Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

(Surat al-Baqara; Madani; it has two hundred and eighty-seven verses)
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾: These are expressions used to refer to the letters of the alphabet (huruf al-mu'jam). Among them are the disjointed letters written at the beginnings of the noble surahs, which are names for them, because they fall under the definition of the noun (ism). This is confirmed by the features that befall them, such as definiteness, indefiniteness, plurality, diminutive forms and other properties of the noun. The leading scholars of Arabic grammar have stated this. As for what occurs in the statements of earlier scholars explicitly calling them letters (harf), it is to be understood as a figurative looseness of expression.

As for what is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites a letter from the Book of Allah, he has a good deed, and the good deed is multiplied tenfold. I do not say 'Alif-Lam-Mim' is a letter; rather, 'Alif' is a letter, 'Lam' is a letter, and 'Mim' is a letter." And in the narration of al-Tirmidhi and al-Darimi: "I do not say 'Alif-Lam-Mim' is a letter, nor 'Dhalika al-Kitab' is a letter; rather, the 'Alif' is a letter, the 'Lam' is a letter, the 'Mim' is a letter, the 'Dhal' is a letter, and the 'Kaf' is a letter." This has absolutely no bearing on what we are discussing. The application of the term "letter" (harf) to what is contrasted with the noun and the verb is a new convention, coined by the masters of the discipline. The term "letter" among the earlier scholars referred to the simple letters from which words are composed; it was sometimes also applied figuratively to the word itself. So the noble hadith was intended to remove the suspicion of figurative usage and to specify more clearly the intended literal meaning, so that it becomes clear that the promised good deed is not measured by the number of Qur'anic words, but by the number of its letters as written in the copies of the Qur'an. This is suggested by the mention of "the Book of Allah" rather than "the speech of Allah" or "the Qur'an". This is not, as some have said, an instance of naming a thing by the name of its referent. How could it be, when what is judged to be a letter and to bring a good deed is in fact the simple entities occurring in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, whether they are expressed by their names or by themselves, as in your saying: "The sin is unpointed (muhmala); the shin is pointed and has three dots," and other such statements, in which the predicate applies only to the subject itself and not to its composed names, as when you say: "The alif is composed of three letters"?! Just as the good deeds in the recitation of His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Dhalika al-Kitab﴾ ("That is the Book") correspond to its simple letters and match their number, so also in the recitation of His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ they correspond to its three written letters and match their number, not to its pronounced names and the alifs that match in number. For the ruling that each of them is a single letter entails the ruling that each brings one good deed. Thus what matters is what is referred to, not the expression used to refer to it. Perhaps the secret in this is that the bringing of a good deed depends on conveying the meaning intended by the Qur'anic words. Just as the rest of the noble words convey their meanings only by pronouncing their letters themselves, so too the written disjointed letters convey the intended meanings only by expressing them by their names. Thus this is treated as pronunciation of the named entities, like the first category (p-21), with no difference between them. Do you not see that in the last narration the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Dhal is a letter, and the Kaf is a letter," how he referred to both of them by their names, even though they are pronounced themselves?! Indeed, a wonderful subtlety has been observed in this naming, in that each named entity, being of the category of words, is placed first before its name, so that it is what is understood from it, most prominent of the prominent. Except that the Alif, since it is impossible to begin with it, has the hamza substituted in its place; and the hamza is inflected, since there is no resemblance between it and the original indeclinable form. Yet, as long as governing words do not precede it, it remains with a quiescent ending in pause, as with numerals and others when they are free of governing words. For this reason it is said "Sad" and "Qaf," with the two quiescent letters joined together, and it is not treated like "ayna" (where), "kayfa" (how) and "ha'ulaa'" (these), which take inflection if a governing word precedes them. Also, the shortening of what ends in an alif during spelling is for the sake of lightness, not because its pattern is one that is sometimes shortened and sometimes lengthened to become its name, as in the verse of Hassan (may Allah be pleased with him):

"He never said 'la' (no) except in his tashahhud,
Were it not for the tashahhud, no 'la' would have been heard from him."

This, and they have spoken concerning these noble beginnings and what is meant by them. It has been said: they are among the hidden knowledge and the concealed secrets. It is narrated from al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "Every book has a secret, and the secret of the Qur'an is the beginnings of the surahs." And from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "Every book has an elite, and the elite of this Book are the letters of the alphabet." And from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: "The scholars were unable to comprehend them." When al-Sha'bi was asked about them, he said: "It is the secret of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so do not seek it." It has been said: they are names of Allah (Exalted is He). It has been said: each letter of them is a reference to one of the names of Allah (Exalted is He), or one of His attributes. It has been said: they are attributes of actions: the Alif is "ala'" (bounties), the Lam is His "lutf" (kindness), and the Mim is His "majd" (glory) and "mulk" (dominion). This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. It has been said: they are from the category of calculation. It has been said: the Alif is from "Allah," the Lam from "Jibril," and the Mim from "Muhammad," meaning: Allah sent down the Book through Jibril upon Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon them both). It has been said: they are oaths sworn by Allah (Exalted is He) by these unpointed letters, because of their nobility, insofar as they are the foundations of languages, the origins of His revealed books, and the constituents of His noble names. It has been said: it is an indication of the end of one speech and the beginning of another. It has been said... and it has been said... But what is relied upon is either that they are names for the surahs that begin with them, and this is the consensus of most scholars, and it is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh. They said: they were named by them as a notice that they are Arabic words, well known in their composition from the named entities of these utterances. Thus there is in this an allusion to the inimitability and the challenge, in the manner of awakening: had it not been a revelation from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, they would not have been unable to oppose it. Close to this is what al-Kalbi, al-Suddi and Qatada said, that they are names for the Qur'an. Naming with three names or more is only considered objectionable in the Arabic language when they are combined and made into one name, as in "Hadramawt." But when they are scattered, there is no objection to them. The named entity is the whole collection, not the opening alone, so that the name and the named would have to be unified. At most, the name enters the named, and there is no prohibition in that, just as there is no prohibition in the reverse, as you have realized a moment ago. The figures of the named entities, rather than the figures of the names, are written in the copies of the Qur'an, because they are more indicative of how they are to be pronounced, which is in the manner of spelling rather than combination, and because it avoids lengthiness, especially in the five-letter openings. Moreover, the script of the Mushaf is not to be disputed on grounds of violating analogy. Or they are recited in a sequence, in the pattern of enumeration, and this is the view to which the investigators inclined. They said: they came in this form so as to awaken those who were challenged by the Qur'an and to alert them that it is composed of the very same material from which they compose their speech. Thus, had it not been that it lies beyond the capacity of humans and descends from the presence of the Creator of powers and destinies, their strength would not have diminished, nor would their ability have collapsed, while they are the champions of the arena of debate and the chiefs of speech in the assembly of pride, without producing anything approaching it, let alone opposing it with something equal to it, despite their mutual rivalry in hostility and harm, and their eagerness for contention and opposition. Or so that the opening of what is recited to them would stand out by a kind of strangeness, serving as a model of the kinds of inimitability in what follows. For the pronunciation of the letters themselves within the course of speech, even if in a trifling manner, is comprehended by the elite and the common alike, from the Bedouin and the non-Arabs. But pronouncing their names can only be achieved by one who has studied and written. As for one who has never approached this at all, it is rarer than the eggs of the phoenix and further than the stars of the Pleiades' rival, especially when it is in a strange pattern and a wondrous style, indicative of a secret of secrets, built upon a unique and extraordinary method, such that the minds of the intelligent are bewildered in understanding it and the intellects of the masters are incapable of grasping it. How could it not be so, when these openings occur in twenty-nine surahs, matching the number of the letters of the alphabet, comprising roughly half of it, so that they contain approximately half of its categories, in verification or approximation, as becomes evident upon examination and investigation, as explained by one of the excellent leading scholars of tafsir. Glory be to Him whose wisdom is too subtle to be perceived by the eyes, and whose power is too exalted to be reached by the hands of thoughts. The presentation of some of them singly, and some of them as pairs up to five-letter groups, follows the custom of variety, while taking into account the patterns of words and their distribution across the surahs, rather than presenting all of them once for this purpose. There is also in repetition and reiteration an increase in benefit. The assigning of each of them to its own surah is something for which no way exists to demand the reason. The counting of some of them as verses and not others is based on pure tradition (tawqif). As for "Alif-Lam-Mim," it is a verse wherever it occurs. It has been said that in "Al 'Imran" it is not a verse. "Alif-Lam-Mim-Sad" is a verse. "Alif-Lam-Mim-Ra" was not counted as a verse. "Ta-Ra" is not a verse in any of its five surahs. "Ta-Sin-Mim" is a verse in its two surahs. "Ta-Ha" and "Ya-Sin" are two verses each. "Ta-Sin" is not a verse. "Ha-Mim" is a verse in all its surahs. "Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad" is a verse. "Ha-Mim-'Ayn-Sin-Qaf" is two verses. "Sad," "Qaf" and "Nun" were not counted as verses. This is according to the opinion of the Kufans. It has been said that all the openings are verses in their view in all surahs, without distinction between them. As for those other than them, they did not count any of them as a verse. Furthermore, even on the assumption that they are presented in the pattern of enumeration, they show no trace of inflection and are to be stopped upon with a complete pause. On the assumption that they are names for the surahs or for the Qur'an, they have a share of inflection: either nominative (raf'), as an inchoative subject (mubtada') or as a predicate (khabar); or accusative (nasb), by a suppressed verb such as "udhkur" (remember), or by the estimation of the verb of oath, in the manner of "By Allah, I will surely do," or genitive (jarr), by the estimation of its preposition, as the context requires and the arrangement demands. There is no pause in other than the nominative case as a predicate, and all are pronounced in the manner of quotation, with quiescent endings. Except that those among them which are single letters, like "Sad," "Qaf" and "Nun," may also receive lexical inflection. They have been read in the accusative by supposing a suppressed verb, meaning "remember" or "recite": "Sad; Qaf; Nun." They are not given tanwin because of the prohibition of declension. Likewise, those among them which are equivalent to a single word, such as "Ha-Mim," "Ya-Sin" and "Ta-Sin," equivalent in weight to "Qabil" and "Habil," for which Sibawayh permitted similar treatment. He said, in the chapter on the names of surahs of his book: some of them have recited "Ya-Sin wal-Qur'an" and "Qaf wal-Qur'an," so it is as though they made it a foreign proper name, and then he said: "Recite Ya-Sin," end of quotation. Al-Sirafi also related from some of them a recitation of "Ya-Sin" (with a vowel). It is possible that this applies to all of them, as movement to avoid the meeting of two quiescent letters. There is no room for accusative by a suppressed verb of oath, because what follows them, "the Qur'an" and "the Pen," is what is sworn by. And they have found it objectionable to combine two oaths upon one object sworn to before the first is complete. This is the secret of making the other than the first waw in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ ﴿and by the day when it reveals itself﴾ ﴿and by Him who created the male and the female﴾ conjunctive. There is no room for conjunction here, because of the difference in case between the first and the second. Yes, that is permissible by making the first one genitive.

with the hidden bāʾ of oath (al-bāʾ al-qasamiyya), fatḥa being used because it is indeclinable (ghayr munṣarif). It is also read "Ṣ" and "Q" with kasra, on the basis of movement (al-taḥrīk), because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn). In "Ṭā Sīn Mīm" it is permissible for its nūn to be given fatḥa, and it is placed among the type of "Dārā Bijird," as mentioned by Sībawayh in his book. As for the other disjointed letters (al-fawātiḥ) apart from these, there is in them nothing but reporting (al-ḥikāya). The detailed rulings of each of them will come, explained in their places, by the permission of God, mighty is His authority.

As for this noble opening (al-fātiḥa al-sharīfa): if it is made a name for the surah, or for the Qur'an, then its position is in the nominative case (raf'), either as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtadaʾ), the estimate being "This is Alif Lām Mīm," meaning named by it; and the pointing to the Qur'an, in part or in whole, was valid even though it had not been mentioned before, because by virtue of its being about to be mentioned it became in the status of what is present and witnessed, as one says: "This is what so-and-so bought." Or it is a subject (mubtadaʾ), i.e., "the one named by it," and the first is the more apparent, because what is made the title of a topic should, by right, be already known to be attributed to it by the addressee; and since there is no prior knowledge of the naming, its due is to inform of it. The claim of its fame is rebutted by the hesitation over whether what is named is the surah or the whole Qur'an.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 2 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾: "ذا" is a demonstrative noun (ism ishara). The "lam" is an "imad" (a supporting particle, *imad*) brought in to indicate the distance of the thing pointed to. The "kaf" marks address (*khitab*). The thing pointed to is the named entity (*al-musamma*). It is treated as though it were present to the sight, and the sense of distance it carries, despite the nearness of the time of reference, is to signal the exaltedness of its rank and its being at the furthest extent of excellence and nobility, following the mention of its name with honour. As for what has been said, that it is by way of considering it distant because of the completeness of its investigation, or because of the arrival from the sender to the one to whom it is sent, which is in the rule of the distant: although this justifies its use, it is far from being preferred over using what is set for pointing to the near. Its masculine form, on the assumption that the named entity is the surah, is because the thing pointed to is the named entity under the name mentioned, insofar as it is named by it, not insofar as it is named as a surah. And if it is claimed that the second consideration is taken into account in the first, on the basis that naming serves to distinguish the surahs from one another, then that is for the sake of recalling what follows it. It is, on the first view, a separate subject (*mubtada'*), and on the second view, a second subject (*mubtada' thani*).

وَقَوْلُهُ - عَزَّ وعَلا -: ﴿الكِتابُ﴾: either it is its predicate (*khabar*) or it is an attribute (*sifa*). If it is its predicate, then on the first view the sentence is a new independent sentence (*mustaanifa*), confirming what the first sentence conveyed of the high standing of the named entity, and has no place in the grammatical structure (*la mahalla laha min al-i'rab*). On the second view it is in the nominative position (*mahall al-raf'*), as a predicate of the first subject, and the demonstrative noun suffices in place of the resumptive pronoun (*al-damir al-rabit*). And "al-Kitab" is either a verbal noun (*masdar*) used as a name for the passive participle, for emphasis, like *al-khalq* and *al-tasvir* for the created and the shaped; or it is a form *fi'al* built for the passive, like *al-libas* (the garment) from *al-kitb*, which is the joining of letters to one another, its root meaning being gathering. Joining is in matters that are apparent to the sight, and from it comes *al-katiba* for an army; just as the root of *al-qira'a* (recitation) is gathering and joining in things hidden from it. The application of "al-Kitab" to what is arranged is an expression, since its eventual outcome is writing (*al-kitaba*). The intended meaning, on the assumption that the named entity is the surah, is the whole of the Noble Qur'an, even though it was not fully revealed at the time the surah was revealed, either in terms of its realization in the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, or in terms of its being established in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh*), or in terms of its being sent down all at once to the lowest heaven, as mentioned at the opening of the Book (*fatihat al-kitab*). The "lam" is for previous knowledge (*al-'ahd*), and the meaning is: this surah is the Book, that is, its supreme pillar (*al-'umda al-qusva*). It is as though, in attaining excellence, it is the whole of the known Book, which needs no description of perfection, because of its fame for that among the books, following the manner of his saying (ﷺ): "The Hajj is 'Arafa" (*al-Hajj 'Arafa*).

And on the assumption that the named entity is the whole Qur'an, then "al-Kitab" means the genus, and the "lam" is for reality (*al-haqiqa*). The meaning is: that is the complete Book, deserving to be singled out by the name "the Book," because of its far superiority over the rest of the individuals in possessing the perfections of the genus, as though the other heavenly books were excluded from it in relation to it, as one says: "He is the man," that is, the perfect one in manhood, who combines what is found among men of praiseworthy qualities. On this is the saying of the one who said:

> ∗∗∗ They are the people, all the people, O mother of Khalid.

The praise, as you see, is from the aspect of restricting the perfection of the genus to one of its individuals; and in the first case it is from the aspect of restricting the perfection of the whole to a part. There is no room there for taking "al-Kitab" as the genus, because its known individual is the totality of the Qur'an, which stands opposite all its other individuals among the heavenly books, not a part of it which the name "the Book" applies to by virtue of being a part of this individual, and not by virtue of being a particular of the genus on its own. Also, restricting perfection to the surah implies the deficiency of the rest of the surahs, although the restriction is not in relation to them, so as to establish the difference between them. This is on the assumption that "al-Kitab" is a predicate of "dhalika." And if it is an attribute of it, then "dhalika al-Kitab" (that Book), on the assumption that "Alif-Lam-Mim" is the predicate of an omitted subject, is either a second predicate, or a substitute (*badal*) for the first predicate, or an independent subject whose predicate is what follows it. And on the assumption that it is a subject, it is either its predicate, or a second subject whose predicate is what follows it, and the sentence is the predicate of the first subject. The pointed-to thing, on both assumptions, is the named entity, whether it is the surah or the Qur'an. The sense of distance is what has been mentioned of the implication of exalted rank. The meaning is: that Book, of wondrous standing, reaching the furthest levels of perfection. It has been said: the pointed-to thing is the promised Book, and then the sense of distance is clear, except that if the named entity is the surah, the promise should be taken as what is in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, We shall cast upon you a weighty word﴾, as has been said. And if it is the Qur'an, then it is what is in the Torah and the Gospel. This is on the assumption that "Alif-Lam-Mim" is a name for the surah or the Qur'an. As for the assumption that they are recited in the manner of enumeration, then "dhalika" is a subject, and "al-Kitab" is either its predicate or its attribute, and the predicate is what follows it, in the manner already passed; or a subject is assumed, meaning: the Book composed of these letters is that Book. And it has been read: "Alif-Lam-Mim, the sending down of the Book" (*tanzil al-Kitab*).

And His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿لا رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾ (there is no doubt in it): either it is in the nominative position, on the basis that it is a predicate of "dhalika al-Kitab," in the three forms mentioned; or it is a second predicate of "Alif-Lam-Mim," or of "dhalika," on the assumption that "al-Kitab" is its predicate; or of the subject assumed last, on the opinion of one who permits the second predicate to be a sentence, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿فَإذا هي حَيَّةٌ تَسْعى﴾ (then behold, it was a serpent moving swiftly). Or it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of "dhalika" or of "al-Kitab," the operative being the sense of pointing. Or it is a new independent sentence with no place in the grammatical structure, confirming what precedes it. The word "la" is a negation of the genus, conveying totality (*istighraq*), working in the manner of "inna" by analogy with it, since it is its opposite, and it is necessarily attached to the noun as it is necessarily attached. Its noun is built on the fatha, because it is singular and indefinite, not an annexed noun, nor resembling one. As for what al-Zajjaj mentioned, that it is inflected and the tanwin was omitted for lightness, it is among things on which no reliance is placed. The cause of its being built is that it includes the meaning of the "min" of totality, not that it is compounded with it in the manner of *khamsata 'ashara* (fifteen), as was imagined. Its predicate is omitted, meaning: "there is no existing doubt," or something similar, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿لا عاصِمَ اليَوْمَ مِن أمْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ (there is no protector today from the command of Allah). The adverbial phrase (*zarf*) is an attribute of its noun, and its meaning is: negation of existence in absolute terms and its removal from the doubt assumed in the Book. Or the predicate is the adverbial phrase, and its meaning is: removal of existence of doubt from it in absolute terms. The omitted predicate has been made an adverbial phrase, and the mentioned one has been made a predicate of what follows it. And it has been read: "la raybun fihi" (there is no doubt in it), on the basis that "la" has the meaning of "laysa" (is not). The distinction between this and the first is that the first implies totality, while this permits it.

The word *al-rayb* is in origin the verbal noun of "rabani," when unease arises in you. Its reality is restlessness and agitation of the soul. Then it was used in the sense of doubt generally, or with suspicion, because it disturbs the soul and removes tranquility. And in the hadith (*fi al-hadith*): "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt." The meaning of negating it from the Book is that it is of such lofty standing and clear proof that there is no room for anyone to doubt its reality, or that it is a revelation sent down from Allah (Exalted is He). It does not mean that no one at all doubts it. Do you not see how that was permitted in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿وَإنْ كُنْتُمْ في رَيْبٍ مِمّا نَزَّلْنا﴾ (and if you are in doubt about what We have sent down), etc.? For it is in effect as if it were said: "And if there is doubt for you about what We have sent down," or "If you doubt about what We have sent down," etc. However, the style was altered, in that it is supposed that they are in doubt, not that doubt is in it, for the sake of greater exaltation of the sanctuary of the revelation above it, with a kind of implication that this comes from their side, not from its lofty side. That implication is not intended here, just as the implication of the establishment of doubt in the rest of the books is not intended, so that the context requires the fronting of the adverbial phrase, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿لا فِيها غَوْلٌ﴾ (wherein is no intoxication).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 2 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿Guidance﴾ (hudan): a verbal noun (masdar) from "hadahu," like *al-sura* (the journey by night) and *al-buka* (weeping). It is the gentle indication of what leads to the desired goal, i.e., that which by its nature has this effect. It has been said that it is the indication that actually leads to the goal, as evidenced by the fact that error (dalala) is set in opposition to it, in His words (exalted is He): ﴿They are those who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ [2:16]; and His words (exalted is He): ﴿And indeed, either we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [34:24]. There is no doubt that non-arrival (at the goal) is taken into account in the concept of error; therefore arrival is taken into account in the concept of its opposite. And from the necessity of taking it into account there, it is taken into account in the concept of guidance as a transitive (muta'addi) action, since there is no difference between them except in terms of influencing and being influenced. Its upshot is that guidance is the directing that arrives, because what is necessary is the directedness that arrives; the evidence being that its opposite, which is error, is a directedness that certainly does not arrive. And this, as you see, rests on two matters: taking arrival as obligatory in the concept of the intransitive (lazim), and taking the existence of the intransitive as obligatory in the concept of the transitive. Both matters are far from being established.

As for the first: the axis of opposition between guidance and error is not arrival and its absence in an absolute sense, but rather both are taken into account in their concepts in a specific manner, so that the opposition between them is realized. Its clarification: guidance necessarily involves taking into account a directedness, with knowledge, toward that which by its nature brings one to the goal; just as error necessarily involves taking into account a deviation from intent toward that which by its nature certainly does not bring one (to the goal). This level of consideration is agreed upon by both parties, and it realizes the opposition between them. The dispute is only over whether the capacity of arrival at the goal is sufficient for the attainment of the concept of guidance, or whether arrival must come out from potentiality into actuality, just as the actual non-arrival is certainly taken into account in the concept of error. Having established this, we say: if what is meant by taking actual arrival into account in the concept of guidance is taking it as concomitant with it in existence in time, in accordance with taking its absence into account in the concept of its opposite, then that is clearly invalid. For arrival is the end point of that directedness, so it certainly terminates it, since it is impossible for directedness to be toward attaining what is already attained. What remains after that is either directedness toward steadfastness upon it, or directedness toward increasing it. And because directedness toward the destination is gradual, while arrival at it is instantaneous, their coexistence in existence is necessarily impossible. As for non-arrival: since it is a continuous matter, as error requires, it is necessary that it accompany it throughout all the times of its existence; for if it were separated from it at any instant of those times, then at that instant it would be accompanied by its opposite, which is arrival, and so what we supposed to be error would not be error.

And if what is meant is taking it into account insofar as it is an end point for it that must necessarily follow from it, then it would follow that the directedness accompanying the utmost effort in the journey toward that which by its nature leads to arrival, when it fails to reach it due to an external obstacle, such as death overtaking him for example, without any negligence or deviation on the part of the one directed, and without any defect on the part of the path, would be error; since there is no intermediary between them; yet in it there is a deviation from intent at all. Thus the taking of the necessity of arrival in the concept of the intransitive is certainly invalid. (p-26) And it has become clear from this that it is not taken into account in the concept of the transitive necessarily.

As for taking the existence of the intransitive into the transitive as obligatory, which is the second matter, its explanation rests on laying down a principle: the action of the agent in reality is that which proceeds from him and is completed by him. But since its realization in itself cannot be without its relation to its object, that is certainly taken into account in the signification of its name. Then, since it has, by consideration of the manner of its proceeding from its agent and the manner of its relation to its object, and other than that, various effects that follow from it, distinct in themselves, independently requiring rulings that necessitate singling them out with special names; and there occurs to it—in relation to each of those effects—a special relation distinguished from the other relations occurring to it in relation to the rest; and those effects were following it in realization, never separate from it at all (since there is no influencer for them other than its agent), they are counted among its completions; and the relation occurring to it in accordance with them is taken as included in its signification. Like the pressing that is connected to a body, for example: it was assigned—by consideration of the relation occurring to it from the breaking of that body, which is a special effect of that pressing—the name "breaking"; and by consideration of the relation occurring to it from the severing that is another of its effects, the name "severing"; and so on with the other relations occurring to it in relation to its necessary effects. This is a consistent matter regarding its natural effects. As for the effects that it has a role in bringing about in general, without necessitating them—following it sometimes and separating from it other times, according to the existence or non-existence of their causes that necessitate them—like the voluntary acts proceeding from their influencers through its being a motive for them; since those effects are independent in themselves, grounded in their influencers, not necessarily following from it in the way natural effects follow it, they are not counted among its completions, and the relation occurring to it in accordance with them is not taken as included in its signification. Like the relation occurring to a command in accordance with the commanded one's compliance, and the relation occurring to a summons in accordance with the summoned one's response. For compliance and response, although they are counted as effects of the command and the summons by virtue of their generally following from them, nevertheless, since they are voluntary acts of the commanded and the summoned, independent in themselves, not necessitated by the command and the summons, they are not counted among their completions; and the relation occurring to them in accordance with them is not taken as included in the signification of the names "command" and "summons." Rather they are made to express the very demand relating to the commanded and the summoned, whether compliance and response occur or not.

Having established this, we say: just as compliance and response are two acts independent in themselves, proceeding from the summoned and the commanded by their own choice, not necessitated by the command and the summons in the way natural effects are necessitated by the acts that bring them about—even though they follow from them in general—similarly, the guidance of the one guided (i.e., his directedness toward what was mentioned of the path) is an act independent in itself, proceeding from him by his choice, not necessarily following from guiding—I mean, directing toward it—in the way the mentioned natural effects necessarily follow; even though it follows from them in general. Since they (compliance and response) were not counted among the completions of command and summons, and the relation occurring to them in accordance with them was not taken as included in their signification, it is known that the necessary (lazim) guidance is not counted among the completions of guiding, and the relation occurring to guiding in accordance with it is not taken as included in its signification.

If it is said: guidance in relation to guiding is not like compliance and response in relation to their two roots. For the relation of command and summons to the commanded and the summoned requires nothing more than their being characterized as commanded and summoned; and it is not necessarily implied that they are characterized by compliance and response, since there is no necessary connection between them and the former at all. Unlike guidance in relation to guiding, for its relation to the one guided requires that he be characterized by it. For the relation of the transitive verb in the active voice to its object indicates that he is characterized by its verbal noun taken from the passive voice, certainly; and that necessitates his being characterized by the verbal noun of the intransitive verb. And is this anything other than taking the existence of the intransitive in the signification of the transitive necessarily?

We say: just as the relation of command and summons to the commanded and summoned requires only their being characterized by what was mentioned, (p-27) without any reference to compliance and response, either affirmatively or negatively; likewise the relation of guiding, which is the aforementioned indication, to the one guided requires only his being characterized by the state of being indicated, which is the expression of the verbal noun taken from the passive voice; without any reference to his accepting that indication, as is the meaning of necessary guidance, nor to his not accepting it. Rather, guiding is the very same as summoning to the path of truth, and being guided is the very same as response. So how can it be taken into their signification? And the implication of being characterized by the verbal noun of a transitive verb in the passive voice for being characterized by the verbal noun of an intransitive verb in general is only in natural acts, like being broken and breaking, and being severed and severance. As for voluntary acts, they are not so, as you have realized previously.

If it is said: learning is among voluntary acts, yet it is certainly taken into account in the signification of teaching; so let guidance be likewise with guiding. We say: that is not because it is a voluntary act in an absolute sense, nor because teaching is an expression for bringing knowledge about to the learner, as has been said. For the teacher is not independent in that; so ascribing it to him involves a kind of figurative usage. Rather, it is because each of them depends in its realization and attainment on the other. For teaching is an expression for casting the principles of knowledge upon the learner and driving them into his mind little by little, in an order that the situation requires, such that some of them are not driven to him except after his receiving others. So each of them completes the other and is taken into account in its signification. As for guidance, which is an expression for the aforementioned directedness, it is a voluntary act, independently effected by its agent; guiding has no part in it except that it is a motive for bringing it about by his choice. So it is not among its completions, nor is it taken into account in its signification.

If it is said: teaching is a kind of guiding, and learning is a kind of being guided; so taking it into the signification of teaching is taking guidance into the signification of guiding. We say: applying the term "guiding" to teaching occurs only when the path is clear and the learner independently follows it, with no role for teaching in it except being a motive toward it. And you have known the clarity of the matter on that assumption.

If it is said: is not the failure of guidance to follow guiding like the failure of learning to follow teaching? So, since that is not teaching in reality, let guiding likewise not be guiding; and let the naming of what does not entail guidance by it be taken as figurative. We say: the difference between the two failures is vast. For the failure of learning to follow teaching is due to a deficiency in it, just as the failure of breaking to follow a weak blow is due to that (weakness). But the failure of guidance to follow guiding is not due to any admixture of deficiency on its part; rather, it is only due to the absence of its cause that necessitates it on the part of the one guided, after the completion of what is accomplished by the guide.

With this clarification, the way of guiding has become clear, and it has been shown that it is an expression for the absolute indication toward what by its nature leads to the goal, by defining its landmarks and clarifying its paths, without requiring in its signification arrival or acceptance. And that the indication that accompanies either of them, or one of them, or that is separate from them—all of that, setting aside the condition of accompaniment or its absence—are real instances of it. And that what is in His words (exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [28:56], and His words (exalted is He): ﴿And had He willed, He would have guided you all﴾ [16:9], and similar to that in which arrival is taken into account, is of the figurative category. And it has become evident that the cosmic indications placed within the souls and the horizons, and the legislative clarifications revealed in the heavenly books, in an absolute sense, in relation to all of creation—its righteous and its wicked—are true guidances flowing from Allah, glorified is He. And praise be to Allah who guided us to this; and we would not have been guided had Allah not guided us.

**For the God-conscious** (*lil-muttaqin*): that is, those characterized by *taqwa* (God-consciousness, piety), whether presently or in their final outcome. The specification of guidance for them is because they are the ones who draw light from it and benefit from its effects, although it encompasses every beholder, believer and unbeliever alike. On this basis God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾. *Al-muttaqi* is an active participle of the *ifti'al* pattern (Form VIII) from *al-wiqaya* (protection), which is extreme guarding. In the terminology of the Sacred Law (*al-shar'*), *taqwa* refers to the perfection of guarding oneself against what would harm one in (p-28) the Hereafter. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The sum of *taqwa* is in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah orders justice and excellence﴾," the verse.

It is reported from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that he said: it is abandoning what Allah has forbidden and performing what Allah has obligated. It is reported from Shahr ibn Hawshab: the *muttaqi* is one who abandons what is not objectionable, out of fear of falling into what is objectionable. It is reported from Abu Yazid that *taqwa* is abstention from everything that contains doubt. It is reported from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya that it is avoiding everything that distances you from Allah, Exalted is He. It is reported from Sahl: the *muttaqi* is one who disavows his own power and ability. It has been said: *taqwa* is that Allah does not see you where He has forbidden you, nor miss you where He has commanded you. It is reported from Maymun ibn Mihran: a man is not God-conscious until he is more severe in calling himself to account than a stingy partner and a tyrannical ruler. It is reported from Abu Turab: before *taqwa* there are five obstacles, and whoever does not pass them will not attain it: preferring hardship to ease, preferring weakness to strength, preferring humiliation to honor, preferring toil to rest, and preferring death to life. It is reported from some of the sages that a man does not reach the summit of *taqwa* unless his inner state is such that, if what is in his heart were placed on a tray and carried through the market, he would not be ashamed before anyone who looks at it. It has been said: *taqwa* is that you adorn your inner self for the Truth just as you adorn your outward self for people.

The verified position is that *taqwa* has three levels. The first: guarding oneself against the everlasting punishment by disavowing unbelief, and to this refers His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and He made them hold fast to the word of *taqwa*﴾. The second: avoiding everything that incurs sin, whether by act or omission, even minor sins according to some, and this is what is commonly understood by *taqwa* in the Sacred Law; it is what is meant by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If only the People of the Book had believed and been God-conscious﴾. The third: that one purify oneself of everything that occupies one's inner self away from the Truth, Mighty and Majestic is He, and devote oneself to Him entirely; this is the true *taqwa* commanded in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, be conscious of Allah with the consciousness due to Him﴾. This level is broad, and its people vary in ranks according to the variation in the degrees of their innate capacities, which overflow upon them in accordance with the Divine will, which is founded on lofty wisdoms. Its furthest reach is what the aspirations of the Prophets, peace be upon them, attained, for they combined thereby the leadership of prophethood (*nubuwwa*) and sainthood (*wilaya*). Attachment to the world of forms did not hinder them from ascending to the realms of spirits, and their engagement with the welfare of creation did not prevent them from being absorbed in the affairs of the Truth, owing to the perfect readiness of their pure souls, supported by holy power.

The guidance of the Manifest Book encompasses all the holders of these levels. If by its being a guidance for the God-conscious is meant its guiding them to attain and reach the first level, then those intended are those approaching *taqwa*, figuratively, since attaining what has already been attained is impossible. [The author] preferred this for the sake of brevity. The opening of the noble surah with mention of His friends and magnifying their status: if by it is meant guiding them to attain one of the last two levels, then if by the God-conscious are meant the people of the first level, the literal meaning (*haqiqa*, the proper, non-figurative sense) is determined; if by them are meant the people of one of the last two levels, the figurative meaning (*majaz*) is determined, because reaching those two is only realized through the guidance that is awaited from Him. The same applies to the relationship between the second and third levels: if by guidance is meant guiding to attain the third level, then if by the God-conscious are meant the people of the second level the literal meaning is determined, and if by them are meant the people of the third level the figurative meaning is determined. The word "guidance" (*al-hidaya*) is literal in all these cases. As for if by its being a guidance for them is meant keeping them firm in what they are upon, or guiding them to increase in it, on the condition that its concept is included in the meaning used, then it is necessarily figurative. The word "the God-conscious" (*al-muttaqin*) is literal in every case. The preposition *lam* (*li-*) is connected to *hudan* (guidance), or to an omitted element that functions as a qualifier of it, or as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from it. The grammatical position of *hudan* is nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is guidance; or as a predicate together with *rayba fihi* (no doubt in it) for *dhalika al-kitab* (that Book); or as a subject whose predicate is the preposed adverbial phrase, as has been indicated; or it is accusative in the circumstantial sense from *dhalika* (that), or from *al-kitab*, the governing element being the sense of the demonstrative; or from the pronoun in *fihi* (in it), the governing element being the sense of the verb negated in the preposition-and-object phrase. It is as if it were said: doubt did not arise in it while it was guiding. This is so that the negation is a qualifier of the negation and not of what is negated. Its summary: doubt is negated from it while it is guiding. Its indefiniteness (*rayb*) is for magnification. Its being attributed to *al-kitab* is either for emphasis, as if it were the very essence of guidance, or to make the verbal noun (*masdar*) carry the sense of an active participle.

This is so. What the eloquence of the revelation requires regarding the arrangement of these sentences is that they be coherent, with each subsequent one confirming the preceding one. For this reason no conjunction intervenes between them. *Alif-Lam-Mim* (الم) is a sentence in itself, either as the predicate of an implied subject, or a group of letters of the alphabet standing independently, indicating that the challenge is directed at a composition of the same kind as that from which they compose their speech. *Dhalika al-kitab* (That is the Book) is a second sentence confirming the aspect of the challenge, by virtue of what it indicates of its being described with superlative perfection. Then it recorded its supreme excellence by negating doubt from it, for there is no excellence higher than what belongs to Truth and certainty. *Hudan lil-muttaqin* (a guidance for the God-conscious), together with what is supposed as its omitted subject, is a sentence emphasizing that it is a truth around which no trace of any doubt hovers, and indicating its completion after its perfection. Alternatively, the later sentences follow the earlier ones as evidence follows what it proves: since it first drew attention to the inimitability of what was challenged, in that it is of the same kind as their speech, and they were utterly unable to oppose it, it became manifest that it is the Book reaching the highest levels of perfection. That necessarily entails that it is in the utmost purity from the place of doubt, for nothing is more deficient than what is subject to suspicion. Whatever is like this is necessarily a guidance for the God-conscious. In each of these there are refined subtleties and superior features, the magnificence of whose station is evident, as you have verified.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 3 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾: It may be a relative clause (mawsul) attached to "the God-conscious" (al-muttaqin), and its place in i'rab (grammatical inflection) is the genitive (jarr), as a descriptive qualifier (sifah muqayyidah) of them if taqwa is interpreted as abstaining from sins alone, in which case it follows from it as embellishment follows clearing away (al-tahliyah 'ala al-takhliyah). It is an explanatory qualifier (muwaddihah) if taqwa is interpreted in its legally recognized sense and as customarily understood, namely performing acts of obedience and abstaining from evil deeds together. For then it is a detailing of what the noun of the described (al-mawsuf) comprised in summary, because these two (i.e., faith and prayer, and charity) include what is the pillar of deeds and the foundation of good works: faith, prayer and charity, for they are the mother-principles of the inward deeds and of the bodily and financial acts of worship, which entail all the other acts of nearness to God and which generally call one to avoid sins. Do you not see His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, prayer prevents indecency and wrongdoing﴾; and His saying (upon him be prayer and peace): "Prayer is the pillar of religion, and zakat is the bridge of Islam"? Or it is a praising qualifier of those described with taqwa, interpreted as above as performing acts of obedience and abstaining from evil deeds. The singling out of the three qualities mentioned for mention is to show their nobility and their superiority over all the other good deeds that fall under the name of taqwa. Or it is in the accusative (naşb) by way of praise, with the implied "I mean" (a'ni); or in the nominative (raf') by way of praise, with the implied "they are." And it may be separated from what precedes it, being in the nominative by way of a new inceptive subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is the clause introduced by the demonstrative (ism al-ishara), as will be explained. Then the pause on "the God-conscious" (al-muttaqin) in this case is a complete pause (waqf tamm), because it is a pause on something that is a new beginning, and what follows it is also a new beginning. But according to the first possibilities it is an acceptable pause (hasan), since what is paused on is self-standing but not complete, as what follows is connected to it and dependent on it. As for the case of the genitive as a descriptive, this is clear. As for the case of the accusative or the nominative by way of praise, this is because it has been established that the accusative and the nominative are praised, even if they have departed from following what precedes them in form, since they did not follow it in i'rab. For this reason they were called "cut off" (qat'), but they are in truth dependent on it. Do you not see how they were bound to omit the verb and the subject in the accusative and the nominative, out of intention to make each of them resemble a complement of what precedes it, and to alert to the intensity of connection between them? Abu 'Ali said: When attributes are mentioned for praise and the i'rab of some of them is varied, it is varied for the sake of variety (iftinan), that is, for the variety that causes the listener to be awakened and moved to serious attention in listening. For changing the speech directed to a meaning among meanings, and turning it away from its established course, indicates a new concern on the part of the speaker with its matter and draws greater desire in it from the addressee. If it is said: There is no doubt that the status of the relative clause when it is the predicate of an omitted subject, like its status when it is the subject whose predicate is ﴿those are upon guidance﴾, in that it forms a nominal sentence conveying the God-conscious's possession of the excellent qualities, since each of the omitted pronoun and the relative refers to "the God-conscious," and since each of their possession of faith and its branches and their attaining guidance and success are sublime attributes, then what is the secret in the first case that it was made one of the followers of the God-conscious and the pause was counted as incomplete, while in the second it was cut off from it and the pause was counted as complete? We say: The secret in this is that the subject in both cases, although it refers to "the God-conscious," yet the predicate in the first case, since it was a detailing of what the subject comprised in summary, as you have realized, and its attribution to him was known and free of doubt, did not convey anything to the listener beyond the benefit of detailing and clarification. So it was arranged within the row of attributes, out of regard for the meaning, even though it is called "cut off," out of regard for the wording. How could it not be so, when it is well known in the discipline that a predicate whose attribution to the subject is known should be a description of it, just as a description whose attribution to the described is not known should be a predicate of it? To the point that they said: attributes before knowledge of them are predicates, and predicates after knowledge of them are attributes. As for the predicate in the second case, since it was not like that, but rather included meanings befitting the context that the subject does not indicate, as you will come to understand, it was a predicate conveying to the addressee pleasing benefits. So it was made cut off from what precedes it, in order to preserve both the form and the meaning.

"Faith" (al-iman) is an form (ifa'al) derived from "security" (al-amn), which is transitive to one object. One says: "I made him secure" (amantuhu). By transitivity it becomes transitive to two objects; one says: "Another made me secure from it" (amannanihi ghayri). Then it was used for "affirmation" (al-tasdiq), because the one who affirms makes the affirmed one secure (yu'ammin al-musaddaq), that is, makes him safe from denial and opposition. Its usage with the preposition "bi" (in) is to include in it the meaning of "acknowledgment" (al-i'tiraf). It is sometimes applied to "trust" (al-wuthuq), for the one who trusts becomes one possessing security and tranquility. From this is what is related from the Arabs: "I was not secure that I would find a companion," that is, I did not become one possessing security and calm. Both aspects are acceptable here. In the legal sense it is not realized without affirming what is known necessarily to be from the religion of our Prophet (upon him be prayer and peace), such as monotheism, prophethood, resurrection, recompense, and their like. Is this sufficient for that, or is it necessary to add acknowledgment (al-iqrar) to it for one who is able to do it? The first is the opinion of Shaykh al-Ash'ari and those who followed him, for acknowledgment according to him is an indicator for the application of rulings. The second is the doctrine of Abu Hanifa and those who followed him, and it is the truth, for he made the two parts of it. Except that acknowledgment is a pillar which may be dropped with an excuse, as under compulsion. It is the combination of three matters: belief in the truth, acknowledgment of it, and acting in accordance with its requirement, according to the majority of later scholars, the Mu'tazilah, and the Khawarij. Whoever neglects belief alone is a hypocrite; whoever neglects acknowledgment is an unbeliever; whoever neglects action is a sinner by consensus, but an unbeliever according to the Khawarij, and outside faith; he is not included in unbelief according to the Mu'tazilah. It was read "yu'minun" without a hamza. "The unseen" (al-ghayb) is either a verbal noun (masdar) described by it as the absent one, for emphasis, like "the witnessed" (al-shahadah) in His saying: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾; or it is the form "fay'il" lightened, like "qayl" from "qayyil," "hayn" from "hayyin," and "mayt" from "mayyit," but the original form was not used in it as it was used in its counterparts. In any case, it is that which is absent from the senses and the intellect with complete absence, such that it is not perceived by either of them at first by way of immediate self-evidence. It is of two kinds: a kind for which there is no proof, which is what is meant by His saying (glorified is He): ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾; and a kind for which a proof has been set up, such as the Creator and His attributes, the prophethoods and what relates to them of rulings and laws, and the Last Day and its states of resurrection, gathering, reckoning and recompense. This is what is intended here. So the "bi" is a complement of "faith," either by including in it the meaning of acknowledgment, or by making it a metaphor for trust, in which case it occupies the place of the direct object; or the verbal noun remains as it is, like "absence," and then it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial state (hal) of the agent, as in His saying: ﴿Those who fear their Lord in the unseen﴾, and His saying: ﴿That he may know that I did not betray him in the unseen﴾. That is: they believe while being in a state of absence, either regarding what is believed in, meaning absent from the Prophet (ﷺ), not witnessing what is in him of signs of prophethood; for it is related that the companions of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) mentioned the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and their faith, and he (may Allah be pleased with him) said: The affair of Muhammad (upon him be prayer and peace) was clear to whoever saw him; but by Him other than whom there is no god, no believer has believed with a better faith than faith in the unseen; then he recited this verse. Or, either regarding the people, meaning absent from the believers, unlike the hypocrites who, when they meet those who believe, say "We believe," but when they go privately to their devils, say "We are with you." It was also said: the intended meaning of "the unseen" is the heart, for it is hidden; and the meaning is: they believe with their hearts, not like those who say with their mouths what is not in their hearts. Then the "bi" is in that case for instrumentality. The omission of mention of what is believed in, on all three interpretations, is either for the purpose of bringing about the act itself, as in the saying: "So-and-so gives and withholds," meaning they perform faith; or for relying on what will come, for the divine books speak clearly of the details of what must be believed.

﴿And establish prayer﴾: Establishing it is an expression for correcting its pillars and preserving it from any deviation in any of its obligations, sunnahs and etiquettes. It is from "aqama al-'ud" (he set the stick straight), when he straightened it and made it even. It was also said: it means persistence in it, derived from "qamat al-suq" (the market became brisk) when goods sold well, and "aqamtuha" (I made it brisk) when you made it sell well; for when it is preserved, it becomes like the brisk goods that are desired. It was also said: it means perseverance, for performing it without slackness or negligence, from their saying: "qama bi al-amr" and "aqamahu" when one strives and exerts oneself in it. It was also said: it means performing it; it is expressed by "establishing" because it includes standing, just as it is expressed by "qunut," which is standing, and by bowing, prostration and glorification. The first is the most apparent, because it is the most well known, and closer to the literal reality. "Salat" is the form "fa'lah" from "sallá" when it means to supplicate, like "zakat" from "zakka." They were written with a waw in accordance with the emphatic pronunciation of the word. The specific action was named "salat" because it includes supplication. It was also said: the original root of "sallá" is "he moved the two salawayn," which are the two protruding bones at the top of the thighs, because the one praying does this in his bowing and prostration. The prevalence of the word in the second meaning rather than the first does not detract from its transmission from it. The one who supplicates was called "musalli" (one who prays) by way of likening him, in his humility, to the one who bows and prostrates.

﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾: "Rizq" (provision) in the language means gift, and it is applied to the portion given, like "dhibh" (slaughter) for the slaughtered thing and "ri'y" (pasture) for the pastured thing. It was also said: with a fatha it is a verbal noun, and with a kasra it is a noun. In customary usage it is what the living being benefits from. The Mu'tazilah, since they deemed it impossible for God (exalted is He) to enable one to [take] the unlawful, because He forbade benefiting from it and commanded restraint from it, said: provision does not include the unlawful. Do you not see that He (exalted is He) attributed provision to Himself, as an announcement that they spend from pure lawful sustenance, for spending the unlawful is far from deserving praise? And He censured the polytheists for forbidding some of what God (exalted is He) had provided them, by His saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you have made some of it unlawful and some lawful?﴾ Our companions (i.e., the Ash'arites) held that the aforementioned attribution is for exalting and encouraging spending, and the censure is for forbidding what He did not forbid, and that "what We have provided them" is restricted to the lawful by the context. They relied, for the inclusion of provision of both, on what is related from him (upon him be prayer and peace) in the hadith of 'Amr ibn Qurrah, when he came to him and said: O Messenger of Allah, God has written misery upon me, and I see that I am not provided for except from my drum by my palm; so permit me to sing without indecency. He (upon him be prayer and peace) said: "I will not permit you; there is no honor for you, nor blessing of the eye. You have lied, O enemy of God! By God, God has provided you with what is lawful and good, but you have chosen what God has forbidden you of His provision in place of what God has made lawful for you of His lawful things." And because if the unlawful were not provision, one who was nourished by it throughout his life would not have been provided for; and God (exalted is He) has said: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾. And "infaq" (spending) and "infad" (expending) are brothers; except that (...)

In the second case, the meaning is removal entirely, unlike the first. The intended sense of this spending is directing it toward the path of good, whether it is obligatory (fard) or voluntary (nafl). Whoever interprets it as zakat has mentioned its most excellent kind, and the principle in this matter is that; or he restricted it to zakat because it is paired with what is its sibling (i.e., prayer). The clause is coordinated with what precedes it among the relative clauses (silah). The fronting of the object is for emphasis and for preserving the rhyme of the verse endings (ru'us al-ayy). The insertion of the partitive "min" (min al-tab'idiyyah) before it serves to restrain from extravagance (tabdhir). This is it.

It has also been permitted that it means spending from all the provisions that Allah (Exalted) has granted them, of the apparent and hidden blessings. This is supported by his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Indeed, knowledge by which one does not attain [benefit] is like a treasure from which one does not spend." And to this view went the one who said: "And from what We have granted them of the lights of knowledge, they bestow."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 4:**

﴿Those who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you﴾: It is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the first relative clause (al-mawsul al-awwal), on both assumptions about whether it is connected to what precedes it or separated from it. It is included together with it in the group of the God-fearing (al-muttaqun), either in both form and meaning or in meaning alone, as the inclusion of two specific groups under a general one. For the first group (al-awwalun) refers to those who came to faith after polytheism and heedlessness regarding all the laws (shara'i'), as the expression "the unseen" for what is believed in indicates. The second group (al-akharun) refers to those who came to faith in the Qur'an after believing in the books sent down earlier, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his like. Alternatively, it is conjoined to "the God-fearing," with the first group alone intended by them, and the specification of them by the attribute of God-consciousness (al-ittiqa') serves to announce their complete disassociation from their former state, because of its perfect ugliness and its opposition to all the laws, which necessitates abstaining from it. This contrasts with the second group, who did not wholly abandon what they had been upon, but rather held fast to the fundamentals of the laws, which hardly differ with the differences of the eras. It is also permissible to make both relative clauses refer to the whole, included under "the God-fearing." The placing of the conjunction (al-'atif) between them is then not due to a difference in essences but to a difference in attributes, as in his saying:

*To the king, the lord of the chieftains, the son of the valiant,*
*and the lion of the battalion in the crush.*

And his saying:

*Alas for Zayyaba, for al-Harith, the early morning raider,*
*the one who takes booty, the one who returns.*

This is to announce that each of the belief in what has been indicated as unseen matters, and the belief in what attests to their establishment from the heavenly books, is a noble quality in itself, of great consequence, entailing many rulings, worthy of being given a separate independent description, and that one of them should not be made a completion of the other. The first has been paired with the performance of prayer and almsgiving, which are among the laws included under those believed matters, as a completion of it, for the perfection of knowledge is action. The second has been coupled with certainty regarding the Hereafter, although it is subsumed under the first, to draw attention to the perfect soundness of that belief and to hint at the defects in the beliefs of the People of the Two Books, as will come. This is on the assumption that the preposition (ba') is connected to "belief." Judge the circumstantial clause (hal) by analogy when it is connected to the omitted verb, for each of the unseen belief accompanied by what confirms it of the two acts of worship, together with setting aside consideration of what is believed in, and the belief in the revealed books that explain the details of the matters that must be believed in, joined with what is joined to them, is an outstanding virtue calling for what has been mentioned. And God (Exalted) knows best. It has been understood to mean that they are those who combine belief in what the intellect grasps in summary, and the performance of the physical and financial acts of worship that attest to it, with belief in what has no path to it except revelation. The repetition of the relative pronoun serves to draw attention to the difference between the two categories and the divergence between the two ways, so let this be considered. It is also possible that, after all are included in the first, the second relative clause refers to a particular group among them, namely the believers among the People of the Book, who are singled out by mention, as Gabriel and Michael are singled out, following the mention of the angels (peace be upon them), to honor their status and to encourage their like and peers to attain the perfection that is theirs.

Sending down (al-inzal) is conveying from above to below. Its connection to meanings is only through the mediation of its connection to the concrete things that entail them. Thus the sending down of the books of God other than the scrolls (al-suhuf) to the messengers (peace be upon them), and God (Exalted) knows best, is by the angel receiving them from His presence (Mighty and Majestic) in a spiritual reception, or by his preserving them from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), then descending with them to the messengers and conveying them to them (peace be upon them). The intended meaning of "what has been sent down to you" is the Qur'an in its entirety and the law in its entirety. The expression of its sending down in the past tense, although some of it was still awaited at that time, serves either to give precedence to what is established over what is measured, or to treat what is certain in its occurrence as if it had occurred, as in his saying (Exalted): ﴿Indeed, we have heard a Book sent down after Moses﴾, although the jinn had not heard the whole Book, nor was the whole of it then sent down. By "what was sent down before you" is meant the Torah, the Gospel, and the rest of the earlier books. The omission of mention of those to whom the prophets (peace be upon them) were sent is for the sake of brevity, since the purpose does not depend on detail, unlike its connection to it in his saying (Exalted): ﴿Say: We believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us, and what was sent down to Abraham and Ishmael﴾, and so on.

Belief in all of it in summary is an obligation (fard), and belief in the Qur'an in detail, insofar as we are obliged to act upon its details, is a communal obligation (fard kifaya), for its being an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) upon everyone would entail clear hardship and disruption of the affairs of livelihood. The construction of the two verbs in the passive voice serves to announce that the agent is determined, and to follow the manner of majesty. Both have also been read in the active voice.

﴿And in the Hereafter they are certain﴾: Certainty (al-iyqan) is mastering knowledge of a thing by removing doubt and uncertainty from it. For this reason, God's knowledge (Exalted) is not called certainty. That is, they know with definitive knowledge that dispels the doubts and delusions that the People of the Book had, among which is their claim that no one enters Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian, and that the Fire will not touch them except for a few numbered days. Also among them is their disagreement over whether the bliss of Paradise is of the same kind as the bliss of this world or not, and whether it is everlasting or not. The fronting of the prepositional phrase (al-sila), and the construction of "they are certain" upon the pronoun, contains an allusion to those other than them among the People of the Book, for their belief concerning matters of the Hereafter is far from soundness, let alone reaching the level of certainty. "The Hereafter" (al-akhira) is the feminine of "the last" (al-akhir), just as "the world" (al-dunya) is the feminine of "the nearer" (al-adna). Both became dominant as names for the two abodes, so they function as proper nouns. It has been read with the hamza dropped and its vowel transferred to the lam. It has also been read "yu'qinun," with the waw converted into a hamza, treating the vowel before it as its vowel in "wujuh" (faces) and "wuqqitat" (were appointed a time). A parallel to this is in his saying:

*Dearer to me are the two fire-kindlers, Musa and Ja'da,*
*when the fire has lit them up.*

(p-33)

His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to those whose praiseworthy qualities were mentioned, in terms of their being characterized by them. It indicates that they are distinguished by these qualities in the most complete distinction, and that by means of them they are placed within the order of the observable matters. The sense of distance in it serves to signal the loftiness of their rank and the remoteness of their station in excellence. It is the subject (mubtada'), and His saying, mighty and exalted is He: ﴿upon guidance﴾ is its predicate (khabar). The indefiniteness conveyed by the indefinite form (al-tankir), with the ambiguity it implies, is for the sake of the utmost magnification of it, as if it were said: "upon what sort of guidance?" A guidance whose reality cannot be reached and whose measure cannot be estimated. The use of the word for elevation ('ala, "upon") is based either on representing their state of being engaged with guidance by the state of one who mounts a thing and takes control of it, so that he disposes of it as he wishes; or on its being used metaphorically (isti'ara), a subsidiary metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya) derived from likening their holding fast to guidance to the rider's mounting and sitting firmly upon his mount; or on making it a qarina (indicator) for a metaphor by way of allusion (isti'ara bi'l-kinaya) between guidance and the mount, to announce the strength of their firm establishment in it and the completeness of their steadfastness therein.

His saying (exalted is He): ﴿from their Lord﴾ is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of it (guidance), clarifying its magnificence in relation (to them), after the statement of its intrinsic magnificence, and confirming it. That is: upon a guidance coming from Him (exalted is He). It encompasses all kinds of His guidance (exalted is He) and the varieties of His success. The mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyya) together with its being attributed to their pronoun is for the utmost magnification of the described and of what is attributed to them, for honouring both, and for increasing the verification of the content of the sentence and establishing it by stating what necessitates and requires it. The nun (of min) has been assimilated into the ra' (of Rabbihim), with ghunna (nasalization) or without ghunna (idgham).

The sentence, on the assumption that the two relative clauses are joined to "the God-fearing" (al-muttaqin), is independent, having no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical case), confirming the content of His saying (exalted is He): ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾, together with additional emphasis and verification of it. How could it not be so? For the Book being guidance for them is one of the varieties of that guidance which they have been granted and upon which they have settled, as you have verified, especially when one considers what it entails of success and prosperity?

It has been said: it occurs in the position of an answer to a question that may arise from what preceded, as if it were said: What is it for those described with what has been mentioned of these attributes that they have been singled out for the guidance of that Book of supreme importance? And are they deserving of that preference? So it is answered: that by reason of their being characterized by that, they possess the reins of the root of guidance, which comprises its varieties and entails success and prosperity; so what doubt is there regarding their deservingness of what is a branch of its branches? Whoever said in establishing this answer that those described are not unlikely to succeed, to the exclusion of people, in guidance in this world and in prosperity in the next, has strayed from the course of correctness.

As for the case where the two relative clauses are separated from it (i.e., not joined to al-muttaqin), then it occupies the position of raf' (nominative), on the basis that it is the predicate (khabar) of the subject (mubtada') which is the first relative pronoun, and the second is conjoined to it. And this sentence is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) that occurs as an answer to a question which the mind is led to from singling out what was mentioned for the God-fearing before the explanation of the principles of their entitlement to it. As if it were said: What is the matter with the God-fearing that they are specified with it? So it is answered by explaining what their name comprehensively contains of attributes of perfection, and by clarifying the result that it demands; that is: those whose affairs are these are deserving of what is greater than that. Like your saying: I love the Helpers who fought in defence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and gave their lives in the way of God; those are the apple of my eyes and the blackness of my heart.

Know that this method is pursued at times by repeating the name of the one from whom the discourse has been resumed, as in your saying: "I did good to Zayd; Zayd is worthy of kindness." And at other times by repeating his attribute, as in your saying: "I did good to Zayd; your old friend is fit for that." And there is no doubt that this is more eloquent than the first, because it contains an explanation of what necessitates the ruling. The use of the demonstrative is equivalent to repeating the described with his mentioned attributes, together with what it contains of signalling his complete distinction by them, and his being placed by means of that within the order of observable matters, and an allusion to the remoteness of his station, as has passed. This is all.

It has also been permitted that the first relative pronoun be attached to "the God-fearing," as has been detailed, and the second be the subject (mubtada'), and "those" etc. its predicate; and their being singled out for guidance and prosperity is taken as an indirect reference (ta'ridh) to non-believing People of the Book, since they used to claim that they were upon guidance and aspired to attain prosperity.

﴿And those are the ones who prosper﴾: the repetition of the demonstrative is to show further concern for the matter of those referred to, and to draw attention to the fact that their being characterized by those qualities necessitates attaining each one of those two distinctions, and that each of them suffices to distinguish them by it from others. The placement of the conjunction between the two sentences supports this, unlike what is in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Those are like cattle; nay, they are further astray; those are the heedless﴾, for the ascription to them of complete heedlessness is an expression of what the likening of them to beasts conveys; so the second sentence is confirmatory of the first.
