As for prosperity (al-ifla"), which is an expression for attaining the sought object, since it is distinct from guidance and a result of it, and since each of them in itself is the most precious aim for which competitors compete, it has been done as it has been done. And "they" (hum) is a separating pronoun (damir fasl), which separates the predicate from the qualifier, and confirms the attribution, and conveys the restriction of the predicated to the subject. Or it is a subject, whose predicate is "the prosperers," and the sentence is the predicate of "those." The definiteness of "the prosperers" (al-muflihun) serves to indicate that the God-fearing are the people whom you have heard are the prosperers in the Hereafter; or it is an allusion to what every person knows of the reality of the prosperers and their characteristics.

This is all. And in explaining the singling out of the God-fearing for attaining these lofty ranks, by means of many fine considerations, as has been pointed to within the course of the commentary on this noble verse, there is encouragement to follow their footsteps and guidance to emulate their course, the place of which is not hidden. And God is the Guardian of guidance and success.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 6:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾: This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a sentence that begins a new topic), brought to explain the condition of the disbelievers, who are misguided, obstinate and insolent, following the description of their opposites, who are characterized by perfect qualities and who attain their aims both in the present and in the future. The conjunction between the two has been omitted, and it has not been used in the manner of His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, the righteous are in bliss﴾ ﴿and indeed the wicked are in the Blazing Fire﴾, because of the opposition between them in style and the contrast in purpose. The first is brought to explain the exalted status of the Book in guidance and direction, while the reference to the condition of those guided by it occurs by way of digression (istitrad, a digression from the main topic). This holds whether the relative pronoun is joined to what precedes it or separated from it, because the resumptive sentence is built upon a question that arose from the preceding discourse, so it is inevitably one of its consequences. As for the second, it is brought principally to explain the condition of the disbelievers, and how their affair extends in error and misguidance to the point where warning and good tidings are of no benefit to them, and admonition and reminder have no effect on them. They have swerved from the path of sound reason into the wilderness of error and corruption, and they ride upon every hard and easy path of stubbornness and obstinacy. This manner was preferred, and the discourse was not founded on explaining that the Book is a guide for the earlier generations and useless for the later ones, because the final title is not something that bestows perfection, so that it should be mentioned in the course of enumerating perfections. "Inna" (indeed) is one of the particles that resemble the verb in the number of its letters, in being built on the fatha (vowel), in being restricted to nouns, in taking the protective nun (nun al-wiqayah) such as in "inna-ni" and "la'alla-ni" and similar forms, in giving its meanings, and in being transitive, especially when it governs two nouns. For this reason it operates in its secondary function, which is the accusative for the first noun and the nominative for the second, to indicate that it is a branch in its operation and an intruder into it. According to the Kufans, it has no operation on the predicate, but the predicate remains in its original state by virtue of presumption of continuity (istishab). It is answered that the nominative status of the predicate is conditional on being free of governing particles, since otherwise the predicate of "kana" would not be in the accusative, and it has ceased to be so with the entry of "kana". Therefore the operation of the particle is confirmed. Its effect is the emphasis and affirmation of the attribution, and for this reason it is used to introduce oaths, it begins responses, and it is employed in situations of doubt and denial to repel and refute them. Al-Mubarrad said: When you say, "Abd Allah is standing," it is a report of his standing; "Indeed, Abd Allah is standing" is an answer to one who asks about his standing while doubting it; and "Indeed, Abd Allah is certainly standing" is an answer to one who denies his standing. The definiteness of the relative pronoun is either for a specific reference, and what is meant by it is particular people, such as Abu Lahab, Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira and their like, and the rabbinical leaders of the Jews; or it is generic, and from it are excluded those who do not persist, by what is attributed to it in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿it is all the same for them﴾, etc. Disbelief (kufr) in the lexical sense is the concealment of a favour, and its root is "al-kafr" with a fatha, that is concealment. From this, the farmer and the night are called "kafir". He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿like rain whose vegetation pleases the tillers (kuffar)﴾, and upon this is the verse of Labid:

*In a night the clouds concealed its stars*

From it also comes "al-mutakaffir" in his weapons, which is the armoured man whose weapons cover his body. In the Sharia, it is the denial of what is known by necessity to be brought by the Messenger (ﷺ). The wearing of the distinguishing belt (ghiyar) and the tying of the zunnar without necessity, and similar things, are considered disbelief, because they indicate denial, for whoever believes the Prophet (ﷺ) would hardly dare to do such things, since there is no motive for them, just as with fornication and drinking wine. The Mu'tazilites argued for the createdness of the Qur'an from what came in it in the past tense in the form of reporting, since this necessarily requires the prior existence of what is reported. It is answered that this is one of the requirements of the relation (ta'alluq), and the createdness of the relation does not necessitate the createdness of the speech, just as the createdness of the relation of knowledge to the known does not necessitate the createdness of knowledge.

﴿It is all the same﴾: It is a noun in the sense of equality, described by it as the verbal nouns are described for emphasis. He (Exalted is He) said: ﴿Come to a word that is common between us and you﴾. His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿for them﴾ is connected to it, meaning "with them." Its nominative status is because it is the predicate of "inna". His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿whether you warned them or you did not warn them﴾ is in the nominative as its subject, because the interrogative hamza and "am" are stripped of the meaning of question, to establish equality between the two elements they introduce, just as the imperative and prohibitive are stripped of their meanings for this purpose in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾. The vocative particle in your saying, "O Allah, forgive us, O company," is stripped of the meaning of request for the mere purpose of specification, as though it were said: "Indeed those who disbelieve, your warning and its absence are equal for them," as when you say, "Indeed Zayd, his brother and his cousin are disputing." Or it is the subject, and ﴿it is all the same for them﴾ is the predicate, placed before it for the sake of emphasis on its matter, and the sentence is the predicate of "inna". The verb is only excluded from being the subject of a statement when it remains in its real meaning. But if it is intended to refer to the wording, or to the bare event implied by it, by way of extension, then it is like a noun in being an object of addition and being attributed to it, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿This is a day on which the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness﴾, and His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption"﴾, and in the saying: "You hear of al-Mu'aydi as better than seeing him." As though it were said: "Your warning and its absence are equal upon them." The turn to the verb is because of what it implies of renewal, and the means to bring in the hamza and its counterpart before it is to establish and affirm the meaning of equality, as has been indicated. It has been said that "sawa'" is the subject and what follows it is its predicate, but this is not correct, because the context requires explaining that warning and its absence are equal, not explaining that those for whom they are equal are warned and not warned.

Warning (al-indhar) is informing of what is feared, so as to be wary of it. It is of the form "if'al" from "nudhira bi-al-shay'", when one knows of a thing and beware of it. What is meant here is frightening from the punishment of Allah (Exalted is He) and His retribution for sins. Restricting the discourse to it is because they are not at all deserving of good tidings, and because warning is more effective in hearts and has a stronger impact on souls, for repelling harms is more important than bringing benefits. So since they are not affected by it, they will certainly not raise their heads at good tidings. It was recited with an alif inserted between the two hamzas while making both clear, and with its insertion while the second is between-between (a intermediate pronunciation), and with the second lightened to between-between without insertion, and with the deletion of the interrogative particle, and with its deletion while the vowel of it is transferred to the preceding quiescent consonant, as in the reading "qad aflaha" (qad aflaha). It was also recited with the second hamza changed to an alif. This has been attributed to solecism.

﴿They do not believe﴾: It is an independent sentence, emphasizing what precedes it and clarifying what is ambiguous in it regarding the equality. It therefore has no place in terms of grammatical case; or it is an emphasizing circumstantial clause (hal) of it; or a substitute (badal) for it; or a predicate of "inna". What precedes it is an interjection with what is the cause of the ruling, or a second predicate according to the opinion of one who permits it when it is a sentence. The noble verse is among the proofs used for permitting the imposition of what cannot be borne. He (Exalted is He) has informed about them that they do not believe, so the impossibility of their belief becomes evident, since this entails the impossible, which is that His report (Exalted is He) would not correspond to reality, while they are commanded to believe and remain under obligation. Moreover, among what they were obligated to is believing in their own persistent non-belief. The truth is that imposing what is impossible in itself, even if it is rationally permissible in terms of the fact that rulings do not require purposes, especially compliance, nonetheless it does not occur, by inductive observation. The report of the occurrence or non-occurrence of a thing does not negate the capacity to do it, like His report (Exalted is He) of what He does or what the servant does by his choice. What they were obligated to believe is not the details of what the Qur'an has stated, so that it would follow that they were obligated to believe in their persistent non-belief. Rather, it is belief in all that the Prophet (ﷺ) brought, in summary, while it is not known to them that the relative pronoun refers to them. The benefit of the warning, after knowing that it does not benefit them, is to establish the proof against them and to secure for the Messenger (ﷺ) the merit of conveying the message. For this reason it was said: ﴿it is all the same for them﴾, and it was not said "for you," just as it was said to the idol-worshippers: ﴿It is all the same for you whether you call upon them or you remain silent﴾.

In the noble verse there is a report of the unseen, in accordance with what is the case, if the relative pronoun is intended to refer to particular individuals. Therefore it is among the dazzling miracles.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 7:**

﴿God has sealed their hearts﴾: This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf ta'lili*) giving the reason for the ruling that precedes it, and an explanation of what that ruling requires; or it is an explanation and emphasis of it. By "the heart" (*qalb*) is meant the seat of the rational faculty within the inner heart (*fu'ad*). "Sealing" (*khatm*) upon a thing means securing it by striking a seal (*khatam*) upon it, to protect it, or because of what is in it that exposes it to threat, as with an empty house or a full bag. The first sense is the more fitting to the context, since the aim is not to protect what is in their hearts, but to produce a state which, because of their persistence in error, their immersion in blind imitation (*taqlid*), and their turning away from the path of sound reasoning (*nazar*), makes warning ineffective in them and truth not penetrate them at all. This may be understood either by way of metaphor (*isti'arah tab'iyyah*), by likening that to the striking of a seal, in the manner of the doors of abandoned dwellings built for habitation, the likening of an intellectual thing to a sensible one, with an intellectual common element, namely the containment of preventing the receptive thing from what it should rightly receive, and the term "seal" is borrowed for it, and then the past-tense form is derived from it; or by way of representation (*tamthil*), by likening the condition abstracted from their hearts, upon which has been done what has been done of producing that preventive state, so that what the hearts were created for, namely the beneficial religious matters, cannot reach them, and they are entirely cut off from it, to a condition abstracted from an impossibility, prepared to receive what would settle in it, a settling that entails important benefits; and it has been prevented by sealing over it, and it is entirely cut off from what it was prepared for. Then there is borrowed for it a term indicating the condition likened to it. Thus each of the two sides of the comparison is composed of several elements; from the side of the likened-to, only that on which the matter turns in depicting that condition and abstracting it has been selected, which is the seal, while the rest is implied, intended in purpose by imagined expressions through which the composition is realized. Although these expressions contribute to realizing the aspect of resemblance, which is an intellectual matter abstracted from them, namely the impossibility of benefiting from what is prepared for it because of a strong preventive cause, nevertheless none of them individually is a figurative usage (*tajawwuz*) in light of this metaphor; rather they remain as they are, whether literal, metaphorical or allusive (*kinayah*). The figurative usage lies only in the whole. And since the meaning of the whole is the totality of the meanings of those expressions, which contain no customary figurative usage, and since the condition abstracted from them is not a conventional signification of them, such that what indicates the condition likened-to, when used for the condition likened, would be used in other than what it was coined for, and thus fall under metaphor, which is a type of linguistic metaphor, defined as a word used in other than what it was coined for: the earlier eminent scholars, such as Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir (al-Jurjani) and his like, held that representation (*tamthil*) is a separate category. Whoever seeks to reduce the categories considers that condition likened-to as among the conventional significations, and makes the speech conveying it, when used for what is likened to it, a different condition abstracted from other matters, of the kind of metaphor; and he calls it a representational metaphor (*isti'arah tamthiliyyah*). The attribution of the production of that state in their hearts to God (Exalted) is because all events, in our view, are ascribed to Him in terms of creation, glorified and exalted is He. The noble verse, coming to censure them for their evil conduct and the gravity of their outcome, is because their acts, in terms of acquisition (*kasb*), are ascribed to them; for their creation by Him, glorified is He, is not by way of compulsion (*jabr*), but by way of consequence upon the abominations they committed, as His saying (Exalted) indicates: ﴿Rather, God has set a seal upon them for their disbelief﴾, and the like. As for the Mu'tazilah, they took the path of interpretation (*ta'wil*), and mentioned several sayings on this, among them: that when the people turned away from the truth, and that became firmly established in their hearts, until it became like a nature for them, it was likened to a created attribute to which they were inclined. Among them also: that what is meant is the representation of their hearts by the hearts of beasts which God (Exalted) created devoid of perception (*fatn*); or by hearts for which God's sealing is supposed, as in "the valley carried him off" meaning he perished, and "the phoenix carried him off" meaning his absence was prolonged. Among them also: that this is the act of Satan or of the unbeliever, and its ascription to Him (Exalted) is in terms of His enabling and empowering it. Among them also: that when their roots (*a'raq*) took firm hold in disbelief and became established, to the point that no way remained to bring about their faith except compulsion and coercion, and then He did not do that, in order to preserve the wisdom of obligation (*taklif*), this was expressed by "sealing," because it is a complete blocking of the path of their faith; and in it is an indication of the far-reaching nature of their matter in error and obstinacy, and the extreme extent of their immersion in evil and corruption. Among them also: that this is a report of what the disbelievers used to say, like their saying: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings from what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a veil﴾, mocking them. Among them also: that this refers to the Hereafter, and it was reported in the past tense because its occurrence is certain; and His saying (Exalted) supports it: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind and mute﴾. Among them also: that what is meant by the sealing is the marking of their hearts with a mark which the angels recognize, so they hate them and turn away from them.

﴿and upon their hearing﴾: This is conjoined (*'atf*) to what precedes it; it falls under the ruling of the sealing, because of His saying (Glorious and Mighty is He): ﴿And He sealed upon his hearing and his heart﴾; and by the consensus (*wifaq*) on pausing upon it (at "their hearts") and not on "their hearts"; and because the two share in perception from all sides. The repetition of the preposition is for emphasis and to indicate the difference of the two sealings. The mention of the sealing of their hearts first is to signal that it is the root of non-faith, and to indicate that its sealing is not by way of consequence upon the sealing of their hearing, on the basis that the latter is a path to it; rather the sealing upon it is a sealing upon them, but they are sealed with a separate seal, such that even were there no sealing upon their hearing, it would remain in its state, as He (Exalted) makes clear: ﴿And had God known any good in them, He would have made them hear; and had He made them hear, they would have turned away while they were averse﴾. Hearing (*sam'*) is the perception of the faculty of hearing, and it may be applied to that faculty and to the organ bearing it; and this is what is meant here, since it is the primary object of the sealing. The mention of its condition before the condition of their sight is either because of the commonality between it and their hearts in that state, or because their offence in respect of hearing, through which the legal rulings are received and through which warning is realized, is greater than in respect of sight, through which the conditions indicating unity are witnessed; so its explanation is more deserving of precedence and more fitting to the context. They said: hearing is superior to sight, because He (Mighty and Exalted) when mentioning both, placed hearing before sight; and because hearing is a condition of prophethood, for this reason God (Exalted) never sent a deaf messenger; and because hearing is a means to completing reason through knowledge which is received from its possessors. The singular form (*tawhid*) is used for safety from ambiguity, and in view of the basic form, or by assuming an elided genitive, i.e., "and upon the sense-faculties of their hearing." The discussion of placing the seal upon this is as was said before.

﴿and upon their sight there is a covering﴾: "Absar" is the plural of "basar". The discussion of it is as you have heard in the case of hearing. "Ghishawah" is the pattern *fi'alah* from *taghshiyah*, i.e., covering; it is formed for what envelops a thing, like "'isabah" (headband) and "'imamah" (turban). Its indefiniteness is for magnification and awe. According to the view of Sibawayh it is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is the fronted adverbial phrase, and the clause is conjoined to what precedes it. The choice of the nominal sentence is to signal the continuance of its content, for what is perceived by the seeing faculty of the signs set up in the horizons and in the selves, since they are constant, their blindness to these is likewise constant. As for the signs received through the hearing faculty, since their reaching it occurs from time to time, the verbal sentence was chosen in expressing the sealing upon it, and upon what is one of the two ways of knowing it, namely the heart. According to the view of al-Akhfash, it is raised as the agent (*fa'iliyyah*) of what the preposition depends upon. It is also read in the accusative, on the assumption of an implied governing verb, i.e., "and He placed upon their sight a covering." It has been said: by elision of the preposition and conveying the sealing to it, and the meaning is: "and their sight was sealed with a covering." It is read with *damm* and *raf'*, with *fath* and *nasb*, these being two dialects for it. "Ghishwah" with *kasr* in the nominative, and with *fath* in the nominative and accusative; and "'ashawah" with the unpointed *'ayn* and in the nominative.

﴿and for them there is a great punishment﴾: This is a threat and an explanation of what they deserve in the Hereafter. "'Adhab" (punishment) is like "nakal" (exemplary punishment), in form and meaning. It is said: "a'dhaba 'an al-shay'" when he refrained from it; and from this comes "al-ma' al-'adhb" (sweet water), because it quells and repels thirst; and for this reason it is called *nuqakh*, because it breaks and shatters thirst; and *furat*, because it spreads over the heart and breaks it. Then the usage was extended, and it was applied to every grievous pain, even if it is not a punishment whose aim is to deter the offender from repetition. It has been said: its derivation is from *ta'dhib*, which is the removal of the 'adhab, like *taqdhiyah* and *tamridh*. "Al-'azim" (great) is the opposite of "al-haqir" (small); and "al-kabir" (big) is the opposite of "al-saghir" (little). Hence, since the *haqir* is below the *saghir*, the *'azim* is above the *kabir*. They are used of physical bodies and of events; one says: "a great man" (*rajul 'azim*) and "a big man" (*rajul kabir*), meaning his body, or his importance. The punishment is described by it to emphasize what the indefiniteness conveys of magnitude, awe and exaggeration in that. The meaning is that upon their sight there is a kind of covering, outside what people customarily know, and it is the covering of blindness to the signs; and for them there is a kind of great pain of which the reality cannot be reached and whose extent cannot be grasped. O God, we seek refuge in You from all of that, O Most Merciful of the merciful.

﴿And among the people﴾: This begins an explanation that some of those whose past conditions have been described are not limited to the mere persistence in disbelief and obstinacy that has been mentioned. Rather, they add to it other kinds of evil and corruption. It also enumerates their shameful crimes, which entail dreadful conditions, both in this world and in the Hereafter.

The original form of *nās* (people) is *unās* (أُناس), as is attested by *insān* (إنسان), *anāsī* (أناسيّ), and *ins* (إنس). Its hamza was dropped for lightness, as has been said in the case of *lūqah* in *alwiqah*. The definite article (*al*) was substituted for it, which is why the two are hardly ever combined. As for what occurs in the verse:

*Indeed the deaths look down*
*upon the people who feel secure*

this is anomalous. They were so named because of their visibility (*zuhūr*) and because people are attached to them, just as *jinn* were named *jinn* because they are hidden (*ijtinān*). Some scholars held that its root is *al-nawas* (النَّوَس), which means movement. Its *wāw* became an *alif* because it was vowelled and preceded by a vowel that was open. Others held that it is derived from *nasiya* (نَسِيَ, to forget). Its final radical was moved to the position of the middle radical, so it became *nayas* (نَيَس), and then the *yā'* was changed to an *alif*. They were so named because of their forgetfulness. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "Man (*al-insān*) was named *insān* because a covenant was made with him, and he forgot."

The definite article in it is either for specific reference (*al-ʿahd*) or for the category (*al-jins*) restricted to the persistent ones, as stated in the discussion of the relative pronoun. It is as if it were said: "And among them" or "among those." The shift to *al-nās* (the people) is to indicate that they are numerous, as the partitive (*tab'īḍ*) implies.

The prepositional phrase (*al-ẓarf*) is in the nominative position, either as a predicate (*mubtada'*) with regard to its content, or as a qualifier of an unstated subject, as in His, Exalted and Majestic is He, saying: ﴿And some of us are other than that﴾, meaning: "and a group of us." And *man* (مَن) in His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿who says﴾ is either a relative pronoun (*mawṣūlah*) or a qualifying noun (*mawṣūfah*), and its position is nominative as a predicate (*khabar*). The meaning is: "and some of the people," or "and some of the people who say," as in His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾, and so on. Or it means: "a group who say," as in His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿Among the believers are men﴾, and so on. In this case, the core of the benefit and the primary intent is their being characterised by what falls within the scope of the relative clause or the qualifier, together with all the attributes connected to it, and not that they are the very persons mentioned.

As for making the prepositional phrase the predicate, which is the common usage in contexts of use, this is rejected by the eloquence of the meaning. Their being from among the people is evident, so informing about it is devoid of benefit, as has been said. This is because its basis is the suspicion that the intended meaning of "the people" is humanity in general. The answer to this is likewise that the benefit is to draw attention to the fact that the attributes mentioned contradict humanity. Thus, whoever is characterised by them should not be known to be among the people, so that one would be informed of it and marvel at it. You know well that "the people" refers either to those already known, or to the category restricted to the persistent ones. In either case the benefit is clear. Indeed, the predicative use of the prepositional phrase requires that the characterisation of these people by those ugly attributes, detailed in thirteen verses, be a heading (*ʿunwān*) for the subject, taken as given, not intended in itself. The core of the benefit then is their being among those mentioned. No one doubts that the sublime text must be interpreted according to its most excellent and complete meanings.

The pronoun in *yaqūlu* (says) is singular, in view of the word *man*, while its plural in His saying ﴿We believe in God and the Last Day﴾ and what follows it is in view of its meaning. The "Last Day" refers to the period from the Gathering (*ḥashr*) without end, or until the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, since there is no limit beyond that. Singling them out for belief in both, with the repetition of the preposition *bi* (in), claims that they have attained faith from both sides and encompassed it from both ends, and that they believe in each of the two fundamentally and firmly. Yet they have concealed beneath this the corrupt beliefs they hold, since their belief in neither of the two is belief in reality. They are polytheists with respect to God by their saying: ﴿Ezra is the son of God﴾, and deniers of the Last Day by their saying: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾, and similar statements. The reporting of their words serves to demonstrate the completeness of their wickedness and corruption. For what they said, if it had issued from them not in the manner of deception and hypocrisy, while their belief is what it is, would not be faith. How much more so when they say it to deceive the believers and to mock them.

﴿And they are not believers﴾: This is a refutation of what they claimed and a negation of what they professed. The *mā* here is of the Ḥijāzī type (*ḥijāziyyah*, the dialect of the Hijaz, which makes the predicate of *mā* take the accusative and allows the preposition *bi* to be added to it). This is because the permissibility of adding *bi* to its predicate for emphasis of negation is conventional, unlike the Tamīmī dialect (*tamīmiyyah*, which does not treat *mā* as operating on the subject and predicate). The choice of the nominal sentence over the verbal one, which would agree with their claim being refuted, is for emphasis in the rejection, by conveying the negation of faith from them at all times, not only in the past as the verbal sentence would indicate. One should not imagine that a positive nominal sentence indicates the continuity of the affirmation, so that when negation enters it, the meaning must be the negation of continuity. Rather, with the aid of the context, it definitely indicates the continuity of the negation, just as the present-tense verb free of the particle of prevention indicates the continuity of existence, and when the particle of prevention enters it, it indicates the continuity of prevention, not the prevention of continuity, as in His, Exalted and Majestic, saying: ﴿And if God were to hasten evil upon the people as they seek to hasten good, their term would surely have been decreed for them﴾. The non-execution of their term is for the continuity of the non-hastening, not for the non-continuity of the hastening.

The omission of the word "belief" from what they had restricted it with is to indicate that they are not of the kind of belief at all, let alone belief in what they mentioned. It has been permitted that the intended meaning is this, and that the unqualified use is for clarity. The implication of the noble verse is that whoever shows belief while his inner conviction is contrary to it is not a believer. Thus there is no proof in it for the Karrāmiyyah (a sect that held that whoever utters the two testimonies, with his heart empty of what agrees with or contradicts them, is a believer), who maintain that whoever pronounces the two testimonies of faith, with his heart empty of what agrees with or contradicts them, is a believer.

﴿They deceive Allah and those who believe﴾: an explanatory clause (bayan) for "yaqulu" [﴿they say﴾], and a clarification of their aim in what they say. Or it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence that answers an implied question) that came in reply to a question the mind naturally leads to, as if it were said: "Why do they say that when they are not believers?" So it was answered: "They deceive Allah," and so on. That is: they cheat (yakhda'un). This reading has also been transmitted. The use of the form of mutual action (mufa'ala, "yukhadi'un") serves to convey intensity in the manner of the act, since when an action is practised against someone with full effort, it is certainly carried out with great intensity. Or it conveys intensity in quantity, as in habitual practice and persistence, since they were constant in deception. Deception (khada') means to make one's victim imagine the opposite of what one intends for him of harm, in order to bring it upon him from a direction he does not expect. Or it means to make him imagine that one is helping him with what he himself intends, so that he is deceived and escapes easily. This is from the expression "a deceptive lizard" (dabb khadi') and "khuda'" (a deceptive creature), which is the one that, when the hunter passes his hand over the entrance of its hole, makes him think it is coming toward him, and so it comes out through its other opening. Both meanings suit the context, for they intended by what they did to learn the secrets of the believers and then spread them to the hostile ones, and to protect themselves from what afflicts the rest of the disbelievers. Whatever the case, attributing this to Allah (exalted is He) is either by way of metaphor (isti'ara) and figurative representation (tamthil), to convey the full abominableness of their crime, meaning that they are treated as deceivers. Or it is by way of rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), by attributing to Him (exalted is He) what properly belongs to the Messenger (ﷺ), to show his high standing with Him (exalted is He), as indicated by His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are pledging allegiance only to Allah; the hand of Allah is over their hands﴾, and His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾; while also conveying the full abominableness, as already mentioned. Or it is merely a preparation and introduction for what follows, namely its attribution to those who believe, and a signal of the strength of their particular association with Him (exalted is He), as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, and His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, those who harm Allah and His Messenger﴾. The form of deception is kept in its literal meaning, based on their corrupt assumption and as a rendering of their false belief, as if it were said: "They claim that they deceive Allah, while Allah deceives them." Or the word is taken as a subsidiary metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya), or as a representation of the image of their conduct toward Allah (exalted is He) and the believers, and His conduct toward them by applying the rulings of Islam to them, while in His sight they are the most wicked of the disbelievers and the people of the lowest level of the Fire, as a means of lulling them (istidraj). The Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers complying with Allah's command (exalted is He) in this is a requital to them with the like of their conduct, in the form of the conduct of those who deceive one another, as has been said. This is what sound taste does not approve. As for the first, if the hypocrites believed that Allah (exalted is He) deceives them in return for their deception of Him, it would not be conceivable that they would undertake to deceive. As for the second, the requirement of the context is to present their condition in particular, to depict it in the abominable form that suits it, and to explain its harmful outcome, which returns to them from a direction they do not expect, as indicated by His saying (mighty and majestic is He): ﴿And they deceive none but themselves﴾. Therefore, dwelling on the condition of the other side would impair the context's due fulfilment. ﴿وَما يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ [﴿and they are not aware﴾] is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yukhadi'un" (they deceive), meaning: they do what they do while the situation is that they harm by it none but themselves, since the scope of their action is confined to themselves. Or: they do not in reality deceive anyone but themselves, by feeding them falsehoods, so they cast them into the pits of destruction. It has been read as "wa-ma yukhadi'un," and the meaning is the same. Whoever keeps the form in what precedes says: "And they are not treated with that treatment resembling the treatment of deceivers except themselves, because its harm befalls none but them." Or: "They do not deceive in reality anyone but themselves, by making them hopeful of falsehoods; and these in turn deceive them and make them vain hopes." It has also been read as "wa-ma yukhda'un" (from takhdi'), and "ma yakhtadi'un" (meaning: they deceive themselves), and "yukhda'un," and "yukhadhu'un," in the passive voice. The word "anfusahum" (themselves) is in the accusative by removal of the preposition. The "nafs" (self) is the essence of a thing and its reality. It is also used for the spirit, because the life of a living being is by it; and for the heart as well, because it is the seat of the spirit or what the spirit is connected to; and for blood as well, because the sustenance of the body depends on it; and for water as well, because of its great need for it. The meaning intended here is the first meaning, because the purpose is to show that the harm of their deception returns to them and does not pass over them to others. His saying (exalted is He): ﴿وَما يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ [﴿and they are not aware﴾] is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "ma yakhda'un," meaning: they confine themselves to deceiving themselves, while the situation is that they are not aware, that is, they do not perceive it, because of their persistence in error. The omission of the object is either because it is evident, or because it is general, meaning: they are not aware of anything at all. The arrival of the consequence of what they did has been made, in its manifestness, like a matter perceived by the senses, which is not hidden except from one whose senses are impaired and whose perceptions are disordered.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 10:**

﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾: "Disease" (*maradh*) is an expression for what befalls the body and takes it out of the proper balance (*i'tidal*) suited to it. It causes disorder in its functions and leads to death. It is used here as a metaphor (*isti'ara*) for what is in their hearts of ignorance, corrupt belief, enmity toward the Prophet ﷺ (p-42) and other kinds of disbelief that lead to spiritual ruin. The indefinite form (*tankir*) indicates that it is a vague kind, not the sort of disease people commonly know. The clause confirms what is implied by His saying: ﴿And they are not believers﴾, namely that their non-belief is continuous. Or it gives the reason for it, as if it were said: "What is the matter with them that they do not believe?" And it is answered: "In their hearts is a disease that prevents it."

﴿So Allah increased them in disease﴾: by sealing their hearts, because He knew that reminder and warning would have no effect on them. This clause is conjoined (*ma'tuf*) to what precedes it, and the *fa'* (so) indicates that its content follows from it. Through this it becomes clear that they are among the disbelievers whose hearts are sealed, with added explanation of the cause. It has also been said: He increased them in disbelief by the increase in legal obligations, because whenever the obligations increased with the descent of revelation, they increased in disbelief. It is also permissible that "disease" is a metaphor for the weakness, cowardice and feebleness that entered their hearts when they witnessed the might of the Muslims. Then His increasing them in disease is what He did to them by casting terror and fear into their hearts when religion was made mighty through the support of the Prophet ﷺ by the sending down of angels and his being aided with various kinds of victory and establishment. Then His saying: ﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾, etc., is at that point a resumptive explanatory clause (*isti'naf ta'lili*) for His saying: ﴿They deceive Allah﴾, etc., as if it were said: "What is the matter with them that they deceive and flatter? And why do they not openly declare what is in their hearts of disbelief?" And it is answered: "In their hearts is a double weakness." This is their state in this world. ﴿And for them﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿is a painful punishment﴾, i.e., one that causes pain. It is said *alam* (pain) and *huwa alim* (it is painful), like *wajaʿ* (ache) and *huwa wajiʿ* (it is aching). The punishment is described with it for emphasis, as in his saying:

*Their greeting among them is a painful striking*

according to the manner of "his majesty is majestic" (*jadda jiddhu*). For pain and ache are truly attributes of the one in pain and the one struck, just as majesty belongs to the majestic. It has been said that it means "causing pain" (*mu'lim*), like "hearing" (*sami'*) meaning "making hear" (*musmi'*). But this is not established, as will come in His saying: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾.

﴿Because they used to lie﴾: The *ba'* is causal (*sababiyya*) or for exchange (*muqabala*). The *ma* is verbal (*masdariyya*), and in reality it enters upon "they lie." The word "used to be" (*kanu*) is inserted to indicate the continuity and renewal of their lying. That is: because of their lying, or in return for their continuous and persistent lying, which is their saying: ﴿We believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, while they are not believers. For this is a report that they have produced belief in the past, not a performance of belief (*insha'*). And even if it were granted that it is an act, it would contain a report of its issuing from them, and that is not the case, because there is absolutely no inner assent in the sense of submission and acceptance. It is also permissible that it be taken at face value, according to the view of those who permit the incomplete *kana* to have a verbal noun, as has been stated in the verse of the poet:

*By generosity and forbearance the young man became lord among his people, and your being him is easy for you.*

That is: for them is a painful punishment because they habitually lie. The ordering of the punishment upon this among all its other strong causes is either because the intended meaning is to explain the punishment specific to the hypocrites, on the basis that their partnership with the open disbelievers in the great punishment mentioned is apparent, according to their sharing in what necessitates it, namely persistence in disbelief, as His saying indicates: ﴿And among the people﴾, etc. Or it is to signal that for them, in return for all their great crimes, there is a punishment beyond description. Or it is an allusion to the utter ugliness of lying, considering the apparent wording, which suggests that it alone is the cause, while the listener knows that the punishment reaches them from various directions; and that restricting it to this is to indicate the extreme ugliness of it and to cause aversion from it.

From Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him). It is also related with a *marfu'* chain to the Prophet ﷺ: "Beware of lying, for it is contrary to faith." As for what is related, that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) told three lies, the meaning there is allusion (*ta'ridh*), and it was called lying only because of its outward resemblance to it.

It has also been said: *ma* is relative (*mawsula*), and the returning pronoun is omitted, i.e., "with that which they deny." It is also read *yukadhdhibun* (with doubling), and the object is omitted, which is either the Prophet ﷺ or the Qur'an. Here *ma* is verbal: i.e., because of their denying him (peace and blessings be upon him), or the Qur'an. Or it is relative: i.e., with what they deny, with the returning pronoun omitted. It is also permissible that the *taf'il* form is for emphasis, as in *bayyana* (for *bana*, to become clear) and *qallasa* (for *qalasa*, to shrink); or for multiplicity, as in *mawwatat al-bahaʾim* (the beasts died in numbers) and *barrakat al-ibil* (the camels knelt); and that it derives from the saying "the wild animal lied" (*kadhaba al-wahshi*), when it runs a course and then stops to look at what is behind it. For the hypocrite is hesitant in his affair and wavering in his opinion, and for this reason he is called *mudhabdhab* (vacillating).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 11:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth"﴾: This begins the enumeration of some of their vile deeds, which branch out from the disbelief and hypocrisy mentioned about them. "Idha" (إذا) is an adverb of future time, and it generally carries the meaning of a conditional. It is used only with a matter that is certain, or whose occurrence is considered likely. The "lam" (اللام) is connected to "qila" (قيل, "it was said"), and its meaning is notification and communication. The element standing in for the subject of the verb is the clause "la tufsidu" (لا تُفْسِدُوا, "do not cause corruption"), with the understanding that what is meant by it is the utterance itself. It has also been said that the subject is a pronoun referring back to something implied, which the mentioned clause explains. Corruption (fasad, فساد) is the departure of a thing from the condition appropriate to it, and righteousness (salah, صلاح) is its opposite. Corruption on the earth is the stirring up of wars and strife, which entails the loss of uprightness in the affairs of the servants and the disruption of the order of their livelihood and their hereafter. What is meant by what they were forbidden is that which leads to such corruption, such as disclosing the secrets of the believers to the disbelievers, inciting the disbelievers against them, and other kinds of evil. This is like saying to a man, "Do not kill yourself with your own hand," or "Do not throw yourself into the fire," when he is about to do what has such an outcome. This clause is either conjoined to "yaqulu" (يَقُولُ, "says"), in which case, if the word "man" (مَن) is taken as a relative pronoun, it has no place in the grammatical analysis, and there is no harm in the interposition of an explanatory clause or a resumptive clause, and what is connected to them between the parts of the relative clause, for that is not an intrusion of a foreign element. If "man" is taken as a qualifying (descriptive) term, then its place is in the nominative case. The meaning is: among the people is one who, when he is forbidden by the believers from the corruption on the earth in which they are engaged, ﴿says﴾, showing the forbidders that such conduct does not come from them, while their original intention is to deny that it is corruption and to claim that it is pure reform, as will be explained: ﴿Indeed, we are only reformers﴾; that is, restricted only to pure reform, such that no trace of corruption or ruin attaches to it, indicating by the word "innama" (إنما, "indeed only") that this is so evident that one should not doubt it. Or it is a resumed statement, brought to enumerate their abominations. As for its being conjoined to "yakdhibun" (يَكْذِبُونَ, "they lie"), with the meaning "for them is a painful punishment for their lying and for their saying, when they were forbidden from corruption, 'Indeed, we are only reformers,'" as has been said, this is rejected, because this type of causal explanation should be attached to descriptions whose causal relation is apparent, whose attribution to the described party is established, and which need no clarification, due to the fame of the attribution of these descriptions in the hearer's mind, or because they have been explicitly mentioned earlier, as in His (Exalted) saying: ﴿because of what they used to lie﴾, for its content is an expression of what was related about them concerning their saying: "We believe in God and the Last Day." Or it is because what is mentioned implies it with clear implication, as in the saying of Him, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, those who stray from the way of God, for them is a severe punishment because they forgot the Day of Reckoning﴾; for what is mentioned of straying from the way of God necessarily entails forgetting the side of the Hereafter, of which the Day of Reckoning is a part. And when the matter is not like that, its proper form is that its causal basis be stated intentionally, as in His (Exalted) saying: ﴿That is because they said, "The Fire will not touch us"﴾, etc., and His saying: ﴿That is because God sent down the Book with truth﴾, etc., and so on. There is no doubt that this conditional statement, and the two conditional statements that follow it and are conjoined to it, the content of none of them is known to be attributed to them in the hearer's mind by any of the aforementioned means, such that it could qualify to be included in the chain of the stated causal explanation. Therefore, its proper form is that these be presented in the manner of enumerating their abominations, in one of the two ways, serving to establish that they possess each one of those attributes, intentionally and independently. How is it not...

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 12:

And His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Surely it is they who are the corrupters﴾; this proclaims it with a clear (p-44) proclamation? For it is a rejection from Him, exalted is He, of their claim as reported, the most eloquent rejection and the most indicative of great wrath, in that it follows the method of resumption (isti'naf, a new sentence that resumes the discourse) which leads to the ruling becoming more firmly fixed in the mind of the hearer. The sentence is introduced by the two emphatic particles "alā" (a particle of alerting that draws attention to the certainty of what follows) and "inna" (which confirms the predication). The interrogative hamza of denial (al-hamza al-inkariyya), when it enters upon a negation, definitively establishes the affirmation, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾. For this reason the sentence that follows it almost never occurs except when introduced by that which accompanies an oath. Its sister, "amā," is among the harbingers of an oath. It has also been said that they are two simple particles set for alerting and initiating speech. The predicate is definite, and the separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl, the pronoun placed between subject and predicate to restrict and confirm it) is placed in the middle, to answer what their claim of restricting themselves to reform implies by way of insinuation against the believers. Then He corrects it with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But they do not perceive﴾, to indicate that their being corruptors is among the matters that are perceptible, but they have no sense by which they could perceive it. The same applies to the two conditional clauses that come next and what follows them, and to the refutation of their content. Had the aim not been to detail their crimes, enumerate their abominations and blunders, then to manifest their corruption and demonstrate its falsehood, this door would not have been opened. And Allah knows best what is correct.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 13:

﴿And when it is said to them﴾: from the side of the believers, by way of enjoining the right (al-amr bi'l-ma'ruf) after forbidding them from the wrong (al-nahy 'an al-munkar), completing the counsel and perfecting the guidance: ﴿Believe﴾: the object of belief (al-mu'min bihi) has been omitted because it is evident; or it is intended: "Do belief" (ifʿalu al-iman). ﴿as the people have believed﴾: the kaf (ka) is in the accusative position, as an adjective (na't) to an omitted emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkad), meaning: "Believe with a belief similar to their belief." Thus "ma" is either verbal-source (masdariyyah) or restrictive (kafffah), as in "rubbama," for it restrains the particle from operating and makes it correct for it to enter upon the sentence, and it is for comparison between the contents of the two clauses, meaning: "Make your belief real as their belief became real." The lam is for the genus (li'l-jins), and by "the people" is meant those perfect in humanity, who act according to the dictate of reason; for the generic noun, just as it is used for its referent, is also used for what gathers the special meanings proper to it that are intended by it; therefore it is negated of what is not so, and it is said: "He is not a human being." And the one who combined both said:

*When people are people and the time is time*

Or it is for the specific (al-'ahd), and by it is meant the Messenger ﷺ and those with him, or those among their own kind who believed, such as Ibn Salam and his like. The meaning is: "Believe with a belief joined with sincerity, purified of the taints of hypocrisy, similar to their belief." ﴿They said﴾: responding to the enjoining of the right with denial, describing the sound, weighty ones with the opposite of their fine qualities: ﴿Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?﴾; pointing with the lam to those among the people who were indicated as perfect, or those known, or to the genus as a whole, while they include themselves in it according to their corrupt assumption. Safah (foolishness) is lightness and flimsiness of opinion, produced by deficiency of intellect, and its opposite is forbearance and deliberateness. They attributed them to it although they were at the furthest extreme of right-guidedness, steadiness and dignity, because of the complete immersion of their own souls in foolishness, their persistence in error, and their being among those for whom the evil of their deeds was made attractive so that they saw it as good; for whoever considers misguidance to be guidance will inevitably call guidance misguidance. Or it is to belittle their standing, since many of the believers were poor, and among them were freedmen such as Suhayb and Bilal. Or it is for showing boldness and indifference toward those among them who believed, on the supposition that the intended meaning of "the people" is Abdullah ibn Salam and his like. Whichever it is, what the sublimity of the revelation requires and the grandeur of its exalted matter demands is that this statement came from them in the presence of the believers who were advising them, as a response to their counsel. And since its import was to make foolish those famous luminaries and to impugn their faith, it follows that they were openly declaring themselves and hypocrites, and this is something the context and the sequence barely support. Hence they said: it must be that this took place among themselves, not in the presence of the believers. Imam al-Wahidi said: they used to express this statement among themselves, not in the presence of the believers, so God (Exalted is He) informed His Prophet, peace be upon him, and the believers of it as having come from them. You know that to bring out what issued from one of two speakers in private, in the course of what passed between them in a context of dialogue, is something not customary in speech, let alone in what holds the station of inimitability. Therefore the truth from which there is no escape is that their statement, though it issued from them in the presence of the advisers, does not require that they were openly declaring themselves; for it is a kind of refined disbelief and an ancient art of hypocrisy, fashioned after their saying: ﴿And hear, unheard﴾; just as that is a double-meaning speech of their sort, capable of bad sense, by being taken as: "Hear from us, unheard, a speech you would like," and the like, and capable of good sense, by being taken as: "Hear, unheard, something disagreeable," which they used to address to the Messenger of God ﷺ mockingly, showing the latter meaning while concealing the former in their souls, reassured by it; and for this they were forbidden. Likewise this statement admits of a bad meaning, as was mentioned in its interpretation, and a good meaning, by being taken as a claim to belief, like the belief of the people, and a denial of what they were accused of, namely hypocrisy, in the sense: "Shall we believe as the foolish and the madmen have believed, whose belief would not be counted even if they believed? And shall we not believe as the people believe until you order us to that?" They addressed the advisers with it mockingly, feigning, while showing the latter meaning, and relying on the former; so God returned this upon them with His saying (Mighty is He, speaking): ﴿Surely they are the foolish, but they do not know﴾, the most eloquent refutation, and they were charged with the most shameful ignorance, since the sentence is introduced with the two particles of emphasis, as has been indicated earlier, and foolishness is confined to them and carried to the point that they know they are fools. From this the secret of what was said in the interpretation of His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿We are only reformers﴾ becomes clear; for taking it in the latter meaning, as is the opinion of the majority, is necessarily incompatible with their condition: their addressing the advisers, claiming that what they were forbidden from, namely corruption, is reform, as was said earlier, is a manifestation on their part of enmity, and the emergence of their persons from the tunnel of hypocrisy; and the excuse that what they were forbidden from was their conciliation of the polytheists, as mentioned in some exegeses, and that the reform they claim is reform between themselves and the believers, and that the meaning of His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Surely they are the corrupters﴾ is that in that dealing they are corrupters of the believers' interests, since it indicates the giving of a lowly thing and reveals their weakness, which compelled them to engage someone who undertakes the reconciliation of affairs, let alone their being reformers, which is certainly impossible. For His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿but they do not perceive﴾ is explicit in refuting this; how could it not be, since it would require that the hypocrites in that claim be truthful, intending reform, while corruption comes upon them without their perceiving it? There is no doubt that in it they are liars, who associate with them only to harm the religion and betray the believers. So the way to resolve the difficulty is none other than what has been indicated: their saying "We are only reformers" admits of being taken as a lie; and the denial that the corruption attributed to them issued from them, in the sense "We are only reformers; there does not proceed from us what you forbid us from of corruption," they addressed to the advisers mockingly and as a display, to show this meaning, while they deviate toward the former meaning; so He returned upon them with His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Surely they are the corrupters﴾, the verse. And God, glorified is He, knows best what He deposited within the folds of His hidden Book of the concealed secret; we ask Him for protection and success, and guidance to the right path.

The detailing of this noble verse with "they do not know" is because it corresponds more closely to the mention of foolishness, which is a branch of ignorance; and because the knowledge that the believers are steadfast upon the truth while those others are upon falsehood depends on distinguishing truth from falsehood, which cannot be achieved except by reflection and inference. As for hypocrisy and what it contains of sedition and corruption, and what follows from it of the one who is characterized by it being a corrupter, this is an evident matter that anyone possessing awareness comprehends; therefore the preceding noble verse was detailed with "they do not perceive."

﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe."﴾ This shows the variation of their states and the contradiction of their statements during their dealings and conversations, according to the variation of those they address, and the context in which their story is introduced, in order to expose their creed and reveal their hypocrisy. For this reason, the faith itself is not mentioned here, so there is no trace of repetition. It is narrated that: "Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions went out one day, and a group of the Companions met them. Ibn Ubayy said, 'Look how I will turn these fools away from you.' When they drew near to them, he took the hand of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and said, 'Welcome to the Siddiq, the chief of the Banu Tamim, the elder of Islam, the second of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the cave, the one who gave his soul and his wealth for the Messenger of Allah.' Then he took the hand of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and said, 'Welcome to the chief of the Banu Adi, al-Faruq, the strong in his religion, the one who gave his soul and his wealth for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.' Then he took the hand of Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and said, 'Welcome to the cousin of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his son-in-law, and the chief of the Banu Hashim, other than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.' Then the verse was revealed. It is also said that Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said to him, 'O Abdullah, fear Allah and do not be a hypocrite, for the hypocrites are the worst of Allah's creation (exalted is He).' He said to him, 'Gently, O Abu al-Hasan! Do you say this about me? By Allah, our faith is like your faith, and our belief is like your belief.' Then they separated. Ibn Ubayy said to his companions, 'How did you see me act? When you see them, do the same as I did.' They praised him and said, 'We will remain in good so long as you live among us.' The Muslims returned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and informed him of this, and then the verse was revealed." The word *al-liqa'* (meeting) means encountering or coming upon; it is said: *laqituhu* and *laqitu* (I met him), meaning I encountered him and came before him. It is also read as *"idha laqaw"*.

﴿And when they are alone﴾: from *khalawtu ila fulan*, meaning I was alone with him. It may also be used with *bi* (with). Or it may be from *khala* in the sense of "passed away," as in the phrase "the generations that passed (*al-qurun al-khaliya*)." Their saying "khalaka dhamm" (may he who has passed you be a reproach) means he surpassed you and went away from you. It has also been permitted that it is from *khalawtu bihi*, meaning I mocked him, with *ila* in His saying (exalted is He), ﴿to their devils﴾, because it implies the sense of conveying; that is, "when they convey the mockery to them," and so on. You know that restricting their saying as reported to that conveying is something without any basis. The meaning of *shayatinihim* (their devils) is: those among them who resemble the devil in rebellion and obstinacy, who openly display their disbelief; and attributing them to them is for sharing in disbelief. Or it means the great hypocrites, while the speakers are their lesser ones. Sibawayh made the *nun* of *al-shaytan* (the devil) sometimes original, so its pattern is *fay'al*, derived from *shatana*, meaning he went far away, since it is far from good and mercy; their saying *tashaytana* supports this. And sometimes it is additional, so its pattern is *fa'lan*, derived from *shata*, meaning he perished or became null; and among his names is *al-batil* (the falsehood). It was also said that its meaning is: he was agitated and burned.

﴿They say, "We are with you"﴾: that is, in religion and belief; we do not part from you in any state. They addressed them with the nominal sentence emphasized, because what they claim to them is establishing firmness upon the religion they were on, and the emphasis is to indicate the sincerity of their desire and the abundance of their eagerness; it is not to deny the devils. This is unlike their dealings with the believers, for they only claim to them the creation of faith, because they are certain that the claim of perfection in it, or of persistence upon it, will not be accepted. ﴿"We are only mocking"﴾: that is, in showing faith before the believers, ﴿them﴾, without faith ever occurring to our minds in reality. This is a resumptive statement (*istinaf*) built upon a question arising from the claim of being with them. As if it was said to them, when they said, "We are with you": "Then why do you agree with the believers in uttering the word of faith?" So they said, "We are only mocking them." That does not harm their being with you; rather it emphasizes it. They have included in their answer that they humiliate the believers and consider that support for their religion. Or it is an emphasis of what came before it, for the one who mocks a thing is persistent in its opposite. Or it is a substitute for it, because whoever belittles Islam has exalted disbelief. *Al-istihza'* (mockery) of a thing is ridiculing it; it is said *hazi'tu* and *istahzi'tu* with the same meaning. Its origin is lightness from *al-hazw*, which is swift killing; *hazi'a* and *yahza'u* means he died on the spot; and *tahza'u bihi naqatuhu* means his she-camel hastens with him and becomes light.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 15:**

﴿Allah mocks them﴾: i.e., He requites them for their mockery. The recompense for it is named by its name, just as the recompense for an evil deed is called an evil deed. This is either for *al-mushakalah* (consonance in wording, the same word being used for a related thing), or for *al-muqaranah* (the accompaniment in existence). Or the harmful consequence of the mockery returns upon them, so that He is as one who mocks them. Or He inflicts upon them the abasement and humiliation that is the necessary result of mockery. Or He treats them as one who mocks them. In this world, this is by applying to them the rulings of the Muslims, by *istidraj* (gradual leading on) through reprieve, and by increasing their blessings while they persist in their transgression. In the Hereafter, it is by what is related: a door to the Garden is opened for them, so they hasten towards it, and when they reach it, the door is shut against them. This is His saying (exalted is He): ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾. It was phrased as a new sentence (*isti'naf*) to signal that they had gone to such an extreme in mocking the believers that its vileness became apparent to the listeners and it weighed so heavily upon them that it compelled them to say: "What is the fate of these people? What is the outcome of their condition?" In this there is also the indication that He (exalted is He) is the One who takes charge of their affair and does not need to oppose them with the like of their conduct, and that He mocks them with a more eloquent mockery, the mockery of which is not, in His estimation, of the kind of mockery, since He inflicts upon them punishment and brings upon them abasement and humiliation beyond description. The choice of the form of the imperfect (*al-istiqbal*) indicates renewal and continuity, as His saying (exalted is He, who is Mighty and speaks) expresses: ﴿Do they not see that they are tested once or twice every year?﴾ And they were not, for most of the time, free from the tearing of veils, the uncovering of secrets, the descent of revelation concerning them, and the sense of fear of that, as His saying (Mighty and Majestic is He) indicates: ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down upon them informing them of what is in their hearts. Say: "Mock on; surely Allah will bring forth what you fear."﴾

﴿And He extends them﴾: i.e., He increases them and strengthens them, from "madda al-jaysh" (the army was reinforced) and "amaddahu" (he supplied it) when he increases it and strengthens it. From this comes: "I replenished the inkwell (*maddat al-dawah*) and the lamp (*al-siraj*)" when I supplied them with ink and oil. The choice of this verb over "yazidu-hum" (increases them) is to signal that this is contingent upon their own poor choice, since it is only realised in the case of seeking supply (*al-istimdad*) and what is similar to it of the need that calls for it, as in the examples mentioned. It has been read as "yumiddu-hum" from *al-imdad* (supplying), and this is explicit that the well-known reading is not from *madd* (extension) in the sense of lengthening one's life. Moreover, the verb is used with the preposition *lam*, like *al-imla'* (dictation), as He (exalted is He) said: ﴿And We extend for him of the punishment an extension﴾. The omission of the preposition and the attachment of the verb directly to the pronoun, contrary to the original usage, is not resorted to except with evidence.

﴿in their transgression﴾: it is connected to "yamuddu-hum" (He extends them). *Al-tughyan* is exceeding the limit in every matter, and what is meant is their excess in insolence and their extremism in disbelief. It has also been read with a kasra on the *ta'* (*tughyan*), and this is a dialect form of it, like *liqyan*, a dialect form of *luqyan*. The attribution of it to them indicates that it is specific to them, and it confirms what was pointed out concerning the extension being consequent upon their poor choice.

﴿they wander blindly﴾: it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in the accusative or genitive position, since the noun it is attached to is a verbal noun (*masdar*), so it is in the nominative in terms of its ruling. *Al-'amah* in insight is like blindness in sight, and it is bewilderment and hesitation, to the extent that one does not know where to turn. The attribution of this extension to Allah (exalted is He), together with its attribution in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And their brothers extend them in error﴾, confirms the principle of the People of Truth (*ahl al-Haqq*) that all things are ultimately traced to Him (glorified is He) in terms of creation, although the actions of servants are attributed to them in terms of acquisition (*al-kasb*). As for the Mu'tazilah, when it became impossible for them to keep the noble text on its course, they turned to the byways of interpretation. First, they replied that when they persisted in their disbelief, Allah (exalted is He) forsook them and withheld His favours from them, so the rust (*al-rayn*) in their hearts increased, and this was called an extension in transgression, and therefore its causing was attributed to Him (exalted is He). Thus there is a linguistic metaphor (*majaz lughawi*) in the word, and a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*) in the attribution, because it is the attribution of the act to the one who causes it. Its real agent is the disbelievers. Second, they said that what is meant by extension in transgression is the abandonment of compulsion and obstruction towards faith, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾. So the metaphor is in the predicate only. Third, they said that what is meant is its literal meaning, which is the act of Satan, but it was attributed to Him (glorified is He) metaphorically, because it occurs through His enabling and empowering.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 16:

﴿Those﴾: a demonstrative referring to the people mentioned earlier, on account of their being characterized by the abominable attributes mentioned, which distinguish them from others in the most complete way, such that they become as if they were present, witnessing what they are upon. The sense of distance in it indicates the remoteness of their station in evil and the badness of their condition. Its position is nominative, as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is His (exalted) saying: ﴿who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾. The sentence is brought to confirm what precedes it and to explain the completeness of their ignorance regarding the sayings and deeds related of them, by showing the extreme ugliness of these and depicting them in a form that one with even the slightest discernment would hardly practise, let alone rational people.

"Error" (ḍalāla) is deviation from the straight course, and "guidance" (hudā) is turning toward it. The first has been used metaphorically for swerving from what is correct in religion, and the second for remaining firm upon it. "Buying" (ishtirā') is exchanging a commodity for a price, i.e. taking it in return for that price, not paying it in order to obtain the commodity, as some have said, although it entails that. The essential notion in the contract of purchase is acquisition, not relinquishment, which is what is essential in the contract of sale. Then it was used metaphorically for taking something by giving what is in one's hand, whether each of the two is a concrete thing or an abstract meaning, and not for turning away from what is in one's hand while thereby obtaining something else, as some have said, although that entails it, for the reason whose secret has passed. From this is his saying:

I took by the forelock a bald head,
and by the bright, gleaming front teeth, the worn ones;
and by the long life, a short one,
as the Muslim bought (with it) when he became a Christian.

So "buying error with guidance" is metaphor for taking error as a substitute for it, a taking governed by desire for it and turning away from guidance. Since this requires that what functions as the price be already in the possession of the disbelievers before the contract, and what functions as the goods not be in their possession at that time, as is the case in the verse, and there is no doubt that they were far from guidance, constantly persisting in error, the context requires establishing what functions as the two counter-values. So we say, and with God is success: the object of the buying here is not the genus of error, encompassing all kinds of disbelievers, such that it would be present for them beforehand. Rather it is its complete particular form peculiar to these people, and the article is for definiteness, namely their blindness combined with being prolonged in transgression, which is consequent upon the evil deeds related of them. This arises for them only when there is despair of their being guided and a seal is set upon their hearts. Likewise, what is in the place of the price is not guidance itself, but full capacity for it, through the mutual support of causes, and the preliminaries entailing it are taken figuratively, as if it were guidance itself, by the common participation in bringing about benefit. There is no doubt that this degree of capacity was present for them through the manifest signs and overpowering miracles they witnessed from the Messenger (ﷺ), and through the admonitions of the believers they heard, among which is the prohibition on corruption on earth and the command to sound faith, which were related. They cast these behind their backs and took in their place the enormous error, which is blindness in the bewilderment of transgression. Taking guidance to mean the original innate nature present in everyone is rejected, because its loss is not peculiar to these people. And if it is taken to mean the complete loss reaching the point of the seal upon the hearts peculiar to them (p-49), then the loss of it alone is not as shameful as losing it together with its supports, both rational and transmitted. Moreover, that would lead to the mention of what has been detailed from the beginning of the surah up to here being wasted. Even more remote is taking the buying of error with guidance as merely preferring it over guidance, without regard to its being in their hands, on the basis that it is used loosely for preferring one of two things that are both in a position of honour over the other. For this, despite being entirely devoid of the aforementioned features, disrupts the splendour of the following *tarshīḥ*. This is when the stated buying is taken as an expression for their previous dealings related above, which is the most suitable with the harmony of the parts of the noble composition. But if it is taken as an expression for another of their offences, then guidance means what they possessed of knowing the truth of the Prophet's (ﷺ) prophethood and the reality of his religion, through what they saw of his descriptions in the Torah, and they were certain of it, to the extent that they would seek victory through him against the polytheists, saying: "O God, help us through the Prophet sent at the end of time, whose description we find in the Torah." And they would say to them: "The time of a prophet who will come confirming what we have said has drawn near, and we will kill you with him as the killing of ʿĀd and Iram." So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in him, as will come. There is no room for taking guidance to mean what they used to display when meeting the believers, for that is a doubled error.

﴿So their commerce did not profit﴾: a conjunction upon the relative clause, within its scope. The fa' indicates that the content follows from it. "Commerce" (tijāra) is the trade of merchants, which is engaging in buying and selling to obtain profit, that is, the surplus over the capital. One says: "So-and-so profited in his commerce," meaning he gained and obtained profit. Attributing its absence, which is a figure for loss, to the commerce itself, while it belongs to its owners, is based on the extension grounded in the connection between them. Its purpose is to intensify their ruin, because it implies the abundance and comprehensiveness of the loss, which entails its spreading to whatever is connected to them. Mentioning these two right after the buying, which is used metaphorically for the stated exchange, is a *tarshīḥ* for the metaphor, and a depiction of the benefits of guidance they have lost in the form of the loss of commerce, which everyone shuns, for the sake of completeness in ruin and regret. That commerce itself is a metaphor for their immersion in what they are upon, preferring error over guidance and habituating themselves to it, does not conflict with this, indicating that this has become a firmly rooted craft for them. For it is not essential to *tarshīḥ* that what remains on the literal sense and follows the metaphor be intended only to strengthen it, as in your saying: "I saw a lion with full claws," where you intend by "claws" nothing but to increase the depiction of the brave man as a complete lion, without intending another meaning by the word "claws." Indeed it may be borrowed from a term suited to the original metaphor, for a term suited to the thing it stands for, and yet it is still a *tarshīḥ* of the root metaphor, as in his saying:

When I saw the vulture overpower the son of Da'ya,
and nested in its two nests, my chest surged for him.

Here the word "nests" (wakrayn), though borrowed from its real meaning, which is a place a bird makes for hatching, is a *tarshīḥ* in terms of its original meaning for the metaphor of "vulture" for white hair and "son of Da'ya" for black hair, meaning the two sides of the head.
