Likewise the word "nesting" (ta'shīsh), though borrowed for continuous settling and descent, is a *tarshīḥ* for those two metaphors in the stated respect.

It is read "tijārātuhum" (their commerces), and its plurality corresponds to the plurality of those to whom it is attributed. ﴿And they were not guided﴾: that is, to the paths of commerce. For the aim of commerce is the preservation of the capital together with gaining profit. If profit is lost in one deal, it may perhaps be made up in another, since the principal remains. But the total destruction of everything is certainly not of the nature of commerce. Thus these people, whose capital was guidance, exchanged it for error, and so they lost both aims, and remained failed, losers, distant by a thousand stages from the path of commerce. The sentence therefore returns to the *tarshīḥ*, joined to what precedes it, sharing with it the ordering upon the buying mentioned (p-50). It is preferable to join it to "they bought," etc.

﴿مَثَلُهُمْ﴾: an added unveiling of their condition, and a depiction of it. The depiction is after the depiction of what leads to loss in terms of its outcome, by the form of what leads to loss in terms of its essence, in order to magnify it and make its horror clear. For the parable (tamthil) is the most subtle means to bring the imagination under the command of the intellect and to bring it down from its position of defiance against the intellect, and the most powerful means to make the ignorant and dull understand and to subdue the wild rage of the stubborn and the proud. How could it not be so? It lifts the veil from the faces of hidden intelligibles, brings them forth in the display of clear sensible things, shows the reprehensible in the form of the commendable, and reveals the savage in the guise of the familiar. The word "mathal" (parable) originally means "mithl" (likeness) and "naẓīr" (equivalent). It is said "mithl," "mathal," and "mathīl," like "shibh," "shabah," and "shabīh." Then it was applied to a saying that circulates, whose point of application is compared with its source. Since it is nothing but a wondrous saying, with a strangeness that makes it worthy of being carried through the lands and deserving of acceptance among every present and desert dweller, it is borrowed for every state, attribute, or story that has a wondrous importance and a strange weight, without any comparison being noticed between it and something else. From this is His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلِلَّهِ المَثَلُ الأعْلى﴾ (And to God belongs the highest description), that is, the attribute that has a great importance and a noble weight. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿مَثَلُ الجَنَّةِ الَّتِي وُعِدَ المُتَّقُونَ﴾ (The description of the Garden promised to the God-fearing), that is, its wondrous story.

﴿كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي﴾: that is, "like those who" (alladhī, singular relative, used for the plural), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَخُضْتُمْ كالَّذِي خاضُوا﴾ (and you plunged in as those who plunged in). Except that the pronoun is made singular in His saying: ﴿اسْتَوْقَدَ نارًا﴾ (he kindled a fire), with regard to the image. This is permissible even though it is not permissible to place the singular in the position of the plural, because what is intended by the description is the clause that falls as its relative clause, not the word itself. It is merely a link for describing the definite nouns by it. Also, because it deserves lightening, since it is lengthened by its relative clause, and therefore it was emphasized: its "yā'" was deleted, then its kasra, then it was limited to the "lām" in the forms of the active and passive participles. Also, because it is not a complete noun but is like a part of itself, its proper form is that it should be pluralized and that the singular and the plural should be the same in it, as is the case with its sister words. "Alladhīna" is not its sound plural; rather the "nūn" in it is an added letter to indicate an increase in meaning. For this reason it always comes with "yā'," according to the eloquent dialect. Or it is intended as the genus of the kindler, or the group or the party that kindles. Fire is a subtle, luminous, hot, burning substance. Its derivation is from "nāra, yanūru," meaning to flee, because in it there is movement and agitation. "Istīqād" (kindling) is seeking its fuel, that is, its blazing and the rising of its flame. Its indefiniteness (nakīr) is for magnification (tafkhīm, expressing grandeur).

﴿فَلَمّا أضاءَتْ ما حَوْلَهُ﴾ (When it illuminated what was around him): "ilā'" (illumination) is the excess of lighting, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿هُوَ الَّذِي جَعَلَ الشَّمْسَ ضِياءً والقَمَرَ نُورًا﴾ (It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light). It comes transitively and intransitively. The "fā'" indicates that it is consequent upon the kindling; that is, "when the fire illuminated what was around the kindler," or "when what was around him was illuminated." The feminine is because it refers to places and things. Or: the fire itself illuminated what was around it, and that is a place-adverb for the shining of the fire, placed in the position of the fire itself, not for itself. Or "mā" is an added particle and "ḥawlahu" is an adverb. The formation of "ḥawl" is for revolving, and the year is called "ḥawl" because it revolves.

﴿ذَهَبَ اللَّهُ بِنُورِهِمْ﴾ (God took away their light): "nūr" is the light of every luminous thing. Its derivation is from fire. The pronoun refers to "alladhī," and the plural is according to meaning. That is: God extinguished their fire, which is the source of their light. He attached the taking away to the light rather than to the fire itself, because the purpose of kindling is light, not warmth and the like, as His saying indicates: ﴿فَلَمّا أضاءَتْ﴾ (when it illuminated), where He did not say "when its blaze rose" or something similar. This clause is the answer to "mā" (the particle that introduced the conditional), or it is a resumptive sentence answering a questioner who says: "What is the matter with them, that their state resembles the state of one who kindled a fire that went out?" Or it is an explanatory substitution for the parabolic clause. The pronoun in both cases refers to the hypocrites. The answer is omitted, as in His saying: ﴿فَلَمّا ذَهَبُوا بِهِ﴾ (when they took him away), for brevity and for security from ambiguity. It is as if it was said: "When it illuminated what was around it, it died down, and they remained in darkness, groping, bewildered, failing after their struggle to kindle it." Attributing the taking away to God, Exalted is He, is either because everything is by His creation, or because the extinguishing occurred through a hidden cause, or a heavenly matter, such as a wind or rain, or it is for emphasis, as indicated by the transitivity of the verb with "bi" rather than with the hamza (of causation), because it contains the meaning of retaining and holding. It is said: "The sultan took his wealth," if he seized it. And what God, Exalted and Majestic, seizes and holds, no one can release after Him. For this reason, one turns from "ḍiyā'" (radiance), which is what the apparent sense requires, to "nūr" (light), because the going away of radiance may coexist with the remaining of light in general, since the absence of the strong does not necessitate the absence of the weak. What is meant is its complete removal, as His saying, Exalted is He, makes clear: ﴿وَتَرَكَهم في ظُلُماتٍ لا يُبْصِرُونَ﴾ (and left them in darkness, they do not see). For darkness, which is the absence of light, and the complete obliteration of it, especially when it is multiplied and piled up, one layer upon another, as indicated by the plural and the indefinite form used for magnification (tafkhīm), and what follows it in His saying: ﴿لا يُبْصِرُونَ﴾ (they do not see), is not realized except after no trace or vestige of light remains. Or the light meant is what God does not approve of, from the metaphorical fire, which is the fire of sedition and corruption, as in His saying: ﴿كُلَّما أوْقَدُوا نارًا لِلْحَرْبِ أطْفَأها اللَّهُ﴾ (Whenever they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it). Describing it with the illumination of what is around the kindler is by way of "tarshīḥ" (completing the metaphor with a supporting detail). Or it is the literal fire that the deviators kindle so that they may reach some sins through it, and be guided by it in the paths of mischief and corruption, and God extinguished it and frustrated their hopes. "Taraka," originally means "to cast away" and "to leave," and it has one object, so it was made to include the meaning of "to make" and it operates like the verbs of the heart. The poet said:

"So I left him as prey for the beasts, who gnaw at him,
devouring the beauty of his fingers and wrist."

"Ẓulmah" (darkness) is derived from their saying: "What prevented you (mā ẓalamaka) from doing such and such?" That is, what prevented you? Because it blocks sight and prevents it from seeing. It is read "fī ẓulumāt" with the "lām" sukūn, and "fī ẓulmah" in the singular. The object of "lā yubṣirūn" (they do not see) is of the type of what is left unstated, as if the verb were intransitive, and the meaning is that their strange condition, which is their purchase of error, which is an expression for the two darknesses of disbelief and hypocrisy, which entail the darkness of God's wrath and the darkness of the Day of Resurrection, ﴿يَوْمَ تَرى المُؤْمِنِينَ والمُؤْمِناتِ يَسْعى نُورُهم بَيْنَ أيْدِيهِمْ وبِأيْمانِهِمْ﴾ (On the Day you will see the believing men and believing women, their light running before them and on their right), and the darkness of everlasting punishment, in exchange for guidance, which is the innate light confirmed by what they witnessed of the proofs of truth, or by the guidance they had acquired from the Torah, as has been mentioned, is like the state of one who kindled a great fire, until he almost benefited from it, and then God extinguished it, and left him in terrible darkness, in which seeing is impossible.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 18:**

﴿Deaf, dumb, blind﴾: These are predicates (akhbar, sing. khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada’), which is the pronoun referring to the hypocrites. Alternatively, they are one predicate, according to the well-known interpretation, as in their saying: "This is sweet-sour" (hadha hulw hamid). Deafness (al-samam) is an affliction that prevents hearing. Its original meaning is hardness and the compacting of parts. From it come "the solid stone" (al-hajar al-asamm) and "the hard spear" (al-qanah al-samma'). The stopper of a bottle (simam al-qarurah) is its plug. The term was applied to the loss of the faculty of hearing, because its cause is the compacting of the inner ear canal (al-simakh) and the blocking of its openings, such that air can hardly enter it, and sound is produced by its vibration. Dumbness (al-bakam) is muteness. Blindness (al-'ama) is the absence of sight in that which is capable of seeing. They are described with these, despite the soundness of their well-known faculties, because when they stopped their ears from paying attention to the verses and the Wise Reminder recited to them, and refused to receive them with acceptance and to speak them with their tongues, and did not behold the manifest miracles that they witnessed at the hands of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and did not look upon the verses of monotheism placed in the horizons and in themselves with the eye of reflection, and persisted in that, to the point that there was no longer any possibility for them to refrain from it, they became like those who have wholly lost those faculties. This, according to the eloquent masters of rhetoric, is from the category of eloquent figurative expression (al-tamthil al-baligh), founded on forgetting the comparison (tanasi al-tashbih), as in the saying of one who said:

*He ascends until the ignorant one thinks*
*That he has some need in the sky.*

This is because what is implied in the structure is treated as if it were spoken, and it is not of the type of metaphor (isti'arah) in which the mention of the borrowed-for term is entirely omitted, even if there is no indication to direct it toward the literal meaning, as in the saying of Zuhayr:

*Near a lion, armed, thrust forward, having a mane,*
*Whose claws have not been trimmed.*

﴿So they do not return﴾: The fa’ (fa’) indicates that what follows is consequent upon what precedes it. That is: they, because of their being characterized by the attributes mentioned, do not return to the guidance which they abandoned and neglected, or away from the misguidance which they adopted. The verse is a result (natijah) of the figurative expression, serving to increase its terror and horror, for the utmost of the figurative expression is their remaining in immense darkness without touching upon the two faculties of hearing and speech, and with the faculty of sight being impaired. It has been said: the omitted pronoun and what follows it refer to the relative pronoun, in view of its meaning, like the preceding pronouns. Thus the noble verse is a completion (tatimmah) of the figurative expression and its perfection (takmil), in that what befell them is not merely the extinguishing of their fire and their remaining in thick, immense darkness, while the faculty of sight remains in its condition; rather, all their faculties became impaired, and they were characterized by those attributes in the manner of comparison (tashbih) or of literal description (haqiqah). So they remained motionless in their places, not returning, and not knowing whether they should advance or retreat, and how could they return to that from which they began? The shift to the nominal sentence (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah) serves to indicate the continuity of that state in them.

It was also read as "ṣummān bukman ‘umyan" (in the accusative). This is either for dispraise (al-dhamm), as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿the carrier of firewood﴾ (111:4), and the one singled out for dispraise is the hypocrites or those who kindled the fire. Or it is in the accusative of state (al-hal) from the pronoun in "tarakahum" (He left them), or from the nominative pronoun in "la yubsirun" (they do not see). Or it is in the accusative as an object (al-maf'uliyyah) of "tarakahum," and the two pronouns then refer to the ones who kindled the fire.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 19:**

﴿Or like a downpour﴾: This is a parable for their condition following the earlier parable, so that the explanation from it covers every minute and grand detail, and its due share of frightening and dreadful description is fulfilled. Their varied forms of disbelief and misguidance, and their shifting from one condition to another within them, deserve that parables be coined about their matter, that the reins of speech be let loose in their arena, that the tent-ropes of elaboration (*itnab*, expansive exposition) be extended to explain them, and that chapters and sections be devised for their sake. This is because every speech has a share of eloquence and a portion of strength and skill, and it is necessary that the due of each of the two situations, elaboration (*itnab*) and brevity (*ijaz*), be fulfilled in it. So what do you think of what is at the peak of inimitability in the Glorious Revelation? Indeed, in this parable the details of their crimes have been censured. It is a conjunction with the first, with the omission of a modifying word (*mudaf*) because of the pronouns that follow, which call for it. That is: "Like the likeness of people of a downpour." The word "or" (*aw*) signifies that the two stories are equal in being independently sufficient for the aspect of comparison, and in the validity of the parable with each of them individually and with both together.

And "*al-sayyib*" (the downpour) is on the pattern *fay'il*, from *al-sawb*, which is the descent that has impact and effect. It is applied to rain and to clouds. Al-Shammakh said:

*"Its marks were effaced by the weaving of the south wind together with the east wind, and a dark, low-hanging cloud, true in its promise, a downpour."*

Probably the first meaning is what is intended here, because it implies the second. Its being indefinite is because a kind of it that is severe and terrifying is meant by it, like the fire in the first parable. Its intensity is reinforced by the emphases contained in it from the aspect of its first root, namely the emphatic *ṣād*, the doubled *yā'*, and the strong *bā'*, and from the aspect of its second root, namely *al-sawb*, which indicates intensity of pouring, and from the aspect of its structure which indicates persistence. It has also been read as "*ka-ṣā'ib*" (like a striking one).

﴿from the sky﴾: It is connected to "*ṣayyib*" (downpour), or to an omitted word that serves as its modifier. By "the sky" is meant this canopy. Originally it is everything that is above you of a roof or the like. It is reported from al-Hasan that it is a restrained wave, that is, held back from flowing by the power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Its definiteness is to indicate that the emergence of the downpour is not from a single horizon, for each horizon of its horizons, that is, everything encompassed by each horizon of it, is a separate sky. The poet said:

*"...and from the distance of a land between us and a sky."*

Just as each layer of its layers is a sky. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And He revealed in each sky its command﴾. The meaning is that it is a general downpour, descending from an enveloping cloud, seizing the horizons. It has been said that by "the sky" is meant the cloud, and the *lām* is for defining the reality.

﴿in it are darknesses﴾: That is, kinds of them. These are: the darkness of its density and its thickening through the successive drops; the darkness of the shade of the cloud that accompanies it, the black, enveloping cloud seizing the horizons; together with the darkness of the night. He made it the locus of them, although some of them belong to something else, like the two darknesses of the cloud and the night, because they have been made to be among the consequences of its darkness, as an exaggeration of its intensity and an amplification of its matter, and an indication that it is of such severity and terror that its darkness overwhelms the darknesses of the night and the cloud. This is the secret of not making "darknesses" the principal (*al-asl*) that the rest follow, along with the clear indication of its being a container for all of them. For if it had been said: "Or like darknesses in which is a downpour," and so on, it would not have indicated that the downpour has a darkness peculiar to itself, let alone that its darkness predominates over the others.

﴿and thunder﴾: It is a sound heard from the cloud. It is well known that it arises from the clashing of the bodies of clouds against one another, or from the tearing of some of them from others, when they are agitated by the winds driving them with violent driving.

﴿and lightning﴾: It is what gleams from the cloud, from "*baraqa al-shay'u bariqan*," meaning "it gleamed." Both are originally verbal nouns, and for that reason neither is pluralized. Their being in the downpour is with regard to their being in its upper part and its place of pouring, and the arrival of their effect to it, and their being in the darknesses that exist in it. The nunation in all of them is for magnification and dread, as if it were said: "In it are intense, pitch-black darknesses, and a crashing thunder, and a snatching lightning." The nominative case of all of them is by the adverbial phrase as the subject, since the condition of operation is established by agreement. It has also been said that they are in the nominative as the subject-matter (*mubtada'*). The clause is either a modifier of "*ṣayyib*" or a circumstantial clause (*ḥal*) from it, since it is specified by the modifier, or by the operation on what follows it of the prepositional phrase, or of the pronoun hidden in the first adverbial phrase, on the assumption that it is a modifier of "*ṣayyib*."

The pronouns in the statement of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿they put their fingers into their ears﴾ refer to the omitted noun whose place is taken by the noun in the genitive, for its meaning remains even though its wording is dropped, relying on the indication, as in His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And how many a city We destroyed, so Our punishment came upon it by night or while they were resting at midday﴾. For the pronoun refers to the people, understood from the city that has taken their place. Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

*"They give to drink whoever comes to al-Barisa, of them, from the Barada, which is mixed with the pure wine."*

For the masculine form of the hidden pronoun in "*yusaffaq*" (is mixed) refers to the water attached to Barada; otherwise it would have been feminine necessarily. And out of preference for making what indicates the continuance of the connection and the persistence of the settling apply to the entering, which only indicates the mere movement from outside to inside, for the sake of exaggeration in explaining the blocking of the ears in terms of time, just as the mention of "fingers" instead of "fingertips" is for completeness in explaining their blocking in terms of the whole, as if they blocked them with their entirety, not merely with their fingertips, as is customary. It is also possible that this is an allusion to the perfection of their bewilderment, the extremity of their astonishment, and their reaching a point where they are not guided to using their limbs in the customary manner. Likewise the situation regarding not specifying the usual finger, namely the index finger. It has been said that this is for observing good manners (*adab*).

The clause is a resumption with no place in grammatical construction (*i'rab*), built on a question arising from the speech, as if it were said when describing their dreadful conditions: "So what do they do amid that severity?" Then it was said: "They put..." etc.

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿because of the thunderbolts﴾: It is connected to "they put," that is, for the sake of the thunderbolts accompanying the thunder, from the saying: "He gave him to drink from the *ʻaymah*" (a sickness of thirst). The thunderbolt is a crash of terrible thunder, with which a burst of fire descends that does not pass over anything without consuming it, from "*al-ṣa'q*," which is intensity of sound. Its form is either an adjective for the crash of thunder, or for the thunder, and the *tā'* is for intensification, as in the narration; or it is a verbal noun like "*al-'āfiyah*." It is sometimes applied to every terrifying thing heard or seen. It is said: "The thunderbolt struck him" (*ṣa'aqathu al-ṣā'iqah*), if it destroyed him by burning or by the intensity of the sound. The blocking of the ears benefits only on the second assumption, not the first. It has also been read as "*mina al-ṣawāqi'*" (from the thunderbolts), and this is not a transposition from "*al-ṣawā'iq*," since both patterns are equal in use. It is said: "The rooster crowed" (*ṣaqa'a al-dik*), and "*khaṭīb miṣqa'*," meaning one who raises his voice loudly in his sermon.

﴿because of the fear of death﴾: It is in the accusative governed by "they put," as a cause (*'illah*), even though it is definite by annexation, like his statement:

*"I forgive the shameful deeds of the noble, storing them up, and I overlook the abuse of the base, out of generosity."*

There is no harm in there being more than one object of cause, for the act may be caused by various causes. It has been said that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning: they are wary with a wariness like the wariness of death. "*Al-ḥadhar*" and "*al-ḥidhār*" mean intense fear. It has been read as "*ḥidhāra al-mawt*." Death is the cessation of life. It has been said that it is an accident opposed to it, based on His statement, the Exalted: ﴿He created death and life﴾. This was refuted on the grounds that "creation" means "decree," and annihilation is also a decree.

﴿And Allah encompasses the disbelievers﴾: That is, they cannot escape Him, just as the encompassed cannot escape the encompassing. He likened the inclusion of His power over them, and the enfolding of His dominion upon them, to the encompassing of the encompasser over what it encompasses, in the impossibility of escape. Or He likened the configuration abstracted from His affairs with them to the configuration abstracted from the conditions of the encompasser with the encompassed. So the metaphor based on the first comparison is a subordinate metaphor in the attribute, branching from the metaphor contained in its verbal noun. The one based on the second is an allegorical representation (*tamthiliyyah*), in which only the core element is mentioned from the side of the thing likened, namely the encompassing, from which the configuration to be likened is abstracted. The remainder is implied through imagined expressions, by which the composition required in the allegory is achieved, as its explanation has already passed in His statement, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Allah has sealed their hearts﴾. The clause is parenthetical, alerting that what they did of blocking their ears with their fingers does not avail them anything, for decree is not repelled by caution, and devices do not turn back the might of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The benefit of placing "the disbelievers" in the position of the pronoun referring to the people of the downpour is to indicate that the dreadful matters that befell them, described here, are because of their disbelief, in the manner of His statement, the Exalted: ﴿Like the likeness of a wind in which is a bitter cold, which struck the tilth of a people who had wronged themselves, and destroyed it﴾, for destruction arising from wrath is more severe. It has been said that this parenthetical clause is among the circumstances of the thing likened, on the basis that by "the disbelievers" are meant the hypocrites; by it He indicated that there is no one to repel them from the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, in this world and the Hereafter. It was placed in the middle of the circumstances of the thing likened, although the analogy would require placing it before or after them, in order to show the utmost care and the extreme concern with the matter of the thing likened.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 20 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿يَكادُ البَرْقُ﴾: This is another resumptive sentence (*istiʾnaf*, a sentence that begins a new point without grammatical connection to what precedes it). It answers an implied question, as if it were said: "What is their condition with that lightning?" So it is said: ﴿The lightning almost snatches away their sight﴾, meaning it steals and seizes it swiftly. *Kāda* ("to almost") is one of the verbs of approximation (*afʿāl al-muqārabah*). It is set for the approach of an event to existence, when its causes are gathered and its beginnings reinforce one another, but the event has not yet occurred, either because a condition is missing or because an obstacle has arisen. Its predicate (*khabar*) is only ever a present-tense verb (*muḍāriʿ*) without *anna*. Its coming as a plain noun is rare, as in the line of verse:

*"So I returned to understanding, though I had almost not returned."*

Likewise it may come with *anna*, analogizing it to *ʿasā* ("perhaps"), as in the words of Ru'bah:

*"It has almost, from the long wear of time, been effaced."*

Just as *anna* may be elided after it, so too *kāda* may be treated as analogous to *ʿasā* because of their shared connection in the notion of approximation. It has none of the element of the performative (*inshāʾiyyah*) that *ʿasā* has.

It is read as *yakhṭifu* (with the *ṭāʾ* vowelled with kasra), *yakhtaṭifu*, and *yakhaṭṭafu* (with fatḥah on the *yāʾ* and *khāʾ*, moving the fatḥah of the *tāʾ* to the *khāʾ* and assimilating it into the *ṭāʾ*), and *yikhiṭṭafu* (with kasra on both), in order to match the vowel of the *yāʾ* and *khāʾ*. Also read *yakhaṭṭafu* from the *tafʿīl* form, and *yatakhaṭṭafu*, from His words (exalted is He): ﴿and people are snatched away from around them﴾.

﴿كُلَّما أضاءَ لَهُمْ﴾: *Kull* is an adverb of time (*ẓarf*), and *mā* is a verbal-source particle (*maṣdariyyah*), with the time-noun omitted, meaning: "every time of illumination." It is also said that *mā* is an indefinite qualified noun (*nakirah mawṣūfah*), meaning "time," with the returning pronoun omitted, meaning: "every time it lit up for them within." The governing element of *kullamā* is its response (*jawāb*). This is a third resumptive sentence, as if it were said: "What do they do amid that terror? Do they do with their eyes what they did with their ears, or not?" So it is said: whenever the lightning illuminates for them a path and a way (on the view that *aḍāʾa* is transitive and its object is omitted), or whenever it flashes for them (on the view that it is intransitive, supported by the reading *kullamā ḍāʾa*), ﴿they walk in it﴾, that is, in that path, or in the place where its light falls, ﴿a few steps,﴾ while fearing that their sight will be snatched away. The preference for *mashy* (walking) over what is above it, such as running or dashing, indicates that they are unable to do either.

﴿وَإذا أظْلَمَ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾: That is, the lightning became hidden and concealed. The verb *aẓlama* (intransitive in form) is used, but since darkness revolves around the concealment of the lightning, it is attributed to it figuratively (*majāz*), to establish the intended emphasis on the causes of their confusion. It has also been permitted that it is transitive, transferred from *ẓalama al-layl* ("the night became dark"). From this is what Abu Tammam said:

*"They two darkened my two states, then they revealed, after their darkness, the face of a beardless young man turned grey."*

This is supported by the reading *uẓlima* (in the passive voice).

﴿قامُوا﴾: That is, they stood still in their places, in the same state they had been in, bewildered, watching for another flash in hope that they may reach the destination, or seek refuge in a shelter that protects them. The use of *kullamā* with illumination and *idhā* with darkness is to signal that they are eager to walk and wait for what enables it, so whenever they find an opportunity they seize it. Standing still is not like this. In it is an indication of complete bewilderment and the scattering of reason beyond description.

﴿وَلَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ لَذَهَبَ بِسَمْعِهِمْ وأبْصارِهِمْ﴾: The word *law* links the occurrence of a past matter, which is the response (*jazāʾ*), to the occurrence of a supposed matter in it, which is the condition (*sharṭ*), because of the actual or claimed mutual dependence between them. From the nature of the condition being supposed is that it indicates its definite non-occurrence. Whoever disputes this is being obstinate. As for whether it indicates the non-occurrence of the response, it has been said yes and it has been said otherwise. The truth from which there is no escape is this: if the dependence between them, whether total or partial, is what the ruling is built upon, then it indicates it by means of its conventional meaning without doubt, since the non-existence of the cause necessitates the non-existence of the effect. As for the case of total dependence, as in His words (exalted is He): ﴿If He had willed, He would have guided you all﴾, and your saying: "If you had come to me, I would have honoured you," it is evident, because the existence of the will is actually a cause for the existence of guidance, and the existence of coming is claimed to be a cause for the existence of honouring. Both have been negated by the supposition, so their effects are necessarily negated. Then the speech may be used to explain the negation of the response by the negation of the condition, as in the two examples mentioned, and this is the common usage of the particle *law*. For this reason it has been said that it indicates the impossibility of the second because of the impossibility of the first. It may also be used to argue from the negation of the second, because it is evident, or accepted, in order to show the first, because it is hidden, or disputed, as in His words (glorified is He): ﴿If there had been in them gods other than God, they would both have been corrupted﴾, and in His words (exalted is He): ﴿If it had been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾. The corruption of the two heavens and the earth is necessarily tied to the plurality of gods in reality, and the non-precedence of the believers to faith is necessarily tied to its goodness, according to the claim of the disbelievers. There is no doubt about the negation of the two necessary consequences, so the negation of the two conditions is established: in reality for the first, and as a false claim for the second, since the negation of the consequence necessitates the negation of the antecedent. However, this is not by way of external causation, as in the first two examples, but by way of rational inference, which goes back to the causation of knowing the negation of the second for knowing the negation of the first. Whoever is not alert to this thinks that the first is negated because of the negation of the second.

As for partial dependence, as in your saying: "If the sun had risen, light would have existed," the response tied to the condition, which is the sun's rising, is not the existence of any light at all, such as moonlight, which coexists with the non-rising, for example. Rather it is the existence of the specific light arising from the rising, and there is no doubt about its negation with the negation of the rising. This applies when the ruling is built upon the consideration of the dependence. But if it is built upon its absence, then either it is considered that there is the realisation of another dependence for it, or not. If it is considered, then the indication follows the state of that dependence. If there is an incompatibility between it and the negation of the first, then the indication is determined, as when you say: "If the sun had not risen, light would have existed." The existence of light, although it is formally tied to the non-rising, is in reality by another cause, necessarily so, because the non-rising, in and of itself, is not in reality a dependence for the existence of light. It was placed in the position of a dependence only because it reveals the realisation of another dependence for it. So it is as if it were said: "If the sun had not risen, light would have existed by another cause, such as the moon, for example." There is no doubt that this response is negated when the condition is negated, because the existence of moonlight at sunrise is impossible. If there is no incompatibility between them, then the absence of indication is determined, as in his words, peace be upon him, concerning the daughter of Abu Salamah: "If she had not been my stepdaughter in my care, she would not have been lawful to me; she is the daughter of my brother through fosterage." The dependence considered within the condition, namely her being the daughter of his brother through fosterage, is not incompatible with the negation of what he is about, namely her being his stepdaughter, peace be upon him. Rather it coexists with it, and it necessarily entails the coexistence of their two effects: the prohibition arising from her being his stepdaughter, and the prohibition arising from her being the daughter of his brother through fosterage. If no realisation of another dependence is considered there, but the ruling is built upon the consideration of its absence, then the speech does not indicate that at all. How could it not? Since the context of the speech at that point is to demonstrate the establishment of the response in every state, by tying it to what contradicts it, so that its establishment may be known when what does not contradict it occurs, a fortiori. As in His words (mighty and majestic is He): ﴿Say: If you possessed the treasuries of the mercy of my Lord, you would have held them back for fear of spending﴾, and His words, peace be upon him: "If faith were in the Pleiades, men from Persia would have attained it." And the words of ʿAli, may God be pleased with him: "If the veil were lifted, I would not have increased in certainty." Here the aforementioned responses are tied to what contradicts them and calls for their opposites, as a declaration that they are in themselves such that their establishment is necessary even with the supposed negation of their causes, or the realisation of the causes of their negation. How much more so when it is not like this, in the manner of the concessive *law* (*law al-waṣliyyah*), as in His words (exalted is He): ﴿Its oil would almost give light even if no fire touched it﴾. It has detailed and branching explanations, which we have set down in our commentary on His words (exalted is He): ﴿He said: Even if we were unwilling?﴾. Also the words of ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him: "Suhayb is an excellent servant; if he did not fear God, he would not disobey Him." If this is taken to tie the non-disobedience, within the absence of fear, to another dependence, such as modesty, veneration, and others which coexist with fear, then it is of the kind of the hadith about the daughter of Abu Salamah. If it is taken to show the impossibility of his disobedience as an emphasis, then it is of this kind too.

The noble verse is given in the common usage, conveying the utmost gravity of their condition and the extreme terror of the hardships that befell them, and that they have reached such severity that, if God's will (exalted is He) were to be attached to removing their senses, their senses would be removed, because what requires it is fully realised.

It has been said that the word *law* here serves to link its response to its condition, without indicating the negation of one because of the negation of the other, in the manner of the word *in* ("if"). The object of the will is omitted, following the established rule: when it occurs as a condition and its object is what the response guarantees, it is hardly ever mentioned, unless it is something strange, as in the line:

*"If I willed to weep blood for him, I would have wept, but the courtyard of patience is wider."*

That is, if He willed to take away their hearing and sight, He would have done so, but He did not will it, because of the wisdom and interests it requires. It is read *la-adhhaba bi-asmāʿihim* ("He would have taken away their hearing"), with the added *bāʾ*, as in His words (exalted is He): ﴿and do not cast yourselves by your own hands into destruction﴾. The singular form in the well-known reading is because *samʿ* (hearing) is originally a verbal noun.

The conditional sentence is coordinated with what precedes it of the resumptive sentences. It has been said that it is coordinated with *kullamā aḍāʾa* and so on.

His words (exalted is He): ﴿Indeed God is over all things capable﴾ are a causal justification for the conditional sentence and a confirmation of its content, which speaks of His power (exalted is He) to remove their senses by way of demonstrative proof. The word *shayʾ* ("thing"), according to its lexical concept, applies to everything that can be known and spoken of, whatever it is. Originally it is the verbal noun of *shāʾa* (to will), and it was applied to the object of will, relying on the consideration that the will relates to it, in terms of knowledge and speaking about it only. Here it has been specified as the possible, whether existent or non-existent, because the power relates to it specifically, since power is an expression for the ability to bring into existence and to annihilate, which are specific to it. It has been said that power is an attribute that requires that ability. The *qādir* (capable) is the one who, if he wills, acts, and if he does not will, does not act. The *qadīr* (all-capable) is the one who accomplishes everything he wills, as he wills. For this reason it is not attributed to anyone other than the Creator, may His majesty be exalted.

The meaning of His power (exalted is He) over the possible existent while it exists is that if He wills its continued existence, He continues it, for the cause of existence is the cause of continuance. This has been verified in our explanation of His words (exalted is He): ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾. If He wills its annihilation, He annihilates it. The meaning of His power over the non-existent while it is non-existent is that if He wills to bring it into existence, He brings it into existence, and if He does not will, He does not bring it into existence.

It has been said that human power is a state by which one is able to do and to refrain from doing, while God's power (exalted is He) is an expression for the negation of incapacity. The derivation of *qudrah* (power) is from *qadr* (measure), because the capable one performs the act according to the measure his will requires, or according to the measure of his strength. In this is evidence that what the servant is able to do is, in reality, something God (exalted is He) is able to do, because it is a thing, and every thing is within God's power (exalted is He).

Know that each of the two similes, although it may be of the kind of the detached simile (*tamthīl al-mufarraq*), as in the line:

*"As if the hearts of birds, moist and dry, beside their nest are the ʿunnāb fruit and the decayed dried fig."*

...by likening the hypocrites, in the first parable, to those who kindle a fire; their innate guidance (al-hudā al-fiṭrī) to the fire; their support for it through the evidences they witnessed of its kindling; their full capacity to benefit from it by its lighting what is around them; its removal through the taking away of the fiery light; and the seizing of misguidance by its opposite, their being enveloped in dense darkness and remaining in it. And they are likened, in the second parable, to the wayfarers; and the Qur'an, with what it contains of knowledge and insights upon which eternal life depends, to the downpour, which is the cause of earthly life; and the distresses and sorrows that befall them with its descent; and the darkening of their minds by the darknesses; and what it contains of promise and threat, to the thunder and lightning; and their deafness to what strikes their ears of threat, by the condition of one whom thunder and lightning terrify, so that he fears its thunderbolts and stops his ears against them, and has no escape from them; and their agitation at what glimmers for them of right guidance that they perceive, or of provision that they secure, by their walking in the place where the lightning's light falls, whenever it lights up for them; and their bewilderment in their affair when a calamity befalls them, by their standing still when it grows dark upon them. However, applying the parable as a compound parable (al-tamthīl al-murakkab), in which it is not required that each individual element on one side be likened to a single individual element on the other side in detail, but rather a configuration (hay'a) is abstracted from the elements on the side of the likened (al-mushabbah) and is likened to another configuration abstracted from the elements on the side of the likened-to (al-mushabbah bihi), such that a distinct configuration is abstracted from the hypocrites and their states as detailed in each of the two parables, and a separate configuration is abstracted from each of the fire-kindlers and the people of the downpour and their narrated states, then likening each of the first two to what corresponds to it from the latter two is what the eloquence of the revelation requires and what the grandeur of its sublime matter calls for; because it includes the first likeness in summary, together with an additional matter, namely the likeness of the configuration, and its indication that the gathering of those elements results in a wondrous configuration, truly worthy of being a parable in strangeness.

(p-58) ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾: After Allah (Exalted) mentioned the high rank of His Noble Book, and how people divided into three groups concerning it, (a group) believing in it and keeping to its laws and rulings, (a group) disbelieving in it and casting it behind their backs openly and in opposition, and another wavering between the two through deceit and hypocrisy, and after He described each group with its own qualities and conditions and explained what awaits them as their final destination and outcome, He turned to them with direct address in the manner of *iltifat* (the shift from third person to second person), to rouse them to listen, to turn their hearts toward receiving (the message), and to soften for them the burden of worship with the pleasure of being addressed directly. So He commanded them all to worship Him and forbade them from associating anything with Him.

"Yā" (O) is a particle set for calling someone distant, though it may be used for someone near, treating him as if he were distant. This is either out of reverence, as in the words of the supplicant, "O Allah" and "O my Lord," though He is closer to him than his jugular vein, or to make the speaker belittle himself and consider himself unworthy of the gatherings of nearness and the stations of those brought close (to Allah). Or it is to alert the one addressed to his heedlessness and poor understanding. It may also be intended to alert that what follows is a grave matter that deserves attention.

"Ayyu" (which) is an ambiguous noun, used as a bridge to call one who is defined by the article "al-" (the). It is not that it is itself the principal one called, but that it is a qualifying descriptor clarifying the (noun) and removing its ambiguity. Its nominative case is obligatory, even though the modified noun is in the accusative position, to indicate that the noun is the intended one of the call. The particle of alerting (*kalimat al-tanbih*, here "hā") is inserted between them, both to emphasise the meaning of the call and to compensate for what "ayyu" deserves of a genitive complement (*mudaf ilayhi*). Because this construction is distinctive in carrying several kinds of emphasis and intensification, it is frequently used in the Glorious Revelation. How could it not be, when all the judgments and laws addressed to the servants throughout it, and other matters, are weighty affairs, truly deserving to make the skin shiver, to reassure the noble hearts, and to be received by attentive ears? Yet most people are heedless of them. Thus the situation required intensification and emphasis in awakening and alerting.

"Mankind" (*al-nās*) is meant to include all the responsible (*mukallafūn*) persons existing in that age, since plural nouns and their definite forms with "al-" are general in meaning, as proven by the validity of an exception from them and by emphasis with what denotes generality, as in His words: ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾. The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, deriving evidence from its generality, is widespread and well known. As for those who came after them and will exist later, they are not included in the direct address, but they are included under its ruling, because it is necessarily established from his religion (ﷺ) through mass transmission that the implication of his address and rulings encompasses the responsible persons existing (at the time) and those who will exist among them until the Hour is established. The generality is not undermined by what is narrated from ʿAlqama and al-Hasan al-Basri, that everything revealed with "O mankind" is Meccan, because it does not follow from its being revealed in Mecca, may Allah exalt it, that its ruling is restricted to its people, nor does it follow from its being restricted to them that it is restricted to the disbelievers, since not all of its people were disbelievers at that time. Nor is there any harm in the worship being realised by some of the responsible persons before this command was revealed, since what is commanded is the shared element, which includes initiating worship, persisting in it, and increasing it, while it is repeated according to the repetition of its causes. Nor (is there harm) in the absence of its condition in others among them, namely faith, because the command to it includes the command to what it cannot be completed without, and it is known from the religion, as a necessity, that it is conditional upon faith. For the command to one who is in a state of ritual impurity to pray necessarily entails the command to perform ablution.

It has been said that the meaning of worship includes the acts of the heart as well, since it expresses the utmost of humility and submission. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that everything in the Qur'an concerning acts of worship has the meaning of monotheism (*tawhid*). It has also been said that the meaning of "worship" (*uʿbudū*) is: affirm the oneness (of Allah), and obey (Him).

Nor is there any objection in the fact that some of the last two groups, those for whom warning is of no avail, are (addressed), by the authority of the decisive text, because the purpose of the command is to cut off excuses (p-59), and it does not contain imposing on them what is beyond their capacity, namely faith, while their faith does not exist at all. For no one among them has certainty that he is included under the ruling of the text. The text's revelation about them is because they, by their own bad choice, are in that state, and not that their being in that state is because of the text's revelation. So there is no compulsion at all. Yes, there is a subtle reason for restricting the address to the polytheists, which we shall examine when we reach His words: ﴿while you know﴾.

Mentioning Him (Exalted) with the title of Lordship (*rubūbiyya*), together with the attribution to the pronoun of those addressed, serves to emphasise the reason for the command, by alerting to its being the cause of worship.

﴿Who created you﴾: This is a descriptive attribute applied to Him (Glorified is He) for honour and as a further reason, following another reason. It has been permitted that it be (a) restrictive and clarifying (adjective), based on restricting the address to the polytheists and interpreting "lord" (*rabb*) as something more general than the true Lord, and the deities they call lords. *Khalq* (creation) is bringing a thing into being in measure and proportion; its origin is measurement. It is said: "He created the sandal," meaning he measured it and made it even by the measure. It is also read: "khalaqkum" with the qaf assimilated into the kaf.

﴿And those before you﴾: This is coordinated with the pronoun in the accusative (*ka-kum*), and completes what is intended by the glorification and the reasoning. For the creation of their forebears necessitates worship, just as does the creation of themselves. "Min" (from) is for the starting point, related to an omitted (verb): i.e., they existed from a time before your time. It is also said: He created them before your creation, so the verb "created" was omitted and the pronoun put in its place. What is meant by them are all the earlier nations that preceded them. It follows from the generality of the address that His creation extends to all. Restricting it to the polytheists leads to not touching upon the creation of those others among their contemporaries. The sentence is placed in the position of a relative clause whose attribution to the relative pronoun should be known to them as well, although they do not acknowledge the ultimate purpose of creation, even if they acknowledge its agent, as His words indicate: ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say: Allah﴾, to announce that their creation for piety is so evident that it is impossible for anyone to deny it. It is also read: "wa khalaqa man qablakum" and "wa-alladhina min qablakum," with the second relative pronoun inserted between the first and its clause, for emphasis, like the insertion of the particle *lam* between the two genitive-linked nouns in "abā laka" (your father's...). Or (it may be read) by making it a qualifier with the adverbial phrase, as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "those who are people existing before you."

﴿So that you may be mindful﴾: The literal meaning of the word "la'alla" (perhaps/so that) is to create an expectation of a matter which is uncertain between occurring and not occurring, with the first (occurring) more probable. If the matter is desirable, it is called hope (*tarajjī*); if it is undesirable, it is called apprehension (*ishfāq*). That meaning may be considered as actually realised, either from the side of the speaker, as in your saying: "Perhaps Allah will have mercy on me," and this is the common usage, because the meanings of the performative utterances (*insha'at*) subsist in him; or from the side of the addressee, treating him as if he were the speaker in fully engaging in the conversation taking place between them, as in His words (Glorified is He): ﴿Speak to him gently, perhaps he will be mindful or fear﴾. It may also be considered as realised potentially, by a kind of figurative usage, indicating that the matter in itself is a sign of the expectation, possessing an aspect that makes it valid, without there being any expectation actually occurring from an expecting person at all. If, in the noble verse, the side of the speaker is taken into account, it becomes impossible to intend that meaning, since expectation is impossible from the All-Knowing of the Unseen (Mighty and Majestic is He). So one turns either to metaphor, by likening His (Exalted) seeking of piety from His servants, while they are a sign of it because its causes are mutually supporting, to the hope of one who hopes from one from whom he hopes for something easily obtained, in that the object of each is uncertain between occurring and not occurring, with the first more probable. So the particle "la'alla" is used for it as a verbal metaphor (*isti'āra tab'iyya harfiyya*), to emphasise the strength of the demand and the nearness of the desired matter to occurring. Or one turns to analogy (*tamthil*), by considering His creating them prepared for piety, and His demanding it from them while they are able to achieve it and possess its causes, and abstracting from that a configuration, which is likened to a configuration abstracted from the one who hopes, and his hope from the one from whom he hopes for something easily attainable. Thus what properly belongs to the second configuration is used for the first, so that there is a metaphor of analogy (*isti'āra tamthiliyya*), in which the element that is the core of abstracting the configuration compared to is explicitly stated in its words, namely the word for hope, while the rest is implied with imagined words.

The composition that is considered valid in the allegorical representation (tamthil) results, as has been mentioned many times. As for taking the one being likened (al-mushabbah) to be His (Exalted is He) will in the metaphor (isti'arah) and the allegorical representation, this is a matter founded on the principle of the Mu'tazilah (al-I'tizal), who hold that what is willed may differ from His will (Exalted is He).

The sentence is in the accusative of circumstance (hal), either from the subject of "khalaqakum" (He created you), meaning: seeking from you piety (al-taqwa); or from its object, together with what is conjoined to it, by way of giving precedence to the addressees over the absent ones, since they are the ones commanded to worship. That is: He created you and them, seeking piety from you. Or it is a cause ('illah) for it: their creation in that state is equivalent to their creation for the sake of piety, as if it were said: "He created you so that you may be pious," or "in order that you may be pious." This is either based on permitting the explanation of His acts (Exalted is He) by purposes that return to the servants, as many of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) held; or by treating the attainment of the end as a result of what is its fruit as if it were the attainment of the purpose from what is its purpose. For the fact that His acts (Exalted is He) entail ends and perfectly executed, sublime benefits, without those being a final cause for them such that without them they would not have been undertaken, is something about which there is no dispute. The restriction of their creation by what has been mentioned, whether as circumstance or cause, serves to complete its causality with respect to the commanded matter and to confirm it, for their bringing about what they were created for is more binding in obligation.

The choice of "tattaqun" (that you may be pious) over "ta'budun" (that you may worship), despite its agreement with His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾, is for the sake of emphasis in making worship obligatory and of intensifying its imposition, since piety is the utmost of the worshipper's effort and the limit of his striving. So when piety is binding upon them, what is lesser than it is more binding, and bringing it about is easier.

If the aspect of the addressees is taken into account, then "la'alla" (perhaps/so that) retains its literal meaning, and the sentence is a circumstance from the pronoun in "u'budu" (worship), as if it were said: "Worship your Lord, hoping to be enrolled in the company of the pious who attain guidance and success." On this reading, piety means its third rank, which is devoting oneself entirely to God (Mighty and Majestic is He) and being purified from everything that preoccupies the inner self from watching over Him. This is the furthest aim of worship, for which competitors compete. By "being enrolled" is meant the common element between undertaking it and remaining steadfast in it, so that the people of this rank may hope for it, and for what is below it, namely the two ranks of guarding against the everlasting punishment and avoiding everything that is sinful, whether an act or an omission, as has been explained in the commentary on "al-muttaqin" (the pious).

Perhaps placing the circumstance from the subject between the two descriptions of the object is because, with the preposing, the indication that the first description is the greatest of the rulings of lordship, and that it is deeply rooted in imposing worship, would be lost; and in postponing it there is the added length of speech. This is according to the view that the realization of the expectation is taken as actual. But if its realization is taken as potential, then the sentence is a circumstance from the object of "khalaqakum" (He created you), and what is conjoined to it in the manner mentioned: that is, He created you and them in a state in which all of you are such that every hoper hopes that you will be pious. For when He (Glorified and Exalted is He) brought them into being prepared for piety, combining its beginnings, both external (al-afaqiyyah) and internal (al-anfusiyyah), their condition was such that every hoper hopes from them that they will be pious without doubt. This condition is concurrent with their creation, even if the hope is not definitively realized.

Know that the noble verse, although by its wording it declares the obligation of His unity (Exalted is He) and makes His worship binding upon all people, also guides them by its allusion to the contemplation of the signs of creation (al-ayat al-takwiniyyah) set up within the selves and the horizons, and to what decides this with perfect decision. It has first shown among those signs what relates to themselves, from their own creation and the creation of their forebears, because it is the stronger testimony and the more evident indication. Then it followed with what relates to their livelihood. So it was said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 22:

﴿Who made the earth a bed for you﴾: It is in the accusative position, as a second qualifier (sifa, an attribute or descriptive adjective) of "Rabbakum" (your Lord), either clarifying (muwaddiha) or praising (madiha). Or it is governed by an implied "I specify" (akhussu) or "I praise" (amdahu). Or it is in the nominative position, for praise and exaltation (al-madh wa-al-ta'zim), with an implied mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence). Ibn Malik said: the verb is obligatorily omitted in the accusative used for praise, to signal that it is an act of creation (insha'), as in the vocative (al-munada); and the mubtada' is omitted in the nominative so that both constructions follow one pattern. As for it being a mubtada' whose predicate (khabar) is "so do not set up," as some have said, this would require that the focus of the prohibition be only what lies within the relative clause (silah), without their creation and the creation of those before them having any part in it, even though that is of greater significance.

"Ja'ala" (made) here means "sayyara" (made into), and the two accusatives after it are its two objects. It has also been said that it means "khalaqa" (created), in which case the second accusative is a circumstantial state (hal). On both interpretations the adverbial phrase ("for you") depends on it. Placing it before the direct object serves to hasten the joy by showing that what follows is a benefit to the addressees, and to create anticipation for it, because the soul, when something that should come first is delayed, especially after being told of its benefit, waits eagerly for it, so that it settles in the heart most fully when it arrives. Or it is for the sake of what comes later and what is conjoined to it, which is a kind of length; had it been put first, the harmony of the parts of the noble structure would have been lost.

The meaning of "made it a bed" is: He made part of it project above the water, although its nature is to sink. He made it intermediate between hardness and softness, suitable for sitting upon and sleeping on, like a spread carpet. It does not follow from this that it is a true flat surface, for the sphericity of its shape, together with its great mass, makes its being spread out (iftirash) possible. It was also read as "bisatan" (a carpet) and "mihadan" (a cradle).

﴿and the sky a structure﴾: It is conjoined to the two previous objects. The earth is mentioned first because their need of it and their benefit from it are greater and more evident. That is, He made it a dome erected over you. "Al-sama'" (the sky) is a collective noun that applies to one or many. It may also be the plural of "samawa" or "simaa'a." "Al-bina'" (building) is originally a verbal noun (masdar) that came to be used for the thing built, whether a house, a dome, or a tent. From it comes the saying "banā 'alā imra'atihi" (he consummated the marriage with his wife), because when they married a woman they would pitch a new tent over her.

﴿and sent down water from the sky﴾: It is conjoined to "made." That is, He sent it down from its direction, or from it, to the clouds, and from the clouds to the earth, as has been related from him (ﷺ). Or "the sky" means the direction of height, as the use of the apparent noun in place of a pronoun indicates. On the first two interpretations, the repetition is for the sake of emphasis. The "min" (from) denotes the starting point of the motion and depends on "sent down," or on an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial state of the object, meaning "being from the sky." It is placed before its noun because the noun is indefinite. As for placing the adverbial phrase before the direct object on the first interpretation, even though it should come after the direct object, this is either because the sky is its origin and starting point, or because of the anticipation mentioned earlier, together with the greater coherence it gives between it and His saying (exalted is He): ﴿and brought forth with it﴾, that is, by means of the water, ﴿fruits as provision for you﴾.

This happens in that He placed in the water an active power and in the earth a receptive power, and from their interaction the kinds of fruits were produced. Or it happens in that He continued His customary practice of pouring forth the forms of fruits and their diverse qualities upon the matter formed from the two. Although the true agent is His power and will, He, exalted is He, is able to bring all things into existence without intermediate causes or materials, just as He originated the souls of the first principles and causes. But in creating them as things that change in their conditions and transform through their stages, He, mighty and majestic is He, has wondrous wisdoms that renew lessons for people of insight and greater reassurance in His great power and subtle wisdom, which the sudden creation of them would not provide.

The "min" here is partitive (lil-tab'id), since He said ﴿and We brought forth with it fruits﴾ and since it falls between two indefinite nouns, "water" and "provision." It is as if it were said: He sent down some of the water from the sky, and by it brought forth some of the fruits, to be some of your provision. This is indeed what happens, for He did not send down all the water from the sky, nor bring forth from the earth all the fruits, nor make all that is provided for into fruits. Or the "min" is explicative (lil-tabyin). "Rizqan" (provision) is an object in the sense of "the thing provided," and "min al-thamarat" (of the fruits) explains it or is a circumstantial state of it, as when you say: "I spent of the dirhams a thousand." It is also permissible for "min al-thamarat" to be the object and "rizqan" a circumstantial state of it, or a verbal noun (masdar) of "akhraja," since it carries the sense of "razaqa" (provided). The plural "thamarat" (fruits) was used rather than "thimar" although the context calls for plurality, because by "thamarat" is meant the plural of "thamara" as in your saying: "I obtained the fruit (thamara) of his orchard." This is confirmed by the reading in the singular. Or because plural nouns may sometimes stand in place of one another, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿How many gardens and springs they left behind﴾, and His saying: ﴿three periods﴾. Or because it is definite by the article "al-" and goes beyond the limit of paucity.

The "lam" (for) depends on an omitted element that functions as a qualifier of "rizqan," on the supposition that it is the thing provided, meaning: a provision that is for you. Or it is a support strengthening the action of "rizqan" on the supposition that it is a verbal noun, as if it were said: a provision for you.

﴿So do not set up rivals to God﴾: This either depends on the preceding command, following from it, as if it were said: since you are commanded to worship One who has this character, with these exalted attributes and beautiful deeds, then do not set up a partner for Him. The phrase "rivals" (andad) is used in view of what actually happens, and not because the basis of the prohibition is plurality. It was also read as "nidd." Placing the glorious name in the position of the pronoun serves to identify the worshipped One by His essence after identifying Him by His attributes, and to give the reason for the ruling by the quality of divinity, on which the matter of oneness and the impossibility of association depend, and to indicate that the other attributes follow from it.

Or it is conjoined to the preceding, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Worship God and associate nothing with Him﴾. The "fa'" (so) indicates that what precedes it, namely the attributes applied to Him (exalted is He), is the cause of the prohibition, or of the cessation (from the prohibited act). Or it indicates that the final outcome of the prohibition is the command to restrict worship to Him (exalted is He), which follows from its basis. It is as if it were said: worship Him, so single Him out for it. The use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is for the reason mentioned just above.

It has been said that this is a negation put in the subjunctive by an implied "an" as a response to the command. This is rejected, because that construction applies when the first is a cause of the second, and there is no doubt that worship is not a cause of monotheism, which is its foundation and basis. It has also been said that it is in the subjunctive governed by "la'alla" (perhaps), like "fa-attali'a" (so that I may look) in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Perhaps I may reach the means, the ways of the heavens, so that I may look upon the God of Moses﴾. That is: He created you so that you might guard yourselves and fear His punishment; so do not liken Him to His creation. Since the basis of this subjunctive is the resemblance of "la'alla" to "layta" (would that) in the remoteness of the hoped-for, there is in it an admonition to their failing, in that they treat the near hoped-for as if it were a distant wish.

It has also been said that it depends on His saying (exalted is He): ﴿the One who made﴾ ... etc., on the supposition that it is in the nominative for praise. That is: He is the One who surrounded you with these mighty signs and clear proofs, so do not take partners for Him. In this view there is what has already been mentioned, namely that the creation of them and of their forefathers would be outside the scope of the prohibition, despite their relevance to it. It has also been said that it is the predicate (khabar) of the relative pronoun, with the implication of "a thing said concerning him." You already know what is wrong with this, together with the necessity of adopting the view of al-Akhfash (that a proper noun may stand in place of a pronoun), as in your saying: "Zayd stood, Abu 'Abd Allah," when that is his kunya (patronymic).

"Al-nidd" is an equal counterpart, from "nadda, nududdan," meaning he fled or ran away. "Nadadtuhu" means I opposed him. The term is restricted to a contrary that is identical in essence, just as the equal is restricted to one that is identical in quantity. Calling what the polytheists worship besides God "rivals," although they did not claim that these resemble Him (exalted is He) in His attributes, nor that they oppose Him in His actions, is because when they abandoned His worship for the worship of these, and named them gods, their condition resembled that of one who believes they are beings necessary in essence, able to ward off from them the might of God (mighty and majestic is He) and to grant them what God has not intended for them of good. Thus He ridiculed them and condemned them for making rivals for the One for whom it is impossible to have even a single rival. Concerning this, the monotheist of the Jahiliyya, Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, said:

Is it one Lord, or a thousand lords, that I should worship,
when affairs are divided?

I have abandoned al-Lat and al-'Uzza, all of them,
as the discerning man does.

His saying (exalted is He): ﴿while you know﴾ is a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "do not set up," directing the restriction to what the prohibition conveys of the ugliness of what is forbidden and the obligation of avoiding it. The object of "ta'lamun" (you know) is omitted entirely, as if it were said: do not do that, for it is ugly and must be avoided, while you are among those who know the subtleties of matters and hit upon right judgment. Or the omitted object is supplied as the context requires, such as: while you know the falsehood of that; or you know that nothing resembles Him; or you know the disparity between Him and them; or you know that they do not do the like of His actions, as in His saying: ﴿Is there any of your partners who does any of that?﴾ Or it is something else. The essence of this is to stimulate the addressees and urge them to cease what they have been forbidden. This is what the general address of the prohibition requires, by taking the forbidden as the common element that unites the initiation of cessation, which is what is demanded of the unbelievers, and the persistence in it, which is the condition of the believers, as has been said of the same construction in the command. As for directing the restriction to the prohibition itself, it necessarily requires limiting the address to the unbelievers, since the restriction to the state of knowledge cannot be achieved that way, because the obligation extends to both the one who knows and the ignorant one who is able to know. Rather, it is achieved only by way of intensifying the rebuke and reproach, on the basis that committing ugly acts is more ugly when done by those who know their ugliness, and this can only be imagined regarding the unbelievers. Whoever directs the restriction to the prohibition itself while also extending the address to the believers has strayed from precision.

If you say: Does not limiting the address to the unbelievers in the command and the prohibition free us from such strained interpretations, and provide a good coherence between what precedes and what follows? For there is no escape, in the verse of challenge, from setting the address apart and restricting it to the unbelievers necessarily, along with the other considerations, such as the elevation of the believers' station and the exaltation of their rank above being forced into the same thread as the unbelievers, and the indication that they are persistent in obedience and worship, as already mentioned at the beginning of the noble surah, and that they are independent of command and prohibition in this matter. I say: Indeed, that is a subtle view and a straight path; whoever takes it does not go astray, and whoever firmly plants his foot upon it does not slip. So reflect.

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 23 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾: This begins the establishing that the Noble Book, of which the two noble verses recited above are a part, the two verses that declare the obligation of worship and monotheism, is sent down from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, upon His Messenger (ﷺ). Likewise, the signs of creation mentioned in those two verses, which point to this, proceed from Him (exalted be He). This is to clarify His attribution of the noble qualities mentioned at the beginning of the blessed surah, among which is His being free from any doubt whatsoever. The expression of their belief about Him in terms of doubt, although they are certain that it is the speech of a human, is indicated by His saying (exalted be He): ﴿if you are truthful﴾. This is either to inform that the utmost that can come from them, even though they are in the extreme of obstinacy and stubbornness, is doubt about its matter; and as for the certainty mentioned, it is outside the circle of possibility. Likewise, its being indefinite (nakirah) and its being introduced with the word of doubt (in raybin) indicates that its proper status is to be weak and doubtful in occurrence. Or it is to alert that their certainty in that is like a weak doubt, because of the complete clarity of the proofs of inimitability and the utmost strength of those proofs. The reason He did not say "and if you doubt what We sent down..." is what was pointed out earlier of the exaggeration in declaring the sanctity of the revelation free from any trace of doubt occurring in it, as expressed by His saying (exalted be He): ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾, and to indicate that if any doubt occurs, it comes from their side, not from His exalted side. Considering their settling in it and its encompassing them does not contradict considering its weakness and scarcity, since what that requires is the continuity of their involvement with it, not its strength and abundance.

The "min" in "mimma" (from what) is for beginning (ibtida'iyyah), related to an omitted element that occupies the position of an attribute of "raybin" (doubt). Taking it to mean causation (sababiyyah) might give the impression that it (the revelation) is a locus of doubt in some sense, and far be that from it. The "ma" (what), whether relative (mawsulah) or descriptive (mawsufah), refers to the Noble Book itself, not to the common notion shared between it and its parts. The meaning of their being "in doubt about it" (p-64) is not their doubt about the correctness of its meanings or the soundness of its rulings, but about the very fact that it is a revelation sent down from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The choice of the term "tanzil" (sending down), which indicates gradualness, over the general term "inzal" (sending down), is to remind of the source of their doubt. Building the challenge upon it is to give rein and widen the field, for they had taken its gradual descent as a means to deny it. So this was made one of the starting points of acknowledging it, as if it were said: "If you doubt the matter of what We sent down gradually and in stages, then produce yourselves a single chapter like one of its installments and one solitary star of its stars, for that is easier for you than that it be sent down all at once and you be challenged with the whole." This, as you see, is the utmost in rebuke and removing excuses. And in mentioning him (ﷺ) with the title of servanthood, together with its attribution to the pronoun of majesty, there is an honour, an elevation, and an alert to his being specific to Him (exalted be He) and his submission to His commands (exalted be He), which is not hidden.

It has been read as "upon Our servants" (ʿibadina), and the intended meaning is him (ﷺ) and his community, or all the prophets (peace be upon them). In that there is an indication that doubt about it is doubt about what was sent down before it, because it confirms what came before and is a guardian over it.

The command in His saying (exalted be He): ﴿then produce a chapter﴾ is of the category of showing inability and silencing (ilqam al-hajar), as in His saying (exalted be He): ﴿then bring it from the west﴾. The "fa" (then) is for the answer (of the condition), and the causality of the doubt for the command, or for bringing about what is commanded, because of what was pointed out, that it is an expression of their aforementioned certainty. For it is a cause for the first absolutely, and for the second on the assumption of truthfulness. As if it were said: "If the matter is as you claim, that it is the speech of a human, then produce its like, for you are capable of what all the rest of your species are capable of."

The "surah" (chapter) is a portion of the Mighty Qur'an, distinct, and its least is three verses. Its "waw" is original, transferred from "sur al-balad" (the walls of a city), because it encloses a portion of the Qur'an, separate and set apart on its own, or contains refined fields of knowledge, like the enclosure of a city's walls over what is within it. Or it is from "sawra" (rank), as the poet said:

*And for a band of Harrab and Qadhdh there is a rank*
*in glory, whose crow is not put to flight.*
