For the chapters of the Qur'an, although they are in themselves ranks in terms of excellence and nobility, or in terms of length and shortness, they are, by their arrangement with their sisters in the codex, stages which the reader ascends little by little. It has been said that its "waw" is substituted from a hamza, so its meaning is "the remainder of a thing." Its problem is not hidden.

The "min" in His saying: ﴿of its like﴾ is explicative (bayaniyyah), related to an omitted element that occupies the position of an attribute of "surah". The pronoun refers to "what We sent down", meaning: a chapter that is of its like in loftiness of rank, sublimity of level, refined arrangement, and wondrous eloquence, possessing all the other qualities of inimitability. Making it partitive (tab'idiyyah) gives the impression that it has an established like, for whose part they were intended to be shown incapable of bringing. As if it were said: "Then produce a part of what is its like", which suggests that likeness is part of what they are incapable of, rather than likeness being the very basis of the incapacity, although that is what is intended. The framing of the command on accommodating them, according to their reckoning, since they used to say: ﴿If we willed, we would say the like of this﴾, or on mocking them, is refuted by what preceded of treating it as a doubt, for the basis of mockery is accepting that from them, and deferring it, even if not seriously. It has been said that "min" is extra (ziyadah), according to the opinion of al-Akhfash, based on His saying (exalted be He): ﴿then produce a chapter like it﴾, and ﴿ten chapters like it﴾. It has been said that it is for beginning (ibtida'iyyah), so the pronoun then refers necessarily to the one upon whom it was sent down, since its return to what was sent down would give the impression that it has an established like, for which the command of showing incapacity by bringing something from it has come. You already know its problem. Unlike its return to the one upon whom it was sent down, for the existence of his like (peace be upon him) in humanity, in the Arabic language, and in being unlettered, eases the matter in general. Except that restricting the challenge to a single person who shares with him (peace be upon him) the stated qualities that are incompatible with bringing what is commanded does not indicate the incapacity of those who are not like that among their scholars. Rather, it may give the impression that they are able to do so in some measure, individually or collectively. Moreover, it requires that what was sent down be bare of the qualities detailed, which necessitate the impossibility of its like existing. So where is this from challenging a great community and commanding them to gather in the arena of opposition (p-65) with their horsemen and their infantry, as His saying (exalted be He) expresses: ﴿and call your witnesses apart from Allah﴾, and to cooperate in bringing a small amount similar in the qualities of perfection to what one of their own kind brought in its entirety?

"Shuhada'" (witnesses) is the plural of "shahid", in the sense of "present", or "one who bears witness", or "helper". The meaning of "dun" (apart from) is the nearest place to a thing; it is said: "this is dun that" when it is slightly lower than it. Then it was borrowed for difference in conditions and ranks, so it is said: "Zayd is dun 'Amr", meaning in excellence and rank. Then it was extended and used for every crossing of a limit to another limit, and transgressing one ruling to another ruling, without regard to one being lower than the other. So it came to function like the particle of exception. The word "min" (from) is either related to "ud'u" (call), in which case it is for the starting point of the end (ibtida' al-ghayah), and the adverbial phrase is stable, and the meaning is: "Call, transgressing Allah (exalted be He), those who are present to support you, whoever they may be; or those present in your gatherings and assemblies, from your leaders and nobles, to whom you turn in calamities and rely upon in important matters; or those who bear witness among you in your affairs, your trustees who are entrusted with recovering rights by carrying out the statement before the rulers; or those who stand with you in support, in reality or in claim, from humans and jinn, so that they may help you." Excluding Him (glorified and exalted be He) from the ruling of calling in the first case, despite His being included in presence, is to emphasize His encompassing all that is other than Him, not to explain His sole authority over the power to do what they were charged with. For that would give the impression that if they called Him (exalted be He), He would answer them. As for the other aspects, it is for clarifying from the outset their disavowal of Him (exalted be He), and their being on the edge of opposition and hostility toward Him, seeking support from other than Him. The turn to a different mode (iltifat) is to bring in awe and cultivate dread. It has been said: the meaning is: "Call, apart from the friends of Allah, your witnesses who are the notables of the people and the knights of debate and counter-argument, so that they may bear witness for you that what you have brought is its like", indicating that they refuse to accept for themselves the testimony to the correctness of what is manifestly false and clearly impossible. In this there is that it indicates that the challenge does not include those leaders. It has been said: the meaning is: "Call your witnesses, and thereby validate your claim, and do not call upon Allah (exalted be He) as witness, saying: 'Allah bears witness that what we claim is true,' for that is the habit of one who is refuted." In this there is that if what they claim is meant to be the truth of the false religion they hold, then it has no bearing on the position of challenge; and if what is meant is the likeness of what they brought to what was challenged, then, with its not fitting the beginning of the challenge, it gives the impression that they had undertaken opposition and brought something of uncertain state, wavering between likeness and its absence, and that they claimed it while seeking witness in that from Allah (exalted be He). For at that point there is a need for the command to seek testimony from people and the prohibition from seeking testimony from Him (exalted be He). But how could they do that, when no vein of theirs throbbed and they did not utter a word?

Or it is related to "shuhada'akum" (your witnesses), and what is meant by them is the idols, and "dun" is in the sense of "beyond", with it being a stable adverbial phrase that occurred as a circumstantial state from the pronoun of the addressees, and the governing element is what "shuhada'akum" indicates. That is: "Call your idols whom you have taken as gods, transgressing Allah (exalted be He) in taking them thus." The word "min" is for beginning, for taking is a beginning from transgression. The naming of the idols as "witnesses" is to specify the basis of seeking support through them, by reminding of what they claimed: that they have a standing with Allah (exalted be He), and that they benefit them by their testimony for them that they are upon the truth. For what is of this nature must be a refuge for them in every important matter, and a place to which they resort in every grave calamity. As if it were said: "Those are your support, so call them for this calamity that has overtaken you." So the purpose of the turn (iltifat) is to inform of the complete foolishness of their minds, in that they preferred over the worship of Him who possesses divinity, comprising all the qualities of perfection, the worship of what has no lowliness greater than it. It has been said: the word "dun" is borrowed from its conventional meaning, which is the nearest place to a thing in front of it, as in the saying of al-A'sha:

*You show him the mote in front of her, while she is beneath it.*

That is: "You show him the mote in front of her, and she is in front of the mote." Then it is an adverbial phrase, a loose adverbial (zarf laghw), governed by "shuhada'akum", because the scent of the verb is sufficient in it without need for (p-66)

...not to reliance (i'timad), nor to the supplying (taqdir) of "yashhadun" (they bear witness). The meaning is: call your witnesses who bear witness for you before God (Exalted), so that they may help you in the opposition (mu'arada). Its being presented under this designation indicates, as has passed, the basis for seeking their aid. The purpose of the shift (iltifat, a change of grammatical person) is to cultivate awe (mahaba) and to strengthen that meaning, for whoever undertakes this matter in that grave situation deserves to be sought for help in every aim. As for their being commanded in both respects, namely that they should back you in opposing the Qur'an, which silenced every eloquent speaker, with inanimate things, by way of mockery at them, that is beyond description. The word "min" (from) here is partitive (tab'idiyya), because they say "jalasa bayna yadayhi wa khalfahu" (he sat before him and behind him) with the meaning of "fi" (in), since these two are the two extremities of the action; and "min bayni yadayhi wa min khalfihi" (from before him and from behind him), because the action only occurs in part of those two directions, just as you say "ji'tuhu min al-layl" (I came to him from the night), meaning part of the night. It has also been said that the "min" which precedes "dun" is in all positions with the meaning of "fi" (in), as in the rest of the adverbs which do not inflect and are always in the accusative as adverbials of place, and are only governed by "min" specifically. It has been said that the intended "shuhada" (witnesses) are the leaders of the people and the notables of the assemblies and gatherings, and "dun" is a stationary adverbial (zarf mustaqirr), and "min" is initial (ibtida'iyya, indicating origin). That is: call those who bear witness for you that what you have produced is its like, going beyond God's friends in that, and its summary is: witnesses other than them, as a notice that they too do not bear witness to that. The annexed noun (mudaf) to God (Exalted) was supplied in observance of the antithesis, for God's friends (Exalted) are opposed to the friends of the idols, just as the mention of God (Exalted) is opposed to the mention of the idols. The purpose of this command is to give free rein and to lead them on toward the final reproach, as if it were said: We have left off obliging you with witnesses who have no inclination to either side, as is customary, and we have been content with your well-known witnesses who defend you, for they too do not bear witness for you, out of fear of blame and disdain for a testimony whose falsity is clear. How could they? The matter of the inimitability (i'jaz) has reached such clarity that there is no way left to deny it with certainty. In this there is what has passed of the lack of suitability to the beginning of the challenge (tahaddi), and the lack of its addressing those witnesses, and the implication that they had confronted the opposition and produced something for which they needed witnesses to establish its equivalence to what was challenged. How far apart they are from that!

﴿If you are truthful﴾, that is, in your claim that it is from his speech, peace and blessings be upon him. This is a conditional whose apodosis has been omitted, because what preceded indicates it. The meaning: If you are truthful, then produce a surah of its like, etc. The implication of the antecedent for the consequent is that their truthfulness in that claim requires their capacity to produce its like, by the necessity of their sharing with him, peace and blessings be upon him, in humanity and in Arabic, together with their long practice of sermons and poetry, their frequent exercise of the styles of verse and prose, and their great care in preserving events and days, especially in mutual support and cooperation. And there is no doubt that capacity for a thing is among the requirements of performing it and of the motives to command it.

﴿فَإنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلُوا﴾: That is, if you do not do what you were commanded, which is producing the like of it, after you have exerted every effort in the striving and have exceeded every known limit, grasping at the skirts of the matter and mounting the back of every difficult and easy thing. The verse did not state the action explicitly, to signal that there is no need for it, since their eagerness for it is fully evident. In the conditional clause the verb is given in its absolute form, and the verbal noun of the commanded act is made an object of cause (maf'ul lahu). This is a concise eloquence (i'jaz badi') that dispenses with lengthiness and repetition, along with a subtle secret that the context itself demands, namely the indication that what is intended by the obligation is the very performance of the act commanded, to manifest their inability to perform it, not the obtaining of the object, that is, the thing brought about. This is because it is impossible to bring about the like of it. The response of the conditional, namely the command to guard against the Fire, rests on their inability to perform the act, not on the failure to obtain the object. The meaning of the word "verb" (al-fi'l) is the essences of the specific actions, whether intransitive or transitive, without regard to their relations to their particular objects. When it is connected to a specific transitive verb, what is intended is the performance of that very act and bringing it out from potentiality into actuality. As for its relation to its specific object, that lies outside the meaning of the absolute verb, and it is derived only from the specific verb. For this reason you find them using this to strip transitive verbs of their objects and treating them as intransitive verbs. They say, for example: the meaning of "so-and-so gives and withholds" is "he performs giving and withholding." This is guided by His (Exalted) saying: ﴿فَإنْ لَمْ تَأْتُونِي بِهِ فَلا كَيْلَ لَكم عِنْدِي ولا تَقْرَبُونِ﴾ ("But if you bring him not to me, there shall be no measure for you with me, nor shall you come near me"), after His saying: ﴿ائْتُونِي بِأخٍ لَكم مِن أبِيكُمْ﴾ ("Bring me a brother of yours from your father"). For since the aim of Joseph (peace be upon him) in the command, and the target of his purpose in the obligation, was to bring Benjamin into his presence, he did not suffice, in the conditional that impels them to earnestness in compliance and striving to realize what was commanded, with the general reference to the act that was ordered, by saying "If you do not do," but rather repeated it exactly, connected to its object, to affirm his demand and to express his intention. This is it. It has been said: the verb was used absolutely but intended as bringing, together with what is connected to it, either by way of expressing apparent nouns through pronouns referring back to them, to avoid repetition, or by way of mentioning the necessary concomitant and intending the thing necessitating it, because of the mutual implication between them that justifies the transition with the aid of the indications of the situation. Then consider the choice of the word "in" (if), which indicates doubt, over "idha" (when), even though there is certainty of their not doing it, in accommodation to them according to their supposition before testing, or in mockery of them.

﴿وَلَنْ تَفْعَلُوا﴾: The word "lan" is for negating the future, like "la", except that "lan" carries additional emphasis and intensity. Its origin, according to al-Khalil, is "la an"; according to al-Farra', it is "la", whose alif was replaced by a nun; according to Sibawayh, it is a particle independent in itself for the aforementioned meaning. This last is one of the two narrations from al-Khalil. The clause is a parenthetical insertion between the two parts of the conditional, confirming the content of its antecedent and affirming the obligation to act upon its consequent. This is a brilliant miracle, in that He, whose knowledge of the unseen is exclusive to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, informed of it, and the matter came to pass exactly so. How could it be otherwise? For had they opposed it with anything resembling it in general, the narrators would have transmitted it, generation after generation.

﴿فاتَّقُوا النّارَ﴾: This is the response to the condition, on the basis that guarding against the Fire is a metonymy for abstaining from obstinacy, since through it its being caused by obstinacy and its consequence following from it are realized. It is as if it were said: "If you are unable to produce its like, as is established, then guard yourselves against denying that it is sent down from God, glory be to Him, for that entails punishment by the Fire." But the aforementioned metonymy was preferred over this, being founded on depicting obstinacy in the form of fire, and making the attribute of it the very same as being engulfed in it, in order to exaggerate its terror and its grave matter, to show complete care in warning the addressees against it, in repelling them from it, and in urging them to earnestness in realizing what is meant by the metonymy. In this there is a brilliant concision that is not hidden, for the original would be: "If you do not do it, then its truth has been confirmed for you. If that is confirmed, then your persistence in obstinacy and your abandonment of belief in it is a cause for your deserving punishment by the Fire. So guard against it, and guard against the Fire ﴿الَّتِي وقُودُها النّاسُ والحِجارَةُ﴾ ("whose fuel is men and stones")." This is a description of the Fire, bequeathing to it increased terror and atrocity (may God protect us from that). The "waqud" (fuel) is that with which the fire is kindled and raised from firewood. It has been read with a damma on the waw, and it is a verbal noun used as a name for the object, for intensity, just as one says "so-and-so is the pride of his people and the adornment of his city." The meaning is that it is so intense that it does not touch anything, moist or dry, without burning it, unlike the fires of this world, which in their blazing require fuel of firewood or grass. This attribute was made a relative clause for the relative pronoun, implying that its connection to what it is described as belonging to is known to the addressee. This is on the basis that they heard it from the People of the Book before that, or from the Messenger (ﷺ), or they heard before this Medinan verse His saying: ﴿نارًا وقُودُها النّاسُ والحِجارَةُ﴾ ("a fire whose fuel is men and stones"). So what they had heard first is referred to here. That the sura of Prohibition (al-Tahrim) is Medinan does not entail that all its verses are so, as is well known. As for the attribute also needing to be known to the addressee as belonging to the described thing, the matter is easy here, since the addressees are the believers, and it is evident that they heard that from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). What is meant by "stones" is the idols, and by "men" themselves, as stated in His saying: ﴿إنَّكم وما تَعْبُدُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ حَصَبُ جَهَنَّمَ﴾ ("Indeed you and what you worship besides God are the firewood of Hell"), and so on.

﴿أُعِدَّتْ لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾: That is, it has been prepared for those who disbelieve in what We have sent down, and made a provision for their punishment. The intended meaning is either the genus of disbelievers, with the addressees entering among them by primary inclusion, or specifically them. "Al-kafirin" (the disbelievers) was placed in the position of their pronoun, to censure them and to make the ruling depend on their disbelief. It has been read "u'tiddat" from "al-'atad", meaning "al-'uddah" (provision). This indicates that the Fire is created and exists now. The clause is a resumption, with no place in terms of i'rab, confirming the content of what precedes it, affirming the obligation to act upon it, and clarifying who is meant by "men", thereby repelling the possibility of generality. It has been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) with "qad" implied, referring to "the Fire", not to its pronoun in "its fuel", because that would involve separating the two with the predicate. It has also been said that it is a relative clause after a relative clause, or a conjunction with the relative clause without a conjunction particle.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 25:**

﴿And give good tidings to those who believe﴾: that is, that it (the Qur'an) is sent down from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This clause is conjoined (*ma'tuf*, coordinated by *'atf*) to the preceding sentence. However, the intent is not to coordinate the matter itself, such that a counterpart would have to be sought to which it can properly be conjoined. Rather, it is conjoined in the sense that the account of the believers in the Qur'an and the description of their reward are placed alongside the account of the disbelievers in it and the manner of their punishment, following the divine practice of pairing encouragement with warning and promise with threat. It seems that the change in construction serves to evoke the complete contrast between the state of the two groups. It is also recited as *"wa-bushshira"* (and it was given good tidings), in the passive verbal form, conjoined to *"u'iddat"* (it was prepared), and in that case it is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new independent sentence). The linking of the good tidings to the relative pronoun indicates that it is motivated by what is contained in the relative clause of faith and righteous deeds. Yet it is not on account of these two in themselves, for they do not match the previous blessings, let alone entail a reward in the future. Rather, it is by the legislator's appointment and the requirement of his promise, and by making their relative clause a verb indicating occurrence (*hudūth*), after the mention of the disbelievers in the form of the active participle, in order to urge the addressees to guard themselves by bringing about faith and to warn them against persisting in disbelief. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ. It has been said that it is addressed to everyone who is able to give good tidings, as in his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Give good tidings to those who walk to the mosques in the darkness of the nights with the perfect light on the Day of Resurrection." He, peace and blessings be upon him, did not command this of one specific person, but of everyone who is able to do so. In this there is an allusion that the matter, because of its greatness and the magnificence of its status, is fitting for everyone who is capable of it to undertake giving good tidings of it. *Bishārah* (good tidings) is news that brings joy, by which the effect of happiness appears on the skin; and *tabāshīr al-ṣubh* are the first beginnings of its light.

﴿and do righteous deeds﴾: *ṣāliḥah* (righteous), like *ḥasanah* (good), functions as a noun; it is every deed that is upright, by the proof of reason and transmission. The article *al-* here denotes the genus, and the plural indicates that what is meant is a collection of righteous deeds, the principal ones of which were alluded to at the beginning of the noble surah, and some of which vary according to the varying states of the responsible persons in their obligations. The conjoining of deed to faith indicates that they are distinct, and it signals that the basis for deserving the good tidings is the combination of both matters, for faith is a foundation, and righteous deeds are like the building upon it, and there is no benefit in a foundation without a building upon it.

﴿that for them are gardens﴾: it is in the accusative by the omission of the preposition and the reaching of the verb to it; or it is in the genitive by a preposition understood, like the phrase "by Allah, I will surely do it." *Jannah* (garden) is the single instance of the verbal noun of *janna-hu*, meaning to cover him, when he concealed him. It is applied to palm trees and to dense trees that shade by the interlacing of their branches. Zuhayr said:

*As if my two eyes, in the two sides of a waterwheel's drawing, were irrigating a tall, sparse garden.*

That is, tall palm trees. As if, because of the intensity of their density, their interlacing, and their covering of what is beneath them, they were in a single instance the very act of covering. And *jannah* is also applied to the land that has trees on it. Al-Farra' said: *jannah* is that in which there are palm trees, and *firdaws* is that in which there are vines. Thus the root of the verbal noun, in that case, should be derived from the passive verb. The abode of reward was named *jannah* although it contains things that cannot be described, such as lofty rooms and palaces, because it is the locus of its bliss and the greater part of its delights. Its plural with indefiniteness is because they are seven, according to what Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, mentioned: the Garden of Firdaws, the Garden of 'Adn, the Garden of Na'im, the Abode of Eternity, the Garden of Refuge, the Abode of Peace, and 'Illiyyun. In each of them there are levels and degrees that vary according to the variation of deeds and their people.

﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾: it is in the accusative position as a description (*ṣifah*) of *"jannāt"*. If by them are meant the trees, then the flowing of rivers beneath them is evident. If by them is meant the land that contains them, then a noun must be supplied: that is, beneath their trees. If by them is meant the whole of the land and the trees, then the consideration of "beneath" is with regard to the apparent part, which validates applying the name "garden" to the whole. It is reported from Masruq that the rivers of Paradise flow without a trench. The definite article in *"al-anhār"* (the rivers) is for the genus, as in your saying: "For so-and-so there is a garden in which is flowing water, and figs, and grapes." Or it is a substitute for the genitive complement, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the head has flared with white hair﴾. Or it is for a known reference, pointing to what was mentioned in His saying, Mighty and Exalted is He: ﴿rivers of water unaltered﴾, and so on. *Nahr* (river), with a fatha or with a sukun on the ha', is the wide watercourse, above the small stream and below the sea, like the Nile and the Euphrates. The root carries the sense of width. What is meant by it is its water, by ellipsis, or by linguistic metaphor; or the watercourses themselves, and flowing has been attributed to them as a rational metaphor (*majāz 'aqlī*), as in "the gutter has flowed."

﴿Whenever they are provided with a fruit from them as provision, they will say, "This is what we were provided with before." ﴾: this is another description of *"jannāt"*, delayed after the first because the flowing of rivers beneath them is a description of them in respect of their own essence, whereas this is a description of them in respect of their people who enjoy them. Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, or a resumptive sentence, as if, when the gardens were described with what has been mentioned of description, there occurred to the mind of the hearer: are their fruits like the fruits of the gardens of this world or not? So their state was explained. *"Kullamā"* (whenever) is in the accusative as an adverb of time; *"rizqan"* (as provision) is the direct object; the first *"min"* and the second are for the beginning (of a point), and they are in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). It is as if it were said: at every time they were provided with a provision begun from the gardens, begun from a fruit; so that the provision is restricted by its being begun from the gardens, and its beginning from them is restricted by its being begun from a fruit. Thus the possessor of the first circumstance is *"rizqan"*, and the possessor of the second is its pronoun concealed within the circumstance. It is permissible that *"min thamarah"* (from a fruit) is an explicative (*bayān*) placed before what it explains, as in your saying: "I saw from you a lion." This *"hādhā"* (this) points to what they were provided with, even if it falls upon one particular instance of it, as in your saying, pointing to a flowing river: "This water does not cease." For if you point to what you see by outward appearance, yet you only mean by that the known and constant kind, then the meaning is: this is like what we were provided with before, that is, before this, in this world. But because the resemblance between them became firm, its essence was made to be its essence. The fruit of Paradise was made like the fruits of this world so that the soul would incline toward it when it sees it, for natures incline toward what is familiar and shrink from what is unknown, and so that its excellence and the reality of the blessing in it would become clear to the soul; for if it were a kind not previously known, it would be supposed that it could not be otherwise than that. Or: "like what we were provided with before" in Paradise, because its food is similar in appearance. As is related from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him: one of them is brought a dish, and he eats from it; then another is brought, and he sees it as the first, and so he says that; and the angel says: "Eat, for the color is one but the taste is different." Or as it is reported that he ﷺ said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, a man of the people of Paradise reaches out for a fruit to eat it, but it has not yet reached his mouth before Allah, exalted is He, replaces it with another like it." The first is more fitting, for it preserves the generality of *"kullamā"*, since it indicates that they repeat this statement every time they are provided with it, not only on the first occasion. They display boastfulness and extreme astonishment, because of the great disparity between them in terms of pleasure, despite their unity in form and color, as if they were saying: "This is the very thing we were provided with in this world; so from where does it have this degree of pleasure and goodness?" Nor does what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, detract from this, namely that there is nothing in Paradise of the foods of this world except the name. For that is to explain the complete disparity between them in terms of pleasure and beauty, not to explain that there is no resemblance between them at all. How could it be so, since the application of names depends with certainty on specific unity? Moreover, this noble verse has been explained to mean that the pleasures of the people of Paradise, in comparison with what they were provided in this world of knowledge and acts of obedience, are varied in state; so they may mean: this is the reward of what we were provided in this world of acts of obedience. This is not supported by restricting it to the fruits, for Paradise and what is in it of kinds of honors are of the category of reward.

﴿And they will be brought it in resemblance﴾: a parenthetical clause (*i'tirāḍ*) confirming what precedes it. The pronoun in the genitive, on the first view, refers to what the content of the speech indicates, namely what they were provided in both abodes, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If he is rich or poor, Allah is more entitled to both of them﴾; that is, to the two kinds of the rich and the poor. On the second view it refers to the provision.

﴿and for them therein are purified spouses﴾: that is, free from the repugnant conditions found in the women of this world, such as menstruation, filth, the impurity of nature, and bad character; for purification is used of bodies, of morals, and of deeds. It is recited also as *"muṭahharāt"* (purified, feminine plural), and both are eloquent dialects: one says "al-nisā' fa'alat" and "fa'alna" (the women did), and "hunna fā'ilah" and "fawā'il" (they are doer, and doers). The poet said:

*And when the virgins were veiled with smoke, and hastened to set the pots, and grew weary.*

So the plural follows the form, and the singular follows the interpretation of the group. It is recited also as *"muṭṭahirah"* with the ṭā' shaddah and the kasrah on the hā', meaning *"mutaṭahhirah"*. *"Muṭahharah"* is more emphatic than *"ṭāhirah"* and *"mutaṭahhirah"*, to indicate that a purifier purified them, and that is none other than Allah, glorified and exalted is He. As for self-purification, it may be from their own selves, as during their ritual bathing. The word *"zawj"* (spouse) is applied to the male and the female, and in its original sense it is a name for what has a companion of its own kind; there is no consideration of procreation in its meaning, which is the basis of the continuation of the species, so that it would not be correct to apply it to the spouses of the people of Paradise, because they are eternal in it and independent of offspring. Just as the sense of being the basis for the continuation of the individual is not a condition in the meaning of the name "provision", such that this would invalidate its application to the fruits of Paradise.

﴿and they will abide therein forever﴾: that is, they will remain. *Khulūd* in its original sense is lasting stability for a long time, whether it endures or not. For this reason the three stones of the hearth and rocks are called *al-khawālid* (the everlasting ones), and the part of a human that remains in its state is called *khalad*. Had its basic meaning been permanence, it would not have been restricted by the word "eternity" in His saying, Mighty and Exalted is He: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾; and it would not have been used where there is no permanence. But what is meant here is certainly permanence, because of the verses and the established practices that point to it. As for what has been said, that bodies are composed of parts that are contrary in quality, liable to changes that lead to dissolution and separation, its basis is the analogy of that complete world to what is observed in the world of generation and corruption. Moreover, it is possible that the Creator, exalted is He, may restore them in such a way that change does not afflict them and dissolution certainly does not befall them, by making their parts varied in their qualities, equal in their powers, such that none of them, at the time of interaction, is able to transform the other; intertwined, interdependent, such that no part separates from another; and this proportion remains balanced among them forever, not altered by eating, drinking, movement, or other things. Know that most of the sensory pleasures, since they are confined to dwellings, foods, and marriages, as induction indicates, and since the foundation of all of these is lasting and stability (for every blessing, however great, is in the process of passing away and on the verge of vanishing, and it is clouded, not pure of the admixtures of pain), He gave good tidings to the believers of these things and of their permanence, to perfect joy and happiness. O Allah, grant us success in what pleases You, and keep us firm upon what leads to it, in belief and in action.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 26 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike a parable of a gnat or what is above it﴾: This begins the clearing of the sanctity of the revelation from any particular doubt that might attach to it, arising from the matter of the striking of parables, and an explanation of its wisdom and a realisation of the truth, following its being cleared of any general doubt, through the challenge, the silencing, and the confounding of all eloquent people, both of settled and of nomadic (lit. "of the towns and of the hair-tents") dwellings. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the hypocrites criticised the striking of parables with fire, darkness, thunder and lightning, and said: "Allah is too exalted and high for the striking of parables." 'Ata' narrated, may Allah be pleased with him: this criticism came from the polytheists. It is also narrated from him that when the saying of Allah (exalted is He) was revealed: ﴿O people, a parable has been struck, so listen to it﴾, and the verse: ﴿The parable of those who take protectors besides Allah﴾, the Jews said: "What worth do the fly and the spider have, that Allah (exalted is He) should strike parables with them?" And they made that a pretext for denying that it is from Allah (exalted is He), although it is not hidden from anyone who has discernment that it is not something in which doubt could be imagined, let alone denial; rather it is among the clearest proofs that it lies beyond the capacity of humans and descends from the Creator of powers and decrees. How could it not be so? Indeed, the parable, as has passed, is nothing but the bringing forth of the intended meaning in the form of a visible matter, and the adorning of the intelligible with the adornment of the sensible, and the depicting of elusive meanings in the form of the familiar, in order to win over the imagination and bring it down from its opposition to the intellect and its refusal of it, in grasping subtle realities and understanding refined fine points, so that it follows what the intellect requires and complies with what it approves. For this reason, parables became widespread in the divine books and the prophetic words, and spread through the expressions of the eloquent and the allusions of the wise. And from the necessity of similarity between the one represented and that by which it is represented in the ground of comparison: the representing of the great by the great and the small by the small. The Gospel has represented the rancour of the breast by the bran, and the opposition of the foolish by stirring up wasps. And there came in the expressions of the eloquent: "More comprehensive than an atom," "Bolder than the fly," "Keener of hearing than a tick," "Weaker than a gnat," and other examples too many to count. Modesty (al-haya') is the soul's change and withdrawal from what is blamed for it or censured because of it; one says: "The man became ashamed (haiya al-rajul)" and "he is shy (huwa haiyy)." Its derivation is from "life" (al-hayah), in the manner of the derivation of "shadhiya," "nasiya," and "hashiya," from "al-shazy," "al-nasy," and "al-hashy": one says "the horse's (shadhiya al-faras; nasiya; hashiya) those limbs became diseased," as if the one overtaken by modesty has his animal strength weakened and diminished. "Istahya" has the same meaning, except that it is transitive both directly and by means of a preposition: one says "istahyaytuhu" and "istahyaytu minhu," and the first is only transitive by means of a preposition, and one of the two yaʾs may be dropped from it, and from it is his saying:
"Do not the kings feel shame before us, and guard our sacred things, so that blood is not avenged by blood?"
And his saying:
"When they feel shame of water, it presents itself to them; they drink in a cup of roses."

So just as when it is ascribed to Him, glorified is He, affirmatively, as in his saying ﷺ: "Indeed Allah is shy before the Muslim elder who is grey-haired, to punish him" (ﷺ), and his saying, upon him be prayer and peace: "Indeed Allah is Modest and Generous; He is shy, when a servant raises his hands to Him, to return them empty until He places good in them" — what is meant by it is the specific abstention, by way of representation, where in the two noble hadiths is represented His abstaining from punishing the grey-haired, and the disappointing of the servant from His gift, by the abstention of one who abstains from them out of modesty. Likewise, when it is negated of Him (exalted is He) in specific matters, as in this noble verse, and in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And Allah is not ashamed of the truth﴾, what is meant is the negation of that specific abstention which resembles the abstention of the one who is ashamed of it, not the negation of the attribute of modesty from Him (exalted is He) altogether, as in your saying: "Indeed Allah is not described by modesty," because restricting the negation to some matters gives the impression that affirmation is in some respect proper to Him (exalted is He). So what is meant here is the non-abstention from striking a parable similar to the abstention of one who is ashamed to strike it. And in it is an allusion to the convergence of motives for striking it and the interlocking of impulses toward it, since modesty is only conceivable in acts that are acceptable to the soul and pleasing to it. And it is possible that its occurrence is by way of mushakala (conformity of expression), for they used to say: "Does not the Lord of Muhammad feel shame to strike a parable with trifling things?" as in the saying of one who said:
"Who will convey to all the tribes of Ya'rub that I built the neighbour before the house?"

The striking of a parable (darb al-mathal) means using it in its place of application and matching it to it, not its fashioning and creation in itself; otherwise the creation of the proverbs that circulate in their sources would be a striking of them, rather than their use afterwards in their places of application, since creation would be absent there. The parables that occur in the revelation, although their use is in their places of application, are themselves identical with their creation in themselves; yet the expression of it by "striking" is not in this sense but in the first sense, decisively. It is derived either from the striking of the seal, by the common factor of application: just as its striking is its application with its mould, so the use of parables in their places of application is their application to them; as if the places of application were moulds into which the parables are struck according to their form; but not in the sense that they arise in accordance with them after not having been so, rather in the sense that they are brought forth fitted to them, whether their creation then—as with the general run of revealed parables, whose places of application are their moulds—or before that—as with the other circulating proverbs, for although they were made beforehand, their application, that is, their being brought forth fitted to their places of application, only takes place at the time of striking. Or it is derived from the striking of clay on a wall so that it sticks to it, by the common factor of adhesion: as if the one who uses them sticks them to their places of application and makes them a striking that does not separate from them, because of the strength of their attachment to them. The position of "an yadriba" — on the supposition that "yastahyi" is transitive directly — is accusative as an object; but on the supposition that it is transitive by the preposition, then according to al-Khalil it is genitive, with "min" understood; and according to Sibawayh it is accusative, the verb reaching it after the deletion of the preposition. "Mathalan" is the object of "yadriba"; and "ma" is nominal, indefinite, which adds to the indefinite noun it accompanies indefiniteness and generality, as in your saying: "Give me a book, any (ma)"; as if it were said: "a parable of any kind of parables, whatever parable it may be"; so it is an adjective of what precedes it. Or it is particle, extra, for strengthening and emphasising the relation, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿So by a mercy from Allah﴾. "Ba'udatan" is a substitute for "mathalan"; or an explicative apposition according to those who permit it in indefinites; or an object of "yadriba"; and "mathalan" is a circumstantial accusative placed before it, because it is indefinite; or the two of them are its two objects, because it includes the meaning of making and rendering. It has also been read in the nominative, on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "it is a gnat"; and the clause, on the supposition that "ma" is a relative with its relative clause, has its beginning omitted, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Completion upon the one who did well﴾, according to the nominative reading; and on the supposition that it is an adjective of a qualifying noun, likewise. The position of "ma" on both readings is accusative, either as a substitute for "mathalan" or as an object of "yadriba"; and on the supposition that it is indefinite, it is an adjective of "mathalan" likewise. As for on the supposition that it is interrogative, then it is its predicate: as if, when their objection to striking a parable was conveyed, it was said: "What is a gnat? And what obstacle is there in it, that a parable should not be struck with it? Rather He (exalted is He) may represent with what is smaller than it and more insignificant, such as its wing, as occurred in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: 'If the world were weighed before Allah as much as the wing of a gnat, He would not have given the unbeliever a sip of water from it.'" "Al-ba'uth" (the gnat) is "fa'ul" from "al-ba'd," which is "the cutting," like "al-bad'" and "al-'adb"; it became specific to this kind, like "al-khumus" in the dialect of Hudhayl, from "al-khamsh," which is "scratching."

﴿So what is above it﴾: a coordination with "ba'udatan," on the supposition of its being accusative according to the aspects mentioned; and "ma" is relative or qualifying, its complement the adverbial phrase. As for on the supposition of its being nominative, it is coordinated with the first "ma," on the supposition of its being relative or qualifying; and as for on the supposition that it is interrogative, it is coordinated with its predicate, namely "ba'udatan," not with itself, as has been said; and the meaning is: "What is a gnat, then what is above it? Or is there something above it, so that a parable should not be struck with it?" Likewise on the supposition that it is an adjective of the indefinite noun, or extra; and "ba'udatun" is the predicate of the omitted pronoun. The mention of the gnat and "what is above it" from among the kinds of the parable is only by way of representation, not by specification and restriction; so it does not undermine the generality but rather establishes and confirms it, by way of priority. The "being above" is meant either as increase in the meaning that the representation intends—namely smallness and insignificance—or as increase in size and bulk, but not extending to any limit whatever, rather in general, like the fly and the spider. On the first supposition it is permissible that the second "ma" alone be an interrogative of denial, and the meaning is that Allah is not ashamed to strike a parable with a gnat: so what thing is above it in smallness and insignificance? Thus He (exalted is He) may represent with whatever He wills. A parallel in admitting both meanings is what is related that a man in Mina fell upon the rope of a tent, and when this was mentioned to 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, she said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'No Muslim is pricked by a thorn or anything above it, but a degree is written for him by it, and a sin is erased from him by it.'" For it admits what exceeds the thorn in smallness, such as the sting of an ant, by his saying, upon him be prayer and peace: "Whatever befalls the believer of harm is an expiation for his sins, even the sting of an ant," and what exceeds it of pain, such as the like of what is related about the heat.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 26 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿As for those who believed﴾: This begins the detailed explanation of what follows from the parable's divine wisdom, after establishing that it truly comes from Him (exalted is He). The *fa'* (then) indicates that what follows is a consequence of what precedes it. It is as if it were said: "He sets forth the parable, and as for those who..." etc. Placing the condition of the believers before what is related of the disbelievers requires no explanation of the reason. Opening both sentences with *amma* (as for) emphasizes the praise of the believers and the censure of the disbelievers, which is clear. *Amma* is a particle that contains the meaning of the conditional noun, and its verb is in the position of "whatever may be the case," which is why it is answered by *fa'*. Its purpose is to emphasize what it introduces and to detail the divisions in the speaker's mind. Sometimes all of them are mentioned, and sometimes only one of them is, as in the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾, etc. Sibawayh said: "*Amma Zaydun fa-dhahibun*" means: "Whatever the case regarding Zayd, he is certainly going." It is a firm assertion. The original arrangement was for the *fa'* to enter upon the sentence, since it is the response (*jaza'*). But they disliked placing it directly after the conditional particle, so they placed it on the predicate, and the subject was substituted for the condition in form. The term "those" refers to the known group of believers, just as the relative pronoun that follows refers to the group of disbelievers, not to those who accept the parable and those who reject it, because that would disrupt the meaning. That is, "as for the believers," ﴿they know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾, like all that comes from Him (exalted is He). *Al-haqq* (the truth) is that which is established and whose establishment is necessary, such that the intellect has no way to deny it. It does not mean whatever is established in any sense. The *lam* indicates that it is attested to be true, and that it has wisdoms and benefits. *Min* (from) indicates the figurative starting point, and its governing verb is omitted. It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring either to the pronoun hidden in *al-haqq*, or to the pronoun referring to the parable, or to its setting forth, meaning: existing and issuing from their Lord. The mention of the title of Lordship, together with the addition to their pronoun, is for their honour, and to indicate that the setting forth of the parable is an education for them and a guidance to what brings them to their perfection, which befits them. The clause takes the place of the two objects of *ya'lamun* (they know) according to the majority, and according to al-Akhfash, it takes the place of its first object while the second is omitted, meaning: "they know its truth to be established." Perhaps the mention of their knowledge without mentioning their acknowledgment of its consequence, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And those firmly rooted in knowledge say: "We believe in it; all is from our Lord"﴾, is to indicate the strength of the necessary connection between the two and its clarity, which needs no mention.

﴿And as for those who disbelieved﴾, from among those whose words and conditions have been related: ﴿they say: "What did Allah intend by this as a parable?"﴾ *Yaqulun* (they say) is preferred over *la ya'lamun* (they do not know), contrary to what the apparent sense of its counterpart would require, to indicate the completeness of their excess in disbelief and the extremity of their obstinacy in rebellion. Mere lack of knowledge of its truth is not equal to denying it and openly mocking it. It also prepares for enumerating what is censured of them within the reply, such as misguidance, wickedness, breaking the covenant, and other abominations that follow from their saying. Moreover, lack of knowledge of its truth does not apply to all of them, for among them are those who know it, but they say what they say out of stubbornness and obstinacy. Restricting it to the sense of not submitting and not accepting, which encompasses both ignorance and obstinacy, is a clear forcing of meaning. That said, it has been said that the proper form should have been: "And as for those who disbelieved, they do not know," to match its counterpart and to correspond to its pair. But since their saying this is a clear proof of their ignorance, it was used in its place by way of implication, so that it would serve as evidence against them. So reflect, and hold to the clear truth. *Madha* (what) is either composed of the interrogative word and *dha*, placed as the subject, whose predicate is *dha* in the sense of *alladhi* (which), and whose relative clause is what follows it, with the returning pronoun omitted. In that case, the best is for its answer to be in the nominative. Or it is treated as a single word in the sense of "what thing," in which case the best answer is in the accusative. *Al-irada* (will) is the soul's inclination and tendency toward an act, such that it moves it toward that act; or it is the power that is its source. The first is together with the act, and the second precedes it. Both are things that cannot be conceived in relation to the Exalted. Therefore they differed concerning His will (Mighty and Majestic is He). It was said that His will regarding His acts is that He is neither heedless nor compelled in them, and regarding the acts of others it is His command to them. Thus sins do not occur by His will (exalted is He). It was also said that His will is His knowledge that the matter includes the most perfect order and the most beneficial aspect, for this calls the capable one to achieve it. The correct view is that it is an expression for preponderance of one of the two sides of what is within capacity over the other, and specifying it with one aspect rather than another, or with a meaning that necessitates it. It is more general than choice, for choice is preponderance together with preference. The word *hadha* (this) contains contempt for what is pointed to and belittlement of it. *Mathalan* (parable) is in the accusative either as a specifier (*tamyiz*) or as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you﴾. Their intention by this grand statement was not to ask about the wisdom in setting forth a parable, nor to find fault with its containing benefit, since they acknowledge that it issues from Him (exalted, high is He). Rather, their aim was to alert by claiming that it is so base and worthless that no matter from among those that fall under His will may properly be connected to it, on the basis that it is impossible for the setting forth of such a parable to come from Him (glorified is He). Therefore His saying (Mighty and Majestic is He): ﴿He misguides many by it and guides many by it﴾ is an answer to that false claim and a refutation of it, by explaining that it contains a sublime wisdom and a beautiful end, namely that it is a means to guiding those who are prepared for guidance, and to misguiding those who are immersed in error. Thus the two verbs are placed in the position of the verb that occurs in the question, for emphasis in indicating their realization, since willing them is different from their actually occurring. It also avoids placing misguidance together with guidance in the same series under the heading of will, lest it imply that they are equal in their connection, which is not the case. The essential purpose of setting forth a parable is remembrance and guidance, as indicated by His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And these parables We set forth for people, that perhaps they may reflect﴾, and its like. As for misguidance, it is an incidental matter that follows from their own bad choice. The form of the future tense is preferred to indicate renewal and continuity. It has also been said that the two verbs are placed in the position of their verbal nouns, as if it were said: "He wills the misguiding of many and the guiding of many." Misguidance is mentioned before guidance, although the condition of the guided was mentioned before that of the misguided earlier, so that the first thing to strike their ears from the reply is a terrible matter that distresses them and weakens their resolve. This is the secret in singling out this benefit for mention. It has also been said that this is an explanation of the two sentences introduced by *amma*, and a recording that knowing that it is true is guidance, and that ignorance of the reason for its being set forth and denial of its excellent placement is misguidance and wickedness. The multitude of each group is considered only in relation to themselves, not in comparison to their opponents. Therefore the fewness of the people of guidance in relation to the people of misguidance does not detract from this, as indicated by His saying: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾, and the like. Considering their intrinsic multitude rather than their relative fewness serves to complete and multiply the benefit of setting forth the parable. It is also possible that what is meant by the first group is multitude in number, and by the latter group is multitude in excellence and nobility, as in the words of the one who said:

*Indeed the noble are many in the lands, even if they are few; as others are few, even if they are many.*

The attribution of misguidance, meaning the creation of error, to Him (glorified is He) is based on the principle that all things are created by Him (exalted is He), even though the acts of servants, in terms of acquisition (*kasb*), are ascribed to them. Taking it as ascribing an act to its cause is rejected by the explicit mention of the cause. It was read: ﴿He is misguided by it many, and guided by it many﴾, in the passive voice. The repetition of *bihi* (by it), although the first would suffice, serves to increase the emphasis on the causal relation and to confirm it.

﴿And He does not misguide by it﴾: that is, by the parable, or by its setting forth, ﴿except the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqin)﴾. This is coordinated with what precedes it, and completes the reply and refutation. It is an added specification of those whose misguidance is intended, by describing their ugly attributes that entail it, and an indication that this is not initial misguidance, but rather confirmation upon what they were already upon of various kinds of error, and an increase in it. It was also read: ﴿And it is not misguided by it except the defiantly disobedient﴾, in the passive voice. *Al-fisq* (defiant disobedience) in the linguistic sense means going out. It is said: "The ripe date (*rutbah*) went out of its skin," and "the mouse went out of its hole," meaning it came out. Ru'bah said:

*They go off in a wide valley and a deep depression, defiant, deviating from their course.*

In the legal sense, *fisq* is going out of obedience to Allah (Mighty and Majestic is He) by committing a major sin, of which persisting in minor sins is among the types. It has three levels. The first is negligence, which is committing it occasionally while disapproving of it. The second is immersion in indulging in it. The third is persistence in it while denying its ugliness. This last level is among the degrees of disbelief. So as long as the wicked person has not reached it, the name "believer" is not removed from him, because he possesses the affirmation upon which faith turns, and because of His saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾. The Mu'tazilah, since they held that faith is an expression for the totality of affirmation, acknowledgment, and action, and disbelief is an expression for denying the truth and rejecting it, and could not place the wicked person within either of these, made him a category between the two categories of believer and disbeliever, because each of them shares in some of his rulings. The intended sense of "the defiantly disobedient" here is those who are rebellious, obstinate in disbelief, transgressing its limits, among those of whom were related what was related of denying the speech of Allah (exalted is He) and mocking it. The singling out of misguidance for them, as following from the attribute of defiant disobedience and the ugly acts that were imposed upon them, serves to indicate that this is what prepared them for misguidance and led them to error. Their disbelief, their turning away from the truth, and their persistence in falsehood turned the faces of their attention away from reflecting on the wisdom of the parable, toward the baseness of the thing used as a parable, until their ignorance became firmly fixed and their error increased. So they denied it and said about it what they said.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 27:**

﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah﴾: an attribute of "the defiantly disobedient" (al-fasiqin), given to censure them and to confirm the defiant disobedience they are upon. *Al-naqd* (breaking) means undoing the structure of composite physical things, such as a rope, spun thread, and the like. Its use for annulling a covenant is a metaphor (*isti'ara*), since a rope is borrowed for the covenant because of the binding of one of the two parties' statements to the other. If it is accompanied by "rope" and "rope" is meant as the covenant, it is *tarshih* (a supporting term that reinforces the metaphor). If it is linked to "covenant," it is a hint (*ramz*) at what belongs to its associated meanings, and a notice of its place, and that what is mentioned has been borrowed for it, as one says: "A brave man who devours his rivals; a scholar from whom people draw water," to indicate that he is a lion in his bravery and a sea in his generosity.

*Al-'ahd* (covenant) means a binding pledge. One says: "He charged him with such-and-such" (*'ahida ilayhi kadha*) when he enjoined it upon him and bound him to it. What is meant here is either the covenant taken by the intellect, which is the proof established upon His servants, indicating His existence, His oneness, and the truthfulness of His Messenger (peace be upon him). On this basis His statement (exalted is He): ﴿And He made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes"﴾ has been interpreted. Or it is the apparent meaning of the word. Or it is what is taken from the Messengers (peace be upon them) on behalf of the nations: that when a Messenger confirmed by miracles is sent to them, they should believe him, follow him, not conceal his matter, his mention in the earlier scriptures, and not oppose his judgment, as His statement (Mighty and Majestic is He) indicates: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book: "You shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it"﴾, and its like. It has been said that the covenants of Allah (exalted is He) are three. The first: what He took from all the descendants of Adam (peace be upon him), that they should acknowledge His lordship. The second: what He took from the prophets (peace be upon them), that they should establish the religion and not divide over it. The third: what He took from the scholars, that they should make the truth clear and not conceal it.

﴿after its ratification﴾: *al-mithaq* is either a noun for that by which binding and firm commitment is achieved, or a verbal noun meaning "the act of binding," like *al-mi'ad* in the sense of "the promise." On the first reading, if the pronoun refers to the covenant, *al-mithaq* means what they bound themselves to, namely acceptance and commitment. If it refers to the name of Allah, what is meant is His signs, His books, and the warnings of His Messengers (peace be upon them). The noun being omitted (*al-mudaf mahdhuf*) is the case on both readings, meaning: after the establishment of His covenant. On the second reading, if the pronoun refers to the covenant, and *al-mithaq* is a verbal noun from the active form, the meaning is: after they bound it by acceptance and commitment; or: after Allah (Mighty and Majestic is He) bound it by sending down the books and the warnings of the Messengers. If it is a verbal noun from the passive form, the meaning is: after its being bound, either by their binding it through acceptance, or by His (exalted is He) binding it through sending down the books and the warnings of the Messengers.

﴿and cut what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾: this admits of every severance with which Allah (glorified and exalted is He) is not pleased, such as severing the ties of kinship, allying with unbelievers against believers, distinguishing between the prophets (peace be upon them) and the books in confirmation, abandoning the obligatory congregations, and all else that involves rejecting good or engaging in evil. For it severs what lies between Allah (exalted is He) and the servant of the connection which is the very purpose of every joining and separating. *Al-amr* (command) is the speech that seeks an act from a position of superiority. It has been said: from a position of elevation. By it the matter (*al-amr*), which is the singular of "affairs" (*al-umur*), is named, by naming the object with the verbal noun, since it is among what is commanded, as one says: "He has a concern" (*sha'n*), which means intention and seeking. This is because it is an effect of the concern. Likewise one says: "He has a thing" (*shay'*), which is a verbal noun of "he willed" (*sha'a*), because it is an effect of the will. The position of ﴿to be joined﴾ (*an yuwsal*) is either in the accusative as a substitute (*badal*) for the relative pronoun, or for its pronoun; the second is preferable both in wording and meaning.

﴿and spread corruption on the earth﴾: by preventing people from belief, by mocking the truth, and by severing the connections on which the order and wellbeing of the world's system revolve.

﴿Those are﴾: a reference to the defiantly disobedient, in view of their being characterized by the detailed ugly attributes mentioned. It contains a notice that they are distinguished by these in the most complete distinction, and that by this they are placed in the rank of perceptible things. The sense of distance in it indicates how far their rank is in corruption.

﴿they are the losers﴾: those who lost by neglecting the intellect's reflection, by failing to seize what would give them eternal life, by exchanging denial and slander of the signs for belief in them and reflection upon their realities and drawing from their lights, by buying breaking for fulfilment, corruption for righteousness, severance for connection, and punishment for reward.

(p-77)

﴿How do you disbelieve in God?﴾: This is a turn (*iltifat*) to address those who were mentioned. It is based on bringing up their earlier ugly deeds that were enumerated, because the anger that calls for direct address with rebuke and reproach has intensified. The interrogative is a denial (*istinkari*), not in the sense of denying that the act occurs, as in His (exalted) saying: ﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists with God and with His Messenger?﴾, etc. Rather, it denies the reality, deems it unlikely, and expresses wonder at it. In this there is an emphasis not found in directing the denial at disbelief itself, by saying, "Do you disbelieve?" Because every existing thing must necessarily exist in some state, if all the states of its existence are negated, then its existence is negated by way of demonstration. His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿while you were dead﴾, up to the end of the verse, is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the pronoun of address in "you disbelieve." It reinforces the denial and the deeming of it unlikely, through the great matters enumerated in it that call to faith and deter from disbelief, insofar as they are a general blessing, and insofar as they indicate complete power, like His (exalted) saying: ﴿And He created you in stages.﴾

"How" (*kayfa*) is in the accusative. According to Sibawayh it is treated as an adverb of time (*zarf*), and according to al-Akhfash as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). That is: in what state, or in which state, do you disbelieve in Him (exalted), while you were dead, that is, bodies without life: elements, nutrients, drops of semen, clots, shaped and unshaped? The word *amwat* is the plural of *mayyit*, like *aqwal* is the plural of *qayl*. Its application to those bodies is based on the absence of life absolutely, as in His (exalted) saying: ﴿a dead land﴾, and His (exalted) saying: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth.﴾

﴿Then He gave you life﴾: by breathing souls into you. The *fa'* indicates sequence, since the giving of life occurs right after their being dead, even though successive stages occurred to them in that condition, some of them following others at intervals, as was pointed out just above. ﴿Then He causes you to die﴾: that is, when your terms come to an end. That causing death is among the signs of power is clear. As for its being a blessing, it is because it is a means to the second life, which is the true life and the greatest blessing. The delay indicated by "then" is relative to the time of giving life, not to the time of living, since the time of causing death is not separated from it. ﴿Then He gives you life again﴾: by resurrection on the day when the Trumpet is blown, or for questioning in the graves. Whichever it is, it is delayed from the time of death, even though it follows the time of continuous death. ﴿Then to Him you will be returned﴾: after the gathering, not to anyone else, so He will recompense you for your deeds, good for good and evil for evil. Or: to Him you will be raised up from your graves for reckoning.

These verbs, although some of them are past and some future, cannot be made to coincide in time with that which is their circumstance. But the circumstance in reality is the knowledge connected to them, as if it were said: "How do you disbelieve in God while you know these states that prevent it?" Its outcome is wonder at its occurrence, together with the certainty of what negates it. The later giving of life and the return, which they deny, have been placed in the same series as the earlier giving of life and causing death, which they acknowledge, treating their capacity to know through the decisive signs they have witnessed as if it were actual knowledge, in removing excuses and pleas.

"Life" (*hayat*) is literally the sensory faculty, or whatever necessitates it, and by it the animal is named *hayawan*. Figuratively it is the growing faculty, because it is among its precursors. Likewise, in what pertains to humans, it refers to reason, knowledge, and faith, insofar as these are its perfection and its goal. "Death" (*mawt*), its opposite, is applied to whatever is opposed to each of these levels. He (exalted) said: ﴿Say: God gives you life, then causes you to die﴾; He (exalted) said: ﴿Know that God gives life to the earth after its death﴾; and He (exalted) said: ﴿Is one who was dead and whom We brought to life, and made for him a light by which he walks among the people?﴾ When He (exalted) is described by it, what is meant is the soundness of His being described by knowledge and power, which are necessary for this faculty in us, or a meaning subsisting in His essence (exalted), necessitating that.

It has been recited as *tarji'un* (you are returned) with an open *ta'*. The first reading is the more fitting to the context.

﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it﴾ (p-78): This is an affirmation of the denial (of the preceding clause), and a reinforcement of it from the two aspects mentioned. Its structure is changed from the structure of what precedes it, although both share the same purpose, to make clear the difference between them. For what relates to their own selves, namely giving life, causing death, and resurrection, is more effective in urging belief and restraining from disbelief than what relates to their livelihoods and what is similar to them. Also, making the pronoun a subject and the relative clause a predicate indicates the majesty (of Allah) in a manner that is not hidden. Placing the adverbial phrase before the direct object serves to hasten the joy by stating that it is beneficial to those addressed, and to create eagerness for it, as has passed. That is: He created for your sake all the existing things that are on the earth, so that you may benefit from them in the affairs of your worldly life, directly or indirectly, and in the affairs of your religion by reasoning from them to the states of the Creator, exalted is His majesty, and by taking each one of them as evidence for what suits it of the pleasures and pains of the Hereafter. The statement covers all that is on the earth, not the earth itself, except if by "earth" is meant the direction of the lower part, just as "heaven" is meant as the direction of the upper part. Indeed, it covers every part of its parts, for it is among what is in it, since the part is necessarily present in the whole. The word "jami'an" (all of it) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the second relative pronoun, reinforcing the generality contained in it. For every single item of what is on the earth, indeed every part of the parts of the world, has a role in the continuation of the suitable order upon which the arrangement of human interests depends. As for the aspect of livelihood, it is evident. As for the aspect of religion, there is nothing in the world that is related to the consideration (of reason) or that is not related to it, except that it is a proof of the Capable, the Wise, exalted is His majesty, as has passed in the explanation of His statement (exalted is He): ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾; even if no one actually reasons from it.

﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾: That is, He intended it by His will and His purpose, with a straight intention, without any diverting factor that turns Him away, nor any inclination that bends Him from willing the creation of something else within the folds of its creation, or other than that. It is derived from their saying: "istawa ilayhi ka-al-sahm al-mursal" (he went straight toward it like an arrow shot). Its specification by mention here is either because its realization is not present in the creation of the lower things, due to what is narrated from al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him) that the creation of the heavens intervened between the creation of the earth and its spreading out: Allah (exalted is He) created the earth in the place of Bayt al-Maqdis, like the shape of a flat stone (fihr), with smoke over it clinging to it; then He raised up the smoke, created the heavens from it, held the flat stone in its place, and spread out from it the earths. This is His statement (exalted is He): ﴿The two were a closed mass, then We parted them﴾. Or it is to show the completeness of care in originating the higher things. It was also said: "istawa" means "istawla" (he took control) and "malaka" (he possessed). The first is the apparent meaning. The word "thumma" (then) is to indicate the excellence and superiority it has over the creation of the lower things, not for temporal delay, for its precedence over the creation of what is on the earth, which is later than its spreading out, is beyond doubt, by His statement (exalted is He): ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾; and due to what is narrated from al-Hasan. What is meant by "the heaven" is either the celestial bodies, for turning toward them by will does not require prior existence; or the directions of height. ﴿Then He made them complete seven heavens﴾: that is, He perfected them, set them in order, and created them from the beginning, preserved from crookedness and fissures, not that He (exalted is He) made them complete after they had not been so. The fine placement of the juxtaposition of "taswiyah" (making complete) and "istiwa'" (turning) is not hidden. In it is an indication that there is no change in them by growth or decay, as in the lower things. The pronoun, according to the first aspect, refers to "the heaven," since it has the sense of a genus. It was said: it is the plural of "sama'a" or "samawa." According to the second aspect, it is ambiguous, explained by His statement (exalted is He): ﴿seven heavens﴾, as in their saying: "rubbahu rajulan" (a man, indeed him). According to the first aspect, it is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun. The delay in mentioning this wondrous creation after mention of the creation of what is on the earth, although it is stronger than it in indicating the perfection of irresistible power, as has been pointed out, is because the benefits attached to what is on the earth are more numerous, and the connection of human interests to that is more evident; although in the origination of the higher things there are also innumerable religious and worldly benefits. This is what they have said; and further verification and detail will come in "Ha Mim al-Sajda," with Allah's permission (exalted is He).

﴿And He is, of every thing, Knowing﴾: a parenthetical concluding clause (i'tirad tadhyili), confirming what precedes it: of the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is in them, in this wondrous pattern, which contains supreme wisdoms and fitting benefits. For His knowledge (may He be glorified and exalted) of all things, the apparent and the hidden, the manifest and the concealed, and what suits each one of them, requires that He create everything He creates in the most excellent manner. It was read: "wahwa" with the sukun on the ha', assimilating it (to the preceding sound), which is supported.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 30 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And [mention] when your Lord said﴾:
This is an explanation of another matter of the same kind as the matters preceding it, which confirm the denunciation and the astonishment. For the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, and the noble honours with which He distinguished him, as related here, are among the greatest blessings, calling his descendants to gratitude and faith and restraining them from disbelief and disobedience. It is also a confirmation of the content of what came before it, His (exalted) saying: ﴿He created for you all that is on earth﴾; and an clarification of how to dispose of and benefit from what is in it.

The shift of address, by directing it specifically to the Prophet ﷺ, indicates that the import of the speech is not something reached through rational proofs, like the matters observed, by which the disbelievers were admonished through direct address. Rather, its way is only the specific revelation to him, peace and blessings be upon him. Also, in mentioning the title of Lordship (rubbubiyya), which indicates the bringing to perfection, together with its attribution to his pronoun, peace and blessings be upon him, there is an indication of his honour, peace and blessings be upon him, which is not hidden.

And "idh" (إذ) is an adverb, established for the time of a past relation in which another similar relation occurred, just as "idha" (إذا) is established for the time of a future relation in which another similar relation occurs. For this reason, both must be annexed to clauses. Its accusative case is governed by an implied verb, of which the like has been stated explicitly in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And remember when you were few and He multiplied you﴾; and His saying (exalted): ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of ʿAd﴾.
