Directing the command to remember toward the time, rather than the events that occurred in it—although the events are the primary intended matter—is for the sake of emphasising the obligation of remembering them, because the obligation to remember the time entails, by way of demonstrative proof, the obligation to remember what occurred in it; and because the time encompasses them, so when it is brought to mind they are present with their details, as if witnessed directly. It was also said:

It is not that its accusative case is that of the object; rather, it is by way of interpreting it as "remember the event that occurred in it," by deleting the adverbial complement and placing the adverb in its position. In any case, it is conjoined to another implied verb, to which the speech extends. As if it were said to him, peace and blessings be upon him, after what had been revealed to him: the revelation that was addressed to the disbelievers, containing the details of the preceding matters, which restrains them from disbelief in Him (exalted):
Remind them of that, and recount to them this blessing, so that by it they may become alert to the falsehood of what they are in, and desist from it. As for what has been said, that the implied element is: "Give thanks for the blessing of the creation of the heavens and the earth," or: "Reflect upon that," it is not sound, since the requirement of the context is to remind the negligent of the obligations of gratitude and to alert them to what it requires; and where is that from his exalted station, peace and blessings be upon him?

It was also said:
Its accusative case is governed by His (exalted) saying: ﴿They said﴾; but this is refuted by the fact that it entails that it alone is the primary intended matter, not the rest of the narrative. It was also said: by what preceded in His (exalted) saying: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe﴾; but its distance is not hidden. It was also said: by an implied element indicated by the content of the preceding verse, like: "And He began your creation when He said..." etc. There is no doubt that there is no benefit in restricting the beginning of creation to that time. It was also said: by "He created you," or "He gave you life," as an implied element; and there is much to be said about this. It was also said: "idh" is superfluous; this is attributed to Abu ʿUbayd and Maʿmar. It was also said: it means "qad" (قد).

The "lam" in His saying, Mighty is He and speaking: ﴿to the angels﴾ is for conveying the message. The fronting of the prepositional phrase in this context is regular, because the spoken content is generally long, together with the concern for what has been fronted and the arousing of curiosity about what has been postponed, as has passed many times. "Malaʾika" (الملائكة) is the plural of "malak" (ملك), considering its origin, which is "malʾak" (ملأك), with the hamza being an added letter, like "shamaʾil" (الشمائل) as the plural of "shamʾal" (شمأل); and the "ta" is for emphasising the feminine form of the collective. Its derivation from "malak" is because it contains the sense of severity and strength. It was also said: it is inverted from "maʾlak" (مألك), from "al-alūka" (الألوكة), which is the message; that is, the place of the message; or it is "mursal" (مرسل) in the sense of a verbal noun with the meaning of a passive participle, for they are intermediaries between God (exalted) and people, so they are His messengers, or they are in the position of His messengers, peace be upon them.

The rational thinkers differed about their reality, after agreeing that they are existing beings, self-subsisting. The majority of the theologians held that they are subtle bodies, capable of taking various forms, citing that the messengers used to see them thus, peace be upon them. The philosophers held that they are immaterial substances, in reality distinct from the rational souls, and that they are more complete in power and more knowledgeable, flowing from them as the sun flows light. They are divided into two kinds: a kind whose concern is complete absorption in the knowledge of the Truth and freedom from occupation with anything else, as God, Mighty and Majestic, described them in His saying: ﴿They glorify Him night and day, they do not slacken﴾; and they are the exalted and the brought near. And a kind that governs the affair from heaven to earth, in accordance with what the pen of decree and destiny has run; and they are "those who arrange the affair" (المدبرات أمرا); among them are heavenly ones and among them are earthly ones. A group of Christians said: they are the virtuous human souls, separated from bodies.

It was related in explanation of their multitude that he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The heaven creaks, and it has right to creak: there is no place the size of a foot in it but there is an angel prostrating or bowing." It was also narrated that the children of Adam are a tenth of the jinn; these two are a tenth of the land animals; all of these are a tenth of the birds; all of these are a tenth of the sea creatures; and all of these are a tenth of the appointed angels of the earth; all of these are a tenth of the angels of the lowest heaven; all of these are a tenth of the angels of the second heaven; and so on...
up to the seventh heaven; then all those, in comparison with the angels of the Kursi, are a tiny little bit; then all of these are a tenth of the angels of one canopy of the canopies of the Throne, whose number is six hundred thousand; the length of each canopy, its breadth, and its thickness, when compared with it, the heavens and the earth and what is in them and what is between them have no perceptible measure in its regard; and there is not a measure of a span in it but there is an angel prostrating, or bowing, or standing, having a chanting of glorification and sanctification. Then all of these, in comparison with the angels who circle around the Throne, are like a drop in the sea; then the angels of the Tablet, who are the followers of Israfil, peace be upon him, and the angels who are the hosts of Jibril, peace be upon him, whose kinds no one counts, nor the lengths of their lives, nor the manners of their worship, except their Creator, the All-Knowing, the All-Aware; as He (exalted) said: ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾. It was also narrated that when he, peace and blessings be upon him, was taken up to the heaven, he saw angels in a place of honour, some walking opposite others; so the Messenger of God ﷺ asked Jibril, peace be upon him: "Where are they going?" Jibril said: "I do not know, except that I have seen them since I was created, and I have not seen any one of them before that." Then they asked one of them: "Since how long have you been created?" He said: "I do not know, except that God, Mighty and Majestic, creates a star every four hundred thousand years, and since He created me He has created four hundred thousand stars." Glory be to such a God; how great is His station! And how vast is His dominion!

It has been disputed about the angels to whom what was said was said. It was said: they are the angels of the earth. Al-Dahhak related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, that they were the chosen ones who were with Iblis when God, Mighty and Majestic, sent him to fight the jinn, since they were the inhabitants of the earth; they corrupted in it and shed blood, so he killed them except a few; he had driven them out of the earth and joined them to the islands of the seas and the summits of the mountains; and he inhabited the earth; God (exalted) lightened the worship for them, and gave Iblis the dominion of the earth, the dominion of the lowest heaven, and the treasury of Paradise; so he worshipped God (exalted) at times on earth, at times in heaven, and at other times in Paradise; then pride seized him, and what happened to him happened.

Most of the Companions and the Followers—may God's good pleasure be upon them—said that they are all the angels, because of the generality of the wording and the absence of a specifier.

His (exalted) saying: ﴿Indeed I am placing in the earth a successor﴾ is within the sphere of the accusative, as the object of "said"; and the form of the active participle is in the sense of the future; for this reason it operates as its verb does; and it contains what the imperfect form does not contain of indication that He is certainly the one who does that. It is from "jaʿl," in the sense of "taṣyīr" (making/rendering), which is transitive to two objects. It was said: the first of them is "khalīfa" (successor), and the second is the adverbial phrase fronted, according to what the grammatical craft requires; for the two objects of "taṣyīr" in reality are the subject and predicate of "ṣāra" (became); the first of them is the first, and the second is the second; and they are a subject and predicate. The original is: "in the earth a successor"; then it was said: "a successor became in the earth"; then: "making a successor in the earth"; so its meaning, after all these alternatives, is: "I am making a successor from among the successors, or a specific successor, existing in the earth." For the predicate of "ṣāra" in reality is the implied "being," which governs the adverbial phrases. There is no doubt that this is not at all what the context requires; rather, what the context requires is the announcement of making Adam a successor in it, as the answer of the angels, peace be upon them, indicates. So then His (exalted) saying: ﴿successor﴾ is the second object, and the adverbial phrase is connected to "jāʿil," fronted over the explicit object, for the reason already mentioned, concerning the arousing of curiosity about what is postponed; or it is governed by an implied element that functions as a circumstantial qualifier of what follows it, because it is indefinite. As for the first object, it is omitted, relying on the context that indicates it, as in His saying (exalted): ﴿And do not give the foolish your wealth which God has made for you a means of support﴾, where the first object has been omitted, which is the pronoun referring to "wealth," due to the indication of the situation; and likewise in His saying (exalted): ﴿And let not those who are stingy with what God has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them﴾, where the first object has been omitted, due to the indication of "yabkhalūna" (they are stingy) upon it; that is: "Let not the stingy think that their stinginess is good for them." There is no doubt about the establishment of the indication here; as for if it is taken as an omission at the time of the reported event, it is clear, because it occurs in the course of his, peace and blessings be upon him, mention, as we shall detail; as if it were said: "I am creating a human from clay, and placing in the earth a successor." As for if it is taken to mean that it was not omitted there, but rather it was said—for example—"and making him a successor in the earth," but it was omitted at the time of reporting, then the indication is what has been mentioned from the answer of the angels, peace be upon them. The allamah al-Zamakhshari said, in his commentary on His (exalted) saying: ﴿When your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I am creating a human from clay"﴾:

"If you say: how is it correct that He says to them, 'a human,' when they did not know what a human is, nor were they acquainted with him?

I say: its aspect is that He had said to them, 'Indeed I am creating a creature whose description is such and such'; but when He related it, He confined Himself to the name."

End.

Since it is permissible to suffice, when relating that detail, with the mere name, without any indication pointing to it, what then do you think of what we are concerned with, when there is an evident indication with it?!

It is also permissible that it be from "jaʿl" in the sense of "khalq" (creation), transitive to one object, which is "khalīfa"; and the adverbial phrase is in its connection and fronting, as has passed; in that case, what will come later of the angels' speech is not consequent upon it directly, but through an intermediary. For it has been related that when He (exalted) said to them, ﴿Indeed I am placing in the earth a successor﴾, they said: "Our Lord... and what will that successor be?" He (exalted) said: "He will have descendants who will corrupt in the earth, envy one another, and some will kill others." Thereupon they said what they said; and God (exalted) knows best.

And the "khalīfa" is one who succeeds another and takes his place; it is "faʿīl" in the sense of "fāʿil"; and the "ta" is for intensification; and what is meant by it is:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 30 (part 2 of 2):

Either it refers to Adam, peace be upon him, and his descendants. He is mentioned alone only because his mention makes theirs unnecessary, just as a tribe is referred to by the name of its ancestor, such as "Mudar" and "Hashim." From this comes the caliphate (khilafa, succession or vicegerency) of the Quraysh. Or it refers to whoever succeeds, from the verb "khalafa yakhlufu," so that it includes him, peace be upon him, and the other successors among his offspring. The meaning of khilafa is either:

the vicegerency from Him, glory be to Him, in executing His rulings, carrying out His commands among people, and governing creation, but not because He has any need for this, rather because of the inadequacy of the readiness of those made successors and their unfitness to receive the overflow directly, so it is restricted to the elite among his descendants. Or it is the succession of those who were on the earth before that, in which case it includes everyone.

﴿Qalu﴾ (they said): this is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) that answers what the minds would naturally move toward, as if it were said: "What did the angels say at that time?" So it is said: ﴿They said: Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it?﴾ This also comes from "ja'ala" (to place, make), which is transitive to two objects, and what has been said about the first applies to both. The apparent view is that the first object is the word "man" (من), and the second is omitted, relying on what was mentioned in the preceding speech, just as the first was omitted there, relying on what is mentioned here. One of them said:

"Do not leave us in consolation for you, for indeed ... the enemies have long slandered us,"

with the second object omitted, meaning: do not leave us grieving over your consolation. The meaning is: "Will You place in it, as a successor, one who causes corruption in it?" The first adverbial phrase (فيها, "in it") is connected to "tajalu" (You place), and its being placed first is for reasons already mentioned many times. The second is connected to "yufsidu" (causes corruption), and its purpose is to emphasize the improbability, because appointing one who corrupts in the very place of his corruption carries a remoteness that is absent in appointing him elsewhere. This is it. It has also been permitted that it comes from "ja'l" in the sense of "khalq" (creating), which is transitive to one object, namely the word "man." But you know that the focus of their astonishment is not the creation of one who causes corruption on the earth, how could it be, since what follows it of the circumstantial clause, which declares their greater right to it than him, requires its invalidity necessarily? For there is no validity to a claim of greater right to creation from him when they themselves are created. Rather, its focus is that he be made a successor to develop the earth and reform it, by executing the rulings of God, the Exalted, and His commands, or that there be appointed in place of those who are naturally inclined to obedience one whose kind is by nature inclined to corruption and the shedding of blood. Although he, peace be upon him, is exempt from this, his appointment entails the appointment of his offspring, who are generally not free of it. They only expressed their astonishment in seeking to uncover what was hidden from them of the wisdoms that surpass those corruptions and nullify them, and in asking about what would remove their doubt and guide them to knowing the virtues that he, peace be upon him, possesses, which make him fit for this. It is like a student's question about what arises in his mind, not an objection to the act of God, glory be to Him, nor a doubt that it includes wisdom and benefit in general, nor a slander against him, peace be upon him, nor against his descendants by way of backbiting, for their rank is too exalted for such things to be imagined of them. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾ ﴿who do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾. They knew what they said either by information from God, the Exalted, as was reported earlier, or by receiving it from the Preserved Tablet, or by inference from what was fixed in their minds about the exclusivity of infallibility to them, or by analogy of one of the two worlds (jinn and humans) to the other.

﴿And shed blood﴾: al-safk, al-safh, al-sabk, and al-sakb are kinds of pouring. The first two are specific to blood, indeed the first is used only for unlawful blood, that is, by killing souls unlawfully and without right. Expressing it as "shedding blood" is because it is the worst kind of killing and the most heinous. It has been read as "yusfiku" with a damma on the fa', and as "yusfiku" and "yasfiku," from "asfaka" and "safaka." It has also been read as "yusfaku" in the passive, and the pronoun referring back to "man," whether relative or descriptive, is omitted, meaning: he sheds blood among them.

﴿And we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾: this is a circumstantial clause, confirming the earlier astonishment and emphasizing it, in the manner of one who works hard at serving his master while ordering others to do so, saying: "Will You employ the disobedient while I strive in it?" It is as if it were said: "Will You appoint one whose descendants are by nature inclined to corruption, while there exists one who is not at all of that nature?" The purpose is to present their greater right to the succession and to ask about what preferred him over them, together with the obstacles expected from them, not out of self-admiration or boasting. It seems they perceived in themselves the appetitive power, whose extreme vice is corruption on earth, and the irascible power, whose extreme vice is shedding blood, so they said what they said, and they were unaware that if reason commands these two and trains them toward good, there results from that a height of rank that falls short of reaching the level of the rational power when it acts alone, such as comprehending the details of particular affairs, deriving crafts, extracting benefits of existing things from potentiality to actuality, and other matters entrusted to the office of succession.

Tasbih (glorification): declaring God, the Exalted, free of and far removed from what does not befit His majesty, in belief, speech, and action, from "sabaha fi al-ard wa al-ma'" (he swam in the land and the water), when he went far in them and penetrated deeply. From this comes "faras sabub" (a horse that runs far), meaning one with wide stride. Likewise taqdis (sanctification) of Him, the Exalted, from "qadasa fi al-ard" (he went into the land and went far). It is said "qaddasahu," meaning "tahharahu" (purified him), since purifying a thing removes it far from filth.

The ba' in ﴿bi-hamdika﴾ is connected to an omitted verb which is in the circumstantial position relative to the pronoun, meaning: we declare You free of everything that does not befit Your station, while joined with Your praise for the blessings You have bestowed upon us, of which our being guided to this worship is one. So tasbih is to manifest the attributes of majesty, and hamd is to recall the attributes of bounty. The lam in ﴿laka﴾ may be extra, meaning "we sanctify You"; or it may be connected to the verb, as in "sajadtu lillah" (I prostrated to God); or it may be explanatory, as in "suqyan laka" (watering to you), in which case it is connected to an omitted verb, meaning: we sanctify a sanctification for You, that is, we describe You with what befits You of exaltedness and might, and we declare You free of what does not befit You. It is also said that the meaning is: we purify our souls of sins for Your sake. As if they set corruption, whose greatest form is associating partners with God, against glorification, and the shedding of blood, which is defiling the soul with the most hideous crimes, against purifying the soul of sins, not as self-praise, nor to display favor, but as an explanation of the reality.

He said: this is a resumptive sentence, as preceded. ﴿I know what you do not know﴾: the intention is not to state that He, the Exalted, knows things they do not know, whatever they may be, for that is something about which they have no doubt, so as to need to be alerted to it, especially with emphasis. Rather, it is to state that in him, peace be upon him, there are meanings that call for his appointment, since these are what was hidden from them, and on them they built their astonishment and their judgment of improbability. So "ma" (what), whether relative or descriptive, refers to those meanings. The meaning is: "I know what you do not know of the motives for the succession in him." He did not limit himself to stating that these were realized in him, peace be upon him, by saying, for example, that in him is what requires it, without referring to God's comprehensive knowledge of it and their unawareness of it, in order to magnify his status, and to indicate that the matter of God, the Exalted, is founded on firm knowledge and perfected wisdom, and that their words came from heedlessness. It is also said that its meaning is: "I know, regarding his appointment, of benefits that are hidden from you." This is guidance for the angels that all of God's acts, the Exalted, are good and wise, even if the aspect of goodness and wisdom is hidden from them. You know that this implies they did not know this before, and their astonishment would be based on their hesitation about whether this act includes some wisdom, and that does not befit their station, for they know that it includes some wisdom, but they are uncertain what it is: whether it is a matter that returns to the pure ruling of God, Mighty and Majestic, or to a virtue on the part of the one appointed. So God, glory be to Him and exalted, first explained to them in general and vague terms that in it are virtues hidden from them, so that they would look forward to them, then revealed to them a portion of them, so that they would witness it openly, the marvelous work and wisdom would become manifest to them, and their doubt would be entirely removed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 31:

﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾: This begins a detailed account of what occurred after the general answer, confirming its content and explaining its ambiguity. It is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "He said" (qāla). Beginning with the narration of the teaching indicates, on its apparent reading, that the preceding conversation that was related took place after Adam's creation, in his presence. This is the more fitting reading, given the angels' attentiveness to his circumstances, namely that it was said, immediately after the breathing of the spirit into him: "Indeed I am placing him as a successor (khalīfa)." Then what was said was said, as was indicated (p-84). Mentioning him, peace be upon him, by his proper name serves to further specify the intended referent of "successor," and because mentioning him by the title of succession does not suit the context of laying down its foundations. The name is non-Arabic (aʿjamī). The more likely view is that its pattern is fāʿil, like shālikh, ʿādhir, ʿābir and fāligh, not afʿal. As for deriving it from al-udma or al-adama (with a fatḥa), meaning "pattern/exemplar," or from adīm al-arḍ ("surface of the earth"), based on what is related from the Prophet ﷺ that "He (exalted is He) took a handful from all the earth, its plain and its rough parts, and created Adam from it," and for this reason his offspring differ in colour, this is one approach. Deriving it from al-adm or al-adama, meaning "affection," is far-fetched, like deriving Idris from al-dars, Ya'qub from al-'aqb, or Iblis from al-iblas.

The ism (name), in terms of etymological derivation (ishtiqāq), is that which serves as a sign of a thing and an indicator that raises it to the mind, from among words, attributes and actions. Its customary usage is for a word assigned to a meaning, whether singular or compound, whether it is the subject or the predicate, or a link between them. Its technical usage (iṣṭilāḥ) is for a singular term that signifies a meaning in itself, not connected with time. What is intended here is either the first or the second, and the second entails the first, since knowledge of words, in terms of their signifying meanings, is preceded by knowledge of them. Teaching, in the strict sense, is an expression for an act that necessarily results in knowledge, without fail. This is not achieved merely by the attribution of the teacher, but depends on the learner's readiness to receive the overflow (fayḍ) and to take it from its source, as was mentioned in the explanation of "guidance" (hudā). This is the reason for choosing it over ʿilām and inbāʾ (informing and reporting), since those depend only on hearing news, which both humans and angels share. By it, his superiority to them for the succession, peace be upon them, becomes evident, since their nature is not disposed to comprehend the detailed circumstances of corporeal particulars by report. Thus the meaning of His (exalted is He) teaching him is that He creates in him, at that time, according to the requirement of his readiness, a detailed, necessary knowledge of the names of all named things, their states, and their properties appropriate to each of them. Or He casts into his heart, in detail, that this is a horse and its characteristics are such-and-such, and that is a camel and its condition is such-and-such, and so on regarding the states of existing things. He receives them, peace be upon him, in accordance with what his readiness requires and what his capacity, which branches from his nature, demands, a nature containing diverse temperaments, differing powers and distinct elements. Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with them, said: He taught him the names of all things, even the bowl (qaṣʿa), the small bowl (quṣayʿa), the large dish (jafna) and the (vessel) miḥlab, and He connected the benefit of each thing to its kind. It was also said: the names of what has been and what will be until the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: the meaning of His (exalted is He) words "And He taught Adam the names" is that He created him from different parts and diverse powers, readied to perceive types of perceptibles, whether intelligibles, sensibles, imaginables or estimatives, and inspired him with knowledge of the essences of things, their names, their properties, their realities, the foundations of knowledge, the rules of crafts, the details of their tools, and the modes of their use. Then the conversation mentioned would have been before his creation, peace be upon him. It was also said: the teaching is on its apparent meaning, but there are omitted clauses (jumal maṭwiyya) to which the mentioned matter is conjoined, meaning: so He created him, shaped him, breathed into him the spirit, taught him, and so on.

﴿Then He presented them to the angels﴾: The pronoun refers to the named things, indicated by the names, as in His (exalted is He) words "and the head glistened with grey" (wa-ishtaʿala al-raʾsu shayban). The masculine form is used to give precedence to rational beings over others. It is also read as "ʿaradahunna" and "ʿaradahā," meaning: He presented their named things (musammayātihinna or musammayātihā). In a hadith it is stated that He (exalted is He) presented them like ants (dharr). Perhaps He, mighty and majestic, presented to them, from the individuals of each species, what could serve as a model from which the states of the rest and their rulings might be known.

﴿He said: Tell Me the names of these﴾: as a rebuke to them and a demonstration of their inability to fulfil what they had hoped for regarding the matter of succession. For conduct, management and the establishment of justice without knowledge of the ranks of readinesses and the measures of rights is almost impossible. Inbāʾ (telling) is a report containing information, and for this reason it takes the place of each of the two (informing and reporting). What is intended here is what is free of that. Its being preferred over ikhbār (reporting) serves to signal the elevated status of names and the magnitude of their importance, since naba' (news) is only applied to a weighty report and a great matter.

﴿If you are truthful﴾: that is, in your claim that you are more deserving of the succession than the one I have appointed, as your statement indicates. Truthfulness (taṣdīq), as it applies to speech in terms of its explicit content, may also apply to it in terms of what it necessarily entails from reporting. For the lowest rank of entitlement is knowing the names of what is on the earth. As for what has been said, that the meaning is: "in your claim that I am appointing among the earth those who cause corruption and shed blood," this is not what the context requires, even if it is interpreted as: "in your claim that I appoint one whose dominant trait is corruption and shedding of blood, without his having any other distinguishing quality," since it has no connection to their matter with the reporting. The apodosis of the conditional is omitted, because what is mentioned indicates it.

﴿They said﴾: This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) occupying the place of an answer, as though it were said: "What did they say then? Did they discharge the obligation of what they were charged with, or not?" So it was said: they said: ﴿Glory be to You﴾. It was said that it is a proper noun (ʿalam) for tasbih (glorification), and it is hardly ever used except in construction with a following noun (muḍaf). It has come unconstructed, irregularly, as indeclinable (ghayr munṣarif) due to definiteness and the added alif and nun, as in his words:

*"Glory be to ʿAlqama the boaster..."*

As for what occurs in his words:

*"Glory be to Him, then glory, which we seek refuge in..."*

it was said that he declined it (ṣarafahu) out of necessity (li-l-ḍarura). It was also said that it is an indefinite verbal noun (maṣdar munakkar), like "ghufran", and not a verbal noun in the sense of an ism al-maṣdar (noun of verbal action). Its meaning, according to the first view, is: "We glorify You above what is not befitting Your most sacred Majesty, among the matters of which is that Your actions are devoid of wisdoms and benefits." By this they meant a glorification arising from complete tranquillity of the soul and firm certainty that the appointment of Adam, peace be upon him, comprises profound wisdoms. According to the second view, it means: "You are exalted above that, an exaltation arising from Your very essence." He intended by it that they said it in submission, having known in general terms that he, peace be upon him, would be charged with what they had been charged with, and that he would be able to do what they had been unable to do, of what the caliphate depends upon.

His words, Mighty and Exalted is He: ﴿We have no knowledge except what You have taught us﴾ are an acknowledgment from them of their incapacity regarding what they had been charged with. Its meaning is: "We have no knowledge except what You have taught us, in accordance with our receptivity, of the sciences suited to our world; and we have no capacity for what lies outside the scope of our preparedness, such that even if we were prepared for it, You would have bestowed it upon us." The "mā" in ﴿mā ʿallamtanā﴾ is either a relative pronoun (mawṣūla) whose returning pronoun has been omitted from its relative clause, or it is a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle. They negated knowledge of the names from themselves in an emphatic manner, in that they did not restrict themselves to declaring its absence by saying, for example, "We have no knowledge of them," but rather made it among the category of things they do not know, and they indicated that its being in that category is too clear to need explanation.

﴿Indeed You, You are the All-Knowing﴾: the One from whom nothing is hidden. This is an indication of their verification of His words (Exalted is He): ﴿Indeed I know what you do not know﴾. ﴿The All-Wise﴾: that is, the One who perfects His creatures and is the doer of them, according to what wisdom and benefit require. The second word is a predicate following a predicate, or an adjective of the first. The word ﴿anta﴾ is a separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl), having no place in the grammatical structure (i'rab); or it has a place in it, sharing the case of what precedes it, as stated by al-Farrāʾ; or the case of what follows it, as stated by al-Kisāʾī. It was also said that it is an emphatic appositive of the particle "kāf" (you), as in your saying: "I passed by you yourself." It was also said that it is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is what follows it, and the whole clause is the predicate of "inna" (indeed). This clause is a reason (taʿlīl) for the restriction of their knowledge to what God (Exalted is He) taught them, and for what is understood from it of Adam's knowledge of what was hidden from them. So it is as though they said: "You are the Knower of all the known things, among which is Adam's preparedness, peace be upon him, for which we are far from being prepared, of the hidden sciences related to the kinds of created beings that are on the earth, upon which revolves the sphere of the caliphate of the All-Wise, who does only what wisdom requires; and among its elements is the teaching to Adam, peace be upon him, of what is receptive of universal sciences and particular knowledge connected with the rulings that apply to what is on the earth, and the establishment of the matter of the caliphate upon them."

He said: [this is] a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf), as has already passed. ﴿O Adam, inform them﴾, that is, tell them. [The verb] anbiʾhum ("inform them") was preferred over anbiʾnī ("inform me"), as occurred in the case of the angels, even though the purpose is also achieved with it, which is the manifestation of Adam's excellence over them, peace be upon them. This makes clear the evident difference between the two matters. It also signals that his knowledge, peace be upon him, of these names is a clear matter, not in need of what functions as a test, and that he, peace be upon him, is worthy of teaching them to others. It is also read with the hamza changed to a yāʾ, and also with it omitted, and the hāʾ is kasra in both readings. ﴿of their names﴾, which they had been unable to know, and they acknowledged the shortness of their aspirations in reaching their rank.

﴿So when he informed them of their names﴾: the fāʾ is eloquent (faṣīḥa, a fāʾ that signals an implied element), conjoining the conditional clause to an omitted element that the context requires and that the discourse implies, to signal that it is settled and that it need not be mentioned, and to indicate that it occurred as quickly as possible, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So when he saw it [placed] firmly before him﴾, after His words, Glorified is He: ﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you﴾. The use of the nouns in the place of the pronoun is to show the complete concern with their matter, and to signal that he, peace be upon him, informed them of them in detail, not in summary. The meaning is: he informed them of their names in detail, and made clear to them the conditions of each of them, their properties, and their rulings related to livelihood and the afterlife. So they knew that, when they saw that he, peace be upon him, did not falter in any of the details he mentioned, along with the agreement between the names and what they name in terms of correspondences and resemblances, and other indicators that necessitate the truthfulness of his statements, peace be upon him. So when he informed them of that, He, Mighty and Majestic, said, confirming the previous general answer and bringing it to mind: ﴿Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth?﴾ However, this is not to confirm Himself, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Did your Lord not promise you a good promise?﴾ and its like, but rather to confirm what it indicates of the realization of the motives for the caliphate in Adam, peace be upon him, since its fulfilment becomes manifest. The mention of ﴿what you do not know﴾ under the heading of the unseen, joined to the heavens and the earth, is for emphasis in showing the completeness of the comprehensiveness of His encompassing knowledge and the extent of its breadth, along with signalling that what appeared of their incapacity and of Adam's knowledge, peace be upon him, is among the matters related to the people of the heavens and the people of the earth. This is clear evidence that what is meant by ﴿what you do not know﴾ in what preceded is what was pointed to there, as if it were said: Did I not tell you that I know in it [i.e., in Adam] of the motives for the caliphate what you do not know in it, namely this which you have witnessed?

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And I know what you reveal and what you have been concealing﴾ are conjoined to the clause ﴿Did I not tell you﴾, not to ﴿I know﴾, since it does not fall under the saying. The word "mā" in both places is a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: I know what you reveal and what you conceal. The change of style signals the continuation of their concealment. It has been said: what they reveal is their saying: "Will You place in it...", etc., and what they conceal is their inner conviction that they are deserving of the caliphate and that He, Exalted is He, will not create a creation more excellent than them. It is related that when God, Exalted is He, created Adam, peace be upon him, the angels saw his wondrous nature and said: Let Him do what He wills; our Lord will not create any creation except that we will be more honoured before Him than it. It has also been said: it is what Iblis concealed within himself of arrogance and refusal to prostrate. Then attributing the concealment to all of them is of the type of saying: "The Banu so-and-so killed so-and-so," when the killer is one of them.

They said: the noble verse indicates the nobility of humankind, the distinction of knowledge, and its excellence over worship; that this is the basis for the caliphate; that teaching may properly be applied to God, Exalted is He, even though the term "teacher" (muʿallim) may not be applied to Him, because it is customarily restricted to one who practises it as a profession; that languages are revelation-based (tawqīfiyya, meaning that they are divinely taught and not merely conventional), since names indicate words, specifically or generally, and teaching them clearly consists of presenting them to the learner while explaining their meanings to him, and this requires a prior establishment, which can only come from God, Exalted is He; that the concept of wisdom (ḥikma) is additional to the concept of knowledge; that repetition is more likely; that the knowledge and perfections of the angels accept increase, while the philosophers denied this for the highest class of them, and interpreted in this sense His words, Exalted is He: ﴿There is none of us but that he has a known station﴾; that Adam is more excellent than these angels, because he, peace be upon him, is more knowledgeable than them; and that He, Exalted is He, knows things before they occur.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 34 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when We said to the angels﴾: this is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with the first temporal clause. It is in the accusative governed by the implied verb that governed that clause, or by an independent governing verb conjoined to its governor, as the narrative is conjoined to the narrative. The meaning is: "Remember the time when We said to them." It has also been said that it is governed by a verb indicated by the context, meaning: "They obeyed at the time when We said..." etc. You have already learned what is involved in such constructions. The singling out of this statement for mention, although the apparent expectation would be to present it in the same manner as the preceding reported statements connected with it, is to indicate that what falls within its scope is a sublime, independent narrative, worthy of being mentioned and recalled on its own. The shift to the first-person plural ("We") serves to manifest majesty and to cultivate awe, along with what it contains of emphasis on independence. Likewise, the use of the noun "the angels" in place of a pronoun is for the same reason. The discussion concerns the particle "li-" (to) and its placement before its object together with its prepositional complement, as has already been explained. It has also been read with a ḍamma on the tāʾ of "al-malāʾika" (the angels), by assimilation to the ḍamma of the jīm in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾; and it has been read with a kasra on the dāl in His words, exalted is He: "Al-ḥamdu lillāhi" (All praise is due to Allah), by assimilation to the kasra of the lām; and this is a weak dialect. Prostration (sujūd) linguistically means submission and humbling oneself; in the Sharīʿa it means placing the forehead upon the ground with the intention of worship. It has been said: they were commanded to prostrate to him (peace be upon him) as a form of greeting and honouring, in exaltation of him, in acknowledgment of his merit, in fulfilment of the right of his having been taught, and as an apology for what had occurred from them concerning him. It has also been said: they were commanded to prostrate to Allah (exalted is He), and Adam was made the direction (qibla) of their prostration only to magnify his status, or as the cause for its obligation. Thus it is as though Allah (exalted is He), when He created him as a model for all originated beings and a copy encompassing the connection of the spiritual world with the physical world and their blending in a wondrous pattern, commanded them to prostrate to Him (exalted is He), because of what they witnessed of His great power. In that case the lām is as in the words of Hassan (may Allah be pleased with him):

Was he not the first to pray toward your qibla,
and the most knowledgeable of people in the Qur'an and the Sunnah?

Or it is as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾. The first explanation is the more evident. As for His words, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿So they prostrated﴾: this is conjoined to "We said," and the fāʾ indicates their haste in complying and their lack of hesitation in that. It is related from Wahb that the first to prostrate was Jibril, then Mikail, then Israfil, then ʿIzrāʾīl, then the rest of the angels (peace be upon them all). As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿except Iblis﴾: this is a continuous exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil), because he was a jinn who was singular, submerged among thousands of angels, having the attributes of them; so they (the angels) predominated over him in "they prostrated." Then he was excepted as one of them. Or because among the angels there is a species who reproduce, called "the jinn," as related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), and he was one of them. Or because the jinn too were commanded to prostrate to him, but the mention of the angels sufficed in place of mentioning them. Or it is a discontinuous exception (munqaṭiʿ), and it is a non-Arabic name, and for this reason it is not declined. Whoever took it to be derived from "iblās" (despair), which is "yaʾs," said: it is formed in analogy to non-Arabic names, since no one was named with it, and so it was like a non-Arabic name.

Know that what this noble verse requires, and what is in the surah of al-Aʿrāf in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," so they prostrated, except Iblis﴾, and the verse..., and what is in the surah of Banī Isrāʾīl, the surah of al-Kahf, and the surah of Ṭāhā, in His words, exalted is He: "And when We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam,' so they prostrated," and the verse..., is that the prostration of the angels was consequent solely upon the immediate command issued after his creation, his formation, and the breathing of the spirit into him; as is hinted at by the narration of their compliance with the expression of prostration, not with the event which the conditional command was tied to. But what is in the surah of al-Ḥijr in His words, exalted and most high is He: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I will create a human from clay, from black mud altered"﴾ ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down to him in prostration﴾ ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾; and what is in the surah of Ṣād in His words, exalted is He: ﴿When your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I will create a human from clay"﴾, to the end of the verse, both by their apparent meaning require that it be consequent upon the conditional command found in them, without anything intervening between them other than what the eloquent fāʾ (al-fāʾ al-faṣīḥa) expresses of creation, proportioning, and the breathing of the spirit into him (peace be upon him). It is related from Wahb that the prostration occurred, as soon as the spirit was breathed into him, without delay. The interpretation of the preceding verses holds what is in them of command to be a report of the conditional command after the conditioned matter has been realised in general terms; for then it has the ruling of an immediate command. This is contradicted by what is in the surah of al-Aʿrāf, namely the word "thumma" (then), which signals the delay of the command's issuance after the formation, which is delayed after creation, which is delayed after the conditional command. And the excuse of taking the delay to be in rank (rutbī) or the delay in reporting, or that the conditional command, before the realisation of the conditioned matter, since in not obligating the commanded act it is as nothing, is treated as though it occurred only after its realisation, and so is narrated in the form of an immediate command; this leads, after much ado, to the conclusion that what took place between Him and them (peace be upon them) concerning the matter of the caliphate, and what they said about it, and what they heard, occurred only after the prostration, which was preceded by knowledge of the sublimity of his rank (peace be upon him), and after Iblis had departed from the scene by the perpetual curse because of his obstinacy, and after their witnessing all of that with their own eyes. And is this anything but a breach of the principle of reason and transmitted text? Resorting, in order to escape it, to interpreting the breathing of the spirit as meaning the bestowal of whatever gives life to souls, of which the teaching of the names is one part, is a forced reading which reveals the narrowness of the field. What verification requires, and what refined reflection demands, after perusing the repositories of the hidden Book and searching out the secret it contains, is this: their prostration to him (peace be upon him) was consequent upon the immediate command, which branches from the manifestation of his merit (peace be upon him), which is grounded in the dialogue preceded by the announcement of his caliphate, all of this being gathered into the thread of what the conditional command was attached to, namely the proportioning and the breathing of the spirit. For it is not a requirement of that matter that the prostration be obligatory immediately upon the breathing of the spirit into him; the conditional fāʾ (al-fāʾ al-jazāʾiyya) is not explicit in requiring that the content of the consequent occur immediately upon the existence of the condition without any delay, since it is certain that running (to the Friday prayer) is not obligatory immediately upon the call, by His words: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, then hasten﴾, to the end of the verse; nor is establishing the prayer obligatory immediately upon being at rest, by His words: ﴿So when you are secure, then establish the prayer﴾; rather, the obligation arises only upon the entry of the time. How could it be otherwise, when the wisdom which called for the conditional command in question, following what has been mentioned, is in fact to get the angels to reflect upon his matter (peace be upon him), so that they may contemplate all his circumstances, comprehend what he possesses by way of knowledge, inquire into whatever might be obscure to them concerning his matter (peace be upon him), because it is founded upon lofty wisdoms and hidden secrets concealed from their knowledge, and so that they may stand upon the clear state of affairs before the immediate command arrived and compliance became binding. And they spoke, in accordance with that, what they spoke, and witnessed what they witnessed. And the fact that the immediate command is not arranged in the thread of the matters mentioned in the two surahs at the time of narration does not require that it is not arranged within it at the time the narrated event occurred; just as the non-mention of the conditional command at the narration of the immediate command in the noble surah mentioned does not necessitate that it was not preceded by it. For the narration of one statement in different styles, according to what the context requires and the fine arrangement demands, is not rare in the Mighty Book. And consider what has been transmitted regarding the explanation of His words: ﴿a human﴾, despite the angels not having prior knowledge of that, and since it has been resorted to, although no transmission has come with it; so what do you suppose about what has been explicitly stated in many places? Perhaps all that the immediate command depends upon in general was communicated to them from the outset, by saying, for example: "I am creating a human from such-and-such, and I am making him a caliph on earth; so when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, and his matter has become clear to you, then fall down to him in prostration." So He created him, proportioned him, and breathed the spirit into him, and then they said what they said at that time. Or the news of the caliphate was communicated to them after the enumerated conditions had been realised, by saying, immediately upon the breathing of the spirit into him: "I am making this one a caliph on earth." Then they mentioned concerning him (peace be upon him) what they mentioned, and Allah (exalted and majestic is He) strengthened him by teaching him the names, so they witnessed from him what they witnessed. At that point the immediate command came, in attention to the matter of what was commanded and in specifying its time. Some matters have been narrated in some places and some in others, sufficing with what is mentioned in each place about what is left out in another place. What closes the door to confusion is that the words in the surah of Ṣād, in His words, exalted is He: ﴿When your Lord said to the angels﴾, etc., are a substitution (badal) for His words, exalted is He, preceding them: ﴿when they dispute﴾, in His words: ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they disputed﴾; that is, by their speech during their disputing. By "the Exalted Assembly" is meant the angels, Adam, and Iblis, as the majority of the community agreed. By their disputing is meant what passed between them concerning the matter of Adam's caliphate, a debate of which part was what issued from him (peace be upon him) regarding the announcement of the names. It is a requirement of substitution that the dispute mentioned occurs within the details of what was mentioned in it, namely the conditional command, what was tied to it of creation, proportioning, and breathing of the spirit into him, what resulted from it of the prostration of the angels (peace be upon them), the obstinacy of Iblis, the curse that followed it, his expulsion from among the angels, and what occurred after that of deeds and sayings. And since the completion of the dispute did not come after the prostration of the angels and the arrogance of Iblis, which entailed his expulsion from among them, because, as you know, he was one of the disputants; just as it was not before creation, owing to the impossibility of announcing the names at that time. So it is, then, after the breathing of the spirit and before the prostration, necessarily, by one of the two ways. And Allah, glorified is He, knows best the reality of the matter.

﴿He refused and was arrogant﴾: this is a resumptive statement (istiʾnāf), explaining the manner of the non-prostration understood from the exception, and that it was not out of hesitation or deliberation. "Ibāʾ" (refusal) is abstaining by choice; "takabbur" (haughtiness) is that one sees oneself as greater than others; "istikbār" (arrogance) is seeking that, through feigning greatness. That is: he refused what he was commanded, and he was arrogant against honouring him or taking him as a means in the worship of his Lord. The placement of "refusal" before "arrogance," although arrogance is its cause, is because it is more manifest and its effect is clearer. In the surah of Ṣād, only the mention of arrogance is given, being sufficient; and in the surah of al-Ḥijr only the mention of refusal is given, where it is said: ﴿He refused to be among the prostrators﴾.

﴿And he was among the disbelievers﴾: that is, in the knowledge of God (exalted is He). For his origin was from the disbelieving jinn; therefore he committed what he committed, as His saying (exalted is He) makes clear: ﴿He was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord﴾. So the sentence is parenthetical, confirming what preceded of refusal and arrogance. Or he became one of them by considering abhorrent God's command (exalted is He) to him to prostrate before Adam (peace be upon him), claiming that he was superior to him; and the superior does not fittingly be commanded to submit to the inferior, as His saying reveals: ﴿I am better than him﴾, when it was said to him: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I created with My hands? Did you become arrogant, or were you among the exalted?﴾. Not by abandoning the obligation alone. So the sentence is conjoined to what precedes it; and the choice of the particle "wa" (and) over "fa" (so) is to indicate that bare refusal and arrogance is disbelief, not that they are two causes of it, as the particle "fa" would imply.(p-90)

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 35:**

﴿And We said﴾: This begins the narration of what took place between Allah (Exalted is He) and Adam (peace be upon him), after the completion of what took place between Him (Exalted is He) and the angels and Iblis, of words and deeds. The account of Iblis's rebuke, his response, his curse, his request for respite, and his being granted respite has been omitted, being sufficiently detailed in the other noble surahs. This clause is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "We said to the angels." The difference in their times does not harm this, for the time indicated by the word "idh" (when) is an extended period, broad enough for both sayings. It has also been said that it is conjoined to "idh qulna" (when We said), with "idh" implied. This is a reminder of another blessing that calls for gratitude and prevents disbelief.

The opening of the speech with the vocative in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾ serves to alert the listener to the importance of receiving the command. Restricting the primary address to him (peace be upon him) indicates his primacy in carrying out the command.

"Uskun" (dwell) is from "al-suknā", which means staying, residing, and settling, not "al-sukūn", which is the opposite of motion. "Anta" (you) is a pronoun used to emphasize the concealed pronoun in "uskun", so that the conjunction to it is valid.

Scholars differ regarding the time of the creation of his wife. Al-Suddi reported, from Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, and some of the Companions, may Allah's good pleasure be upon them all, that when Allah (Exalted is He) expelled Iblis from the Garden and settled Adam in it, Adam remained in it alone, and there was no one with him to keep him company. So Allah (Exalted is He) cast sleep upon him, then took a rib from his left side and put flesh in its place, and created Eve from it. When he awoke, he found her sitting at his head, so he asked her: "What are you?" She said: "A woman." He said: "Why were you created?" She said: "So that you may find comfort in me." The angels then said, to test his knowledge: "Who is this?" He said: "A woman." They said: "Why was she named a woman?" He said: "Because she was taken out of man (al-mar')." They said: "What is her name?" He said: "Ḥawwāʾ." They said: "Why was she named Ḥawwāʾ?" He said: "Because she was created from a living thing (shayʾ ḥayy)."

It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: Allah (Exalted is He) sent a host of angels who carried Adam and Eve on a throne of gold, as kings are carried, and their garments were light, until they brought them into the Garden. As you see, this indicates that she was created before entering the Garden. By "the Garden" is meant the abode of reward, since it is the one that is known. It has also been said that it is a garden in the land of Filastin, or between Fars and Kirman, which Allah (Exalted is He) created as a test for Adam (peace be upon him). The descent (ihbāṭ) is interpreted as a moving from it to the land of Hind, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Descend into a city [Misran]﴾, because the creation of him (peace be upon him) was on earth, without disagreement. Nothing is mentioned in this story about his being raised to the heaven, and had that occurred it would have been more worthy of mention and reminder, since it is one of the greatest blessings. Also, if it had been the abode of eternity, Iblis would not have entered it. It has also been said that it was in the seventh heaven, as evidenced by "descend." Then the first descent was from it to the lowest heaven, and the second from it to the earth. It has also been said that all of these are possible, and the transmitted proofs conflict, so it is necessary to suspend judgment and refrain from certainty.

﴿And eat from it﴾: that is, from its fruits. The address was directed to both of them to generalize the honor and comfort, and as an emphasis in removing excuses and pretexts, and to indicate that they are equal in carrying out the command, since Eve is an example for him (peace be upon him) in eating, unlike dwelling, in which she follows him.

﴿Plentifully﴾ (raghadan): an adjective of the emphatic verbal noun, meaning: abundant, comfortable eating. ﴿Wherever you wish﴾: that is, any place from it that you desire. This, as you see, is a general permission, in that eating from it was permitted to them in a manner of broad and complete ease that removes all reasons, and not some of the eating was forbidden to them, nor some of the places containing foods, so that they would have no excuse in taking what they were forbidden by His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And do not approach﴾, with the vowel of the letter rāʾ being fatḥa, from "qaribtu al-shayʾ" with kasra, "aqrabuhu" with fatḥa, meaning when you are involved with it and expose yourself to it. Al-Jawhari said: "qaruba", with ḍamma, "yaqrubu, qurban", means to draw near; and "qaribtuhu", with kasra, "qurbānan", means I approached it.

﴿This tree﴾ (hādhihi al-shajara): accusative, either as an apposition (badal) to the demonstrative noun, or as an attributive adjective (naʿt) to it, by interpreting it with a derived noun, meaning: this present tree. That is: do not eat from it. The prohibition was linked to approaching it only as an exaggeration in forbidding eating and in the obligation to avoid it. What is meant by it is: wheat, or grapes, or figs. It has also been said: it is a tree that whoever eats from it becomes impure (aḥdatha). The better course is not to specify it without a decisive proof. It is also read as "hādhī" with yāʾ, with kasra on the shīn of "al-shajara" and on the tāʾ of "taqraba"; and it is read as "al-shīra" with kasra on the shīn and fatḥa on the yāʾ.

﴿Lest you be among the wrongdoers﴾ (fa-takūnā min al-ẓālimīn): jussive (majzūm), either as conjoined (maʿṭūf) to "taqraba", or accusative as a response (jawāb) to the prohibition. Whichever it is, the approaching, that is, eating from it, is a cause of their being among the wrongdoers, that is, those who wronged themselves by committing disobedience, or who diminished their portions by engaging in what harms honor and bliss, or who transgressed the limits of Allah (Exalted is He).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 36:

﴿فَأزَلَّهُما الشَّيْطانُ عَنْها﴾ ("So Satan caused them to slip from it"): i.e., he caused their slip (izlal, "causing to slip"); that is, he made them slip, and he drove them to the slip by means of it. A parallel to this is what is in His (Exalted) saying: ﴿وَما فَعَلْتُهُ عَنْ أمْرِي﴾ ("And I did it not of my own accord" [lit. "not from my command"]). Or: "he caused them to slip away from the Garden," in the sense of "he removed them and kept them far from it." It is said: "zalla 'anni kadha" (so-and-so went away from me), when it has gone away from you. It is supported by the reading "azalahuma" ("he removed them"), and the two are close in meaning, for izlal (causing to slip) necessarily entails the slipper's departure from his place, absolutely. His causing them to slip was his saying to them: ﴿هَلْ أدُلُّكَ عَلى شَجَرَةِ الخُلْدِ ومُلْكٍ لا يَبْلى﴾ ("Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?"), and his saying: ﴿ما نَهاكُما رَبُّكُما عَنْ هَذِهِ الشَّجَرَةِ إلا أنْ تَكُونا مَلَكَيْنِ أوْ تَكُونا مِنَ الخالِدِينَ﴾ ("Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels or become of the immortals"), and his swearing to them: ﴿إنِّي لَكُما لَمِنَ النّاصِحِينَ﴾ ("Indeed, I am to you among the sincere advisers"). These verses indicate that he (peace be upon him) was not commanded to dwell in the Garden in the manner of eternity, but in the manner of honour and distinction, because of the caliphate of the earth that he was entrusted with until the time of being raised up to it. There is disagreement concerning the manner in which he reached them, after it was said to him: ﴿فاخْرُجْ مِنها فَإنَّكَ رَجِيمٌ﴾ ("So get out of it, for indeed you are expelled"). It was said: he was only prevented from entering in the manner of honour, as the angels enter it, and he was not prevented from entering for the purpose of whispering, as a trial for Adam and Eve. It was said: he stood at the gate and called out to them. It was said: he took the form of an animal and entered, and the guardians did not recognise him. It was said: he entered into the mouth of the serpent, and entered with it. It was said: he sent some of his followers, and they caused them to slip. And knowledge is with God, Glorified is He.

﴿فَأخْرَجَهُما مِمّا كانا فِيهِ﴾ ("So He brought them out of that in which they were"): i.e., from the Garden, if the pronoun in "from it" refers to the tree; and the expression about it in this way is to indicate its grandeur and majesty, and their being in it; i.e., from the great place in which they were settled, or from honour and bliss, if the pronoun refers to the Garden.

﴿وَقُلْنا اهْبِطُوا﴾ ("And We said: Go down"): the address is to Adam and Eve (peace be upon them), by the evidence of His (Exalted) saying: ﴿اهْبِطا مِنها جَمِيعًا﴾ ("Go down from it, all of you"). The pronoun is in the plural because they are the origin of the species, so they are as if they were the entire species. It was said: the address is to them, and to the serpent, and to Iblis, on the basis that he was expelled from it a second time, after he had been entering it for the purpose of whispering; or he entered it stealthily; or he was sent down from the sky. It was also read with a dammah on the ba' (ihbutu).

﴿بَعْضُكم لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ﴾ ("Some of you are enemies to others"): a circumstantial clause in which the waw is dispensed with by means of the pronoun; i.e., mutually hostile; some of you transgress against others by misleading them. Or it is a resumptive clause with no place in the grammatical structure. The singular "'aduww" (enemy) is either in view of the wording of "ba'd" (some), or because its pattern is that of a verbal noun, like "qabul" (acceptance).

﴿وَلَكم في الأرْضِ﴾ ("And for you on the earth"): which is the place of descent. The adverbial phrase is connected to what the predicate is connected to, namely "lakum" (for you), from ﴿مُسْتَقَرٌّ﴾ ("a dwelling place") [i.e., the sense of settling]: i.e., a settlement; or a place of settlement; ﴿وَمَتاعٌ﴾ ("and enjoyment"): i.e., enjoyment of life and benefiting from it; ﴿إلى حِينٍ﴾ ("for a time"): it is the time of death, on the basis that the limit is the enjoyment of each individual of those addressed; or the Resurrection, on the basis that it is the enjoyment of the species within some of the individuals. The sentence, like what precedes it, is circumstantial in that it is [in the sense of] "deserving of settling and enjoyment"; or it is a resumptive clause.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 37:**

﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾: That is, he received them by taking them, accepting them, and acting upon them, when he came to know them and was granted success in them. It has also been read with *Adam* in the accusative and *kalimat* (words) in the nominative, to indicate that the words reached him and came to him. They are His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾, and the verse [continues]. It has also been said: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You; blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty; there is no god but You. I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You." And on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, he said: "He said: 'O my Lord, did You not create me with Your hand?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'O my Lord, did You not breathe into me of Your spirit?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'O my Lord, did Your mercy not precede Your wrath?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Did You not settle me in Your Garden?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'O my Lord, I have repented and made amends; will You return me to the Garden?' He said: 'Yes.'" The *fa'* (then) indicates that the repentance occurred immediately after the command to descend, before the commanded matter was realized. The mention of the title of Lordship (*rububiyyah*), together with its attribution to him (peace be upon him), is for honour, and to signal that it is the cause of the bestowing of the words, which is implied by his receiving them.

﴿So He turned to him in forgiveness﴾: That is, He returned to him with mercy and accepted his repentance. The *fa'* indicates that this result follows from the reception of the words, which contain the meaning of repentance (*tawbah*), the term for acknowledging the sin, regretting it, and resolving not to return to it. The account is confined to Adam (peace be upon him) because Eve follows him in the ruling; for this reason the mention of women is omitted in most places in the Book and the Sunnah.

﴿Indeed He is the Oft-Returning, the Most Merciful﴾: That is, the One who returns to His servants with forgiveness; or, the One who greatly helps them to repent. The root of *tawb* is returning. When it is attributed to the servant, it means returning from disobedience; when it is attributed to the Creator (mighty and exalted), it means returning from punishment to forgiveness.

﴿the Most Merciful﴾: the one who intensifies mercy. Combining the two attributes is an eloquent promise to the penitent of goodness, together with pardon and forgiveness. The sentence is a justification for His saying (exalted is He): ﴿So He turned to him in forgiveness﴾.

﴿We said﴾: This is an *isti'naf* (a resumptive clause), built upon an implied question that the speech carries with it, as if it were said: "What happened after the acceptance of his repentance?" So it was said: ﴿We said: Go down from it, all of you﴾. The command to descend was repeated to signal that its requirement is binding and that it will certainly be realized, and to forestall what might arise in the mind of Adam, peace be upon him, that the acceptance of repentance entails pardon for that (descent). It also shows a kind of compassion toward him, peace be upon him, given the clear difference between the two commands. How could it not be so? The first is mixed with a measure of displeasure, and is followed by a statement that their place of descent is a house of trial and mutual enmity, in which they will not dwell forever. The second is coupled with the promise of the bestowal of guidance, which leads to salvation and success. As for the threat of punishment contained in it, it is not intended by the obligation as a primary aim; rather, it revolves around the bad choice of those who are obligated. It has been said: in this is an admonition that the prudent person is sufficiently restrained from opposing the judgment of God, exalted is He, by the fear of descent, coupled with one of these two matters; so how much more so by one coupled with both? So reflect. It has also been said: the first descent is from the Garden to the lowest heaven, and the second is from it to the earth; but the reference to their settlement on the earth in the first (command) rejects this, as does the return of the pronoun (p-93) to the Garden in the second. And "jami'an" (all of you) is a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier) in form and an emphasis in meaning, as if it were said: "Descend, you all, altogether." Therefore it does not require that they descend together at one time, as in your saying: "They came all of them" (*ja'u jami'an*), in contrast to your saying: "They came together" (*ja'u ma'an*).

﴿Then if there comes to you from Me guidance﴾: The *fa'* (then) is for ordering what follows upon the descent understood from the command to it. "*Imma*" (if, or whenever) is composed of the conditional "*in*" and the superfluous "*ma*," which emphasizes its meaning. The verb is in the position of the jussive after the conditional particle, and it is built (*mabni*) because it is joined to the energetic nun (*nun al-tawkid*). It has been said that it is *mu'rab* (inflected) absolutely; it has been said that it is *mabni* absolutely; and the correct view is a distinction: if the nun is attached to it, it is built; otherwise it is inflected, as in: "Will the two of them stand?" The fronting of the adverbial phrase before the subject is for what has passed more than once. The meaning is: if there comes to you from Me guidance, through a messenger whom I send to you, and a Book which I send down upon you. The answer to the condition is His saying: ﴿Then whoever follows My guidance, there shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve﴾, as in your saying: "If you come to me, then if I am able, I will do good to you." The use of the word of doubt (*kalimat al-shakk*), together with the certainty that the coming will certainly occur, is to signal that faith in God and monotheism do not require the sending of messengers or the revelation of Books; rather, for their obligation it suffices that reason is bestowed, that the signs of the horizons and of the souls are set up, and that one is enabled to reflect and to infer. Or it is to follow the custom of the great in using "*'asa*" (perhaps) and "*la'alla*" (perhaps) in places of certainty and decisiveness. The meaning is: whoever among you follows My guidance, there shall be no fear for them, in either abode, of encountering something disliked; nor shall they grieve over the loss of something desired. That is, there does not befall them what necessitates that (fear and grief); not that such (fear and grief) befalls them but they do not fear and do not grieve; nor that the very fear and grief never befall them at all; rather they continue in joy and vigor. How could it not be so? For the sense of fear and awe, out of magnifying the majesty and awe of God, exalted is He, and out of regarding one's striving and effort in fulfilling the rights of servanthood as insufficient, is among the distinguishing traits of the elite and the near ones. The intended meaning is to state the continuance of the negation of these two, not the negation of the continuance of them, as might be imagined from the fact that the predicate in the second clause is a present verb; for it is established in its proper place that negation, even when it enters upon the present verb itself, conveys permanence and continuity, according to context. The mention of "guidance" as an annexed noun to the divine name is to magnify it and to emphasize the obligation of following it; or because what is meant by the second (guidance) is more general than the legislative guidances, and includes what has been mentioned of the bestowal of reason and the setting up of the signs of the horizons and of the souls, as has been said. It was also read: "*hudayya*" (My guidance), according to the dialect of Hudhayl; and "*la khawf*" (there is no fear) with a fatha.

﴿Those who disbelieve and deny Our signs﴾: This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "those who follow" (man tabiʿa), and it is its counterpart (qasīm). It is as if it were said: "and those who do not follow it." The commentator chose this formulation over a simple statement of contrast to express the horror of the state of error and to make clear the full extent of its ugliness. The relative pronoun is given in the plural form to indicate the large number of disbelievers. The combination of disbelief (kufr) and denial (takdhīb) indicates that guidance has taken the form of both of these kinds mentioned. The use of the "We" of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama) serves to cultivate awe and to bring in dread. The attribution of the signs (āyāt) to Him expresses the full ugliness of denying them. That is: "those who disbelieved in Our messengers who were sent to them, and denied Our signs revealed to them." It has also been said that the meaning is: they disbelieved in God and denied His signs, which He sent down upon the prophets, peace be upon them, or which He manifested through their hands, from among the miracles. It has also been said: they disbelieved in the signs in their hearts and denied them with their tongues; in that case both verbs are directed at the prepositional phrase.

The word "āyah," in its original sense, means the apparent sign. Al-Nābigha said:

"I perceived signs in her and recognized them after six years, and this year is the seventh."

It is also applied to created things insofar as they point to the Creator (exalted is He), His knowledge, and His power; and to each group of the words of the Qur'an that is distinguished from others by a separation, because it is a sign of the separation of what precedes it from what follows it. It has also been said that it is because it gathers words from it, so it comes from the saying: "So-and-so went out with his āyah," that is (p-94) with his company. He said:

"We went out from the two houses, no tribe is like ours; with our āyah we drive the nursing she-camels with their young."

Its derivation is from "ayy" (which), because it clarifies one thing from among another; or from "awā ilayhi," meaning "returned to it." Its original form is "awyah" or "ayyah," and its ʿayn was replaced by an alif contrary to analogy; or it is "awayah" or "ayayah" like "ramakah," and it underwent i'lal (morphological alteration); or it is "āʾiyah" like "qā'ilah," and the hamzah was dropped for lightness.

﴿Those﴾: a demonstrative referring to the described subject, in consideration of its being characterized by the disbelief and denial contained in the relative clause. It implies that they are distinguished by that attribute, a distinction that justifies the use of a sensory demonstrative; and the sense of distance it contains indicates the remoteness of their station. It is the subject (mubtadaʾ). The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿the companions of the Fire﴾: that is, those who remain in it, cling to it, and are inseparable from it; this is its predicate (khabar), and the sentence is the predicate of the relative pronoun. Alternatively, the demonstrative is a substitute (badal) for the relative pronoun, or an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to it, and "the companions of the Fire" is its predicate. The words of the Exalted: ﴿they therein abide eternally﴾ are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), because this is explicitly stated in His words, exalted is He: ﴿the companions of the Fire, abiding therein eternally﴾. It has also been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause of "the Fire," since it contains its pronoun, and the operating element is the sense of the annexation (idāfah), or the implied preposition (lām). Or it is in the nominative position, as another predicate of "those," according to the view of one who permits a sentence to be a second predicate. "Therein" is related to "abiding eternally."

"Khulūd," in its original sense, means a long stay; and consensus has been established that what is meant by it is perpetuity (dawām).

(p-95)

﴿O Children of Israel﴾: a shift in address, directed to a particular group of the disbelievers contemporary with the Prophet ﷺ, in order to remind them of the various kinds of blessings showered upon them. This follows the address to the Messenger of God ﷺ and his command to remind them all of the general blessing given to the whole of the children of Adam, through His words (exalted is He): ﴿And when your Lord said﴾, etc.

﴿And when We said to the angels﴾, etc. Because the meaning, as has been indicated, is: "Convey My words to them, and mention to them when We made their father a khalifah (vicegerent) on the earth, and an object of prostration for the angels, peace be upon them, and We honoured him by teaching him the names, and accepted his repentance." And "ibn" (son) is from "binaʾ" (building), because he is the building of his father. For this reason the made thing is attributed to its maker, so it is said "Abu al-Harb" (the father of war) and "bint fikar" (the daughter of thought). "Israel" is the epithet (laqab) of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, and its meaning in Hebrew is "the chosen one of God" (safwat Allah). It has also been said to mean "the servant of God."
