It has been read as "Isra'il" with the yaʾ omitted, and "Isra'l" with both omitted, and "Israyil" with the hamzah changed to a yaʾ, and "Isra'al" with an open hamzah, and "Isra'il" with a kasrah-marked hamzah between the rāʾ and the lām. The singling out of this group for mention and reminder is because they are the people most abundantly blessed and the most ungrateful for them.

﴿Remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you﴾: by reflecting upon it and by standing up in thanks for it. In this there is an indication that they had entirely forgotten it and had not brought it to mind, not merely that they had neglected to give thanks for it. The attribution of the blessing to the Divine Name (ḍamīr al-jalālah) is to honour it, and to make obligatory the singling out of its thanks for Him (exalted is He). The restriction of the blessing to them is because man is naturally inclined to love blessings; when he considers what has overflowed upon him of blessings, this leads him to contentment and thankfulness. It has been said that what is meant is what He bestowed upon their forefathers, of the blessings whose details will come, and upon them, of the various kinds of blessings, the most excellent of which is attaining the age of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. It has also been read as "idhdhakkarū" (with the iftiʿāl form, in which the tāʾ of the reflexive pattern has assimilated into the dhāl). And "niʿmatiya" (My blessing) is read with the yāʾ silent and dropped in continuous speech, which is the view of those who do not vocalise a yāʾ preceded by a kasrah.

﴿And fulfil My covenant﴾: by faith and obedience; ﴿I shall fulfil your covenant﴾: by good recompense. The "ʿahd" (covenant) is attributed to each of the two parties who undertake its two sides. Probably the first is attributed to the agent and the second to the object, for He (exalted is He) pledged to them faith and righteous deeds, by setting up proofs, sending messengers, sending down scriptures, and promising them reward for their good deeds. For fulfilling these two there is a broad scope: the first of its levels from us is to utter the two words of testimony, and from God (exalted is He) the preservation of blood and property; and the last of its levels from us is being absorbed in the sea of monotheism, to the extent that we become heedless of ourselves, let alone others; and from God (exalted is He) is attaining everlasting meeting. As for what has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both: "Fulfil My covenant in following Muhammad ﷺ; I shall fulfil your covenant in removing the burdens and the shackles," and from others: "Fulfil by performing the obligations and abandoning the major sins, I shall fulfil by forgiveness and reward," or: "Fulfil by steadfastness upon the straight path, I shall fulfil by honour and lasting bliss"; these are according to the means (wasāʾiṭ). It has been said that both are attributed to the object, and the meaning is: "Fulfil what you have pledged to Me of faith and undertaking obedience; I shall fulfil what I have pledged to you of good recompense." The detail of the two covenants is His words (exalted is He): ﴿And God had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾, up to His words: ﴿And We will surely admit you into gardens﴾, etc. It has been read as "ūfi" (with shaddah) for emphasis and intensification.

﴿And fear Me alone﴾: in what you do and what you leave undone, especially in breaking the covenant. It is more emphatic in conveying exclusivity than "Iyyāka naʿbudu" (You alone do we worship), because of what it contains, together with the fronting (of the object), of the repetition of the object, and of the fāʾ of consequence, which indicates that the speech implicitly carries the sense of a condition, as if it were said: "If you are fearing anything, then fear Me." Ar-rahbah (fear) is fear accompanied by caution. The verse includes promise and threat, indicates the obligation of gratitude and of fulfilling the covenant, and that the believer should fear none but God (exalted is He).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 41:

﴿And believe in what I have sent down﴾: He singled out belief in the Qur'an with the command to it, because it is the supreme foundation regarding the fulfilment of covenants.

﴿Confirming what you already have﴾: that is, the Torah. The expression "what you already have" is used to signal that they know it confirms the Torah, since being "with you" implies repeated reference to it and close attention to what it contains, which leads to knowledge that it confirms the Torah. The meaning of its confirming the Torah is that it has been sent down in accordance with the description of it found there, or that it agrees with the Torah in its narratives, its promises, its call to monotheism (tawhid), its justice among people, and its prohibition of sins and abominations. As for what appears to be a contradiction with the Torah in some particular rulings, which vary according to the differing eras, it is not in reality a contradiction. Rather, it is in agreement with it, since each of them is true relative to its own era and time, and includes the wisdoms upon which the orbit of legislation revolves. The Torah contains no indication that its abrogated rulings (mansukhah) are permanent, so that what abrogates them would contradict them. It only indicates their legitimacy in general, without addressing their continuation or cessation. Indeed, we say that it explicitly states the abrogation of those rulings, since its affirmation of the truth of the abrogating Qur'an is an explicit statement of their abrogation. Therefore, the basis of the contradiction in abrogated rulings is only the difference of era. Even if the earlier revelation had been delayed, it would have been revealed in conformity with the later one; and if the later revelation had come first, it would have definitely agreed with the earlier one. For this reason, he (ﷺ) said: "If Moses were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me." Restricting the revealed text to being a confirmation of what they already have serves to emphasise the obligation to comply with the command, since their belief in what they have necessarily entails belief in what confirms it.

﴿And do not be the first to reject it﴾: that is, do not hasten to disbelieve in it. Your duty is to be the first to believe in it, since you know its status and its truth through transmission from the divine books you possess, just as you know your own sons. You used to seek victory through it and to give good tidings of its time, as will come. So do not place yourselves in a position other than what is expected of you, and do not do what is required of you, nor what is imagined to come from you: becoming the first to reject it. The phrase "the first to reject it" as a predicate of the plural pronoun is to be understood either as "the first group" or "the first company," or as "let not each one of you be the first to reject it," like your saying "he clothed us in a robe" (kasana hullatan). The prohibition against them being foremost in disbelief in it, although the idolaters of the Arabs are older than them, is because the intended meaning is an allusion (ta'ridh) and not the literal indication of what the apparent wording states, like your saying: "As for me, I am not ignorant." This is because the intended meaning is to forbid them from becoming the first unbelievers among the People of the Book, or among those who disbelieve in what they have, since whoever disbelieves in the Qur'an has disbelieved in what confirms it; or like those of the idolaters of Mecca who disbelieved. "Awwal" (first) is an elative form (af'al) with no verb from which it is derived. It has been said that its original form is "awwal," from "wa'ala ilayhi," meaning to escape and find safety, so the hamzah was replaced by a waw for lightness, in a non-analogical way. Or it is "a'wal," from "ala" (to return), so its hamzah was changed to a waw and assimilated.

﴿And do not trade My signs﴾: that is, do not take in exchange for yourselves a substitute for them, ﴿for a small price﴾, from worldly pleasures. Even if they are great, they are small and contemptible in comparison with what they have lost of the pleasures of the Hereafter by abandoning belief. It has been said: they had leadership among their people, and customary dues and gifts, and they feared losing these if they followed the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so they chose them over belief. The expression "trade" is used for what is bought, which is the principal element in contracts of exchange and the thing intended in them, but it is expressed with "price," which normally serves as the means in them. The signs, which by right should be the object of competition for those who compete, are connected with the preposition "bi" (with), which accompanies means. This signals the reversal of their state, since they made the primary aim a means, and the means an aim.

﴿And fear Me alone﴾: by believing, following the truth, and turning away from the trash of this world. Since the preceding verse contains what is like the foundations for what is in the second verse, it is distinguished by fear (rahbah), which is one of the preliminaries of piety (taqwa). Or, because the address in it encompasses both the learned and the imitators (muqallid), they were commanded in it to have fear, which applies to both groups. As for the address in the second, since it is restricted to the scholars, they were commanded in it to have piety (taqwa), which is the ultimate goal.

﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾: This is conjoined (*'atf*) to what precedes it. *Al-labs* means mixing, and it may entail confusion between the two things mixed. The meaning is: do not mix the revealed truth with the falsehood that you invent and write, so that one becomes indistinguishable from the other. Or: do not make the truth ambiguous through the falsehood that you write within its lines or mention in its interpretation.

﴿and conceal the truth﴾: This is in the jussive mood (*majzum*) and falls under the scope of the prohibition, as if they were commanded to believe and to abandon error, and forbidden from misleading others through obscuring the truth from those who have heard it and concealing it from those who have not heard it. Or it is in the accusative mood (*mansub*) by the implied "an" (*idmar "an*), with the *waw* indicating joint occurrence, meaning: do not combine mixing the truth with falsehood and concealing it. This is supported by its reading in the codex (*mushaf*) of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa-taktumūna," meaning "while you conceal," i.e., as concealers. This implies that the mixing is abominable because it is accompanied by the concealment of the truth. The repetition of "the truth" is either because the latter refers to something other than the former, namely the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) that they concealed, writing something else in its place, as will come in His words (exalted is He): ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands﴾; or it is to intensify the reprehensibility of what is forbidden, since explicitly naming "the truth" conveys what is not in its own implication.

﴿while you know﴾: That is, while you are aware that you are mixing and concealing; or: "while you know that it is the truth"; or: "while you are among the people of knowledge." The mention of the circumstance is not to restrict the prohibition by it, as in His words (exalted is He): ﴿Do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated﴾; rather, it is to intensify the reprehensibility of their state, since the ignorant person may perhaps be excused.(p-97)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 43:

﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾: that is, the prayer of the Muslims and their zakat; for other than these two are far from being prayer and zakat. Allah (Exalted) commanded them with the branches (furu') of Islam after commanding them with its foundations (usul).

﴿And bow with those who bow﴾: that is, in their congregation; for the congregational prayer is preferred over the prayer of the solitary person by twenty-seven degrees, because in it souls support one another in intimate communion with God. The prayer is expressed by bowing (ruku') as a safeguard against being confused with the prayer of the Jews. It has also been said: ruku' means submission and compliance with what the Lawgiver obligates upon them. Al-Adba' ibn Quray' al-Sa'di said:

؎ Do not belittle the weak, for perhaps ∗∗∗ you will bow one day while time has raised him up.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 44:**

﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people?﴾: This is a *tajrid* (a turning of the address away from the general audience to a particular group), after it had been directed at everyone. The *hamza* (the interrogative particle) here expresses affirmation together with rebuke and astonishment. *Al-birr* (righteousness, piety) means the broadening of goodness, derived from *al-barr*, which is the wide open space. It encompasses all kinds of goodness. For this reason it has been said: *al-birr* is of three kinds: righteousness in the worship of Allah (Exalted); righteousness in caring for relatives; and righteousness in dealing with strangers.

﴿and you forget yourselves﴾: that is, you leave yourselves out of righteousness, like those who are forgotten. On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, it was revealed concerning the rabbis of Madinah, who would secretly command those they advised to follow the Prophet (ﷺ), while they themselves did not follow him, out of greed for the gifts and benefits that reached them from their followers. It has also been said that they would enjoin giving charity while not giving charity themselves. Al-Suddi said: "They would command the people to obey Allah (Exalted) and forbid them from disobeying Him, while they themselves abandoned obedience and rushed into disobedience." Ibn Jurayj said: "They would command the people to pray and to give zakat, while they themselves abandoned both." The focus of the denunciation and rebuke is the conjoined clause, not the clause to which it is conjoined.

﴿while you recite the Book?﴾: This is a *tabkit* (a silencing rebuke) and *taqri'* (a reprimand), like His saying (Exalted): ﴿while you know﴾. That is, while you recite the Torah, which describes his attributes (ﷺ), and commands belief in him, or commands the promise of doing good and the threat against corruption, obstinacy, abandoning righteousness, and the contradiction between speech and action.

﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾: That is, "Do you recite it and yet not understand what is in it, or the ugliness of what you do, so that you would refrain from it?" The denial is directed at the absence of reason after the realization of what would necessitate it, so the emphasis is in terms of manner. Alternatively: "Will you not reflect and then understand?" The denial is then directed at both matters, and the emphasis is in terms of quantity. *Al-'aql* (reason, intellect) originally means restraint and holding back, and from it comes *al-'iqal*, the cord tied from the leg of a camel to its foreleg to restrain it from movement. The spiritual light by which the soul perceives necessary and theoretical knowledge is named after it, because it restrains the soul from engaging in what is ugly and guides it toward what is good. The verse, as you see, censures everyone who admonishes others but is not admonished by his own bad conduct and lack of effect, and whose action is that of one ignorant of the sacred law, or a fool devoid of reason. Its intended meaning, as has been indicated, is to urge the purification of the self and the devotion to perfecting it, so that it may stand for the truth and thereby set others upright, not to prevent the sinner from being admonished.

It is related that there was a scholar among the learned whose speech was influential and who had strong power over hearts. Often one or two of the people of his assembly would die from the intensity of the effect of his admonition. In his town there was an old woman who had a righteous son, tender of heart and quick to be moved, and she would guard him closely and prevent him from attending the preacher's assembly. One day he attended it when she was unaware, and there befell him what Allah (Exalted) decreed. Then one day the old woman met the preacher on the road and said:

> Would you guide mankind while you yourself are not guided?
> Surely that does not benefit.
>
> O whetstone, how long will you sharpen iron
> yet never cut?

When the preacher heard this, he gave a great gasp and fell from his horse unconscious. They carried him to his house, and he died to the mercy of Allah, Glorified be He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 45:

﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾: This is connected to what precedes it; as if, when they were charged with what involves hardship, namely leaving leadership and turning away from wealth, they were treated with this. The meaning: seek help in your needs through awaiting success and relief, trusting in God (Exalted is He); or through fasting, which is patience in abstaining from things that break the fast, because it breaks desire and purifies the soul; and through seeking means (tawassul) in prayer (salah) and turning to it, for it encompasses the types of acts of worship, both spiritual and physical: purity, covering the private parts, spending wealth on these two, facing the Ka'bah, devoting oneself to worship, showing humility with the limbs, sincerity of intention in the heart, striving against Satan, intimate conversation with the Truth, recitation of the Qur'an, and uttering the testimony of faith, and restraining the self from the two most pleasant things, until they become eager to attain their aims and to remedy calamities. It is narrated that he (ﷺ) "when a matter distressed him, he would turn to prayer." It is also permissible that prayer here means supplication (du'a).

﴿And indeed it﴾: that is, seeking help through these two, or prayer. Singling it out by returning the pronoun to it is due to its great importance and its encompassing of various kinds of patience, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And when they saw a trade or amusement, they dispersed to it﴾; or [it refers to] the whole of what they were commanded and forbidden.

﴿is indeed burdensome﴾: heavy, difficult, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿It is grievous to the polytheists what you call them to﴾;
﴿except for the humble﴾: khushu' (humility) is submission (ikhbat), and from it comes "al-khush'ah," for a low-lying sandy slope. Khudu' is gentleness and compliance; for this reason it is said: khushu' is with the limbs, and khudu' is with the heart. It is not burdensome for them because they anticipate what has been prepared for them in exchange for it, so it becomes easy for them; and because they become absorbed in intimate conversation with their Lord, so they do not perceive the hardships and toils that befall them. For this reason he (ﷺ) said: "The coolness of my eye is in prayer." The clause is circumstantial (ḥāliyyah), or a parenthetical concluding clause (i'tirāḍ tadhyīliyy).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 46:

﴿Those who think that they will meet their Lord, and that they will return to Him.﴾ That is: they expect to meet Him (exalted is He) and to attain what is with Him of rewards. The mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyya), together with the attribution to them, is to signify the overflowing of His beneficence towards them. Or: they are certain that they will be gathered to Him for recompense, so they act accordingly, out of desire (raghba) and dread (rahba). As for those who do not have certainty regarding recompense, nor hope for reward, nor fear punishment, the [prayer] is for them a pure hardship, so it weighs heavily upon them, like the hypocrites and the show-offs. Thus the mention of the aforementioned title serves to indicate the causal link of Lordship and the sovereignty over judgment. This is supported by the fact that in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, the reading is: "they know" (ya'lamun). It is as though ẓann (thinking), since it resembles 'ilm (knowledge) in being a strong probability, was applied to it, by way of implying the meaning of expectation. He said:

*So I sent him, certain in his conjecture that he would penetrate what lies between the ribs, piercing through.*

And making the predicate of "anna" in both places a noun indicates the affirmation of the meeting and the return, and their being established in their minds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 47:

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾: The reminder is repeated for emphasis, and to connect what follows it of severe warning with it.

﴿And that I preferred you﴾: This is a conjunction with "My favour," the conjunction of the specific with the general (ʿatf al-khass ʿala al-ʿamm), for its completeness; meaning: "I preferred your forefathers"; ﴿over the worlds﴾: meaning, "the worlds of their times, by what I granted them of knowledge, faith, and righteous deeds, and by making them prophets and just kings"; and they are their forefathers (p-99) who lived in the era of Musa, peace be upon him, and after him, before they changed.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 48:**

﴿And guard against a Day﴾: that is, the reckoning of a Day, or the punishment of a Day; ﴿on which no soul will avail another soul in anything﴾: that is, it will not discharge for it any of the rights (of others). The accusative of "shay'an" (anything) is then as the object (maf'ul bih, direct object). Or: (it means) anything of the recompense, in which case its accusative is as a verbal noun (masdar). It has also been read as "la tujzi'" (will not suffice), meaning: will not avail it, in which case the accusative as a verbal noun is definite. Its being indefinite, together with the indefiniteness of "nafs" (soul), is for generality and for complete despair. The clause is a qualifier of "yawman" (a Day), and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: "will not avail in it." Whoever does not permit the omission says: the expression has been extended, so the preposition was dropped, the genitive was treated as the object, and then it was dropped, as in the words of one who said:

*"I do not know whether distance has changed them, and the long passage of time, or the wealth they have acquired."*

That is, "they have acquired it."

﴿Neither will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any ransom be taken from it﴾: that is, from the second soul, the disobedient one; or from the first. "Shafa'ah" (intercession) is from "shaf'" (even, a pair), as if the one for whom intercession is made was single, and the intercessor made him a pair. "'Adl" (ransom) is compensation; it has been said it means substitute, and its original meaning is "equalising." It is called by this name because the ransom equals the one ransomed and stands in its place. ﴿Nor will they be helped﴾: that is, they will not be prevented from the punishment of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The pronoun refers to what is indicated by the second, indefinite soul, which occurs in a negative context, from among the many souls; the masculine form is used because it refers to servants and human beings. "Nusrah" (help) here is more specific than "ma'unah" (assistance), since it is restricted to repelling harm. It seems the verse intends the negation that anyone should repel punishment from anyone in any possible way. For that is either by compulsion or not. The first is "nusrah." The second is either without payment or not. The first of these is intercession. The second is either by paying the very thing that was owed, which is that one suffices in its place, or by paying something else, which is giving a ransom in its place. The Mu'tazilah have held to this verse to deny intercession for the people of major sins (kaba'ir). The answer is that it is specific to the disbelievers, because of the verses that come concerning intercession and the hadiths narrated about it. This is supported by the fact that the address is with them, and by the purpose of refuting their belief that their forefathers, the prophets, would intercede for them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 49:

﴿And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾: This is a reminder of the details of what was summarized in His (exalted) saying: ﴿My favor which I bestowed upon you﴾; among the varieties of bounty and the kinds of blessings. That is: remember the time of Our delivering you, i.e., your forefathers, for their deliverance is a deliverance for their descendants. It was also read: "anjaytukum" (We delivered you). The original form of "ali" (family/people of) is "ahl" (folk), since its diminutive is "uhayl"; and it was specially joined by idafa (annexation) to the possessors of high station, such as the prophets, peace be upon them, and the kings. "Fir'awn" (Pharaoh) is a title for whoever ruled the Amalaqa, like "Kisra" for the king of the Persians, "Qaysar" for the king of the Romans, and "Khaqan" for the king of the Turks. From his tyranny (utuw) is derived "tafarʿana al-rajul" (the man acted like Pharaoh), when he transgressed and rebelled. The Pharaoh of Moses, peace be upon him, was Mus'ab ibn Rayyan; it is said that he was his son Walid, from the remnants of 'Ad. It is also said that he was an Isfahani perfumer, whom debts overwhelmed, so he went bankrupt and was compelled to leave. He went to al-Sham, but could not settle there, so he entered Egypt. He saw in the outskirts a load of melons for a dirham, and in himself [the desire for] a melon for a dirham. He said to himself: "If it becomes possible for me to pay the debt, this is its way." So he went out to the countryside and bought a load for a dirham, then headed with it to the market. Every tax-collector (makkas) he met took melons from him, so when he entered the town he had with him only a single melon, which he sold for a dirham, and went on his way. He saw the people of the town left neglected and unattended, no one administering their affairs; a great plague had struck them. So he headed toward the graveyards, and saw a dead man being buried. He approached his relatives and said: "I am the trustee of the graveyards, and I will not let you bury him until you give me five dirhams." They paid it to him. He went on to another, and another, until in the span of about three months he had gathered a great amount of money, and no one ever opposed him. Then one day he approached the relatives of a dead man and demanded from them what he had been demanding from others; they refused and said: "Who appointed you to this post?" They took him to Pharaoh. He said: "Who are you, and who installed you in this position?" He replied: "No one installed me; I only did what I did so that someone would bring me to your assembly, and I would alert you to the disorder of your people. By this way I have gathered this amount of money." So he presented it and handed it to Pharaoh. Pharaoh said: "Entrust your affairs to me; you will find me a trustworthy and capable man." So he appointed him, and he governed them with a good administration; the affairs of the army were organized and the conditions of the subjects were set right. He remained among them a long time, and his reputation for justice and righteousness spread. When Pharaoh died, they set him in his place, and he did what he did. The Pharaoh of Joseph was Rayyan, and between them were more than four hundred years.

﴿yasumunakum﴾: That is, they seek to inflict upon you, from "sامه خسفا" (he imposed injustice upon him), when he inflicted oppression on him; its original meaning is "going in pursuit of a thing". ﴿suʾ al-ʿadhab﴾ (the evil of torment): that is, its most grievous and most vile [form] in comparison with the rest of it. "Al-su'" is a verbal noun from "saa, yasuu" (to be evil). Its accusative is as the object of ﴿yasumunakum﴾. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the pronoun in ﴿najjaynakum﴾, or from "ali Fir'awn", or from both together, since it contains pronouns referring to both.

﴿yudhabbihuna abnaʾakum wa-yastahyuna nisaʾakum﴾ (they slaughter your sons and spare your women): This is an explanation of ﴿yasumunakum﴾; for this reason the conjunction between them was omitted. It was also read "yadhbahuna" with the lighter form. They did to them what they did because Pharaoh saw in a dream, or the soothsayers informed him, that a boy would be born among them who would take away his kingdom; so their efforts did not repel anything of the decree of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is said they killed, by that method, nine hundred thousand (or: ninety thousand) newborns. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, had granted the soul of Moses, peace be upon him, the power of disposal that those slain would have been given had they been alive; for this reason his miracles were manifest and dazzling.

﴿wa-fi dhalikum﴾: a reference to what was mentioned of slaughter and sparing of women, or to the deliverance from it; the pronoun is in the plural for the addressees. According to the first, the meaning of His saying ﴿balaʾun﴾ is: a trial and affliction; and the sparing of their women, that is, leaving them alive, was a trial, even though it was a pardon and a leaving off of punishment, because they were used for hard labor. According to the second, it is a blessing. The original meaning of "balaʾ" is testing; but since that is impossible with respect to Him, glory be to Him, and what functions as testing for His servants is sometimes by affliction and sometimes by bestowal, the term was applied to both. It is also said that "dhalikum" may refer to the whole clause, and "balaʾ" may be intended as the common notion encompassing both.

﴿ʿaẓim﴾ (great): an adjective of "balaʾ"; and the indefinite form of both is for magnification. In this noble verse there is an admonition that what befalls the servant of happiness and hardship is by way of testing; so upon him is gratitude in times of joy, and patience in times of harm.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 50:

﴿And when We divided the sea for you﴾: This explains the cause of the deliverance and depicts how it happened, following the reminder of it, and clarifies its greatness and terror. Within this he also clarifies another magnificent blessing, namely being saved from drowning. That is: "Remember when We split it for you by your passage through it, or while you were within it, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿a tree that grows out of Mount Sinai, yielding oil﴾ [23:20], or because of your deliverance; and We separated part of it from part until pathways came into being." It is also read with the shaddah (tashdid, doubling of the letter), for intensification, because the pathways were twelve, according to the number of the tribes (asbat).

﴿Then We delivered you﴾: That is, from drowning, by bringing you out onto the shore. This is indicated by the shift to the form af'ala (the Ifal form), after mentioning the rescue from Pharaoh in the form fa''ala (the Taf'il form). Likewise His saying (exalted is He): ﴿and We drowned the family of Pharaoh﴾ [2:50]. What is meant is Pharaoh and his people. They are mentioned only as "the family" because it is known that he is more deserving of it than they are. It has also been said that what is meant is his person alone, as it is narrated that al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him) used to say: "O Allah, send blessings upon the family of Muhammad," meaning his person. By mentioning him, his people are dispensed with.

﴿while you were watching﴾: That is, that [event], or their drowning, or the sea closing over them, or the splitting of the sea into dry, smooth paths, or their corpses which the sea cast onto the shore, or that some of you were looking at one another. It is narrated that (exalted is He) commanded Musa (peace be upon him) to travel by night with the Children of Israel. So he set out with them, and Pharaoh and his soldiers caught up with them at dawn and encountered them on the shore of the sea. Then Allah (exalted is He) revealed to him: "Strike the sea with your staff," and he struck it with it, and twelve dry paths appeared in it. They traversed them, but they said: "We fear that some of our companions may drown, and we would not know." So Allah (exalted is He) opened windows in the paths, so they could see one another and hear one another, until they crossed the sea. When Pharaoh reached it and saw it split apart, he plunged into it along with his soldiers, and so there covered them what covered them.

Know that this event, just as it is a great miracle for Musa and a mighty blessing for the earliest Children of Israel, which obligated them to be grateful for it, so too its narration as it is, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), is a magnificent miracle by which proud hearts are reassured and by which dull souls are brought to submission. It obligates their descendants to receive it with acceptance. Yet their forefathers were not affected by witnessing and seeing it, and their latter generations were not reminded by its being recounted and related. How lamentable a band, how rebellious! And how grievous a people, how insolent!

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 51:**

﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾: When they returned to Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh, Allah (Exalted) promised Moses, peace be upon him, that He would give him the Torah, and He set for him an appointed time: the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah and the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. It is said that Moses, peace be upon him, had promised the Children of Israel, while they were still in Egypt, that if Allah destroyed their enemy, He would bring them a Book from Allah (Exalted) containing an explanation of what they should do and what they should refrain from. When Pharaoh died, Moses asked his Lord for the Book, and He commanded him to fast thirty days, which is the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah, and then added ten days from Dhu al-Hijjah. He expressed these as nights because nights are the beginnings of the months (ghurar al-shuhur). The form *wa'adna* (from the root *w-'-d*, with the pattern *mufa'alah*, Form III) has the meaning of the trilateral form (*thulathi*, Form I). It is also said that it retains its original meaning, with Moses' acceptance being treated as a promise (*wa'd*) through a process of *tanzil* (a figurative application, lit. "lowering" a concept to a different status).

"Forty nights" (*arba'in layla*) is the second object of *wa'adna*, with an elided noun governed by it (*hadhf al-mudaf*), meaning: "the completion of forty nights." It is read as *wa'adna* in one reading.

﴿Then you took the calf﴾: as a god and an object of worship, through the seduction of the Samiri. The *thumma* ("then") here indicates a difference in rank (*al-tarakhi al-rutbi*), not merely a difference in time.

﴿after him﴾: that is, after his departure to the appointed time, with an elided noun (*hadhf al-mudaf*): "after the time of his departure."

﴿while you were wrongdoers﴾: by associating partners with Allah and by placing a thing in other than its proper place. This clause is either a *hal* (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in *ittakhadhtum*, or a parenthetical concluding clause (*i'tiradh tadhyili*), meaning: "and you are a people whose habit is wrongdoing."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 52:

﴿Then We pardoned you﴾; when you repented. And al-'afw (pardon) is the effacing of the crime; from "'afahu," meaning "darasahu" (he obliterated it); and it may come intransitively. He said:

"I recognised the abandoned dwelling, / effaced after its conditions."

"Every pouring rain effaced it, / abundant in its heavy downpour, incessant."

And His saying (exalted is He): ﴿after that﴾: that is, after the taking (of the calf) which is extreme in ugliness; to indicate the complete remoteness of the pardon after that degree of wrongdoing; ﴿so that you might give thanks﴾: so that you would give thanks for the blessing of pardon; and persist thereafter in obedience.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 53:

(p-102) ﴿And [remember] when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion (al-Furqan)﴾: that is, the Torah, combining being a book (kitab) and a proof (hujjah); it distinguishes between the truth and falsehood. It was also said: what is meant by al-Furqan is his miracles, which separate the truthful claimant from the liar in his claim; or between disbelief and faith. It was said: it is the Law (al-shar') that distinguishes between the lawful (halal) and the unlawful (haram); or it is the victory by which He separated him from his enemy, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿the Day of the Criterion﴾, meaning the Day of Badr. ﴿So that you may be guided﴾: so that you may be guided by reflecting upon it and acting by what it contains.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 54:

﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾: an explanation of how the aforementioned pardon came about. ﴿O my people, you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf﴾: i.e., as a deity. ﴿So repent﴾: i.e., resolve upon repentance. ﴿To your Originator (bari')﴾: i.e., to He who created you free of defects, deficiency and disparity, and distinguished some of you from others by diverse forms and shapes. The root meaning of this construction (tarkib) is disengagement from another, either by way of escaping, as in "the patient became well (bara'a al-mariḍ)," or by way of origination, as in "God originated (bara'a) Adam from clay." Mentioning the title of "Originator" serves to indicate that they had reached the utmost of ignorance and the furthest extreme of error, in that they abandoned the worship of the All-Knowing, the All-Wise, who created them by the subtlety of His wisdom free of disparity and discord, in favour of the worship of a cow, which is a proverb for stupidity. And whoever does not recognise the rights of his benefactor deserves to have those (blessings) taken back from him; for this reason they were commanded to kill and to dismantle the composition (of their being). ﴿So kill yourselves﴾: as a completion of your repentance, by exhaustion (bakh') or by cutting off the desires. It was said: they were commanded that some of them should kill others. It was also said: whoever had not worshipped the calf was commanded to kill whoever had worshipped it. It is narrated that a man would see his relative and was unable to proceed with God's command (exalted is He); so God sent a mist and a black cloud, so that they could not see one another, and they began killing from the morning until the evening, until Moses and Aaron (peace be upon them both) supplicated, whereupon the cloud was lifted, the repentance was granted, and the slain numbered seventy thousand. The first "fa" (so) denotes causation, and the second denotes sequence. ﴿That﴾: a reference to what has been mentioned of repentance and killing. ﴿Is better for you with your Originator﴾: because it is a purification from polytheism and a means to eternal life and everlasting joy. ﴿Then He relented toward you﴾: a conjunction with an elided element, on the basis that it is an address from Him (glorified is He), in the manner of the iltifat (shift) from the first person, which the context and the flow of the noble composition require; for the whole is built on the first person shifting to the third person, so that it serves as a means to attributing the act to the pronoun of "your Originator," which entails an indication of the causality of the title of Originator, of creation and of giving life, for the acceptance of repentance, which is an expression for pardon of the killing. Its supposed form: "You did what you were commanded, so your Originator relented toward you." And it was not said "then He relented toward them," although the pronoun refers to the people, because that is a blessing whose remembrance is intended for those addressed, not for their forebears. This is the position. It has also been permitted that "then He relented toward you" be linked to an elided element, on the basis that it is from the speech of Moses (peace be upon him) to his people, the supposed form being: "If you do what you were commanded, then he has relented toward you." It is not hidden that this is wholly incongruous with the majesty of the status of the revelation; how could it not be? For then it would be a report of Moses (peace be upon him) promising his people the acceptance of repentance from Him (exalted is He), not of His acceptance of it as a certainty. You have already understood that the noble verse is an elaboration of the manner of the acceptance reported in what precedes, and that the purpose is to remind the addressees of that blessing.

﴿Indeed, He is the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful﴾: a causal explanation (ta'lil) of what precedes; i.e., He who abundantly grants the sinners success in repentance, exceeds in accepting it from them, and in bestowing favour upon them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 55:

﴿And when you said, "O Musa, we will never believe you until we see Allah openly"﴾: a reminder of another blessing upon them, after there had proceeded from them what had proceeded of the great offense, which is the taking of the calf (as a god). That is: "we will never believe (in) on account of your saying and your call," or: "we will never acknowledge you." The thing believed in is: Allah (exalted is He) giving him the Torah; or His speaking to him; or that he is a prophet; or that He (exalted is He) made their repentance conditional upon their killing themselves. ﴿Until we see Allah openly﴾; that is, directly (ʿiyanan). It is originally the verbal noun of your saying, "I recited aloud (jahartu bi'l-qira'a)," and it was borrowed for direct observation, because of the unity between them in clarity and disclosure; except that the first (jahr) is for things heard, and the second for things seen. Its accusative (nasb) is as a verbal noun (masdar), because it is a kind of seeing; or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject or the object. It has also been read with a fatha on the ha', as a verbal noun like "al-ghalaba," or as a plural like "al-kataba," in which case it is a circumstantial clause from the subject only. The speakers are the seventy chosen men for the appointed time of repentance from the worship of the calf. It is narrated that when they regretted what they had done and said, ﴿If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers﴾, Allah (exalted is He) commanded Musa (peace be upon him) to gather seventy men and to attend with them at the Mount (al-Tur), that they might manifest that repentance there. When they went out to the Mount, a column of cloud descended upon it and enveloped it entirely, and Allah (exalted is He) spoke to Musa (peace be upon him), commanding him and forbidding him; and whenever He (exalted is He) spoke to him, He cast upon his forehead a dazzling light, which none of the seventy could bear to look at. And they heard the speech of Allah (exalted is He) with Musa (peace be upon him): "Do, and do not do." At that point they coveted the seeing, and said what they said, as will come in surah al-A'raf, if Allah (exalted is He) wills. It has also been said: they were ten thousand of his people. ﴿So the thunderbolt seized you﴾, because of excessive obstinacy, insolence, and seeking the impossible; for they thought that He (glorified and exalted is He) is of the kind that resembles bodies, and that seeing relates to Him as it relates to them, by way of facing one another in directions and locations. There is no doubt in its impossibility. What is possible regarding Him (exalted is He) is the seeing that is absolutely free of modalities; and that is for the believers in the Hereafter, and for particular prophets who attained such purity of essence that you see them as if they were in garments of their bodies, having stripped them off and detached from them into the world of holiness, in some states in this world. It has been said: a fire came down from heaven and burned them. It has been said: a cry. It has been said: troops whose rustling they heard, so they fell down stunned and dead for a day and a night. And from Wahb: they did not die; rather, when they saw that awesome form, trembling seized them and they shook until their joints nearly separated and their backs nearly broke, and they came close to perishing. At that point Musa (peace be upon him) wept and called upon his Lord, and Allah (exalted and majestic is He) removed that from them, and their minds and senses returned to them. The stunning of Musa (peace be upon him) was not death but a swoon, due to His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And when he recovered﴾; ﴿while you were looking on﴾; that is, what befell you (was) by itself or by its effects.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 56:

﴿Then We revived you after your death﴾; with that thunderbolt (al-sa'iqa). He restricted the resurrection (al-ba'th) to it because it may be from fainting (al-ighma'), and it may be from sleep (al-nawm); as in His (Exalted) saying: ﴿Then We revived them that We might know﴾; etc.

﴿so that you may give thanks﴾: that is, for the blessing of the resurrection; or for what you disbelieved in, having seen the might (ba's) of Allah (Exalted).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 57:

﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾: that is, We made them such that they cast their shade upon you. That is because He (Exalted is He) subjected to them (p-104)

the clouds, which moved with their movement while they were in the wilderness (al-tih), shading them from the sun; and at night there descended a pillar of fire, by whose light they traveled; their garments did not become soiled, nor did they wear out. ﴿And We sent down upon you the manna and the quails﴾: that is, the tarantabin (a sweet exudation) and the quails. It was also said: the manna would descend upon them like snow from dawn until sunrise, a ṣāʿ (a measure of volume) for each person; and the south wind would bring quails to them, so that a man would slaughter from them what sufficed him. ﴿Eat﴾: implying the verb of saying, that is, saying to them, or it was said to them: ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾, from its delicacies. And "what" (mā), whether it is a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun, refers to the manna and the quails.

﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾: this is a statement diverted from the course of the preceding address, to signal that the offenses of those addressed necessitate turning away from them and enumerating their ugly deeds before others, by way of reproach. It is conjoined to an implied clause that has been omitted for brevity and to convey that it is a certainty, needing no explicit mention; that is: "so they wronged, by denying those magnificent blessings; and they did not wrong Us thereby." ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾: by ingratitude, since it is necessarily not beyond them. The fronting of the object indicates restriction (qasr), which the preceding negation requires; and in it there is a form of mockery toward them. The combining of the past and the present tense forms indicates their persistence in wrongdoing and their continuance in disbelief.

And when We said: a reminder of another of His blessings (exalted is He), and another ingratitude of their forefathers. That is: remember the time when We said to your fathers, right after We had rescued them from the wandering (al-tīh): ﴿Enter this town﴾. It is in the accusative, as an adverbial of place (al-ẓarfiyyah) according to Sibawayh, and as a direct object (al-maf'ūliyyah) according to al-Akhfash. It is Bayt al-Maqdis, and it has been said that it is Jericho (Arīhā). ﴿Then eat from it wherever you wish, plentifully﴾: that is, abundantly and comfortably. Its accusative is either as an absolute infinitive (al-maṣdariyyah) or as a circumstantial qualifier (al-ḥāliyyah) referring to the addressees. In this is an indication that what was commanded was entering to settle and reside. This returns to His words in Surat al-A'rāf: ﴿Dwell in this town﴾. ﴿And enter the gate﴾: that is, the gate of the town, according to what is reported, that they entered Jericho in the time of Mūsā (peace be upon him), as will come in Surat al-Mā'idah. Or it is the gate of the dome (al-qubbah) which they used to face in prayer, for they did not enter Bayt al-Maqdis during the lifetime of Mūsā (peace be upon him). ﴿Prostrating﴾: that is, humbling themselves, submissive, or prostrating to God (exalted) in thanks for bringing them out of the wandering. ﴿And say: ḥiṭṭah﴾: that is, our request for forgiveness; or: your command is ḥiṭṭah. It is a noun of the form fi'lah derived from al-ḥaṭṭ (removal), like jilsah. It was read in the accusative according to the original form, meaning: remove from us our sins, a removal. Or it is the direct object of "qūlū", meaning: say this word. It has been said that its meaning is: show us ḥiṭṭah, that is, that we may set down our baggage in this town and settle there. ﴿We will forgive you your sins﴾, for what you do of prostration and supplication. It was read with the yā' and the tā', in the passive form. The original of khaṭāyā is khaṭāyi'u, like khaḍā'i'u. According to Sībawayh, the extra yā' was replaced by a hamzah because it came after an alif, and two hamzahs came together; the second was replaced by a yā', then turned into an alif, and since the hamzah was then between two alifs, it was replaced by a yā'. According to al-Khalīl, the hamzah was placed before the yā', and then what has been mentioned was done to it. ﴿And We will increase the good-doers﴾ in reward. Compliance was made a repentance for the wrongdoer and a cause of increased reward for the good-doer. This has been taken out of the form of a response into the form of a promise, as a notice that the good-doer is poised for this even if he has not yet done it; so how much more so if he has done it? And he will certainly do it.

(p-105) ﴿So those who did wrong substituted﴾ a word other than what they had been commanded, namely repentance and seeking forgiveness, by turning away from it and bringing in in its place ﴿another saying﴾ that held no good. It is narrated that they said, instead of "ḥiṭṭah" (remove [our sins]), "ḥinṭah" (wheat). It is also said that they said, in Nabataean, "ḥuṭan samqāthan," meaning "red wheat," mocking the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Other than what had been said to them﴾ is an attribute of "saying." It was stated explicitly, although the substitution could not occur without some difference, in order to confirm their defiance and to state explicitly that the difference was in every respect.

﴿So We sent down﴾, that is, immediately after that, ﴿upon those who did wrong﴾ by what was mentioned of the substitution. The relative pronoun was placed in the position of a pronoun referring back to the first relative pronoun, for the sake of giving the reason, intensifying the censure and reproach, and to state explicitly that by what they did they wronged themselves by exposing themselves to the wrath of Allah (Exalted).

﴿A plague from the sky﴾, that is, a punishment decreed from it. The tanwin (indefinite ending) is for magnifying and emphasizing the matter. ﴿Because they used to defiantly transgress﴾: because of their persistent defiance, as is indicated by combining the past and present verb forms. Stating the cause of sending down the plague, after indicating its cause as their wrongdoing, serves to signify that this is defiance, departure from obedience, and excess in wrongdoing, and that their punishment was for all the abominations they committed, not merely for their failure to repent, as is suggested by the connecting of the result to that with the particle fa'. "Rijz" (plague/filth) originally means what is loathed; likewise "rijs." It has also been read with a ḍammah (rujz), which is a dialectal variant of the same word. The intended meaning is the plague (ṭā'ūn). It is narrated that twenty-four thousand people died from it in a single hour.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 60:

﴿And when Musa (Moses) asked for water for his people﴾: a reminder of another blessing that they disbelieved. This occurred during the wandering (al-tih), when severe thirst overcame them. The change in order, concerning what has been pointed out repeatedly, is for the purpose of highlighting each of the enumerated matters within the context of an independent command that must be remembered and called to mind. Had the chronological order been observed, it would have been understood that all of them were one matter, which he was commanded to mention. The lam (preposition) is connected to the verb, meaning: he asked for water for the sake of his people.

﴿So We said: Strike the rock with your staff﴾: It is related that it was a Tur (Sinai) rock, cubical, which he carried with him, and from each of its faces three springs gushed forth, each spring flowing in a stream to one tribe. They were six hundred thousand, and the width of the encampment was twelve miles. Or it was a rock that Allah (Exalted) sent down with Adam (peace be upon him) from Paradise, and it came into the possession of Shu'ayb (peace be upon him), who gave it to Musa (peace be upon him) along with the staff. Or it was the rock that fled with his garment when he placed it upon it to bathe, and Allah (Exalted) cleared him through it of what they had accused him of, the swelling of the testicles; then Jibril (Gabriel) (peace be upon him) gestured to him to carry it. Or it was a rock of ordinary stones, and this is the most apparent in terms of argument. It has been said: Musa (peace be upon him) was not commanded to strike a specific rock, but when they said, "What will become of us if we reach a land with no stones in it?", he carried a rock in his bag, and he would strike it with his staff when he dismounted, and it would gush forth; and when he departed he would strike it and it would dry up. They said: "If Musa loses his staff, we will die of thirst." So Allah (Exalted) revealed to him: "Do not strike the rock; speak to it and it will obey you, so that perhaps they will take heed." It has also been said: the rock was of marble, its size one cubit by one cubit, and the staff was ten cubits in length, of the wood of Paradise's myrtle, and it had two branches that shone in the darkness. (p-106)

﴿Then there gushed forth﴾: this is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon an implied element that the speech carries along; it has been omitted to indicate the complete swiftness of the realisation of the gushing, as if it occurred immediately after the command to strike; meaning: so he struck, and there gushed forth ﴿from it twelve springs﴾. As for attaching the fa' (so) to an omitted element, meaning: if you strike, then it has gushed forth, this is not worthy of the sublime status of the noble composition, as is not hidden from anyone. It was also read as "ʿashirata" with a kasra on the shin and with a fatha on it; both are also dialectal forms. ﴿Every people knew their drinking place﴾: each tribe knew their own specific spring. ﴿Eat and drink﴾: with the implication of saying. ﴿Of the provision of Allah﴾: this is what He provided them of manna, quails, and water. It has also been said that it is water alone, because from it grows what is eaten of crops and fruits. What rejects this is that what was commanded was eating the blessing that was ready, not what they would seek. Its attribution to Him (Exalted), while everything is ascribed to Him in creation and ownership, is either for honour, or because it appeared without an ordinary cause. And He did not say "of Our provision," as the phrase ﴿So We said﴾ and so on would require, to indicate that the command to eat and drink was not in the form of direct address, but through the mediation of Musa (peace be upon him).

﴿And do not act wickedly on the earth﴾: al-ʿathy (ʿathy) is the most severe corruption. So it was said to them: do not persist in corruption while ﴿being corrupters﴾. It has also been said that it was restricted by this because al-ʿathy originally means absolute transgression, though it predominates in corruption; it may also occur in other than corruption, as in confronting the oppressor who transgresses by his action, and it may contain a predominant good, like the killing of the boy by al-Khidr (peace be upon him) and his damaging of the ship. Its counterpart is al-ʿabath (aimless mischief), except that it predominates in what is perceived by the senses.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 61:**

﴿And when you said﴾: a reminder of another offence committed by their forebears, of their ingratitude for the blessing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and of their inclination toward the baseness and meanness in which they were living. The attribution of the quoted speech to their descendants, and the directing of the rebuke at them, is because of the unity (ittihad) between them.

﴿O Musa, we will not endure one kind of food﴾: Perhaps they did not mean by this that they wanted to combine what they had asked for with the blessing they already had, nor that the blessing should cease and what they asked for should take its place, since that would entail being exposed to solitude. Rather, they wanted this to be at one time and that at another. It is related that they were farmers, and they inclined toward their former ways (ukar), so they found the abundant blessing they had been enjoying tedious because of its uniform kind and its continuity, and their souls longed for hardship.

﴿So pray to your Lord for us﴾: that is, ask Him on our behalf by your supplication to Him. The fa' (so) indicates that their lack of patience causes the supplication. Mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyya) is to prepare the ground for the granting of the answer.

﴿He will bring forth for us﴾: that is, He will make manifest for us and bring into existence. The jazm (apocopation) is in response to the imperative. ﴿From what the earth grows﴾: this is a figurative attribution (isnad majazi), by placing the recipient in the position of the agent. The "min" is partitive (tab'idiyya). The "min" in His words, may He be exalted, ﴿from its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils and its onions﴾, is explanatory (bayaniyya) and occupies the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), meaning: being from its herbs, and so on. It has also been said that it is a substitute (badal), with the preposition repeated. "Baql" (herbs) means the greens that the earth produces, and what is intended is their choice edibles that are eaten, such as mint, celery, leeks and the like. "Fum" means wheat; it has also been said to mean garlic. It is also read as "qutha'ihā" with a damma on the qaf, which is a dialectal variant of the same word.

He (Allah, exalted, or Musa, peace be upon him) said, in rebuke of them. This is a fresh sentence (isti'naf) that answers an implied question, as if it were said: "What did He say to them?" It was then said: He said, ﴿Do you exchange﴾, that is, do you take for yourselves and choose; ﴿that which is lower﴾, that is, nearer in rank and lesser in value, easy to obtain and readily attainable, because it is not desirable and is trivial, despicable and of little worth. The original meaning of "dunuww" (lowness) is nearness in place, and it was borrowed for baseness, just as distance is borrowed for nobility and elevation; so one says "far in station" and "far in aspiration." It is also read as "adna'" from "dana'a" (baseness), and the familiar reading is understood as having its alif substituted for a hamza; ﴿for that which is better﴾: that is, in exchange for what is better. The "ba'" (for) accompanies the thing that departs and passes away, not the thing that comes and is attained, as in the case of exchange (tabdil) in His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾, and His words: ﴿And We replaced their two gardens with two gardens bearing bitter produce﴾. There is nothing in it that definitely indicates that they wanted the manna and quails to cease entirely and what they asked for to be obtained in their place, as in the actual establishment of substitution, in the scenario of alternation mentioned above.

﴿Go down to a city﴾: they were commanded to do so, as an explanation of the baseness of their request, or as a fulfilment of their aim; that is, descend to it from the wilderness. One says "habata al-wadi" (he descended the valley). It is also read with a damma on the ba'. "Misr" means a great city; its original sense is a boundary between two things. It has been said that it is intended as a proper name, and it is diptotic (ghayr munsarif) only because of the sukun in its middle, or because it is interpreted as "city" rather than "metropolis." This is supported by the fact that in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it is without tanwin. It has also been said that its original form was "Misrayim," which was then Arabized.

﴿For you will have what you asked for﴾: this is the rationale for the command to descend; that is, for you there is in it what you requested. Perhaps the expression of the things requested by "ma" (what) is to express disdain in mentioning them, as if it were said: "For it is abundant there, commonplace, which everyone attains without hardship."

﴿And humiliation and wretchedness were stamped upon them﴾: that is, they were made to surround them, like a tent encompassing the one upon whom it is pitched; or they were made to cling to them and were made a stamp that does not leave them, as a recompense for their disbelief, like the stamping of clay on a wall. This is by way of metaphor by implication (isti'arah bi-l-kinayah). The Jews are for the most part humble and wretched, either in actual fact, or for fear that their poll-tax (jizya) would be increased.

﴿And they returned﴾: that is, they came back; ﴿with anger﴾, great anger. His words, may He be exalted, ﴿from Allah﴾, are connected with an omitted element and are a qualifier of "anger," emphasising what the tanwin conveyed of intrinsic magnitude with the magnitude of attribution; that is, with anger that proceeds from Allah, may He be exalted. Or they became deserving of it, from the saying of people: "Fulan returned (ba'a) with Fulan," meaning he became deserving of being killed in retaliation for him. From this is the saying of the one who said: "Return (bu') with the thong of the sandal of Kulayb." The original meaning of "ba'" is equality.

﴿That﴾: a reference to what has passed of the stamping of humiliation and wretchedness, and of returning with great anger; ﴿because﴾: owing to the fact that; ﴿they used to disbelieve﴾, continually; ﴿in the signs of Allah﴾, the dazzling miracles that are the brilliant proofs manifested at the hand of Musa, peace be upon him, both those that have been enumerated and those that have not been enumerated.

﴿And they killed the prophets without right﴾, such as Sha'ya, Zakariyya and Yahya, peace be upon them all. The purpose of the qualification, although killing prophets could never be rightful, is to indicate that this was also, in their view, without right, since no one among them believed in the rightfulness of killing any of the prophets, peace be upon them. What moved them to that was love of this world, following of desire, excess in disobedience, and transgression, as His words, may He be exalted, make clear: ﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾. That is, disobedience and persistence in aggression drove them to what has been mentioned of disbelief and the killing of the prophets, peace be upon them, for minor sins, if persisted in, lead to major ones, just as persistence in minor acts of obedience leads to seeking out the major ones. It has also been said that the demonstrative was repeated to indicate that what befell them, just as it was because of disbelief and killing, was also because of their committing sins and their transgression of the limits of Allah, may He be exalted. It has also been said that the demonstrative refers to disbelief and killing. The "ba'" here means "with." It is permissible to refer to a plural with a singular, by interpreting it as "what has been mentioned" or "what has preceded," as in the verse of Ru'ba ibn al-'Ajjaj:

*There are in it streaks of black and white,*
*as if on its skin is the spreading of leprosy.*

That is, "what has been mentioned was." What made this acceptable in pronouns and vague demonstratives is that their dual and plural forms are not used in their literal sense; for this reason "alladhi" is used with the meaning of "alladhina" (those who).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 2, verse 62:**

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾: that is, with their tongues only; and they are the hypocrites (munafiqun), as indicated by their being grouped in the same category as the disbelievers. The expression used for them is this, rather than the designation of hypocrisy, to make clear that this state, even though it is described as belief, does not benefit them at all, and does not rescue them from the predicament of disbelief in any way. ﴿And those who were Jews﴾: that is, those who became Jews (tahawwadu), from "hada," when one enters Judaism. As for "Yahud" (Jews): it is either Arabic, from "hada," meaning "he repented." They were so named when they repented from worshipping the calf, and this name was specifically given to them because their repentance was tremendous. Or it is an arabized form of "Yahudha" (Judah), as if they were named after the eldest of the sons of Ya'qub, peace be upon him. ﴿And the Christians (al-Nasara)﴾: the plural of "Nasran," like "nadama," the plural of "nadman." It is said: a man is "nasran," and a woman is "nasrana." The yā' in "nasrani" is for emphasis (mubalagha), as in "ahmari." They were named this because they helped (nasaru) the Messiah, peace be upon him. Or because they were with him in a village called "Nasran," so they were named after it, or were attributed to it, and the yā' is for ascription (nisba). Al-Khalil said: the singular of "al-Nasara" is "nasri," like "mahri," and "mahara." ﴿And the Sabians (al-Sabi'un)﴾: they are a people between the Christians and the Magians. It is said: the origin of their religion is the religion of Nuh, peace be upon him. It is also said: they are worshippers of the angels. It is also said: they are worshippers of the stars. If it is Arabic, then it is from "saba'a," meaning he left one religion for another. It has also been read with a yā' (al-Sabiyin), either for lightness, or because it is from "saba," meaning he inclined, since they inclined away from all other religions towards what they were upon, or from the truth towards falsehood. ﴿Whoever believes in God and the Last Day﴾: that is, whoever among these groups produces sincere belief in the Origin and the Return, in the proper manner. ﴿And does﴾ an action; ﴿righteous﴾: as belief in what has been mentioned requires. ﴿For them﴾, in return for that, ﴿is their reward﴾, which was promised to them, ﴿with their Lord﴾: that is, the Owner of their affair, and the One who brings them to their fitting perfection.

So "man" (whoever): it may be in the nominative position, as the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is the clause "for them is their reward." The fa' (then) is because the relative pronoun includes the meaning of a condition, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who tormented the believers﴾, and so on. The plural of the three pronouns is in accordance with the meaning of the relative pronoun, just as the singular of what is in the relative clause is in accordance with its wording. The clause, as it is, is the predicate of "inna," and the returning pronoun to its subject is omitted, meaning: "whoever believes among them..." etc. Or it may be in the accusative position, as an apposition (badal) to the subject of "inna" and what is conjoined to it, and its predicate is "for them is their reward." And "ʿinda" (with) is connected to what is connected to "lahum" (for them), from the sense of being established. Its being attributed to the Lord, which is attributed to their pronoun, shows additional kindness towards them, and indicates that their reward is certain to be established and secure from being lost.

﴿And no fear shall be upon them﴾: a conjunction to the clause "for them is their reward." That is: no fear shall be upon them at the time when the disbelievers fear punishment. ﴿Nor will they grieve﴾: at the time when those who fall short grieve over wasting their lives and losing reward. The purpose is to state the continuous negation of these two, not the negation of their continuity, as the fact that the predicate in the second clause is in the present tense might suggest, because of what has been stated before: that negation, even when it enters upon the present tense itself, indicates permanence and continuity, according to the context. This is it.

It has been said: the intended meaning of "those who believe" is those who adhere to the religion of Islam, sincere ones among them and hypocrites. In that case it is necessary to interpret "whoever believes" as "whoever among them is characterized by sincere belief in the Origin and the Return," in an unrestricted sense, whether that is by way of steadfastness and persistence in it, like the belief of the sincere ones, or by way of initiating and producing it, like the belief of the hypocrites and the rest of the groups. The benefit of including the sincere ones in the generalization is to further encourage the others to believe, by showing that their delay in acquiring it does not harm their being an example for those earlier ones in deserving the reward and what follows it of lasting security. As for what has been said in its interpretation: "whoever among them was, in his religion, before it was abrogated, believing in his heart in the Origin and the Return, acting according to the requirement of his law," this is something that has no way to be sustained at all. This is because the requirement of the context is encouragement towards the religion of Islam, whereas describing the state of those who passed on another religion before its abrogation has no connection to the context whatsoever. Rather, it may even undermine its requirement, in terms of its indication that it was true in its time, in general. Moreover, the hypocrites and the Sabians cannot have what has been mentioned applied to them. As for the hypocrites: if they are from the people of polytheism, the matter is clear. If they are from the People of the Book, then those among them who passed before the abrogation were not hypocrites. As for the Sabians: they have no religion that could be permissibly observed at any time. Even if it is granted that they had a heavenly religion, then they departed from it, the ones who passed from the people of that religion before their departure from it are not from the Sabians. So how is it possible to return the connecting pronoun between the subject of "inna" and its predicate to them, or to the hypocrites? And to commit to returning it to the collection of the groups as a whole, not to each one of them individually, intending to include the group mentioned in it? This is because whoever among the People of the Book acted according to the requirement of his law before its abrogation, from among the collection of the groups, by virtue of its including the Jews and the Christians, even if he was not from the hypocrites or the Sabians, is something from which the sanctity of the revelation must be kept free. Moreover, the sincere ones, despite being included in the domain of the subject of "inna," have no trace or effect in the domain of its predicate. So reflect, and be upon the clear truth.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 63:

﴿And [remember] when We took your covenant﴾: a reminder of another transgression of your forefathers; that is, "Remember the time when We took your covenant to uphold what is in the Torah." ﴿And We raised the mount above you﴾: this is coordinated with His saying "We took" (akhadhna), or it is a circumstantial clause; that is, "while We had raised the mount above you, as if it were a canopy." It is narrated that when Musa (peace be upon him) brought them the Torah and they saw what it contained of arduous obligations, they found them heavy and refused to accept it. So Jibril (peace be upon him) was commanded, and he uprooted the mountain (al-Tur) and held it over them until they accepted. ﴿Take﴾, with the implied meaning of "saying": ﴿what We have given you﴾, from the Book, ﴿with strength﴾: with earnestness and resolve. ﴿And remember what is in it﴾: that is, preserve it and do not forget it; or reflect upon it, for that is remembrance by the heart; or act upon it. ﴿So that you may become righteous﴾: in order that you may refrain from sins; or that you may be saved from the ruin of both abodes; or in hope from you that you may be enrolled among the righteous; or in seeking that. Its verification has already passed.

Then you turned away, that is, you refused to fulfil the covenant, after the taking of that solemn covenant. ﴿But for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾: by granting you the ability to repent; or through Muhammad (ﷺ), since he calls you to the truth and guides you to it. ﴿You would certainly have been among the losers﴾: that is, the cheated, by immersing yourselves in sins and stumbling into the abysses of misguidance during the interval (al-fatra). It was said: but for His grace upon you through granting respite and delaying the punishment, you would have been among the ruined. This is the more fitting reading with what follows.

The word لَوْلا (lawla) is either simple or compounded from لَوْ (law), the particle of impossibility, and the particle of negation. Its meaning is the impossibility of one thing because of the existence of another, just as لَوْ indicates the impossibility of one thing because of the impossibility of another. According to Sibawayh, the noun that follows it is a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence) whose khabar (predicate) is obligatorily omitted because the context indicates it, and the answer (jawab) has taken its place. The estimated sentence is: "But for the grace of Allah (being present)..." According to the Kufans, the noun is the fa'il (agent) of an omitted verb, meaning: "Had the grace of Allah been established upon you..."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 65:

﴿And you certainly knew﴾; i.e., you recognized; ﴿those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath﴾. It is narrated that they were commanded to devote the day of the Sabbath entirely to worship, to free themselves for it, and to abstain from hunting. But some people among them transgressed in this during the time of Dawud (peace be upon him), and they busied themselves with hunting. They lived in a town on the seashore called "Aylah." When the Sabbath day came, no fish remained in the sea without rising to the surface and extending its snout; and when the day passed, they dispersed. So they dug pools and ran channels to them, and the fish would enter them on the Sabbath, and they would catch them on Sunday. The meaning is: by Allah, you certainly knew of them, when they did what they did of the kinds of your own offenses, that We did not give them respite and did not delay their punishment, but hastened it. ﴿So We said to them, "Be apes, despised and driven away."﴾; i.e., combining the form of apes and the state of ﴿khasi'in﴾, which means expelled and humiliated. [The word] ﴿khasi'in﴾ is an attribute of ﴿qiradah﴾ (apes). It is also said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) of the subject of "kunu" according to those who permit the operation of "kana" on adverbs of time and circumstance; and it is said that it is a circumstantial clause of the pronoun concealed in ﴿qiradah﴾, because it carries the meaning of "transformed" (mamsukhin). Mujahid said: their forms were not transformed, but their hearts were; so they were depicted as apes, just as they were depicted as a donkey in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿like the example of a donkey carrying books﴾. The purpose of the command is to express the speed of the bringing into being, and that they became so, as He (mighty and majestic is He) intended. It is also read "qaridatan" with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the ra, and "khasin" without a hamza.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 66:

﴿So We made it﴾: that is, the transformation (into apes) and the punishment; ﴿a deterrent﴾: a lesson that deters the one who takes heed from it, that is, prevents him and restrains him; and from this comes "al-nakl" (the shackle), for the fetter; ﴿for what was before it and what was after it﴾: for what came before it and what came after it, of the nations, since their condition is recorded in the scriptures of the earlier ones and their stories are well known among the later ones; or for their contemporaries and those after them; or for the towns near it and those far from it; or for the people of that town and those around it; or because of what preceded it of their sins and what followed from it; ﴿and an admonition for the God-conscious﴾: from among their people; or for every God-conscious person who hears of it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 67:

﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾: another rebuke to the descendants of the Children of Israel, by reminding them of some crimes committed by their forefathers; that is: "Remember the time when Moses, peace be upon him, said to your forefathers: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾." The cause of this was that among the Children of Israel there was a wealthy elder, whom his cousins killed, out of greed for his inheritance; they then threw him at the gate of the city and came demanding his blood-money (diyah). So Allah (exalted be He) commanded them to slaughter a cow and strike him with a part of it, so that he would come to life and tell them who his killer was. ﴿They said﴾: this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), occurring as an answer to what the discourse leads to; as if it were said: "What did they do? Did they hasten to comply or not?" So it was said: they said: ﴿Do you make us a mockery?﴾ with a damma on the zay and the hamza changed into a waw; it is also read with the hamza together with damma and with sukun (huzu'an, huzu, huzuan); that is: "Do you make us into an object of mockery, or people of mockery, or ones who are mocked, or mockery itself?"
