This is said as a denial of what he had said and as a contempt for him. ﴿He said﴾: a resumptive clause, as mentioned before: ﴿I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant﴾, because mocking while conveying the command of Allah (glorified be He) is ignorance and foolishness. He (peace be upon him) negated what they had imagined about him in the most emphatic and forceful manner, by phrasing it as something from which no harm would follow, through seeking refuge from it, as a way of expressing abhorrence of it and magnifying the enormity of what they had dared to do, the great offense they had directed at him to his face (peace be upon him).

Qālū (they said): this is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf), as previously explained; it is as if it was said: "What did they say after that?" So it was answered: they turned toward compliance, and said: "Od'u lanā" (pray for us) — that is, on our behalf — "rabbaka yubayyin lanā mā hiya" (your Lord to make clear to us what it is). "Mā" is the subject (mubtadaʾ), and "hiya" is its predicate (khabar), and the clause is in the position of an accusative (fī ḥayyiz al-naṣb). "Yubayyin": that is, "yubayyin lanā jawāba hādhā al-suʾāl" (make clear to us the answer to this question). They were asking about its state and its attributes, since there had reached their ears what they had not known of a dead cow, by a part of which the dead would be struck so that he would come to life. For "mā," although it is used to seek the concept of a thing and its reality, as in the explanatory "mā" and the real "mā," it may also be used to seek an attribute and a condition. You say: "Mā Zayd?" and it is answered: "A physician," or "a scholar." It was said that its proper form was to be asked with "ayyu" (which), but when they saw that what they were commanded regarding was in a state different from that of its kind, they removed it from the reality and made it a kind on its own.

[Mūsā] said — that is, Mūsā (peace be upon him), after he had asked his Lord (Mighty and Majestic) for clarification, and revelation came to him: "Innahu" (He, Exalted) "yaqūlu innahā" (says: it is) — that is, the cow commanded to be slaughtered — "baqaratun lā fāriḍun wa lā bikrun" (a cow neither old nor young): that is, neither aged nor youthful. It is said: "faraḍat al-baqaratu furūḍan," meaning it became aged, from "al-farḍ" in the sense of "cutting," as if it had cut its teeth and reached its end. The root b-k-r is for primacy, and from it come "al-bakara" (early morning) and "al-bākūra" (early fruit). "ʿAwān" — that is, middle-aged, neither worn out nor a suckling calf. He said:

*Tiwālun mithla aʿnāqi al-hawādī* ... *nawāʿimu bayna abkārin wa ʿūn*

"Bayna dhālika" (between that): a reference to what was mentioned of the "fāriḍ" and the "bikr"; for this reason "bayna" was given the form of an addition to it, because it is specific to being added to a plural. "Fa-fʿalū" (so do): a command from Mūsā (peace be upon him), derived from what came before it of explaining the attribute of what is commanded. "Mā tu'marūn" (what you are commanded): that is, what you are commanded to do, meaning "you are commanded to do it," as in the line:

*Amartuka al-khayra fa-fʿal mā umirta bihi* ...

For the omission of the preposition has become common with this verb, to the extent that it has come to be treated like verbs that take two objects. This command from him (peace be upon him) was to urge them toward compliance and to deter them from further questioning; yet despite this they were not satisfied with it. And His (Exalted) saying:

﴿They said﴾: This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new clause that answers an implied question), as mentioned earlier. It is as if it were said: "What did they do after this clear explanation and this repeated command?" So it is said: ﴿They said: Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is﴾, so that the cow to be sacrificed may be made clear to us. He said, i.e., Musa (peace be upon him), after intimate conversation with Allah (Exalted) and the coming of the explanation: ﴿Indeed, He (Exalted) says: It is a yellow cow, bright in its color﴾. The attribution of the explanation each time to Allah (Exalted and Majestic) is to show the complete assistance in answering their request with their words "make it clear for us." The form of the future tense is used to bring the image to mind. "Al-fuqu‘" (intense brightness) means the purity and clarity of yellowness, and for this reason it is used for emphasis. It is said: "aṣfar fāqi‘" (intensely yellow), just as it is said: "aswad ḥālik" (intensely black) and "aḥmar qāni'" (intensely red). In attributing it to the color, although it is one of the states of the colored thing, because of its close connection with it, there is an emphasis that is not hidden. It is as if it were said: "yellow, its yellowness is intensely yellow," as in "jadda jiddu-hu" (his fortune was great). It is narrated from al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him) that it means "black, intensely black." It is also explained this way in His (Exalted) words: (p-112)﴿Camels, yellow﴾. It is said: Perhaps the expression of blackness by yellowness is because yellowness is among its preliminary stages; or because the blackness of camels is overlaid with yellowness. But this is rejected by its description in His (Exalted) words: ﴿that pleases the beholders﴾, just as it is rejected by its description with the brightness of color. Surur (delight) is a pleasure in the heart upon obtaining a benefit or anticipating it, derived from "sirr" (inner joy). It is narrated from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "Whoever wears a yellow sandal, his worry becomes little."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 70:**

﴿They said﴾: a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnaf*), like its counterparts. ﴿Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is﴾: an additional request for disclosure of its condition, as if they were asking for a clarification of its true nature, such that it would be distinguished from all others that share with it the described attributes and the explained conditions in the course of the clarification. For this reason they gave as the reason for their request their saying: ﴿Indeed, the cattle have become confused to us﴾, meaning that many cows share the counted attributes, and we cannot be guided by them to identify which one is the one commanded, since they apply to all the individuals of the species. It is read: "Inna al-bāqira" (the collective noun for a herd of cattle), and "al-abāqir," and "al-bawāqir," and "yatashābahu" with a *yāʾ* and with a *tāʾ*, and "yushābahu" with the *tāʾ* dropped and with assimilation (*idghām*), in the masculine and feminine forms, and "tashābahat" lightened and doubled, and "tashabbahu" meaning "tatashabbahu," and "tashabbaha" in the masculine, and "mutashābihun," and "mutashābihatun," and "mutashabbihun," and "mutashabbihatun." In this there is an indication that they had distinguished it from some of what was other than it in general, but a confusion remained, awaiting removal. This is indicated by their saying: ﴿And indeed, if God wills, we will surely be guided﴾, emphasized with several kinds of emphasis; that is, we will surely be guided, by what we have asked of the clarification, to the one commanded to be slaughtered. And in a hadith: "Had they not made the exception (*istithnāʾ*), it would never have been made clear to them until the end of time."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 71:**

﴿He said: Indeed, He says it is a cow neither trained for ploughing, that stirs up the earth, nor waters the tilth.﴾ That is, it has not been made submissive for ploughing or for watering the tilth. "Neither trained" (*la dhalul*) is an attribute of "cow," meaning "not trained." The second "la" (not) emphasizes the first. The two verbs are attributes of "trained" (*dhalul*), as if it were said: "Neither trained, ploughing, nor watering." It is also read as *la dhalula* (with a fatha), meaning "wherever it is," like your saying, "I passed by a man, neither stingy nor cowardly," meaning "wherever he is." It is also read *tusqi* (with a damma on the initial letter and the verb in the causative form from *asqa*). ﴿Sound﴾ means that Allah (Exalted) made it free from defects, or qualified it for work, or that its colour was pure, from "salima lahu kadha" when it became pure for him. This is supported by His words (Exalted): ﴿there is no blemish in it﴾, that is, there is no colour in it that differs from the colour of its skin, even its horn and hoof. The word *shiya* is originally a verbal noun of "washa, washyan, shiyatan," when one mixes another colour with its colour.

﴿They said﴾, when they heard these descriptions: ﴿Now you have brought the truth﴾, that is, the true description of the cow, such that you have distinguished it from all others, and no confusion remains regarding it at all. This is unlike the first two times, for what you brought in those two cases was not at this level of specification. Perhaps they had seen it before and found it to comprise all the attributes detailed in the three instances, without any other sharing with it in what was mentioned the last time. Otherwise, how would they have known that the final descriptions are specific to it and not to anything else? It is also read *a-al-an* (with a prolonged alif, as an interrogative), and *al-an* (with the hamza omitted and its vowel transferred to the lam). ﴿So they slaughtered it﴾: the fa is an eloquent *fa* (a conjunction implying an unstated clause), as in "fa-infajarat" (then it burst forth). That is, they obtained the cow and so slaughtered it. ﴿And they almost did not do it﴾: "kad" (a verb of approximation) is placed to indicate that the report is close to occurring. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun of "they slaughtered," meaning: they slaughtered it while they, before that, were far from it. Or it is a concluding parenthetical clause (*i'tiraDh tadhyili*), and its purpose is to express disapproval of their disobedience and reproach them, and that, due to their great prolixity and their many objections, the thread of their elaboration nearly did not come to an end concerning it. It is said: forty years passed from the beginning of the matter until compliance. It is also said: "And they almost did not do that" because of the high price of it.

It is narrated that among the Children of Israel there was a righteous old man who had a young calf. He brought it to the thicket and said: "O Allah, I have entrusted it to You for my son until he grows up." He was dutiful to his parents. Then the old man died, and the calf grew up and became one of the finest and fattest cows. They bargained with the orphan and his mother until they bought it for its hide filled with gold, because it was unique with the mentioned attributes. At that time the cow was worth three dinars.

Know that there is no disagreement that the apparent meaning of the noble wording is an unrestricted, indefinite cow, and that compliance at the end occurred only by slaughtering a specific cow; so that if they had slaughtered any other, they would not have been free of the obligation of the command. However, it has been disputed regarding what was intended by the command: was it the specific cow, while the clarification was delayed beyond the time of address? Or was it the indefinite one, which was then subsequently changed to the specific one because of their sluggishness in compliance and their persistence in probing and investigating? Some went to the first view, holding that the pronouns in the answers, namely "Indeed, it is a cow... to the end," refer definitely to the specific cow, and it follows from this that the question too must be so. And there is no doubt that the question concerns only the cow commanded to be slaughtered, so it would be the specific one. This is rejected by the claim that when they were astonished at a dead cow, by part of which a dead man would be struck so that he would live, they assumed it to be specific, outside the attributes and properties common to its kind. So they asked about it, and the pronouns then returned to the specific one in their supposition and belief. Then Allah (Exalted) specified it as a severity upon them, even though what was intended at first was not the specific one. The truth is that it was indefinite at the beginning, such that if they had slaughtered any cow whatsoever, compliance would have been achieved, by the indication of the apparent meaning of the noble wording, and by the repetition of the command before the clarification of the colour, and what follows it, of its being sound, and so on.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If they had taken any cow at random and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed them." The same is narrated from the leader of the exegetes, Abdullah ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Then the first ruling was abrogated (*naskh*) by the second, and the second by the third, as a severity upon them. But this was not in the manner of the complete removal of the ruling of the unrestricted and its transfer to the specific, but rather in the manner of restricting it and specifying it bit by bit. How could it be otherwise? For if it were not so, their reported objections would not be counted as crimes, but rather as acts of worship. Compliance with a command without knowing what is commanded is hardly attainable. So their questions are of the nature of concern for compliance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 72:

﴿وَإذْ قَتَلْتُمْ نَفْسًا﴾: It is in the accusative (mansub) governed by a suppressed verb (mudmar), as its parallels have passed; and the address is to the Jews contemporary with the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The attribution of the killing and the disputing to them is because of the attribution of the offenses of the predecessors to the successors, as has passed, for rebuke and reproach; and their being singled out for attribution, rather than the other lapses that have passed from them, is due to the evident ugliness of killing, and its attribution to others. That is: "Remember the time when you killed a soul (nafs) that was forbidden (to kill)." ﴿فادّارَأْتُمْ فِيها﴾: that is, you disputed concerning it, since each of the adversaries repels the other; or: you pushed the blame onto one another, with each one casting the killing of it onto another. Its original form is "tadarra'tum" (تَدارَأْتُمْ), so the taa' was assimilated into the daal, and a hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamza) was brought in for it. ﴿واللَّهُ مُخْرِجٌ ما كُنْتُمْ تَكْتُمُونَ﴾: that is, He is the one who will undoubtedly bring forth what you were concealing. The combination of the two forms, the past and the present (future), is for indicating continuity; and "mukhrij" (مُخْرِجٌ) was made to govern (a‘mala) because it is a narration of a past state (hikayat hal madiyah).

﴿فَقُلْنا اضْرِبُوهُ﴾: It is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "fa-iddārāʾtum" (﴿and you disputed﴾). What lies between them is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ, an interjected phrase that breaks the flow of the sentence). The shift (iltifāt, a change in grammatical address) serves to cultivate awe. The pronoun refers to "the soul" (nafs). The masculine form is used because the word denotes a man, or is construed as "the person" (al-shakhṣ) or "the slain man" (al-qatīl). ﴿bi-baʿḍihā﴾: that is, with some part of the cow, whatever part it was. It has been said: with its two smaller parts; it has been said: with its tongue; it has been said: with its right thigh; it has been said: with its ear; it has been said: with its ʿujb (the coccyx, the bone at the base of the spine); it has been said: with the bone that adjoins the cartilage (ghuḍrūf). This is the beginning of the story, as the pronoun referring back to the cow indicates. It is as if it were said: "And when you slew a soul and disputed concerning it, We said: slaughter a cow, then strike him with part of it." The order was altered in the narration to repeat the reproach and to double the rebuke, for each of the following is a grave offence: killing a soul unlawfully, mocking the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), presuming upon his command, and failing to hasten to comply with it. Each therefore deserves to be censured on its own. Had the story been related in the order in which events occurred, the independent force of each element, with the reproach specific to it, would not have been apparent. The command to slaughter is related as coming from Mūsā (peace be upon him), although it is from Allah (Exalted and Majestic), just like the command to strike; this is because their offences consisted in their referring matters to him (peace be upon him) and presuming upon his judgement.

﴿كَذَلِكَ يُحْيِي اللَّهُ الْمَوْتى﴾: This is based on the assumption of a conjoined statement dependent upon an implied element to which the discourse extends. That is: "So they struck him, and he came to life; and We said: Thus does Allah give life…" The eloquent fa' (al-fāʾ al-faṣīḥa, a fa' that indicates an omitted intermediate step) in "fa-ḥayiya" has been elided, together with what was conjoined by it, and what it was conjoined to, since "kadhālika" indicates that. The address in "kadhālika" is then to those present at the time of the slain man's revival. It is also permissible that it refers to those present at the time of the revelation of this noble verse; in that case there is no need to posit an implied "saying," and the narrative ends at His (Exalted) words ﴿bi-baʿḍihā﴾, together with what is supposed after it. The sentence is then a parenthetical clause, meaning: "Just as with that wondrous giving of life, Allah (Exalted) will give life to the dead on the Day of Resurrection."

﴿وَيُرِيكُمْ آيَاتِهِ﴾: and He shows you His signs, His proofs indicating that He (Exalted) is powerful over everything. It is also permissible that "the signs" refers to this giving of life; its expression in the plural is because it contains wondrous matters: the life restored to a dead limb, the report of its killer, and the extraordinary circumstances accompanying it.

﴿لَعَلَّكُمْ تَعْقِلُونَ﴾: that is, so that your minds may be perfected, and you may know that He who is able to give life to one soul is able to give life to all souls; or that you may act in accordance with the demands of your minds.

It may be that the wisdom in the conditions attached to the giving of life, despite the manifest completeness of His power to give life directly and without any intermediary at all, lies in its comprising: drawing near to Allah (Exalted); performing an obligation; benefiting an orphan; drawing attention to the blessing of trusting in Allah (Exalted); compassion towards children; the benefit of dutifulness to parents; that the seeker has a right to offer a means of drawing near; that the one who draws near has a right to seek the best and to pay a high price for it. This is as is related of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), that he sacrificed a noble she-camel which he had bought for three hundred dinars. Also: that the one who truly effects is Allah (Exalted), and that causes are merely signs with no real influence of their own. And also: that whoever wishes to know the most hostile of his enemies, who strives to bring about his true death, the path to that is to slaughter the cow of his own self, which is his appetitive power, once the excess of youthful vigour has left it and the weakness of old age has not yet overtaken it, while it remains pleasing and fair of appearance, not made base through pursuit of the world, pure of its defilements, bearing no mark of its ugliness, such that its effect reaches his own self, and he lives by it a good life. It also makes clear what reveals the true state of affairs, and removes what lies between the intellect and the imagination of disputation and contention.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 74:

﴿Then your hearts hardened﴾: The address is to the contemporaries of the Prophet (ﷺ). Qaswa (hardness) is an expression for coarseness, harshness, and firmness, as in a stone. It is used metaphorically for the hearts' being impervious to being affected (p-115)

by admonitions and calamities, by which mountains melt and rocks are softened. The use of the verb indicating the occurrence of hardness, although their hearts are still hard, is because the purpose is to explain that they have reached a particular stage of the stages of hardness that came into being. Or because persistence in something after the arrival of what requires abandoning it is a new matter and a recent act. And "thumma" (then) is for expressing the improbability of hardness after witnessing what removes it, as in His (Exalted) saying: ﴿Then those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾.

﴿after that﴾: It is a reference to what was mentioned of the raising of the dead man, or to all that was enumerated of the signs that necessitate the softening of hearts and their turning towards the truth; that is, after hearing that. The sense of distance in it is to indicate the remoteness of its rank and the loftiness of its class. The singular form of the address particle, despite the plurality of those addressed, is either by interpreting them as a group, or because the purpose is mere address and not the specification of an addressee, as is the well-known view. ﴿So they are like stones﴾ in hardness; ﴿or harder﴾ than them; ﴿in hardness﴾. That is: they are in hardness like stones, or exceeding them in it, or they are like them, or like what is harder than them in hardness, such as iron. The genitive noun has been omitted and the noun in the genitive has been placed in its position; and the reading in the genitive, as a conjunction with "stones," supports this. The use of a nominal sentence, although what preceded it was verbal, is to indicate the continuity of the hardness of their hearts. The "fa" (so) is either to derive their resemblance to them from the mentioned hardness, the derivation of a simile from the explanation of the aspect of resemblance, as in your saying: "His cheek is red; so it is like the rose"; or it is for causation, as in your saying: "Worship your Lord; so worship is due to Him." And it was not said "or more hard than them" because of the greater emphasis in stating the intensity and the clear indication of the two hardnesses sharing in intensity. The inclusion of the preferred term with the addition of the particle "waw" is for choice or for ambiguity, in the sense that whoever knew their state likened them to stones or to what is harder; or whoever knew them likened them to stones, or said: they are harder than stones. The omission of the pronoun of the comparative object is because there is no fear of confusion.

﴿And indeed among stones there are those from which rivers gush forth﴾: It is an explanation of the greater hardness of their hearts than stones in hardness, and of their non-being affected, and the impossibility of good proceeding from them; meaning that stones may be affected, since among them are some from which great waters gush forth; ﴿And indeed among them are those that split open﴾; that is, they split; ﴿so water comes out of them﴾; that is, springs; ﴿And indeed among them are those that fall down out of fear of God﴾; that is, they tumble from the high to the low, by virtue of the heaviness that God, Mighty and Majestic, has placed in them, which draws them to the center; and it is a metaphor for submission to His command (Exalted). The meaning is that there is no single stone that is not submissive to His command (Mighty and Exalted), performing what it was created for without disobedience; and their hearts are not like that, so they are, without doubt, harder than them in hardness. The lam in "lamma" is the lam of commencement, entering upon the subject of "inna" because the predicate has been moved forward. It has been read as "in" (if), as a lightened form of the heavy particle, with the lam being distinguishing. It has been read "yahbutu" with a damma. ﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾: "ʿan" is connected to "ghafil" (unaware), and "ma" is a relative pronoun with the returning pronoun omitted; or it is a verbal (infinitival) "ma." It is a severe warning concerning their state of hardness of hearts and the evil deeds that follow from it. It has been read with "ya" (they) by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person). And His (Exalted) saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 75:

(p-116)﴿Do you then hope?﴾ This is a shift in address, turning away from the Jews after their shortcomings and crimes had been enumerated and censured, to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers who were with him. The interrogative *hamza* serves to deny and to find improbable the event that has occurred, as in your saying: *Are you going to strike your father?* It does not deny the occurrence itself, as in his saying: *Shall I strike my father?* The *fa'* (then) serves as a conjunction to an implied element that the context requires and that the structure of the discourse calls for. However, it is not intended to direct the denial at both conjoined elements together, as in *"Will you not then see?"* (﴿أفَلا تُبْصِرُونَ﴾), where the conjoined item is taken as negated, meaning: "Do you not look, so that you do not see?" Thus what is denied is both matters. Rather, the denial is directed at the consequence of the second upon the first, together with the necessity that its opposite should follow from it. The same applies when the first is taken as affirmative, meaning: "Do you look, so that you do not see?" Here what is denied is the consequence of the second upon the first, together with the necessity that its opposite should follow from it. That is, "Do you hear their reports and know their conditions, so that you hope?" The sense of the matter is: after you have come to know the details of their affairs, which despair you of them, do you hope ﴿that they will believe﴾? For they are alike in their intense stubbornness and their blameworthy characters. Nothing can come from their characters except the like of what came from their forebears. The *"an"* (that) is a verbal-source particle (*maṣdariyyah*), from which the preposition has been omitted; the original is *fī an yu'minū* (regarding that they believe). It, together with what follows it, occupies a position either in the accusative or in the genitive, according to the well-known scholarly disagreement. The *lam* in *"lakum"* (for you) is for the implication of the meaning of responding, as in His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿So Lut believed in him﴾, meaning: regarding their belief, responding to you. Or it is for causation, meaning: that they bring about belief for the sake of your call. The complement of *al-īmān* (belief) is omitted, since it is evident that what is meant by it is its legal meaning. You will be made to stand upon what it contains of excellence, if Allah (Exalted) wills.

﴿And indeed there was a group among them﴾: *al-Farīq* (the group) is a collective noun (*ism jam'*) that has no singular from its own form, like *al-Rahṭ* (the company) and *al-Qawm* (the people). The prepositional phrase is in the nominative position, meaning: a group existing from among them. His saying (Exalted): ﴿who used to hear the speech of Allah﴾ is the predicate of *kāna* (was). It has been read as *"kalima Allāh"*. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), emphasizing the denial and cutting off the source of hope, in the manner of their shameful conditions related in what has passed, following the method of His saying (Exalted): ﴿and they are an enemy to you﴾, after His saying (Exalted): ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies besides Me?﴾ That is: while the state is that a party among them, according to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, were people from the seventy chosen for the appointed time, who used to hear His speech (Exalted) when Musa (peace be upon him) spoke to him at Mount Tur, and what he was commanded and forbidden. ﴿Then they distort it﴾ from its places. This is not because their understanding was too limited to grasp its details as they should, due to the overwhelming awe and majesty, as the station of greatness requires. Rather, ﴿after they had understood it﴾: that is, they comprehended it and retained it with their minds, and there remained for them no doubt at all about its content or about its being the speech of the Lord of Might. When they returned to their people, the truthful ones conveyed it to them as they had heard it. But these ones said: "We heard Allah (Exalted) say, at the end of His speech: 'If you are able to do these things, then do them; and if you wish, do not do them; there is no harm.'" So *thumma* (then) indicates delay in time or in rank. Al-Qaffal said: they heard the speech of Allah and understood His intended meaning from it, but then interpreted it with a corrupt interpretation. It has been said: they are the leaders of their forebears who undertook the distortion of the Torah after they had encompassed what it contains in knowledge. It has also been said: they are those who altered the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his time, and changed the verse of stoning. But this is rejected by the combination of the two past and future verb forms, which indicates the occurrence of the hearing and the distortion in what has passed, unless that is understood as preceding the time of the revelation of this noble verse, not as preceding his time (peace and blessings be upon him). This is it. The first view is more suitable to the hearing and the speech, since (p-117)

the Torah, although it is the speech of Allah (Exalted and High), is more famous by the name "the Book," and the effect of distortion is more evident in it, and the description of the Jews by reciting it is more frequent, especially their leaders who directly carried out the distortion, since their function is recitation, not hearing. So the more fitting expression then would be: "They recite the Book of Allah (Exalted)." The meaning is: Do you hope that these people will believe through you and respond to you, while their forebears, who share with them in evil qualities, used to hear the speech of Allah without intermediary, then distorted it after they had known it with certainty, and did not respond to it? Far-fetched indeed! From here appears the grandeur and eloquence in preferring *"lakum"* (for you) over *"bi-Allah"* (by Allah). His saying (Exalted and Majestic): ﴿while they know﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the subject of *yuḥarrifūnahu* (they distort it). It conveys the complete ugliness of their state, and indicates that their distortion of it did not proceed from forgetting what they had understood, or from error in some of its premises. Rather, it occurred while they were knowing, mindful of it. Or it means: while they knew that they were liars and fabricators.

﴿وَإذا لَقُوا﴾ ("And when they meet"): this is a resumptive (mustaʾnafah) clause, brought in right after the account of what had come from their likes, in order to explain what came from them directly: the shameful reports that despair of their faith, namely the hypocrisy of some of them and the reproach others among them directed at them. Alternatively, it is coordinated (maʿṭūfah) with the preceding circumstantial clause (al-jumlah al-ḥāliyyah). The pronoun refers to the Jews, for reasons you will come to understand, and not to their hypocrites alone, as has been said. This is so that the agent of the two verbs in the conditional and the consequent is truly one and the same. ﴿الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ ("those who believe"): from among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. ﴿قالُوا﴾ ("they said"): that is, the ones who met them. However, this is not by way of all of them actually undertaking the speech. Rather, it was by the direct action of their hypocrites, with the silence of the rest, as one says: "The sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," when the killer is only one of them. This is more effective in disparaging the state of those who first remained silent and then reproached, because it shows their hypocrisy, the variation of their states, and the contradiction of their opinions. The attribution of the speech to those who directly performed it alone, with the omission of a noun (taqdīr al-muḍāf), means: their hypocrites said, ﴿آمَنّا﴾ ("We believe"). They did not restrict themselves to this, but gave a reason for it: they found the description of the Prophet ﷺ in the Torah (al-Tawrah, the Jewish scripture), and they knew that he was the prophet who had been foretold. The reason it was not stated explicitly is that they relied on the testimony of the rebuke that follows. ﴿وَإذا خَلا بَعْضُهُمْ﴾ ("And when some of them are alone"): that is, some of those mentioned, namely those of them who were silent. That is, when they were finished with occupying themselves with the believers, turning and gathering ﴿إلى بَعْضٍ﴾ ("with one another"), another group among them, namely their hypocrites, such that no one else remained with them. This is an explicit statement that the silent ones shared in meeting the believers, as was indicated just before, since being alone occurs only after occupation. Also, because their reproach is tied to being alone by itself, and if they had not been present during the discussion, it would have been necessary to make their hearing of it part of the condition. And because it adds further condemnation of them for their silence and then their reproach. ﴿قالُوا﴾ ("they said"): that is, the silent ones, rebuking their hypocrites for what they had done: ﴿أتُحَدِّثُونَهُمْ﴾ ("Do you tell them"), meaning the believers, ﴿بِما فَتَحَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ ("what Allah has disclosed to you"). The word "ma" ("what") is a relative pronoun, and its returning pronoun (al-ʿāʾid) is omitted. That is: what He made clear to you alone in the Torah, of the description of the Prophet ﷺ. The expression of it as "disclosure" (fatḥ) signifies that it is a hidden secret and a closed door that no one can reach. As for the permissibility that this rebuke came from the hypocrites to their successors, in order to show firmness in their religion, as a group has held, this is not fitting for the status of the glorious revelation. The lām in His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿لِيُحاجُّوكم بِهِ﴾ ("so that they may argue against you with it"), is connected to the telling (al-taḥdīth), not to the disclosure (al-fatḥ). The purpose is to emphasize the denunciation and intensify the rebuke, for telling them of that, although it is itself objectionable, is even more so when the telling is for this purpose, which hardly issues from a sensible person. That is: do you tell them of that so that they may argue against you with it and silence you? Those who report it, even if they did not intend that aim, since their act necessarily entails it, are treated as if they were doing it for the mentioned purpose, and this displays the complete foolishness of their minds and the feebleness of their opinions. ﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّكُمْ﴾ ("before your Lord"): that is, in His judgment and His Book, as one says: "It is so-and-so before Allah," meaning in His Book and His law. It was also said: "before your Lord on the Day of Resurrection." This was refuted on the grounds that concealment does not prevent it, since they know that on that day they will be argued against, whether they reported it or not. The excuse that the believers' imposing this upon them and rebuking them, by saying to them, "Did you not tell us in this world what is in your Book of the truth of our religion and the truthfulness of our Prophet?", is more shameful. Thus it is possible that what they feared was this imposition, by referring the pronoun in "bihi" ("with it") to the telling rather than to what was told. There is no doubt that this is refuted by concealment, which the following noble verse does not support, as you will come to know, God willing, Exalted and Majestic is He. ﴿أفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ﴾ ("Do you not then understand?"): this is part of the rebuke and reproach. The "fa" (فاء, "then") here is for coordination with an implied element to which the speech is attached. That is: "Do you not pay attention, so that you do not understand this gross error, or any of the things of which this is one?" In this case, the denounced matter is the absence of understanding from the outset. Or: "Do you do that, so that you do not understand its falsehood, despite its clarity, to the point that you need to be alerted to it?" In this case, the denounced matter is the absence of understanding after the act. This is it. As for what has been said, that it is an address from Allah, glorified is He, to the believers, connected to His saying: ﴿أفَتَطْمَعُونَ﴾ ("Do you then hope"), and the meaning being: "Do you not understand their state, and that you have no hope in their faith?", this is rejected by His saying, Exalted is He:

**Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 2, verse 77:**

﴿Do they not know?﴾ Its continuation (to the end) is a rebuke for them from Him (Exalted is He), concerning what He related about them. So the insertion of the address to the believers in the middle of it is like separating the tree from its bark. Moreover, restricting the address to the believers involves excessive strain (ta'assuf), and extending it to the Prophet ﷺ as well, as in "Do you then hope..." (afatat'amun), involves a breach of good manners that is not hidden. The hamza (the interrogative particle, hamzat al-istifham) here expresses denial and reproach, as it does before it. The waw is the conjunction of coordination (wawu al-'atf) on an implied element that the mind is led to, and the pronoun refers to those being rebuked. That is: do they blame them for the aforementioned speech, out of fear of being argued against, and do they not know ﴿that God knows what they conceal﴾? That is, what they keep secret among themselves from the believers, or what they harbour in their hearts. The ruling therefore applies to that by way of priority (bi-al-tariq al-awla). ﴿And what they disclose﴾: that is, what they show to the believers, or to their companions, as has preceded. Then God (Exalted is He) brings out what they wished to hide, through revelation to the Prophet ﷺ, so the argument is established and the rebuke takes place, as happened in the verse of stoning and in the prohibition of some forbidden things for them. What then is the benefit of blame and reproach? From here it becomes clear that what they dreaded was the argument by what God (Exalted is He) had opened up to them, and this is present in both worlds, whether they speak of it or not, not merely by speaking of it, so that it might be averted by concealment. It has been said: the pronoun refers to the hypocrites alone, or to them and to those being rebuked, or to their distorting forefathers. That is: do they do what they do without knowing that God (Exalted is He) knows all that they conceal and all that they disclose? Among that is their concealing of disbelief and their showing of faith, their concealing of what God (Exalted is He) has opened to them and their showing of other than it, their hiding of God's command (Exalted is He), and their showing what they displayed as a fabrication. The concealing is mentioned before the disclosing only to announce their exposure, and the occurrence from the outset of what they were wary of, and to emphasise the all-encompassing scope of His knowledge over all knowable things, as if His knowledge of what they conceal were prior to His knowledge of what they disclose, though in reality both are equal. For His knowledge (Exalted is He) of His objects of knowledge is not by way of the acquisition of their forms; rather, the existence of each thing in itself is knowledge in relation to Him (Exalted is He). (p-119) In this respect the situation does not differ between things that are manifest and things that are hidden. A parallel to this is His saying (Mighty and Exalted is He): ﴿Say: whether you conceal what is in your breasts or disclose it, God knows it﴾, where concealing is placed before disclosing because of the secrecy mentioned, in the reverse of what occurs in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And whether you disclose what is in your selves or conceal it, God will call you to account for it﴾, since the primary object of accountability is what is manifest, not what is hidden. It is possible that this is by consideration that the level of the secret is prior to the level of the open, for there is nothing that is made public except that it, or its beginnings, was previously concealed in the heart, to which secrecy usually attaches. Thus the connection of His knowledge (Exalted is He) to its first state precedes its connection to its second state.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 78:

﴿And among them are unlettered folk (ummiyyun)﴾; it is also read with the yā' lightened; it is the plural of ummiyy (the unlettered, one who is unable to write or read); and it has been disputed as to its derivation. It is said: it is derived from umm (mother), in the sense that he resembles his mother in ignorance of writing and reading, for these are not among the affairs of women but rather among the attributes of men; or in the sense that he remains in the state in which his mother bore him, empty of knowledge and writing. It is said: it is derived from ummah (community), in the sense that he remains upon its simplicity, devoid of knowledge of things, like their saying "āmmiyy" (common), meaning: upon the custom of the common people. It is narrated from ʿIkrimah and al-Ḍaḥḥāk that what is meant by them are the Christians of the Arabs. It is said: they are a people from among the People of the Book whose scripture was lifted because of sins they committed, so they became unlettered. And it is narrated from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that they are the Magians. The truth from which there is no escape is that they are the ignorant among the Jews. The sentence is resumed, brought to explain their abominations after the explanation of the atrocities of the earlier groups. It is said: it is conjoined to the preceding circumstantial clause and what follows it, for ignorance of the Book is not on a par with the contradiction of faith, like the distortion of the words of Allah after hearing them and knowing their meanings, as occurred from the earlier ones; or with hypocrisy and the prohibition against manifesting what is in the Torah, as occurred from the two other groups. That is: among them is a group of ignorant people, unable to write or recite, ﴿who do not know the Book﴾; that is, they do not know the Torah so as to peruse it and verify what is in its folds of proofs of prophethood, so that they might believe. Taking "the Book" to mean "writing" is rejected by the coherence and context of the noble text.

﴿except wishful fancies (amani)﴾; with shaddah; it is also read lightened; it is the plural of umniyyah (wish), whose original form is "umnuwiyyah," on the pattern "uf'ulah," from manna (meaning "to determine") or in the sense of "to recite," like tamanna in his saying:

؎ He wished for the Book of Allah at the first of his night

and it was made defective like "sayyid" and "mayyit." Its meaning on the first reading is what a person determines in himself and desires; on the second it is what he recites. On both readings the exception is disjunctive, since what is wished for or recited is not of the same kind as knowledge of the Book; that is: they do not know the Book, but they wish wishful fancies, as their rabbis have fed them, such as that Allah—glorified is He—will pardon them, and that their fathers the prophets will intercede for them, and other vain wishes founded on the Book according to the claim of their leaders. Or: they do not know the Book, but they receive it only to the extent that it is recited to them, so they accept it without being able to reflect upon it. As for taking "amani" to mean lies of every sort in general, with no connection to the Book, the noble text does not support it.

﴿And they are only assuming (yazunnun)﴾: they are a people whose utmost condition is supposition and imitation, without reaching the rank of knowledge; so how can faith founded on the foundations of certainty be expected from them? Having explained the state of these in clinging to the ropes of wishful fancies and following supposition, he followed with an explanation of the state of those who led them into that predicament, disclosing the manner of their misguidance and specifying the return of all to the Hereafter; so it is said—by way of invocation against them—:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 79:**

﴿Woe﴾: it and similar words, derived from *wayh*, *ways*, *wayb*, *wayh*, *wayk*, and *'awl*, are verbal nouns (*masadir*, sing. *masdar*, "verbal noun") put in the accusative by an implied verb whose form is not stated. It is never permissible to state that verb. If the word is put in construct with a pronoun, it takes the accusative, as in *waylaka* and *wayhaka*. If it is separated from the construct, it takes the nominative, as in *waylun lahu*. The meaning of *al-waylu* is extreme evil, as stated by al-Khalil [ibn Ahmad]. Al-Asma'i said: *al-waylu* is lamentation, and *al-wayhu* is compassion. Sibawayh said: *waylun* is for one who has fallen into destruction, and *wayhun* is a rebuke to one who has come close to destruction. It has also been said that *al-waylu* is grief. Do *wayh*, *wayb*, and *ways* have that same meaning, or is there a distinction between them and it? It has been said that *waylun* is used in cursing against someone, while *wayhun* and what follows it are used in showing compassion for someone. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "*Al-waylu* is painful punishment." Sufyan al-Thawri reported that it is the pus of the people of Hell. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "*Al-waylu* is a valley in Hell, in which the disbeliever will fall for forty autumns before he reaches its bottom." Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: "It is a valley in Hell; if the mountains of this world were moved through it, they would melt from the intensity of its heat." Ibn Buraydah said: "It is a mountain of pus and blood." It has been said that it is a cistern in Hell. Al-Zahrawi related that it is a gate of the gates of Hell. In every case, it is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is the statement of Him, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿for those who write the Book﴾, that is, the altered text, or what they wrote of corrupt interpretations. ﴿with their own hands﴾ is an emphasis to remove the suspicion of metaphor, as when you say, "I wrote it with my right hand." ﴿Then they say, "This is from Allah"﴾: that is, all of them, according to the first reading, or specifically those responsible, according to the second. It is reported that the rabbis of the Jews feared the loss of their revenues and the end of their leadership when the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Medina. They therefore schemed to keep the lower-ranking Jews away from faith. They deliberately changed the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Torah, which was there: "good-looking, with beautiful hair, with dark eyes, of medium height." They altered it and wrote in its place: "tall, blue-eyed, straight-haired." When their followers asked them about this, they read to them what they had written, and the followers found it contrary to his description, upon him be blessings and peace, so they denied him. The word *thumma* ("then") indicates a sequence of rank, since attributing altered text and corrupt interpretation to Allah, Glorified be He, explicitly, is far more heinous than the alteration and interpretation itself. ﴿so that they may trade it﴾: that is, so that they may take for themselves, in exchange for it. ﴿for a price﴾ is what they took in bribes in exchange for their alteration and interpretation. The thing purchased, which is the primary aim in a contract of exchange, is expressed by the price, which is merely a means in it, to indicate their reversal, since they made the primary aim a means and the means a primary aim. ﴿a little﴾: it is not worth regarding, for although that [price] may be great in itself, it is far less than a little when compared with the eternal punishment they deserve.

﴿So woe to them﴾: this repeats what came before for emphasis, and it explicitly states its cause, which is "what their hands have written," after having alluded to it earlier, by mentioning part of it in the relative clause (*sila*) and part of it in the context of the purpose. The *fa'* indicates that the woe follows from it. The *min* in His statement, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿from what their hands have written﴾ is causal, and it is connected either to *waylun* or to the stability within the predicate. The *ma* is a relative noun (*ismiyya mawsula*), and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning "they wrote it"; or it is a verbal *ma* (*masdariyya*). The first is more effective in deterring one from engaging in alteration, and the second in deterring one from alteration itself. ﴿And woe to them for what they earn﴾: the discussion of it is like that of what came before it. The repetition is for the emphasis and intensity already mentioned, and to aim at the cause of each of the two crimes, and to not address their statement, "This is from Allah," because it is among the beginnings of marketing what their hands have written, so it is (p-121) included in the cause stated by it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 2, verse 80:**

﴿And they say﴾: this explains another of their crimes. Its separation from what precedes it indicates that it is among the lies they fabricated, which they did not write in the Book. ﴿Never will the Fire touch us﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿except for a few days, numbered﴾: a small number, limited, equal to the number of days of their worship of the calf, forty days, the period of Musa's (peace be upon him) absence from them. Al-Asma'i related from some Jews that the number of days of their worship of the calf was seven. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid that the Jews said: the age of the world is seven thousand years, and we will only be punished one day for every thousand years. Al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Jews claimed they found in the Torah that the distance between the two edges of Hell is a journey of forty years, until they reach the tree of Zaqqum, and that they would traverse each journey of one year and complete it.

﴿Say﴾ (to them), as a rebuke and reproach: ﴿Have you taken﴾ with the omission of the connective hamza (hamzat al-wasl, the hamza that is added at the beginning of words), because it occurs in continuous recitation (al-darj, connected reading), and with the pronunciation of the dhal. It has also been read with its assimilation into the ta' (idgham, assimilation). ﴿a covenant from Allah﴾, a report or a promise regarding what you claim, for what you assert can only be based on a firm promise. For this reason it was expressed as a covenant. ﴿Then Allah will not fail His covenant﴾. The fa' here is the eloquent fa' (fa' al-fasiha, which indicates an omitted condition), which expresses an omitted condition, as in the words of the one who said:

*They said: "Khurasan is the farthest that we are aimed at, then the return," but we have come to Khurasan.*

That is: if the matter is as you say, then He will not fail it. The clause is parenthetical. The mention of the noble Name here is to indicate the reason for the ruling, for not failing is a requirement of divinity. The covenant is mentioned with the pronoun referring to Him, glorified and exalted, for the reason mentioned, or because what is meant by it is all of His covenants, due to its generality through the annexation. Thus the covenant in question is included in it primarily. In this there is a deliberate avoidance of explicitly affirming the realization of the content of their statement, even though it is conditioned on something that scarcely has any scent of existence, namely the taking of a covenant.

﴿Or do you say﴾, fabricating, ﴿about Allah what you do not know﴾, its occurrence? The rebuke is attached to their attributing to Him, glorified is He, what they do not know to occur, although what they attributed to Him is of the kind that they know does not occur, for the sake of intensifying the rebuke. The indefiniteness is also significant, for rebuking the lesser entails rebuking the greater all the more. Their stated saying, although it is not an explicit fabrication against Him, glorified is He, nonetheless entails it, because such certainty can only be based on attributing its cause to Him, exalted is He.

"Am" here is connected (am muttasila, the connected 'am), and the interrogative is for affirmation leading to rebuke, since knowledge of the final part is established, as if it were said: "Did you not take it? Rather, you fabricate against Him, exalted is He." Or it is disconnected (am munqati'a, the disconnected 'am), and the interrogative is for denying the taking and negating it. The meaning of "bal" (rather) in it is a turning away and a transition from the rebuke by denial of taking a covenant to what its hamza indicates of rebuke for fabricating against Allah, glorified is He, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Has Allah permitted you, or do you fabricate against Allah?﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 81:

﴿Yes...﴾; to its end: it is a response to their stated claim, and a refutation of it from His side (exalted is He); and an explanation of the reality of the situation in detail, within a general legislation that includes them and all the disbelievers, after the manifestation of their lie in summary. The entrusting of this to the Prophet ﷺ is because argument and obligation are among his duties - upon him be prayers and peace - together with what it contains of an indication (p-122) that it is a matter that is easy, depending only on instruction. And "bala" (yes/indeed) is a particle of affirmation, specific to responding to a negation, whether a declarative or an interrogative one. ﴿Whoever earns an evil deed﴾: a grave matter among the evil deeds; that is, a major sin among the major sins; like the way of these disbelievers. And "kasb" (earning) is seeking to acquire benefit; and its connection with "evil deed" is in the manner of ﴿so give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾.

﴿And his sin encompasses him﴾: from all of his sides; such that no side of him remains - of his heart, his tongue, and his limbs - except that it has been comprised of it and it has overtaken it; ﴿his sin﴾: which he earned, and which has become a特 property of his, as the attribution to him indicates; and this is only realized in the disbeliever; and for this reason the early scholars (al-salaf) interpreted it as disbelief, as related by Ibn Abi Hatim from Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hurayrah - may Allah be pleased with them - and Ibn Jarir from Abu Wa'il, Mujahid, Qatadah, 'Ata', and al-Rabi'. It is also said: the "evil deed" is disbelief, and the "sin" is a major sin; and it is said the reverse; and it is said: the difference between them is that the first may be applied to what is intended directly, while the second predominates over what is intended incidentally, because it is from error. It was also read as "khati'atuhu" and "khatiyyatuhu" (by metathesis and assimilation in both), and "khati'atuhu" and "khataya-hu" (plural forms); and in that is an indication of the abundance of the varieties of their disbelief.

﴿Then those﴾: a subject (mubtada'); ﴿companions of the Fire﴾: its predicate; and the clause is the predicate of the subject; and the "fa" (then) is because it includes the meaning of a condition; and the use of the demonstrative noun, which indicates the bringing to mind of the one indicated with his attributes, is to indicate that these attributes are the reason for being companions of the Fire; and what it contains of the sense of distance serves to alert to the distance of their rank in disbelief; and they are referred to with the plural designation, observing the sense of the word "man" after observing the form in the three pronouns, because that is what suits what was attributed to them in those two states: the earning of evil deeds and the encompassing of their sins around them in the state of isolation, and companionship with the Fire in the state of gathering; that is: those described with what was mentioned of earning evil deeds and their sins encompassing them are companions of the Fire, that is, they will be bound to it in the Hereafter, just as they were bound to the causes that necessitate it in this world, among which is what they are upon of denying the signs of Allah (exalted is He), distorting His speech, slandering Him, and other things. The answer was not specifically restricted to their situation, by saying - for example: "Yes, indeed they are companions of the Fire..." etc., because of what generality contains of awe-inspiring force, and of clarifying their situation by proof and evidence, together with what has passed of the intention to indicate the cause.

﴿They therein abide forever﴾; permanently, eternally. How, then, could they be freed from it after seven days, or forty, as they claimed? So there is no proof in the noble verse for the eternity of the one who commits a major sin, since, as you have come to know, it is specific to the disbeliever; and there is no need to interpret "abiding" as a long stay; moreover, that would lessen the gravity of the matter in a context of awe.

The divine custom has been to pair promise with threat, in keeping with what wisdom requires in guiding the servants: encouragement at one time and warning at another, good tidings at one moment and admonition at another.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 83:

﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾: This begins (p-123)

an enumeration of further ugly deeds of the forefathers of the Jews, which proclaims the non-faith of their descendants. The word "idh" (when) is in the accusative by means of an implied verb addressed to the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, so that reflection on their circumstances may lead them to cut off hope of their faith; or it is addressed to the Jews present in the age of Prophethood, as a rebuke for the evil conduct of their forefathers. That is: remember when We took their covenant; ﴿that you shall worship none but Allah﴾; on the assumption of the saying, i.e. "We said", or "saying": you shall not worship, etc. It is a report in the sense of a prohibition, like His (exalted) saying: ﴿Let no scribe or witness be harmed﴾; and like when you say: "You go to so-and-so", and you say: "Such-and-such"; and it is more eloquent than explicit prohibition, because it gives the impression that the one prohibited ought to hasten to desist from what he has been forbidden, so it is as if he has desisted, and so the prohibiter informs of it. It is supported by the reading "do not worship" (la ta'budu), and by the conjunction of "say" (qulu) to it. It has also been said: its estimate is "that you do not worship" etc., so the governing particle (an) is elided and the verb is put in the nominative, as in his saying:

Ala ayyuhadha al-zajiri ahdura al-wagha * wa-an ashhada al-ladhdhati hal anta mukhlidi?

It is reinforced by the reading "that you not worship" (alla ta'budu), in which case it is either a substitute for the covenant or an object of purpose, with the preposition elided. It has also been said: it is the answer to an oath indicated by the meaning, as if it were said: "And We made them swear that they would not worship except Allah". It has been read with the letter ya' (ya'budun, "they not worship"), because they are in the third person.

﴿And to parents, good treatment﴾: it is connected to an implied verb, i.e. "and you shall be good to", or "be good to".

﴿And to kindred, orphans, and the needy﴾: it is conjoined to "parents". "Yatama" is the plural of "yatim", like "nadama" is the plural of "nadim"; and this is rare. "Miskin" is "mif'il", from "sukun" (stillness), as if poverty had kept him from movement and weighed him down from turning about.

﴿And speak to people good words﴾: that is, a good saying; he called it "husn" (goodness) as an intensification. It has also been read thus; and "husun" with two dammas, which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz; and "husna", like "bushra". What is meant by it is that which contains good moral conduct and guidance. ﴿And establish prayer and give zakat﴾: these are what was prescribed for them in their law.

﴿Then you turned away﴾: if the governing element of the time-clause is taken as addressed to the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, then this is a shift to addressing all the Children of Israel, giving precedence to their descendants over their forefathers, since the mention of all of them then runs in the manner of the third person; for the earlier addresses to their forefathers are related and fall within the scope of the implied saying before "you worship", as if they were summoned at the mention of their crimes, and so these were announced against them. And if it is taken as addressed to the Jews contemporary with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers, then this is a generalization of the address, by treating the forefathers as the descendants; just as it is also a generalization of the turning away, by treating the descendants as the forefathers, for the sake of intensifying the rebuke; that is: you turned away from proceeding according to the requirement of the covenant, and rejected it; ﴿except a few of you﴾; and they are: among the forefathers, those who upheld Judaism in its proper form before abrogation; and among the descendants, those who embraced Islam, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his like; ﴿and you are averse﴾: a concluding sentence; that is: and you are a people whose habit is aversion from obedience and observance of the rights of the covenant. The root of "i'rad" (aversion) is going away from confronting, and turning toward the side of the breadth.

﴿وَإذْ أخَذْنا مِيثاقَكُمْ﴾: The word إذْ (idh, "when") is in the accusative (manṣūb), governed by an implied verb (fiʿl muḍmar). It is addressed to the Jews as a whole, in the manner of taghlīb (giving precedence to the dominant group in the address), as has been mentioned. It censures them for failing to observe the obligations of the covenant that was taken from them concerning the rights of people (ḥuqūq al-ʿibād), in the manner of a prohibition, following the statement of what they did with the covenant taken from them concerning the rights of God, exalted is He, and what is comparable to it, in the manner of a command. The primary purpose of the prohibition against worshipping other than God (exalted is He) is the command to devote worship exclusively to Him, exalted is He. That is: "Remember the time when We took your covenant (p-124) in the Torah."

﴿لا تَسْفِكُونَ دِماءَكم ولا تُخْرِجُونَ أنْفُسَكم مِن دِيارِكُمْ﴾: Like the preceding clause, this is a statement with the meaning of a prohibition. The construction was changed to it because of the point of emphasis (mubālagha) mentioned earlier. What is meant is a strong prohibition against some of the Children of Israel attacking others by killing them or expelling them. The expression of this as shedding their own blood (anfus) and driving them out of their own homes is based on each one of them being treated as himself, because of the strong bond between them in lineage and religion, in order to intensify the obligation to observe the rights of the covenant, by depicting the forbidden act in a form that every soul dislikes and every nature recoils from.

Accordingly, the pronoun in أنْفُسَكم (your souls) necessarily refers to the addressees, since the act of treating the expelled as the addressees' own is realised through it. Likewise, the pronoun in دِيارِكُمْ (your homes) definitely refers to those who are expelled, since what is feared is their being driven from their homes, not from the homes of the addressees insofar as they are addressees. This is made clear by what follows in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿مِن دِيارِهِمْ﴾ (from their homes). The address here is by way of treating their homes as the homes of the addressees, based on treating their souls as the addressees' own souls, for the sake of emphasis (taʾkīd) of the point of exaggeration and intensifying the reproach.

As for the pronoun in دِماءَكُمْ (your blood): it admits of two interpretations. The first implies that the blood shed is, in a figurative sense (iddiʿāʾiyya), the blood of the addressees, while the second implies that it is, in a literal sense (ḥaqīqiyya), the blood of the addressees in a figurative sense. Both come close in conveying the point of exaggeration, so reflect.

As for what has been said, that the meaning is: "Do not engage in what leads to the killing of your own souls by retaliation (qiṣāṣ), or what permits the shedding of your blood and your expulsion from your homes"; or: "Do not do what destroys you and turns you away from eternal life, for that is killing in reality, and do not commit what bars you from Paradise, which is your abode, for that is true exile": this is something the noble context of the text does not support. Rather, the text is explicit in what we have said, as you will see.

﴿ثُمَّ أقْرَرْتُمْ﴾: That is, you acknowledged the covenant and the obligation to uphold it.

﴿وَأنْتُمْ تَشْهَدُونَ﴾: This is an emphasis (taʾkīd) of the acknowledgment, like your saying: "So-and-so acknowledged, as a witness against himself." You, the present ones, bear witness today to the acknowledgment of your forefathers of this covenant.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 85:

﴿Then you are these﴾: an address specific to those present; in it is severe reproach and a strong expression of astonishment at what they committed after the covenant, the acknowledgement of it, and the testimony upon it. "Antum" is the subject (mubtada'); and "ha'ula'" is its predicate (khabar). The locus of the benefit (manat al-ifadah) is the difference of attributes, which is treated as the difference of essence. The meaning is: "You, after that, are these ones: witnesses, breakers, self-contradicting, as the following sentences explain." For His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿you kill yourselves﴾ ... etc., is an elaboration of it and a detailing of their abominable states, which are implicitly included under the demonstrative. As if they had said, "How are we?" So it was said: ﴿you kill yourselves﴾, i.e., those who run in the place of your own selves, as has been indicated. It is also read "tuqattilun" with the doubled letter, for intensification. ﴿and you expel a group of you from their homes﴾: the pronoun may refer either to the addressees, with a suppressed genitive (i.e., "from your own selves"); or to the slain, and the address is in view of their being made the selves of those addressed. Otherwise there would be no equivalence between the slain and the expelled under that heading, around which revolves the orbit of exaggeration in stressing the covenant, as has been stated; and the full ugliness of their crimes in breaking it does not appear. ﴿from their homes﴾: the pronoun refers to the group. The choice of the third person, although the second person would also be permissible, is based on considering the aforementioned heading, as was mentioned regarding the covenant, to guard against the supposition that the intent is to expel them from the homes of the addressees insofar as they are the addressees' homes, rather than insofar as they are the homes of the expelled. It has been said: "ha'ula'" is a relative pronoun (mawsul), and the two clauses are within its relative clause, and the whole is the predicate of "antum." ﴿you back one another against them﴾: with one of the two tas' elided; it is also read with both retained, and with assimilation; and "tazzahharun," with one of the two tas' dropped from "tatazahharun." The meaning of all of them is: you assist one another. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "tukhrijun," or from its object, or from both together, clarifying the manner of the expulsion, and removing the supposition that the prohibition applies only to expulsion directly and independently, and not to backing and aiding. ﴿with sin﴾: connected to "tazahharun," a circumstantial clause from its subject, i.e., "while being involved in sin." It is the act which deserves blame and reproach by its doer; and it has been said: it is what the soul recoils from and the heart does not find at rest with. ﴿and aggression﴾: which is transgression in wrongdoing. ﴿And if they come to you as captives﴾: the plural of "asir," which is one who is taken by force, a form "fa'il" in the sense of "maf'ul," from "al-asr," i.e., binding; or the plural of "asra," which is the plural of "asir," like "jarha" and "jarih"; and it has been read "asra." Its position is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. ﴿you ransom them﴾: i.e., you bring them out of captivity by giving ransom; it is also read "tafdu-hum." Al-Suddi said: God, Exalted is He, took from the Children of Israel in the Torah a covenant that none of them would kill another, nor expel one another from their homes; and whichever slave or maidservant you find from the Children of Israel, you are to buy them and free them. Qurayzah were allies of the Aws, and al-Nadir were allies of the Khazraj, when there was between them what there was of enmity and hatred. So each group fought with its allies; and when they prevailed, they ruined their homes and expelled them from them. Then, when a man from either of the two groups was taken captive, they gathered wealth for him and ransomed him. The Arabs reproached them and said: "How do you fight them, and then ransom them?" They would reply: "We were commanded to ransom them, and fighting them was forbidden to us; but we are ashamed to let our allies be humiliated." So God, Exalted is He, censured them for the contradiction. ﴿And it is forbidden to you, their expulsion﴾: "huwa" is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), placed as the subject; and "muharram" contains a pronoun standing in place of the subject, placed as the predicate, from "ikhrajuhum"; and the clause is the predicate of the pronoun of the matter. It has been said: "muharram" is the predicate of the pronoun of the matter, and "ikhrajuhum" is in the nominative as the substitute for the unnamed subject. It has also been said: the pronoun is ambiguous, explained by "ikhrajuhum," or refers to what is indicated by "tukhrijun" of the verbal noun; and "ikhrajuhum" is an emphasis or an explanation; and the clause is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "tukhrijun," or from "fariqan," or from both, as has passed, after considering the restriction by the earlier circumstantial clause. The specification of the explanation of the prohibition here to expulsion, although it was paired with killing when the covenant was taken, is because it is a place where leniency in the matter is expected, due to its lesser gravity relative to killing; and because the thrust of the speech is to rebuke them and reproach them for their crimes and the contradiction of their actions together; and that is specific to the case of expulsion, since no report is transmitted from them of making amends for the slain with any blood-money or retaliation. This is the secret in specifying the backing with it earlier. As for his placing the conditional "man" (in ﴿wa-in ya'tukum﴾) in an interposed position, although its proper place is at the front, as al-Wahidi mentioned, it is because arranging their contradictory deeds on one string of mention is more effective in showing their falsehood.

﴿Do you believe in part of the Book﴾: that is, the Torah, in which the aforementioned covenant was taken. The interrogative hamza is for reproachful denial, and the fa' is for coordination with an implied element demanded by the context; i.e., "Do you do that, then believe in part of the Book, namely the ransoming?" ﴿and disbelieve in part﴾: namely the prohibition of fighting and expulsion? Although from the requirement of believing in part is believing in the rest, since the whole is from God, Exalted is He, and is included in the covenant; so the basis of the reproach is their disbelief in part, along with their belief in part, as the order of the noble composition indicates. For the fronting here, in the discursive context, requires the primacy of what is fronted and its precedence in some respect necessarily; and since that is not the case here with regard to denial and reproach upon it, it is by consideration of actual occurrence, certainly; not their belief in part along with their disbelief in part, as would be understood if it were said: "Do you disbelieve in part of the Book and believe in part?" Nor mere disbelief in part and belief in part, as would be indicated by saying: "Do you combine belief in part of the Book with disbelief in part?" or the reverse.

﴿So what is the recompense of those who do that﴾: "ma" is negating; and "man," if taken as a relative pronoun, then "yaf'alu" has no place in grammatical analysis; and if taken as a qualifying noun, then its place is in the genitive, being its attribute. "Dhalika" is a pointer to the disbelief in part of the Book together with belief in part, or to what they did of killing and expulsion together with ransoming the captives. ﴿among you﴾: a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yaf'alu." ﴿except disgrace﴾: an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh), which stands as the predicate of the subject. "Khizy" is humiliation, debasement, together with disgrace; and the indefiniteness is for magnification. It is the killing of the Banu Qurayzah and the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir to Adhri'at and Ariha' in Syria; and it has been said: the jizyah (poll tax). ﴿in the life of this world﴾: in the place of nominative, being an attribute of "khizy," i.e., a disgrace existing in the life of this world; or in the place of accusative, being an adverb of time for the disgrace itself. Perhaps the statement of their recompense by way of restriction, as mentioned, is to cut off their vain hopes from the fruits of their belief in part of the Book, and to show that it has no effect whatsoever when joined with disbelief in part. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned﴾: it is also read with the taa' (turadduna); the plural form is chosen, in view of the meaning of "man," after the singular was chosen in view of its wording, because returning occurs only collectively. ﴿to the most severe punishment﴾: because their disobedience is the most severe of disobediences. It has been said: "the most severe punishment" is relative to what they have in this world of humiliation and abasement. The arrangement of the noble composition was changed, in that it did not say, for example, "and the most severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection," to signal the complete contrast between the recompense of the two abodes; and the fronting of "the Day of Resurrection" before mentioning what occurs in it is to magnify the gravity and make the state appear dreadful from the outset. ﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾: of the abominations, of which this reprehensible act is part. It is also read with the yaa' (yuradduna), following the pattern of "yuraddun"; and it is an emphasis of the threat.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 86:

﴿Those﴾: those described with the ugly qualities mentioned above. It is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is the statement of Him, exalted is He: ﴿who have bought the life of this world﴾; that is, they preferred it and exchanged it ﴿for the Hereafter﴾, and turned away from it, although they were able to obtain it. For the disbelief in some of the rulings of the Book that was mentioned was only out of regard for the side of their allies, because of some worldly, base benefits that came back to them from them. ﴿So the punishment will not be lightened for them﴾, whether it is worldly or otherwise-worldly; ﴿nor will they be helped﴾ by having it averted from them, through intercession or compulsion. The clause is conjoined to what precedes it: the conjunction of a nominal clause to a verbal clause. Or "they will be helped" explains an elided element before the pronoun, in which case it is the conjunction of a verbal clause to a similar one.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 87:**

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾: This begins the explanation of another of their crimes. Introducing it with a oath-clause shows the great care taken with it. By "the Book" is meant the Torah (the Tawrah, the revealed scripture of Moses). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that when the Torah was sent down all at once, Allah (exalted is He) commanded Moses (peace be upon him) to carry it. He could not bear it, so Allah sent an angel with each letter of it, and they too could not bear to carry it. So Allah (exalted is He) lightened it for Moses (peace be upon him), and he carried it.

﴿And We followed him up with messengers﴾: It is said "qaffahu bihi" (he followed him up with him) when one makes someone follow another. That is, "We sent them in his footsteps," as in His words (exalted is He): ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾. They are: Joshua (Yushu'); Samuel (Ashmawil); Simeon (Shim'un); David (Dawud); Solomon (Sulayman); Isaiah (Sha'ya); Jeremiah (Armiya); Ezra ('Uzayr); Ezekiel (Hizqil); Elijah (Ilyas); Elisha (al-Yasa'); Jonah (Yunus); Zechariah (Zakariyya); John (Yahya); and others, peace be upon them all.

﴿And We gave 'Isa, son of Maryam, the clear proofs﴾: the clear miracles, such as raising the dead, healing the blind and the leper, and informing of unseen matters. Or it means the Injil (Gospel). "'Isa" in Syriac is "Ishu'", meaning "the blessed". "Maryam" means "the servant" and in Hebrew, for women, it is like "zir" for men. This is how the verse of Ru'ba is explained:

*I said to a zir whom Maryam did not reach,*
*misled by the desires of youth, its regret...*

Its pattern is "maf'al", since "fa'yal" is not attested.

﴿and We supported him﴾: that is, We strengthened him. It is also read as "wa-ayyadnahu". ﴿with the Holy Spirit﴾: read with a damma on the dal and also with it sukoon (sakin), meaning "with the holy spirit", which is the spirit of 'Isa (peace be upon him). It is like your saying "Hatim of generosity" and "a man of truthfulness." It is described as holy because of his honour, or because the loins did not contain him and the wombs of the menstruating did not hold him. It is said it refers to Jibril (peace be upon him), and it is said to the Injil, just as it was said of the Qur'an: ﴿a spirit from Our command﴾. It is also said it refers to the Greatest Name of Allah, by which he used to raise the dead.
