Singling him out from among the messengers (peace be upon them) for mention, describing him with what was mentioned of being given clear proofs and being supported with the Holy Spirit, is because their mission was to implement and confirm the rulings of the Torah, whereas 'Isa (peace be upon him) abrogated many of its rulings by his law. It also serves to cut off the root of their false belief about him (peace be upon him) by showing his truth, and to make clear how utterly ugly was what they did to him (peace be upon him).

﴿Is it then that whenever a messenger came to you﴾: from those messengers; ﴿with what your souls did not desire﴾: of the truth from which there is no escape. That is, what you do not love. From "hawiya" (he desired), like "fariha" (he rejoiced), when one loves. Expressing it this way indicates that the basis of their acceptance or rejection is opposition to the desires of their souls, or agreement with them, and nothing else. The insertion of the hamza between the fa' and what it connects to of the preceding verbs is to rebuke them for following that with this, and to express wonder at their condition. It is also permissible for the fa' to be a conjunction to something implied that suits the context, meaning: "Did you not obey them? So whenever a messenger from among them came to you with what your souls did not desire, ﴿you became arrogant﴾ and refused to follow him and to believe in what came from Allah (exalted is He)?" ﴿So a group﴾ of them ﴿you denied﴾, without troubling them with any other harm. The fa' here indicates cause or sequence. ﴿And a group﴾ of them ﴿you killed﴾, not content with denying them, like Zechariah, John, and others (peace be upon them). Placing "a group" first in both places is for emphasis and to arouse the listener's curiosity about what they did to them, not for restriction. The use of the present tense for killing is to bring its terrible image to mind, or to hint that they were still of that intention, as they plotted against him (peace be upon him) and failed to achieve their aim against him. They also bewitched him and poisoned a sheep for him, until the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The morsel of Khaybar has kept coming back to me, and now is the time that it has severed my aorta."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 88:**

﴿And they said﴾: This explains another category of their ugly deeds, using a shift to the third person (*iltifat*, a change of grammatical address) to indicate that they have been removed from the rank of direct address, because of the disgraceful acts already detailed that call for turning away from them. It also relates similar statements for everyone among the people of truth who understands their falsehood and ugliness. Those who said it were those present in the time of the Prophet (peace be upon him).

﴿Our hearts are ghulf﴾: This is the plural of *aghlaf*, borrowed from *al-aghlaf*, meaning one who has not been circumcised. That is, they are covered with natural coverings, so that what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought hardly reaches them and they do not comprehend it, like their saying: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings from what you call us to﴾. It has also been said that it is a lightened form of *ghulf*, the plural of *ghilaf* (covering). This is supported by what is narrated from Abu 'Amr, reading it with two dammas (*ghuluf*). They mean: our hearts are receptacles for knowledge, so we are self-sufficient with what we have, without needing anything else. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata'. Al-Kalbi said: they mean that no statement reaches our hearts without them retaining it, and even if there were good in your statement, they would have retained it too.

﴿Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾: This is a rejection of what they said and a denial of their claim. The meaning according to the first reading is: rather, Allah, glorified is He, has removed them far from His mercy, by forsaking them and leaving them to themselves, because of their incidental disbelief, and their nullifying of their readiness through their completely bad choice, and their being in a state where kindness (*al-iltaf*) does not benefit them at all, after He created them upon the natural disposition and the ability to accept the truth. According to the second reading: rather, He has removed them far from His mercy, so how could they claim knowledge, which is the greatest of its effects? According to the third reading: rather, He has removed them far from His mercy, therefore they do not accept the truth that leads to it.

﴿So little is it that they believe﴾: *Ma* (ما) here is superfluous (*za'idah*) for emphasis; that is, they believe with little faith, which is their belief in some of the Book. It has also been said: they believe for a little time, which is what they said: ﴿Believe in what has been revealed to those who believed at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end﴾. Both of these are not faith in reality. It has also been said: by "little" is meant nothing, and the *fa'* (ف) indicates that the cursing is the cause of their non-belief.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 89:

﴿And when there came to them a Book﴾: it is the Qur'an; its indefiniteness is for magnification; and its description by His saying, Exalted and Glorified is He: ﴿from Allah﴾; that is, existing from Him (exalted is He), for honour; ﴿confirming what is with them﴾ of the Torah; He expressed it by that because being "with them" necessitates becoming acquainted with what is within its contents, which leads to knowledge of its being a confirmer of it. It was also read "muṣaddiqan" (confirming), as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "Book", because it has been specified by the description. ﴿And they had previously been seeking victory over those who disbelieved﴾; that is, from before its coming; ﴿they used to seek victory over the polytheists through it﴾ before its coming, and they would say: "O Allah, grant us victory through the Prophet sent at the end of time, whose description we find in the Torah," and they would say to them: "The time of a prophet who will emerge to confirm what we have said has drawn near, and we will kill you along with him with the killing of ʿAd and Iram." Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning the Banu Qurayzah and the Nadir, who used to seek victory over the Aws and the Khazraj through the Messenger of Allah ﷺ before his mission. It has also been said: the meaning of yastaftiḥūn (they seek victory) is: they would open (the matter) against them, and inform them that a prophet who will be raised among them has drawn near in time; the sin (in yastaftiḥūn) is for emphasis, as in "istaʿjaba" (he marvelled); that is, they would ask of themselves victory over them, or some of them would ask others that victory be granted over them. On both interpretations, the clause is circumstantial, expressing the completeness of their obstinacy and stubbornness. His saying, Exalted and Most High: ﴿So when there came to them﴾: is a repetition of the first, due to the long interval caused by the intervening circumstantial clause. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿what they recognised﴾: is an expression for the Book mentioned earlier, because knowing the one upon whom it was sent down is knowing it; and seeking victory through it is seeking victory through him. The use of the relative pronoun rather than merely a pronoun is to show the completeness of their obstinacy, for recognising what had come to them is inevitably among the foundations and motives of belief in it. The fa' (so) indicates that his coming follows upon their seeking victory through it, without any forgotten interval between them. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿they disbelieved in it﴾: is the response to the first "mā" (when), as is the view of al-Mubarrad; or its response is both together, as Abu al-Baqa' said. It has also been said: the response of the first is omitted, because what is mentioned points to it; so His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they had been﴾, etc., is a clause conjoined to the conditional clause, conjoining one narrative to another. The meaning of "what they recognised" is the Prophet ﷺ, as is the meaning of "what they used to seek victory through". So the meaning: when there came to them a Book confirming what was with them, they denied it; and before its coming they had been seeking victory through the one upon whom that Book was sent down; then when there came to them the Prophet whom they recognised, they disbelieved in him. ﴿So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers﴾: the definite article is for reference (al-ʿahd); (p-129) that is, upon them; and placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun is to indicate that the descent of the curse upon them is due to their disbelief; just as the fa' is to signal its consequence from it; or the article is for the genus, and they are included in the ruling primarily, since the discourse concerns them; and whichever it is, it confirms the content of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 2, Verse 90:**

﴿Wretched is that for which they have sold themselves﴾: "ma" (ما) is indefinite (nakira), meaning "a thing." It is in the accusative and serves as an explanatory specification (mufassira) of the subject of "bi'sa" (بِئْسَ, a verb expressing blame, "how wretched"). "Ishtaraw" (اشْتَرَوْا) is its descriptive qualifier (sifa). The meaning is: "How wretched is the thing for which they sold their souls." It has also been said that the meaning is: they bought it [i.e., their souls] with it, in their own estimation, since they believed that by what they did they would rescue themselves from punishment. This is rejected by the fact that what is blamed must be what they actually obtained, not what was removed from them.

The object of the blame is His statement (Exalted is He): ﴿that they disbelieve in what Allah has sent down﴾, i.e., in the Book that confirms what is with them, after they had come to know its truth. The substitution of "sending down" (inzal) with "coming" (maji') is to signal that. ﴿Out of envy﴾: that is, out of jealousy, and seeking what is not theirs. It is the cause (illa) of "that they disbelieve," definitively, not of "they sold," because of what has been said about the separation (fasl) by something that is foreign in relation to it, even though it is not foreign in relation to the act of blame and its agent. Moreover, envy has no connection at all to the concept of selling; especially since it is given as the reason for what follows, namely Allah's sending down of His bounty upon whomever He wills. What links them is only their disbelief in what Allah has sent down. The meaning is: how wretched is the thing for which they sold their souls, namely their disbelief, which is caused by envy, for the sake of: ﴿that Allah should send down of His bounty﴾, which is the revelation, ﴿upon whomever He wills﴾, i.e., whomever He wills to bestow it upon and chooses, ﴿of His servants﴾, those who are qualified to bear the burdens of the message. The ultimate result is that their disbelief in what was sent down is explained by their envy of the one upon whom it was sent down. The use of the form of intensification (taf'il) here is to signal the renewal of their envy in accordance with the renewal of the sending down and its multiplicity.

﴿So they returned with wrath upon wrath﴾: that is, they returned laden with anger, which was upon anger, deserving it in accordance with the disbelief upon disbelief they committed, for they disbelieved in the true Prophet and transgressed against him. It has also been said: they disbelieved in Muhammad (upon him be blessings and peace) after Jesus; and it has been said: after their saying: ﴿Ezra is the son of Allah﴾, and their saying: ﴿the hand of Allah is chained﴾, and other forms of their disbelief. ﴿And for the disbelievers﴾: that is, for them. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to indicate that their disbelief was the cause of what befell them. ﴿A humiliating punishment﴾: it is intended to humiliate them and abase them, since their disbelief in what Allah (Exalted is He) sent down was founded on envy, which was founded on the hope that revelation would descend upon them, and on the claim of superiority over people, and on contempt for the one upon whom it was sent down (upon him be blessings and peace).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 91:

﴿وَإذا قِيلَ﴾; from the side of the believers; ﴿لَهُمْ﴾; that is, the Jews. The fronting of the prepositional phrase has already been explained, especially with the *lam al-tabligh* (the lam of conveying a message). ﴿آمِنُوا بِما أنْزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾; [meaning] of the divine books, all of them. What is intended is the command to believe in the Qur'an, but [the verse] adopts the general form to signal that compliance is mandatory, insofar as the Qur'an shares with what they believed in (what is within the scope of the relative clause) and agrees with it in content; and to alert that belief in anything other than it, without belief in it, is not belief in what Allah has sent down. ﴿قالُوا نُؤْمِنُ﴾: that is, we will continue to believe in ﴿بِما أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْنا﴾; they mean by it the Torah, and what was sent down to the prophets of the Children of Israel, (p-130)

for the purpose of confirming its rulings. They insinuate that whatever else is not sent down to them. By the first-person pronoun, they mean either themselves, so the meaning of "sent down to them" is the imposing on them of the rulings contained in what was sent down; or the prophets of the Children of Israel, which is the apparent meaning, because it includes the merit of signaling that their non-belief in the Criterion (al-Furqan) is due to the rebellion and envy mentioned earlier, toward its being sent down to someone who is not of them. Also, although what they mean by the relative pronoun is the Torah and what is in its ruling specifically, presenting it under the heading of being sent down to them is based on the claim that what is other than it is not like that, by way of allusion, as has been pointed out. So if by being sent down to them is meant the imposing of obligations mentioned, it would follow, from the difference between the Qur'an and what was sent down to them (as his saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, indicates: ﴿وَيَكْفُرُونَ بِما وراءَهُ﴾, "and they disbelieve in what is beyond it"), that they are not obligated by what is in it; just as it would follow, on the latter interpretation, that it was not sent down to any one of the Children of Israel. Isolating the relative pronoun, when it is used with a pronoun, from what they alluded to is an unwarranted strain, which is not hidden. The word *al-wara'* (وراء) originally is a verbal noun used as an adverb of place; when it is annexed to the subject, it means what hides something, namely behind it; when annexed to the object, it means what conceals it, namely in front of it. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun of "qalu" (قالوا), with an implied subject, meaning: they said what they said while they disbelieve in what is other than it. The intent is not merely to state that singling out their belief in what was sent down to them by mention serves to negate their belief in what is beyond it; rather, it is to state that the belief they claim is not in fact belief in what was sent down to them. For His saying, Mighty is His name: ﴿وَهُوَ الحَقُّ﴾, "and it is the truth", that is: known for being true, deserving that the name al-Haqq (the Truth) be applied to it absolutely, is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yakfuruna" (يكفرون). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿مُصَدِّقًا﴾, "confirming", is a circumstantial clause emphasizing the content of the sentence; its referent is either the pronoun of "al-Haqq" (الحق), and its governing element is the verbal sense contained in it, as Abu al-Baqa' said; or a pronoun indicated by the context, and its governing element is an implied verb, meaning: I acknowledge it as confirming. ﴿لِما مَعَهُمْ﴾, "of what is with them", that is, of the Torah. The meaning is: they say, "We believe in what was sent down to us," while they disbelieve in the Qur'an, and the situation is that it is the truth, confirming what they believed in. Thus disbelief in what they believed in is entailed for them; and its upshot is that they claim belief in the Torah, while in fact they disbelieve in what entails disbelief in it.

Say (to them), as a rebuke from Allah, Mighty is the Speaker, by demonstrating the contradiction between their statements: ﴿فَلِمَ﴾; its origin is *lima* (لِما), the alif was dropped from it to distinguish the interrogative from the declarative (*ma*). ﴿تَقْتُلُونَ أنْبِياءَ اللَّهِ مِن قَبْلُ﴾; the address is to the Jews present and to their predecessors, by way of prioritizing the present group; and since they shared in the covenant and the practice, objection to their forefathers is an objection to their descendants. The form of the present tense is used to narrate a past situation. It is the answer to an omitted conditional clause, meaning: say to them, "If you are believers in the Torah as you claim, then for what reason did you kill the prophets of Allah in the past, while it is forbidden in it?" It has also been read as *"anbi'a'"* (أنبئاء), with hamza. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ مُؤْمِنِينَ﴾, "if you are believers", is a repetition of the objection, to reinforce the obligation and intensify the threat, meaning: if you are believers, why do you kill them? In each of the two conditional clauses, something has been omitted, relying on what is stated in the other. It has also been said: there is no omission in it, rather the answer precedes the condition; but that is not possible except according to the opinion of the Kufan grammarians and Abu Zayd. It has also been said that *"in"* (إن) here is negative, meaning: you were not believers; otherwise you would not have killed them.

[It is] among the completions of the rebuke and reproach; it falls under the command, and is not a repetition of what was recounted in the midst of the enumeration of blessings, of which the pardon for worshipping the calf is one.

The lam is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam); i.e., "By God, Moses did indeed come to you accompanied by the manifest miracles (al-mu'jizat), which are: the staff; the hand; the years of drought (al-sununa); the diminishing of the fruits; the blood; the flood; the locusts; the lice; the frogs; and the splitting of the sea." The Torah (al-Tawrah) has been counted among them, but this is not clear, since its coming was after the story of the calf.

﴿Then you took the calf﴾: i.e., as a god. ﴿After him﴾: i.e., after his coming with them. It is said: after his going up to the Mount (al-Tur); in which case the Torah would then be among the clear signs. The "then" (thumma) indicates remoteness in rank and signifies the extreme ugliness of what they did. ﴿While you were wrongdoers﴾: a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "you took"; meaning: you took the calf while being wrongdoers by worshipping it, placing worship in other than its proper place; or by neglecting the rights of God's (exalted is He) signs. Or it is a parenthetical statement (i'tiradh); i.e., "you are a people whose habit is wrongdoing."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 2, Verse 93:**

﴿And when We took your covenant﴾: this is a rebuke from God (Exalted is He) and a refutation of their claim to believe in what was revealed to them, by reminding them of their crimes, which speak to their lying. That is: remember when We took your covenant. ﴿And We raised the mount above you﴾, saying: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength and listen.﴾ That is: take hold of what you were commanded in the Torah, and listen to what is in it, listening with obedience and acceptance. ﴿They said﴾: this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What did they say?" So it is said: ﴿They said, "We hear"﴾ your word, ﴿and we disobey"﴾ your command. Now, when their forefathers responded to such an emphatic address, while witnessing such a dazzling miracle, with such a monstrous outrage, and disbelieved in what is contained within the Torah, how can it be conceived that their descendants would believe in what is in it? ﴿And the calf was made to sink into their hearts﴾: this is an ellipsis of the annexed noun (hadhf al-mudaf) with the annexed-to noun put in its place, for emphasis. That is: its love penetrated them, and its image became firmly fixed in their hearts, due to their excessive infatuation with it and their eagerness to worship it, just as dye penetrates cloth and drink penetrates the depths of the body. The phrase ﴿in their hearts﴾ specifies the place of the sinking, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿They only eat fire into their bellies﴾. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the pronoun in "they said," with "qad" implied. ﴿Because of their disbelief﴾: because of their previous disbelief, which necessitated this. It has been said that they were anthropomorphists (mujassima) or incarnationists (hulooliyya), and they had not seen a body more wondrous than it, so what the Samiri had embellished for them took firm root in their hearts.

*Say*: this is addressed as a rebuke to the present Jews, following what became clear of the states of their leaders, whom they follow in everything they do and leave undone. ﴿Wretched is what your faith commands you﴾, in respect of what was revealed to you of the Torah, according to your claim. The thing being dispraised is omitted; that is, what was mentioned of their saying "We hear and we disobey" and their worship of the calf. Attributing the command to faith is a form of mockery of them, and the annexation of "faith" to them is to indicate that it is not true faith in reality, as His saying (Exalted is He) indicates: ﴿If you are believers﴾. For this is a discrediting of their claim to believe in what was revealed to them of the Torah, and an invalidation of it. Its meaning is: if you are believers in it, acting upon what was mentioned of the speech and the deed, and upon what is in it, then wretched is what your faith in it commands you to do. Since faith in it does not permit such abominations, you are definitely not believers in it. The answer to the conditional clause, as you see, is omitted, due to what preceded indicating it.

Say: He repeated the command although the earlier command was recent, because this is a command to rebuke them and expose their lie, in another branch of their falsehoods. However, it was not related from them before the command to refute it; rather, it was alluded to within the discourse, where it was said: ﴿If the Abode of the Hereafter is yours﴾; that is, Paradise, or the bliss of the Abode of the Hereafter (p-132) ﴿with God, exclusively﴾; that is, pure and safe for you, specifically yours, as you claim that none will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian. Its accusative case is as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from "the Abode"; and "with" (ʿind) is an adverbial complement of stability in the predicate, meaning "for you." And His saying (exalted is He): ﴿apart from other people﴾ is in an accusative position (maḥall naṣb) governed by "exclusively." It is said: "such-and-such became pure for me from such-and-such" (khalaṣa lī kadhā min kadhā). The lām is for the genus; that is, all people; or for a specific reference; that is, the Muslims. ﴿Then wish for death﴾; for whoever is certain of entering Paradise yearns to be freed from the abode of ruin and the place of troubles, especially if it is exclusively his, as ʿAlī (may God ennoble his face) said: "I do not care whether I fall upon death or death falls upon me." ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir said at Ṣiffīn: "Now I meet the beloved ones, Muhammad and his party." Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān, when he was dying, and he had wished for death before, said:

*A beloved has come upon poverty,*
*so none will prosper today who has regretted.*

That is, regarding the wishing. And His saying (exalted is He): ﴿if you are truthful﴾ is a repetition of the statement, to intensify the obligation, and to alert that the consequence of the answer is not based on the realization of the condition in reality alone, but also in their belief; and that they have claimed that. The answer is omitted, relying on the indication of what preceded it; that is: if you are truthful, then wish for it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 95:

His (Exalted is He) saying: ﴿And they will never wish for it, ever﴾ is a resumptive statement (kalam mustanaf), not included under the command. It was brought from His side, glory be to Him, to explain what they would refrain from of that to which they were called, which indicates the falsity of their claim.

﴿Because of what their hands have sent forth﴾: because of what they had done of sins that necessitate entry into the Fire, such as disbelief in the Prophet (peace be upon him) and the Qur'an, and distortion of the Torah. Since the hand (yad), among the limbs of a human being, is the locus of most of his crafts and the pivot of most of his benefits, it is used at times to express the self (nafs), and at other times to express power (qudrah).

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾: that is, of them. The choice of the explicit noun over the pronoun is to censure them and to record upon them that they are wrongdoers in all matters, among which is the claim to what is not theirs, and the negation of it from others. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to what precedes it, confirming its content: that is, He is All-Knowing of them and of what proceeded from them of the varieties of wrongdoing and sins that lead to the varieties of punishment, and of what will come from them of guarding against what leads to that. So the matter occurred as He mentioned, and none of them wished for death, for had that happened it would have been transmitted and become well known.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "If they had wished for death, every person among them would have choked on his saliva and died in his place, and not a single Jew would have remained upon the face of the earth."

The verse says: ﴿And you will find them the most eager of people for life﴾. *Wijdan* (intellectual perception, here used in the sense of rational finding) is used in the sense of *'ilm* (knowledge), except that it is specific to what occurs after experience and the like. Its two objects are the pronoun (the *-hum*) and *aḥraṣa* (most eager). The indefinite form in His words ﴿upon life﴾ indicates that what they intend is a particular kind of it, namely the long-drawn-out life. It has also been read with the definite article.

﴿And of those who associated partners﴾: this is coordinated with what precedes it in meaning, as if it were said: "most eager of the people, and of those who associated partners." Singling them out for mention, although they are included among the people, indicates that they are distinguished among them by the intensity of their eagerness, for the sake of emphasising the rebuke of the Jews. Their eagerness, while they acknowledge the requital, was greater than the eagerness of the polytheists who deny it, which shows that they were certain of their destination in the Fire. It is also permissible to take it as the omission of a coordinated element, relying on the preceding term to indicate it, meaning: "and [most eager] than those who associated partners." Then His words, ﴿one of them wishes﴾, are an explanation of the increase in their eagerness, in the manner of a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*). It is also permissible that it be in the position of the nominative, as a qualifier of an omitted subject whose predicate is the preceding adverbial phrase, on the basis that the intended referent of "the polytheists" is the Jews, because of their saying: ﴿Uzayr is the son of God﴾. That is: "and among them is a group, one of whom wishes, whichever of them it was, that is, each one of them, ﴿if he were given a life of a thousand years﴾." This is a report of their wish, as if it were said: "I wish I were given life." It was put in the third person because of His words ﴿wishes﴾, just as you say: "He swore by God that he would do it." Its position is the accusative, as the object of "wishes," treating it as if it were a saying, since it is a verb of the heart.

﴿And he is not one who will remove him from the punishment﴾: *mā* is the Hijazi negation, the pronoun referring back to "one of them" is its subject, and *bi-muzaḥziḥihi* is its predicate, with the *bā'* being superfluous. ﴿That he be given life﴾ is the agent of *muzaḥziḥihi*, that is, "and none of them is one whose long life would move him away from, that is, distance him from, and save him from, the punishment." It has been said that the pronoun refers to the verbal noun implied by "be given life," and "that he be given life" is its substitute. It has also been said that it is ambiguous (*mubham*), and "that he be given life" explains it, and the clause is a circumstantial phrase (*ḥāl*) of "one of them," with the governing element being "wishes," not "be given life," and not as a circumstantial phrase of its pronoun, because the meaning would be corrupted; or it is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tirāḍ*). The original form of *sana* ("year") is *sanawa*, given the saying *sanawāt* and *sinriyya*. It has been said that it is *sanha*, like *jabha*, given the saying *sānahtuhu* and *sunayha*, and "the palm tree aged" (*tasannahat*) when the years passed over it.

﴿And God is seeing of what they do﴾: *al-baṣīr* in the speech of the Arabs means the one who knows the reality of a thing and is acquainted with it. From this is the saying: "So-and-so is *baṣīr* in jurisprudence," meaning he is knowledgeable of its subtleties. That is, He is knowing of the hidden aspects of their deeds, and so He will certainly requite them for them. It has been read with the second-person *tā'* as a shift of person (*iltifāt*), and in it is an intensification of the threat.

**﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel﴾**: It was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Suriya, one of the rabbis (aḥbār) of Fadak. He argued with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and asked him about the one who brings down the revelation to him. The Prophet, upon him be peace, said: "Gabriel, upon him be peace." He (Ibn Suriya) said: "He is our enemy. If it had been anyone else, we would have believed in you." In some narrations: "Our messenger is Michael; if it were he who came to you, we would have believed in you." Gabriel had opposed us many times, and the most severe of these was that he brought down to our Prophet that Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) would be destroyed by Bukhtnasar (Nebuchadnezzar). So we sent someone to kill him, but he met him in Babylon as a poor young boy, and Gabriel, upon him be peace, repelled him and said: "If your Lord commanded him to destroy you, then He will not give him power over you; and if not, by what right do you kill him?" It is also said: God commanded him to place prophethood among us, but he placed it among others.

It is related that ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, had land in the upper part of Medina, and his route passed by the schools of the Jews. He used to sit with them and listen to their speech. They said: "O ʿUmar, we love you, and we hope for you." He said: "By God, I do not come to you out of love for you, nor do I ask you out of doubt in my religion. I only enter upon you so that I may increase in insight regarding the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), and so that I may see his traces in your Book." Then he asked them about Gabriel, upon him be peace. They said: "That one is our enemy; he informs Muhammad of our secrets, and he is the one in charge of every sinking (of the earth) and punishment. Michael brings fertility and peace." He said to them: "What is their rank with God, exalted is He?" They said: "Gabriel is nearer in rank; he is on His right, and Michael is on His left, and the two are enemies." ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "If they are as you say, then they are not enemies. You are more disbelieving than donkeys! Whoever is an enemy to one of them is an enemy to the other, and whoever is an enemy to both of them is an enemy to God, glorified is He." Then ʿUmar returned and found that Gabriel had already preceded him with the revelation. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Your Lord has agreed with you, O ʿUmar." ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "After that, I found myself in my religion firmer than stone."

It has been read as "Jabraʾīl," like "Salsabīl"; and "Jabraʾl," like "Jaḥmarish"; and "Jibrīl"; and "Jibriʾīl"; and "Jibrāʾīl," like "Jibrāʿīl"; and "Jibrāʾil," like "Jibrāʿil." The prohibition of its declension (ṣarf, i.e., taking nunation) is due to its being a proper name (taʿrīf) and being non-Arabic in origin (ʿujma). It is also said that its meaning is "servant of God" (ʿAbdullāh).

**﴿for indeed he has sent it down﴾**: This is a causal explanation for the answer of the conditional (sharṭ), standing in its place. The pronoun "he" (the first hidden one) refers to Gabriel, upon him be peace, and the second refers to the Qur'an. It was made hidden without prior mention, to signal the greatness of his station and his independence from being mentioned, because of the complete fame and prominence of his name, especially when some of his attributes are mentioned.

**﴿upon your heart﴾**: This adds emphasis to the revelation by specifying the locus of the inspiration, for the heart is the first recipient of it, and it is the seat of understanding and memorization. The choice of direct address (khiṭāb) instead of first-person speech (takallum), which would have been based on relating God's words exactly, is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, because quoting in these exact words adds emphasis to the content of the statement.

**﴿by God's permission﴾**: That is, by His command and facilitation. It is a metaphor borrowed from facilitating a barrier (ḥijāb). In it there is an allusion to the complete readiness of Gabriel, upon him be peace, for its descent, and to the sincerity of his determination, upon him be peace. This phrase is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the agent of "sent it down."

His saying, exalted is He: **﴿confirming what is before it﴾**: That is, of the divine books, most of which is the Torah, is a circumstantial clause referring to its object. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: **﴿and a guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾**. The governing element (ʿāmil) for all of these is "sent it down."

The meaning is: whoever among the People of the Book is an enemy to Gabriel, there is no justification for his enmity, rather it is obligatory for him to love him, for he has sent down to you a Book confirming their books. Or, the cause of their enmity to him is his sending down a book that confirms their book and agrees with it, while they are averse to it. For this reason they distorted their book and denied its agreement with it, because acknowledging that would necessitate faith in him, and that would bring about the reversal of their conditions and the loss of their leadership.

It is also said that the answer (of the conditional) is: "then he has removed the noose of fairness," or "then he has disbelieved in what is with him of the books," or "then let him die of rage," or "then he is an enemy to me, and I am an enemy to him."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 98:

﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah﴾: By enmity towards Him (exalted is He) is meant opposing His command out of obstinacy, and departing from obedience to Him out of arrogance; or it means enmity towards His elite and His near ones. However, the statement begins with His glorious Name to magnify their status, and as a notification that their enmity is the enmity of Him, mighty and exalted; just as in His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾. Then the intended meaning is stated explicitly, so it is said: ﴿and His angels and His messengers, and Jibril and Mika'il﴾. These two are singled out for mention, although they are the first to be included under the heading of angelhood and messengerhood, in order to show their excellence, as if they were of another kind, nobler than what has been mentioned; this treats difference in description as if it were difference in kind. It also serves as an indication that enmity towards one of them is enmity towards the other, to cut off the root of their false belief concerning them, since they claimed that the two are adversaries; and to indicate that opposing one or all of them is equal in disbelief, and that enmity brings enmity from God (glorified is He); and that whoever is hostile to one of them is as if he were hostile to all of them. As for His words (exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾: that is, to them. It is the answer to the conditional clause, and the meaning is: whoever is hostile to them, Allah (exalted is He) is hostile to him, and punishes him with the most severe punishment. The choice of the nominal sentence indicates certainty and permanence; and placing "the disbelievers" in the position of the pronoun indicates that enmity towards the aforementioned is disbelief, and that this is evident and does not need to be reported; and that the basis of His (exalted is He) enmity towards them, and His wrath which necessitates the most severe punishment and torment, is their aforementioned disbelief. And it has been read: "Mikha'il" (Mīkāʾīl), like "Mikā'il"; and "Mīkā'īl", like "Mīkā'īl"; and "Mīkaʾil", like "Mīkaʿil"; and "Mīkaʾīl", like "Mīkaʿīl".

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 99:

﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear signs﴾: clear in their indication of their meanings, and clear in showing that they are from Allah, Mighty and Majestic; ﴿and none disbelieves in them except the defiantly disobedient﴾: that is, those who are rebellious in disbelief, who have transgressed its limits; for whoever is not of that description among the disbelievers would not dare to disbelieve in such clear signs. Al-Hasan said: When the word fisq (defiant disobedience) is used for a type of sin, it applies to the greatest individuals of that type, whether of disbelief or other than it. "And on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: Ibn Suriya said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'You have brought us nothing that we recognize, and no sign has been sent down to you that we would follow you in; so this was revealed.'" The lam (in al-fasiqun) is for specific reference (al-'ahd); that is, the particular defiantly disobedient people known to be meant, namely the People of the Book who distorted their Book and went outside their religion. Or it is for the genus (al-jins), and they enter into it in the first place.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 100:

﴿Is it that whenever they make a covenant, a party of them throws it aside?﴾: The hamzah (the interrogative particle, used here for censure) and the waw (the conjunction, which links to an implied clause required by the context) are used; that is, "Did they disbelieve in it while it was in the utmost clarity?" And "whenever they made a covenant". Among the instances of this is what is indicated by His (exalted) saying: ﴿And before this they used to seek victory over those who disbelieved﴾. This is from their saying to the polytheists: "The time of a prophet has drawn near, who will come confirming what we have said, and we will kill you along with him the killing of 'Ad and Iram." The waw is also recited with a sukun (silent), on the basis that the implied sense of the noble composition is: "None disbelieve in it except those who are defiantly disobedient," or "they broke their covenants many times." It is also recited as "ʿūhidū" (passive) and "ʿahidū" (active). His saying (exalted), ﴿a covenant﴾: it is either an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid) for "ʿāhadū" without its own root word, or an object of purpose (maf'ūl lah) on the basis that it means "they gave the covenant." ﴿A party of them threw it aside﴾, that is, they cast it off with the reins and rejected it. It is recited as "naqaḍahu" (broke it). The attribution of the throwing aside to "a party of them" is because not all of them threw it aside. ﴿But most of them do not believe﴾: that is, in the Torah. This is a rebuttal of what might be imagined, namely that those who threw it aside were the minority, and that whoever did not throw it aside openly still believes in it in secret.

And when there came to them a Messenger ﴿وَلَمّا جاءَهم رَسُولٌ﴾: he is the Prophet ﷺ. The indefiniteness (al-tankir) is for magnification (li-l-tafkhim). ﴿مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾ "from Allah": it is related to "came" (jaa'a), or to a omitted element that serves as a qualifier (sifah) of "a Messenger", to convey further exaltation of him, by emphasizing the grandeur that the indefiniteness had conveyed, namely inherent grandeur, with grandeur by annexation (al-fakhamah al-idafiyyah). ﴿مُصَدِّقٌ لِما مَعَهُمْ﴾ "confirming what was with them": that is, the Torah. This is in that he ﷺ affirmed its authenticity and established the truth of the prophethood of Musa, peace be upon him, through what was revealed to him. Or it is in that he, peace be upon him, came in accordance with what was described of him in it.

﴿نَبَذَ فَرِيقٌ مِنَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ﴾ "a party of those who were given the Book threw away": that is, the Torah. They were the Jews who were in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, among those who had previously sought victory through it (yastaftihuna bihi). It does not refer to those who were in the time of Sulayman, peace be upon him, as has been said, because such a casting away at the coming of the Prophet ﷺ is not conceivable from them. The singling out of this casting away for mention, although it is included under His saying, Exalted and Mighty is He: ﴿أوَكُلَّما عاهَدُوا عَهْدًا نَبَذَهُ فَرِيقٌ مِنهُمْ﴾ "Is it that every time they make a covenant, a party of them throws it aside?", is because it is the greatest of their crimes, and because it paves the way for mentioning their following of what the devils recite and their preference for it over it.

The meaning of "given it" (ita'ihā) is either the granting of its knowledge through study, memorization and comprehension of what is in it; so the relative pronoun refers to their scholars. Or it is merely its being sent down to them, in which case it refers to all of them. In either of the two interpretations, placing the relative clause in place of the pronoun serves to signal the complete contradiction between what was affirmed for them in the relative clause and what proceeded from them of casting away.

﴿كِتابَ اللَّهِ﴾ "the Book of Allah": that is, the one that was given to them. Al-Suddi said: When Muhammad ﷺ came to them, they opposed him with the Torah, and the Torah and the Furqan (the Qur'an) agreed, so they cast away the Torah and took up the book of Asaf and the magic of Harut and Marut, which did not agree with the Qur'an. This is the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَلَمّا جاءَهم رَسُولٌ مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ﴾ and so on. He referred to it as "the Book of Allah" only to honor it, to magnify its right upon them, and to make dreadful what they dared to disbelieve in of it.

It was also said: "the Book of Allah" is the Qur'an. They cast it away after it had become binding upon them to receive it with acceptance, especially since they had previously sought victory through it, for that is an acceptance of it and an adherence to it. Thus disbelief in it at its coming is a casting away of it, as if it were said: "the Book of Allah which he brought," since the coming of the Messenger indicates the coming of the Book. ﴿وَراءَ ظُهُورِهِمْ﴾ "behind their backs": this is a metaphor for their abandonment of it and turning away from it entirely. It is a figure drawn from what is thrown behind the back, in indifference to it and paying it little attention. ﴿كَأنَّهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ "as if they did not know": this is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah). That is: they cast it behind their backs, being likened to those who do not know it.

If by them are meant their rabbis, then the meaning is: as if they knew it with certainty, yet they did not recognize what it contains of the proofs of his prophethood, peace be upon him. In this there is an indication that their knowledge of it is firm, but they feign ignorance. Or: as if they did not know that it is the Book of Allah; or they do not know it at all. The same applies if by them is meant all of them. In these two interpretations there is additional intensification of their turning away from what is in the Torah of the proofs of prophethood.

This is so. If by what they cast away of the Book of Allah is meant the Qur'an, then the knowledge negated in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿كَأنَّهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ is the knowledge that it is the Book of Allah. In it there is what is in the first interpretation of indicating that they are certain of that, and that they disbelieve in it only out of arrogance and obstinacy.

It has been said: The generation of the Jews consists of four groups. One group believed in the Torah and upheld its rights, like the believers among the People of the Book, and they are the fewest, referred to in His saying, Exalted and Mighty is He: ﴿بَلْ أكْثَرُهم لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ "Rather, most of them do not believe." Another group openly cast aside the covenants and transgressed the limits, in rebellion and wickedness, and they are the ones meant by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿نَبَذَهُ فَرِيقٌ مِنهُمْ﴾. Another group did not openly cast it aside, but cast it aside out of their ignorance of it, and they are the majority. Another group held fast to it outwardly but cast it aside secretly, and they are the ones who feign ignorance.

**﴿And they followed what the devils recited﴾**: This is coordinated with the answer of "lamma" (when), meaning: they cast aside the Book of God and followed the books of the sorcerers which the devils used to read. The devils here are the rebellious among the jinn. The verb "tatlu" (recited) is a narration of a past state. By "following" is meant deep immersion in it and devoting oneself to it entirely, since the basic following was already present before the coming of the Messenger (ﷺ). Therefore it cannot be coordinated with the answer of "lamma," and for this reason it has been said that it is coordinated with the clause [of the preceding verse], and it has been said that it is coordinated with "ushribu" (were made to drink).

**﴿over the kingdom of Solomon﴾**: That is, in the era of his kingdom. It has been said: the devils used to eavesdrop, and they would add to what they had heard lies that they fabricated, and they would cast these to the soothsayers (kahana), who would write them down and teach them to people. This spread in the time of Solomon, peace be upon him, to the point that it was said: the jinn know the unseen. They used to say: "This is the knowledge of Solomon, and his kingdom was not complete except by this knowledge, and by it he subjected mankind, the jinn, the birds, and the wind that moves by his command." It has also been said: Solomon, peace be upon him, had buried many of the sciences with which God, exalted is He, had singled him out, beneath his throne of kingship. When a period of time had passed over that, some hypocrites reached them and wrote during that interval things from the branches of magic that correspond in some respects to those buried things. Then, after his death, when people came upon those books, they led them to believe that it was from the work of Solomon, peace be upon him, and that he had attained this rank only by means of these things.

**﴿And Solomon did not disbelieve﴾**: This is a declaration of the innocence of his sanctuary, peace be upon him, from magic, and a refutation of the one who slandered him by claiming that he believed in it and practised it. The mention of it as disbelief is for the sake of emphasis in demonstrating his purity, peace be upon him, and the falsity of those who accused him of it.

**﴿But the devils disbelieved﴾**: It has been recited with the lightened "lakinna" and the nominative "ash-shayatin" (devils). The "wa" is conjunctive, joining the corrective clause to what precedes it. The fact that the lightened particle is, according to the majority, for conjunction applies only when there is no "wa," and when what follows it is a single word.

**﴿disbelieved﴾**: by employing magic and recording it.

**﴿teaching people magic﴾**: as misguidance and leading astray. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "kafaru," or from "ash-shayatin." For what is in "lakinna" of the scent of the verb suffices to govern the state. Or it is in the nominative position, as a second predicate of "lakinni," or a substitute for the first predicate. The form of the present tense indicates the continuity and renewal of the teaching. Or it is a resumptive clause. This is according to the assumption that the pronoun refers to the devils. As for the assumption that it refers back to the subject of "ittaba'u," then it is either a circumstantial state from it, or merely a resumptive clause.

Know that magic has kinds. Among them is the magic of the Chaldeans (Kaldaniyyin), who existed in ancient times; they were a people who worshipped the stars and claimed that they were the governors of this world, and from them proceed good, evil, happiness, and misfortune. They would produce marvels by mixing celestial powers with earthly powers. They were the ones whom God, exalted is He, sent Abraham, peace and blessings be upon him, to refute their doctrine. They are three groups. One group of them claims that the spheres and the stars are necessarily existent in themselves; these are the Sabians (Sabi'a). Another group says that the spheres are divine, and they take for each one of them a temple (haykal) and busy themselves with serving them; these are the idol-worshippers. A third group affirmed for the spheres and the stars an agent acting by choice, but they said that He gave them a high, penetrating power in this world and entrusted its governance to them.

Among them is the magic of people of illusions and strong souls, for they claim that a human's soul, through purification, can reach in power and influence the point where it is able to bring into existence, annihilate, give life, and change structure and form. Among them is the magic of one who seeks help from earthly spirits, which is called "'azA'im" (incantations) and the subjugation of the jinn. Among them are the imaginative deceptions that seize the eyes, called sha'wadha (sleight of hand).

There is no disagreement among the community that whoever believes the first is an unbeliever, and likewise whoever believes the second, which is the magic of people of illusions and strong souls. As for one who believes that a human, through purification and recitation of incantations and charms, can reach the point where God, glorified is He and exalted, creates after that, by way of the customary course, some marvels, then the Mu'tazila agreed that he is an unbeliever, because by this belief he cannot know the truthfulness of the prophets and messengers, unlike others. Perhaps the verified position is that if that person is good, observant of the law in everything he does and forbears, and the one from whom he seeks help is of the good spirits, and his incantations and charms do not contradict the rulings of the noble Sharia, and there is no legal harm to anyone from the marvels that appear in his hand, then that is not of the kind of magic. But if he is wicked and does not adhere to the noble Sharia, then it is evident that the one from whom he seeks help is necessarily of the evil, wicked spirits, since the mutual alliance and cooperation between them cannot be realized without sharing in wickedness and vileness; so he is an unbeliever with certainty. As for sleight of hand and what runs in its course, such as the display of wondrous matters by arranging engineering devices, dexterity of hand, and the use of the special properties of medicines and stones, then the application of the term "magic" to them is by way of metaphor, or because of their subtlety, since in origin it is a designation for whatever its source is subtle and whose cause is hidden, or from diverting from the customary direction, since in the original language "sarf" means diversion, as related by al-Azhari from al-Farra' and Yunus.

**﴿and what was sent down to the two angels﴾**: This is coordinated with "sihr" (magic); that is, they teach them what was sent down upon the two. The intended meaning of the two is one, and the coordination is for the difference of consideration, or it is a stronger kind of it, or it is coordinated with "ma tatlu" (what [the devils] recited), with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion, meaning: "and they followed what was sent down..." etc. These two were angels sent down to teach magic as a trial from God, exalted is He, for people, just as the people of Talut were tested with the river. Or [they were sent] to distinguish it from the miracle, lest people be deceived by it. Or because sorcerers had multiplied in that age, and had devised strange branches of magic, and claimed prophethood; so God, exalted is He, sent these two angels to teach people the branches of magic so that they could counter those liars and make their affair manifest to people.

As for what is related, that when the angels, peace be upon them, saw the sins ascending from the children of Adam, they reproached them and said to God, glorified is He: "These are the ones You chose to be vicegerents on earth; they disobey You in it." He, exalted and majestic, said: "If I had installed in you what I installed in them, you would disobey Me." They said: "Glory be to You; it is not fitting for us to disobey You." He, exalted is He, said: "Choose from your best two angels." They chose Harut and Marut, and they were among the most righteous and most devout of them. So they were sent down to earth after there had been installed in them what is installed in humans of desire and other powers, so that they might judge between people by day and ascend to heaven by night. They had been forbidden from associating partners with God, from killing without right, from drinking wine, and from fornication. They used to judge among them by day, and when evening came they would mention the Greatest Name of God and ascend to heaven. Then one day a woman, among the most beautiful of women, named Zuhra, came to them with a dispute. She was from Lakhm; it has been said she was a queen in her land from the people of Persia, and her dispute was with her husband. When they saw her they were captivated by her, and they sought to seduce her, but she refused. They insisted upon her, and she said: "No, unless you judge in my favour against my opponent." So they did. Then they asked her what they had asked, and she said: "No, unless you kill him." So they did. Then they asked her what they had asked, and she said: "No, unless you drink wine and prostrate to the idol." So they did each of these after much back and forth. Then they asked her what they had asked, and she said: "No, unless you teach me what you ascend to heaven with." So they taught her the Greatest Name, and she invoked it and ascended to heaven. God, glorified is He, transformed her into a star. They then set out to ascend according to their custom, but their wings did not carry them. They knew what had befallen them. This was in the time of Idris, peace be upon him, so they sought refuge with him to intercede for them, and he did so. God, exalted is He, gave them the choice between the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, and they chose the first, because it would end sooner. So they are being punished in Babylon. It has been said: they are suspended by their hair; it has been said: they are hanging upside down, being struck with whips of iron until the Hour arises. As for this, there is no reliance upon it, since its basis is a narration of the Jews, together with what it contains of contradiction to the proofs of reason and transmission. Perhaps it is from the category of parables and symbols by which the guidance of the discerning and intelligent is intended, through encouragement and warning. It has also been said that they were two men, called "angels" because of their righteousness. This is supported by the reading "al-mali'kayni" (the two kings) with a kasra.

**﴿at Babil﴾**: The "ba'" is in the sense of "fi" (in), and it is connected to "unzila" (was sent down), or to a deleted element which occurs as a circumstantial state of "al-malakayn," or of the pronoun in "unzila." It is the Babylon of Iraq. Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, said: Babil is the land of Kufa. It has been said: it is the mountain of Damavand. The prohibition of its declension is due to foreignness and proper-namehood, or to femininity and proper-namehood.

**﴿Harut and Marut﴾**: These are an explanatory apposition to "al-malakayn." They are proper names for them. Their declension is prohibited due to foreignness and proper-namehood. Even if they were from "al-harat" and "al-marat," meaning "breaking," they would be declinable. As for one who reads "al-malikayn" with a kasra on the lam, or who says that they were two righteous men, he says: these are their names. It has been said: they are the names of two tribes of the jinn, and they are the intended meaning of "al-malikayn" with a kasra. It has also been recited with the nominative: "they are Harut and Marut."

**﴿And they did not teach anyone﴾**: The "min" is superfluous in the direct object, to give emphasis to the comprehensiveness that the word "ahad" (anyone) conveys, not to convey comprehensiveness itself as in your saying: (p-139) "No man came to me." It has been recited as "yu'limani," from "al-i'lam" (informing).

**﴿until they say, "We are only a trial"﴾**: "Fitna" means testing and examination. Its being singular while they are two is because it is a verbal noun; and attributing it to them is a strong emphasis, as if they were themselves the trial. The restriction is to clarify that they have no concern in what they practise other than it, so that people may turn away from learning it. That is: they do not teach what was sent down upon them of magic to anyone of its seekers until they counsel him before teaching and say to him: "We are only a trial and a test from God, mighty and majestic." Whoever acts upon what he has learned from us and believes in its truth becomes an unbeliever; and whoever refrains from acting upon it, or takes it as a means of guarding himself against being deceived by its like, remains upon faith.

Note on the passage: the text is marked "part 2 of 2" and begins mid-argument, so I translate it exactly as given.

﴿So do not disbelieve﴾ by holding that it is true and that acting upon it is permissible. (It is evident that the goal of the prohibition is not this statement alone; rather, part of it is the addressee's commitment to what the prohibition requires, though this was not mentioned because it is obvious; and the discourse concerns the attention the two angels gave to advice and guidance.) The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "yu'allimūn" (they teach), not conjoined to it, as has been said. That is: "But the devils disbelieved, teaching people sorcery and what was sent down to the two angels, and leading them to act upon it, through seduction and misguidance, while the state of affairs is that the two do not teach anyone until they have forbidden him to act upon it and to disbelieve because of it." As for what has been said, that "mā" in His words (Exalted is He): ﴿and what was sent down﴾, etc., is negative, and the clause is conjoined to His words (Exalted is He): ﴿and Solomon did not disbelieve﴾, it was brought for the refutation of the Jews in the story, meaning: the permission of sorcery was not sent down to the two angels; and that Hārūt and Mārūt are a substitute (badal) for the devils, as two tribes of the jinn singled out for mention because of their nobility, and the rest of the devils are their followers; and that the meaning is: they do not teach anyone until they say, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve," and thus become like us; this is rejected, because the context of describing the devil with disbelief and the misguiding of people is not suited to describing their leaders with the prohibition from disbelief as mentioned, along with what it involves of disturbing the order of the discourse, for substitution has the effect of setting aside the thing substituted.

﴿Then they learn from both of them﴾: conjoined to the negated clause, for it has the force of an affirmative clause, as if it were said: they teach them after their saying, "We are only..." etc. The pronoun refers to "anyone" (aḥad), taken according to its meaning, as in His words (Exalted is He): ﴿So among you there is none who could withhold from Him﴾.

﴿What they cause division with﴾: that is, by means of it and by using it, ﴿between a man﴾; it is also read with a damma and a kasra on the mīm, with a hamza, and with a shadda on the rā' without a hamza; ﴿and his wife﴾; by God (Exalted is He) causing hatred, enmity and discord between them when they did what they did of sorcery, according to the customary divine practice of creating effects upon the occurrence of ordinary causes, as a trial; not that sorcery is the one that has an effect in that. It was said: they learn from them what they act upon, so people see it and believe it to be true, and so they disbelieve, and thus their wives are separated from them.

﴿But they cannot harm anyone thereby﴾: that is, by what they have learned and used of sorcery; ﴿anyone﴾: that is, anyone; and "min" is superfluous, for what was mentioned in His words (Exalted is He): ﴿and they teach no one﴾; and the usual rule, though its superfluity is in the object of a negated verb, is that the nominal here is treated as verbal, as if it were said: they do not harm anyone thereby; ﴿except by God's leave﴾; because it and other causes are far removed from having effect in themselves; rather it is by His command (Exalted is He). So when they use sorcery He may create among His acts an effect as a trial, and He may not create it. The exception is an exception of the emptied (mufarragh) type; the "bi" is related to an omitted element and occurs as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "ḍārrīn" or from its object, even though it is indefinite, because it relies on the negation, or from the pronoun in the "bihi" governed by the preposition; that is: they do not harm anyone thereby except conjoined with God's leave (Exalted is He). It is also read "biḍārrī", as an annexation, by making the preposition part of the genitive noun, and separating the two elements of the annexation by the adverbial phrase.

﴿And they learn what harms them﴾, because they intend thereby to act, or because knowledge generally leads to action; ﴿and does not benefit them﴾; this is stated explicitly to indicate that it is not among the matters mixed with benefit and harm, but is pure evil and unmitigated harm, because they do not intend by it to free themselves from being deceived by the falsehoods of one who claims prophethood, for example, from among the sorcerers, nor to rescue people from it, so that there would be some benefit in it in general. In this is the principle that abstaining from what its harms cannot be safeguarded against is better, like learning philosophy, which cannot be guaranteed not to lead to error; even though someone has said:

I came to know evil, not for the sake of evil,
but to guard against it;
and whoever does not know evil
among people will fall into it.

﴿And they certainly knew﴾: that is, the Jews whose crimes have been related; ﴿that whoever purchased it﴾: that is, exchanged what the devils recite for the Book of God, Mighty and Majestic. The first lām is the answer to an omitted oath; the second is the lām of the beginning, to which "knew" is suspended from action; and "man" is a relative pronoun in the nominative position as subject; "purchased it" is its relative clause; and His words (Exalted is He): ﴿he has no portion in the Hereafter﴾, that is: no share, is a clause of subject and predicate; "min" is superfluous in the subject; and "fi al-ākhira" is related to an omitted element and occurs as a circumstantial clause from it; had it been placed after it, it would have been a qualifier of it; the sense being: he has no share in the Hereafter. This clause is in the nominative position, as the predicate of the relative pronoun; and the clause in the accusative position fills the place of the two objects of "knew", if it is made transitive to two, or of its single object if it is made transitive to one. So the clause "and they certainly knew..." etc. is what is sworn to, not the clause "whoever purchased it..." etc. This is the view of the majority, and it is the position of Sibawayh. But al-Farrā' said, and Abu al-Baqā' followed him: the last lām is a preparatory lām for the oath; "man" is conditional, in the nominative as subject; "purchased it" is its predicate; and "he has no share in the Hereafter" is the answer to the oath; the answer of the condition is omitted, being sufficed by the answer of the oath, for when a condition and an oath come together, the earlier of the two is generally answered; then both clauses are what is sworn to.

﴿And wretched is that for which they sold their souls﴾: that is, they sold them; the lām is the answer to an omitted oath; the object of the dispraise is omitted, that is: "By God, wretched is what they sold their souls for, namely sorcery, or disbelief." In this is the indication that they, in casting the Book of God behind their backs, have exposed themselves to destruction, and sold them for what increases them only in perdition. Interpreting the sale as meaning purchase is not tenable, for the purchased thing is determined, which is what the devils recite; and because the object of the dispraise is what was taken, not what was cast away, as was pointed out in the explanation of His words (Glorified is He): ﴿Wretched is that for which they sold their souls, in that they disbelieve in what God has sent down﴾.

﴿If only they knew﴾: that is, if they acted upon their knowledge; they were made as those without knowledge because they did not act in accordance with what their knowledge required; or: if only they reflected upon it; or knew its ugliness with certainty; or the reality of what follows it of punishment for it. Moreover, what was first affirmed for them with an oath-emphasis is innate reason, or general knowledge of the ugliness of the act, or the ordering of punishment without verification. The answer to "law" (if only) is omitted; that is: they would not have done what they did.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 2, verse 103:**

﴿And if they had believed﴾: that is, in the Messenger referred to in His (Exalted) saying: ﴿And when there came to them a Messenger from Allah...﴾ and so on. Or in what was sent down to him of the clear signs mentioned in His (Exalted) saying: ﴿We have certainly sent down to you clear signs, and none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient﴾. Or in the Torah, which is meant by His (Exalted) saying: ﴿A party of those who were given the Scripture threw the Book of Allah behind their backs﴾, for disbelief in the Qur'an and in the Messenger (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him) is disbelief in it.

﴿And had they been mindful [of Allah]﴾, that is, had they refrained from the acts of disobedience reported about them. ﴿A reward from Allah would have been better﴾: this is the response (jawab) of "law" (lau, "if"). Its underlying form is: "They would have been rewarded with a reward from Allah, better than what they sold their souls for." The verb was deleted and the construction was altered to the form in which the noble text stands, to indicate the certainty of the reward for them and the affirmation of its being better. The comparative object was deleted, out of reverence for the one being preferred, so that it would not be attributed to him. The word "reward" (mathubah) is indefinite to indicate lessening (of quantity or quality). The word "min" ("from") is connected to an omitted element and functions as a descriptive qualifier of honour for mathubatun ("a reward"), meaning: "some reward proceeding from Him (Exalted) is better." It has been said that the response of "law" is omitted, meaning: "they would have been rewarded," and what follows is a new independent clause, because the occurrence of an independent nominal clause as the response of lau is not familiar in Arabic usage. It has also been said that lau here expresses wishing (tamanni), and its meaning is that their situation is so dreadful that the one who knows (the truth) wishes for their faith and their God-consciousness, out of grief over them. It is also read as lamathubatun (with a different vowelling of the word). The reward is called thawab and mathubah only because the doer of good "returns" (yathub) to it. ﴿If only they knew﴾ that the reward of Allah is better: they were attributed to ignorance because they did not act in accordance with what knowledge requires.

O you who have believed: this is an address to the believers, containing guidance toward what is good, and an allusion to another of the crimes of the Jews.

﴿Do not say "Ra'ina"﴾: al-Mura'a (attentiveness) means exaggerating in caring for something; it is guarding another's interests, managing his affairs, and attending to his welfare. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would convey some knowledge to the Muslims, they would say, "Ra'ina, O Messenger of Allah," meaning: attend to us, wait for us, and be patient with us, until we understand your speech and memorize it.

The Jews had a word in Hebrew or Syriac that they used to revile one another among themselves: "ra'ina." It was said that its meaning was: "Listen, may you not hear." When they heard the believers say this, they seized upon it and made it a pretext (dhari'a, means) to achieve their aim. They began addressing the Prophet (ﷺ) with it, intending by it that abuse, or attributing to him (ﷺ) the quality of ra'an, which is foolishness and stupidity.

It is narrated that Sa'd ibn 'Ubada (may Allah be pleased with him) heard them say it, and said: "O enemies of Allah, the curse of Allah be upon you! By Him in whose hand my soul is, if I hear any one of you say it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I will surely strike his neck." They said: "Do you not say it yourselves?" Then the verse was revealed, and the believers were forbidden from this, to cut off the tongues of the Jews from deception (tadlis, concealment and misleading), and they were commanded with what has the same meaning, since deception is not accepted.

So it was said: ﴿And say, "Unzurna"﴾: meaning, look upon us (unzur ilayna), with the omission and the connecting of the preposition; or: wait for us (intazirna), taking it from "nazarahu," when one waits for him. It has also been read as "anzirna," from "al-nazra" (respite), meaning: grant us respite until we memorize. It has also been read as "ra'una," in the plural form, out of reverence; and "ra'inan," in the form of the active participle, meaning: a statement containing ra'an, like "dari'un" and "labin," because it resembled their saying "ra'ina," and since it became the cause of reviling with ra'an, it was described by it.

﴿And listen﴾: and listen well to what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) speaks to you and the questions he puts to you, with attentive ears and present minds, so that you will not need to ask for protection and for a request for consideration. Or: listen to what you have been charged with of prohibition and command with earnestness and care, so that you do not return to what you have been forbidden. Or: listen with the listening of obedience and acceptance, and let your listening not be like the listening of the Jews, when they said: "We hear and we disobey."

﴿And for the disbelievers﴾: that is, the Jews, who used your aforementioned statement as a means to their disbeliefs, and made it a cause for belittling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and said to him what they said. ﴿There is a painful punishment﴾: for what they dared against him of the great offence. This is a conclusion (tadhyil) to what preceded; it contains a severe threat to them and a kind of warning to the addressees against what they have been forbidden.

﴿Those who disbelieve do not wish﴾: *al-wudd* is love of a thing together with desiring it, and for this reason the word is used for each of the two. Negating it is a metonymy for dislike. Placing the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) in place of the personal pronoun indicates that what is in its clause (*sila*) is the cause, namely their not loving. Perhaps its connection to what precedes is that the forbidden speech often occurred at the time of the descent of revelation, which is expressed in this verse as "good." It is thus implied that the reason for their distortion of it is what is reported of them, since it occurred in the course of the arrival of the good they disliked. It has also been said: a group of the Jews used to show love to the believers and claim that they wished them good, so this was revealed to refute them in that claim. And "min" in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿from the People of the Book nor the polytheists﴾ is explanatory (*lil-tabyin*), as in His saying, exalted and high is He: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not [going to desist]﴾. And "la" is superfluous (*mazidah*), for reasons you will understand. ﴿That there be sent down upon you﴾: it is in the place of the accusative, as the object of "yawaddu." The verb is in the passive voice for confidence in the identity of the agent. The explicit mention that comes next in His saying (exalted is He), ﴿of good﴾, is what stands in place of its agent. "Min" is superfluous for comprehensiveness (*lil-istighraq*). The negation, although it does not directly govern it apparently, is nonetheless extended to it in meaning. The good is the revelation. Interpreting it as encompassing that and other things, such as knowledge and support, as has been said, is rejected by its being described afterward with restriction. Fronting the adverbial phrase before it, although its proper place is after it, is to show complete care for it, because it is the basis of their not loving. "Min" in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿from your Lord﴾ is for the starting point (*ibtida'iyyah*). Mentioning the title of Lordship is to indicate its causality for the sending down of good. The addition to the pronoun of the addressees is to honour them. Their dislike is not for its being sent down upon the addressees in terms of their worship of what preceded it and their exposure thereby to the happiness of both abodes. How could it be otherwise? For they are, in that respect, among those upon whom good descended. Rather, it is in terms of that descent falling upon the Prophet ﷺ. The plural form is to announce that the basis of their dislike is not a meaning specific to the Prophet ﷺ, but a quality shared by all: emptiness of learning according to the Jews, and of leadership according to the polytheists. The meaning is: they see themselves as more worthy that revelation be sent to them, and they dislike, so they envy you that any part of revelation should descend upon you. As for the Jews, it is on the basis that they are the People of the Book and sons of the prophets, raised in the places of descent of revelation, while you are unlettered. As for the polytheists, it is out of pride in the status and wealth they had, supposing that the leadership of prophethood is like other worldly leaderships, bound to apparent causes. For this reason they said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?﴾ And since the Jews were more notorious for this disease, especially in the course of mentioning their being tested with it, it did not follow from negating their love for what was mentioned the negation of the polytheists' love for it. So the word "la" was added to emphasise the negation.

﴿But Allah singles out for His mercy﴾: an initial sentence (*jumlah ibtida'iyyah*), brought to establish what preceded of the sending down of good, to draw attention to its wisdom, and to humble those who dislike it. By His mercy is meant revelation, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Do they apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ It is expressed in terms of its descent upon the believers as good, and in terms of its being attributed to Him (exalted is He) as mercy. 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: by His prophethood, with which He singled out Muhammad ﷺ. So the verb is transitive, and the form *ifti'al* indicates selection. Choosing it over "tanzil" (sending down), which suits the context and agrees with His saying (exalted is He): ﴿that Allah should send down of His bounty upon whom He wills﴾, is to increase the honour of the Prophet ﷺ and to despair them of what they had attached their empty hopes to. The *ba'* (with) is attached to the intended object, i.e., He bestows His mercy ﴿upon whom He wills﴾ of His servants, and makes it restricted to him, on account of his inherent worthiness, which overflows upon him according to His will, glorified and exalted is He, by way of bounty; it does not extend beyond him to another. It has also been said: the verb is intransitive (*lazim*), and "man" is its agent; the pronoun referring back to "man" is omitted under both interpretations. His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And Allah is the possessor of great bounty﴾ is a concluding phrase (*tadhyil*) to what preceded, confirming its content. In it is an indication that bestowing prophethood is from His great bounty, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, His bounty upon you has been great﴾; and that the deprivation of one who is deprived of that is not due to the narrowness of the scope of His bounty, but to His will, which operates according to the paths of perfect wisdom. The beginning of both sentences with the sublime Name is to indicate the magnificence of their two meanings, and that each of them is independent in its matter; for the pronoun in the second indicates its dependence on the first.

(p-143)

﴿Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾: This is a resumed statement, brought to explain the secret of abrogation (naskh), which is one of the forms of the descent of revelation, and to refute the claims of those who criticize it. It follows the establishment of the reality of revelation and rejects outright the words of those who dislike it.
