It was said that it was revealed when the polytheists, or the Jews, said: "Do you not see Muhammad ordering his companions to do something, then forbidding them from it, and ordering the opposite?" In language, naskh means removal and transfer. It is said, "The wind abrogated the trace," meaning it removed it, and "I copied the book," meaning I transferred it. The abrogation of a verse is the clarification that the obligation of reciting it, or of the ruling derived from it, or of both together, has come to an end. Its causing to be forgotten means removing it from hearts. "Ma" is a conditional particle that governs "nansakh" in the jussive mood, and it is in the accusative as its object. It was also read as "nunsikh," from "ansakha," meaning: We command you, or Gabriel, to abrogate it, or you find it abrogated. It was read as "nansa'uha," from "al-nasʾ," meaning: We delay it. It was read as "nunassihā" with the doubled letter, and as "tansahā" and "tunsahā," addressing the Messenger (ﷺ), in the active and passive voices. It was also read as "mā nansakh min āyatin aw nunsikaha," and as "mā nunsik min āyatin aw nansakhhā." The meaning is that every verse We take away, in accordance with what wisdom and benefit require, by removing its wording, or its ruling, or both together, is replaced by another, or is not replaced at all. ﴿We bring a better than it﴾: that is, a different kind which is better for the servants in terms of benefit and reward than the one that has gone. It was also read with the hamza changed to an alif. ﴿Or its like﴾: that is, in the benefit and reward mentioned. This ruling is not restricted to the abrogation of a complete verse and what is above it, but applies also to what is less than that. Its specification by mention is in view of what is most common. The text, as you see, indicates the permissibility of abrogation. How could it not, when the descent of the verses on which the orbit of the legal rulings revolves is according to what wisdom and benefits require? These differ with the differing of circumstances, and change with the change of persons and eras, like the circumstances of livelihood. Many a ruling that wisdom requires in one situation, wisdom requires its opposite in another situation. So, if abrogation were not permitted, the order between wisdom and the rulings would be disrupted.

﴿Do you not know﴾: The hamza is for confirmation, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?﴾ and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ The address is to the Prophet, upon him be peace and blessings. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that Allah is over all things competent﴾ fills the place of the two objects of "taʿlam" according to the majority, and fills the place of its first object according to al-Akhfash, with its second object omitted. The purpose of this confirmation is to cite his knowledge of what has been mentioned as evidence of His power, exalted is He, to abrogate and to bring what is better than the abrogated or its like, because that is among the things subjugated under His power, exalted is He. Whoever knows that His power, exalted is He, encompasses all things, knows with certainty His power to do that. The turn to the use of the august Name in place of the pronoun is to cultivate awe and to indicate the basis of the ruling, for the comprehensiveness of power over all things is among the attributes of divinity. The same is the case in His saying, mighty is His authority:

Did you not know that Allah—to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾? For the title of divinity is the basis of the rulings concerning their dominion. The prepositional phrase (*al-jar wa al-majrur*) is a fronted predicate (*khabar muqaddam*). "*Mulk al-samawat wa al-ard*" (the dominion of the heavens and the earth) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and the whole clause is the predicate of *inna* (*khabar li-inna*). The choice of this structure over saying "*inna li-Llahi mulk al-samawat wa al-ard*" is intended to strengthen the ruling through the repetition of the predication. This is either a repetition for emphasis (*taqrir*) and a restatement to provide evidence for what was mentioned before. The reason *inna* is not conjoined (*lam yu'taf*) with the *inna* clause that is within its scope, as with similar earlier instances, is to add emphasis and to indicate that knowledge of each of the two matters is independent and sufficient for grasping the intended meaning. Or it is an independent affirmation (*taqrir mustaqill*) serving as evidence for His, exalted is He, power over all things, meaning: "Did you not know that Allah possesses the overpowering authority and the dominating control, which necessitate complete power over the total disposal of them, by bringing into existence, annihilating, commanding and forbidding, as His will requires, with none opposing His command and none reversing His judgment? Whoever has such a status, how could anything escape His power?"

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And you have no protector or helper apart from Allah﴾ is conjoined (*ma'tuf*) to the clause that is the predicate of *inna*, and it falls together with it under the established scope of knowledge. It also contains an indication that the two preceding addresses include the community as well. The reason He singled out the Prophet, peace be upon him, with them is that their knowledge is based on his knowledge, peace be upon him. The placing of the noble Name in the position of the pronoun referring back to the subject of *inna* serves to cultivate awe, and to signal the conjunction of guardianship and support with strength and might. The purpose of this is to cite, as evidence, what is connected to it of knowledge concerning the connection of His, exalted is He, will to what was mentioned of bringing what is better than the abrogated (*al-mansukh*) ruling, or its like. Mere power on His part, exalted is He, over that does not necessitate its actual occurrence at all. What necessitates it is that He, exalted is He, is, along with that, their guardian and helper. Whoever knows that He, exalted is He, is his guardian and helper independently, knows with certainty that He does to him only what is good for him. So he entrusts his affair to Him, exalted is He, and no doubt about the matter of abrogation (*naskh*) or anything else occurs to his mind at all.

The difference between the guardian (*wali*) and the helper (*nasir*) is that the guardian may be weak in giving support, while the helper may be a stranger to the one he supports.

As for *ma*: it is either the *tamimiyya* (the *ma* of the Banu Tamim dialect, a particle that governs nothing), with *lakum* as the fronted predicate and *min waliyy* as the postponed subject, to which the word *min* has been added for generality (*li-l-istighraq*). Or it is the *hijaziyya* (the *ma* of the Hijazi dialect, which operates like *laysa*), with *lakum* as its predicate in the accusative, according to those who permit placing it first, and its subject being *min waliyy*, where *min* is added for the reason mentioned. And *min duni Llah* lies in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of its subject, because originally it was an attribute of it, and when it was fronted it took the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier. Its meaning is "other than Allah."

The meaning is that the requirement of knowledge of the three matters mentioned is certainty and firm conviction that He, exalted is He, does not do to them, in any matter of their religion or their worldly affairs, except what is good for them. Acting upon its implication, through trust in Him, reliance upon Him and entrusting the matter to Him, without listening to the statements of the disbelievers and their doubts, among which is what they said concerning the matter of abrogation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 108:

And His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Or do you desire﴾ is a stripping away of the address from the Prophet (ﷺ) and a restriction of it to the believers. The "am" (or) is disjunctive (munqati'a). The meaning of "bal" (rather) in it is a turning away (idrab) and a transition (intiqal) from urging them to act according to what they know of what was mentioned, when some signs of leniency (makhabil al-musahala) in that matter and indications of being influenced by the words of the disbelievers appeared among them, to warning them against that. The meaning of the interrogative hamza (al-hamza) is a denial that the desire occurred from them, and a judgment that it is unlikely, because the requirement of faith restrains them from it. The denial is directed at the desire rather than at its object, in order to emphasize the denial and the unlikelihood of it, by making clear that it is something that a rational person would not produce, let alone carry out. The meaning is: rather, do you desire ﴿to ask﴾ ﴿your Messenger﴾, while you are believers, and he is at that level of elevated rank, and to propose to him what you desire, not trusting in the grace of Allah (Exalted is He) as your knowledge of His affairs requires? It has been said: perhaps they were asking him (peace be upon him) to explain the details of the wisdoms that call for abrogation (naskh). It has also been said: a group of Muslims asked the Messenger (peace be upon him) to make for them a dhat anwat, as the polytheists had, which is a tree that they used to worship and hang food and drink upon.

And His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿as Moses was asked﴾ is a comparative verbal noun (masdar tashbihi), that is, a qualifier of a deleted emphatic verbal noun. The "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), meaning: a question resembling the question of Moses (peace be upon him), when it was said to him: "Make for us a god," and "Show us Allah openly," and other things. The apparent requirement would be to say: "as they asked Moses," because the thing compared is the verbal noun of the active form, namely the questioning (sa'iliyya) of the addressees, not the verbal noun of the passive form, namely the being questioned (masu'liyya) of the Messenger (ﷺ), so that it could be compared with the being questioned of Moses (peace be upon him). Perhaps the comparison was intended in both together, but the expression was made concise: the questioning is mentioned on the side of the compared, and the being questioned on the side of the thing compared to, each side being satisfied with what is mentioned in it in place of what is omitted in the other, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm, there is none to remove it but He; and if He wills good for you, there is none to repel His bounty﴾. It has also been permitted that "ma" be a relative pronoun (mawsula), with a deleted returning pronoun, meaning: like the question that Moses (peace be upon him) was asked. His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿from before﴾ is connected to "was asked," and it was brought for emphasis. It was also read as "sil" with a kasra on the sin, and with the hamza facilitated between bayn bayn (between hamza and its vowel-sound, i.e., facilitated, bayn bayn).

﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief﴾: that is, chooses it and takes it for himself, ﴿for faith﴾, in exchange for it, as a replacement for it. It was also read as "wa man yubdil," from "abdala." The apparent requirement would be to say: "and whoever does that," that is, the aforementioned questioning, or its desire. Its sum is: whoever abandons confidence in the clear signs sent down, according to the interests of which the abrogating verses are part, which are pure good and unmixed truth, and proposes other than them, ﴿has indeed strayed from the right way﴾: that is, he deviated and went astray, without knowing it, from the straight path that leads to the landmarks of truth and guidance, and wandered in the bewilderment of desire, and fell into the pits of destruction. This wording of the noble composition was preferred over saying "whoever does that becomes a disbeliever" in order to state from the outset that it is disbelief and apostasy, and that its being so is a matter clear enough to need no informative statement, and is worthy of being counted among the established truths, and placed as the antecedent of the conditional, in order to emphasize the severity of the deterrence and the excess of the restraint. The phrase "sawa' al-sabil" (the right way) is of the type of the attribute's annexation to the thing described, for the purpose of emphasizing the strength of the attribution, as if it were the very essence of rightness, following the pattern of the form's occurring in the form that has come about. It has been said: the address is to the Jews, when they asked that Allah (Exalted is He) send down to them a book from heaven. It has also been said: it is to the polytheists, when they said: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾, and so on. The annexation of the Messenger (ﷺ) to them on both views is by considering that they are of the community of the call. The meaning of "the exchange of disbelief for faith while they are far removed from faith" is: abandoning the directing of their capacity toward it, despite their being able to do so, and preferring disbelief over it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 109:**

﴿Many of the People of the Book wish⁠﴾: They were a group of the rabbis (aḥbār) of the Jews. It is narrated that Finḥāṣ ibn ʿĀzūrāʾ, Zayd ibn Qays, and a number of Jews said to Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān and ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, may Allah be pleased with them both, after the Battle of Uhud: "Have you not seen what befell you? Had you been upon the truth, you would not have been defeated. So return to our religion, for it is better and more excellent for you, and we are better guided in the path than you." ʿAmmār said: "How would the breaking of the covenant be among you?" They said: "It is grave." He said: "Then I have covenanted that I will not disbelieve in Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) as long as I live." The Jews said: "As for this one, he has apostatized." Ḥudhayfa said: "As for me, I am content with Allah as Lord, with Muhammad as Prophet, with Islam as religion, with the Qur'an as leader, with the Kaʿba as qibla, and with the believers as brothers." Then the two went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him, and he said: "You have done well and prospered." Then this verse was revealed. ﴿If they could turn you⁠﴾: This is a report of their desire. The particle ﴿لَوْ﴾ (law, "if") here carries the sense of wishing (tamannī). The form of the third person (ghayba) is as in the phrase "he swore he would certainly do it." It is also said that ﴿لَوْ﴾ here has the function of ﴿أنْ﴾ (an, the particle that governs the subjunctive), so it has no answer clause; from it and what follows it a verbal noun (maṣdar) is formed, which functions as the object of ﴿وَدَّ﴾ (wadda, "wished"). The sense is: "They wished your turning back." It is also said that it is in its literal meaning, and its answer clause is omitted, its implied sense being: "If they were to turn you back as disbelievers, they would be delighted by that."

﴿after your belief⁠﴾: (p-146) This is connected to ﴿يَرُدُّونَكُمْ⁠﴾ (yaruddūnakum, "turn you back"). The words ﴿كُفّارًا⁠﴾ (kuffāran, "disbelievers") are the second object (mafʿūl thānin) of it, on the basis of the verb ﴿الرَّدُّ⁠﴾ (al-radd, "turning back") being construed with the sense of ﴿التَّصْيِيرِ⁠﴾ (al-taṣyīr, "making/rendering"), meaning: "they make you disbelievers," as in the verse of the poet:

*Time has struck the women of the family of Saʿd*
*with a decree; they became motionless in its grip.*

*So it turned their black hair white,*
*and turned their white faces black.*

It is also said that ﴿كُفّارًا⁠﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) of its object, but the first view is more suitable, because it explicitly indicates that the disbelief is imposed by way of compulsion. The mention of the adverbial phrase (ẓarf), ﴿مِن بَعْدِ إيمانِكُمْ⁠﴾, even though there is no need for it, since the addressees are believers and it is impossible for a turning back to disbelief to occur without prior faith, and although it is placed between the two objects, serves to show the complete ugliness of what they intended and the extreme remoteness of its occurrence. Either it is to increase its repulsiveness, which diverts the intelligent person from engaging in it, or it is because faith resists it; as if it were said: "after your firm faith." In this there is an affirmation of the believers that is not hidden.

﴿out of envy⁠﴾: This is the cause (ʿilla) of ﴿وَدَّ⁠﴾ (wadda, "wished"); or it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) in which the attribute of the plural is intended, meaning: envious of you. Envy (ḥasad) is grief over one who has good, on account of his good. ﴿from themselves⁠﴾: This is connected to ﴿وَدَّ⁠﴾, meaning: they wished that out of their own desires and personal interests, not out of religious devotion or inclination toward the truth, even if by their own assumption. Or: with envy; that is, envy originating from the root of their souls, reaching its furthest degree.

﴿after the truth has become clear to them⁠﴾: through the manifest miracles, and through the proofs they witnessed in the Torah, and they knew that you hold firmly to it, while they were immersed in falsehood.

﴿so pardon and overlook⁠﴾: Pardon (ʿafw) is leaving off punishment and retribution; overlooking (ṣafḥ) is leaving off reproach and rebuke.

﴿until Allah brings His command⁠﴾: which is the killing of the Banū Qurayẓa, the expulsion of the Banū al-Naḍīr, and their humiliation by imposing the jizya (poll tax) upon them; or the permission for fighting. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is abrogated (mansūkh) by the verse of the sword (āyat al-sayf). The stipulation of a limit does not detract from this, because the limit is known only through revelation, and the ruling conveyed by it does not cease to be an abrogating ruling (nāsikh). It is as if it were said: "Pardon and overlook until the revelation of the abrogating ruling."

﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent⁠﴾: so He will take vengeance upon them when their time comes and their appointed hour arrives. This is an explanation (taʿlīl) of what the preceding part indicates.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 110:

﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾: It is conjoined to "so pardon" (fa-u'fu); they were commanded to be patient, to be forbearing, and to take refuge in God (exalted is He) through bodily worship and worship by wealth; ﴿and whatever good you send forth for yourselves﴾, such as prayer, or charity, or other than that; that is: whatever of the good deeds you send forward for the benefit of your own souls; ﴿you will find it with God﴾, that is: you will find its reward; it has been read as "tuqdimu" (you send forward), from "aqdama"; ﴿indeed God is Seeing of what you do﴾; so no deed is lost in His sight; this is a promise to the believers; and it has been read with the ya' (yaʿmalūna, "they do"), in which case it is a warning to the disbelievers.

﴿And they say﴾: this is coordinated with ﴿wadda﴾ (وَدَّ, "wished"), and the pronoun refers to the People of the Book collectively. ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians.﴾ That is, the Jews said: "None will enter Paradise except Jews," and the Christians said: "None will enter Paradise except Christians." He combined the two statements, trusting that the hearer would attribute each to its own speaker. A similar construction is: ﴿And they say: Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided﴾. By "those" (أُولَئِكَ) they do not mean those who established Judaism and Christianity in their original form before abrogation (al-naskh, "the abrogation of earlier law") and distortion (al-tahrif, "alteration"), but rather themselves, as they are, because they only say this to mislead the believers and return them to disbelief.

"Hud" (هُودًا) is the plural of "hA'id" (هائِدٌ), like "'udh" (عُوذٌ), the plural of "A'idh" (عائِذٌ), and "buzl" (بُزْلٌ), the plural of "bazil" (بازِلٌ). The singular in "kana" (كانَ) is in view of the wording of "man" (مَن), and the plural in its predicate is in view of its meaning. It was also read: "illa man kana yahudiyyan aw nasraniyyan" (إلّا مَن كانَ يَهُودِيًّا أوْ نَصْرانِيًّا).

﴿Those are their wishful thinkings﴾: "amani" (الأمانِيُّ) is the plural of "umniyyah" (أُمْنِيَّةٌ), meaning what is wished for, like "al-u'jubah" (الأُعْجُوبَةُ, "a marvel") and "al-udhukah" (الأُضْحُوكَةُ, "a laughing-stock"). The sentence is parenthetical, clarifying the falsehood of what they said. "Tilka" (تِلْكَ, "those") refers to it, and the plural is in view of its having come from all of them. It has been said that there is an omitted modifier, meaning: the wishes like that wish are their wishes. It has also been said that "tilka" refers both to it and to what precedes it, namely that no good from their Lord should descend upon the believers and that they should return them as disbelievers. This is refuted by His saying (Exalted be He): ﴿Say: Bring your proof, if you are truthful﴾, since these two claims are neither things for which proof is sought nor things that admit of truth and falsehood. It has been said that "hatu" (هاتُوا, "bring") originally was "atu" (آتُوا), with the hamza changed to a ha: that is, produce your argument for your exclusive claim to entry into Paradise, if you are truthful in your assertion. This is what the context requires according to the plain sense. But what the inimitability of the revelation calls for is that the rebuking command be understood as a demand for proof concerning the basic entry itself, which the claim of exclusivity to it implies, for

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 112:

His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Bala﴾ ("Yes indeed"); etc. This is an affirmation from Him (exalted is He) of what they denied, which necessarily entails the negation of what they claimed. Since what is affirmed by it is not merely the entry of others into Paradise, even together with them, such that the negated thing would be merely their exclusivity of it while the basic entry remains as it is; rather it is the exclusivity of others with entry, as you will know, God willing (exalted is He), it becomes clear that what is negated is the very entry of them, and it follows necessarily that this is what they were charged to establish proof for, not their exclusivity of it, so that the object of affirmation and negation is unified. He turned away from refuting what they claimed and took this course only to make clear the extent of their deprivation from what they had set their hopes upon, and to show the completeness of their incapacity to establish their claim. For their deprivation from exclusivity of entry, and their inability to establish proof for it, do not necessitate their deprivation from the basic entry itself, nor their inability to establish it. As for entry itself, since their deprivation from it has been established, and their inability to establish it, they are even further from exclusivity with it, and even more incapable of establishing it. Only the one who attains it is the one encompassed by His saying (glorified is He): ﴿Whoever submits his face to God﴾; i.e., devotes himself sincerely to Him (exalted is He), associating nothing with Him. He expressed it by "face" because it is the most noble of the limbs, the gathering place of the senses, the place of prostration, and the manifest sign of humility, which is among the most distinctive characteristics of sincerity; or [it means] his turning toward Him and his intention, such that he does not turn his resolve toward anything other than Him. ﴿And he is a doer of good﴾: a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of "submits"; i.e., while he is a doer of good in all his deeds, of which submission mentioned is one. The reality of ihsan (excellence): performing the act in the proper manner, which is its descriptive goodness that follows its essential goodness. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained it with his saying: "That you worship God as if you see Him; and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you." ﴿Then for him is his reward﴾; which was promised to him for his deed; and it is an expression for entry into Paradise, or for what he enters initially; and whichever it is, the depiction of it in the form of a reward is to signal the strength of its connection with the deed and the impossibility of attaining it without it. His saying (exalted is He): ﴿with his Lord﴾: a circumstantial clause from "his reward"; the element governing it is the meaning of being settled in the adverbial phrase and of "with-ness", for honor; and placing the name "Lord" with a pronoun referring to "whoever submits" in the position of the pronoun for the Majesty is to show further kindness toward him and to affirm the content of the sentence; i.e., his reward is with his owner, his manager of affairs, and the one who brings him to his perfection. The sentence is the response to "whoever" if it is conditional; and its predicate if it is relative; the "fa" is because it includes the meaning of the condition; so the refutation is by His saying (exalted is He) ﴿Bala﴾ alone. It is also permissible that "man" be the subject of an implied verb; i.e., "Yes, whoever submits enters it"; and His saying (exalted is He): ﴿then for him is his reward﴾ is conjoined to that implied verb. Whichever it is, the attachment of the existence of the reward to what has been mentioned of submission and excellence, which are specific to the people of faith, indicates that those claimants of entry into Paradise are far removed, and infinitely far from exclusivity with it. ﴿And no fear shall be upon them﴾; in either abode; of befalling something disliked; ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾; over the loss of something desired; i.e., there befalls them what necessitates that; not that it befalls them while they still fear and grieve. The plural in the three pronouns is in consideration of the meaning of "whoever," just as the singular in the first pronouns is in consideration of the wording.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 113:

﴿The Jews say: The Christians have nothing [of truth] to stand on.﴾ This states that each group misguides the other specifically, after the statement that each misguides everyone else in general. It was revealed when the delegation of Najran came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the rabbis (ahbar, religious scholars) of the Jews came to them. They debated, their voices rose, and they said to them: "You have nothing [of truth] to stand on," meaning: no matter of religion that is worthy of consideration, or "nothing at all" in the sense of having no basis whatsoever, as an exaggeration, as in the saying: "less than nothing." They also rejected Jesus and the Gospel. ﴿And the Christians say: The Jews have nothing [of truth] to stand on,﴾ in the aforementioned manner, and they rejected Moses and the Torah. [This does not mean] that they made this statement on the basis that the Torah had been abrogated (naskh, abrogation). ﴿And they recite the Scripture.﴾ The waw is for the circumstantial clause (hal), and the lam is for the genus: that is, they said what they said while the situation was that each group among them is among the people of knowledge and of the Book. That is, it was the right of each of them to acknowledge the truth of the other's religion, as their own Scripture declares, for the Books of Allah (exalted is He) confirm one another. ﴿Thus﴾: like that which you have heard. The kaf is in the accusative position, either as an adjective (na't) of a deleted verbal noun (masdar) placed before its governing verb to give restrictive emphasis (qasr), meaning: a statement exactly like that statement, a statement different from it. ﴿Said those who do not know﴾: from among the idol-worshippers, the mu'attilah (those who deny the divine attributes), and similar ignorant people. That is, they said to the adherents of every religion: "They have nothing [of truth] to stand on." Or the kaf may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the implied, definite verbal noun indicated by "said," meaning: those who know said the statement while being in the condition of being like that statement which you have heard. ﴿Like their statement﴾: either a substitute (badal) for the position of the kaf, or an object of the negated verb preceding it, meaning: like that statement was said by the ignorant, in the same manner as the statement of the Jews and the Christians. This is a severe rebuke of them, since they placed themselves, despite their knowledge, in the same category as those who have no knowledge at all. ﴿So Allah will judge between them﴾: that is, between the Jews and the Christians, for the thrust of the wording is to explain their condition. The mention of the statement of others is only to demonstrate the complete falsity of their own statement, and because the dispute requiring a judgment occurred between them. ﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾: this is connected to "will judge," and likewise what precedes and what follows it; there is no harm in this, since the meanings differ. ﴿Concerning that in which they used to differ﴾: by apportioning to each group the punishment that befits it. It has also been said: His judgment between them is that He will refute them and cause them to enter the Fire. The final adverbial phrase is connected to "they used to differ," and it was placed before it to preserve the rhyme of the verse endings (ru'us al-ay), and not connected to "used to be."

(p-149) ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah﴾: This is a denial and a deeming of it improbable that anyone could be more unjust than one who does such a thing, or equal to him. Although the structure of the expression does not explicitly address the denial of equality, its negation is attested by common usage and consistent practice. Thus, when one says, "Who is more generous than so-and-so?!" or "None is more excellent than so-and-so," what is definitively meant is that he is more generous than every generous person and more excellent than every excellent person. This ruling is general for everyone who does this, in whatever mosque it may be, even if the occasion of revelation was the action of a specific group in a specific mosque. It is narrated that the Christians used to throw filth into Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and prevent people from praying therein, and that the Romans invaded its people, destroyed it, burned the Torah, and killed and took captives. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Titus the Roman, king of the Christians, and his companions invaded the Children of Israel, killed their combatants, took their offspring captive, burned the Torah, destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis, cast carrion into it, and slaughtered swine in it; and it remained in ruin until the Muslims rebuilt it in the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. The prevention is attributed to the mosques, although the ones prevented were the people, because their act of casting filth, destruction, and the like relates to the mosque and not to the people, while the mosque remains in its state. The connection of this noble verse with what precedes it is that it refutes the claim of the Christians to exclusive entry into Paradise. It is also said that it refers to the polytheists preventing the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from entering the Sacred Mosque in the year of al-Hudaybiyah; its connection to what precedes it is that the polytheists are among the ignorant who say to everyone else: "They are not upon anything."

﴿that Allah's name be mentioned therein﴾: The second object of "prevented" (manaʿa); as in His saying (exalted is He): "And what prevented the people from believing..." and His saying (exalted is He): "And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them." It is also permissible that this be with the preposition elided along with "an" (that), and that it be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: "lest His name be mentioned therein."

﴿and strove for their ruin﴾: by demolishing them, or by rendering them desolate through the cessation of remembrance.

﴿Those﴾: the preventers, the wrongdoers, the ones striving for their ruin.

﴿It was not for them to enter them except in fear﴾: that is, it was not fitting for them to enter them except in awe and humility, let alone to dare to destroy or render them desolate. Or: it was not right for them to enter them except in a state of reverence and trembling, out of fear that the believers might seize them, let alone that they would gain control over them, govern them, and prevent the believers from them. Or: in the knowledge of Allah (exalted is He) and His decree concerning the Hereafter, it was not for them except this; so it is a promise to the believers of victory and of recovering what was seized from them. The promise has been fulfilled, and to Allah belongs all praise. It is narrated that no Christian enters Bayt al-Maqdis except disguised, stealthily. It is also said that its meaning is a prohibition against enabling them to enter the mosque. The scholars differed on this: Abu Hanifa permitted it absolutely, Malik prohibited it absolutely, and al-Shafi'i distinguished between the Sacred Mosque and others.

﴿For them﴾: that is, for those mentioned.

﴿in this world is disgrace﴾: that is, a grievous disgrace, beyond description, by killing, captivity, and humiliation through the imposition of the jizyah upon them.

﴿and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾: and this is the punishment of the Fire, since its cause, also—namely, the wrongdoing that has been related—is likewise great. The fronting of the adverbial phrase in both places serves to create anticipation for what is mentioned after it, of disgrace and punishment, since delaying what should rightly come first causes the soul to turn toward it, so that it settles most firmly upon its arrival, as in His saying (exalted is He): "Did We not expand for you your breast?" and "And He sent down for you of the cattle eight pairs," and other such instances.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 115:

﴿And to Allah belong the east and the west﴾; that is, to Him belongs the whole earth, which is referred to by the two directions of east and west. He is not restricted to it in terms of ownership and disposal, nor in terms of place: there is no particular spot in it for His worship rather than another. So if you are prevented from establishing worship in the Masjid al-Aqsa or the Masjid al-Haram, ﴿then wherever you turn﴾; that is, wherever you direct your faces toward the qibla, ﴿there is the Face of Allah﴾. "Thamma" (there) is a demonstrative noun for a distant place only; it is indeclinable, built on the fatha, and does not vary in form except for the genitive with "min" (from). It is a predicate preceding its subject, and "Face of Allah" is the subject. The clause is in the position of a jussive (jazm), as the response of the conditional; that is: there is His direction which He has commanded. For the possibility of turning is not restricted to one mosque rather than another, or one place rather than another. Or it means "there is His Essence," in the sense of knowledge-presence; that is, He knows what is done therein and rewards you for it. It was also read with the taa and the lam vowelled with fatha (tawallu), meaning: wherever they face the qibla. ﴿Indeed Allah is All-Encompassing﴾; by His encompassing of things, or by His mercy, He intends to give ease to His servants; ﴿All-Knowing﴾; of their interests and their deeds in all places. The clause is a justification of the content of the conditional sentence. It is related from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it was revealed concerning the prayer of travellers on their mounts: wherever they turn. It was also said: it was revealed concerning a people for whom the qibla was obscured, so they prayed facing various directions, and when morning came they realised their error. On this basis, if a mujtahid errs and then the error becomes clear to him, he is not obliged to make up the prayer. It was also said: this verse is a preparation for the abrogation of the qibla, and a declaration that the Worshipped is exalted above being in a direction.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 116:

﴿And they say, "God has taken a son."﴾ This is a report of another part of their false statements mentioned earlier. It is conjoined to what precedes it in His words (exalted is He): ﴿And they said﴾, etc. It is not conjoined to the relative pronoun "man" (those who), because of the many unrelated sentences between them. The pronoun refers to the Jews, the Christians, and those who share their views among those who do not know. It is also read without the conjunction "wa" (and), in which case it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new sentence that begins a fresh statement). It was revealed when the Jews said, "'Uzayr is the son of God," the Christians said, "The Messiah (al-Masih) is the son of God," and the idolaters of the Arabs said, "The angels are the daughters of God."

The verb "ittakhadha" (to take) may mean either "to make" or "to do", in which case it takes only one object. Or it may mean "to make into" (tasyir), in which case the first object is omitted, meaning: He made some of His creatures a son.

﴿Glory be to Him﴾: this is a declaration of His transcendence and a clearing of Him (exalted is He) from what they say. "Subhan" is a proper noun used for the act of glorifying, like "Uthman" as a man's name. Its position is that of a verbal noun (masdar, a noun derived from the verb expressing the action), and its governing verb is rarely mentioned. That is, "I glorify Him" (usabbihu subhanahu), meaning: I declare Him transcendent in a manner fitting to Him. In it there is an eloquent expression of transcendence in terms of its derivation from "al-sabh", which is going away and distancing in the land; in terms of its transfer to the pattern "taf'il"; in terms of the shift from the verbal noun to a noun reserved for this specific meaning, especially a proper noun pointing to a present reality in the mind; and in terms of its use in place of the verbal noun together with the verb, which is obvious. It has also been said that it is a verbal noun like "ghufran" (forgiveness), with the meaning of "tanazzuh" (transcendence), that is: He is transcendent in His essence in a manner worthy of Him. In this there is emphasis, in that the disavowal is attributed to the holy essence. Although tanzih (declaring transcendence) is the belief in His purity from what does not befit Him, not the affirmation of anything for Him (exalted is He).

﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾: this is a refutation of what they claimed and an alert to its falsehood. The word "bal" (rather) is used for a transition (idrab) away from what their false statement implies, namely His (glorified and exalted is He) being of the same kind as any of the created things, and His swift perishing, which would necessitate taking something to stand in His place. The mere possibility of existence and perishing does not necessitate this. Do you not see that the celestial bodies, despite their possibility and their eventual perishing, are free from what resembles offspring among living beings, by virtue of their continuance and long duration? That is: the matter is not as they claim. Rather, He is the Creator of all existing things, among which are 'Uzayr, the Messiah, and the angels.

﴿All﴾: the tanwin (nunation) here is a substitute for the omitted genitive, meaning: all that is in them, whatever it may be, of those endowed with reason and others, ﴿are devoutly obedient to Him﴾: submissive, not resisting in any respect His creating, His determining, or His will. Whoever is in this state cannot be conceived of as being of the same kind as anything. A son must be of the same kind as the father. The word "ma" (what), which is specific to things other than rational beings, is used to belittle their status and to indicate the complete distance of Him from what they attributed to some of them.

The plural form for the rational ones in "qanitun" (devoutly obedient) is used by way of predominance (taghlib, giving precedence to the rational when mixed with others). Or the meaning is: everyone whom they made a son of God is devoutly obedient to Him, that is: obedient to Him, worshipping Him, acknowledging His lordship (exalted is He), like His words (exalted is He): ﴿Those whom they call upon seek means of access to their Lord﴾.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 117:**

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾: That is, the one who brings them into being (*mubdi'uhuma*), and who creates them (*mukhtari'uhuma*) without a model to imitate or a rule to follow. For *badi'* (originator, from *bada'a*), as it is applied to the one who innovates (*mubtadi'*), is also applied to the one who originates (*mubdi'*). This is affirmed by the pillars of the lexicographers (*asatin ahl al-lugha*). It has also come as *bada'ahu*, like *mana'ahu*, meaning "he brought it into being," like *ibtada'ahu*, as is mentioned in the *al-Qamus* and elsewhere. A parallel to this is *al-sami'* (the hearing), meaning *al-musmi'* (the one who makes hear), in the words of the poet:

*Does Rayhana's caller, the one who makes hear, [...]*

It is also said that it is an attributive adjective (*sifa mushabbaha*, a descriptive form resembling the active participle) in which the noun is put in the genitive to its agent for lightness, after being put in the accusative by likening it to the active participle, as is well known. That is: the originator of its heavens, from *bada'a*, when something is of an exceptional form and a refined beauty. This is another argument for refuting their hideous claim. Its explanation is that the father is the origin of the child, who is affected by the separation of his matter from him, whereas Allah, glory be to Him, is the originator of all things absolutely, exalted above being affected, so He cannot be a father. It is read in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: He is the originator... etc. It is also read in the accusative, as praise, and in the genitive, as a substitution (*badal*, apposition) for the pronoun in *lahu* ("for Him"), according to the view of those who permit substitution from the genitive pronoun, as in the words of the poet:

*Over his generosity, Hatim would be stingy with water [...]*

﴿And when He decrees a matter﴾: That is, He wills something, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿His command, when He wills a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ The original meaning of *al-qada'* is "decreeing" or "making firm." It is applied to the divine will related to the existence of a thing, because it necessarily brings that thing into being. It is also said that *al-qada'* means "command." From this is His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾, etc.

﴿then He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾: Both *kun* and *yakun* are from *al-kawn al-tamm* (complete existence, existence in the full sense), meaning: "Come into being," and it comes into being. The intended meaning is not the literal command and obedience. Rather, it is an illustration of how easily the things decreed are brought about, according to the connection of His will (exalted is He), and a depiction of how quickly they come into being, through what is well known in this domain: the obedience of one who is commanded to the commander who is obeyed. This contains an affirmation of the meaning of origination (*ibda'*) and an allusion to another argument for refuting what they claimed: taking a child is the affair of one who, in achieving his aim, depends on preliminary stages whose arrangement requires the passage of time and the change of states, whereas the action of Allah (exalted is He) is far above that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 118:

﴿And those who do not know said﴾: This is a narration of another kind of their ugly conduct, namely their disparagement of the matter of prophethood, after the narration of their disparagement concerning the matter of tawhid (divine oneness) by attributing a son to Him, glorified and exalted is He. Scholars differed regarding these speakers. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: they are the Jews. Mujahid said: they are the Christians. Describing them as "those who do not know" is either because of their lack of proper knowledge of tawhid and prophethood, as it should be; or because of their lack of knowledge of the implications of their own deeds; or because what is attributed to them does not proceed from one who has any trace of knowledge at all. Qatadah and the majority of the people of tafsir (exegesis) said: they are the polytheists of the Arabs, based on His saying (exalted is He): ﴿So let him bring us a sign as the earlier ones were sent﴾; and they said: ﴿Why does not Allah speak to us, or a sign come to us, or we see our Lord?﴾ [cf. 6:124, 25:21]

﴿Why does Allah not speak to us?﴾: that is, why would He not speak to us directly, commanding or forbidding, as He speaks to the angels? Or: why would He not speak to us, specifying your prophethood? ﴿Or a sign come to us﴾: a proof that shows your truthfulness. They reached such a degree of arrogance and haughtiness that they hoped to attain the rank of direct divine address without the mediation of the Messenger, peace be upon him, or of an angel; and such a degree of obstinacy and stubbornness that they did not count as signs the manifest clear proofs which the solid mountains would crumble before, which Allah has given them. May Allah fight them; how are they deluded?

﴿Likewise﴾: like that shameful saying, arising from obstinacy and corruption. ﴿Said those who came before them﴾: from the past nations, ﴿the like of their saying﴾: this false and shameful claim. So they said: ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾; and they said: ﴿We will not be patient with one kind of food﴾, the verse...; and they said: ﴿Can your Lord do it?﴾, etc.; and they said: ﴿Make for us a god﴾, etc.

﴿Their hearts are alike﴾: that is, the hearts of these and those are alike in blindness and obstinacy; otherwise their false sayings would not be alike. ﴿We have made the signs clear﴾: that is, We revealed them as clear, by making them so in themselves, as in the saying: "Glory be to Him who made the gnat small and the elephant large"; not that We made them clear after they were not clear. ﴿For a people who are certain﴾: that is, who seek certainty and are certain of realities, to whom no doubt or suspicion occurs. This is a rejection of their demand for a sign. In the definiteness of "the signs," in their plurality, and in the use of "made clear," which reveals the perfection of explanation, in place of "come," which they demanded, there is a manifest eloquence. The meaning is that they proposed a single unique sign, while We have made clear the great signs for a people who seek the truth and certainty. The reason their saying ﴿Why does Allah not speak to us?﴾ is not addressed is an indication that its falsehood is so evident that it needs no refutation or answer.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 119:

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾: i.e., accompanied by the Qur'an; as in His (Exalted) saying: ﴿They denied the truth when it came to them﴾; or "with truthfulness"; as in His (Exalted) saying: ﴿Is it true?﴾. His (Exalted) saying: ﴿as a bringer of glad tidings and a warner﴾: is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the object (mafʿul), considering that it is restricted by the first circumstantial clause; i.e., We have sent you accompanied by the Qur'an, being a bringer of glad tidings to those who believe in what has been revealed to you and act upon it, and a warner to those who disbelieve in it; or: We have sent you truthfully, being a bringer of glad tidings to those who affirm you with reward, and a warner to those who deny you with punishment; so that they may choose for themselves what they love, there being no compeller for them to faith. So you are not to blame if they persist and act arrogantly. ﴿And you will not be asked about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾: What is the matter with them that they did not believe after you had conveyed what you were sent with? It has also been read as "You will not be asked" (lan tus'al) and "You are not asked" (ma tus'al); and it has been read as "Do not ask" (la tas'al), in the prohibitive form; signifying the complete severity of the punishment of the disbelievers and magnifying it; as if, due to its extreme horror, the one who reports it cannot utter it with his tongue, or the listener cannot bear to hear its report. Interpreting it as the Prophet ﷺ being forbidden from asking about the state of his parents is supported by the noble composition. "Al-Jahim" (the Blazing Fire): the fiercely kindled part of the fire. In describing them as companions of the Blazing Fire, rather than by disbelief, denial, or the like, there is a severe threat against them and an indication that they are sealed upon, such that faith is definitively not to be expected from them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 120:

His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And the Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion﴾: it is an explanation of the utmost severity of obstinacy of these two groups in particular, following the explanation of what encompasses both of them and the polytheists, namely their persistence in what they are upon until death. The placing of the negative particle "lan" (no) between the two conjoined elements serves to emphasize the negation, due to what has passed, that the obstinacy of the Jews in matters of this magnitude is greater than that of the Christians, and to indicate that the pleasure of each of them is contrary to the pleasure of the other. That is: the Jews will never be pleased with you, even if you leave them to themselves, until you follow their religion; nor the Christians, even if you leave them and their religion, until you follow their religion. The structure has therefore been abbreviated, relying on the clarity of the intended meaning. In this there is such exaggeration in despairing him, peace and blessings be upon him, of their acceptance of Islam that there is no beyond it. For when they were not pleased with him, peace and blessings be upon him, even if he left them to do what they do, but rather they desired from him, peace and blessings be upon him, what can hardly fall within the realm of possibility, namely that he follow their religion, how then could one imagine that they would follow his religion, peace and blessings be upon him, when this is their state within themselves and this is their speech among themselves? As for their having displayed this to the Prophet ﷺ and having said it to him directly, saying, "We will never be pleased with you, even if you strive to seek our pleasure, until you follow our religion," as has been said, the noble composition does not support this; rather it contains what indicates the contrary. For His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the guidance﴾ is explicit that what occurred as a response to this was not the very same expression, but rather what entails its content, or what follows from it of calling to Judaism and Christianity, and claiming that guidance lies in them, like His saying, mighty and majestic is He, quoting them: ﴿Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided﴾. That is: Say, in rejection of them: Indeed, the guidance of Allah, which is Islam, is the guidance in truth, and what truly and rightly may be called guidance; and it is the whole of guidance, with nothing beyond it as guidance; and what you call to is not guidance, but rather desire, as His saying (exalted is He) indicates: ﴿And if you followed their desires﴾; that is, their deviant opinions, issuing from them by the dictate of their own appetites; and these are what was referred to earlier as "their religion," since these are what they adhere to. As for the Sharia that Allah (exalted is He) prescribed for them through the tongues of the prophets, peace be upon them, which is the true meaning of religion, they have altered it with a great alteration; ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾; that is, the revelation, or: the religion whose soundness is known; ﴿you would have from Allah﴾: from His mighty side; ﴿no protector﴾ who would take charge of your affairs in general; ﴿nor any helper﴾ who would ward off His punishment from you. And since the negation of a protector does not necessarily entail the negation of a helper, "lan" has been placed between the two conjoined elements to emphasize the negation. This is the mode of stirring up and kindling; otherwise, how could it be imagined that he, peace and blessings be upon him, could follow their religion? And this is the answer to the oath, which is introduced by the lam, and the answer to the conditional is dispensed with by it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 121:

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾; they are the believers among the People of the Book, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and their like; ﴿who recite it as it should be recited﴾; by observing its wording against distortion (taḥrif), by reflecting upon its meanings, and by acting upon what is in it. This is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddarah), and the predicate is what follows it; or it is a predicate, and what follows it confirms it. ﴿Those﴾: a demonstrative referring to those described as having been given the Book and as reciting it as is its due. The sense of distance contained in it serves to indicate the remoteness of their rank in excellence. ﴿They believe in it﴾; that is, in their Book, unlike the distorters, for they are far removed from belief in it, since belief does not coexist with disbelief in part of it. ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it﴾; by distorting it and by disbelieving in what confirms it; ﴿those are the losers﴾; since they have exchanged disbelief for belief.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 122:

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you﴾; among its components is the Torah. Remembrance of a favor is only (p-154) fulfilled through giving thanks for it, and giving thanks for it is faith in all that is in it; among what is in it is the description of the Prophet ﷺ, and it is a necessity of faith in it to have faith in him, peace and blessings be upon him. ﴿And that I preferred you over the worlds﴾; this favor is singled out for mention, although it is included under the previous favor, because of its excellence among the various kinds of favors.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 123:**

﴿And fear﴾; if you do not believe; ﴿a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all﴾; on that Day; ﴿no soul﴾; of souls; ﴿[will avail] for another soul﴾; [i.e., will suffice for it]; ﴿anything﴾; of things; or anything of recompense; ﴿nor will any compensation be accepted from it﴾; i.e., ransom (fidya); ﴿nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped﴾. Their being singled out by repeating the reminder and restating the warning is for the sake of intensifying counsel, and to signal that this is the conclusion (fadhlaka) of the matter and the purpose of the narrative; because the blessings of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, upon them are greater, and their disbelief in them is more severe and more ugly.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 124:

﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain words﴾: This begins the demonstration that the guidance of God is what the Prophet ﷺ holds to, namely monotheism (tawhid) and submission (Islam), which is the creed (millah) of Abraham, peace be upon him. It also shows that what the People of the Two Books hold are deviant desires, and that their claim to be upon his creed, peace be upon him, is an undoubted falsehood. This is shown by mentioning what was said and done by Abraham and his sons, the prophets, peace be upon them, in words and deeds that affirm the truth of monotheism and Islam, the falsity of polytheism (shirk), the validity of the Prophet's ﷺ prophethood, and that he is the very Prophet whom Abraham and Ishmael, peace be upon them both, asked for, by their saying: ﴿Our Lord, and raise up among them a messenger from among them﴾, and so on.

So "idh" (when) is in the accusative as an object of an implied verb placed earlier, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ by way of changing the mode of address (al-talwin). The meaning is: "Recount to them the time of his testing, peace be upon him, so that they may remember the matters that befell him which call to monotheism and restrain from polytheism, and so accept the truth and abandon the falsehood they are in." Directing the command of remembrance to the time, rather than to the events that occurred in it, although the events are the primary intent, has already been explained in the course of the commentary on His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I am going to place a successor on earth"﴾.

It has also been said that it is in the position of an adverb (zarfiyya), governed by an implied verb placed later, meaning: "And when He tested him, such and such occurred." And it has been said that it is governed by what will come later in His words, Exalted: "He said" etc. The first view is the one more fitting to the eloquence of the revelation. It is not far-fetched that it is governed by an implied verb coordinated with "remember" (udhkuru), addressed to the Children of Israel, so that they may reflect on what is related about those who claim the creed of Abraham and his sons, peace be upon them, of acts and sayings, and so follow them and walk in their path.

Ibtila' (testing), in origin, means examination (ikhtibar), that is, seeking knowledge of the state of the one tested by placing him before a matter that is generally difficult for him to do or to leave undone. This is truly conceivable only from one who does not know the outcomes of affairs. As for the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, it occurs only figuratively, through His granting the servant the power to choose one of two matters before He orders anything from among its ordinary beginnings, like one who tests his servant to learn his state of discernment, and then commands him with what befits his condition in terms of his interests.

"Ibrahim" (Abraham) is a non-Arabic name. Al-Suhayli said: "Often there occurs agreement, or closeness, between Syriac and Arabic. Do you not see that 'Ibrahim' is interpreted as 'a merciful father'? For this reason he and his wife Sarah were made guardians of the children of the believers who die young, until the Day of Resurrection, according to what al-Bukhari related in the hadith of the dream: 'That the Prophet ﷺ saw in the garden Abraham, peace be upon him, and around him were the children of people.'" It is a fronted object (maf'ul muqaddam) because its doer is attached to its pronoun.

Mentioning the title of Lordship (rububiyya) is an honour for him, peace be upon him, and an indication that this testing was a training for him and a preparation for a weighty matter. The meaning: He, glory be to Him, treated him as one who is tested, by assigning him commands and prohibitions through which it becomes evident, by his good performance of their duties, that he is capable of fulfilling the great office of imamate and bearing the burdens of messengership. This treatment, and its mention to people, is for guiding them to the way of perfecting affairs by basing them on trial, and to indicate that the sending of the Prophet ﷺ is also founded upon that firm principle, and occurs after the manifestation of his worthiness, peace be upon him, for general prophethood. How could it not be so, since it is the one by which the supplication of Abraham, peace be upon him, was answered, as will come. The words (al-kalimat) have been differed about. Mujahid said: they are what is mentioned after them. This is refuted, because the fa' in "so he completed them" prevents it, and also the resumption. Tawus said, from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: they are ten characteristics which were obligatory in his law and are sunna in our law: five in the head: rinsing the mouth, sniffing water into the nose, parting the hair, trimming the moustache, and the siwak; and five in the body: circumcision, shaving the pubic area, plucking the armpit hair, clipping the nails, and cleansing with water after defecation. In a report it is said that Abraham, peace be upon him, was the first to trim the moustache, the first to be circumcised, and the first to clip the nails.

'Ikrima said, from Ibn 'Abbas: No one was tested with this religion and then established all of it except Abraham. God, Exalted, tested him with thirty characteristics of Islam: ten of them are in Surat Bara'a: ﴿The repentant﴾, etc.; ten in Surat al-Ahzab: ﴿Indeed the Muslim men and Muslim women﴾, etc.; and ten in Surat al-Mu'minun: "A questioner asked", up to His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And those who are attentive to their prayers﴾.

It has also been said: God, glory be to Him, tested him with seven things: with the sun, the moon, and the stars; with circumcision in old age; with the fire; with the slaughter of the son; and with the migration; and he fulfilled them all. It has been said that they are his disputation with his people; prayer; zakat; fasting; hospitality, and patience upon them. It has been said that they are rites, such as the tawaf, the sa'y, the stoning, the ihram, the standing at 'Arafat, and other things. It has been said that they are his, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿He who created me, it is He who guides me﴾, and the verses that follow.

Then it has been said: this testing occurred before prophethood, and this is the apparent view. It has been said: after it, because it implies a prior revelation. It was answered that unrestricted revelation does not entail sending to the creation.

It was also read with the nominative for "Ibrahim" and the accusative for "Rabbuhu" (his Lord), meaning: He (his Lord) called him by words of supplication, as one who tests, to see whether he would answer them or not. ﴿So he completed them﴾: that is, he upheld them with the due upholding, and performed them in the finest manner, without neglect or laxity, as in His words, Exalted: ﴿And Abraham, who fulfilled [his covenant]﴾. According to the last reading: God, Exalted, gave him what he asked without any deficiency. This is supported by what is related from Muqatil that he interpreted the words as what Abraham asked of his Lord in saying: ﴿My Lord, make [this city secure]﴾, up to the verses.

As for His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿He said﴾: on the assumption that "idh" is governed by an implied verb, this is a resumptive sentence (jumla musta'anifa) which comes as an answer to a question arising from the discourse. For the testing is a preparation for a great matter, and the manifestation of the tested one's excellence is among the motives for bestowing kindness upon him. So after their narration the soul looks forward to what came after them, as if it were said: "What happened after that?" So it is said: ﴿He said, "Indeed I will make you an imam for the people"﴾. Or it is an explanation of His words, "tested" (ibtala), according to the view of one who takes the words as an expression of what its effect has been mentioned, namely the imamate, the purification of the House, the raising of its foundations, and other things. And on the assumption that "idh" is governed by "said" (qala), the sentence is coordinated with what precedes it, a narrative joined to a narrative, and the waw in meaning enters on "said", meaning: "And he said, 'He tested'..." etc.

"Ja'l" (making) here means "appointing"; its first object is the pronoun (ka, "you"), and the second is "imaman" (an imam). The active participle (ism al-fa'il) here has the sense of the present tense, and is more emphatic than it, because it indicates that He is indeed making it for him, definitively, without any diverting obstacle or any turning aside. "Lil-nas" (for the people) is connected to "ja'iluka" (making you), meaning: for the sake of the people; or it is connected to an omitted element that falls as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "imaman", for if it were placed after it, it would be a qualifier of it. "Imam" is a noun for one who is followed, and every prophet is an imam for his community. His imamate, peace be upon him, is general and perpetual, since no prophet was sent after him except that he was of his offspring, commanded to follow his creed.

"Qala" (he said): a resumptive sentence based on an implied question, as if it were said: "What did Abraham, peace be upon him, say in response?" So it is said: ﴿He said, "And of my offspring"﴾: it is coordinated with the kaf (you); and "min" (of) is partitive, connected to "ja'il" (making), meaning: "And [will you make] a part of my offspring [imams]?" Like saying, when someone says, "I will honour you": "And Zayd?" Or it is connected to an omitted element, meaning: "And make a group of my offspring imams." The restriction of the imamate to a part is because it is obvious that the imamate of all of them is impossible, even if they are upon the truth. It has been said that the estimate is: "And what will be of my offspring?" "Dhurriyya" (offspring) is the progeny of a man; it is of the pattern fu'ula, from dharawtu or dharaytu, and the origin is dhuruwwa or dhurriyya. Two waws gathered in the first: one additional and one original, so the original was changed to a ya', and it became like the second; so a waw and a ya' gathered, and one of them was preceded by sukun, so the waw was changed to a ya', and the ya' was assimilated into the ya', and it became dhurriyya. Or it is fi'ayla from both; the origin of the first is dhuraywa, and the waw was changed to a ya' for the reason mentioned, from the gathering of the two and the preceding of one by sukun; so it became dhurriyya like the second, and the ya' was assimilated into its like, and it became dhurriyya. Or it is fi'ila from dhar'  (creating), meaning creation; the origin is dhir'iyya, and the hamza was lightened by changing it to a ya', like the hamza of khati'a (error), then the additional ya' was assimilated into the changed one. Or it is fi'ila from al-dharr (scattering), meaning dispersal; the origin is dhirrira, the last ra' was changed to a ya' to avoid the succession of like letters, as in tasarri, taqaddi, and tazanni, then the ya' was assimilated into the ya', as already mentioned. Or it is fu'ula from it, the origin being dharurra; the last ra' was changed to a ya', and assimilation came about. It was read also with a kasra on the dhal, which is a dialect form of it, and Abu Ja'far al-Madani read it with a fatha, which is also a dialect form of it.

"Qala" (He said): a resumptive sentence based on an implied question that the mind is led to, as already mentioned. ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾: this is not a rejection of his supplication, peace be upon him, but a hidden answer to it, and a general promise from Him, Exalted, to honour some of his offspring, peace be upon him, by attaining the covenant of imamate, in accordance with his, peace be upon him, request, without specifying for them any descriptive attribute distinguishing them from all others. For the explicit statement that the wrongdoers are deprived of it has no bearing on that distinction, since its meaning is not that it reaches everyone among them who is not a wrongdoer, because that is impossible, as has been pointed out. Perhaps the choice of this method over specifying in general or in detail those who combine the principles of imamate among his offspring, and leaving the rest, is so that the followers among the imams of the community will not be counted among those deprived. In detailing each group there is prolixity that is not hidden. Moreover, in this method there is a disappointment of the disbelievers who used to wish for prophethood, and a cutting off of their empty hopes of attaining it. The verb "attain" (nal) was preferred over "make" (ja'l) as an indication that the imamate of the prophets, peace be upon them, from his offspring, peace be upon him, such as Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Aaron, David, Solomon, Job, Jonah, Zechariah, John, Jesus, and our master Muhammad, may abundant peace be upon him, is not an independent appointment, but is attained within the imamate of Abraham, peace be upon him, reaching each of them at a time God, Mighty and Majestic, has decreed.

It was read "al-zalimun" (the wrongdoers, nominative), on the basis that "my covenant" is an object placed before the subject out of concern and for the sake of the rhyme (fawasil). In it is evidence for the infallibility of the prophets, peace be upon them, from major sins absolutely, and that a wrongdoer is not fit for the imamate.

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We made the House﴾: that is, the honoured Ka'bah, which became preeminent over it as a star is preeminent over the Pleiades. It is coordinated with "when He tried" (idh ibtala), on the basis that its governing element (al-'amil) is the same governing element; or it is an independent implied verb, coordinated with the first implied verb. And "made" (al-ja'l) is either in the sense of "rendered" (al-tasyir), in which case His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿a place of return (mathaba)﴾, meaning a place to which visitors return after they have dispersed from it, or their likes, or a place of reward where they are rewarded for their pilgrimage and visit (i'timar), is its second object. Or it is in the sense of "originating" (al-ibda'), in which case mathaba is a circumstantial clause (hal) of its object. The preposition lam in His saying, the Exalted, ﴿for the people﴾, is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of "mathaba", meaning: existing for the people; or it is connected to "We made", meaning: We made it for the sake of the people. It is also read as "mathabat" (places of return), in view of the multiplicity of those who return. ﴿And a sanctuary (amnan)﴾: that is, secure, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a sanctuary secure (haraman aminan)﴾, with the verbal noun placed in the position of the active participle for emphasis; or with an omitted noun (al-mudaf), meaning possessing security; or by metaphorical attribution, meaning secure from the punishment of the Hereafter is whoever performs the pilgrimage to it, inasmuch as the pilgrimage wipes out what came before it; or: whoever enters it is secure from being subjected to punishment, even if he is a criminal, until he leaves, according to the opinion of Abu Hanifah. It is also permissible to consider security in relation to everything whatsoever, and the security of people enters it primarily. Security of game animals is also customary within it, to the extent that a dog would intend to hunt outside the sanctuary, then flee from it while it pursues him; but when game enters the sanctuary, the dog does not pursue it.

﴿And take, from the station of Ibrahim, a place of prayer﴾: on the basis that a saying is intended; it is coordinated with "We made", or it is a circumstantial clause of its subject, meaning: "and We said" or "saying to them: take..." etc. It has been said: it is itself coordinated with the command implied in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a place of return for the people﴾, as if it were said: "return to it, and take..." etc. It has been said: it is coordinated with the implied element that governs "idh". It has also been said: it is a resumptive independent sentence, and the address in the last of these views is to him (peace be upon him) and to his community. The first is the most fitting to the eloquence of the noble composition. The command, whether explicit or understood from the narration, is for recommendation (istihbab). The "min" (from) is partitive (tab'idiyyah). "Maqam" is a noun of place; it is the stone upon which is the trace of his foot, peace be upon him, and the place where he stood and called the people to the pilgrimage, or when he raised the foundations of the House; and it is his place today. The intended meaning of "musalla" is either the place of prayer or the place of supplication. It is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) took the hand of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "This is the Station of Ibrahim." So 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Shall we not take it as a place of prayer?" He said: "I have not been commanded to that." Then the sun had not set until it was revealed. It has also been said that what is intended by it is the command to the two rak'ahs of the circumambulation (tawaf), for what Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, related: that when he (peace be upon him) finished his circumambulation, he went deliberately to the Station of Ibrahim and prayed two rak'ahs behind it, and recited: ﴿And take, from the station of Ibrahim, a place of prayer﴾. For al-Shafi'i there are two opinions regarding their obligation. It has also been said: the Station of Ibrahim is the entire sanctuary. It has also been said: the places of the pilgrimage are 'Arafah, Muzdalifah and the jimar; and taking them as a place of prayer means that one supplicates in them and draws near to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. It is also read as "wa-attakhadha" (and the people took), in the past tense, coordinated with "We made", meaning: "and the people took, from the place of Ibrahim, by which he was marked because of his concern for it and for settling his offspring beside it, a qibla to which they pray."

﴿And We charged Ibrahim and Isma'il﴾: that is, We commanded them with an emphatic command; ﴿that purify My House﴾: by their purifying it. This is on the basis that the verbal "an" has had its preposition omitted in a regular manner, because its relative clause may be a command or prohibition, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and that you set your face toward the religion, upright﴾; because the basis for its being a verb is only its indicating the verbal noun, and that is established in both. The obligation that it be declarative in the relative clause of the substantive relative pronoun is only for reaching the qualification of definite nouns by sentences; and these are only qualified by it when they are declarative. As for the particle relative, it is not so. And since declarative and imperative are equal in indicating the verbal noun, it is permissible for command and prohibition to occur as relative clauses, according to the occurrence of the verb; thus it is stripped at that point of the meaning of command and prohibition, similar to the stripping of the verbal relative clause of the meaning of past and future. Or: that is, purify it; on the basis that "an" is explanatory, because the covenant includes the meaning of saying. The attribution of "House" to the Name of Majesty is for honour. Directing the command to purify here to these two, peace be upon them, does not contradict what is in Surat al-Hajj of its being specified to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, [p-158] because that occurred before the building of the House, as is made clear by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We settled for Ibrahim the place of the House﴾; and Isma'il, peace be upon him, was at that time far from the place of address. It is evident that this was after he reached the age of command and prohibition. The completion of the building was by his own labour, as is indicated by its mention right after the account of His making it a place of return for the people... etc. The intended meaning is purifying it from idols, impurities, the circumambulation of one in a state of major impurity, a menstruating woman, and other things unfitting to it. ﴿For those who circumambulate﴾: around it; ﴿and those who abide﴾: those who stay near it, residents there; or those who seclude themselves (i'tikaf); or those who stand in prayer, as in His saying, the Exalted and Most High: ﴿for those who circumambulate and those who stand﴾; ﴿and those who bow and prostrate﴾: plural of "rakiʿ" (bowing) and "sajid" (prostrating); that is, for the circumambulators and the worshippers, because standing, bowing and prostrating are among the postures of the worshipper; and because the last two are close in essence and time, the conjunction between their two qualified nouns was omitted; or: "dedicate it to these, so that others do not frequent it"; and in this there is an allusion that others' association with it, even with the accompaniment of a permissible matter, is among the kinds of defiling and polluting it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 126:

﴿And when Abraham said﴾: a conjunction (*'atf*) with what precedes it in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And when We made﴾, and so on. It is either directly governed or governed by its implied verb, as has passed. ﴿My Lord, make this a secure land﴾: secure, meaning possessing security, like ﴿a pleasing life﴾; or "secure" in the sense that its people are secure, like "a night of one sleeping," i.e., make this valley one of the secure lands. This was the first thing for which he, peace be upon him, came to Mecca, as Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that when he, peace and blessings be upon him, settled Isma'il there and left Hajar there, and turned back heading for Syria, Hajar followed him saying: "To whom are you leaving us in this desolate place?" He did not answer them at all. Then she said: "Has Allah commanded you to do this?" He said: "Yes." She said: "Then He will not let us be lost," and she was content, and he went on. When he reached the ridge of Kada', he turned toward the valley and said: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled﴾, and the verse continues.

The definiteness of "the land" (*al-balad*), together with its being an attribute of "this" in Surat Ibrahim, is explained as follows if the request is taken as having been made more than once: he, peace be upon him, first asked for both matters, the land's being a city and its security, and one of them was granted, while the other was delayed until its appointed time, in accordance with the dazzling wisdom. Then he repeated the request, as is customary in supplication and entreaty. Or the first thing requested was that it be a city and merely a security that makes habitation sound, as in all other lands, and this was granted; then, secondly, the security that is customary. Or what was requested first was also the security, and it was granted, but the second request was for its continuance.
