Limiting the request to the city, with "land" as an attribute of "this," is because that is the primary aim, or because in the case of a city, continuance after establishment is customary, unlike security. If the request is taken as a single request with the account repeated, as is the more obvious reading, then the apparent meaning is that both matters were requested. This has been related here, while there it is confined to narrating the request for security, being sufficient in place of narrating the request for the city by narrating the request that people's hearts be made to yearn toward it, as its detail will come there, with Allah's permission, Mighty and Majestic is He.

﴿And provide its people with fruits﴾: of its varieties, by making villages near it where such things are produced, or having them brought to it from distant regions. Both have occurred, so that the fruits of spring, summer, and autumn gather there on a single day. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that al-Ta'if was part of the land of Palestine, and when Abraham, peace be upon him, made this supplication, Allah, Exalted is He, lifted it and placed it where it is, as provision for the Sacred Precinct. And it is related from al-Zuhri that Allah, Exalted is He, transported a village from the villages of Syria and placed it at al-Ta'if in answer to the supplication of Abraham, peace be upon him. (p-159)

﴿Whoever among them believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾: a substitution (*badal*) for "its people," a partial substitution (*badal al-ba'd*). He singled them out for the supplication, to display the nobility of faith and make clear its worth, and out of concern for his family and regard for good manners. In it there is encouragement for his people to believe and a warning against disbelief, just as in the narration of it there is encouragement and warning for the Quraysh and others among the People of the Book.

﴿He said﴾: a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) built upon the question, as has passed many times. His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾: a conjunction with the object of an implied verb, whose sense is: "Provide for whoever believes, and whoever disbelieves." His words, Exalted is He, ﴿then I shall grant him enjoyment﴾: are conjoined with that verb, or stand in the position of a nominative by way of the inceptive; his words ﴿then I shall grant him enjoyment﴾ are its predicate, meaning "then I grant him enjoyment." The fa' entered it by way of likening it to a conditional. Disbelief, although it is not a cause of unrestricted enjoyment, is nonetheless suitable as a cause of reducing it, and of its being joined to the torment of the Fire. It has been said that it is a conjunction with "whoever believes," a conjunction of instruction, as if it were said: "Say: and provide for whoever disbelieves, for that too is granted." It is as if he, peace be upon him, had analogized provision to the imamate, so Allah, Exalted is He, alerted him that it is a worldly mercy encompassing both the pious and the wicked, unlike the imamate, which is attained through special qualities. It was also read as ﴿then I shall enable him to enjoy﴾, from *amta'a*, and as ﴿then We shall enable him to enjoy﴾. ﴿a little﴾: a small enjoyment, or for a little time. ﴿Then I shall compel him to the torment of the Fire﴾: that is, I shall drive him toward it, driving the one compelled, because of his disbelief and his squandering of the blessings with which He granted him enjoyment. It was also read as ﴿then We shall compel him﴾, in accordance with the reading ﴿then We shall enable him to enjoy﴾. It was also read as ﴿So enable him to enjoy a little, then compel him﴾, with the imperative in both, on the basis that these are part of Abraham's supplication, and "he said" carries his pronoun. He separated it from what precedes it because it is a supplication against the disbelievers. The change in its construction is to signal that disbelief is the cause of their being compelled to the torment of the Fire. As for the provision of those who believe, it is by way of favor and kindness. It was also read with a kasra on the hamza, according to the dialect of those who vowel the prefixed letter of the imperfect with kasra, and as ﴿uṭarrruhu﴾, with the dad assimilated into the ta', which is a disliked dialect, since in the letters of the mnemonic "ḍumma shufr," what is adjacent to them is assimilated into them, not the reverse. ﴿And wretched is the destination﴾: the object of the dispraise is omitted, meaning: "Wretched is the destination, the Fire," or "its torment."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 127:**

﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House﴾: This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with what precedes it, namely His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And when Abraham said﴾, according to one of the two manners mentioned in "And when We made" (ʿiṭf). The use of the present form (ṣīghat al-istiqbāl) is to narrate a past situation, in order to bring its wondrous image to mind, which points to a dazzling miracle. Al-qawāʿid (the foundations) is the plural of qāʿidah, which is the base. It is a predominantly adjectival form from al-quʿūd (sitting), meaning "steadiness" (al-thabāt). Perhaps it is a metaphor, opposed to al-qiyām (standing). From this comes the expression qaʿadaka Allāh (may Allah keep you steady). Raising them (rafʿuhā) means building upon them, because this transfers them from a state of lowness to a state of height. Strictly speaking, what is raised is the one who builds upon them, but since the two have joined and become one thing, it is as if they grew and rose. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the layers (sāfāt) of the building, since every layer is a foundation for what is built upon it. Raising them means building some of them upon others. It has been said that the intended meaning of raising them is raising the station of the House, displaying its honour, and calling people to its pilgrimage. The indefiniteness of them at first, followed by their specification, magnifies their importance in a way that is not hidden. It has also been said that the meaning is: "And when Abraham raises what was laid down of the House and made level," that is, he makes the form of the level foundation high and lofty by building. It is reported that Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, sent down the House as a ruby from the rubies of Paradise, with two doors of emerald, one eastern and one western. He said to Adam: "I have caused to descend for you that which is circumambulated, just as the Throne is circumambulated." Adam then set out from the land of India towards it on foot, and the angels met him and said: "Your pilgrimage is accepted, O Adam. We performed pilgrimage to this House two thousand years before you." Adam, peace be upon him, performed forty pilgrimages from the land of India to Mecca, on his feet. He continued in this manner until Allah raised it during the days of the Flood to the fourth heaven. It is therefore the Bayt al-Maʿmur (the Frequented House). (p-160) Its place remained empty until the time of Abraham, peace be upon him. Allah, glorified is He, commanded him to build it, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, showed him its place. It has also been said that Allah, Exalted is He, sent the Sakinah (tranquillity) to guide him to it, and Abraham, peace be upon him, followed it until they both reached the honoured Mecca. It has also been said that Allah, Exalted is He, sent a cloud the size of the House, and Abraham walked in its shade until it arrived at the honoured Mecca, where it stopped at the place of the House. Then it was proclaimed: "Build upon its shade, and do not add or subtract." It has also been said that he built it from five mountains: Mount Sinai, Mount Zaytā, Lebanon, and al-Judi, and he laid its foundation from Ḥirāʾ. Gabriel, peace be upon him, brought the Black Stone from heaven. It has also been said that Abu Qubays split open and released it, having been hidden in it during the days of the Flood. It had been a white ruby from the rubies of Paradise, but when menstruating women touched it in the Jahiliyyah, it turned black. Al-Fasi said, in Muthir al-Gharam fi Tarikh al-Balad al-Haram: "What is obtained from the totality of what has been said about the number of times the Kaʿbah was built is that it was built ten times. Among them was the building of the angels, peace be upon them, which al-Nawawi mentioned in Tahdhib al-Asmaʾ wa'l-Lughat, and al-Azraqi in his History, and he mentioned that this was before the creation of Adam, peace be upon him. Among them was the building of Adam, peace be upon him, which al-Bayhaqi mentioned in Dala'il al-Nubuwwah, and he related on the authority of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, sent Gabriel to Adam and Eve, peace be upon them both, and said to him and to Eve: 'Build Me a House.' Gabriel drew its outline, Adam began digging, and Eve carried the earth, until they struck water and were called from beneath it: 'That is enough, O Adam.' When they had built it, it was revealed to him that he should circumambulate it, and it was said to him: 'You are the first of mankind, and this is the first House.' Thus al-Azraqi mentioned it in his History, and ʿAbd al-Razzaq in his Musannaf. Among them was the building of the children of Adam when the tent was raised with which Allah, Exalted is He, consoled Adam, peace be upon him, and which had been pitched at the place of the House. His sons then built a house of clay and stone in its place. It remained inhabited, and they and those after them kept it populated until the flood reached it in the time of Noah, peace be upon him. Al-Azraqi mentioned this with his chain of transmission to Wahb ibn Munabbih. Among them was the building of the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him, which is explicitly mentioned in the Qur'an and well known among near and far. Among them was the building of the Amalekites, and among them the building of Jurhum, which al-Azraqi mentioned with his chain of transmission to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. Among them was the building of Quṣayy ibn Kilab, which al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar mentioned in the Book of Genealogy. Among them was the building of Quraysh, which is well known. Among them was the building of ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Among them was the building of al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, but that was not a rebuilding of all of it, only of one of its walls." Al-Hafiz al-Suhayli said: "Its building did not occur over the ages more than five times. The first was when Shith (Seth), peace be upon him, built it." End of quotation. And Allah, glorified is He, knows best.

﴿And Ishmael﴾: This is coordinated with "Abraham." Perhaps its delay after the object is to indicate that the principal in the raising is Abraham, and Ishmael is a follower of him. It has been said that he used to hand him the stones while he was building them. It has also been said that the two of them built it from two sides. ﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾: This is with the intention of saying, meaning: they both say it. It has been recited that way as well, taking it as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the two of them, peace be upon them. It has also been said that it is the governing element of "when" (idh), and the sentence is coordinated with what precedes it. The estimate is: they say, "Our Lord, accept from us," when they are raising, meaning at the time of their raising. It has also been said that "And Ishmael" is a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is an elided saying, which governs "Our Lord, accept from us." Thus Abraham is the one raising and Ishmael is the one supplicating, and the sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: "And when Abraham raises the foundations, while Ishmael says: Our Lord, accept from us." The mention of the attribute of Lordship, which indicates the bestowal of what benefits the one who is nurtured, together with the addition to their pronoun, peace be upon them both, is to set in motion the chain of answering. The omission of the object of "accept" (taqabbal), while it is mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, and accept my supplication﴾ and elsewhere, refers to the acts of nearness and obedience of which building is part, as indicated by making the supplicatory sentence a circumstantial clause. ﴿Indeed You are the All-Hearing﴾: of all things heard, of which our supplication is one. ﴿the All-Knowing﴾: of all things known, of which our intentions in all our deeds are part. The sentence is a justification for requesting acceptance. It is not that His being All-Hearing of their supplication and All-Knowing of their intentions is what makes acceptance possible in general; rather, His knowledge of the soundness of their intentions and the sincerity of their deeds calls for it, by the necessity of His promise, out of grace. The emphasis of the sentence is for the purpose of the full strength of their certainty in its content. The restriction of the two attributes, hearing and knowledge, to Him, Exalted is He, is to show that their supplication is exclusively directed to Him, and that their hope is cut off entirely from anything other than Him. Know that the apparent order is that the first of the events narrated was the trial and what follows it, then the supplication for the city's security and safety and what relates to it, then the raising of the foundations of the House and what follows, then making it a place of return for people and the command to purify it. Perhaps the change in the chronological order within the narration is to arrange the matters originating from His side in one series, and the actions and sayings originating from Abraham and Ishmael, peace be upon them both, in another series. As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾, etc., it occurred within the circumstances related to Abraham because the context required it, and because what preceded in the speech necessitated it, such that there was no alternative to it at all. Likewise, the occurrence of His saying, peace be upon him: ﴿and from my offspring﴾ within His speech, glorified is He, is for that reason.

ﷻ "Our Lord, and make us submissive to You" (﴿رَبَّنا واجْعَلْنا مُسْلِمَيْنِ لَكَ﴾): "devoted to You" (مُخْلِصَيْنِ لَكَ); or: "surrendering" (مُسْتَسْلِمَيْنِ), from "aslama" (أسْلَمَ), meaning to surrender and submit. Whichever it is, what is sought is increase and steadfastness in the sincerity and submission in which they already were. It is also read "Muslimeen" (مُسْلِمِينَ) in the plural form, by including Hajar with them in the supplication; or because the dual is one of the degrees of the plural.

﴿وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِنا أُمَّةً مُسْلِمَةً لَكَ﴾: that is, "and make some of our offspring" (واجْعَلْ بَعْضَ ذُرِّيَّتِنا). They singled out their offspring for the supplication because they are most deserving of compassion, and because when they are righteous, their followers are righteous. They singled out only some of them because they knew that among them there would be wrongdoers (ظَلَمَةً), and that divine wisdom does not require all of them to be sincere and wholly devoted to Allah, Mighty and Majestic; for that would disrupt the affairs of living. For this reason it was said: "Were it not for fools, the world would be ruined." It was also said that by "a community that submits" (الأُمَّةُ المُسْلِمَةُ) they meant the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is permissible that "min" (مِن) is explanatory (مُبَيِّنَةً), placed before what it explains, and that the conjunction and the conjoined are separated by it, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿وَمِنَ الأرْضِ مِثْلَهُنَّ﴾; and the original order is: "and a community that submits to You from our offspring."

﴿وَأرِنا﴾: from "ru'yah" (الرُّؤْيَةُ), in the sense of "seeing" (الإبْصارُ); or in the sense of "making known" (التَّعْرِيفُ); that is, "show us" (بَصِّرْنا), or "make us know" (عَرِّفْنا).

﴿مَناسِكَنا﴾: that is, our acts of worship in the Hajj (مُتَعَبَّداتِنا في الحَجِّ); or our places of sacrifice (مَذابِحَنا). The word "nusuk" (النُّسُكُ), originally, means the utmost limit of worship, and it became common for the Hajj because of the hardship it involves and its departure from customary practice. It is also read "arna" (أرْنا), by analogy with "fakhdh" (فَخْذٌ) for "fakhidh" (فَخِذٌ); but this is deficient, because the kasrah is transferred from the dropped hamzah, which is indicated by it. It is also read with "ikhtilas" (بِالِاخْتِلاسِ).

﴿وَتُبْ عَلَيْنا﴾: a request for repentance on behalf of their offspring, and it is reported from them both to encourage the disbelievers to repent and to believe; or it is a plea for repentance for them both for whatever lapse occurred from them through forgetfulness. They said it out of humility toward themselves and as guidance for their offspring.

﴿إنَّكَ أنْتَ التَّوّابُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾: this is the reason given for the supplication and a further summons to the answering of it. It was said: if a servant wishes to have his supplication answered, let him call upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by those of His names and attributes that are suitable to it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 129:

﴿Our Lord, and send among them﴾: that is, among the Muslim community (p-162)

﴿a messenger from among them﴾: that is, from among themselves. Sending one among them does not necessarily mean sending one from them. None was sent from their descendants except the Prophet ﷺ, and he is the one through whom their supplication (da'wa) was answered, peace be upon them both. It was narrated that it was said to him: "Your prayer has been answered," and that he was at the end of time. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I am the answer to the prayer of my father Abraham, the good news of Jesus, and the vision of my mother." The singling out of Abraham (peace be upon him) for the answer is because he is the origin of the supplication, and Isma'il (peace be upon him) followed him.

﴿who recites to them Your verses﴾: he reads to them and conveys to them the clear proofs that are revealed to him.

﴿and teaches them﴾: according to their theoretical capacity (nazariyya).

﴿the Book﴾: that is, the Qur'an.

﴿and the wisdom﴾: and that by which their souls are perfected, of the rulings of the Sharia and the true knowledges.

﴿and purifies them﴾: according to their practical capacity ('amaliyya). That is, He cleanses them from the filth of polytheism and the various kinds of sins.

﴿Indeed You are the Mighty﴾: the One who cannot be overpowered and is not defeated in what He wills.

﴿the Wise﴾: the One who does only what wisdom and benefit require.

The whole clause is a justification (ta'lil) for the supplication and the granting of what was asked. The attribute of wisdom necessitates bestowing what wisdom requires, among which is the sending of the Messenger (ﷺ). The attribute of might requires that no impediment exists at all.

﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham﴾: a denial and an expression of astonishment that any sensible person would turn away from his religion, which is the plain truth and the sound faith. That is, none turns away from his clear and radiant religion, ﴿except one who makes a fool of himself﴾. That is, he debases himself, makes himself contemptible, and treats himself lightly. It was said: he ruins himself; and it was said: he destroys himself, or he ruins himself, or he makes his own self ignorant. Al-Mubarrad (d. 285 AH, grammarian) and Tha'lab (d. 291 AH, grammarian) said: "safiha" with a kasra is transitive, and with a damma it is intransitive. What supports this is what occurs in a report: "Arrogance is that you deem the truth foolish and look down on people." It was said its meaning is: he went astray from his own side. It was also said that its original form was "safiha nafsuhu" with the subject in the nominative, and then it was put in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification), like "ghabina ra'yuhu" (his opinion was deceived) and "alima ra'suhu" (his head was in pain), and like the verse:

Then after him we take hold of the tails of a life, with a back humped and no hump on it.

And like his saying:

My people are not Tha'labat ibn Sa'd, nor the Fazara with their shaggy necks.

That is because whoever turns away from what none of the sensible turns away from has gone to great lengths in debasing his self, degrading it and humiliating it, since he has opposed by it every sensible soul. It is related that Abd Allah ibn Salam invited his two nephews, Salamah and Muhajir, to Islam. He said to them: "We know that God (Exalted) said in the Torah: 'I will raise up from the offspring of Ishmael a prophet whose name is Ahmad; whoever believes in him has been guided and has taken the right path, and whoever does not believe in him is cursed.'" So Salamah embraced Islam, and Muhajir refused, and so this verse was revealed.

﴿And We certainly chose him in this world﴾: that is, We selected him with prophethood and wisdom from among all of creation. Its original meaning is taking the best (safwa) of a thing, just as the original meaning of ikhtiyar (choosing) is taking the best of it. The lam here is the lam of the answer to an omitted oath, and the waw is i'tiradiyya (a parenthetical insertion), and the clause confirms the content of what precedes it; that is: "By God, We certainly chose him." His saying (Exalted): ﴿and indeed he, in the Hereafter, is among the righteous﴾: that is, among those witnessed to be steadfast in uprightness and goodness. The word "righteousness" (al-sala) is conjoined to it, falls within the scope of the oath, emphasizes its content, and confirms what it confirms. There is no need to make it another parenthetical insertion, or a presumed hal (circumstantial clause), for whoever is chosen among the servants in this world and witnessed to be righteous in the Hereafter is deserving of being followed; none turns away from his religion except a fool, or one who makes himself a fool, who has debased his self through ignorance and turning away from reflection and contemplation.

The choice of the nominal sentence is because his inclusion in the company of the righteous people of the Hereafter is a continuous matter in both abodes, not something that happens in the Hereafter. The emphasis with "inna" and the lam is because the matters of the Hereafter are hidden from the addressees, so their need for emphasis is greater than for matters whose effects are witnessed. The word "fi" (in) is linked to "al-salihin" (the righteous), while the lam is the lam of definiteness, and it is not a relative pronoun, so there is no need to front part of the relative clause over it. Moreover, something may be tolerated in an adverbial phrase that is not tolerated elsewhere, as in his saying:

I raised him until he became a man grown, and my reward for that was that I be beaten with a stick.

Or it may be linked to an omitted element of the same wording, meaning: "And he is indeed righteous in the Hereafter, among the righteous"; or to an omitted element not of the same wording, meaning: "I mean: in the Hereafter," like "laka ba'du ra'yan" (for you, after this, is a pasture). It was also said it is linked to "isṭafaynāhu" (We chose him), with the Noble Text containing a reordering, its implied sense being: "And We certainly chose him in this world and the Hereafter; and indeed he is among the righteous." (p-163)

﴿Idh (when)﴾ is an adverbial complement (ẓarf) governed by "iṣṭafaynāhu" (﴿We chose him﴾), because the intervening element is not foreign to it. Rather, it confirms it, since his being chosen in this world was for prophethood and for what relates to the good of the Hereafter. Or it is a causal explanation of it. Or it is in the accusative governed by "udhkur" (remember), as if it were said: remember that time, so that you may understand that he was the chosen, righteous one, deserving of leadership and precedence, and that he attained what he attained only by hastening to submission and compliance with what he was commanded, and by sincerely devoting his inner self in the best manner, when ﴿his Lord said to him, "Submit"﴾, that is, to your Lord. ﴿He said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds."﴾

The matter is not to be taken literally; rather it is a figurative representation (tamthīl). The meaning is that he brought to mind the proofs of monotheism (tawḥīd), which lead to knowledge and call to Islam, from the star, the moon and the sun. It has also been said: "Submit" means "yield and obey." It has also been said: "Remain firm upon what you are upon of Islam and sincerity," or "Be upright and entrust your affairs to God (Exalted)." In that case the command is taken literally.

The shift of grammatical person (iltifāt) together with the mention of the title "Lord" (rubūbiyya) and its attribution to him, peace be upon him, serves to show greater kindness toward him and care for his upbringing. The attribution of "Lord" in his reply, peace be upon him, to "the worlds" serves to announce the completeness of the strength of his Islam, since he was certain, upon reflection, that His lordship encompasses all the worlds entirely, not himself alone, as is the command required.

**[Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*, on Surah 2, verse 132]**

﴿And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons﴾: This begins an account of his (peace be upon him) perfecting others, following the account of his perfection in himself. It also emphasizes the obligation to desire his (peace be upon him) religion. *Tawsiyah* (enjoining, or bequeathing advice) means advancing toward another with what contains good and benefit for the Muslims, whether by action or by speech. Its root is *al-wasla* (connection). It is said "*wassahu*" when one connects him, and "*fassahu*" when one separates him. It is as if the one who enjoins connects his action with the action of the one enjoined. The pronoun in "*bi-ha*" (by it) refers to the religion (*millah*), or to his saying ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾, by way of interpreting it as the word (*kalimah*), just as it is used to express his saying (exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, I am free of what you worship, except He who originated me﴾, and in His saying (mighty and majestic is He): ﴿And He made it a word that remains among his descendants﴾. It is also read as "*awsa*" (he enjoined), but the first reading is more eloquent. ﴿And Jacob﴾ is coordinated with "Abraham," meaning: he too enjoined it. It is also read in the accusative case, coordinated with "his sons." ﴿O my sons﴾: this is according to an implied *qawl* (saying) in the view of the al-Basriyyun (the grammarians of Basra), and it is dependent on "*wassa*" (enjoined) in the view of the al-Kufiyyun (the grammarians of Kufa), because it has the meaning of saying, as in the poet's words:

*Two men from Dabba informed us*
*that we saw a man naked.*

According to the first group it is by way of implying the saying, and according to the latter it is dependent on the informing, which has the meaning of saying. It is also read "*an ya baniyya*" (that, O my sons). The sons of Abraham (peace be upon him) were four: Isma'il, Ishaq, Madyan, and Madan. It is said they were eight, and it is said twenty-four. The sons of Jacob were twelve: Ruwbin, Shim'un, Lawi, Yahudha, Yashshukhur, Zabulun, Zuwana, Taftuna, Kuwdha, Ushir, Binyamin, and Yusuf (peace be upon him). ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen for you the religion﴾: the religion of Islam, which is the elite of religions, and there is no religion other than it with Him (exalted is He). ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾: its apparent meaning is a prohibition against dying in a state contrary to Islam, but the intended meaning is a command to remain steadfast upon Islam until the time of death, meaning: hold firm to it and never part from it, like your saying: "Do not pray except while you are humble." The change of expression indicates that their dying not upon Islam is a death in which there is no good, that its proper due is that it should not befall them, and that they must beware of it with the utmost caution. A parallel to this is: "Die while you are a martyr." It is narrated that the Jews said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do you not know that Jacob enjoined Judaism upon his sons on the day he died?" Then this was revealed:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 133:**

﴿Or were you witnesses when death came to Ya'qub (Jacob)﴾: "Am" (أمْ) is *munqati'a* (disjunctive, a conjunction that introduces a new question, in which "am" is taken as "bal", "rather", combined with the interrogative hamza). The address is to the People of the Book who turned away from the religion of Ibrahim (Abraham). "Shuhada'" (شُهَداءَ) is the plural of "shahid" or of "shahid" in the sense of "hadir" (present). "Idh" (إذْ) is an adverb of time (*zarf*) governing "shuhada'". The intended meaning of the presence of death is the presence of its causes. Ya'qub (peace be upon him) is placed first for the sake of emphasis on him, since what is meant is the manner of his bequest to his sons, after this had been stated in general terms. The meaning of "bal" (بَلْ) is the change of subject (*idrab*) and the transition from rebuking them for their aversion from the religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) to rebuking them for their false attribution to Ya'qub (peace be upon him) of Judaism, as is related about them. As for generalizing the false attribution here to all the prophets (peace be upon them), as has been said, this is excluded by the specification of Ya'qub by mention, and by what will follow in His saying (Exalted and Majestic is He): ﴿Or do you say that Ibrahim﴾ and so on. The meaning of the hamza is the denial that they were witnesses at his deathbed (peace be upon him) and a rebuke to them. His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿when he said﴾ is an appositive substitute (*badal*) for "idh hadara" (when he was present), that is: you were not present at his deathbed (peace be upon him).

His saying: ﴿to his sons, "What will you worship after me?"﴾: that is, what thing will you worship after my death? So from where do you have the right to claim against him (peace be upon him) what you claim, guessing at the unseen? At this point the rebuke, the denial and the reproach are complete. Then He explained that the matter had turned out contrary to what they alleged, and that he (peace be upon him) intended by his question to establish his sons upon monotheism and submission (Islam), and to take their pledge to remain steadfast in both, since by this he completes his bequest, with his saying: ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾. "Ma" (مَا) is used to ask about anything whose nature is not known; when it is known, "man" is used for rational beings when one asks about a particular thing. If one asks about its attribute, it is said: "Ma Zayd? Afaqih am tabib?" (What is Zayd? A jurist or a physician?).

His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*), which came as an answer to a question arising from the report of the question of Ya'qub (peace be upon him), as if it were said: "What did they say at that?" So it was said: ﴿They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God; and to Him we are submitting."﴾ This accords with what their father intended by the question; that is: we will worship the God whose existence, divinity and the obligation of worshipping Him are agreed upon. The counting of Isma'il among his fathers is by way of predominance (*taghlib*) of the father and the grandfather, in accordance with his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): "The paternal uncle of a man is the twin of his father," and his saying (peace and blessings be upon him) concerning al-'Abbas: "This is the remnant of my fathers." It was also read as "Abika" (أبِيكَ), considered a plural with the sound masculine ending (*jam' bil-waw wal-nun*), as in the verse:

*So when they perceived our voices,*
*they wept and ransomed us with their fathers.*

The nun was dropped due to the *idafa* (construct). Or it is singular. "Ibrahim" (إبْراهِيمَ) is an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*) to it. "Isma'il" and "Ishaq" are conjoined to "Abika" (in the sense of being coordinated with it). "Ilahan wahidan" (إلَهًا واحِدًا) is a substitute (*badal*) for "ilaha aba'ika" (the God of your fathers), like His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿by the forelock, a lying, sinful forelock﴾. Its benefit is the explicit statement of monotheism and the removal of the misconception that arises from repeating the annexed noun, since coordination with the genitive is not possible; or it is put in the accusative on the basis of specification (*ikhtisas*). ﴿And we are to Him Muslims﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject of "na'budu" (we worship), or from its object, or from both together. It is possible that it is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraḍ*) confirming the content of what preceded.

﴿That is a community﴾: a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence, here "that") and a *khabar* (predicate, "a community"). The demonstrative refers to Ibrahim, Ya'qub and their descendants who affirmed the Oneness of God. The *ummah* (community) is the group that the various groups of people make for, i.e., they intend it and take it as their model. ﴿Which has passed away﴾: a *sifah* (qualifying clause) for the predicate. It means it has passed on through death and has been separated from those who came after it. Its root meaning is that it went to the *khala'* (wasteland), which is the land where no one dwells. ﴿For it is what it earned﴾: this is a resumptive sentence (*jumlah mustaanifah*) with no place in the *i'rab* (grammatical case-inflection). Alternatively, it is another qualifier of *ummah*, or a *hal* (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in *khalat*. *Ma* is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*) or an indefinite qualifying term (*mawsufah*), and its returning pronoun is omitted. That is, it is for them what they earned of righteous deeds, as related, which does not pass over to others. The fronting of the predicate (*musnad*) entails restricting the predicated element (*musnad ilayh*) to it, as is well known. ﴿And for you is what you earned﴾: this is coordinated (*'atf*) with its counterpart on the first interpretation, and is an independent sentence (*jumlah mubtada'ah*) on the last two, since it has no connecting pronoun, which is necessary in a qualifier, and there is no simultaneity of time, which is necessary in a *hal*. That is, for you is what you yourselves earned, not what others earned. The fronting of the predicate may also be intended to restrict it to the predicated element, as was said regarding His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿For you is your religion and for me is my religion﴾, meaning: my religion is for me, not your religion. Reading the first sentence as a restriction in the sense that those people will benefit only from what they themselves earned, as some have said, does not fit the context, since no one would imagine that these people benefit from the earnings of those, such that it would need to be explained that this is impossible. What is actually imagined is that these people benefit from their own earnings, so He explained that this is impossible because their righteous deeds are specific to them and do not pass over to others, and these people have only what they earned, so their affiliation to those ancestors does not benefit them. What benefits them is following those ancestors in their deeds. As he, upon him be peace, said: "O Banu Hashim, let not people come to me with their deeds while you come to me with your lineages."

﴿And you will not be questioned about what they used to do﴾: If the question is taken in its apparent sense, the sentence confirms the content of the two preceding sentences, a clear confirmation. If it is meant in terms of its cause, namely the recompense, then it is a completion of what came before, functioning as a conclusion (*natijah*) to it. In either case, the aim is to disappoint the addressees and cut off their vain hopes of benefiting from the good deeds of the bygone community. The verb "deeds" is used without specification in order to establish the ruling through a demonstrative method within a universal rule. It has also been said that "questioning" is an expression for "being held to account," and "what they did" for their evil deeds. So it was said: that is, you will not be held accountable for their evil deeds, just as you will not be rewarded for their good deeds. There is no doubt that this is not befitting the status of the revelation, for how could it be? They are free from earning evil deeds, so how could it be imagined that these are imposed on others, such that one would undertake to explain the benefit of that?

﴿And they said﴾: a beginning of the explanation of another kind of their disbelief, namely their leading others astray, following the explanation of their own straying. The pronoun refers to the People of the Two Books, in the manner of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person), which indicates that their condition warrants removing them from the position of being addressed, turning away from them, and enumerating their crimes before others. That is: they said to the believers: ﴿Be Jews or Christians﴾. This statement was not said by all of them, nor by every group of the two communities. Rather, it is distributed between them in a particular way that their circumstances require, a requirement that makes it unnecessary to state it explicitly. That is: the Jews said, "Be Jews," and the Christians said, "Be Christians." Thus the noble wording has been treated as his (Exalted) saying was treated: ﴿And they said: None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾, relying on the clarity of the intended meaning. ﴿You will be guided﴾ is the answer to the imperative; that is: if you become like that, you will be guided.

﴿Say﴾: an address to the Prophet ﷺ; that is: say to them, by way of refuting them, clarifying what the truth is in their own view, and guiding them to it: ﴿Rather, the religion of Abraham﴾; that is: we shall not be as you say, but we shall be the people of his religion (peace be upon him). It has also been said: rather, we follow his religion (peace be upon him). It has been permitted that the meaning is: rather, you yourselves follow his religion (peace be upon him), or: be the people of his religion. It was also read in the nominative (*marfu'*), meaning: rather, our religion is his religion, or our affair is his religion; or: we are his religion, that is, the people of his religion. ﴿Upright (*hanifan*)﴾: that is, inclining away from falsehood toward truth. It is a *hal* (circumstantial accusative) from the *mudaf ilayhi* (the noun governed by the genitive after the construct), as in the phrase *ra'aytu wajha Hindin qa'imatan* ("I saw Hind's face standing"); or from the *mudaf* (the construct noun), as in His (Exalted) saying: ﴿And We removed what was in their breasts of rancor, as brothers﴾; etc.

﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾: an indirect rebuke to them, and a declaration of the invalidity of their claim to follow him (peace be upon him), given their association of partners with God by their saying: "Uzayr is the son of God," and "The Messiah is the son of God."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 136:

﴿Say﴾: This is an address to the believers, following His address to the Prophet (peace be upon him) to refute their shameful statement in general terms, and as guidance for them toward the path of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness) and faith, in a certain degree of detail. That is: say to them, in response to what they said, as confirmation and as implicit guidance for them toward it:﴿We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us﴾; meaning the Qur'an. It is mentioned first before the rest of the divine books, although it was revealed later than them, because it is specific to us and because it is the means of believing in them. ﴿And in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes﴾: meaning the scrolls. Although they were revealed to Abraham (peace be upon him), those after him, since they were worshippers bound by its details and subject to its rulings, were treated as though they had been sent down to them, just as the Qur'an was treated as sent down to us. Al-asbat (the Tribes) is the plural of "sibt," which means grandson; the intended meaning is the grandsons of Jacob (peace be upon him), or his twelve sons and their descendants, for they are the grandsons of Abraham and Isaac. ﴿And in what was given to Moses and Jesus﴾: from the Torah and the Gospel, and all the manifest miracles that appeared through the hands of both of them, as detailed in the Glorious Revelation. The mention of "given" (ita') is to generalise what has been indicated, and the specific mention of these two is because the discourse is with the Jews and the Christians. ﴿And in what was given to the prophets﴾: that is, all those mentioned and others; ﴿from their Lord﴾: of the clear signs and the dazzling miracles; ﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾: unlike the practice of the Jews and the Christians, who believed in some and disbelieved in others. The non-distinction between them is considered, although the discourse concerns what was given to them, because non-distinction between them entails affirmation and denial alike, since there is no distinction between what was given to them. The hamza of "ahad" (any one): either it is original, so it is a noun, established for whoever may be addressed, in which the singular, dual, plural, masculine and feminine are equal; for this reason it is correct for "bayn" (between) to govern it, as in the phrase "the wealth is between the people"; and from this is what is in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The spoils of war were not made lawful for any black-headed person other than you," where it is described with the plural. Or it is substituted from the waw, so it means "wahid" (one), and its generality arises from its occurrence in the context of negation, and the correctness of "bayn" governing it is by considering a conjoined term that has been omitted because it is evident, that is: "between any one of them and another," as in the verse of al-Nabigha:

"There was not between Khayr, had he come safely, and Abu Hajar, except a few nights."

That is: between Khayr and me. In it there is clear indication of the realisation of non-distinction between each individual of them and anyone else, whoever they may be, which is not present in the mere statement "We make no distinction between them." The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "We believe." His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And we are submitting to Him﴾: that is, sincerely devoted to Him and humbly obedient; it is another circumstantial clause from it, or a conjunction with "We believe."

(p-167)﴿Then if they believe﴾: The fa' (fa) indicates that what follows is consequent upon what precedes. The faith of the addressees, as described in the revised manner, is a basis for expecting the faith of the People of the Two Books, since it includes what is acceptable to them. ﴿with the like of what you have believed﴾: That is, with what you have believed in, in the manner that has been explained in detail. The word "like" (mithl) is here taken as superfluous, as in His (exalted) saying: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like﴾, meaning "to it." This is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, "with what you have believed in," and the reading of Ubayy, "with that which you have believed in."

It is also permissible that the bā' (ba') be instrumental (li-l-isti'ana), with the object of belief omitted because it is evident from what has just passed. Or the verb may be treated as intransitive: that is, "if they believe in what has been set forth in detail," or "if they perform belief through a testimony like your testimony." The first alternative (fa-in) may be taken as superfluous, and the second as a complement (silah) of "you believed," with "mā" being a verbal-masdar (maṣdariyyah) particle: that is, "if they believe a belief like your belief in what has been mentioned in detail." The bā' may also be for accompaniment (li-l-mulabasah), meaning: "if they believe while associated with what you believed while associated with it," or "if they believe a belief associated with what you believed, a belief associated with it, of submission (idh'an), sincerity (ikhlas), and not distinguishing between the Prophets, peace be upon them. For what was found in them and proceeded from them of testimony, submission, and other things, is like what the believers have, not identical to it. This is unlike the object of belief, for multiplicity cannot be conceived in it. ﴿Then they are guided﴾ to the truth and have attained it, just as you have been guided, and unity and agreement have come about among you.

As for what has been said, that the meaning is: "if they seek faith by a path that guides to the truth, like your path, then they are guided," this is not acceptable, for the unity of purpose does not preclude the plurality of paths. What rules it out is that the context of specifying the path of truth and guiding them to it precisely does not suit allowing that there might be another path beyond it.

﴿And if they turn away﴾: That is, they turn away from faith in the manner mentioned, by neglecting some part of it, such as believing in some and disbelieving in others, as is their religion and their habit. ﴿Then they are only in opposition (shiqaq)﴾: Al-mushaqqah and al-shiqaq derive from "al-shaqq" (splitting), like "al-mukhalafah" (opposition) and "al-khilaf" (difference) derive from "al-khulf," and "al-mu'adah" (hostility) and "al-'adaʾ" derive from "al-'udwah," meaning "the side." For one of two opposing parties turns away from the other, either in appearance or in meaning, turns his back to him, and takes a side other than his side and a direction other than his direction. The tanwīn is for magnification: that is, they are settled in a great opposition, far from the truth. This is to remove what might be imagined as the possibility of agreement, because of their believing in some of what the believers believe in.

The sentence is either the answer to the condition, as it is, with the meaning being their opposition arising after their turning away from faith, like the answer to the first conditional. The nominal sentence was preferred to indicate their steadfastness and firm settlement in that. Or it is by interpretation: "Know that they are only in opposition." This is what the sublime greatness of the noble revelation requires.

It has also been said that His (exalted) saying ﴿Then if they believe﴾, etc., is in the manner of challenge and rebuke, following the pattern of His saying ﴿Then bring a surah like it﴾. The meaning is: if they obtain another religion like your religion, equal to it in correctness and rectitude, then they are guided. Since that is impossible, their being guided is impossible too. There is no doubt that this is not suitable to bear the noble composition.

Since the indefiniteness of "opposition" indicates the impossibility of agreement, and that this inevitably leads to dispute and fighting, He followed it with consoling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and gladdening the believers with the promise of victory, triumph, the guarantee of support and honor. He expressed it with the particle sīn, which indicates the certainty of occurrence without doubt. So He said: ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾: that is, He will suffice you against their opposition, for sufficiency pertains not to persons but to actions. And He, Mighty and Majestic, has fulfilled His noble promise by killing the Banu Qurayza, enslaving them, and expelling the Banu (p-168) al-Nadir. The shift of address by singling out the Prophet (ﷺ), although that sufficiency is from Him, Glory be to Him, for everyone, is because he is the foundation and the principal in that. It also signals that undertaking the affairs of war, bearing its burdens and hardships, and enduring its difficulties in confronting enemies are among the duties of leaders. Therefore His (exalted) blessing of sufficiency and victory in regard to him, upon him be prayer and peace, is more complete and perfect.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾: This is an appendix (tadhyil) to the promise that preceded and a confirmation of it. The meaning is that He (exalted) hears what you call upon Him with, and knows what is in your intention of making the religion manifest, so He will respond to you and bring you to your aim. Or it is a threat to the disbelievers: that is, He hears what they utter and knows what they conceal in their hearts of what has no good in it, and He will punish them for it. It is not hidden how this emphasizes the preceding promise, for the threat to the disbelievers is a promise to the believers.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 2, verse 138:**

﴿Symbol of Allah﴾: "الصِّبْغَةُ" (aṣ-ṣibgha) is derived from "الصَّبْغُ" (aṣ-ṣabgh, dyeing), like "الجِلْسَةُ" (al-jilsa) from "الجُلُوسُ" (al-julūs). It is the state in which the dyeing takes place. By it he expressed the faith mentioned above, in the manner that was detailed, because it is a purification of the believers from the filth of disbelief, an adornment that beautifies them with its lovely effects, and something that penetrates their hearts, just as the matter of dye relates to cloth. It was also said that it is for the estimated participation (al-mushāraka at-taqdīriyya), since the Christians used to immerse their children in yellow water, which they called al-ma'mūdiyya (baptism), and claimed that it was a purification for them, and that by it their Christianity was established. Its attribution to Allah, Exalted and Majestic, together with its being supported earlier by the pronoun of the speakers, is for honour and to announce that it is a gift from Him, glory be to Him, which the servant cannot attain by himself. So it is then a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing His saying (Exalted): ﴿We believe﴾, included with it within the scope of "qūlū" (say), and in the accusative by it, like the accusative of "God's promise" in what precedes it, because it stands in the place of its verb, as if it were said: "Allah has dyed us a dyeing." It was also said that it is in the accusative by a verb of incitement (fi'l al-ighrā'), meaning: hold fast to God's dye. The two conditional clauses and what follows them were placed between them out of concern to clarify that this is the true faith, and that guidance is by it, and out of haste to console him, peace be upon him.

﴿And who is better than Allah in dye?﴾: "مَن" (man) is either the subject or the predicate, and the interrogation is for denial and negation. His saying (Exalted): ﴿dye﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz) of "أحسن" (aḥsan, better), transferred from the subject. The estimate is: "and whose dye is better than His dye (Exalted)?" So the preference runs between the two dyes, not between their doers; i.e., there is no dye better than His dye, in the sense that it is better than every dye, as indicated in His saying (Exalted): ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents﴾, and so on. Since the basis of the preference is the generalization of real and assumed goodness, based on the claim of the disbelievers, it does not necessarily follow that there is any goodness at all in the dye of others than Him. The sentence is parenthetical, confirming the meaning of exultation and rejoicing contained in "God's dye".

﴿and we to Him﴾: i.e., to Allah, who bestowed upon us that great blessing.

﴿worshippers﴾: thanking Him for it and for all His other blessings. The fronting of the adverbial phrase is for emphasis and to respect the fāṣila (verse-ending rhyme). It is conjoined to "we believe" and included with it under the command. The preference for the nominal sentence indicates the continuity of worship. Alternatively, it is conjoined to the verb of incitement, by estimating the saying: "hold fast to God's dye, and say: we are worshippers of Him." In that case, His saying (Exalted): ﴿And who is better than Allah in dye﴾ then functions as a justification (taʿlīl) for the incitement.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 139:

﴿Say, "Do you argue with us concerning God?"﴾: The address is turned exclusively to the Prophet (ﷺ) after a statement that falls under the command addressed in general terms; this is because what he was commanded is among the duties specific to him, upon him be prayers and peace. It is also read with the nun assimilated (idgham, the merging of one letter into the next). The interrogative hamzah is for denial; that is: "Do you dispute with us?" ﴿concerning God﴾; that is, concerning His religion; and you claim that His true religion is Judaism; (p-169)

and Christianity; and you base the entry into Paradise and guidance upon them; and you say, at one time: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾; and at another time: ﴿Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided.﴾

﴿And He is our Lord and your Lord﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah), and so is what is conjoined to it; that is: "Do you dispute with us while the situation is that there is no basis at all for disputation? For He (exalted is He) is our Lord; that is, the Owner of our affair and your affair." ﴿And for us are our deeds﴾; the good ones, which accord with His command; ﴿and for you are your deeds﴾; the evil ones, which oppose His judgment; ﴿and we are sincere to Him﴾; in those deeds; we seek by them nothing but His countenance. So how can you have any argument, or claim that what you are upon is the truth, or hope to enter Paradise through it, or call people to it?

The word "أم" (am) in His saying, ﴿Or do you say﴾, is either a correlative to the interrogative hamza (أ) in His saying, ﴿Do you dispute with us﴾. In that case it falls within the scope of a command, meaning: which of the two matters will you undertake? Will you establish the proof and make clear the evidence for the truth of what you hold, when the situation is as mentioned? Or will you cling to the coattails of blind imitation (taqlid) and to slandering the Prophets? And you say: ﴿Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians.﴾ So we follow them. The intent is to deny both matters and to rebuke them for both.

Or it is disjunctive (munqati'a) and to be read as if it had "بل" (bal, "rather") before it, with the hamza indicating a change of subject (idrab) and a transition from rebuke over disputation to rebuke over slandering the Prophets, upon them be peace.

It has also been read as "أم يقولون" (am yaqulun, "or do they say"), in the third-person form. In that case it is purely disjunctive and not included under the command. It comes from God Most High, rebuking them and denouncing them, not from Him to the Prophet, peace be upon him. This is a shift of grammatical person (iltifat), as this has been said.

As for what has been said, that the meaning is: "Do you dispute with us concerning God's sovereignty and His choosing a prophet from among the Arabs rather than you?", on the basis of a report that the People of the Book said, "All the prophets are from us, so if you were a prophet you would be from us, and so this was revealed," this is not accepted, for the reasons below.

As for His saying, ﴿And He is our Lord and your Lord; for us are our deeds and for you are your deeds﴾, its meaning is that God Most High is not specific to one people over another. He bestows His mercy on whomever He wills of His servants. So it is not unlikely that He honours us for our deeds as He honours you for your deeds. It is as if He obliged them, on every path they follow, to be silenced and rebuked. For the honour of prophethood is either a bounty from God Most High upon whomever He wills, in which case all are equal in it, or it is the outpouring of a right upon those deserving it by persistence in obedience and adornment with sincerity. Just as you have deeds which God Most High may take into account in bestowing what He bestows, so we too have deeds, and we are sincere to Him, not you.

Yet, apart from its incompatibility with the context of the noble composition and its flow, especially if "أم" is a correlative to the hamza, it is in itself invalid, because the deeds referred to from both parties are the righteous and evil deeds that have been indicated. There is no doubt that the matter of righteousness and evil revolves around conformity to the religion founded on the mission (ba'tha) and opposition to it. How then can those deeds be considered as grounds for entitlement to prophethood, and as a preparation for it that precedes the mission by degrees?

﴿Say: are you more knowing or is God?﴾ The repetition of the command is not merely to emphasise the rebuke and intensify the denunciation against them, but to signal that what follows is not directly connected to what precedes; rather, between them there is a statement by the addressees, consequent upon what came before and leading to what follows, which has been omitted for being obvious. It is their declaration of what they were rebuked for, namely slandering the Prophets, upon them be peace. This is like His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿He said, "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Then what is your business, O messengers?"﴾; and His saying, Mighty is He, speaking: ﴿He said, "Shall I prostrate to one whom You created from clay?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Have you considered this one whom You have honoured over me?"﴾. The repetition of "قال" (qala, "he said") in both places, and its insertion between the two sayings of a single speaker, signals that between them there is a statement by its speaker related to the first and the second by way of consequence and sequel, as has been explained in its place. That is: He (God) refuted them in that claim and rebuked them, saying: ﴿Indeed God knows, and you do not know.﴾

He has also cleared Abraham, upon him be peace, of both matters, when he said: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian.﴾ and he was argued against with His saying, Most High: ﴿And the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him.﴾ Those mentioned alongside him, upon him be peace, are his followers in religion by consensus. So how can you say what you say? Glory be to God above what you describe.

﴿And who is more unjust﴾: a denial that anyone could be more unjust; ﴿than one who conceals a testimony﴾ that is established; ﴿with him﴾; existing; ﴿from God﴾. It is His testimony to him, upon him be peace, of being upright (hanifiyya) and of freedom from Judaism and Christianity, as was recited just before. So "عنده" ('indahu, "with him") is a descriptive of "شهادة" (shahada, "testimony"); and likewise "من الله" (min Allah, "from God"). Both were brought to give the reason for the denial and to emphasise it, for the establishment of the testimony with him and its being from the side of God, Mighty and Majestic, is among the strongest motives for upholding it and the sternest deterrents against concealing it. The first is placed before the second, though it is later in existence, to observe the method of ascent from the lower to the higher. The meaning is that there is no one more unjust than the People of the Book, since they concealed this testimony and affirmed its opposite by what has been mentioned of slander. Linking the greatest injustice to mere concealment is to imply that the rank of one who rejects it and testifies to its contrary in injustice lies beyond the scope of explanation. Or the meaning is: there is no one more unjust than us if we concealed it. So by concealing it is meant not establishing it in the place of disputation. This contains an allusion to the utmost injustice of the People of the Book, in the manner indicated.

In applying the word "testimony" while the intended meaning is the specific testimony mentioned, there is an allusion to their concealment of God's testimony, Mighty and Majestic, to the Prophet ﷺ in the Torah and the Gospel.

﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾: of kinds of evil deeds. So their concealment of His testimony, glorified is He, and their slandering of the Prophets, upon them be the blessings and peace, enter it at the first level. That is: He encompasses all that you do and all that you leave undone, and so He will punish you for that with the sternest punishment.

It has been read as "عما يعملون" ('amma ya'malun, "of what they do"), in the third-person form. Then the pronoun refers either to "من كتم" (man katama, "one who concealed") according to meaning, or to the People of the Book.

His saying, Most High: ﴿And who is more unjust﴾, through to the end of the verse, is directed from Him, Most High, to describe them with the utmost injustice and to threaten them with the warning.

This is a commentary passage on verse 141 of Surah al-Baqarah, and I will translate it as it stands.

﴿That is a community that has passed away; theirs is what they earned, and yours is what you earn; and you will not be questioned about what they used to do.﴾: This is a repetition for the sake of emphasis in rebuking them for their boasting of their forefathers and their reliance upon their own deeds. It has been said: the address preceding it was to them, and this is for us, as a warning against following their example. It has also been said: what is meant by the first community are the Prophets (peace be upon them), and by the second, the predecessors of the Jews.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 142:**

﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾: i.e., those whose minds are light, who have made their intellects cheap through blind imitation (taqlid), turning away from reflection and consideration. This is from the expression "a foolish garment" (thawb safih), when it is thin in its weave. It was also said: the safih is the one who lies and fabricates, who deliberately contradicts what he knows. It was also said: the one who is wrongdoing and ignorant. By "the foolish" are meant the Jews, as is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, may God be pleased with them, who said this in denial of abrogation (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by another) and out of dislike of the change, since they were content with the Prophet's agreement with them regarding the qiblah (the direction of prayer). It was also said: they are the hypocrites, and this is the most fitting reading in light of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Surely they are the foolish﴾. They only said it for the sake of mockery and defamation, not because they believed the former qiblah to be true and the latter to be false, since not all of them were Jews. It was also said: they are the polytheists, who did not say it out of dislike of the change to Makkah, but as an attack on the religion, for they used to say: "He has turned away from the qiblah of his fathers, then returned, and he will surely return to their religion too." It was also said: they are those who criticize the change among all of them. In that case, His words, exalted is He, ﴿from among the people﴾, i.e., the disbelievers, serve to clarify that this statement reported here did not come from every individual of those three groups, but from their wretched ones who habitually engage in every kind of corruption. This is the most apparent reading, for if by them were meant a particular sub-group, the statement that they are "from among the people" would add little benefit. Specifying their foolish ones by mention does not imply that the rest accepted the change or approved of it, rather it implies the absence of any utterance of criticism at all, or of the reported words.

﴿What has turned them﴾: i.e., what has diverted them? The interrogative is for denial and negation.

﴿from their qiblah﴾: The qiblah is a form (fi'lah) derived from "facing" (al-muqabalah), like wijhah from "confronting" (al-muwajahah). It is the state in which one thing faces another, just as jilsah denotes the manner in which sitting occurs. One says: "He has neither qiblah nor dibrah," meaning he has not been guided to the direction of his affair. The term became dominant for the direction a person faces in prayer. Here it refers to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Its attribution to the pronoun of the Muslims, and its description by His words, exalted is He: ﴿which they used to follow﴾, meaning that they were steadfast and persistent in facing it, observing it, and believing in its truth, serves to emphasize the denial. For devotion to a thing and persistence in it out of belief in its truth is incompatible with turning away from it. If by the speakers are meant the Jews, then the basis of the denial is their dislike of turning away from it and their claim that the turning is an error. If by them are meant the polytheists, then the basis is merely the intention to attack the religion and disparage its rulings, and to show that both facing it and turning away from it occur without any motive, not because they dislike turning away from it or turning toward Makkah. The denial is attached to what turns them away from it, rather than to what directs them to another, although the two are concomitant in existence, because abandoning an old religion is more distant from reason, and denying its cause is more fitting. This is not to indicate that the deniers are the Jews, on the basis that what they find objectionable is the change from the particular sanctity of Bayt al-Maqdis, which is for them the true qiblah, and not the facing toward the particular sanctity of another qiblah. Nor is it to indicate that they are the polytheists, on the basis that what they find objectionable is abandoning the old qiblah in a manner of attack and disparagement, rather than facing the Ka'bah, since that is the truth in their view. Indeed, how could this be, when the hypocrites are, without doubt, from one of the two groups? The announcement of this before it occurred, although it is among the signs of prophethood since it happened just as he had announced, serves to settle the souls and prepare what will confound them, for the sudden arrival of something hateful upon the soul is harder and more severe, and a ready answer to the clamor of the most stubborn adversary is more effective in repelling it.

﴿Say: To God belong the east and the west﴾: This is a resumptive sentence built upon the question, as if it were said: "What shall I then say in response?" So it was said: "Say..." etc. I.e., to God, exalted is He, belong the two sides of the earth, i.e., all directions, in ownership, dominion, and disposition. Therefore no one side has any special status in itself as a qiblah to the exclusion of others. Rather, it is by the command of God, glorified is He, and His will.

﴿He guides whom He wills﴾: to guide him, by a will that follows hidden wisdoms known to none but Him,

﴿to a straight path﴾: one that leads to the happiness of both abodes. He has guided us to this, in that He commanded us to face Bayt al-Maqdis at one time and the Ka'bah at another, according to what His will requires, accompanied by decisive wisdoms and hidden benefits.

﴿And thus We have made you﴾: this is a turning of the address to the believers, placed between the two addresses directed specifically to the Messenger ﷺ, to reinforce the honor implied in the content of the speech. "Dhalika" ("thus/that") is a pointer to the verbal noun (masdar) of "ja'alnakum" ("We have made you"), not to some other making understood from what preceded, as has been said. The kaf (the "ka" of "dhalika") is singular even though the intended addressees are the believers, because the purpose is merely to distinguish the present from the past, without specifying the addressees. The sense of distance in it indicates the exalted rank of the one pointed to, the remoteness of his station in excellence, the completeness of his distinction, and his being placed by means of it within the line of notable matters. The kaf serves to emphasize the grandeur already conveyed by the demonstrative noun. Its original position is the accusative, as an adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun, and the original estimate is: "We have made you a middle community (ummatan wasatan), a making that is like that making," so it was placed before the verb to convey restriction (qasr). The kaf was regarded as an intensifier (muqhamah), for the reason mentioned, so it became the very verbal noun being emphasized, not an adjective of it. That is: "That wondrous making, We have made you [a middle community]," not some other making lower than it.

"Wasat" (middle) originally is a name for that which the relations of its sides are equal to, like the center of a circle. Then it was borrowed for praiseworthy human qualities, but not because the extremes are quickly subject to defect and deprivation, while the middles are protected and guarded, as has been said. It is cited as evidence for this by the verse of Ibn Aws al-Ta'i:

"She was the protected middle, until calamities surrounded her, until she became an extreme."

That association is of no account in this context, since there is no connection between it and the eligibility for testimony, which was made the goal of the mentioned making. Rather, these qualities are middles between the blameworthy qualities that surround them from the two extremes of excess and deficiency, such as chastity, whose extremes are debauchery and insensibility; courage, whose extremes are recklessness and cowardice; wisdom, whose extremes are cunning and dullness; and justice, which is a balanced state resulting from the combination of those middles surrounded by their extremes. Then the term was applied to the one who possesses them, as an intensification, as if he were those qualities themselves. It is used in the same form for singular, plural, masculine and feminine, observing the original form, like the practice with all other attributive names.

Here a delightful point has been observed: the making referred to is an expression of what was mentioned earlier, namely His (exalted be He) guidance to the truth, which He expressed by the "straight path," which is the upright road, lying in the middle of the crooked roads that deviate from the aim to the sides. For if we draw many lines joining two opposite points, the straight line is the one lying in the middle of those curved lines. And by necessity of its being a middle between the crooked roads, the community guided to it is a middle community among the nations that travel the deviant roads; that is, characterized by praiseworthy qualities, choice, just, and purified by knowledge and action.

﴿That you may be witnesses over mankind﴾: that God, Mighty and Majestic, has made clear the ways and sent the messengers, so they conveyed, advised and reminded; "Is there any who will remember?" This is the goal of the mentioned making, consequent upon it. For justice, as has been indicated, being the balanced state composed of chastity, which is the virtue of the animal appetitive faculty; courage, which is the virtue of the beastly irascible faculty; and wisdom, which is the virtue of the angelic rational faculty, whose rank is indicated by His saying, Mighty and Exalted: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has been given much good﴾. The one characterized by these is standing upon the realities deposited in the Clear Book, which contains the rulings of religion and the conditions of all nations, qualified to meet the requirements of testimony over them.

It is reported that on the Day of Resurrection the nations will deny that the prophets, peace be upon them, conveyed the message. God (exalted be He) will then demand proof from them, to establish the argument against the deniers and to increase their humiliation, by having later nations accuse them. The community of Muhammad ﷺ will be brought and will testify. The nations will say: "How do you know?" They will say: "We knew it through God's informing in His explicit Book, upon the tongue of His truthful Prophet." Then the Prophet ﷺ will be brought at that time and asked about the state of his community; he will vouch for them and bear witness to their justice. This is His saying, Mighty and Speaking: ﴿And the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾.

The word "ʿalā" (over) is used because the witness has the meaning of an observer and a guardian. It has been said: "That you may be witnesses over mankind in this world, regarding matters in which testimony is accepted only from the upright just." The fronting of the adverbial phrase indicates that his testimony, upon him be blessings and peace, is specific to them.

﴿And We did not make the qibla which you were facing﴾: the address was made purely to the Prophet ﷺ, as a symbol that the content of the speech is among the true secrets, such that its knowledge should be specific to him, upon him be blessings and peace. The relative pronoun is not an attribute of "the qibla," but is the second object of "made." What has been said, that making is transforming a thing from one state to another, so that what is connected with the second state is the second object, as in your saying: "I made the clay pottery," would require that the first object be the relative clause and the second be "the qibla." That is an artificial construction that the mind follows according to a superficial view; but proper reflection leads to the reverse. For the intended meaning is not merely making the direction a qibla, as what has been mentioned indicates; rather it is making the actually existing qibla this direction and not another. The relative pronoun refers to the Ka'ba. For he, upon him be blessings and peace, used to pray toward it at first; then, when he migrated, he was commanded to pray toward the rock (Bayt al-Maqdis), to win over the Jews. Or it refers to the rock, in accordance with what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that his qibla, upon him be blessings and peace, while in Mecca was Bayt al-Maqdis, except that he would place the Ka'ba between himself and it. On this report it is not possible for the first qibla to be meant as the Ka'ba; but the rock can be meant on both reports. The meaning on the first view: "We did not make the qibla the direction which you were facing," the most preferred direction, which is the Ka'ba; and on the second: "We did not make it the one which you faced before this time," which is the rock.

﴿Except that We might know﴾: this is an exceptive construction lacking its object (istithna' mufarragh, an exception with no stated excluded item) from the most general of causes; that is: "We did not make that for anything among things, except that We might test people," that is, deal with them as one who tests them, "and know then ﴿who follows the Messenger﴾" in turning toward what he was commanded of the religion, or of the qibla. The shift to the third person, along with mentioning him, upon him be blessings and peace, by the title of messengership, is to indicate the reason for following: ﴿from him who turns back on his heels﴾, who apostatizes from the religion of Islam, or does not turn toward the new qibla. Or: "that We may now know who follows the Messenger from among those who do not follow him." This was for a circumstance which ends when it ends.

On the first interpretation: "We did not return you to what you were upon except that We might know the steadfast in Islam from the one who recoils on his heels because of his unease and weakness of faith." The knowledge meant is the present knowledge around which the sphere of reward revolves; that is, so that Our knowledge may relate to it as an actual existing matter. It has been said that what is meant is the knowledge of the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, and the believers, and its attribution to Him, glorified be He, is because they are His elect. Or: "that the steadfast may be distinguished from the wavering," like His saying (exalted be He): ﴿That God may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾. So knowledge is put in place of distinction, which is its consequence. The reading "li-yu'lama" (in the passive) supports this. "Knowledge" here is either in the sense of recognition, or it is connected with what is in "man" of the meaning of interrogation, or its second object is "from him who turns back..." etc.; that is: "that We may know who follows the Messenger, distinguished from him who turns back on his heels."

﴿And indeed it was difficult﴾: that is, burdensome and heavy. "In" here is the light form of the heavy "inna," entering upon the abrogator of the subject and predicate, and the lam is the one distinguishing it from the negative "in" (ma), as in His saying (exalted be He): ﴿If the promise of our Lord was indeed fulfilled﴾. The Kufans claimed that it is negative, and the lam means "illa" (except), so the meaning is: "it was only great." The pronoun which is the subject of "kana" refers to what is indicated by His saying (exalted be He): ﴿And We did not make the qibla which you were facing﴾, of the making, the turning, the changing, the apostasy, or the qibla. It is read "la-kabirah" (feminine) and also "la-kabirat" (with raising), taking "kana" as superfluous, as in the verse:

"...and brothers of ours who were noble."

Its original form is: "indeed it is great," like "in Zayd la-muntaliq" (indeed Zayd is leaving).

﴿Except upon those whom God has guided﴾: that is, to the secret of the legal rulings, which are founded on wisdoms and benefits, both generally and in detail; and they are those guided to the straight path, who stand firm upon faith and in following the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace.

﴿And God would not have caused your faith to be lost﴾: that is, it is not right for Him, nor does it befit Him, that He should cause your steadfastness upon faith to be lost; rather He appreciated your conduct and prepared for you a great reward. It has also been said: "your faith" refers to your belief in the abrogated qibla and your prayer toward it. For it is reported that when he, upon him be blessings and peace, turned toward the Ka'ba, they said: "How are our brothers who have passed away, who prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis?" So this was revealed.

The "li" in "li-yudi'a" is either connected to the presumed predicate of "kana," as is the view of the Basrans, and the verb after it is in the accusative by an understood "an" (that): meaning "God was not willing, nor disposed, to cause to be lost..." So placing the negation on the willing of the act contains emphasis and intensification not present in negating the act itself. Or it is superfluous for emphasis, governing the verb directly by itself, as is the view of the Kufans; and its being superfluous does not detract from its governing, just as the superfluity of prepositions does not detract from their governing.

His saying (exalted be He): ﴿Indeed God is, toward mankind, Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾: this is a confirmation and establishment of the ruling, and its reason.
