For His being characterized by these two, Mighty and Majestic, necessarily requires that He not waste their rewards and not leave what is good for them. The "bi" is connected with "Ra'uf" (Most Kind). Its being placed before "Rahim" (Most Merciful), even though it is more intensive, is for the reason already explained concerning the placing of "al-Rahman" before "al-Rahim." It has been said: mercy is greater than kindness in quantity, while kindness is stronger in quality, because kindness is the bestowal of blessings free of pains, whereas mercy is the bestowal of blessing absolutely, which may occur together with pain, such as amputating a decaying limb. It is also read "Ra'uf" without the long vowel, like "Nadus."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 144:

﴿We see the turning of your face toward the heaven﴾: that is, its fluctuation, and the shifting of your gaze toward its direction, eagerly awaiting revelation. This was because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would have thoughts arise in his heart, and he would expect from his Lord, mighty and majestic, that He would turn him toward the Ka'bah, because it is the qibla of Ibrahim (peace be upon him); and because it would be more compelling for the Arabs to believe, since it is their pride, their place of visitation, and their place of circumambulation; and to oppose the Jews. So he would watch for the descent of Jibril with the revelation of the change. ﴿So We shall surely turn you to a qiblah﴾: the fa' (fa, "so") indicates the causal link of what precedes to what follows; and in reality it is attached to an omitted oath, indicated by the lam; that is: "By Allah, We shall surely turn you"; that is: We shall surely give it to you, and enable you to face it; from your saying "I made him governor (wallaytuhu kadha)", that is: I made him its governor; or: We shall surely make you take charge of its direction; or: We shall surely change you (lanuhawwilannaka). In that case, the accusative of "qiblatan" is by the omission of the preposition, that is, "toward a qiblah." It has also been said that it is transitive to two objects. ﴿That you are pleased with﴾: you love it and long for it, for religious purposes that accorded with His will (exalted is He) and His wisdom. ﴿So turn your face﴾: the fa' is for deriving the command to turn from the gracious promise; and the specifying of turning with the face is because it is the axis of facing and its measure. It has also been said that what is meant is the whole body; that is: turn it. ﴿Toward the Sacred Mosque﴾: that is, toward it. It is in the accusative as an adverb of place with "walli," or by removing the preposition, or as a second object of it. It has been said: the shatr (side) is originally a noun for what is separated from a thing, and "dar shatur" is a house separated from the other houses; then it was used for its side even if it is not separated, like "al-qutr." And al-haram is the forbidden (muharram), that is: fighting is forbidden in it, or it is protected from the oppressors so that they may not molest it. The mention of "the Sacred Mosque" rather than "the Ka'bah" signifies that observing the direction suffices, because observing the exact point from afar would be a great hardship, unlike someone nearby. It is related from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib that "the Prophet of Allah ﷺ came to Madinah and prayed facing Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen months; then he was turned toward the Ka'bah." It has also been said that this occurred in Rajab, after the sun had declined, about two months before the Battle of Badr; and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in (p-175) the Mosque of Banu Salamah, and he had led his companions in two rak'ahs of the Zuhr prayer; then he turned during the prayer and faced the spout (al-mizab), and the men were moved to the women's place and the women to the men's place; so the mosque was named "the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs." ﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾: the Messenger ﷺ was singled out for the address, to honor his presence and to indicate the granting of his desire; then the address was generalized to the believers, with mention of the difference of their places, to affirm the ruling and to make explicit its generality for all servants, from every settled person and nomad; and to urge the community to follow. "Haythuma" is conditional; and "kuntum" is in a jussive position governed by it; and His saying (exalted is He): ﴿fa-wallu﴾ is its response. It may also be that it is in the accusative as an adverb of place governed by "kuntum," like His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾.

﴿And indeed those who were given the Book﴾: from both groups, the Jews and the Christians; ﴿surely know that it﴾: that is, the change; or: the turning, understood from the act of turning; ﴿is the truth﴾, and nothing else; because of their knowledge that His custom (glory be to Him and exalted) is to assign each law a qiblah, and their witnessing what is written in their books, that he ﷺ would pray toward both qiblahs, as the expression of them by the relative noun with the giving of the Book indicates. "Anna" together with its noun and predicate stands in place of the two objects of "ya'lamun," or in place of its single object, on the basis that "ilm" here means ma'rifah (recognition). His saying (exalted is He): ﴿from their Lord﴾ is connected to an omitted element that falls as a circumstantial clause from "al-haqq," that is: existing from their Lord; or it is a qualifier of it according to the view of one who permits omitting the relative pronoun together with part of its clause, that is: the one existing from their Lord. ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾: a promise and a warning to both groups; and the address is to all, by way of dominance; and it has been read in the third-person form, so it is a warning to the People of the Book.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 145:**

﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Book every sign﴾: He placed the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") in the place of the pronoun (al-mudmar) to indicate the complete wickedness of their state in obstinacy, while the Book that testifies to the truth of what they stubbornly refused to accept is established for them. ﴿Every sign﴾: that is, every decisive proof, indicating the reality of the change of direction. The lam (al-lam) is a preparatory lam (muwatti'a) for the oath. And His saying, ﴿they would not follow your qibla﴾, is the answer to the implied oath, standing in place of the answer to the conditional (sadd masadd jawab al-shart). The meaning is that they did not abandon your qibla because of a doubt that proof could remove, but they opposed you only out of stubborn denial and obstinacy. The address is directed specifically to the Prophet (ﷺ) after it had been generalized to the community, because argumentation and bringing forth a sign are among the functions specific to him (peace be upon him).

And His saying, ﴿Nor are you a follower of their qibla﴾: is a clause coordinated (ma'tufa) upon the conditional clause, not upon its answer. It is sent to cut off their empty hopes, since the Jews said: "If he remains upon our qibla, we would hope that he is the one we are waiting for," as a deception of him (peace be upon him) and in hope of his return. The use of the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) indicates the permanence and continuity of its content. The singular "qiblatahum" is used although they are many, considering their unity in falsehood and opposition to the truth, and so that it is not imagined that the basis of the negation is plurality. It was also read as "bitabi'i qiblatihim" with an idafa (construct). ﴿Nor are some of them followers of the qibla of others﴾: for the Jews face the Rock and the Christians face the rising of the sun, and there is no hope of their agreement, just as there is no hope of their agreement with you, because each group is rigid in what it holds.

﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾: the deviant and conflicting ones, ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾: of their falsehood and of the truth of what you are upon. This hypothetical conditional is presented in the manner of incitement and stirring up, for steadfastness upon the truth. That is: "And if you were to follow their desires, supposing it," ﴿then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers﴾. In it there is gentleness toward the listeners and a warning to them against following desire, for whoever is not of such a character, when he is forbidden from it, and when there is placed upon the supposition of its occurrence what is placed of being included in the line of those firmly rooted in wrongdoing, then what is the assumption about one who is not like that?

The word "idhan" (idhan) is a particle of response and consequence. It is placed between the subject of "inna" and its predicate to establish the relation between them, since its proper place would be to come first or last. It was not placed first, so that it is not imagined that it establishes the relation between the condition and its omitted answer, because what is mentioned is the answer of the oath. It was not placed last for the sake of the rhyme (fawasil). Emphasis has been multiplied in several respects, to magnify the known truth, to encourage adherence to it, to warn against following desire, and to magnify the occurrence of sin from the prophets (peace be upon them).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 146:

﴿Those whom We have given the Book﴾: that is, their scholars, since they are the mainstay in its transmission. The placing of the relative pronoun (al-ladhina, "those who") in the place of the pronoun, despite the proximity of the antecedent, serves to indicate that what follows the relative clause (silah) is the cause of the judgment. The pronoun in the accusative in His words, exalted is He: ﴿they recognize him﴾, refers to the Messenger ﷺ. The shift to the third person (iltifat ila al-ghaybah) signifies that what is meant is not their recognition of him ﷺ in terms of his person and his illustrious lineage, but rather in terms of his being written down in the Book, described therein with the attributes among which is that he ﷺ prays toward both qiblahs. It is as if it were said: Those whom We have given the Book recognize the one whom We have described in it. With this the eloquence of the noble composition becomes apparent. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the antecedent mentioned before it, to indicate the great stature of his ﷺ status, that he is a known knowledge without need of informing; so reflect. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the knowledge (al-'ilm), or its cause which is the revelation (al-wahy), or the Qur'an, or the change of qiblah (al-tahwil). The first view is supported by His words, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿as they recognize their sons﴾; that is, they recognize him ﷺ by his noble attributes written in their Book, and he is not confused for them just as their sons are not confused for them. Their being singled out for mention, rather than what includes daughters too, is because they are better known to them than the females, owing to their being more beloved to them. From Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he asked Abdullah ibn Salam, may Allah be pleased with him, about the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: "I know him better than I know my son." He said: "And why?" He said: "Because I have no doubt about him that he is a prophet; as for my child, perhaps his mother betrayed." Then Umar kissed his head, may Allah be pleased with them both.

﴿Indeed, a party of them surely conceal the truth while they know﴾: they are those who were arrogant and obstinate toward the truth. The rest of them are those among them who believed; for they make the truth manifest and do not conceal it. As for the ignorant among them, they have no knowledge of the Book nor of what is within its contents; so they are neither in a position to manifest nor in a position to conceal it. Their disbelief is rather by way of imitation (taqlid).

The truth [is] from your Lord (al-Haqq): with the nominative (raf'), on the basis that it is a subject (mubtada'); and His saying (Exalted is He): "from your Lord" is its predicate (khabar). The lam is for specificity (al-'ahd), indicating what the Prophet (ﷺ) is upon, or indicating the truth that they conceal; or it is for the genus (al-jins), and the meaning is that the truth is whatever has been established as being from God (Exalted is He), like that which you are upon, and not otherwise, like that upon which the People of the Book are. Or it is on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is the truth." His saying (Exalted is He): "from your Lord" is either a circumstantial clause (hal) or a predicate after a predicate. It has also been read in the accusative (nasb), on the basis that it is a substitute (badal) for the first, or an object (maf'ul) of "they know."

In the mention of the attribute of lordship (rububiyya), together with its being attached to his pronoun (peace and blessings be upon him), there is a manifestation of kindness toward him (peace and blessings be upon him) that is not hidden.

"So do not be of those who doubt" (fa-la takunanna min al-mumtarin): i.e., those who are doubtful about their concealment of the truth, while knowing it. It has been said: [the doubt is] about its being from your Lord; and the intended meaning is not the prohibition of the Messenger (ﷺ) from doubt concerning it, because that is not to be expected from him (peace and blessings be upon him), and it is not by intention or choice. Rather, it is either the confirmation of the matter, and that it is such that no beholder would doubt it, or the command to the Ummah to acquire the knowledge that removes doubt, in the most emphatic manner.

﴿And for each﴾, i.e., for each of the nations, on the basis that the *tanwin* (nunation, the ending "-n" on the noun) is a substitute (*'iwad*) for the noun in the genitive that was added to it. ﴿Direction﴾, i.e., *qiblah* (the direction of prayer). It has also been read this way. Or: for each group of Muslims there is a side of the Ka'bah. ﴿He is turning toward it﴾: one of the two objects is omitted, i.e., "turning toward it his face," or "God is turning them toward it." It has also been read as "wa-li-kulli wijhatin" (with the noun in the genitive), with the meaning: "For every direction God is the one who turns toward it its people." The *lam* is additional, for emphasis and to compensate for the weakness of the governing word. It has also been read as "mawlaha," i.e., the lord of that direction, who has taken charge of it. ﴿So race to the good deeds﴾, i.e., hasten to them, with the preposition dropped, as in the verse of the poet:

"My praise be upon you, family of Harb, and whoever inclines to other than you, then I am guided and not inclining."

This is more emphatic than a command to hasten, because it encourages winning the prize of precedence. By "the good deeds" is meant all their kinds, including the matter of the *qiblah* and other things by which the happiness of both abodes is attained. Or it means the most excellent directions, which are those facing the Ka'bah directly. ﴿Wherever you may be, God will bring you all together﴾, i.e., wherever you are, whether in agreement or opposition, whether your parts are gathered or scattered, God (Exalted) will gather you to the place of assembly for recompense. Or: wherever you are, from the depths of the earth or the peaks of the mountains, He will take your souls. Or: wherever you are, from the various and opposite directions, He will make your prayers like a prayer toward one direction. ﴿Indeed God is over all things Powerful﴾, so He is able to cause death, to give life, and to gather; this is therefore a justification for the preceding ruling.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 149:

﴿And from wherever you set out﴾: an emphasis on the ruling of turning (the face), and an explicit statement that the command does not differ between the two states of travel and residence. The "min" (from) is connected to His (exalted) saying: ﴿then turn﴾; or to an implied element, to which this phrase is conjoined; that is: from whatever place you go out to for travel, then turn; ﴿your face﴾ during your prayer; ﴿toward the Sacred Mosque﴾; or: do what you have been commanded from whatever place you set out, then turn... etc.

﴿And indeed it﴾; that is, this command; ﴿is the truth from your Lord﴾; that is: the established, the one that accords with wisdom; ﴿and Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾; so He will reward you for that with the best of rewards. This is a promise to the believers. It has also been read as "ya'malūna" (they do), in the third-person form, and then it is a warning to the disbelievers.

"And from wherever you set out"—(to it) on your journeys and your expeditions, from near and far dwellings—"then turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque." The discussion of this is as has passed just now. "And wherever you are"—from the regions of the earth, whether residing or travelling—as is indicated by the choice of "you are" (kuntum) over "you set out" (kharajtum), for the address is general to all the believers spread across the horizons, both those present and those travelling. For if it had been said, "And wherever you set out," the address would not have covered those residing in the various places, from where they reside; "then turn your faces"—from your places—"towards it." The repetition is because the qibla has a grave matter, and abrogation is a place of doubt and trial; so it is fitting that its matter be emphasised once after another, although each time he mentioned a separate wisdom.

"So that people will have no argument against you": this is connected to His saying "then turn," and it was said that it is connected to an omitted element indicated by the discourse, as if it was said: "We did that so that..." etc. The meaning is that turning away from the Rock repels the argument of the Jews, that the one described in the Torah, among whose attributes is that he will be turned towards the Ka'bah; and the argument of the polytheists, that he claims the creed of Abraham while opposing his qibla. "Except those of them who do wrong"—and they are the people of Mecca—meaning: so that no one among the people will have an argument, except the obstinate among them, who say: "He only turned to the Ka'bah out of inclination to the religion of his people and love of his land, or a new view occurred to him and he returned to the qibla of his fathers, and he will soon return to their religion." Calling this shameful saying an "argument," though it is the most foul of falsehoods, is of the same kind as in His saying: "their argument is void" (Qur'an 42:16), where they treated it as though it were an argument. It was also said that "argument" here means mere arguing in general; and it was said that the exception serves to emphasise the complete negation of argument, like the one in the verse of poetry:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords have notches from the clashing of battalions."

Since the wrongdoer has no argument. It was also read "Ala alladhina" with the particle of alerting, which makes it a resumption. "So do not fear them": for their reproaches will not harm you at all. "And fear Me": so do not oppose My command. "And that I may complete My favour upon you and that you may be guided": this is a cause of an omitted element indicated by the noble structure; that is: and I commanded you with what has passed, in order to complete the favour upon you, since it is a great blessing, and because of My will that you be guided to the straight path, which leads to the happiness of both abodes, as alluded to in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: "He guides whom He wills to a straight path" (Qur'an 2:213). In expressing the will by the word "la'alla" (perhaps), which is set for hope, by way of subsequent metaphor, there is (a meaning) of utmost care for guidance that is not hidden. Or it is coordinated with an assumed cause, that is: "and fear Me, so that I may protect you from them; and [that I may] complete..." etc. Or it is coordinated with His saying, "so that there will not be," and the interposition of His saying "so do not fear them" etc. between them is for hastening to consolation and reassurance.

It is in a report: "The completion of the favour is entry into Paradise." And from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "The completion of the favour is dying upon Islam."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 151:

﴿Just as We sent among you a messenger from among yourselves﴾: This is connected to what precedes it. The first adverbial phrase (*zarf*) is attached to the verb (*fi'l*, verb). It is placed before its direct object (*maf'ul sarih*, direct object) because of the length of the qualifiers that follow. The second adverbial phrase is attached to an implied verb that functions as a qualifier (*sifa*) of "messenger" (*rasulan*). It clarifies the completion of the blessing, meaning: "And so that I may complete My blessing upon you concerning the matter of the qibla, or in the Hereafter, with a completion like My completion of it by sending a messenger who is from among you." The sending of a messenger, especially one of their own kind, is a blessing that no other blessing can ever equal. It has also been said that this is connected to what follows it, meaning: "Just as you were reminded through the sending, remember Me... etc." The use of the first-person plural form (*sighat al-mutakallim ma'a al-ghayr*, "We") after the singular form used earlier is a stylistic variation (*iftinan*, artistic variation) and a conforming to the manner of divine majesty (*kibriya'*).

﴿who recites to you Our verses﴾: A second qualifier of "messenger", revealing the perfection of the blessing.

﴿and purifies you﴾: A conjunction (*'atf*) on "recites". It means: he leads you to that by which you become pure (*azkiya'*).

﴿and teaches you the Book and the wisdom﴾: Another qualifier, which in existence follows the recitation. The purification (*tazkiya*), which is an expression for the perfecting of the soul according to the practical faculty (*al-quwwa al-'amaliyya*), and its refinement which branches from its perfecting according to the theoretical faculty (*al-quwwa al-nazariyya*), which is attained through teaching that follows from the recitation, has been placed between them. This signals that each of these matters that follow is a great blessing in its own right, deserving of gratitude. Had the order of existence been observed, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses, and teach them the Book and the wisdom, and purify them. Indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾, the understanding would immediately take the whole to be one blessing. A similar case was mentioned in the story of the cow. This is the secret behind the Qur'an being referred to sometimes as "verses" and at other times as "the Book and the wisdom", indicating that each title represents a separate blessing. The inclusion of the legal rulings (*shara'i'*) found within the noble hadiths within the scope of wisdom (*hikma*) does not detract from this.

As for His saying, (Mighty and Majestic is He): ﴿and teaches you what you did not know﴾: it is explicit on this point. The relative clause, although it definitely refers to the Book and the wisdom, has its teaching conjoined to the teaching of these two. This is only for the detailing of the varieties of blessings in a context that calls for it, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And We saved them from a severe punishment﴾, following His saying (exalted is He): ﴿We saved Hud and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us﴾. The meaning of their not knowing is that it is not within their capacity to know it through reflection (*fikr*), contemplation (*nazar*), or other means of knowledge, since the only path is revelation (*wahy*).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 152:

﴿So remember Me⦆: The fa' (fa) indicates the consequence of the command upon what precedes it of its requirements; that is: so remember Me with obedience; ﴿I will remember you﴾: with reward; this is an exhortation to remembrance, together with an indication of what necessitates it; ﴿and be grateful to Me﴾: for the blessings I have bestowed upon you of favours; ﴿and do not be ungrateful to Me﴾: by denying them, and by disobeying what I have commanded you.

﴿O you who believe﴾: He described them with faith right after listing what faith requires and entails, to energize them and to urge them to observe what follows in the command: ﴿seek help﴾ in everything you do and everything you refrain from, ﴿through patience﴾ in matters that are burdensome to the self, among which is opposing the disbelievers and confronting them in a way that leads to fighting them, ﴿and prayer﴾, which is the mother of the acts of worship, the ascent (mi'raj) of the believers, and the intimate conversation with the Lord of the worlds.

﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾: This is a justification (ta'lil) for the command to seek help specifically through patience, since it is the part that needs justification. As for prayer, since it is among the most exalted aims for the believers, as indicated by the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): "And the coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer," the command to seek help through it did not need justification. The meaning of "with" (ma'iyyah) is constant guardianship, which entails victory and the answering of supplication. The use of "ma'a" (with) before "the patient" is because they are the ones who truly practise patience, so they are the ones followed in that respect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 154:

﴿And do not say﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "seek help…" (istaʿīnū); etc. It is brought to explain that there is no harm (ghā'ila) for what one is commanded to do, and that martyrdom, to which patience may sometimes lead, is an everlasting life; ﴿concerning those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead"﴾; i.e., they are dead; ﴿Rather, they are alive﴾; i.e., rather, they are alive; ﴿but you do not perceive﴾ their life. In this there is an indication that it is not something perceived by the apparent senses of physical life; rather, it is a spiritual matter that is not grasped by reason but by revelation. It is also reported from al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, that the martyrs are alive with Allah (Exalted), their provisions being presented to their spirits, so that comfort and joy reach them, just as the Fire is presented to the people of Pharaoh morning and evening, so that pain and suffering reach them. I say: I saw in a dream, in the year (p-180) 939 AH, that I was visiting the graves of the martyrs of Uhud, may Allah (Exalted) be pleased with them all, while I was reciting this verse and what is in Surat Al 'Imran, repeating them while reflecting on their condition, and in my mind was the thought that their life is spiritual, not physical. While I was in that state, I saw a young man among them sitting in his grave, whole of body, complete in form, in the best of appearance and aspect, wearing no clothing, such that what was above the navel was exposed, and the rest was in the grave; except that I knew with certainty that the rest was also as it appeared, but it was not visible because it is a private part (ʿawra). I looked at his face and saw him looking at me smiling, as if alerting me that the matter was contrary to my opinion. Glory be to Him whose word is exalted and whose wisdom is majestic. It was said: the verse was revealed concerning the martyrs of Badr, who numbered fourteen. In it is evidence that the souls are substances subsisting in themselves, distinct from the body that is perceived by the senses, remaining after death perceptive; and this is the view of the majority of the Companions and the Successors (al-Tabiʿūn), may Allah's good pleasure be upon them all. The verses and the Sunnah speak to this. On this basis, the specification of the martyrs with this (status) is due to what the context of exhortation to undertake the beginnings of martyrdom requires, and because of their being singled out for greater nearness to Allah, Mighty and Exalted.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verses 155–156:**

﴿And We will surely test you﴾: We will afflict you as one who tests your conditions afflicts you: will you be patient in the face of trial, and will you submit to the decree? ﴿With something of fear and hunger﴾: that is, with a little of that. What He has shielded them from is, in comparison with what has befallen them, a thousand times greater. Likewise is what befalls their opponents. He informed them of this before it occurred so that they would prepare their souls for it, and so that their certainty would increase when they witnessed it, just as He had told them. And so that they would know that it is a small matter with a praiseworthy outcome. ﴿And loss of wealth, lives and crops﴾: this is coordinated (ʿatf, a grammatical conjunction) with "something". It has also been said that it is coordinated with "fear".

From al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him): "Fear is the fear of Allah; hunger is the fast of Ramadan; loss of wealth is zakat and charity; loss of lives is illness; and loss of crops is the death of children."

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "When a servant's child dies, Allah (Exalted) says to the angels: 'Have you taken the soul of my servant's child?' They say: 'Yes.' He says: 'Have you taken the fruit of his heart?' They say: 'Yes.' Allah (Exalted) says: 'What did my servant say?' They say: 'He praised You and said "Inna lillah wa inna ilayhi raji'un."' Allah, Mighty and Exalted, says: 'Build for My servant a house in Paradise, and name it the House of Praise.'"

﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ ﴿who, when a calamity strikes them, say: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return"﴾: The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to everyone who is capable of giving good tidings. A calamity (muṣībah) is whatever befalls a person of hardship. This is due to the saying of the Prophet (upon him be blessings and peace): "Everything that harms the believer is for him a calamity." Patience is not merely the saying of "istirjaʿ" with the tongue; rather it is with the heart, by his contemplating that he was created for this, and that he will return to his Lord, and by his remembering the blessings of Allah (Exalted) upon him, and seeing that what He has left him with is many times more than what He has taken back. Thus he makes it easier upon his soul and submits. The object of "good tidings" is omitted, its meaning indicated by what follows it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verses 155–156:**

﴿And We will surely test you﴾: We will afflict you as one who tests your conditions afflicts you: will you be patient in the face of trial, and will you submit to the decree? ﴿With something of fear and hunger﴾: that is, with a little of that. ﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ ﴿who, when a calamity strikes them, say: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return"﴾: The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to everyone who is capable of giving good tidings. Thus he makes it easier upon his soul and submits. The object of "good tidings" is omitted, its meaning indicated by what follows it.

﴿Those﴾: a demonstrative referring to the patient ones, in view of their being described by the qualities mentioned. The sense of distance in it is to signal the lofty elevation of their rank. ﴿Upon them are blessings from their Lord, and mercy﴾. Ṣalāh (blessing) from Allah, glorified is He, means forgiveness and tenderness. Its plural form alerts to its abundance and variety. Combining it with mercy (raḥmah) serves emphasis, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿compassion and mercy﴾ and ﴿Kind and Merciful﴾. The indefinite form (tanwīn) in both words serves magnification. The mention of the title of Lordship (rubūbiyyah), together with its attachment to their pronoun, serves to show increased care for them. That is: those described by the mentioned noble qualities, upon them are the varieties of tenderness, flowing from the Master of their affairs, who brings them to the perfections fitting for them. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever says istirjā' (the saying 'Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we will return') at a calamity, Allah will repair his calamity, make his outcome good, and give him a righteous successor whom he is pleased with." ﴿And those﴾: a demonstrative referring to them, either by the earlier consideration, with the repetition serving to show the full extent of care for them, or by consideration of their possession of the mentioned blessings and mercy, which follows from the first consideration. On the first, the guidance (ihtidā') in His saying, exalted and glorified is He: ﴿they are the guided﴾ means guidance to the truth and to what is right, in general, not guidance only to the mentioned istirjā' and submission, because that comes before them, so postponing it beyond what is their result requires a motive that necessitates it, and this is not apparent. The sentence is an interjected clause confirming the content of what precedes it, as if it were said: "And those are the ones specially guided to every truth and what is right; therefore they said istirjā' and submitted to the decree of Allah, exalted is He." On the second, it is the guidance and the attainment of goals: the meaning is "those are the ones who succeed in their religious and worldly aims, for whoever obtains the tenderness and mercy of Allah, exalted is He, will not miss any objective."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 158:

﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah﴾: they are two markers (a'lam) for two hills in the Sacred City of Makkah, like al-Samman and al-Muqattam; ﴿are among the symbols of Allah﴾; among the markers of His rites (manasik). It is the plural of "sha'irah", which means a sign (al-'alamah). ﴿So whoever performs the Hajj to the House or the 'umrah﴾; al-hajj (linguistically: intention, qasd; and al-i'timar: visitation, ziyarah) became dominant in the Shari'ah for intending the House and visiting it, in the two well-known senses, like "al-bayt" and "al-najm" as proper nouns; and once the House is named, it is obligatory to strip the term of attachment to other things. ﴿there is no blame upon him for going around between them﴾; that is, in going around between them. Its original form is "yatatawwaf"; the ta' was changed to ta' (tā') and the first ta' assimilated into the second, so the form is tatawwafa with the doubled letter. The use of the tafa"-ul pattern indicates that the one who circumambulates should exert himself in the tawaf and expend his effort in it. This tawaf is obligatory according to us (the Hanafis); and according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on them both, it is a pillar (rukn). Its expression with the negation of blame, which implies optionality, is because in the time of ignorance there was an idol on al-Safa called Isaf and another on al-Marwah named Na'ilah; when they ran between the two, they would rub themselves against them. When Islam came and broke the idols, the Muslims felt uneasy about going around between them because of that, and so this was revealed. It is also said that it is voluntary (tatawwu'); and the reading of Ibn Mas'ud supports this: "there is no blame upon him that he not go around between them". ﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾; that is, does an act of obedience, whether obligatory or supererogatory, or adds to what was obligatory upon him of Hajj, 'umrah, or tawaf. Here "khayran" is in the accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun; that is, a good voluntary act; or by omitting the preposition and letting the verb reach it directly; or by implying the meaning of "fa'ala". It is also read "yattawwa'", whose original form is "yatatawwa'", like "yattawwafa"; and it is read "wa man yatatawwa' bi-khayr". ﴿then indeed Allah is Shakir﴾; that is, He rewards the obedience; this is expressed by "shukr" as an intensification of benevolence toward the servants. ﴿Knowing (Alim)﴾: exceedingly knowing of things; so He knows the measures of their deeds and their modes, and He does not diminish their rewards in any way. It is the cause for the answer of the conditional, standing in its place, as if it were said: "Whoever volunteers good, Allah (Exalted) will reward him and recompense him; indeed Allah is Shakir, Alim."

(p-182)﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾: It has been said that it was revealed concerning the rabbis of the Jews who concealed what was in the Torah regarding the attributes of the Prophet (ﷺ) and other rulings. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, al-Rabi' and al-Asamm that it was revealed concerning the People of the Book, both Jews and Christians. And it has been said that it was revealed concerning everyone who conceals anything of the rulings of the religion, because the ruling is general to all. The more correct view is the first, for the generality of a ruling does not preclude the specificity of its cause. Concealment (al-katm and al-kitman) is leaving off the manifestation of a thing intentionally, while the need for it is pressing and the call to manifest it is established. This may be merely by covering and hiding it, and it may be by removing it and putting something else in its place, and this is what these people did. ﴿what We sent down of clear proofs﴾: from the clear signs indicating the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿and the guidance﴾: that is, the signs guiding to the reality of his matter and the obligation to follow him and believe in him. It is expressed by the verbal noun for emphasis, and it is not put in the plural, out of regard for the original form. The same is intended by "the clear proofs" as well, and the conjunction is for the difference of the designation, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿a guidance for mankind and clear proofs﴾, etc. It has also been said that the intended meaning of "the guidance" is the rational proofs, but the sending down and the concealing reject this. ﴿after We have made it clear to people﴾: this is related to "they conceal". The intended meaning of "people" is all of them, not only the concealers. The preposition "li" (to) is related to "bayyannahu" (We made it clear), and likewise the adverbial phrase in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿in the Book﴾. The attachment of two prepositional phrases to one verb, when the meanings differ, is undoubtedly permissible. Or the latter is attached to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause from its object, meaning: existing in the Book. Its making it clear to them means summarizing it and explaining it in such a way that each one of them receives it without there being any doubt in it for him. This is a designation different from its being clear in itself. And "guidance" emphasizes the ugliness of concealment; or it means making it understood to them through Musa (peace be upon him). The first is more fitting with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿in the Book﴾. The intended meaning of concealing it is removing it and putting something else in its place, for they erased his description (peace and blessings be upon him) and wrote in its place what contradicts it, as we mentioned in explaining His saying, Mighty and Exalted is He: ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands﴾, etc.

﴿Those﴾: a reference to them in terms of what they were described with, to indicate that it is the cause of what befell them, and the sense of distance in it is to announce the far-reaching nature of their affair and the remoteness of their rank in corruption. ﴿Allah curses them﴾: that is, He drives them away and removes them far from His mercy. The shift to the third person by mentioning the name of the Essence which comprises the attributes (the grammatical device of iltifat, a shift of person) is to cultivate awe and to instill a sense of dread, and to indicate that the source of the cursing from Him, glorified is He, is an attribute of majesty, which differs from the source of sending down and making clear, which is an attribute of beauty and mercy. ﴿and the cursers curse them﴾: that is, those from whom cursing can proceed, that is, invoking a curse upon them, from the angels and the believers of the two species (humans and jinn). The intended meaning is to show the continuation of the curse and its persistence. On this the connected exception (al-istithna' al-muttasil, an exception whose excluded item is of the same category as what precedes it) in

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 160:

His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Except those who repent﴾; that is, from concealment; ﴿and make amends﴾; that is, what they corrupted, by removing the altered wording and writing in its place what they had removed at the time of the alteration; ﴿and make clear﴾; to the people its meanings. For this is other than the amendment mentioned; or they make clear to them what had occurred from them, first and last, for this is more effective in guiding people to the truth and turning them away from the path of error into which they had led them. Or they make clear their repentance, so as to wipe away the mark of what they had been engaged in, and so that their like may follow their example. (p-183) Since this repentance, coupled with amendment and clarification, necessarily entails repentance from disbelief and is built upon it, faith is not explicitly mentioned. His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Those﴾: is a pointing to the relative clause, in view of its being characterized by what is within the scope of the relative clause, to signal that it is the cause of the ruling; and the particle "fa" (then) is for emphasizing that. ﴿I accept their repentance﴾; that is, by acceptance, and by bestowing forgiveness and mercy. His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And I am the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful﴾; that is, the one who is exceedingly accepting of repentance and spreading mercy; it is a concluding parenthetical statement, confirming the content of what precedes it. The shift to the first person singular speaker is for the sake of variety in the noble composition, together with what it contains of allusion and indication to the difference of the source in His two actions (exalted is He), the earlier and the later.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 161:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾: this is a resumptive clause (jumlah musta'nafah), brought in to establish that the curse remains upon them beyond the exception, and to affirm its perpetuity and its continuance upon those who do not repent, as the discourse indicates. The mention of disbelief alone in the relative clause, without addressing the absence of repentance and of reform (islah) and clarification (tabyin), is founded upon what has been pointed out. Just as the presence of those three matters necessitates faith (iman), which entails the absence of disbelief, so too the presence of disbelief necessitates the absence of all of them together. That is to say, this is a continuation upon disbelief, which entails concealment (kitman) and the absence of repentance. ﴿And they die while they are disbelievers﴾: they do not desist from their former state. ﴿Those﴾: the discussion regarding it is as it is regarding what precedes it. ﴿Upon them﴾: that is, settled upon them. ﴿is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together﴾: from those whose cursing is regarded. This is an explanation of its continuance as a fixed state, after the explanation of its continuance as a renewed one. It has been said: the first is their being cursed while alive, and this is their being cursed after death. It has also been read: "and the angels and mankind, all together" (al-malaikatu wa al-nasu ajma'una), in coordination with the place (mahall) of the noun "Allah," since it is the agent in meaning, as in your saying: "The striking of Zayd amazed me, and Umar"; you mean: "that Zayd struck, and Umar." It is as if it were said: upon them is that Allah cursed them, and the angels... etc. It has also been said that it is the subject of an implied verb; that is: "and the angels curse them."

Khalidina fiha (﴿خالِدِينَ فِيها﴾): i.e., in the curse; or in the Fire. It is understood that the reference was omitted without mention, to magnify its matter and to emphasize its terrible nature.

﴿لا يُخَفَّفُ عَنْهُمُ العَذابُ﴾ ("the punishment will not be lightened for them"): this is either a resumptive (mustanʾaf) sentence, explaining the abundance of their punishment in terms of its quality, following the explanation of its abundance in terms of quantity; or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "khalidina" (﴿خالِدِينَ﴾), in the manner of overlapping (tadakhul); or it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "ʿalayhim" (﴿عَلَيْهِمْ﴾), in the manner of synonymy (taradduf).

﴿وَلا هم يُنْظَرُونَ﴾ ("nor will they be given respite"): this is coordinated (ʿatf) with what precedes it, and what applies there applies to it as well. The choice of the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) is to convey the continuity and persistence of the negation. That is, they will not be granted a delay, nor will they be postponed; or: they will not be awaited so that they may make excuses; or: no look of mercy will be cast upon them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 163:

﴿And your God﴾: an address to all of mankind; that is, the one who deserves to be worshipped by you; ﴿is One God﴾; that is, singular in divinity; there is no validity whatsoever in calling anything other than Him "god" at all; ﴿There is no god but He﴾: a second predicate of the subject (mubtada'); or another attribute of the predicate (khabar); or a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD). Whichever it is, it establishes the Oneness (wahdaniyyah) and removes what might be imagined, that there exists in existence a god, but one who does not deserve worship; ﴿the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾: two further predicates of an omitted subject; and this is an affirmation of Tawhid. For He (Exalted is He), since He is the bestower of all blessings, their roots and their branches, their great and their minute, and since all else, whatever it may be, is in need of Him for its existence and for what branches from it of perfections, His Oneness is established without doubt, and the entitlement to worship is confined to Him (Exalted is He) with certainty. It was said: around the Sacred Ka'bah there were three hundred and sixty idols belonging to the polytheists (p-184). When they heard this verse they marvelled, or they said: "If you are truthful, then bring a sign by which we may recognise your truthfulness." So it was revealed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 164:

﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, in their origination in the state in which they are; together with the marvels within them, the lessons, and the wondrous artifacts whose understanding the minds of mankind cannot grasp. The plural "al-samawat" (the heavens) is used in accordance with the well-known view that they are layers of differing realities, whereas "the earth" is singular. ﴿And the alternation of the night and the day﴾: that is, their succeeding one another, and each of them being a successor to the other, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day in succession﴾. Or: the variation of each of them in itself, in increase and decrease, according to what Allah (exalted is He) has decreed. ﴿And the ship that runs in the sea﴾: it is a conjunction with what precedes it. Its feminine form is either by considering it as "the vessel" (al-safina), or because it is a plural, for the vowel of the plural differs from the vowel of the singular in form: the first is as in "humr" (donkeys), and the second as in "qufl" (lock). It has also been read with a ḍammah on the lam. ﴿With that which benefits mankind﴾: that is, connected with what benefits them, of the kinds of benefits carried in it; or by their benefit. ﴿And what Allah sends down from the sky of water﴾: a conjunction with "the ship"; its being placed after the mention of the ship, although it is more general in benefit, is for the sake of the added detail it contains. It has been said that the intended purpose is to take the sea and its states as evidence; the ship is singled out for mention because it is the means of plunging into it and gaining knowledge of its wonders. For this reason it was placed before the mention of the rain and the clouds, since their origin is generally the sea. The first "min" (from) is for the starting point, and the second is explanatory or partitive; and whichever it is, its being delayed is for the reason already mentioned many times: arousing eagerness. By "the sky" is meant the celestial sphere, or the clouds, or the direction of height. ﴿And He gives life thereby to the earth﴾: with kinds of vegetation, flowers, and the trees upon it; ﴿after its death﴾: by the dominance of dryness over it, as its nature requires; and so the mention of death is weighed against the giving of life. ﴿And He spreads throughout it﴾: that is, He scatters and disperses ﴿of every creature﴾: of rational beings and others. The clause is conjoined to "sent down" and falls under the same governing construction. His saying (exalted is He) ﴿so He gives life﴾, etc., is connected to the conjoined item in such a way that both are in the position of one thing, as if it were said: "and what He sent down upon the earth of water, and spread throughout it..." etc. Or it is connected to "gives life", with the prepositional phrase and its pronoun referring to the relative omitted, even though the usual conditions are not fully met, as in the poet's saying:

"Indeed my tongue is a honeyed sweetness by which one is healed, but it is bitter upon the one whom Allah has poured bitterness upon."

That is: bitter upon him. And in his saying:

"Perhaps the one who raised me up will return me to the earth, if the Capable does not will the good."

Meaning: so He gives life to the earth through water, and spreads throughout it every creature, for they grow through fertility and live by the rain. ﴿And the directing of the winds﴾: a conjunction with "what He sent down"; that is, turning them from one quarter to another, or from one state to another. It has also been read in the singular. ﴿And the clouds﴾: a conjunction with "the directing", or with "the winds". It is a collective noun whose singular is "sahaba", named so from its being drawn along (insihab) in the air. ﴿Subjected between the sky and the earth﴾: an attribute of the clouds with regard to their wording; its meaning may also be taken into account, so it is described with the plural, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿heavy clouds﴾. Its subjection is its being turned about in the air through the agency of the winds, according to what Allah's will (exalted is He) requires. Perhaps the delay of the directing of the winds and the subjecting of the clouds in the mention, relative to the running of the ship and the sending down of water, despite the reversal of the external order, is due to what has passed in the story of the cow: it indicates that each of the listed matters is independent in being a sign. Had the external order been observed, it might have been imagined that the whole sequenced group, one following another, constituted a single sign. ﴿Indeed there are signs﴾: the subject of "inna"; the lam has entered upon it because it is delayed beyond its predicate, and the indefiniteness is for magnification, both in quantity and in quality; that is: great signs, many, indicating the power, the manifest wisdom, and the vast mercy, which necessitate that divinity belongs exclusively to Him, glorified is He. ﴿For a people who understand﴾: that is, who reflect upon them and look at them with the eyes of reason. In this there is an allusion to the ignorance of the polytheists, who demanded of the Prophet (ﷺ) a sign that would confirm him, in view of His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And your God is one God﴾; and a censure of them for the feebleness of their minds. Otherwise, whoever contemplates those signs finds each of them speaking of His existence (exalted is He), His oneness, and His other perfect attributes, which necessitate that worship be restricted to Him (exalted is He), and by them one is independent of all else. For each of the listed matters has come into being in one particular form among the possible forms, and not in others, entailing specific effects and particular rulings, without its essence requiring its existence, let alone its existence in a determined pattern entailing an independent ruling. Therefore there must necessarily be a Creator, Powerful and Wise, who brings it into being according to what His wisdom requires and what His will calls for, exalted above the opposition of any other. For if there were with Him another who could do what He can do, it would necessarily follow either that two agents combine upon a single effect, or that there be mutual obstruction leading to the corruption of the world.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 165:

﴿And among the people are those who take, besides Allah,﴾: an explanation of the complete baseness of the opinions of the polytheists, following the affirmation of His oneness - glorified is He - and the clarification of the dazzling signs which compel intelligent people to acknowledge them, which overflow with the impossibility that anything among the existent things should share with Him in any attribute of perfection, let alone sharing in the attribute of divinity. The discussion of its grammatical construction is as was detailed in His - exalted is He - saying: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day"﴾ etc. And "besides Allah" is connected to "takes"; that is, among the people are those who take, besides that one God whose glorious affairs have been mentioned, ﴿equals﴾ - that is, likenesses. And they are their leaders whom they follow in what they do and what they abandon, especially in commands and prohibitions, as is made clear by what will follow of their description as disavowing those who followed them. It was said: they are the idols. The return of the pronoun of intelligent beings to them, in His saying - mighty and exalted is He -: ﴿they love them﴾, is based on their false opinions concerning them, in describing them with what is only described of intelligent beings. And "love" (al-mahabbah) is the inclination of the heart, from "al-habb" (the seed/grain); it was borrowed for the kernel of the heart, then "al-hubb" (love) was derived from it, because it reached it and took firm root in it. Its verb is "habba", on the pattern of "madda"; but the widely used form is "ahabba, hubban, and mahabbatan"; so he is "muhibb" (one who loves), and the other is "mahbub" (one who is loved); "muhabb" is rare, and "habb" is even rarer. The love of the servant for Allah - glorified is He - is the desire to obey Him in His commands and prohibitions, and attentiveness to attaining His pleasure. So the meaning of "they love them" is: they obey them and magnify them. The clause is in the accusative position; either as a description of "equals", or as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "takes". The plural of the pronoun is by consideration of the meaning of "min", just as its singular is by consideration of its wording. ﴿As the love of Allah﴾: is a comparative verbal noun; that is, an attribute of a verbal noun emphasizing the preceding verb. Part of its being in the active voice is that it is also so; and the apparent view is that the agent of both is the same, for they also used to acknowledge Him - exalted is He - and draw near to Him. So the meaning is: they love them with a love existing like their love for Allah - exalted is He; that is, they equate between Him and them in obedience and magnification. It was said: the agent of the love mentioned is the believers (p-186); so the meaning is: a love existing like the love of the believers for Him - exalted is He. It is necessary, then, to consider a resemblance between the two in the essence of love, not in its description as to quantity or quality, because of the clear difference that will follow. It was said: it is a verbal noun from the passive voice; that is, as Allah is loved and magnified. The mention of who loves Him was dispensed with because it is not ambiguous. You are aware that there is no resemblance between their being loved by their equals and His being loved - exalted is He. The conclusion then is what we have previously stated in the interpretation of His saying - mighty and sublime is He -: ﴿as Moses was asked before﴾. The manifestation of the glorious Name in place of the pronoun is to cultivate awe and to magnify the annexed noun, and to show the complete ugliness of what they committed. ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾: a independent nominal clause, brought as a preamble to what follows of an explanation of the weakness of their love and its being a cause of regret for them. The comparative's object is omitted; that is, the believers are stronger in love for Him - exalted is He - than they are for their equals; and its implication is that the love of those for Him - exalted is He - is stronger than the love of these for their equals; in this there is an indication, which is not hidden, that love is a verbal noun from the active voice. It was not made that the comparative's object be their love for Allah - exalted is He - because the intended purpose is to explain its severance and its turning into hatred; and that is only conceivable in their love for their equals, since it is contingent upon corrupt foundations and false origins, which vanish with their vanishing. It was said: and for this reason they used to turn away from them at times of hardship toward Allah - glorified is He; and they used to worship an idol for days, then when they found another they abandoned it for it. Banu Bahilah ate their god in the year of famine, and it was made of "hays" (a mixture of dates, butter and cheese). You are aware that the basis of this is considering the disruption of their love for them in this world; and the discussion is not about that, but about its severance in the Hereafter, when the reality of the situation becomes manifest and the terrors are witnessed, as will follow. Rather, considering it would undermine what the aim of exaggeration in explaining the complete ugliness of what they committed requires, and the extreme magnitude of what they perpetrated. And the choice of the explicit form in place of the pronoun is to magnify the love and to signal its cause.

﴿And if those who did wrong could see﴾; that is, by taking equals and placing them in the position of the worshipped; ﴿when they see the punishment﴾; prepared for them on the Day of Resurrection; that is, if they knew when they witnessed it; and the future form was chosen because it functions as the past in indicating certainty, in the report of the Knower of the unseen; ﴿that power belongs to Allah entirely﴾: fills the place of the two objects of "see"; ﴿and that Allah is severe in punishment﴾: is conjoined to it; its benefit is exaggeration in magnifying the matter and making the affair appalling; for the exclusivity of power to Him - exalted is He - does not necessitate severity of punishment, since He may leave it by pardon while being able to inflict it. The answer to "if" is omitted, to signal its exit from the sphere of explanation; either because of not being able to grasp its reality, or because the expression is too narrow for it, or because mentioning it would require the speaker or hearer to bear what they cannot endure of distress and lamentation over it; that is: if they knew, when they saw the punishment had descended upon them and none of their equals rescued them from it, that power belongs to Allah entirely, and no one has any say in anything at all, they would have fallen into regret and remorse in matters that can hardly be described. It was read: "and if you [singular] could see", with the second-person ta, on the basis that the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit for address; then the answer would be: you would see a matter indescribable in its horror and dreadfulness. It was read: "when they are shown" (idh yurawna), in the passive voice; and "indeed Allah is severe in punishment" on the basis of a new sentence, with an implied "saying".

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 166:

﴿When those who were followed disowned those who followed﴾: it is a substitute (badal) for "when they see" (إذ يرون); that is: when the leaders disowned ﴿those who followed﴾; from the followers; by acknowledging the falsity of what they used to claim in the world, and of the forms of disbelief and misguidance to which they were calling them; and they withdrew from mixing with them, and met them with cursing; like the saying of Iblis: ﴿Indeed, I disbelieve in what you associated me with before﴾. It was also read in the reverse: that is, the followers disowned the leaders. The waw in His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿and they saw the punishment﴾ (p-187) is circumstantial (ḥāliyyah), with "qad" (قد) implied; and it has been said that it is coordinating (ʿāṭifah) upon "disowned"; and the pronoun in "ra'aw" (رأوا) refers to all the described parties. ﴿And their connections were severed from them﴾; and the ties (wuṣul) that had existed between them, of following and being followed, and of agreement upon the deviant creed, and the motives that called to that. The original meaning of "sabab" (سبب) is the rope by which one climbs a tree and the like. It is coordinated (maʿṭūfah) upon "disowned"; and placing the circumstantial clause between them is to draw attention to the cause of the disowning. It has also been permitted that it be coordinated upon the circumstantial clause.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 167:**

﴿And those who followed will say﴾; when they witness the disavowal of the leaders from them, and they regret what they did of following them in the world: ﴿If only we had a return﴾; that is, would that we had a return to the world; ﴿so that we might disavow them﴾; there; ﴿as they have disavowed us﴾; today. ﴿Thus﴾: a demonstrative pointing to the verbal noun (*masdar*) of the verb that follows it, not to anything else understood from what preceded; and what it contains of the sense of distance is to signal the exalted rank of the one pointed to, the remoteness of his station, together with the complete distinction of his case from all others, and its inclusion in the category of observable matters. The particle *kaf* ("like") is superfluous (*muqhamah*), serving to emphasize the grandeur that the demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*) conveys. Its position is in the accusative by way of the verbal noun (*masdariyya*); that is: that dreadful showing. ﴿God will show them their deeds as anguish upon them﴾; that is, severe regrets. For *hasrah* is the intensity of regret and grief, and it is the pain of the heart and its contraction from what pains it. Its derivation is from the saying "*ba'ir hasir*" (a camel that is *hasir*), that is, one whose strength has been cut off. It is the third object of "*yuri*" (to show), if it is from seeing with the heart; otherwise it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The meaning is that their deeds will turn into anguish upon them, so they will see nothing but anguish in place of their deeds. ﴿And they will not be coming out of the Fire﴾: this is a resumed statement (*kalam mustanaf*) explaining their state after entering the Fire. The original form would have been "*wa ma yakhruju-na*" (and they do not come out), but the shift to the nominal form serves to convey the continuity of the negation of exit, and the pronoun (*damir*) serves to indicate the strength of their condition in what is attributed to them, as in his saying:

*They are the ones who spread the felt for every swift steed,*
*and every bare-backed fast racer that outstrips the costly ones.*

﴿يا أيُّها النّاسُ كُلُوا مِمّا في الأرْضِ﴾ ["O mankind, eat of what is on the earth"]; i.e., of some of the kinds of edible things in it, among which is what you have forbidden, fabricating against Allah, from the tilled crops (al-ḥarth) and the livestock (al-an'am). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "It was revealed concerning a people from Thaqif, the Banu 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah, Khuza'ah, and the Banu Mudlij, who forbade for themselves what they forbade of the crops, the baḥā'ir (slit-eared she-camels), the sawā'ib (camels set free), the wasā'il (ewes that bore twin females), and the ḥawāmī (stallions protected from work)."

His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿ḥalālan﴾ ["lawful"] is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from the relative pronoun; i.e., eat it while it is lawful. Or it is a maf'ūl (object) of "kulū" (eat), with "min" being ibtidā'iyyah (indicating origin). It has also been permitted that it be an adjective of an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid); i.e., lawful eating. The first two readings are supported by His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿ṭayyiban﴾ ["good"], for it is an adjective of it, and describing eating with it is not usual.

It was also said: it was revealed concerning a people of the believers who forbade for themselves the choicest foods and clothing. This is refuted by His saying (Mighty and Majestic is He): ﴿وَلا تَتَّبِعُوا خُطُواتِ الشَّيْطانِ﴾ ["and do not follow the steps of Satan"]; i.e., do not take him as a model in following desire. For it is explicit that the address is to the disbelievers. How could it be otherwise? Forbidding the lawful upon oneself out of asceticism is not a case of following the steps of Satan, let alone being an invented saying and fabrication against Allah (Exalted is He). What was revealed concerning them is what is in (p-188) Surat "al-Ma'idah", in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا تُحَرِّمُوا طَيِّباتِ ما أحَلَّ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ﴾ ["O you who believe, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you"], and so on.

It has been read as "khuṭuwāt" with a sukūn on the ṭā' (khuṭwāt); both are dialectal forms for the plural of "khuṭwah" (a step), which is the distance between the two feet of the one walking. It has also been read with two ḍammahs and a hamzah: the ḍammah was placed on the ṭā' as if it were on a wāw; and with two fatḥahs, as the plural of "khaṭwah", which is a single instance of "al-khaṭw" (stepping). ﴿إنَّهُ لَكم عَدُوٌّ مُبِينٌ﴾ ["Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy"] is a reason given for the prohibition; i.e., his enmity is manifest to those of insight, even though he shows friendship to whoever he leads astray. For this reason he is called "walī" (a protector/ally) in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿أوْلِياؤُهُمُ الطّاغُوتُ﴾ ["their protectors are the tyrants"].

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 169:

﴿Indeed, he commands you only to evil and immorality﴾: This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the manner of his enmity, and a detailing of the varieties of his evil and corruption, and that his dealings with them are restricted to this. As for al-su' (evil) in origin, it is the verbal noun of "sa'ahu, yasu'uhu, su'an, wa masa'atan" (he grieved him), when it saddens him. It applies to all acts of disobedience, whether they are deeds of the limbs or actions of the hearts, since all of them share the fact that they harm their doer. Al-fahsha' (immorality) is the most abominable of its kinds and the greatest in harm. ﴿And that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾: This is conjoined (ʿatf) to "al-fahsha'", meaning: and [he commands you] to fabricate against Allah that He has forbidden this and that. The meaning of "what you do not know" is: what you do not know that Allah (exalted is He) has commanded. The linking of His command to their saying about Allah (exalted is He) what they do not know to have occurred from Him (exalted is He), rather than to their saying about Him what they know not to have occurred from Him (exalted is He), is for the sake of intensifying the deterrence. For the warning against the first, although it is less than the second in ugliness and abomination, is a warning against the second in the most emphatic and forceful manner. It also serves to notify that the rational person is obligated not to say about Allah (exalted is He) what he does not know to have occurred from Him (exalted is He), even with the possibility of it, let alone saying about Him what he knows not to have occurred from Him (exalted is He). They said: In this there is evidence for the prohibition of following conjecture (zann) altogether. As for the mujtahid's following of what his conjecture leads him to, it is based on a legal source (madrak shar'i), so its obligation is certain, and conjecture is merely the path to it.

﴿And when it is said to them: "Follow what Allah has sent down"﴾: this is a shift (iltifat) to the third person, in order to record the completeness of their misguidance, to signal the necessity of enumerating what has been mentioned of their offences, to turn the address away from them and direct it to the intelligent, and to detail the evils of their states for them, in the manner of frank speech (al-mubathatha). That is: when it is said to them, by way of sincere advice and guidance, "Follow the Book of Allah which He has sent down," ﴿they say: "No, we will follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾, meaning, "what we found them upon." Either the adverbial phrase ﴿عَلَيْهِ﴾ is related to an omitted verb and stands as a circumstantial clause (hal) of "آباءَنا" (our fathers), and "ألفَيْنا" (we found) is transitive to one object; or it is a second object of "ألفَيْنا" placed before the first. It was revealed concerning the polytheists, who were commanded to follow the Qur'an and the rest of what Allah, exalted is He, had sent down of clear proofs and manifest evidences, but they inclined toward blind imitation (taqlid). The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) here either refers to what preceded of taking rivals to Allah, forbidding good things, and the like, or it remains general, and what has been mentioned enters it as a primary inclusion. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning a group of the Jews, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited, and they said: "Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon, because they were better than us and more knowledgeable." According to this, what Allah, exalted is He, sent down includes the Torah, since it too calls to Islam.

As for His saying, exalted and glorious is He: ﴿Even though their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?﴾: this is a resumed statement issued from Him, exalted is He, refuting their foolish statement and manifesting the falsity of their opinions. The hamza (interrogative alif) is for denying the actual occurrence and finding it abhorrent and astonishing, not for denying its occurrence, like the one in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Even though we were unwilling?﴾. The word "law" (لَوْ) in situations like this one is not used to show the absence of a thing at a past time because of the absence of something else in it; therefore no answer is sought for it, it having been omitted with confidence, by the indication of what precedes it. Rather, it is used to show the certainty of what the preceding statement conveys, directly or through an intermediary, of the affirmed or negated judgment, under every assumed state among the states accompanying it in general terms, by placing it upon the state furthest from it and most contradictory to it, so that by its establishment or its negation alongside it, its establishment or negation alongside all other states is made evident, by way of priority, since whenever a thing is realized alongside a strong contrary, it is even more so realized alongside other than it. For this reason, none of the other states is mentioned with it, and it is sufficient to mention the conjunctive waw linking the sentence to its counterpart opposite it, which encompasses all the states differing from it. This is the meaning of the grammarians' saying that it is for the exhaustive enumeration of states in general terms. This meaning is evident in the affirmative and negative declarative sentence, the imperative, and the prohibition, as in your saying: "So-and-so is generous; he gives even if he is poor, and he is stingy; he does not give even if he is rich," and your saying: "Be good to him even if he wrongs you, and do not humiliate him even if he humiliates you," because it remains in its state. As for what we are dealing with here, there is a kind of obscurity in it, arising from the denial directed at it; but the basis in all of them is one, except that the word "law" in the mentioned forms is connected to the very verb mentioned before it, and what is intended to show its realization under every state is its own signified meaning; and the sentence is a circumstantial clause (hal) of its pronoun, or of what is connected to it; and what falls within the scope of "law" remains as it is, generally, in terms of being considered unlikely. This differs from what we are dealing with, because the word "law" here is connected to an omitted verb required by what is mentioned; and what is intended to show its realization under every state is its signified meaning, not the signified meaning of what is mentioned insofar as it is its signified meaning; and the sentence is a circumstantial clause of what is connected to it, not of what is connected to the mentioned item insofar as it is connected to it; and the primary intent is the denial of its signified meaning in terms of its accompanying the mentioned state. As for estimating its accompaniment with other states, that is for broadening the scope. And what falls within the scope of "law" is not intended to be deemed unlikely in itself; rather, it is intended to indicate that it is a realized matter, but it is presented in the form of something unlikely, dealing with the addressees according to their own belief, lest they wrap themselves in the hide of a leopard by attributing their fathers to complete ignorance and error, and thus persist in obstinacy; and as an exaggeration in the denial regarding their following of their fathers, since it is denounced and deemed abhorrent, given that the possibility that their fathers were as mentioned is a remote possibility; so it is even more denounced when that is realized. The estimate is: "Would they follow that even if their fathers did not understand anything of the religion and were not guided to the right course?" And if they were so, then the sentence is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause of "آباؤُهم" (their fathers), in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Follow the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf﴾. It is as if it were said: "Would they follow the religion of their fathers while being heedless, ignorant, and astray?" as a denial of what their statement implied of following in whatever state of the two states; except that only the second state was mentioned, to draw attention to the fact that it is the one actually occurring, and relying on its clear implication of the first state. For their following, which the denial concerns, when it is realized alongside their fathers being ignorant and astray, is even more so realized alongside their fathers being intelligent and guided. If you say: the denial derived from the interrogative of denial is equivalent to a negation, and there is no doubt that priority in the form of a negation is considered in relation to the negation; do you not see that what is more fitting to be realized in the example of negation mentioned, when in the unmentioned state, namely the absence of wealth, is the absence of giving, not the thing itself? So it should be that what is more fitting to be realized in our case, in the unmentioned state, which is the state of their fathers being intelligent and guided, is the denial of the following itself, not the following itself; for it is what indicates "Would they follow... etc." So why did the situation differ between the two? I say: because the criterion of priority is the judgment whose realization under every state is intended to be shown; and that (p-190) in the example of negation is the absence of giving, derived from the mentioned negated verb; whereas in our case it is the following itself, derived from the omitted verb, since it is what the preceding statement requires, namely their saying: "Rather, we will follow," etc. As for the interrogative, it is outside of that and comes upon it to deny what it conveys and to find abhorrent what it requires, not as part of its completion, as in the case of negation. Likewise the situation is when the hamza is for denying the occurrence and its negation, while it is equivalent to plain negation, as will be verified later in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Even though we were unwilling?﴾. It has been said that the waw is circumstantial (ḥāliyya); but the verified view is that the meaning revolves around the meaning of conjunction in other languages as well.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 171:

﴿وَمَثَلُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ ("And the likeness of those who disbelieve"): this is an independent (ibtida'iyya) sentence, sent to confirm what precedes it by way of depiction (taswir). In it there is an omitted noun (mudaf) which is indicated by the word "mathal" (likeness) standing in its place. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is placed in the position of the pronoun referring back to what the preceding pronouns refer back to, in order to censure them by what lies within the relative clause (sila), and to indicate the cause of the judgment attributed to them. The estimated meaning is: the likeness of that one who calls (the disbelievers to faith), and his state, is truly strange, such that it deserves to be called a "likeness" and to travel through the horizons, concerning what has been mentioned of his summoning them to follow the truth, and their not lifting their heads toward it at all, due to their immersion in imitation (taqlid), their clinging to the misguidance they are upon, and their not understanding from the one who calls to the call, without their directing their minds to what is being conveyed to them. ﴿كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي يَنْعِقُ بِما لا يَسْمَعُ إلا دُعاءً ونِداءً﴾ ("like the likeness of one who shouts to that which hears nothing but calling and crying out"), namely of the cattle, for they hear nothing but the voice of the shepherd and his shouting at them, without any understanding of his speech at all.
