It has also been said: the omitted noun from the second relative (al-mawsul al-thani) is indicated by the word "ma" (that which), for it is an expression for it, and it, together with what lies within the relative clause, indicates that upon which the depiction turns. That is: the likeness of those who disbelieve, in respect of what has been mentioned of their immersion in what they are in, and their failure to reflect upon the signs conveyed to them, is like the likeness of cattle to the one who shouts at them, and they hear from him nothing but the jingle of the tone and the echo of the voice. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the depiction of their following of their fathers according to the outward state of affairs, while ignorant of its reality, by the cattle which hear the voice but do not understand what lies beneath it. It has also been said: the depiction is of their calling upon the idols by the one who shouts at his flock, namely his vocalizing to the cattle; and this is free of the need for an implied element, but the words ﴿إلا دُعاءً ونِداءً﴾ do not support it, for the idols are far removed from that. You have already learned that the excellence of a depiction lies in the resemblance of the individuals of the two sides. ﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ﴾ ("deaf, dumb, blind"): read in the nominative (bi-al-raf'), by way of censure; that is: they are deaf... etc.

﴿فَهم لا يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ ("so they do not understand"): anything, because the path of intellection (ta'aqqul) is reflection upon the first principles of intelligible matters and contemplation of their arrangement; and this is only attained by hearing the verses of God, witnessing His clear proofs, and conferring with one from whom knowledge is taken. So when they are deaf, dumb and blind, the doors of intellection and the ways of understanding are entirely closed to them.

O you who have believed, eat from the good things We have provided for you. That is, from its delicious things. ﴿And be grateful to Allah﴾, who provided them for you. The shift from the third person to the first person (in "We have provided" and then "Allah") serves to cultivate reverence. ﴿If it is Him you worship﴾; for His worship (exalted is He) is not complete except with gratitude to Him.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'Indeed, I and mankind and the jinn are in a great news: I create and others are worshipped; I provide and others are thanked.'"

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 173:

﴿Indeed, He has forbidden you only the carrion﴾; that is, eating it and benefiting from it; and it is that which has died without slaughter (dhakah). The fish and the locust are excluded from it by custom (al-'urf), or by an exception made by the Law (al-istithna' al-shar'i). The spleen is excluded from the category of blood. ﴿And blood, and the flesh of swine﴾; only its flesh was singled out (mentioned), (even though all its other parts are also under its ruling), because the flesh is the most commonly eaten part of the animal, and its other parts are as subordinate to it. ﴿And that over which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾; that is, the voice was raised with it at the time of its slaughter for an idol. Al-ihlal (invocation) originally means: sighting the crescent moon; but since it became customary to raise the voice with takbir at its sighting, that was called "ihlal"; then it was said (to apply) to the raising of the voice, even if it was for other than that. ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing﴾; by monopolizing (the food) against another person who is compelled; ﴿nor exceeding (the necessity)﴾; (that is, exceeding) what suffices to quell the throat and the hunger pangs. It was also said: "neither desiring" means not rebelling against the ruler, and "exceeding" means highway robbery; and according to this, it is not permitted to one who is disobedient by travel; and this is the apparent position of the school of al-Shafi'i and the view of Ahmad, may God have mercy on both of them. ﴿Then there is no sin upon him﴾; in consuming it; ﴿indeed God is Forgiving﴾; for what was done; ﴿Merciful﴾; by granting the concession. If it is said: the word "innama" (indeed/only) restricts the ruling to what has been mentioned, and how many prohibited things are not mentioned! We say: the intended meaning is restricting the prohibition to what has been mentioned out of what they had deemed lawful; not absolutely; or restricting its prohibition to the state of free choice; as if it were said: He has forbidden you these things only so long as you are not compelled to them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 174:

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book﴾ — that is, which includes the various rulings (ahkam), among which are the rulings on what is lawful (muhallalat) and what is unlawful (muharramat), as mentioned just above. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "It was revealed concerning the leaders of the Jews, when they concealed the description (nat) of the Prophet (ﷺ)."

﴿and sell it﴾ — that is, they take in exchange for it — ﴿for a small price﴾ — a base, worthless return. The reason for the expression concerning that "price," which is the means in contracts of exchange (ʿuqud al-muʿawadah), has already been explained.

His (Exalted) saying: ﴿Those﴾ — a demonstrative referring to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), in view of its being characterized by the two abominable attributes contained in its relative clause (silah), which distinguish them completely from all others, making them as though they were present and witnessing what they are doing. The sense of distance in the demonstrative is to signal the extreme remoteness of their rank in evil and corruption. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is His (Exalted) saying: ﴿they eat only the Fire into their bellies﴾. The whole sentence is the predicate of "inna." Alternatively, the demonstrative is a second subject, or a substitute (badal) for the first, and the predicate is "they eat... etc."

The meaning of their eating the Fire is that they eat, in the present, what entails the Fire and necessitates it, so that it is as if it were the very Fire, and their eating is its eating, as in the verse of the poet:

"I have eaten blood, if I do not make you suffer with a co-wife, far from the place where the earring hangs, fragrant in her scent."

Or: they will eat, on the Day of Resurrection, the very Fire, as punishment for their eating bribes in the world. "Into their bellies" is connected to "they eat"; its purpose is to emphasize the eating and to affirm it by stating the place where the food is lodged. It has also been said that its meaning is "filling their bellies," as in the saying "he ate in his belly" and "he ate in part of his belly," and from it: "Eat in part of your bellies, and you will be chaste." Thus it is necessary to resort to attaching it to an omitted element that occurs as a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah) modifying "the Fire," together with its being placed before the exceptive particle; otherwise, attaching it to "they eat" would restrict what they eat to satiety only with the Fire, whereas the intended meaning is to restrict what they eat, absolutely, to the Fire.

(p-192) ﴿Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ — an expression of His great wrath against them, and an indirect allusion to their being deprived of the various honourable and noble favours granted to the believers, and of nearness.

﴿nor will He purify them﴾ — He will not praise them. ﴿And for them﴾, in addition to what has been mentioned, ﴿is a painful punishment﴾ — painful, causing pain.

Those: a demonstrative referring to what was indicated by its counterpart, solely by the aspect mentioned, and not together with what follows of their dreadful conditions, since those have no bearing on the ruling that is intended to be established here. For the purpose is to depict what they engaged in of dealing in an ugly form from which natures recoil and which no rational person would engage in at all, by explaining the reality of what they discarded, revealing the essence of what they took, and showing the awfulness of its consequences. It is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is the relative clause: that is, those who bought with the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, a small price, are not buyers of the price, even if it is small; rather, they are: ﴿who have bought﴾, in relation to the worldly life, ﴿the misguidance﴾, which is certainly not among the things that can be bought, ﴿for the guidance﴾, which is not of the kind that is given in exchange for anything, however great; ﴿and the punishment﴾, that is: they bought, with regard to the Hereafter, the punishment, which it is not imagined could be among the things that are bought, ﴿for the forgiveness﴾, which competitors compete for. ﴿So how patient they are over the Fire!﴾ This is an expression of wonder at their dreadful condition, which is their being involved in what necessitates the Fire with a definite necessity, as though they were its very essence. And "ma" according to Sibawayh is an indefinite complete noun, conveying the meaning of wonder, in the nominative case as a subject (mubtada'), and its specification is like the specification of "sharrun" in: "An evil that has made the one with fangs snarl," its predicate (khabar) being what follows it; that is: something great that has made them patient over the Fire. According to al-Farra': it is interrogative, and what follows it is its predicate; that is: what thing has made them more patient over the Fire?! It has been said: it is a relative (mawsulah); and it has been said: it is a descriptive (mawsufah) with what follows it; and the predicate is omitted; that is: the one who made them patient over the Fire; or a thing that made them patient over the Fire; a matter that is strange and dreadful.

That [punishment] is because God sent down the Book with truth, that is, the genus of the Book, [sent down] accompanied by truth. Therefore, whoever rejects it by denying it and concealing it, and who plunges into the depths of ignorance and error, is certainly afflicted with one of the many forms of punishment like this.

﴿And indeed those who differ concerning the Book﴾: that is, concerning the genus of the divine Book, by believing in some of God's books (Exalted is He) and disbelieving in others; or concerning the Torah, by believing in some of its verses and disbelieving in others, such as the altered verses that contain the matter of the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his noble attributes. The meaning of "differing" is therefore deviating from the true path, or differing over its interpretation (ta'wil, interpretation of the meaning), or differing concerning the Qur'an, such that some of them said it is sorcery, some said it is poetry, and some said it is "the fables of the ancients," as has been related from the exegetes. ﴿Are in extreme dissension﴾: far from the truth and the right course, deserving the most severe punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 177:

﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west.﴾ (البِرُّ, al-birr: a comprehensive term for praiseworthy qualities.) The address is to the People of the Two Scriptures, for they had engaged excessively in discussion about the direction of prayer (al-qiblah) when it was changed to the Ka'bah, and each group claimed that facing its own direction was the better of the two directions mentioned. The mention of the east before the west, despite the later appearance of the Christian religion, is either to observe the order that follows from the order of sunrise and sunset, or because the Jews' facing the west was not because it is the west, but because Bayt al-Maqdis lies to the west of the city of Madinah. So it was said to them: it is not the righteousness you have mentioned, namely turning toward those two directions.

Here, al-birr is the predicate (khabar) of laysa (لَيْسَ), placed before its subject (ism), as in the verse of the poet:

*"Ask me, if you do not know the people about me and about them, / for the knowing and the ignorant are not equal."*

And his saying:

*"Is it not great that a calamity should befall, / and that no one among us should be a spokesman in calamities?"*

This ordering was adopted because the verbal-noun clause (المصدر المؤول, al-masdar al-mu'awwal: the infinitive construction "an tuwallu") is more definite than the noun marked with the definite article (al-), since it resembles a pronoun in that it is neither described nor does it describe. The more definite element has a stronger claim to being the subject. Also, the subject is long, and if the usual order were observed, the harmony of the parts of the noble composition would be lost.

It is also read with the nominative al-birr, as the subject of laysa. This is stronger in meaning, because each group claims that righteousness is this, so the refutation must correspond to their claim, and this is only so if al-birr is the subject, as is made clear by making it the topic of the contrastive clause in His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿But righteousness is in one who believes in Allah﴾. This is the affirmation of the truth after the exposure of falsehood, and a detailing of the qualities of righteousness, some of which do not vary with the variation of the religious laws, and some of which do vary. That is: but the righteousness that is known, that deserves to be cared for and diligently pursued, is the righteousness of one who believes in Allah alone, with a faith free of any trace of association (shirk), not like the faith of the Jews, Christians and polytheists, who say "Uzayr is the son of Allah" and "the Messiah is the son of Allah."

﴿And the Last Day﴾: that is, as it truly is, not as they claim, that the Fire will touch them only for a number of days, and that their forefathers the prophets will intercede for them. So there is an implicit indication that the faith of the People of the Two Scriptures, since it was not as mentioned in the correct manner, was not faith. Placing al-birr with these two directly after its negation regarding turning toward east and west contains an eloquence that is not hidden. It is as if it were said: but righteousness is turning toward the origin and the return, which in reality are the east and the west.

﴿And the angels﴾: that is, and he believes in them, and that they are honoured servants, intermediaries between Him (exalted is He) and His prophets, through the conveyance of revelation and the sending down of books.

﴿And the Book﴾: that is, in the category of the Book, of which the Furqan is one of the instances, which they cast behind their backs. And there is an implicit reference to their concealing the descriptions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and their selling of what Allah (exalted is He) revealed for a small price.

﴿And the prophets﴾: all of them, without distinguishing between any of them, as the People of the Two Scriptures did. The reason for placing the Book between the bearers of revelation and the prophets is clear, and it will come in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Each believed in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers﴾.

﴿And gave wealth, though he loves it﴾: a circumstantial clause (حال, hal) from the pronoun in "gave" (ātā), and the pronoun attached to "wealth" (al-māl) refers back to it. That is: he gave it while loving wealth, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), when he was asked which charity is best: "That you give it while you are healthy and miserly." And the saying of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): "That you give it while you are healthy and miserly, hoping for long life and fearing poverty, and you do not delay, until when it reaches the throat you say: to so-and-so such-and-such, and to so-and-so such-and-such."

It is said that the pronoun refers to Allah (exalted is He): that is, he gave it while it was for His love (exalted is He), not for the purpose of evil and corruption. So there is a kind of implicit reference to those who pay bribes and those who take them, to alter the Torah. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the verbal noun (the act of giving): that is, while loving the act of giving.

﴿Relatives﴾: the first object of "gave" (ātā), whose second object, "wealth," was placed before it for emphasis on it, or because the second object together with what is coordinated with it is long, and if the usual order were observed, the harmony of the parts of the speech would be lost. This is also what required placing the circumstantial clause before it. It is also said that "relatives" is the second object.

﴿Orphans﴾: that is, those among them in need, as indicated by the circumstantial clause. The placing of relatives before them is because giving to them is both charity and kinship ties.

﴿The needy﴾: the plural of miskīn, which is one who is constantly still, because need has immobilised him so that he has no movement; or one who is constantly still in relation to people.

﴿The wayfarer﴾: that is, the traveller; he was named so because he is constantly with the road, just as the one who cuts off the road is called "son of the road." It is also said: the guest.

﴿Those who ask﴾: those whom need and necessity have compelled to ask. The peace and blessings of Allah be upon him said: "Give to the one who asks, even if he comes on a horse."

﴿And for the captives﴾: that is, placing it in the freeing of necks, by assisting those under a contract of manumission (mukātabūn) until they free their necks. It is also said: in freeing captives. It is also said: in buying slaves and setting them free. Whichever is the case, the turn away from mentioning them by a title that makes ownership valid, like those before them, is either to indicate that their ownership of what they are given is not secure, as in the first two interpretations, or that it is not established at all, as in the last interpretation. Or it is to indicate their being firmly entrenched in entitlement and need, because "in" (fī) is for location, which indicates that they are the place for what is given.

﴿And established prayer﴾: that is, the obligatory prayers from among them.

﴿And gave zakah﴾: that is, the obligatory zakah. On the basis that what has passed regarding giving wealth refers to voluntary charity, it is placed before the obligatory as emphasis in urging it. Or what is meant by both is the obligatory: the first explains the recipients, and the second explains the obligation of paying.

﴿And those who fulfil their covenant﴾: coordinated with "those who believe in Allah," for it is in effect as if it were said: "and those who have fulfilled their covenant." The choice of the active participle form indicates the obligation of continuing fulfilment. What is meant by covenant is what does not make lawful what is forbidden nor forbid what is lawful, from among the agreements in force between people. His saying (exalted is He): ﴿when they make a covenant﴾ is to indicate that it is not one of the necessities of the religion.

﴿And the patient﴾: put in the accusative by way of specification (al-ikhtisās). Its construction was changed from what precedes it, as a reminder of the excellence of patience and its distinction. In reality it is coordinated with what precedes it. Abu 'Ali said: when attributes are mentioned for praise or for blame, and some of them are changed in grammatical case, then the change is for variety (lil-iftinān), and this is called qat' (a shift), because changing what is familiar indicates an increase in encouragement to listen to what is mentioned and greater attention to its matter, as has passed at the beginning of the surah. It has also been read: "and the patient ones" (al-ṣābirūn), just as "and those who fulfil" (al-mūfūn) has been read.

﴿In poverty﴾: that is, in destitution and hardship. ﴿And in affliction﴾: that is, in sickness and disability. ﴿And in the time of battle﴾: that is, at the time of fighting the enemy in the places of war. The addition of "time" (ḥīn) indicates that it occurs at times and ends quickly.

﴿Those﴾: a demonstrative referring to those mentioned, in consideration of their being characterised by the beautiful attributes enumerated. The sense of distance in it, as has passed many times, is an alert to the loftiness of their rank and the exaltedness of their standing.

﴿Those who are true﴾: that is, in religion, in following the truth, and in seeking righteousness, since circumstances did not change them and terrors did not shake them.

﴿And those are the God-fearing﴾: that is, guarding against disbelief and all other vices. The repetition of the demonstrative is to increase the emphasis on their status, and the insertion of the pronoun (hum) is an indication that God-fearing is restricted to them.

The noble verse, as you see, contains all human perfections in their entirety, explicitly or allusively, because it, despite the multiplicity of its arts and the diversity of its themes, is confined to three qualities: soundness of belief, good conduct with people, and refinement of the soul. The first has been alluded to by faith, as detailed; the second by giving wealth; and the third by establishing prayer... and so on. Therefore those who possess these qualities were described as truthful, in view of their faith and belief, and as God-fearing, in consideration of their dealings with creation and their conduct toward the Truth. To this his saying (ﷺ) points: "Whoever acts upon this verse has completed faith."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 178:**

﴿O you who have believed⦆: This begins the explanation of some of the legal rulings (aḥkām shar'iyyah), by way of making up for what was neglected by those who had failed in the principles of the religion mentioned above and its foundations, upon which the basis of this life and the Hereafter is built. ﴿It has been prescribed for you⦆, that is: it is obligatory and imposed, upon the demand of the rightful claimant. Thus the capacity of the guardian to pardon does not detract from it, for the obligation is considered only in relation to the rulers or to the killers. ﴿Retribution (qiṣāṣ) for the murdered⦆, that is: because of their killing, as in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat she had tied up," that is: because of her tying it. ﴿The free for the free, and the slave for the slave, and the female for the female⦆: In the Jahiliyyah there was blood between two tribes among the tribes of the Arabs, and one of them had superiority over the other. They swore that they would surely kill the free among you for the slave, and the male for the female. When Islam came, they brought their dispute before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed, and he commanded them to be equal (yatabā'ū). There is no indication in it that a free man is not to be killed for a slave, according to al-Shafi'i as well, because the consideration of the implicit meaning (mafhūm) applies where no apparent reason for specifying the mention appears other than restricting the ruling to the explicit statement (manṭūq). And you have seen the reason here. Al-Shafi'i and Malik, may Allah have mercy on them both, rely on what 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: "A man killed his slave, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lashed him and exiled him for a year, and did not retaliate against him," and on what is narrated from him (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "It is from the Sunnah that a Muslim is not to be killed for one who has a covenant, nor a free man for a slave," and on the fact that Abu Bakr and 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them) did not kill a free man for a slave, among the Companions, without objection, and on analogy with limbs. According to us, a free man is killed for a slave, because of His (Exalted) saying: ﴿that the life is for the life⦆. For the law of those before us, when it is related to us without any indication of its abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by later revelation), acting upon it is obligatory, on the basis that it is a law for us too. And because retribution depends on equality in inviolability (al-'iṣmah), and that is by religion or by abode, and both are equal in these respects. It is also read as "kataba" (in the active voice), with "qiṣāṣ" in the accusative. ﴿So whoever is granted something from his brother⦆, that is: some part of pardon, because "'afā" is intransitive, and its benefit is to indicate that a part of the pardon is like the whole of it in dropping retribution. This is also what commonly happens, since pardon often comes from some of the guardians, so it is "something of the pardon." It has been said: the meaning of "'ufiya" is "left," and "shay'" is the object. This is weak, since "'affāhu" is not established in the sense of "left it," rather "a'fāhu." And the pardon has been taken in the sense of erasure, as in the words of one who said:

*Abodes whose traces were erased by the tyranny of every obstinate one*

and his words:

*Erased by every cloud, abundant in heavy rain, pouring down*

So the meaning becomes: "whoever has something erased for him from his brother." This is a turning of the expression, commonly used in the Book and the Sunnah, away from its well-known and familiar meaning toward what is not familiar in them, nor in the usage of people, for they do not use "pardon" in the matter of offenses except in the sense mentioned earlier. "'Afā" is construed with "'an" to the offender and to the sin. Allah (Exalted) said: ﴿Allah has pardoned you⦆, and He said: ﴿Allah has pardoned it⦆. So when it is construed with the sin, one says: "I pardoned so-and-so for what he committed," as if it were said: "whoever is pardoned for his offense from the side of his brother," that is: the guardian of the blood. Its mention under the title of brotherhood established between them, by virtue of their both being from the children of Adam (peace be upon him), is to stir the chain of tenderness and compassion toward him. ﴿Then let there be a following with kindness⦆: so the command is "following," or "let there be following." The intended meaning is the exhortation of the pardoner to leniency, and the demand of the blood-money (diyah) in a fair manner, without oppression. His (Mighty and Majestic) saying: ﴿and payment to him with good conduct⦆ is an urging upon the one pardoned to pay it with good conduct, without procrastination or diminishing.

﴿That⦆: that is, what has been mentioned of the ruling. ﴿is a lightening from your Lord and a mercy⦆, because of the ease and benefit in it. It has been said: retribution alone was prescribed for the Jews, and pardon and blood-money were forbidden to them; and for the Christians, pardon in absolute terms was prescribed, and retribution and blood-money were forbidden to them; and this community was given the choice among the three, as facilitation for them and a descent of the ruling according to their circumstances. ﴿So whoever transgresses after that⦆, by killing someone other than the killer after the arrival of this ruling, or by killing the killer after pardon or accepting blood-money. ﴿For him⦆, because of his transgression, ﴿is a painful punishment⦆, either in this world, by retaliation for what he killed without right, or in the Hereafter, by the Fire.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 179:

﴿And for you in retaliation (qisas) there is life﴾: an explanation of the excellences of the ruling mentioned, in a wondrous manner whose full extent cannot be attained, since the thing is made the locus of its opposite. Retaliation (qisas) is made definite and life is made indefinite, to indicate that in this category there is a great kind of life that description does not reach. This is because knowledge of it deters the killer from killing, thereby causing the life of two souls. Also, because they used to kill someone other than the killer, and a group for one person, so strife would erupt among them; when retaliation is exacted from the killer, the rest are saved, and this becomes a cause of their life. According to the first explanation there is an ellipsis (idmar), and according to the second there is a specification (takhsis). It has been said: the intended life is the life of the Hereafter, for when the killer is subjected to retaliation in this world, he is not held accountable for it in the Hereafter. The two adverbial phrases (zarfan) are either both predicates of "life," or one is the predicate and the other is a complement to it, or it is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun implicit in it. It was also read as "fi al-qasas," meaning: in what has been recounted to you of the ruling on killing there is life; or: in the Qur'an there is life for the hearts.

﴿O people of understanding (ya uli al-albab)﴾: that is, those possessing pure intellects, free from the admixture of illusions. They were addressed thus after having been addressed by the title of faith, to stimulate them to reflect upon the wisdom of retaliation.

﴿That you may be God-fearing (la'allakum tattaqun)﴾: that is, that you may protect yourselves from laxity in its matter, from neglect in safeguarding it, from ruling by it, and from submitting to it; or, [that you may protect yourselves] regarding retaliation, so that you refrain from killing which leads to it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 180:**

﴿Prescribed for you﴾: an explanation of another ruling among the rulings mentioned. ﴿When death approaches one of you﴾: that is, when its causes arrive and its signs appear, or when the soul draws near to the moment of arrival. The object is placed first to indicate the full certainty of the agent (death) with regard to the soul at the time it reaches it. ﴿If he leaves wealth﴾: that is, property. It is said: much property. This is based on what is reported from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that a freedman of his wished to make a bequest, and he had seven hundred dirhams, and Ali prevented him, saying: "Allah (Exalted) says: ﴿if he leaves wealth﴾, and this is a small amount, so leave it for your dependents." And from Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) that a man wished to make a bequest, and he had dependents and four hundred dinars, and she said: "I do not see in it any surplus." Another man wished to make a bequest, and she asked him: "How much is your property?" He said: three thousand dirhams. She said: "How many are your dependents?" He said: four. She said: "Allah (Exalted) only said: ﴿if he leaves wealth﴾, and this is a small amount, so leave it for your dependents." ﴿The bequest for parents and relatives﴾: is in the nominative case, as the subject of "prescribed" (kutiba). It is placed after what lies between them, for the reason that has been mentioned many times. The choice of the masculine form of the verb, although its feminine form is also permissible, is for the purpose of separation (fasl), or according to the interpretation: "that he make a bequest," or: "the making of a bequest." For this reason the pronoun is also masculine in the statement of Allah (Exalted): ﴿Then whoever alters it after he has heard it﴾. "Idha" (when) is a pure adverb of time, and the governing element in it is "prescribed." However, this is not from the standpoint of the prescribing coming from Him (Exalted), but from the standpoint of its relation to them as an actual relation, entailing the obligation of performance, as the passive construction indicates, and the word of obligation. There is no room for making the governing element the bequest itself, because it comes before it. It is said: it is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is "for the parents," and the sentence is the answer to the condition, with the particle "fa'" (then) elided, as in his statement:

*Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them.*

It is refuted by saying that if it is correct, it is out of poetic necessity. The meaning of "prescribed" is: made obligatory. This ruling was in the beginning of Islam, and then it was abrogated (nusikha) upon the revelation of the verse of the inheritance laws (mawarith, the rules of inheritance), by his statement (peace be upon him): "Indeed Allah has given every person with a right his right; no bequest is valid for an heir." This tradition, although it is among the solitary reports (akhbar al-ahad, reports transmitted by a limited number of narrators), nevertheless, since the community received it with acceptance, it became included in the category of the widely transmitted (mutawatir) reports, in its fitness for abrogation according to our Imams. Yet the verified position is that the actual abrogating text is the verse of the inheritance laws, and the tradition only clarifies the manner of its abrogation, by explaining that He (Exalted) had prescribed for you that you render to the parents and relatives their rights according to their entitlement, without specifying the degrees of their entitlement nor determining the quantities of their shares, but He left that to your opinions, when He said: ﴿in accordance with what is reasonable﴾, that is: with justice. So now that ruling has been lifted from you, by clarifying the classes of entitlement of each one of them, and determining the quantities of their rights specifically, and giving each person with a right of them his right which he deserves by the ruling of kinship, without deficiency or excess, and He did not leave any matter in which your opinion has any place at all, as the negated sentence with "la," the particle that negates the genus, indicates, and its opening with the word of alerting. When you have realized this, it becomes clear to you that what has been said, that the verse of the inheritance laws does not contradict it but rather verifies and confirms it, in that it indicates the precedence of the bequest absolutely, and that the tradition is a solitary report, and the community's acceptance of it does not place it in the category of the widely transmitted, may be what he who explained the bequest as what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, bequeathed of inheritance to the parents and relatives, by His statement (Exalted): ﴿Allah enjoins you﴾, or as the dying person's bequest to them, by the fulfillment of what Allah (Exalted) enjoined upon them, was guarding against, and it is far from verification. Likewise what has been said: that the bequest to an heir was obligatory by this verse, without specifying their shares; then when the verse of the inheritance laws was revealed clarifying the shares, it was understood from it, by the alerting of the Prophet (ﷺ), that what was meant was this bequest which had been obligatory, as if it were said: Indeed Allah (Exalted) enjoined that bequest Himself and did not delegate it to you, so inheritance took the place of the bequest, and this was the meaning of abrogation (naskh), not that there is in it an indication of lifting that ruling. For the implication of the verse of the bequest, since it was a delegation of the matter to the opinions of the responsible persons absolutely, and it was possible to be discharged from the obligation of the duty by performing what their opinions led to, "in accordance with what is reasonable," then the verse of the inheritance laws, which speaks of the degrees of entitlement and the detailed quantities of rights, and definitively rules out any increase or decrease, by His statement (Exalted): ﴿an obligation from Allah﴾, will be abrogating it and lifting its ruling, in a manner that is not unclear to anyone. And His statement (Exalted): ﴿a duty upon the God-conscious﴾: is an emphatic verbal noun, that is: that is due as a due obligation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 181:

﴿Then whoever alters it﴾; that is, changes it, from among the executors (al-awsiya') and the witnesses; ﴿after he has heard it﴾; that is, after it has reached him and become certain to him; ﴿then its sin is only upon those who alter it﴾; that is, the sin of the altering bequest, or the sin of the alteration; ﴿upon those who alter it﴾, because they have betrayed and opposed the ruling of the Shari'ah. The placing of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in the position of the pronoun referring back to "whoever" serves to emphasize the announcement of the causal reason contained in the first relative clause (al-silah al-ula). The choice of the plural is to indicate the enumeration of the alterers as types, or their multiplicity as individuals, and the announcement that the sin encompasses all the individuals; ﴿indeed Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾; a severe warning to those who alter.(p-198)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 182:

﴿Then whoever fears from a testator﴾; i.e., anticipates and knows, from their saying: "I fear that the sky will send down [rain]" (akhaafu an yursila al-sama'); and it has been read as "min muwassin" (from one who bequeaths unfairly); ﴿partiality (janafan)﴾; i.e., inclination through error in the bequest; ﴿or sin (ithman)﴾; i.e., deliberately [committing] partiality; ﴿then he brings about reconciliation between them﴾; i.e., between those to whom the bequest is made, by having them conform to the path of the noble Shari'ah; ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾; i.e., in this alteration; because it is a change from falsehood to truth, unlike the first; ﴿indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾; this is a promise to the one who brings about reconciliation; and the mention of forgiveness corresponds to the mention of sin, and to the fact that the act is of the same kind as that which incurs sin.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 183:

﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you﴾: an explanation of another of the legal rulings of the Sharia; and the repetition of the address (ya ayyuha alladhina amanu) serves to show further concern (for the matter). Al-siyam and al-sawm, in the language, mean abstaining from what the soul inclines towards; and from this is the saying of Him (Exalted): ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any person﴾; and the verse... It was also said: it is abstaining from something absolutely; and from this (comes the phrase) "the wind fasted" (samat al-rih), when it ceased from blowing; and "the horse fasted" (al-faras), when it ceased from running. He said:

Some horses are fasting, and others not fasting, under the dust, while others chew the bits.

In the Sharia, it is abstaining during the day, together with the intention, from the known nullifiers, which are the greatest of what the souls desire.

﴿as it was prescribed﴾: this is in the accusative position, either as an attributive qualifier of the emphatic verbal noun, meaning: a prescription existing as it was prescribed; or as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the definite verbal noun, meaning: fasting has been prescribed for you, the prescribing being likened to what was prescribed. In both cases "ma" is a verbal (masdariyya) particle. Or it is an attributive qualifier of a verbal noun derived from the word "al-siyam", meaning: a fast similar to the fast prescribed upon those before you, in which case "ma" is a relative (mawsulah) particle. Or it is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "al-siyam", meaning: in the state of its being similar to what was prescribed.

﴿upon those before you﴾: from among the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, and the nations, from the time of Adam, peace be upon him. In this there is emphasis on the ruling, encouragement towards it, and consolation for the hearts of those addressed by it, for when a hardship becomes general, its performance becomes easier. By similarity is meant either similarity in the basic obligation, or in the time and the quantity. As it is related that the fasting of Ramadan was prescribed upon the Jews and the Christians. As for the Jews, they abandoned it and fasted one day of the year, which they claimed was the day of the drowning of Pharaoh, and they lied in that; for it was the day of Ashura. As for the Christians, they fasted Ramadan until they encountered intense heat, so the opinions of their scholars converged upon fixing a single season between summer and winter, and they made it in spring, and added to it ten days as expiation for what they had done, so it became forty. Then their king fell ill, or two deaths occurred among them, so they added ten days, and it became fifty.

﴿so that you may become righteous﴾: that is, (righteous) from sins, for fasting breaks the desire that calls to them, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever among you can, let him marry; and whoever cannot, let him fast, for fasting is a shield for him." Or: that you may be wary of neglecting its performance, for it is fundamental. Or: that through it you may attain the rank of taqwa.

(p-199) ﴿Numbered days﴾: fixed to a known number; or: few, for a small quantity of wealth is counted one by one, whereas a large quantity is poured out by handfuls. What is meant by them is either Ramadan, or what was obligatory at the beginning of Islam and then abrogated (naskh) by it, namely the fast of ʿAshura and three days of every month. Its accusative case (inṣiba) is not governed by "al-ṣiyām" (the fasting), as has been said, because a foreign element intervenes between them. Rather, it is governed by an implied verb that it indicates, namely "ṣūmū" (fast), either as an adverb of time (ẓarfiyyah) or as a direct object (mafʿūliyyah), by way of extension (ittisāʿ). It has been said that it is governed by His words (exalted is He) ﴿It has been prescribed﴾, on one of the two readings. But in this there is the objection that the days are not the place of the prescribing, but rather the prescribed thing is; so neither the adverbial sense is realized, nor the objective sense derived from it by extension.

﴿So whoever among you is ill﴾: that is, an illness which the fast harms or makes difficult for him; ﴿or on a journey﴾: remaining on it. In this there is an allusion and a hint that whoever travels during the day does not break his fast. ﴿Then a number﴾: that is, he must fast the number of days of the illness and of the journey; ﴿from other days﴾: if he breaks his fast. The condition and the genitive-governed noun are omitted, relying on what is evident. It was also read in the accusative, meaning "then let him fast a number." This is by way of concession (rukhsah). It has been said that it is obligatory; the Ẓāhiriyyah (literalist school) held this view, and Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) also said so.

﴿And for those who are able to do it﴾: that is, for those who are capable of fasting, even if they break their fast; ﴿a ransom﴾: that is, giving a ransom (fidyah), which is ﴿the feeding of a poor man﴾. It is half a ṣāʿ (a measure) of wheat or of something else according to the people of Iraq, and one mudd according to the people of the Hijaz. This was at the beginning of Islam, because the fast had been prescribed for them while they were not accustomed to it, so it was hard upon them, and therefore they were given leave to break the fast with the ransom. It was also read "yuṭawwiqūnahu" (they are burdened with it), meaning: they are charged with it, or they are bound by it; and "yataṭawwiqūnahu" and "yuṭṭawwiqūnahu" (with the ṭāʾ assimilated into the ṭāʾ); "yuṭayyiqūnahu" and "yuṭṭayyiqūnahu," in the sense of "yataṭayyaqūnahu." Their original forms are "yuṭayawwiqūnahu" and "yataṭayawwiqūnahu," from the pattern faʿyala and tafaʿyala, from "al-ṭawq" (the collar); the yāʾ was assimilated into the wāw after being converted into a yāʾ, as in their saying "tadayyara al-makān wa-mā bihā dayyār" (the place became desolate and no one dwelt in it). In this there are two senses: the first is close in meaning to "yuṭīqūnahu" (they are able to do it); the second is "yukallafūnahu" (they are charged with it), or "yatakallafūnahu" (they undertake it with effort on their part and hardship), and these are the old men and the old women. The ruling for these is breaking the fast and the ransom, and in that case it is not abrogated. It is also possible that this is the meaning of "yuṭīqūnahu," i.e., they fast it to the limit of their effort, their capacity, and the extent of their power.

﴿So whoever volunteers good﴾: so that he adds to the ransom; ﴿it is﴾: that is, the volunteering; or: the good that he volunteers; ﴿better for him. And that you fast﴾: O you who are able, or O you who are burdened, and bear it upon yourselves and exert your capacity; or O you who are granted leave to break the fast, from among the sick and the travellers; ﴿is better for you﴾: than the ransom, or than volunteering good, or than both, or than postponing to other days. The shift to address (iltifāt ilā al-khiṭāb) is for stirring and encouragement; ﴿if you know﴾: that is, what is in your fasting, along with the realization of the permission to break the fast, of virtue. The answer (jawāb) is omitted, relying on its evidence; that is: you have chosen it, or you have hastened to it. It has been said that its meaning is: if you are among the people of knowledge and reflection, you know that fasting is better than that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 185:

﴿Shahru Ramadan﴾: a subject (mubtada'); its predicate (khabar) will come later; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "That is the month of Ramadan"; or it is a substitute (badal) for "al-siyam" (the fasting), with the omission of a modifier (al-mudaf mahdhuf), i.e., "the fasting of the month of Ramadan." It has also been read in the accusative (nasb), by supposing an implied "fast" (sumu) or as the object of "tasumu" (you fast); or it is a substitute for "ayyaman ma'dudat" (certain days).

"Ramadan" is a verbal noun from "ramida," meaning "to be scorched," from "al-ramda'" (scorching sand). The word "shahr" (month) was added to it and it was made a proper name (alam), and it is diptote (mamnu' al-sarf) because of definiteness and the alif and nun, as it was said "Ibn Da'ya" for the crow. The saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): "Whoever fasts Ramadan..." (the hadith) comes with an omitted modifier, for safety from ambiguity. It was named thus either because of their being scorched (irtimada) in it by hunger and thirst, or because sins are scorched by fasting in it, or because it fell in the days of scorching heat (ramd al-harr) at the time when the names of the months were transferred from the older language.

﴿Alladhi unzila fihi al-Qur'an﴾: a predicate of the subject according to the first case, and a qualifier (sifah) of "Shahru Ramadan" according to the remaining cases. The meaning of its being sent down in it is that its revelation began in it, and that was the Night of Decree (laylat al-qadr). Or: it was sent down in it all at once to the lowest heaven, then it descended to the earth in parts, as divine will required. Or: the Qur'an was sent down concerning its matter, which is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿It has been prescribed for you﴾.

And from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): "The scrolls of Abraham were sent down on the first night of Ramadan; the Torah was sent down six nights after it; the Gospel on the thirteenth of it; and the Qur'an on the twenty-fourth."

﴿A guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance and the criterion﴾: two circumstantial clauses (hal) relating to "al-Qur'an"; that is, it was sent down as a state in which it is guidance for mankind, by what is in it of inimitability (i'jaz) and other things; and clear signs, guiding to the truth, distinguishing between it and falsehood, by what is in it of wisdoms and rulings.

﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month﴾: that is, is present in it, and was not a traveler. The placing of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun is for glorification and for emphasis in clarification. The fa' (so) is for consequence and sequence; or because the subject includes the meaning of a condition; or it is superfluous, on the assumption that "Shahru Ramadan" is a subject and the relative clause is its qualifier, and this sentence is its predicate. It has been said that it is a conditional sentence, as if it were said: since fasting has been prescribed for you in that month, whoever is present in it, ﴿let him fast it﴾, i.e., let him fast in it, by omitting the preposition and extending the verb to the object (ittisa'an). It has also been said: whoever of you witnesses the sighting of the crescent of the month, let him fast it, taking it as a direct object, as in your saying "I witnessed the Friday," i.e., its prayer; so what follows it specifies it, as if it were said.

﴿And whoever is ill﴾, and even if he is resident and present in it; ﴿or on a journey﴾, and even if he is healthy; ﴿then a number of other days﴾: i.e., then upon him is the fasting of other days, because the sick and the traveler are among those who witnessed the month. Perhaps the repetition is for this reason, or lest it be thought that it was abrogated, as its counterpart was abrogated.

﴿Allah desires for you ease and does not desire for you hardship﴾: by this concession, out of the utmost of His compassion and the vastness of His mercy.

﴿And that you complete the period, and that you glorify Allah for having guided you, and perhaps you will be grateful﴾: these are causes (ʿilal) for an omitted verb, which is indicated by what precedes; that is, for these matters were the preceding rules legislated: the command for the witness to fast the month, the command for those granted concession to observe the count of the days they broke fast, and the concession in permitting breaking the fast. So His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And that you complete﴾ is the cause of the command to observe the count; and ﴿that you glorify﴾ is the cause of what He made known of the manner of making up the days; ﴿and perhaps you will be grateful﴾ is the cause of the concession and facilitation. The verb of glorifying (takbir) is followed by "ʿala" because it includes the meaning of praising; as if it were said: "and that you glorify Allah, praising Him for having guided you." It is also permissible that it be conjoined to an implied cause, like: "so that He may make it easy for you"; or: "that you may know what you do; and that you may complete..." etc. It is also permissible that it be conjoined to "ease," i.e., "He desires for you that you may complete..." etc., like His saying (exalted is He): ﴿They want to extinguish﴾, etc. The meaning: by glorifying (takbir) is magnifying Him (exalted is He), by praise and commendation of Him. It has been said: the glorification of the day of ʿId; it has been said: the glorification at the sighting of the crescent. The "ma" may be verbal-masdariyya or relative: i.e., for His guidance of you, or for that to which He guided you. It has been read: "wa-li-tukammilu" with doubled letter (tashdid).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 186:

﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me﴾: The shift in address, and its direction toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), contains an evident honouring of him and elevation of his station. ﴿Then indeed I am near﴾; that is, say to them: Indeed I am near. This is a figurative expression for the completeness of His knowledge of the deeds and sayings of His servants and His awareness of their conditions, expressed in the image of nearness of place. It is narrated that a Bedouin said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Is our Lord near, so that we may address Him privately, or far, so that we must call out to Him?" Then this was revealed.

﴿I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾; this affirms the nearness, confirms it, and is a promise to the supplicant of being answered. ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾: when I call them to faith and obedience, ﴿and let them believe in Me﴾: an command to remain steadfast in what they are upon; ﴿that they may be rightly guided﴾, hoping to attain right guidance, that is, the truth. It is also read with the shin both fathah and kasrah (yarshudūn and yarshidūn).

When Allah (Exalted is He) commanded them to fast the month and to observe the prescribed period, and urged them to perform the duties of magnifying and giving thanks, He followed this with this noble verse, which indicates that He (Exalted is He) is aware of their conditions, hears their words, answers their supplications, and recompenses them for their deeds, as an affirmation of this and an incitement to it.

Then he began to explain the rulings of fasting, saying: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go in unto your wives﴾. It is related that when Muslims broke their fast in the evening, eating, drinking and intercourse became permissible for them until they prayed the late night prayer (ʿisha') or went to sleep. Then ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, had intercourse after the ʿisha' prayer, then regretted it, came to the Prophet ﷺ, and apologized to him. Men then stood up and confessed what they had done after the ʿisha' prayer, and this verse was revealed. "The night of the fast" means the night after which one rises fasting. "Ar-rafath" (the sexual approach, lit. obscene speech) is a metaphor for intercourse, since it is hardly free of such speech; it is the explicit mention of what should be veiled by allusion. It is governed by "ila" (to) because it includes the meaning of reaching and going unto. Its choice here serves to express disapproval of what they had committed, and for this reason it was called treachery. It has also been read as "ar-rufuth." Placing the adverbial phrase before the substitute for the subject serves, as has been mentioned many times, to create suspense: when what should come first is delayed, the soul remains expectant for it, so it settles most firmly when it arrives. ﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾: this is a resumptive clause explaining the reason for the permission, namely the difficulty of being patient with them given the intense closeness and frequent contact with them. Each of the man and the woman is made a garment for the other because of their embracing and each wrapping around the other at night. The poet said:

When the bedfellow bends her side, she bends, and becomes a garment over him.

Or because each of them covers the state of the other and keeps the other from immorality. ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾: another resumptive clause, explaining the reason mentioned. "Ikhtiyan" is more intensive than "khiyana," as "iktisab" is from "kasb." The meaning of "takhtanun" is that you wronged yourselves by exposing yourselves to punishment and diminishing your share of reward. ﴿So He turned to you [in forgiveness]﴾: coordinated with "knew"; that is, He turned to you when you repented of what you had committed. ﴿And pardoned you﴾: that is, He erased its trace from you. ﴿So now﴾: since the prohibition was abrogated. ﴿Lie with them﴾: "mubashara" is the contact of skin with skin, used here as a metaphor for intercourse, which necessarily involves it. In this there is evidence for the permissibility of abrogating the Book by the Sunnah. ﴿And seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾: that is, seek what Allah has destined for you and recorded in the Preserved Tablet, namely offspring. In this is the indication that the one who has intercourse should intend offspring, since that is the wisdom behind creating desire and legislating marriage, not merely satisfying desire. It has been said that it contains a prohibition against coitus interruptus (ʿazl); and it has been said against intercourse other than in the proper place. The implied meaning is: seek the place which Allah (Exalted) has decreed for you. ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn﴾: the first appearance of the dawn spreading across the horizon, and the darkness of night that extends with it, is compared to two threads, one white and one black. The explanation of the white thread is given by "from the dawn," which suffices in place of explaining the black thread, since it indicates it. With this they move from metaphor to simile. It is possible that "min" is partitive, since what appears is part of the dawn. It is related that when this verse was revealed, "from the dawn" had not yet been revealed, so men took two threads, one white and one black, and began eating and drinking until they became distinct to them; then it was revealed. Perhaps this was before Ramadan began, and delaying clarification until the time of need is permissible; or they were initially content with the two threads being well known for this, and then the clarification was stated explicitly because it had become unclear to some of them. The permission of intercourse until morning indicates the permissibility of delaying the ritual bath until then, and the validity of the fast of one who enters the morning in a state of major impurity. ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾: a clarification of its final time. ﴿And do not have intercourse with them while you are devoted to worship in the mosques﴾: that is, while you are performing i'tikaf in them. The intended meaning of "mubashara" is intercourse. It is related from Qatada: "A man would perform i'tikaf, then go out to his wife, have intercourse with her, and then return; so they were forbidden from this." In this there is evidence that i'tikaf is in the mosque without being restricted to some mosques over others, and that sexual intercourse during it is forbidden and invalidates it, because a prohibition in acts of worship necessitates invalidity. ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾: that is, the rulings mentioned are limits which Allah (Exalted) set for His servants. ﴿So do not approach them﴾, let alone transgress them. This is a prohibition against approaching the boundary that separates the truth from falsehood, as an intensification of the prohibition against crossing it, just as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed every king has a sanctuary, and the sanctuary of Allah is His prohibitions; whoever pastures around the sanctuary will soon fall into it." It is possible that the limits of Allah (Exalted) mean His prohibitions and what He forbade. ﴿Thus﴾: that is, like this eloquent clarification, ﴿Allah makes clear His verses﴾, which indicate the rulings He legislated, ﴿to mankind that they may be mindful﴾, of disobeying His commands and prohibitions.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 188:

﴿And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾: This is a prohibition against some of them consuming the wealth of others, contrary to the ruling of God (Exalted); following the prohibition against consuming their own wealth during the day of Ramadan. That is: let not some of you consume the wealth of others in a manner that God has not permitted. And "بَيْنَ" (bayn, "between") is in the accusative, either as an adverbial of place (ẓarfiyyah) or as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāliyyah) modifying "أمْوالَكُمْ" (your wealth). ﴿And do not send it [i.e., its case] to the judges﴾: This is conjoined to what is forbidden, or it is in the accusative by the implied "أنْ" (an, "that"). And "al-idlā'" (إدلاء) means to cast or throw; that is: do not cast its litigation before the judges. ﴿So that you may consume﴾: by resorting to judgment before them; ﴿a portion of the wealth of people through sin﴾: by that which entails sin, such as false testimony and a profane oath; or while you are entangled in sin; ﴿while you know﴾: that you are wrongdoers. For the commission of sins, while knowing them, is more heinous.

It is narrated that ʿAbdan al-Ḥaḍrami claimed a piece of land against Imru' al-Qays al-Kindi, and he had no evidence. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) ruled that Imru' al-Qays should take an oath. He intended to do so, and the Messenger (peace be upon him) recited to him: ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of God and their oaths for a small price﴾, to the end of the verse. So he refrained from the oath and handed over the land to ʿAbdan, and the verse was revealed.

It is also narrated that two litigants came before him, and he (peace be upon him) said: "I am only a human being like you, and you bring your disputes before me. Perhaps one of you is more eloquent in his argument than the other, so I rule for him according to what I hear from him. Whoever I rule for him from the right of his brother, I am only giving him a piece of Fire." They both wept, and each of them said: "My right belongs to my companion." (p-203) He said: "Go, and seek what is correct; then cast lots; then let each of you absolve his companion."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 189:

﴿They ask you about the crescent moons.﴾ Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Tha'labah ibn Ghanam asked him, saying: "What is the matter with the crescent, that it appears thin like a thread, then increases until it becomes full, then keeps diminishing until it returns as it began?" ﴿Say: They are times (mawaqit) for the people and for the pilgrimage (hajj, the major pilgrimage to Makkah).﴾ They had asked him (peace and blessings be upon him) about the wisdom in the variation of the moon's state and the change of its condition. So Allah, the Mighty, the Wise, commanded him to answer them that the apparent wisdom in this is that it serves as markers for people in their acts of worship, especially the Hajj, for the time is observed in it, both in performance (ada') and in making up (qada'). Likewise it serves in their dealings, according to what they agree upon. "Mawaqit" is the plural of "miqat" (appointed time), derived from "waqt" (time). The difference between it and "mudda" (duration) and "zaman" (time/age) is that absolute duration is the extension of the motion of the celestial sphere from its beginning to its end; "zaman" is a duration divided into past, present and future; and "waqt" is the time specified for a matter.

﴿It is not righteousness to enter houses from their backs.﴾ When the Ansar (Helpers of Madinah) entered the state of ihram, they would not enter a house or a tent through its door, but would enter and exit through a breach (naqb) or an opening behind it, and they considered that to be righteousness. So it was made clear to them that this is not righteousness. Then it was said: ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah.﴾ That is, the righteousness of one who guards against the prohibited things and the desires.

The connection with what precedes it is that they asked about two matters. Or, when He mentioned that they are times for the Hajj, He mentioned right after it what is among their actions in the Hajj, as a digression (istitrad). Or, when they asked about what did not concern them and was not connected with the knowledge of prophethood (for he (peace and blessings be upon him) was sent to explain the laws, not to explain the realities of things), and left asking about what concerned them and pertains to the knowledge of the message, He followed the answer to what they asked with mention of that, as an alert that what is fitting for them is to ask about such matters as these and to be concerned with knowing them. Or it is intended as an alert to their inversion in questioning, and that it is of the kind of entering a house from its back. The meaning is: "It is not righteousness that you invert your questions; but righteousness is [in] one who guards against that and does not presume to do the like."

﴿And go to houses by their doors.﴾ For there is no righteousness in deviation. Or: deal with matters from their proper directions.

﴿And fear Allah.﴾ Regarding the alteration of His rulings, or in all your affairs. He commanded this explicitly after stating that righteousness is the righteousness of one who fears Allah, to show increased concern with the matter of taqwa (God-consciousness) and as a preparation for His saying (exalted is He): ﴿That you may succeed.﴾ That is, so that you may attain righteousness and guidance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 190:

﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾: that is, strive (jihad) to exalt His religion and raise high His word; and the placing of the adverbial phrase (zarf) "in the way of Allah" before the direct object is to show the utmost concern for the matter placed first. ﴿Those who fight you﴾. It has been said: this was before they were commanded to fight all the polytheists, [and it refers to] those among them who fight and who hold back [from fighting]. It has also been said that its meaning is: those who are set upon fighting you and from whom such fighting is expected, to the exclusion of others, such as the elderly, children, monks and women. Or [it means] the disbelievers all together, since all of them are in a position to fight the Muslims. The first view is supported by what is narrated: "The polytheists prevented the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the year of Hudaybiyah, and they made a treaty with him that he would return the following year, and they would vacate Mecca for him, may Allah exalt it, for three days. So he returned for the 'Umrat al-Qada'. The Muslims feared that they would not keep their word to them and would fight them in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) and in the Sacred Month, and they disliked that, so this verse was revealed." It is also reinforced by its placement amid the explanation of the rulings of the Hajj. ﴿And do not transgress﴾: by initiating the fighting, or by fighting a party with whom there is a covenant, or by surprising them with it without a call [to Islam], or by mutilation, or by killing those whom you have been forbidden to kill, such as women, children, and those who are in their position. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors﴾: that is, He does not intend good for them. This is the reason given for the prohibition.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 191:

﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them﴾; i.e., wherever you find them, ﴿whether within the sanctuary or outside it﴾... 

Note: the passage contains an inline "؛ مِن حِلٍّ؛ أوْ حَرَمٍ؛" which I render as follows.

﴿And kill them wherever you overtake them﴾; i.e., wherever you find them, whether in a place of lawfulness (ḥill) or in the sacred precinct (ḥaram); and the root of "ath-thaqf" (overtaking, catching hold of) is "al-ḥadhq" (skill, dexterity) in grasping a thing, whether by knowledge or by action; and it carries the sense of prevailing over, which is why it is used in that sense. He said:

"If you overtake me, then kill me; but whoever is overtaken, there is no eternity for him."

﴿And expel them from where they expelled you﴾; i.e., from Makkah. This was indeed done to them on the Day of Conquest (Yawm al-Fath) with those of their unbelievers who did not submit. ﴿And persecution (fitnah) is worse than killing﴾; i.e., the trial by which a person is tested, such as expulsion from one's homeland, is harder than killing, because its hardship lasts and the pain of the soul from it endures. It was also said: their polytheism in the Sacred Precinct and their barring you from it is worse than your killing them in it. ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque﴾; i.e., do not initiate fighting with them by killing there, and do not violate the sanctity of the Sacred Mosque; ﴿until they fight you there. But if they fight you﴾; there, ﴿then kill them﴾; there. And do not hesitate to fight them there, because they are the ones who violated its sanctity, so they deserved the severest punishment. In shifting from the form of mufa'alah (mutual fighting) in which the prohibition and the condition were expressed, there is a promise of victory and triumph. It has also been read: "And do not kill them until they kill you; but if they kill you, then kill them," and the meaning is: until they kill some of you, as in their saying: "The Banu Asad killed us." ﴿Thus is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾; they are treated with the same as they did to others.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 192:

﴿Then if they desist﴾; from fighting and from disbelief, after they have seen your fighting; ﴿then indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾; He will forgive them what has already passed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 193:

﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾: that is, shirk (polytheism); ﴿and religion is for Allah﴾; purely, with nothing of it belonging to Satan; ﴿but if they cease﴾; after your fighting them over shirk; ﴿then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers﴾; that is, do not transgress against them, for wrongdoing is only fitting against one who has wronged. So the cause (ʿillah) is placed in the position of the ruling (hukm), and the recompense is called "aggression" (ʿudwān) for the sake of parallelism (mushakalah), as in His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, then transgress against him in the same manner﴾. Or: if you confront those who have desisted, you yourselves become wrongdoers, and the situation is reversed upon you. The first fa' (فَ) is for sequence (taʿqib), and the second is for the consequence (jaza').

The sacred month is for the sacred month (﴿الشَّهْرُ الحَرامُ بِالشَّهْرِ الحَرامُ﴾): The polytheists fought them in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, in Dhu al-Qa'da. So it was said to them, when they set out for the making-up ('Umrat al-Qada') 'umrah also in Dhu al-Qa'da, and [it was said to them] in view of their aversion to fighting in it: this sacred month [is answerable] for that sacred month, and its violation is [answered] by its violation; so do not be concerned about it. ﴿And sacred things are subject to retaliation﴾: that is, every sacred thing, which is what must be preserved, is subject to retaliation. Since they violated the sanctity of your month by obstruction, then do to them the like of it, and enter upon them by force, and kill them if they fight you, as (Exalted is He) said: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾. And this is a summation (fadhlaka), confirming what precedes it. ﴿And fear Allah﴾: in the matter of retaliation; and beware of exceeding what has not been permitted to you. ﴿And know that Allah is with the righteous﴾: so He will guard them and set their affairs right with victory and establishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 195:

﴿And spend in the way of Allah﴾: a command to jihad with wealth, after the command to jihad with lives; i.e., "and do not withhold entirely"; ﴿and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾; by extravagance and by squandering the means of livelihood; or by refraining from the raid (ghazw) and from spending on it, for that strengthens the enemy and empowers them over you. This is supported by what is related from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "When Allah honored Islam and its people multiplied, we returned to our families and our property, to reside in them and tend them, and then this was revealed." Or [it means] by withholding and loving wealth, for that leads to perpetual destruction; and for this reason miserliness (bukhl) was called destruction (halak). Its root meaning is the ending of a thing in corruption. The "ilqa' (casting) is the throwing down of a thing; its transitivity with "ila" (to) is because it includes the meaning of reaching an end; the ba' is redundant (ma'zida); and the intended "hands" are the selves. "Tahlukah" is a verbal noun like "tanshurah" and "tasturah"; it and "halk" and "halak" are one and the same; i.e., do not cause your selves to fall into destruction. It has also been said that its meaning is: do not make them (the hands) grasping by your hands, or: do not cast your selves by your hands toward it, so the object is omitted; ﴿and do good﴾; i.e., in your deeds and your conduct; or: show generosity to the poor; ﴿indeed Allah loves the good-doers﴾; i.e., He wills good for them; and His (Exalted) saying:

﴿And complete the ḥajj and the ʿumrah for Allah﴾: an explanation of the obligation to complete their acts once one has undertaken to perform them, and guidance for people to make up for whatever obstacles may befall them that prevent their completion, such as being prevented (*iḥṣār*, being prevented from completing the rites) and the like, without addressing their legal status in themselves, whether they are obligatory or not. This is like His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾. It is an explanation of the obligation to extend the fast until night, without addressing the obligation of the fast itself, which is derived from His saying: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾, the verse. Likewise, the obligation of ḥajj is derived from His saying: ﴿And for Allah is owed from the people the pilgrimage to the House﴾, the verse. The command to complete an act is not a command to its origin, nor does it necessarily entail that origin at all. So there is no evidence in it for the obligation of ʿumrah with certainty. The claim that the command to complete both is a command to initiate them complete and perfect, as the reading "and establish the ḥajj and the ʿumrah" would suggest, and that a command implies obligation unless evidence indicates otherwise, is without foundation. This is because explanation is not confined to the acts of the obligatory ḥajj, so that such a claim could be conceived. Rather, the truth is that this reading too is to be understood in light of the well-known reading, and it indicates the obligation to perform their acts as they should be performed, without addressing their status in themselves. So the meaning is: complete their pillars, their conditions, and all their acts known by the Sharīʿah, for the sake of Allah (exalted), without any lapse on your part in any of them. This is it. It has been said: completing them means that you enter into ihrām (the sacred state) for both from the dwelling of your family (*duwayrat ahlika*). This was narrated from ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with them. It has also been said: it means that you dedicate a separate journey to each of them, as Muḥammad said: "A Kufan ḥajj and a Kufan ʿumrah are better." It has been said: it means making their expenses lawful. It has been said: it means that you make them sincere for worship and do not mix them with any worldly aims. Whatever the case, there is no reference in the noble verse to the obligation of ʿumrah at all. As for what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: "Indeed the ʿumrah is the companion of the ḥajj," and the saying of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, when a man said to him: "I found the ḥajj and the ʿumrah prescribed upon me, so I entered into ihrām for both," and in another narration: "I entered into ihrām for both together," ʿUmar's words: "You have been guided to the sunnah of your Prophet," this is far from indicating obligation. Moreover, it is opposed by what is narrated from Jābir, who said: "O Messenger of Allah, is the ʿumrah obligatory like the ḥajj?" He said: "No, but if you perform ʿumrah, it is better for you." And by his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "The ḥajj is jihād, and the ʿumrah is a voluntary act." So reflect.

﴿Then if you are prevented﴾: that is, you are kept from the ḥajj. It is said: "ḥaṣarahu al-ʿaduww" and "aḥṣarahu" when the enemy confines him and prevents him from proceeding in his direction, like "ṣaddahu" and "aṣaddahu." What is meant is prevention by an enemy, according to Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah be pleased with them, based on His saying: ﴿Then when you are secure﴾, and because it was revealed concerning Ḥudaybiyyah, and because of Ibn ʿAbbās's saying: "There is no iḥṣār except the iḥṣār of the enemy." According to Abū Ḥanīfa, may Allah be pleased with him, any prevention, whether by an enemy, illness, or otherwise, counts, based on what is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever is broken or lame, then upon him is ḥajj in the following year." ﴿Then what is feasible of the offering﴾: that is, upon you; or, what is feasible is obligatory; or, offer what is feasible. The meaning is that the one in ihrām, when he is prevented and wishes to exit the state, exits by slaughtering an offering (*hady*) that is feasible for him, a camel, a cow, or a sheep, wherever he is prevented, according to the majority. According to us, he sends it to the Sacred Precinct (*Ḥaram*) and appoints a day for the one who was sent with it to be his agreed day. When that day comes and he thinks that it has been slaughtered, he exits the state, based on His saying: ﴿And do not shave your heads until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice﴾. That is: do not exit the state until you know that the offering sent to the Sacred Precinct has reached the place where it must be slaughtered. The earlier scholars understood the arrival of the offering at its place as its slaughter, wherever its slaughter is permitted, whether in the non-sacred area or the Sacred Precinct. Their evidence for this is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ slaughtered there in the year of Ḥudaybiyyah, and it is part of the non-sacred area. We say: the place where the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was restrained was the edge of Ḥudaybiyyah that is toward the lower part of Mecca, and it is part of the Sacred Precinct. It is narrated from al-Zuhrī that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sacrificed his offering within the Sacred Precinct. al-Wāqidī said: Ḥudaybiyyah is the edge of the Sacred Precinct, nine miles from Mecca. The word *maḥill* (with a kasra) is used for both place and time. *Al-hady* is the plural of *hadyah*, like *jadī* and *jadyah*. It was also read *min al-hadiyy*, the plural of *hadiyyah*, like *maṭiyy* and *maṭiyyah*. ﴿So whoever among you is ill﴾: an illness that necessitates shaving the head; ﴿or has an injury on his head﴾: such as a wound or lice; ﴿then an expiation﴾: that is, upon him is an expiation if he shaves; ﴿of fasting, or charity, or a sacrifice﴾: this is an explanation of the type of expiation. As for its amount, it is narrated that "the Prophet ﷺ said to Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah: 'Perhaps your lice have harmed you.' He said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Shave, and fast three days, or give charity of a *faraq* to six needy persons, or sacrifice a sheep.'" The *faraq* is three *āṣuʿ* (measures). ﴿Then when you are secure﴾: that is, from iḥṣār; or when you are in a state of safety or ease; ﴿then whoever benefits from the ʿumrah until the ḥajj﴾: that is, whoever benefits by drawing near to Allah (exalted) through ʿumrah before benefiting by drawing near through ḥajj, within its months. It has also been said: whoever enjoys, after exiting the state from his ʿumrah, the permitted things forbidden by ihrām, until he enters into ihrām for ḥajj. ﴿Then what is feasible of the offering﴾: that is, upon him is an offering that he can afford because of the tamattuʿ (combining ʿumrah and ḥajj in one journey).
