It is a compensatory offering (*dam jubrān*), which he slaughters when he enters into ihrām for ḥajj, and he does not eat from it according to al-Shāfiʿī. According to us, it is like the sacrificial animal of ʿĪd. ﴿Then whoever does not find it﴾: that is, the offering; ﴿then a fast of three days during the ḥajj﴾: that is, in its months, between the two states of ihrām. al-Shāfiʿī said: during the days of being occupied with its rites, after entering into ihrām and before exiting the state. The best is that he fasts on the seventh, eighth, and ninth of Dhū al-Ḥijjah; it is not valid on the Day of Sacrifice or the days of Tashrīq. ﴿And seven when you return﴾: that is, when you depart and have finished with its rites. In one of al-Shāfiʿī's two opinions, it means when you return to your families. It was also read *wa sabʿatan* in the accusative, coordinated with the position of *thalāthat ayyām*. ﴿That is ten complete﴾: a summation of the calculation. Its benefit is that it should not be assumed that the conjunction *wa* means *aw* (or), as in your saying: "Sit with al-Ḥasan and Ibn Sīrīn," and that the number is known in total as it is known in detail, for most Arabs do not know arithmetic. Also, that *seven* refers to the specific number and not to a large quantity, although it may also be used that way. ﴿Complete﴾: an emphatic adjective for "ten," indicating exaggeration in preserving the number. Or it clarifies the completeness of the ten, for it is the first complete number, since with it the units end and its ranks are completed. Or it is restrictive, indicating the complete suitability of its substitution for the offering. ﴿That﴾: a reference, according to us, to tamattuʿ, and according to al-Shāfiʿī, to the ruling mentioned. ﴿For one whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾: this is one who is from the Sacred Precinct at the distance for shortening prayer according to al-Shāfiʿī; and one whose dwelling is beyond the *mīqāt* according to us; and people of the non-sacred area according to Ṭāwūs; and those who are not people of Mecca according to Mālik. ﴿And fear Allah﴾: in preserving His commands and prohibitions, especially in ḥajj. ﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾: for whoever does not fear Him, so that knowledge of Him restrains you from disobedience. Mentioning the noble Name in the place of a pronoun serves to cultivate awe and to instill solemnity.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 197:

﴿The Hajj﴾; i.e., its time; ﴿is in well-known months﴾; known among the people; they are: Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah (according to us; and nine days with the night of sacrifice (laylat al-nahr) according to al-Shafi'i; and all of it according to Malik). The point of disagreement lies in whether what is meant by its time is the time of ihram, or the time of its acts and rites (manasik), or what in it no other rites are proper for at all. Malik disliked performing 'umrah in the remainder of Dhu al-Hijjah; and Abu Hanifah, although he validated entering ihram for it before Shawwal, deemed it disliked. He called two months and part of a month "months" only by giving the part the status of the whole, or by applying the plural to more than one. The masculine sound plural form for non-rational beings comes with the alif and ta' (ending). ﴿So whoever undertakes the Hajj therein﴾; i.e., makes it obligatory upon himself by entering ihram therein, or by talbiyah, or by driving the sacrificial animal (hady); ﴿there shall be no lewd speech, nor wickedness, nor disputing﴾; i.e., no sexual intercourse; or: no obscene speech; nor going beyond the bounds of the Sharia by committing forbidden acts. It was said: by abuse and insulting by nicknames. ﴿Nor disputing﴾; i.e., no quarrelling with servants and companions; ﴿during the Hajj﴾; i.e., during its days. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun serves to show complete concern for its matter and to indicate the reason for the ruling, since visiting the Sacred House, and drawing near to God – Mighty and Majestic – through it, necessitates abandoning the aforementioned matters. The choice of negation is for emphasis in the prohibition and to indicate that this is worthy of not occurring; for what is reprehensible and abhorrent in itself is even more abhorrent within the course of the Hajj, like wearing silk in prayer, or beautifying the recitation of the Qur'an with melody, because it is a departure from the dictates of nature and custom into pure worship. The first two were read with the nominative (raf'), meaning: let there be no lewd speech nor wickedness; and the third with the fatha, meaning the report that there is no dispute in the Hajj. That is because Quraysh used to differ from the rest of the Arabs by standing at the Sacred Landmark (al-Mash'ar al-Haram), so the disagreement was removed by being commanded to also stand at 'Arafat. ﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾; so He will reward it with the best reward; and this is an exhortation to doing good following the prohibition of evil. ﴿And take provision, for the best provision is taqwa﴾; i.e., take provision for your return the taqwa, for it is the best provision. It was said: it was revealed concerning the people of Yemen, who used to perform Hajj without taking provisions, and would say, "We are reliant upon God," so they became a burden upon the people; so they were commanded to take provisions and to avoid pressing and burdening people with requests. ﴿And fear Me, O people of understanding﴾; for the essence of intellect is sensing the fear of God – Mighty and Majestic – and His taqwa; He urged them to taqwa, then commanded that the aim in this be God (Exalted), so that they disassociate themselves from everything other than Him; and this is what reason requires, when free of the impurities of desire; therefore this address is specifically directed to the people of understanding (ulu al-albab).

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 2, verse 198:**

﴿There is no blame upon you﴾ [in] ﴿that you seek﴾: i.e., in seeking, that is, that you seek ﴿bounty from your Lord﴾; i.e., reward and provision from Him, namely profit through trade. (It is said: 'Ukaz, Majanna, and Dhu al-Majaz, their markets in the Jahiliyya, were held during the days of the Hajj seasons, and their livelihoods came from them. When Islam came, they regarded it as sinful [to trade during the pilgrimage], so this verse was revealed.)

﴿Then when you pour forth from 'Arafat﴾: i.e., you press on from it in great numbers, from "afadtu al-ma'" (I poured the water), when I poured it out abundantly. Its original form is "afadtum anfusakum" (you poured forth yourselves), so the object was omitted, like the omission in "daftu min al-Basra" (I pushed from Basra). ﻋَﺮَﻓَﺎتٌ ('Arafat) is a plural that has been named as a proper noun, like ﺃَﺫْﺭِﻋَﺎتٌ (Adhri'at). It is given tanwin and takes a kasra, and it has both proper-name status (ʿalamiyya, the status of a proper noun) and feminine form (ta'nith). This is because the tanwin of the plural is the tanwin of correspondence (tanwin al-muqabala), not the tanwin of declinability (tanwin al-tamakkun). For this reason it can be made definite with the article al-. The loss of the kasra follows the loss of the tanwin without a substitute, because it is not declined (ghayr munsarif). Here, however, the case is not so. Alternatively, the feminine form is either by the ta' mentioned, which is not the ta' of feminine gender but rather, with the alif before it, the sign of the feminine plural, or by a hidden ta', as in "Su'ad." There is no way to this, because the ta' that is mentioned resists being assumed hidden, since it is like a substitute for it, being specific to the feminine, like the ta' of "bint" (daughter). The standing-place was named ʿArafa because Abraham, peace be upon him, was shown it, and when he saw it he recognized it. Or because Gabriel, peace be upon him, used to circle with him through the holy places, and when he saw it he said, "I have recognized (ʿaraftu)." Or because Adam and Eve met there and recognized one another. Or because people recognize one another there. It is one of the coined proper names (al-asma' al-murtajala), except for those who make it the plural of ʿarif.

It is said: in this is evidence for the obligation of standing there (because pouring forth does not happen except after it, and it is commanded by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then pour forth﴾ [Q 2:199]). The Prophet ﷺ said: "The Hajj is 'Arafa; whoever reaches 'Arafa has reached the Hajj." Or [the mention of 'Arafat] is a prelude to the remembrance that is commanded. In this there is a point for consideration, since remembrance is not obligatory and the command to it is not absolute.

﴿Then remember God﴾ by the talbiya, the tahlil, and supplication. It is said: by praying the two evening prayers ﴿at the sacred monument﴾. It is a mountain on which the imam stands, and it is called Quzah. (It is said: it is what lies between the two passes of 'Arafa and the valley of Muhassir. The first view is supported by what Jabir narrated: "When he, peace be upon him, prayed the dawn prayer, meaning at Muzdalifa, in the dark before dawn, he mounted his she-camel until he came to the sacred monument, and he supplicated there, and magnified God, and declared His unity, and he did not cease standing until it became light.") It was called a monument (mash'ar) because it is a sign of worship, and it was described as "sacred" (haram) because of its sanctity. The meaning of ﴿at the sacred monument﴾ is what is adjacent to it and near to it, for that is more excellent. Otherwise, all of Muzdalifa is a standing-place, except the valley of Muhassir.

﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾; i.e., as He has taught you; or: remember Him with a good remembrance, as He has guided you with a good guidance to the rites and other things. The ﻣَﺎ ("ma") is either maṣdariyya (verbal-noun forming) or kaffa (restraining). ﴿And indeed you were before that﴾, before what was mentioned of His guidance to you, ﴿among the astray﴾, those not acting by faith and obedience. The ﺇِﻥْ ("in") is the light form (mukhaffafa), and the lam is the distinguishing lam (al-lam al-fariqa). It is said: it is a negation, and the lam has the meaning of "illa" (except), as in His saying, Mighty and Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed we think you are among the liars﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 199:

﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾: (p-209) That is, from ʿArafah, not from Muzdalifah. The address is to the Quraysh, since they used to stand at Jumʿ (Muzdalifah), while the rest of the people stood at ʿArafah, and they regarded this as a mark of superiority over them, so they were commanded to be equal with them. The "thumma" (then) indicates the difference between the two departures, as in your saying: "Be good to people; then do not be good except to a noble person." It is also said: [the departure is] from Muzdalifah to Mina, after the departure from ʿArafah to it. The address is general. It was also read as "al-nāsi" (with a kasra on the sin), meaning "the forgetful one," referring to Adam (peace be upon him), from His saying (exalted is He): ﴿but he forgot﴾. The meaning is that departing from ʿArafah is an ancient prescription, so do not change it. ﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah﴾, for your ignorance (jahiliyyah) in altering the rites. ﴿Indeed Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾, who forgives the sin of the one who seeks forgiveness and bestows His favor upon him. So this is a reason for seeking forgiveness, or for the command to seek it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 200:

﴿So when you have completed your rites﴾; i.e., your acts of worship connected with the Hajj, and you have finished with them; ﴿then remember Allah as you remember your fathers﴾; i.e., remember Him (exalted is He) abundantly and strive in that, just as you do when mentioning your fathers, their glories and their days; and when the Arabs had completed their rites, they would stand at Mina, between the mosque and the mountain, and mention the glories of their fathers and the fine days of their forefathers. ﴿Or with a greater remembrance﴾: it may be genitive, conjoined to "remembrance," by treating it as the one remembering, in a figurative sense; and the meaning is: remember Allah with a remembrance like your remembrance of your fathers, or like a remembrance greater than it and more eloquent; or it is in the sense of what it is attached to, meaning: or like the remembrance of a people greater in remembrance than you; or it is accusative, conjoined to "your fathers," and "remembrance" is from the verb of the one mentioned, meaning: or like your remembrance of the greatest of your fathers as one mentioned; or it is governed by an implied term indicated by the meaning, its estimate being: or be more intense in the remembrance of Allah than you are in the remembrance of your fathers. ﴿So among the people﴾: a detailing of those who remember, into those who seek by the remembrance of Allah (exalted is He) nothing but this world, and those who seek by it the good of both abodes; and what is intended by it is the exhortation to abundance and to being counted among the latter. ﴿Who say﴾; i.e., in their remembrance; ﴿"Our Lord, give us in this world"﴾; i.e., make our giving and our bounty in this world alone; ﴿and he has no portion in the Hereafter﴾; i.e., no share or allotment, because his concern is confined to this world; so it is an explanation of his state in the Hereafter; or: no portion of seeking [such] a portion, so it is an explanation of his state in this world, and an emphasis on confining his supplication to worldly aims.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 201:

﴿And among them is he who says: "Our Lord, give us good in this world"﴾: it is health, sufficiency, and success in goodness; ﴿and good in the Hereafter﴾: it is reward and mercy; ﴿and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾; by pardon and forgiveness.

It is narrated from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that the good in this world is a righteous woman, and in the Hereafter, the maiden of paradise (al-hawra'); and the punishment of the Fire is a bad wife.

It is narrated from al-Hasan that the good in this world is knowledge and worship, and in the Hereafter, Paradise; and "protect us from the punishment of the Fire" means: guard us from the desires and sins that lead to the Fire.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 202:**

﴿Those﴾: a reference to the second group, on account of their being characterized by the praiseworthy attributes mentioned. The sense of distance in it (the demonstrative used for what is far) points, as has been noted many times before, to the elevation of their rank and the loftiness of their standing in virtue. It has also been said that it refers to both groups together. The tanwin (nunation, the indefinite marker "-n") in His words, exalted is He, ﴿For them is a share of what they have earned﴾, is, according to the first view, for magnification (tafkhim), and according to the second, for specification of kinds (tanwi'): that is, each of them has a kind of share (p-210) of the same type as what they earned, or on account of it, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned﴾. Or it means: of what they supplicated for, We will give them some of it, that which We have decreed. Calling supplication "earning" is because it is one of the deeds. ﴿And Allah is swift in reckoning﴾: He reckons with His servants, despite their multitude and the multitude of their deeds, in the span of a glance. So beware of neglecting obedience to One whose power is of this nature. Or [it means] that He is about to establish the Resurrection and call people to account, so hasten to the acts of obedience and to acquiring good deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 203:

﴿And remember Allah﴾; that is, glorify Him (takbir) after the prayers, at the slaughtering of the sacrificial animals, at the stoning of the pillars (ramy al-jimar), and in other occasions; ﴿during the appointed days﴾; these are the days of tashriq (ayyam al-tashriq); ﴿So whoever hastens﴾; that is, hastens in departing (al-nafr) or in departure (al-nafar), for the form tafa''ala and istif'ala come both intransitive and transitive. It is said: "ta'ajjala fi al-amr" and "ista'jala fihi" and "ta'ajjalahu" and "ista'jalahu." The first is more suitable to the one who delays, as in his saying:

Perhaps the one who takes his time attains some of his need,
and perhaps the hasty one suffers a slip.

﴿in two days﴾; that is, within the completion of two days after the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr), which is the Day of Qarr (yawm al-qarr) and the Day of Heads (yawm al-ru'us); and the day after it, one departs when one has finished stoning the pillars; ﴿and whoever delays﴾; in departing until he stones on the third day, either before noon (al-zawal) or after it; and according to al-Shafi'i, only after it; ﴿there is no sin upon him﴾; for what he did of delay; and what is intended is the choice between hastening and delaying; and the superiority of the second does not detract from this. The negation of sin was stated explicitly as a rebuttal of the people of pre-Islamic ignorance (ahl al-Jahiliyya), who differed: some considered the one who hastens sinful, and others considered the one who delays sinful. ﴿for him who fears (Allah)﴾: a predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'); that is, what has been mentioned of the choice and the negation of sin for the one who hastens or delays; or of the rulings; is for him who fears (Allah), because he is the true pilgrim (al-hajj 'ala al-haqiqa) and the one who benefits from it, or for whose sake it is, so that he is not harmed by abandoning what concerns him of the two. ﴿And fear Allah﴾; in all the matters of your affairs; by performing the obligations and abstaining from the forbidden; so that He may regard you and you may be enrolled among those who profit from the rulings mentioned and the concessions; or: beware of neglecting the rulings mentioned; and this is more fitting with His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And know that you will be gathered to Him﴾; that is, for recompense for your deeds after revival and resurrection (al-ba'th); and the origin of hashr is gathering and bringing together what is scattered. This is an emphasis on the command to piety and a compelling reason to comply with it, for whoever knows of the gathering, the reckoning, and the recompense, that is among the strongest motives to constancy in piety.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 204:

﴿And among the people is one whose speech pleases you﴾: It is a turning away from direct address (tajrid lil-khitab) and a directing of it toward him (ʿalayhi al-salatu wa al-salam) [the Prophet ﷺ]. It is an independent statement (kalam mubtada'), brought to explain the division of people into two parties concerning the matter of God-consciousness (taqwa), and to specify the outcome of each of them. The word "man" (مَن) is either a relative pronoun (mawsula) or a descriptive (mawsufa). Its grammatical analysis is as explained in His (exalted) words: ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in God and the Last Day"﴾. That is: among them is one whose speech pleases you and whose position greatly impresses you, because of what you observe in it of the appropriateness of its content and the grace of its delivery. Ta'ajjub (wonder/amazement) is a bewilderment that comes over a person due to a lack of understanding of the cause of what he marvels at.

﴿in the life of this world﴾: It is connected to "qawluhu" (his speech); that is, what he says concerning the life of this world and its meaning, for it is what he intends by what he claims of faith and love of the Messenger ﷺ. In this there is an indication that he has another speech which does not have this quality. Or it is connected to "yu'jibuka" (pleases you); that is, his speech pleases you in this world by its sweetness (p-211) and its eloquence, not in the Hereafter, because his lying and its ugliness will become apparent there. It has been said: because of the stammering and the impediment in speech that will afflict him there. And you know well that there is then no exaggeration in describing his bad condition, for its outcome is the explanation of the goodness of his speech in this world and its ugliness in the Hereafter. It has also been said: the meaning of "fi al-hayah al-dunya" is "for the duration of the life of this world"; that is, there issues from him in it only good speech.

﴿and he calls God to witness concerning what is in his heart﴾: that is, according to his claim, when he says: "God knows that what is in my heart agrees with what is on my tongue." It is coordinated (ʿataf) upon "yu'jibuka." It has been read as "wa-yashhadu Allah" (and God bears witness). So what is meant by "what is in his heart" is what is actually in it. This is supported by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with them both): "wa-Allahu yashhadu ʿala ma fi qalbihi" (and God bears witness against what is in his heart); here the word "ʿala" (against) indicates that what is witnessed to is harmful to him, so the clause is parenthetical (i'tirad). It has also been read as "wa-yastashhid Allah" (and he calls God to witness).

﴿and he is the most contentious of adversaries﴾: that is, most intense in enmity and hostility toward the Muslims. Here "al-khisam" is a verbal noun (masdar), and the annexation of "alladd" to it carries the sense of "in" (fi), as in their saying "thabit al-ʿudhr" (firm in excuse). Or it means "the most hostile of adversaries toward them in hostility," the word being a plural of "khasm" like "sa'b" and "si'ab." It has been said: this was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafi, who was handsome in appearance and sweet in speech, who professed loyalty to the Messenger of God ﷺ and claimed Islam and love. It has also been said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the genitive in "qawluhu," or from the concealed pronoun in "yushhidu," and it is coordinated upon what precedes it according to the two intermediate readings.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 205:

﴿And when he turns away﴾; i.e., from your assembly. It was also said: when he becomes a governor (wali). ﴿He strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and progeny﴾; as al-Akhnas did to the Thaqif, when he attacked them by night, burned their crops, and destroyed their livestock; or as wicked rulers do by killing, destruction, or oppression, so that God (Exalted is He) withholds rain through their evil, and thus the crops and progeny perish. It was also read: "and the crops and progeny perish" (wa-yuhlika al-harthu wal-naslu), attributing the destruction to them both, coordinated with "strives" (sa'a). It was also read with a fatha on the lam (yahlaka), which is a dialectal form. It was also read in the passive voice from the causative (ihlak). ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾; i.e., He does not approve of it, He hates it, and He is angered at whoever engages in it. This is a concluding parenthetical statement (i'tiraD tadhyiliyy).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 206:

﴿And when it is said to him﴾; in the manner of admonition and advice; ﴿"Fear Allah"﴾; and abandon what you engage in of corruption or hypocrisy, and beware the evil of its outcome; ﴿pride takes him to sin﴾; i.e., arrogance and the zeal of the Jahiliyya carry him to the sin that he was forbidden from, out of obstinacy and defiance. It derives from your saying "akhadhtuhu bi-kadha" (I took him to such-and-such), when you drive him to it or obligate him to it; ﴿so Hell is sufficient for him﴾: it is a mubtada' (subject) and a khabar (predicate), i.e., Hell suffices him. It was also said that "Jahannam" is the fa'il (agent) of "hasbuhu," filling the place of its predicate, and it is a masdar (verbal noun) in the sense of the active participle; and it is strengthened by its reliance on the fa' (fa'), which links the sentence to what precedes it. It was also said that "hasb" is a past-tense verbal noun (ism fi'l madi), i.e., Hell has sufficed him; ﴿and wretched is the resting-place﴾: is the answer to an implied oath, and the object of the blame is omitted because it is evident and determined. "Al-mihad" means the bed; it was also said it is what is spread out for the side (of the body). And the sentence is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 207:

﴿And among the people is one who sells himself﴾: (it is) a mubtada' (subject) and a khabar (predicate), as has passed; i.e., he sells it by expending it in jihad, in the hardships of acts of obedience, and by exposing it to ruin in wars; or (he) enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong, even if it results in his being killed; ﴿seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾; i.e., seeking His approval. This is the perfection of taqwa (God-consciousness). Its mention as a counterpart to the first is (because) that (first person) disdains the command to taqwa, whereas this one enjoins it, even if it leads to destruction. It is said: it was revealed concerning Suhayb ibn Sinan al-Rumi, whom the polytheists seized and tortured so that he would apostatize. He said: "I am an old man; I will not benefit you if I am with you, nor harm you if I am against you. So leave me alone with what I am upon, and take my wealth." So they accepted his wealth from him, and he went to Madina. Thus "yashri" (here) then means "yashtari" (buys), because the situation proceeds in the form of a sale. ﴿And Allah is Compassionate toward the servants﴾; and for this reason He imposes taqwa upon them and exposes them to reward; and the sentence is a parenthetical concluding statement (i'tiradh tadhyili).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 208:

﴿O you who have believed, enter into peace (al-silm) completely⦆; that is, submission (al-istislam) and obedience (al-ta'ah). It has been said: Islam (al-Islam). It is also read with a fatha on the sin (al-sin), which is a dialect form of it, and also with a fatha on the lam.

As for His saying (exalted is He): ﴿kaffah﴾, it is a circumstantial state (hal) either of the pronoun in "udkhulu" (enter), or of "al-silm," or of both together, as in the verse:

I went out with her walking, dragging behind us
on our traces the trailing hem of a fringed, finely-woven cloak.

Originally, kaffah is a noun for a group that restrains its opponent; then it was used in the sense of "all together" (jami'an). Its ta' is not the feminine marker, so there is no need to make "al-silm" feminine like "al-harb" (war), as in the saying of Him, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾; and in the verse:

Peace: take from it whatever you are pleased with,
and war: sips of its breaths will suffice you.

Rather, it is for transfer (naql), as in "ammah" (general), "khassah" (особенно), and "qati'bah" (all of them). The meaning is: submit to God (exalted is He) and obey Him completely, outwardly and inwardly. The address is to the hypocrites; or: enter into Islam in its entirety, and do not mix with it anything else. The address is to the believers among the People of the Book, for they used to observe some of the rulings of their former religion after their conversion to Islam; or (it concerns) all of God's (exalted is He) laws, by believing in all the prophets (upon them be peace) and all the books. The address is to all the People of the Book, and their description as believers is either according to the method of predominance (al-taghlib), or in view of their former faith; or (it concerns) the branches of Islam and all its rulings, so that they neglect none of them. The address is to the Muslims. The People of the Book are addressed with the title of faith even though faith is not valid except with what they are now obligated to, to indicate that what they claim does not become complete without it.

﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾, by division and by causing division, or by opposing what you have been commanded. ﴿Indeed, he is to you a manifest enemy﴾, clearly hostile, or one who displays enmity; and this is a justification for the prohibition, or for the cessation.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on Surah 2, verse 209:

﴿Then if you slip﴾; that is, from entering into peace (silm). It is also read with a kasra on the lam (zalaltum), which is a dialect form of the same verb. ﴿after the clear proofs have come to you﴾; the signs (al-ayat), ﴿the clear ones﴾ (al-bayyinat), and the decisive arguments (al-hujaj al-qat'iyyah) that indicate its reality and make entering into it obligatory. ﴿Then know that Allah is Mighty﴾; overpowering in His command, such that retribution against you does not escape Him; ﴿Wise﴾; He does not neglect what wisdom requires of punishing the criminals, those who are obstinate against His commands.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 210:

﴿Do they wait﴾: an interrogative of denial, meaning a negation; i.e., they do not await, by what they do of obstinacy, opposition in obeying what they were commanded, and failure to desist from what they were forbidden; ﴿except that Allah should come to them﴾; i.e., His command, and His punishment; or Allah should come to them with His command and His punishment. The object brought is omitted because the context indicates it. The shift to the third person (ghayba) is to signal that the evil of their conduct necessitates turning away from them. The mention of their crime is for others among the people of fairness, in the manner of a gentle reproach; and the mention of waiting is to convey that, because they are immersed in what they are in of the causes of punishment, it is as though they were seeking it and awaiting its occurrence; ﴿in shadows﴾, like "qulal" (plural of "qullah"), the plural of "qullah," which is that which overshadows you; it is also read "fi zilal," like "qilal," the plural of "qillah"; ﴿of the clouds﴾; i.e., the white clouds. The punishment comes in them only because they are the locus of mercy; so when punishment comes from them, it is more terrible and cuts off hopes, for the coming of evil from where it is not expected is hard, so how much harder is its coming from where good is hoped for?

﴿And the angels﴾: a conjunction with the Glorious Name; i.e., and the angels come to them, for they are intermediaries in the bringing of His command (exalted is He); rather, they are the ones who actually bring His punishment. The placement of the adverbial phrase between the two is to signal that what comes first is of the kind that accompanies clouds and ordinarily follows from them; as for the angels, although their coming accompanies what has been mentioned of the clouds, that is not by way of habitual occurrence. It is also read in the genitive, as a conjunction with "zulal" or "al-ghamam"; ﴿and the matter is decided﴾; i.e., the matter of their destruction is completed and finished; it is a conjunction with "yatiyahum," falling within the sphere of waiting. The past form was adopted to indicate its certainty, so that it is as though it had already happened; or it is a resumptive clause, brought to announce the occurrence of its content. It is also read "wa qada'u al-amr," as a conjunction with "al-mala'ikah"; ﴿and to Allah﴾, not to other than Him; ﴿are the affairs returned﴾; in the feminine, in the passive voice, from "al-raj'" (causing to return); it is also read in the masculine, and in the active voice in the feminine from "al-ruju'" (returning).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 211:

﴿Ask the Children of Israel﴾: The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ); or it is to everyone among the people addressed. The purpose of the question is to rebuke them (tabkit) and reproach them for this, and to affirm the coming of the clear proofs. ﴿How many clear signs We gave them﴾: a manifest miracle, performed at the hands of the prophets (peace be upon them), and a sign speaking to the truth (haqqiyyah) of Islam, to which one is commanded to enter. The word "kam" (كَمْ) is either declarative (khabariyyah), or interrogative used to affirm (istifhamiyyah muqarrirah). Its place in the sentence is in the accusative as an object (maf'ul), or in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), with the returning pronoun (a'id) from the predicate omitted. "Ayah" (آيَةٍ) is its specifying noun (tamyiz). ﴿And whoever substitutes the blessing of God﴾: which are His dazzling signs; for they are the means to guidance, which is the most noble of blessings. Substituting them means making them a cause of misguidance and of increased defilement (rijs); or distorting them; or interpreting them in a deviant way. ﴿After what has come to him﴾: and has reached him, and he has been able to know them. The explicit statement of this, although substitution cannot be conceived before the coming, serves to indicate that they had substituted them after they had become acquainted with their details, as in His statement, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Then they distort it after they had understood it, while they knew﴾. It is said that its implied sense is: "so they substituted them, and whoever substitutes"; and it was omitted to signal that there is no need to state it explicitly, since it is evident. ﴿Indeed, God is severe in punishment﴾: this is a justification of the answer, as if it were said: whoever substitutes the blessing of God, He will punish him with the most severe punishment, for He is severe in punishment. The explicit mention of the Glorious Name serves to cultivate awe and to instil dread.

﴿Adorned for those who disbelieve is the life of this world﴾: that is, it has become beautiful in their eyes, and love for it has been infused into their hearts, so that they fall upon it greedily and rush headlong into it, turning away from anything else. The adornment, in terms of creation and bringing into being, is attributed to Allah, glory be to Him, as the recitation in the passive form (al-bina' lil-fa'il, the form that names the agent) indicates. For there is nothing that He does not create, and everything, whether Satan, the animal faculties (al-quwa al-hayawaniyya), or the splendid matters and desirable things in this world, is adorned only incidentally.

﴿And they mock those who believe﴾: this is coordinated (ma'tuf) with "adorned." The use of the present-future verbal form (sighat al-istiqbal) indicates the continuation of the mockery directed at them. They are the poor among the believers, such as Bilal, Ammar and Suhayb, may Allah be pleased with them. The disbelievers used to look down on them and ridicule them because they renounced this world and turned toward the hereafter. The "min" here is ibtida'iyya (indicating the starting point), as if they made the mockery originate from themselves.

﴿But those who are mindful of Allah﴾: they are the very same ones who believed, and they were mentioned by the title of taqwa (mindfulness of Allah) only to signal that their turning away from this world was a way of guarding themselves against it, since it impedes their devotion (tabattul) to the sacred presence (janab al-Quds) and distracts them from it.

﴿will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾: because they are in the highest of the high (Illiyyin, the lofty station in Paradise), while the others are in the lowest of the low. Or because they are in the zenith of honour while the others are in the depths of humiliation and abasement. Or because they will look down upon them in the hereafter, and so they will mock them as they mocked them in this world. The sentence is coordinated with what precedes it, and the use of the nominal form indicates the permanence of its meaning.

﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills﴾: that is, in both abodes. ﴿Without measure﴾: without reckoning. So He widens provision in this world at times as a gradual lead-on (istidraj, a gradual drawing toward ruin), and at other times as a trial (ibtila').

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 213:

﴿Mankind was one community﴾: agreeing upon the word of truth (kalimat al-haqq) and the religion of Islam. This was either between Adam and Idris, or Noah (peace be upon them both), or after the Flood. ﴿Then God sent the prophets﴾; i.e., they differed, so He sent... etc. This is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), and the words "and they differed" have been omitted, relying on what is mentioned immediately after it: ﴿as bearers of good tidings and warners﴾. On the authority of Ka'b: "What I know of the number of the prophets (peace be upon them) is one hundred and twenty-four thousand; and those among them who were messengers are three hundred and thirteen; and those mentioned in the Qur'an are twenty-eight." It has also been said: "Mankind was one community," agreeing upon disbelief and error, during the interval (fatra) between Idris or Noah; then God sent the prophets, and they differed concerning them. The first view is more suitable to the noble composition.

﴿And He sent down with them the Book﴾: i.e., the genus of Book; or, with each one of them who had a book, his own specific book, not with each one of them without exception, since some of them had no book, but they would follow the books of those before them. The generality of "the prophets" does not negate the specificity of the pronoun referring to it by the aid of context. ﴿With the truth﴾: a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "the Book"; i.e., combined with the truth. Or it is connected to "sent down," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it descended﴾.

﴿That he might judge﴾: i.e., the Book; or God, glorified and exalted is He; or each one of the prophets; ﴿between the people﴾; i.e., those mentioned; the explicit noun is used in place of the pronoun to add specificity; ﴿concerning that about which they differed﴾; i.e., concerning the truth about which they differed; or concerning what had become confused for them. ﴿And none differed concerning it﴾; i.e., concerning the truth, or concerning the Book sent down while it was combined with it; the waw is circumstantial; ﴿except those who were given it﴾; i.e., the Book revealed to remove disagreement and dispel discord. The expression of the sending down as "giving" serves as an alert from the outset to their complete capacity to grasp the truth contained within its folds, for mere sending down does not yield that benefit. In other words, they reversed the matter, since they made what was sent down to remove disagreement a cause for its entrenchment and firm establishment. ﴿After the clear proofs had come to them﴾; i.e., they took firm root in their minds. The "min" is connected to an omitted element indicated by the context; i.e., they differed, and what they differed about... etc. It has also been said that it is connected to the spoken element, based on the view that "illa" does not prevent this, as in your saying: "No one stood except Zayd on the day (p-215) of Friday."

﴿Out of insolence among themselves﴾: connected to what "min" is connected to; i.e., they differed out of insolence and greed for worldly things. ﴿So God guided those who believed to the truth about which they had differed﴾; i.e., to the truth about which whoever differed had differed. ﴿By His permission﴾; i.e., by His command, or by His facilitation and kindness. ﴿And God guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾; leading to the truth. This is a parenthetical clause affirming the content of what preceded it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 214:

﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed away before you?﴾ This was addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and to those believers who were with him, urging them to be steadfast in perseverance in opposing the disbelievers and in bearing the hardships they suffered at their hands. It follows the explanation of how the nations differed over the prophets (peace be upon them), and it makes clear the outcome of their disagreement, what the prophets and those with them before them endured of severe trials and suffered of anxieties, and that the final outcome of their affair was victory. The "am" (أم) here is disjunctive (munqati'a, introducing a new question), and the hamza (الهمزة) within it is for denial and disapproval, meaning: "Rather, did you think...". ﴿That you would enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed away before you﴾ refers to the prophets and the believers with them. That is, the situation is that their example has not yet come to you, and you have not been tested with the terrible conditions with which they were tested, which are a byword for horror and severity, and which are expected and awaited.

﴿Touched them﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istinaf), which came as an answer to what the mind is led to ask. As if it were said: "What was their example?" So it was said: ﴿Touched them adversity﴾, that is, hardship, from fear and poverty; ﴿and affliction﴾, that is, pains and sicknesses; ﴿and they were shaken﴾, that is, they were violently disturbed by the terrors and dreadful things that overwhelmed them. ﴿Until the Messenger said, and those who believed with him﴾, that is, their affair reached such severity that their weariness compelled them to say, the Messenger, who is the most knowledgeable of people about the affairs of Allah (Exalted), and the most certain of His support, and the believers who follow his traces and are illuminated by his lights: ﴿When?﴾, that is, when will there come ﴿the help of Allah﴾, seeking it and longing for it, and wishing that the period of hardship and distress were shorter. It was also read as حَتّى يَقُولُ (ḥattā yaqūlu, "until he says") with a raised final vowel (ar-raf'), as a narration of a past state (ḥikāyat ḥāl māḍiya). And this, as you see, is the utmost of far-off ends and the ultimate of distant limits. How could it not be so, when the Messengers, despite their high standing in steadfastness and patience, had their patience worn thin, and reached this degree of weariness and lamentation? It is known that the matter had reached an extreme beyond which there is no further aim.

﴿Now surely the help of Allah is near﴾: this is said under an implied "they said" (على تقدير القول), that is, it was said to them at that time, as a relief for their aims. By "near" is meant nearness in time. The choice of the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) over the verbal sentence (al-jumla al-fi'liyya), which would have suited what precedes it, and its opening with the particle of alerting and emphasis (ḥarf al-tanbīh wa-al-ta'kīd), gives an indication of establishing its content and confirming it, which is not hidden. The choice of narrating the promise of victory for us, since it is in the status of issuing a promise to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the limiting of the narration to the promise rather than narrating the victory itself, despite its certainty, is to signal that there is no need for that, because a breaking of the promise is impossible. It is also possible that this came from Him (Exalted) at the time of the narration, as an interjection ( 'alā naḥj al-i'tirāḍ), and not at the time when the narrated event occurred. And in it is an allusion that reaching the presence of holiness is not attainable except by renouncing pleasures and enduring hardships, as his saying (ﷺ) indicates: "Paradise is surrounded by disliked things, and Hell is surrounded by desires."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 215:

﴿They ask you what they should spend.﴾ (p-216) That is: of the kinds of their wealth. ﴿Say: whatever good you spend﴾. "Ma" (whatever) is either a conditional particle, or a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun has been omitted; that is: whatever good you spend of it, of any kind whatsoever. In this is the permission to spend from all types of wealth, and an explanation of what is in the question, except that it has been placed among what falls under the condition or the relative clause, and it is brought forth in the context of explaining the recipients, where it is said: ﴿then for parents and near relatives﴾, to signal that what matters most is the explanation of the enumerated recipients, because the reckoning of spending is according to its occurring in its proper place. And from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, that 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh came, and he was a decrepit old man who had great wealth, and he said: "O Messenger of Allah, what should we spend of our wealth, and where should we place it?" So it was revealed.

﴿And the orphans﴾; that is: those among them who are in need, ﴿and the needy and the wayfarer﴾; and it did not address those who ask, nor the captives (slaves), either being content with what was mentioned in the other passages, or on the basis that they are included under the generality of His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And whatever good you do﴾, for it encompasses every good that occurs, in whatever channel it may be; ﴿indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾; so He will fully reward it. And there is nothing in the verse that contradicts the obligation of zakat so that it would be abrogated by it, as was reported from al-Suddi.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 216:

﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾: [read] with the verb in the passive form (bina' al-fi'l lil-maf'ul) and with "al-qital" in the nominative (raf'); i.e., the fighting of the disbelievers. It was also read with the verb in the active form (bina' lil-fa'il), whose agent is Allah — Mighty and Majestic is He — and with "al-qital" in the accusative (nasb). It was also read "Kutiba 'alaykum al-qatl" (Fighting has been prescribed for you — the killing), i.e., the killing of the disbelievers.

The wa' in His statement (Exalted is He): ﴿and it is hateful to you﴾ is a circumstantial wa' (waw al-hal); i.e., while the state is that it is disliked by you by nature. [This is] on the basis that al-kurh (hatred/compulsion) is a verbal noun (masdar) which is described by the passive participle (al-maf'ul) for emphasis (mubalaghah); or it carries the meaning of the passive participle, like "al-khubz" (the bread) meaning "al-makhbuz" (the baked). It was also read with a fatha (al-fath), on the basis that it means the thing forced upon (al-madmum), like "al-du'f" and "al-du'f" (weakness); or on the basis that it means compulsion (al-ikrah) figuratively, as if they were compelled to it because of the intensity of their dislike of it and its hardship upon them. ﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾: this is all that they were charged with of arduous matters, among which is fighting, for souls dislike it and recoil from it. The sentence is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah), indicating that there is good for them in fighting. ﴿And it may be that you love a thing and it is bad for you﴾: this is all that they were forbidden from among pleasurable matters. It is conjoined to what precedes it, and neither of the two has a place in i'rab (grammatical position). ﴿And Allah knows﴾ what is good for you; therefore He commands you with it. ﴿And you do not know﴾; i.e., you do not know it, and therefore you dislike it. Or: Allah knows what is good and bad for you, and you do not know them both; so do not follow your own opinion in this matter, and comply with His command (Exalted is He).

﴿يَسْألُونَكَ عَنِ الشَّهْرِ الحَرامِ﴾ [They ask you about the sacred month]. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh on an expedition (sariyyah, a small military detachment) in Jumada al-Akhirah, two months before the battle of Badr, to watch for a caravan of Quraysh. Among them was 'Amr ibn 'Abd Allah al-Hadrami, and three others were with him. They killed him, took two prisoners, and seized the caravan with what it held of the merchandise of al-Ta'if. That was on the first day of Rajab, though they thought it was from Jumada al-Akhirah. Quraysh said: "Muhammad has made lawful the sacred month, a month in which the fearful are safe and people disperse to their livelihoods." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) held back the caravan. This was grievous to the companions of the expedition, and they said: "We will not leave until our repentance is revealed." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned the caravan and the captives.

And on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): "When it was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took the spoils." The meaning is: the disbelievers, or the Muslims, ask you about fighting in the sacred month.

As for the words ﴿قِتالٍ فِيهِ﴾ [fighting therein], they are a badal al-ishtimal (an apposition of inclusion, in which the second noun includes or is related to the first) standing in place of "الشَّهْرِ" [the month]. It is indefinite (نكرة, nakirah) because their question concerned fighting in general that occurs in the sacred month, not a specific known fighting. For this reason they did not say, "about fighting in the sacred month." It is also read as ﴿عَنْ قِتالٍ فِيهِ﴾ with the governing preposition repeated, as in ﴿لِلَّذِينَ اسْتُضْعِفُوا لِمَن آمَنَ مِنهُمْ﴾ [to those who were deemed weak, to those among them who believed]. It is also read "قَتْلٍ" [killing].

﴿قُلْ﴾ [Say]: in answer to them, ﴿قِتالٌ فِيهِ كَبِيرٌ﴾ [fighting therein is grave] is a nominal sentence consisting of a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate), and its place in i'rab is accusative by virtue of "قُلْ". The word "قِتالٌ" may stand as a mubtada' although it is indefinite, because it is specified either by a description, if the adverbial phrase "فِيهِ" is attached to an omitted word and so serves as a qualifier meaning "fighting that exists therein," or by its governing function, if the phrase is attached to it. The indefinite form was chosen to avoid the impression of a specific fighting, and to signal that the intended meaning is any fighting that occurs therein, of whatever kind.

It is narrated from 'Ata' that he was asked about fighting in the sacred month, and he swore by Allah that it is not lawful for people to make raids in the Haram or in the sacred month, except if they are attacked there. He said that it was not abrogated. Most opinions hold that it was abrogated (naskh, the replacement of a ruling by a later one) by His words: ﴿فاقْتُلُوا المُشْرِكِينَ حَيْثُ وجَدْتُمُوهُمْ﴾ [then kill the polytheists wherever you find them].

﴿وَصَدٌّ عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ [And hindering from the way of Allah]: this is a mubtada' that is specified by the element governed after it. That is, it means prevention from Islam, which leads the servant to Allah.

﴿وَكُفْرٌ بِهِ﴾ [and disbelief in Him] is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "صَدٌّ" and governs what follows in the same way. That is, it means disbelief in Allah.

Since hindering from the way of Allah is one instance of disbelief in Him, the conjunction mentioned above does not impair the propriety of conjoining His words ﴿والمَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾ [and the Sacred Mosque] to "سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ" [the way of Allah], because it is not wholly foreign to it. It has also been said that it too is conjoined to "صَدٌّ", with an elided genitive-linking noun, so that the sense is "and the hindering of the Sacred Mosque."

﴿وَإخْراجُ أهْلِهِ﴾ [and the expulsion of its people], namely the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, ﴿مِنهُ﴾ [from it], that is, from the Sacred Mosque. This is conjoined to "وَكُفْرٌ بِهِ".

﴿أكْبَرُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ﴾ [is greater in the sight of Allah] is the khabar for the enumerated matters. That is, the grave sins of the questioners are greater in the sight of Allah than what they intended by the question, which is what the expedition did in error and on the basis of supposition. The form "أفْعَلُ" [greater] is used uniformly for the singular, the plural, the masculine and the feminine.

﴿والفِتْنَةُ﴾ [And persecution], that is, what they committed of expulsion, polytheism, and hindering people from Islam, both at its outset and continuing, ﴿أكْبَرُ مِنَ القَتْلِ﴾ [is greater than killing], that is, more monstrous than the killing of al-Hadrami.

﴿وَلا يَزالُونَ يُقاتِلُونَكُمْ﴾ [And they will not cease fighting you] explains the firmness of their enmity and their persistence in persecuting you in religion, ﴿حَتّى يَرُدُّوكم عَنْ دِينِكُمْ﴾ [until they turn you back from your religion], the true one, to their false religion. The attribution of religion to you is made to emphasise the strength of the bond between you and it, which makes separation impossible.

﴿إنِ اسْتَطاعُوا﴾ [if they are able] indicates their obstinacy in their religion and the steadfastness of their stance in it, as if it were said: "and how could they do that?"

﴿وَمَن يَرْتَدِدْ مِنكم عَنْ دِينِهِ﴾ [And whoever of you apostatises from his religion] is a warning against apostasy, that is, whoever does so by leading others astray and misguiding them, ﴿فَيَمُتْ وهو كافِرٌ﴾ [and dies while he is a disbeliever], by not returning to Islam. This contains an encouragement to return to Islam after apostasy.

﴿فَأُولَئِكَ﴾ [those] refers back to the relative pronoun, in view of its being characterised by apostasy and dying upon it as stated in the relative clause. The distal demonstrative, which carries the sense of distance, is used to indicate how far their rank is in evil and corruption. The plural is used in view of the meaning, that is, those who persist in apostasy until death.

﴿حَبِطَتْ أعْمالُهُمْ﴾ [their deeds have become void], the good deeds they had done while in Islam, with a voiding for which there is certainly no remedy, ﴿فِي الدُّنْيا والآخِرَةِ﴾ [in this world and the Hereafter], such that no ruling of the worldly or otherworldly rulings remains for them.

﴿وَأُولَئِكَ﴾ [And those], described by what was mentioned previously and subsequently of foul deeds, ﴿أصْحابُ النّارِ﴾ [are the companions of the Fire], that is, those who are bound to it and abide in it, ﴿هم فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ [they will abide therein forever], like the manner of all disbelievers. (p-218)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 218:

﴿Indeed, those who have believed﴾: It was revealed concerning the companions of the expedition (sariyyah), because it was suspected of them that if they were safe from sin, there would be no reward for them. ﴿And those who emigrated (hajaroo) and strove (jahadu) in the way of Allah﴾: He repeated the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), even though the intended referent of both is one, in order to magnify the matter of emigration (hijrah) and striving (jihad), so that the two are, as it were, independent in realizing the hope. ﴿Those﴾: the ones described with the sublime attributes mentioned. ﴿Hope﴾ (yarjoon): with what they have of the beginnings of success. ﴿The mercy of Allah﴾ (rahmat Allah): that is, His reward. He attributed hope to them without attributing the attainment of what is hoped for, to indicate that they know that the deed does not necessitate the reward, but rather it is by way of His bounty, glory be to Him, not because there is any uncertainty in their attaining it. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving﴾ (ghafur): exceedingly so in forgiving what their servants have neglected by error. ﴿Merciful﴾ (rahim): He bestows abundant reward and recompense upon them. The clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) that confirms the meaning of what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 219:

﴿They ask you about wine and gambling.﴾ Four verses were revealed concerning wine. The first was revealed in Mecca: ﴿And from the fruits of the date-palms and grapes you take from them intoxicant and good provision.﴾ So the Muslims began to drink it. Then 'Umar, Mu'adh, and a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, said: "Give us a ruling, O Messenger of Allah, concerning wine, for it takes away the intellect." So this verse was revealed. Some people drank it and others abandoned it. Then 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf invited some of them, and they drank and became intoxicated. Then one of them led them in prayer and recited: "Say, O disbelievers, I worship what you worship." So this was revealed: ﴿Do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated﴾, and the verse [continues]. So few people drank it afterwards. Then 'Utban ibn Malik invited Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, along with a group. When they became intoxicated, they boasted and recited poetry to one another, until Sa'd recited a poem containing satire of the Ansar. An Ansari struck him with a jawbone of a camel, wounding his head severely. So he complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "O Allah, make clear to us a satisfying clarification regarding wine." Then this was revealed: ﴿Indeed, wine and gambling...﴾, up to His saying (exalted is He): ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "We have desisted, O Lord." And from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "If a drop of it fell into a well and a minaret were built in its place, I would not call the adhan from it. And if it fell into the sea and then it dried up and plants grew in it, I would not graze [animals] there." And from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both: "If I put my finger into it, it would not follow me." This is faith and piety in truth, may Allah be pleased with them all.

The word *khamr* (wine) is a verbal noun from "khamara him", meaning "he covered him", i.e., "he concealed him". The name was applied to the boiled, fermented grape juice that has become strong and has foam thrown up, because it covers the intellect and discernment, as if it were the very essence of a veil. Likewise it was called *sakar* (intoxicant) because it intoxicates, i.e., it restrains them.

The word *maysir* (gambling) is a noun of place or instrument of the form *mif'al* from "yasara", like *al-maw'id* and *al-marji'*. It is said: "yasartahu" when you "qamartahu" (gambled against him). Its derivation is either from *al-yusr* (ease), because it is taking property with ease, without toil, or from *al-yasar* (the left side/wealth), because it is a dispossession of him. Its description is that they had ten arrows (*qidh*, pl. *qidah*), which are the *azlam* (divining arrows). The arrows were: *al-fadhdh*, *al-tawam*, *al-raqib*, *al-hils*, *al-nafis*, *al-musbil*, *al-mu'alla*, *al-manih*, *al-safih*, and *al-wagh*. Each of them had a specified share of a slaughtered camel, which they slaughtered and divided into ten parts. It is said: twenty-eight parts, except the three, which are: *al-manih*, *al-safih*, and *al-wagh*. The *fadhdh* had one share; the *tawam* had two shares; the *raqib* had three; the *hils* had four; the *nafis* had five; the *musbil* had six; and the *mu'alla* had seven. They would put them in the *rababa*, which is a bag, and place it on the hands of a trustworthy person. Then he would shake it, put his hand in, and bring out an arrow for each man by name. Whoever drew an arrow of those bearing shares would take the specified share belonging to it. Whoever drew one of those three would pay the price of the camel and be deprived. They used to give those shares to the poor and would not eat from them, and they would boast of this, while they would disparage whoever entered into it, calling him *al-barm* (the stingy/miserly one). Under its ruling are all kinds of gambling, such as backgammon (*nard*), chess (*shatranj*), and others. From the Prophet (ﷺ) it is related that he said: "Beware of these two wicked games, for they are the gambling of the non-Arabs." And from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that backgammon and chess are from gambling. And from Ibn Sirin: "Everything in which there is a stake is from gambling."

The meaning is: they ask you about their ruling and about what is involved in engaging in them. ﴿Say: In them is great sin﴾, i.e., in engaging in them, because the first (wine) removes the intellect, which is the pivot of religion and of the world, and because each of them destroys wealth. ﴿And benefits for people﴾, from gaining pleasure and delight, from keeping company with youths, from encouraging the coward, and from strengthening temperament. It was read as "great sin" (*ithm kathir*) with the letter *thа'* (with three dots). In placing the statement of their sin first, describing it as great, and delaying the mention of their benefits, while restricting both to "people", there is an indication of the predominance of the first, which is not hidden, as stated by His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And their sin is greater than their benefit﴾, i.e., the corruptions resulting from engaging in them are greater than the benefits resulting from them. It was read as "nearer than their benefit" (*aqrab min naf'ihima*).

﴿And they ask you what they should spend.﴾ This is conjoined to "They ask you about wine..." etc., a conjunction of one narrative to another narrative. That is: what thing do they spend? It was said: this was also 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh. He first asked from what kind of types of property one should spend. When it was clarified that spending from all kinds is permitted, he asked a second time: from which of their varieties should we spend? From their best, or from other than them? Or he asked about the quantity he should spend from it. So it was said: ﴿Say: the surplus﴾, in the accusative, i.e., they spend the surplus, or: spend the surplus. It was also read in the nominative, on the basis that *ma* is interrogative and *dha* is a relative pronoun whose clause is "they spend", i.e., that which they spend is the surplus.

Al-Wahidi said: the original meaning of *al-'afw* in the language is "excess". Al-Qaffal said: *al-'afw* is what is easy and attainable from what exceeds one's sufficiency. This is the view of Qatada, 'Ata', and al-Suddi. The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, used to earn wealth, retaining an amount for expenditure, and giving charity from the surplus. It is related that a man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a golden egg, which he had acquired in some of the spoils, and said: "Take it from me as charity." He turned away from him. He repeated this several times, until the Prophet (ﷺ), angered, said: "Bring it." So he took it, threw it at him with a flick, which if it had struck him would have wounded him. Then he said: "One of you brings all his wealth, gives it in charity, and then sits begging from people. Charity is only from surplus wealth."

﴿Thus﴾: this is a reference to the verbal noun of the verb that follows, and the sense of distance contained in it indicates the elevated rank of what is referred to in excellence, together with its complete distinctiveness, and its being arranged, by reason of that, in the series of manifest matters. The *kaf* is for emphasizing what the demonstrative noun conveys of grandeur. The singular form of the address particle, despite the plurality of those addressed, is considered in terms of the tribe or group, or because there is no intention to specify the addressee, as has already passed. Its position is in the accusative, on the basis that it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., like that clear explanation, which is an expression of what has passed in the answers to the preceding questions. ﴿Allah makes clear to you the verses﴾, which indicate the legal rulings mentioned, not a lesser clarification than that. Its complete verification has already passed in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾. The clarification of the verses means revealing them with their meaning explicit and their significance clear, not that He (exalted is He) clarifies them after they had been ambiguous and confused. The form of the future tense is to bring the scene to mind. ﴿So that you may give thought﴾: so that you may reflect upon them, (p-220) and come to understand their objectives, and act upon what is within their folds.

And his saying (exalted is He): ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾ is connected either to "yubayyinu" (He makes clear), meaning: He makes clear the signs regarding matters that relate to this world and the Hereafter. Or it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of "al-āyāt" (the signs), meaning: He makes them clear to you as existing in both, that is, making clear your conditions that relate to both. The reason was placed before it to give greater attention to the matter of reflection. Or it is connected to his saying (exalted is He): ﴿you may reflect﴾, meaning: you reflect upon the matters relating to this world and the Hereafter, and upon the rulings contained in the answers to the questions mentioned above, so that you choose from them what is suitable for you in both, and avoid what is other than that. This restriction is the one appropriate to the context of enumerating the particular rulings. It is also permissible to generalize it to all matters relating to this world and the Hereafter. In that case, "that" (dhālika) refers to the clarifications that have passed, wholly or partly, and not to the verbal noun (maṣdar) of what follows, since then it is an independent verb that is not an expression for those clarifications. By "the signs" is meant other than what has been mentioned. The meaning is: like that clarification contained in the mentioned answers, God (exalted is He) makes clear to you the signs and proofs, so that you may reflect upon your affairs relating to this world and the Hereafter, take up what is suitable for you and beneficial to you in both, and leave what harms you, according to what those clarifying signs require.

﴿And they ask you about orphans﴾: this is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with what precedes it, as a counterpart of it. It is related that when the verse ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾ was revealed, people avoided mixing with orphans and looking after their property, and that was hard for them, so they mentioned it to the Prophet (ﷺ), and then this was revealed.

﴿Say: Reforming them is good﴾: that is, dealing with their conditions and their property in the way of reform is better than keeping away from them out of caution. ﴿And if you mix with them﴾ and associate with them in a manner that benefits them, ﴿then they are your brothers﴾: that is, they are your brothers, namely in religion, which is stronger than blood kinship, and among the rights and duties of brotherhood is mixing with them through reform and benefit. The mixing has also been interpreted as marriage by alliance (muṣāharah).

﴿And God knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾: "knowledge" here means "recognition" (maʿrifah), which is transitive to one object, and "min" (from) is there because it implies the meaning of distinguishing (tamyīz). That is: He knows who corrupts their affairs when mixing with them, or who intends by his mixing betrayal and corruption, distinguishing him from the one who reforms in them, or intends reform, and He will recompense each of them according to his deed. In this there is both a promise and a warning, except that placing "the corrupter" first adds further threat and emphasis to the warning.

﴿And had God willed, He would have distressed you﴾: that is, had He willed to distress you, meaning to impose upon you what is hard for you, from "ʿanat" (distress), which is "hardship," He would have done so, and would not have permitted you to mix with them. ﴿Indeed God is Mighty﴾: dominant over His command, nothing is difficult for Him among matters, and among those matters is your distress. So this is a justification for the content of the conditional clause. And His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿Wise﴾: that is, He acts in His actions according to what wisdom requires, the wisdom that calls for building obligation upon the basis of capacity. This is evidence for what the word "law" (lau) conveys, namely the negation of its antecedent.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 221:

﴿وَلا تَنْكِحُوا المُشْرِكاتِ﴾: That is: do not marry them (lā tazawwajūhunna). It is also recited with a ḍamma on the tā' (tunkiḥū), from al-inkāḥ (causing to marry), meaning: do not give them in marriage (lā tuzawwijūhunna) (p-221) to Muslims. ﴿حَتّى يُؤْمِنَّ﴾ (until they believe). The intended referent of "them" is either everything that includes the women of the People of the Book as well, as the generality of the two following causes (ʿilla) requires, namely God's words: ﴿وَقالَتِ اليَهُودُ عُزَيْرٌ ابْنُ اللَّهِ وقالَتِ النَّصارى المَسِيحُ ابْنُ اللَّهِ﴾ (The Jews say, "ʿUzayr is the son of God," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of God"), up to His words, glorified be He: ﴿عَمّا يُشْرِكُونَ﴾ (above what they associate). In that case the verse is abrogated (mansūkha) by His words: ﴿والمُحْصَناتُ مِنَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الكِتابَ مِنَ قَبْلِكُمْ﴾ (and chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you). Or the intended referent is other than the women of the People of the Book, in which case the verse stands (is thābita). It is narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent Mirthad ibn Abi Mirthad al-Ghanawi to Makkah to bring out some Muslims from it. He had been attached to a woman during the Jahiliyya named ʿAnāq. She came to him and said: "Will you not be alone with me?" He said: "Woe to you! Islam has come between us." She said: "Would you like to marry me?" He said: "Yes, but I will return to the Prophet (ﷺ) and seek his permission." He sought his permission, and so the verse was revealed.

﴿وَلأمَةٌ مُؤْمِنَةٌ﴾ (And a believing slave-woman): this is a justification (taʿlīl) for the prohibition against associating with them, and an encouragement to associate with believing women. It is introduced by the lam of inception (lām al-ibtidāʾ), which resembles the lam of oath in conveying emphasis, as an intensification in urging restraint. The root of amatun (slave-woman) is amawun; its final radical was dropped contrary to analogy, and the feminine tā' was substituted for it. The evidence that its final radical is a wāw is its return in the plural, and al-Kilābī said:

"As for the slave-women, they do not call me a son
When the sons of the dead (slave-women) claim kinship in shame."

And its appearance in the verbal noun: one says, "She is a slave-woman, clearly of slave status (al-ummawiyya)," and "She acknowledged him as her master (bi-l-ummawiyya)." It has come as the subject of the sentence because of the lam of inception it contains, and because of the descriptive phrase, that is: "And a believing slave-woman," with all the baseness of servitude and lack of standing that she has, ﴿خَيْرٌ﴾ (is better), in terms of religion and worldly affairs, ﴿مِن مُشْرِكَةٍ﴾ (than a polytheistic woman), that is, a polytheist woman, with all the nobility of freedom and elevation of rank she has. ﴿وَلَوْ أعْجَبَتْكُمْ﴾ (even if she pleases you). It has been noted that the word "law" (even if) in such contexts does not indicate the non-occurrence of a thing in the past because of the non-occurrence of something else; therefore no answer (jawāb) is considered for it, having been omitted with confidence in the indication of what precedes it, while the meaning is focused on its implied sense. Rather, it indicates the realization of what the preceding statement conveys of the ruling, in every state assumed among the states accompanying it, in summary, by introducing it upon the most remote of these states and the most incompatible with it, so that by its being established alongside it, its being established alongside everything else among the states becomes evident by way of priority (awlawiyya). This is because a thing, when it is realized alongside a strong contrary, is all the more realized alongside other than it. For this reason nothing of the other states is mentioned with it, and it suffices to mention the conjunctive wāw linking the sentence to its counterpart, which is opposed to it and encompasses all the states differing from it. This is the meaning of their saying that it is for the exhaustive enumeration of states in summary, as though it were said: "Whether or not they please you; and even if they please you." The clause falls in the accusative position, in the state (ḥāl) construction relative to "polytheistic woman," since the result is: "And a believing slave-woman is better than a polytheistic woman in the state of her not pleasing you, and in the state of her pleasing you with her beauty, her wealth, her lineage, and other things of the causes of attraction and the motives of desire for her." That is, in every state. The mention has been restricted to what is most incompatible with the superiority (of the believing slave-woman), as a reminder that since it is realized alongside that, it is all the more realized alongside anything else. It has been said that the wāw is for the state (ḥāliyya), but this is not clear; it has been said that it is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyya), but this is not sound. The truth is that it is conjunctive (ʿāṭifa), entailing the subtle consideration mentioned. Yes, it is permissible that the first clause, together with what is conjoined to it, be a new independent clause (mustaʾnafa) confirming the content of what precedes it. So reflect.

﴿وَلا تُنْكِحُوا المُشْرِكِينَ﴾ (And do not give polytheistic men in marriage): from al-inkāḥ. The intended referent is the disbelievers in general, as already explained. That is: do not give believing women in marriage to them, whether they are free or slaves. ﴿حَتّى يُؤْمِنُوا﴾ (until they believe), and abandon the disbelief they are in. ﴿وَلَعَبْدٌ مُؤْمِنٌ﴾ (And a believing slave): with the humiliation of being owned that he has, ﴿خَيْرٌ مِن مُشْرِكٍ﴾ (is better than a polytheist), with the might of ownership that he has. ﴿وَلَوْ أعْجَبَكُمْ﴾ (even if he pleases you), with what is in him of the motives for desire for him, which return to his essence and his attributes. ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ (Those): a new independent clause confirming the content of the two justifications already mentioned; that is, those mentioned, of the polytheistic women and the polytheistic men, ﴿يَدْعُونَ﴾ (call) whoever associates and mixes with them ﴿إلى النّارِ﴾ (to the Fire), that is, to what leads to it of disbelief and transgression. Therefore one must avoid associating with them and drawing near to them. ﴿واللَّهُ يَدْعُو﴾ (And God calls), through His believing servants (p-222), whoever associates with them, ﴿إلى الجَنَّةِ والمَغْفِرَةِ﴾ (to the Garden and forgiveness), that is, to correct belief and righteous deeds, which lead to these two. The mention of "the Garden" before "forgiveness," although the proper order is to clear away before adorning, is for the sake of the initial correspondence with the Fire. ﴿بِإذْنِهِ﴾ (by His leave): this is connected to "calls." That is: He calls while accompanied by His success, which includes guiding the believers' companions to good and advising them, so they are deserving of association. ﴿وَيُبَيِّنُ آياتِهِ﴾ (and He makes clear His signs), which contain the sublime rulings and the exquisite wisdoms, ﴿لِلنّاسِ لَعَلَّهم يَتَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ (to the people, that they may remember), that is, so that they may remember and act upon what is in them, and thus attain what they have been called to, of the Garden and forgiveness. This is it. It has been said that the meaning of "and God calls" is: "And the friends of God call," who are the believers, by omitting the genitive (muḍāf) and placing the genitive-attached (muḍāf ilayhi) in its position, as an honor to them. But you should know that the pronoun in the conjoined predicate, namely His words: ﴿وَيُبَيِّنُ﴾ (and He makes clear), refers to God, so this would entail a disjunction. It has been said that its meaning is: "And God calls, by His aforementioned rulings, to the Garden and forgiveness, for they lead those who act upon them to both." Although this requires the two pronouns in the two conjoined clauses, which function as predicates of the subject, to have the same referent, it would then lose the fine contrast between it and His words, exalted be He: ﴿أُولَئِكَ يَدْعُونَ إلى النّارِ﴾ (those call to the Fire). The safest way is probably what we clarified first. The mention of "remembrance" here is to indicate that it is evident and needs no reflection, as in the earlier rulings.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 222:**

﴿They ask you about menstruation.﴾ This is coordinated (*'atf*) with what preceded it, of the same kind. The reason these three questions are reported with coordination is that all of them occurred together when they asked about wine. The reason the others are reported without coordination is that each of them occurred at a separate time. *Al-mahid* (menstruation) is a verbal noun from "حاضَتِ المَرْأةُ" (the woman menstruated), like "المَجِيءُ" (the coming) and "المَبِيتُ" (the spending the night). It is related that the people of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period) would not cohabit with menstruating women or eat with them, as was the practice of the Jews and the Magians. People continued in this until Abu al-Dahdah, along with a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, asked about this, and the verse was revealed.

﴿Say: It is a harm.﴾ That is, it is a thing that is loathed and harms whoever approaches it, out of aversion to it and dislike of it. ﴿So keep away from women during menstruation.﴾ That is, abstain from having intercourse with them during the time of menstruation. It was said: the Muslims took the command to "keep away" in its literal sense and expelled them from their houses. Some of the Bedouins said: "O Messenger of Allah, the cold is severe and the clothing is scarce. If we give preference to them, the rest of the household will perish, and if we keep it for ourselves, the menstruating women will perish." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You were only commanded to refrain from having intercourse with them when they menstruate; He did not command you to expel them from the houses, as the non-Arabs do." It was also said: the Christians would have intercourse with them and did not mind menstruation, while the Jews went to excess in keeping away, so the Muslims were commanded to take the middle course between the two. ﴿And do not approach them until they are purified.﴾ This is an emphasis on the ruling of keeping away, and an indication that what is meant by it is not approaching them for intercourse, rather than not being near them at all. It also states its limit, which is the cessation of blood. According to Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him), if that occurs within the majority of the period, approaching them becomes permissible once the bleeding has stopped; otherwise, ritual washing (*ghusl*) or the passing of the time of a prayer is required.
