So it is said: ﴿He said: Would you perhaps, if fighting is prescribed for you, not fight?﴾ The "'asa" and its predicate are separated by the conditional clause for emphasis on it, meaning: have you approached not fighting, as I expect from you? The intent is to affirm that what is expected is established. The reason that what they requested was not mentioned in the conditional, saying "if I send you a king...", despite its being more closely related to their words, but instead he mentioned the prescription of fighting upon them, is for emphasis in showing their failure to do it. For if they do not fight when fighting is made obligatory upon them by God's command, then they are even less likely to fight when it is not obligatory. Also, mentioning what they said might suggest that the cause of their abstention from fighting is the one sent, not fighting itself. It was read "'asitum" with a kasra on the sin, but it is weak. ﴿They said﴾: a resumptive clause, as preceded. ﴿And what is with us that we should not fight﴾: that is, what reason do we have not to fight? ﴿in the way of Allah, when we have been driven out of our homes and our children?﴾: that is, while the situation has arisen that compels us to fight with strong necessity: expulsion from homes and homelands, and estrangement from family and children. The mention of children separately is for greater strengthening of the causes for fighting. That is because Jalut, the head and king of the Amalekites, a tyrant from the descendants of 'Imliq ibn 'Ad, together with those with him among the Amalekites, used to dwell on the coast of the Roman Sea between Egypt and Palestine. They prevailed over the Children of Israel, seized their homes, took their children captive, captured four hundred and forty souls from the sons of their kings, imposed the jizya upon them, and took their Torah. ﴿Then when fighting was prescribed for them﴾: after the Prophet, peace be upon him, asked that, and the king was sent. ﴿They turned away﴾: that is, they turned aside and held back. But not at the beginning of the matter; rather, after witnessing the multitude of the enemy and its might, as its details will come. Here the outcome of their affair is mentioned in summary, to show the contradiction and disparity between their words and their deeds. ﴿Except a few of them﴾: and they were those who were content with a handful of water from the river and crossed it, and they were three hundred and thirteen, according to the number of the people of Badr. ﴿And Allah is Knower of the wrongdoers﴾: a warning to them for their wrongdoing in turning away from fighting, abandoning jihad, and the contradiction between their words and their actions. The sentence is a parenthetical concluding statement (i'tiraD tadhyili).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 247:

﴿And their Prophet said to them﴾: This begins the detailed account of what passed between him (peace be upon him) and them, in words and deeds, following the general indication of the outcome of their situation. That is: he said to them, after what was revealed to him had been revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah has sent Talut (Saul) to you as king﴾. "Talut" is a Hebrew proper name, like "Dawud" (David). Taking it to be "fa'lut" derived from "al-tul" (height) is ruled out by its being diptote (not taking tanwin, its prohibition from declension). "Malikan" (as king) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from it. It is narrated that when he (peace be upon him) asked his Lord to appoint a king for them, he brought a staff by which the one to be made king over them would be measured, and none matched it except Talut. ﴿They said﴾: this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as has passed; ﴿How can he have kingship over us﴾: that is, from where can it come to him, or: how can that be? ﴿While we have more right to kingship than he does, and he has not been given abundance of wealth﴾: the first waw is circumstantial (hali), and the second is conjunctive (atifa), joining the two clauses in judgment. That is: how can he be made king over us when the situation is that he does not deserve kingship, since there exists one who has more right than he, and since he lacks the wealth on which kingship depends? The cause of this incredulity is that prophethood was specific to a particular tribe among the tribes of the Children of Israel, namely the tribe of Levi son of Jacob (peace be upon him), while kingship belonged to the tribe of Judah, from which came Dawud and Sulayman (peace be upon them both). Talut was not from either of these two tribes, but from the descendants of Benjamin. It was said he was a shepherd; it was said a tanner; it was said a water-carrier. ﴿He said: Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you﴾: when they found it improbable that he should be king because of the lowliness of his lineage and his poverty, he answered them, first, that the decisive matter is the choosing of Allah (Exalted), and He has chosen him over you, and He knows the interests better than you; and second, that the principal requirement for it is abundance of knowledge, by which he can know the affairs of governance, and largeness of body, so that his awe will be great in hearts and he will be able to resist enemies and endure wars. Allah (Exalted) has granted him a generous portion of both, and this is His saying (Mighty and Majestic): ﴿And He has increased him broadly in knowledge﴾: that is, knowledge related to kingship, or to it and to religious matters as well. It was also said: he had been given revelation and was made a prophet. ﴿And in physique﴾: it was said: in stature of height, for he was taller than others by his head and shoulders, so that a standing man would stretch out his hand and reach his head. It was also said: in beauty; and it was said: in strength. ﴿And Allah gives His kingship to whom He wills﴾: because He is the Owner of kingship and dominion, the Doer of what He wills, so He may grant it to whomever of His servants He wills. ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾: He widens provision for the poor and makes him rich. ﴿All-Knowing﴾: of whom is fit for kingship and whom it does not suit. The mention of the Majestic Name here is to cultivate reverence.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 248:

(p-241) ﴿And their prophet said to them﴾: His placing (this statement) between his two quoted statements (peh) indicates that one of them is not connected to the other, and that a speech from the addressees intervened, branching off from the preceding and leading to the following. It is as if they had asked him, peace be upon him, for a sign showing that God (Exalted) had chosen Talut (Saul) and made him king over them. It is narrated that they said: "What is the sign of his kingship?" He said: ﴿Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that the chest (al-tabut) will come to you﴾; that is, the coffer (al-sunduq). It is a form of "fa'lut" from "al-tawb," which means return, because whatever comes out of it keeps returning to it. Its ta' is an added letter, not a feminine marker, like "malakut" and "rahabut." The well-known usage is to pause on its ta' without turning it into a ha'; some people do turn it into a ha'. What is meant by it is "the chest of the Torah." God (Exalted) had lifted it after the death of Musa (peace be upon him), as a sign of wrath against the Children of Israel when they disobeyed and transgressed. So when the people asked their prophet for a sign showing the kingship of Talut, he told them: "The sign of his kingship is that the chest will come to you from heaven, and the angels will guard it." Then it came to them as he had described, while the people watched it, until it landed at Talut's place. This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father). The scholars of reports (arbab al-akhbar) said: God (Exalted) sent down to Adam a chest in which were images of the prophets (peace be upon them) from among his offspring; it was made of shamshad wood, about three cubits long, with a width of two cubits. It was with Adam (peace be upon him) until he died; then his descendants inherited it one after another until it reached Ya'qub (peace be upon him); then it remained in the hands of the Children of Israel until it reached Musa (peace be upon him). Musa (peace be upon him) would place the Torah in it, and when he fought he would send it forward, so the souls of the Children of Israel were calmed by it. It remained with him until he died; then it passed among the hands of the Children of Israel. Whenever they disagreed about something they would bring their dispute to it, and it would speak to them and judge between them. When they attended battle they would put it before them and seek victory over their enemy through it. The angels would carry it above the army, and then they would fight the enemy; when they heard a cry from the chest, they were certain of victory. But when they disobeyed and corrupted (the land), God (Exalted) gave power over them to the Amalekites, who defeated them, took the chest as spoil, and placed it in a place of urine and excrement. When God (Exalted) willed to make Talut king, He sent affliction upon them, so that everyone who urinated near it was afflicted with hemorrhoids, and five cities of their land were destroyed. The unbelievers knew that this was because of their contempt for the chest, so they brought it out and placed it on two bulls. The two bulls set off walking, and God (Exalted) had assigned four angels to them, who drove them until they came to Talut's dwelling. When they asked their prophet for proof of Talut's kingship, the prophet said to them: "The sign of his kingship is that you will find the chest in his house." When they found it with him, they were certain of his kingship.

﴿In it is tranquility (sakina) from your Lord﴾: that is, in its coming there is calm for you and reassurance from your Lord; or: in the chest is that in which you find tranquility, which is the Torah deposited in it, based on what has passed, that Musa (peace be upon him), when he fought, would send it forward, so the souls of the Children of Israel were calmed by it. It was also said: the sakina was a figure in it, of emerald or ruby, having a head and tail like the head and tail of a cat, and two wings; it would moan, and the chest would be carried toward the enemy while they advanced with it. When it came to rest, they would stand firm, be calm, and victory would descend. From 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "It had a face like a human face, and in it was a gentle breeze." ﴿And a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun left behind﴾: (p-242) this is the broken pieces of the tablets, the staff of Musa, his garments, and some of the Torah. God (Exalted) had lifted it after the death of Musa (peace be upon him). "Their family" means their descendants, or themselves; the word "al" is inserted to magnify their status. Or: the prophets of the Children of Israel. ﴿Carried by the angels﴾: a circumstantial clause (hal) from the chest; that is, the sign of his kingship is its coming while being carried by the angels. The manner of this has already been mentioned. The carrying by the angels in the last report may be a metaphor for their driving the two bulls that carry it. ﴿Indeed in that﴾: a reference to what has been mentioned about the chest; so it is part of the speech of the Prophet (peace be upon him) to his people. Or it refers to the narration and recounting of the story; in that case it is the beginning of a speech from God (Exalted), brought in before the story is completed, to show complete care for it. The singular form of the address particle, despite the plurality of addressees, under both interpretations, is by treating the group or others as the referent, as has passed. ﴿Is a sign﴾: great; ﴿for you﴾: indicating the kingship of Talut, or the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), in that he reported these details exactly as they were without hearing them from any human. ﴿If you are believers﴾: that is, if you affirm his being made king over you, or any of the signs. The "in" (in) here is conditional, and the answer is omitted, relying on what precedes it. It was also said that it means "idh" (when).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 249:

﴿When Talut set out with the troops﴾: i.e., he departed with them from Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). The original form is "fasala nafsahu" (he separated himself). Since its agent and its object are one and the same, its usage became common with the object omitted, until it took the place of the intransitive (qasir), like "infasala" (he separated). It is also said that "fasala, fusulan" is the origin. It has been permitted that it is a root of its own, distinct from the transitive verb with its verbal noun, as in "waqafa, wuqufan" and "waqafahu, waqfan", "sadda, sududan" and "saddahu, saddan", and "raja'a, ruj'an" and "raja'ahu, raj'an". The preposition "bi" is connected to an omitted verb that functions as a circumstantial clause (hal) for "Talut", meaning: accompanied by them and in their company. It is narrated that he said to his people: "No man who has built a building and not finished it shall go out with me, nor a merchant occupied with trade, nor one who has married a woman and not yet consummated the marriage with her. I seek only the young, energetic, and free." So there gathered to him, from those he had chosen, eighty thousand. The time was summer heat, and they took a barren desert route, so they asked that God (exalted is He) cause a river to flow for them. Then, after what His will had concerned was made clear to him (exalted is He), from the side of the Prophet (peace be upon him), or by way of revelation according to those who hold to his prophethood, ﴿he said: Indeed God is going to test you with a river﴾. It is read with a fatha on the ha', and it is also read with a sukun on it. ﴿So whoever drinks from it﴾: i.e., begins his drinking from the river, by lapping it with the mouth directly (karaʿa), because that is drinking from it in the literal sense. ﴿is not of me﴾: i.e., not of my group and my faithful followers. It is also said: he is not connected to me and not united with me, from the saying "So-and-so is of me", as if he were a part of him, because of the complete mingling of the two. ﴿And whoever does not taste it﴾: i.e., does not sip it, from "ta'ima al-shay'" (he tasted the thing) when he tasted it, whether food, drink, or other. He said:

"And if you wish, I shall forbid women other than you, and if you wish, I shall not taste fresh water nor cold water"

i.e., sleep. ﴿then he is of me, except for one who scoops a handful with his hand﴾: this is an exception from His saying (exalted is He): ﴿So whoever drinks from it, he is not of me﴾. It was placed after the second clause to show the complete care given to it. Its meaning is: a permission to scoop a handful with the hand, but not to lap directly. "Ghurfah" (a handful) is what is scooped. It is also read with a fatha on the ghayn, on the basis that it is a verbal noun, and the preposition "bi" is connected to "ightarafa", or to an omitted verb that functions as a qualifier (sifah) of "ghurfatan", meaning: a handful existing in his hand. It is reported that a single handful was enough for a man to drink, along with his water-skin and his animals. As for those who drank from it, their lips turned black and thirst overcame them. ﴿So they drank from it﴾: it is conjoined to an assumed omitted clause required by the context, meaning: they were tested by it, so they drank from it. ﴿except a few of them﴾: they are the ones indicated earlier, by the exception from "they turned away". It is also read: "illa qalilun minhum" (except a few of them), inclining towards the meaning and setting aside the verbal form, because His saying (exalted is He): ﴿So they drank from it﴾ is effectively the same as saying "they did not obey him", so the excepted noun ought to come in the nominative, as in the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"And time has bitten, O son of Marwan, leaving of wealth nothing but the shaven or the stripped"

For his saying "lam yada'" (did not leave) is equivalent to "lam yabqa" (did not remain). ﴿Then when he crossed it﴾: i.e., the river; ﴿he and those who believed with him﴾: this is conjoined to the attached pronoun, emphasised by the detached one. The adverbial phrase is connected to "jawaza" (crossed), not to "amanu" (believed). It is also said: the "wa" is circumstantial (hal), and the adverbial phrase is connected to an omitted element that functions as the predicate of the relative clause, as if it were said: "when he crossed it, while those who believed were with him, and they are that small number." This indicates that whoever else there was stands entirely apart from faith. ﴿They said﴾: i.e., some of those with him among the believers said to others: ﴿We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops﴾: i.e., to fight them and to oppose them, let alone to have victory over them, because of what they witnessed of their multitude and their severity. It is said that they were a hundred thousand armed fighters. ﴿He said﴾: this is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) built on a question, as if it were said: "What then did those who addressed them say?" So it is answered: ﴿Those who thought that they would meet God said﴾. It is said: i.e., the elect among them, those who are certain of meeting God through resurrection and who look forward to His reward. Singling them out with this description does not negate the faith of the rest, for the ranks of believers in certainty and in hope vary. Or: those who know that they will soon be martyred and so meet God (exalted is He). It is also said that the relative clause refers to all believers, and the pronoun in "they said" refers to those who had been left behind, as if they said it as an excuse for their staying back, the river lying between them. ﴿How many a small company﴾: i.e., a group and a band of people, from "fa'a ra'sahu" when I split it, or from "fa'a ilayhi" when he returned. On the first, its form is "fi'ah", and on the second, "fi'lah". ﴿Has overcome a large company﴾. And "kam", whether it is declarative or interrogative, indicates multiplicity and is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), with its predicate being "ghalabat" (has overcome), meaning: many a small company has overcome large companies. ﴿By God's permission﴾: i.e., by His decree and His facilitation, for the entire affair revolves around His will (exalted is He). Thus whoever He helps is not humiliated, even if his number is small, and whoever He forsakes is not honoured, even if his means and numbers are many. A brilliant subtle point has been observed in the answer: it does not say "they overcame with a large company", as was said in the words of their companions, in order to emphasise the rejection of their claim and to calm their hearts. This answer, as you see, arises from the complete trust they had in God's help and His grace, and the belief that they would meet God through resurrection has no bearing on it, especially through martyrdom, for knowledge of it may perhaps bring despair of victory. Nor does it relate to hope for His reward (exalted is He). There is no doubt that what is mentioned in the relative clause should be the basis for the judgment given about the relative pronoun, so it must at least be a fitting attribute for it. Perhaps the intended meaning of "meeting Him (exalted is He)" is the meeting of His help and support, expressed in this way for emphasis, just as the accompaniment of His help is expressed by the accompaniment of Him (glorified is He), where it says: ﴿And God is with the patient﴾. For the intended meaning there is the certain accompaniment of His help and His grace. Taking it to mean accompaniment through reward, as has been done, is ruled out, because they only said it to complete their answer and to affirm it by way of an explanatory interjection, to encourage their companions and to strengthen them in patience that leads to victory. It has no connection at all with the accompaniment through reward mentioned. The same applies if this is taken as the beginning of a statement from God (exalted is He), brought as confirmation of their words. The meaning is: "Those who thought, or who knew from the Prophet, or from the Ark and the Tranquillity, that they would meet the victory of God the Mighty, said: How many a small company has overcome a large company by God's permission (exalted is He)! So we too shall overcome Jalut and his troops." The expression of the subject of "anna" (that) as a noun, although the meeting is in the future, is to indicate its certainty and realisation. (p-244)

﴿When they came forth﴾: that is, Talut and those believers with him appeared and came out to an open space of the land at the place of battle, ﴿against Jalut and his hosts﴾. They saw the numbers and the equipment that the enemy had, and became certain that they were, by ordinary measure, unable to withstand them. ﴿They said﴾: that is, all together, when the hearts of the first group were strengthened by the words of the second group, humbly beseeching God (Exalted is He) and seeking His help: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾, to endure the hardships of war and to plunge into its difficult and narrow crossings. In the appeal through the attribute of lordship (rububiyya), which indicates bringing [something] to perfection, and in the choice of "pour" (ifragh), which indicates abundance, and in the indefiniteness (tankir) of "patience," which signifies magnitude, there is a eloquence that is not hidden. ﴿And make our feet firm﴾ on the slippery grounds of fighting and the places where combatants slip. The firmness of the foot is an expression for perfection of strength and steadfastness at the moment of clashing, and for not wavering at the time of resistance, not merely for remaining fixed in one place. ﴿And help us against the disbelieving people﴾, by subduing them and defeating them. Placing "the disbelievers" in the position of the pronoun referring to "Jalut and his hosts" serves to indicate the reason for the victory over them. In this supplication they observed a marvelous ordering: they first asked for the pouring out of patience, which is the essence of the matter; then for the firmness of the feet, which branches from it; then for victory, which is the ultimate goal.

**Abu al-Su'ud's Commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 2, Verse 251**

﴿So they routed them﴾, that is, they broke them without delay; ﴿by the permission of Allah﴾, by His help and support, in answer to their supplication. The choice of this phrasing over the wording of His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world﴾, etc., is to preserve the sense of their statement: "A small company has overcome a large company by the permission of Allah." ﴿And David killed Goliath (Jalut)﴾. Iishaa (Jesse), the father of David, was in the army of Talut (Saul), with six of his sons, and David, peace be upon him, was the seventh of them, and he was young, tending the sheep. Allah, exalted is He, revealed to their prophet that it was he who would kill Jalut, so he asked his father for him, and he came, and on his way he passed three stones, each of which said to him: "Carry us, for by us you will kill Jalut." So he carried them in his pouch. It is said: When the news of his brothers in the battle-lines was delayed in reaching their father, David was sent to them to bring him word of them. He came to them while they were in the thick of the fighting, and Jalut had come out himself to single combat, and none could face him in duel. His shadow was a mile long. David said to his brothers: "Is there none among you who will go out against this uncircumcised one?" They rebuked him, so he moved to another side where his brothers were not. Talut passed by him while he was urging the people to fight, and David said to him: "What will you do for the one who kills this uncircumcised one?" Talut said: "I will marry him to my daughter and give him half my kingdom." So David came out to him and struck him with what he had of the stones, by the sling, and it hit him in the chest, and the stones passed through him and killed many people after him. It is also said that the stones spoke to him at the moment he came out against Jalut in the battle, and Talut fulfilled for him what he had promised. It is also said that he (Talut) envied him and expelled him from his kingdom, then regretted what he had done and went seeking him until he was killed. David, peace be upon him, was made king and was given prophethood. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom﴾, that is, the kingdom of the Children of Israel, in the eastern and western parts of the Holy Land; ﴿and the wisdom﴾, that is, prophethood. Before him, kingship and prophethood had not come together among the Children of Israel, except for him. Rather, kingship was in one tribe and prophethood was in another tribe (p-245), and they had never gathered under one king before him. ﴿And taught him of what He willed﴾, that is, of what Allah, exalted is He, willed to teach him, not of what David, peace be upon him, willed, as has been said, because most of what He, exalted is He, taught him is something that hardly occurs to anyone's mind and does not fall within any human wish, so that he could not seek it or desire it, such as the making of coats of mail by softening iron, the speech of birds and beasts, and other such hidden matters. ﴿And were it not that Allah repels some people by means of others﴾, namely those who engage in evil and corruption, ﴿by means of others﴾ among them, by turning them back from what they are upon through what Allah, exalted is He, has decreed of killing, as in the narrated story or otherwise. It is also read as "Difa' Allah" (the defense of Allah), on the basis that the form of mutual contention is for intensification. ﴿The earth would have been corrupted﴾, and its benefits would have ceased, and its interests would have been disrupted, in terms of tillage, offspring, and everything else by which the earth is built up and set right. It is also said: Were it not that Allah gives victory to the Muslims over the disbelievers, the earth would have been corrupted by their mischief and their killing of the Muslims. Or: If He had not repelled them through the Muslims, disbelief would have spread, the wrath would have descended, and the people of the earth would have been utterly uprooted. ﴿But Allah is full of bounty﴾, great, whose worth cannot be measured, ﴿toward the worlds﴾, all of them. This is an allusion to an exceptive syllogism (qiyas istithna'i) composed of the negation of the antecedent, which produces the negation of the consequent, except that what follows from it and necessitates it has been stated, namely His being full of bounty toward the worlds, to indicate that He, exalted is He, is bountiful in that repelling, not that it is obligatory upon Him, and that His bounty, exalted is He, is not confined to this, but is rather one instance of His great bounty. It is as if it were said: But He, exalted is He, repels the corruption of some of them by means of others, so the earth is not corrupted, the interests of the world are ordered by it, and the conditions of the nations are set right.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 252:**

﴿تِلْكَ﴾ (*Those*): a reference to what preceded of the account of the thousands and the report of Talut (Saul), in the detailed manner that has been recorded. The sense of distance in it indicates the exalted rank of what is referred to. ﴿آياتُ اللَّهِ﴾ (*the signs of God*): revealed from Him (Exalted). The clause is independent (*musta'nafah*). His statement (Exalted): ﴿نَتْلُوها عَلَيْكَ﴾ (*We recite them to you*), that is, through Jibril (peace be upon him), may be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to "the signs," with the governing element being the sense of the demonstrative. Or it may be an independent clause having no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis). ﴿بِالحَقِّ﴾ (*with truth*): it is in the accusative position, as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the object of "نَتْلُوها" (*natlūhā*, "We recite them"), meaning: accompanied by certainty, which no one among the People of the Book or the historians doubts, since they find it in agreement with what is in their books. Or it is a circumstantial clause from its subject, meaning: We recite them to you while being in accord with the truth and correctness. Or it is from the pronoun in the genitive position, meaning: accompanied by truth and sincerity. ﴿وَإنَّكَ لَمِنَ المُرْسَلِينَ﴾ (*And indeed you are among the messengers*): that is, among those who were sent to the nations to convey Our messages and to enforce Our commands and Our rulings upon them, for this kind of dealing does not take place between Us and anyone other than them. Thus it is a testimony from Him (glorified is He) to His messengership (peace and blessings be upon him), coming right after the statement of what necessitates it. The emphasis is required by the situation of those who deny it.

﴿Those messengers﴾: This is a resumptive statement, containing an allusion that he (peace be upon him) is among the most excellent of the great messengers, peace be upon them all, following the explanation that he is among their number. The reference is to the group of whom the Prophet ﷺ is one, so the definite article in "the messengers" (al-rusul) is for comprehensiveness (lil-istighraq). The distal demonstrative, with its sense of distance, indicates the lofty rank of these messengers and the elevation of their station. It has also been said that the reference is to those whose knowledge of the Prophet ﷺ is established. ﴿We preferred some of them over others﴾: in degrees of perfection, by singling out each one with glorious distinctions that others did not share, as Our will dictates. ﴿Among them are those to whom God spoke﴾: this is a detailed elaboration of the preference mentioned in summary. That is, He preferred him by speaking to him (exalted is He) without an intermediary. This was Moses, peace be upon him, when God spoke to him on the night of the choice (laylat al-khiyara) and at Mount Sinai (al-Tur). It is also read as "kallama Allaha" with the accusative, and as "kalama Allaha" from "al-mukalama" (conversation), meaning that he spoke to God just as God spoke to him. This is supported by the phrase "Kalim Allah" (the one with whom God spoke), in the sense of "mukalimuhu" (the one who converses with Him). The mention of the Glorious Name by way of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person) serves to cultivate awe, and it alludes to the difference between speaking and elevation, and between the general preference previously mentioned and the clear signs bestowed afterwards, and the support with the Holy Spirit, in terms of disparity. ﴿And raised some of them in rank by degrees﴾: that is, among them is one whom He raised above other messengers, who differ in the ascending stages of excellence, by remote degrees and distant stations. The change of style serves to show the difference in the states of their levels of nobility. The apparent meaning is that this is the Messenger of God ﷺ, as is indicated by the statement that he, peace be upon him, is among them, since that carries the force of "some of them." He was singled out with the general call, numerous proofs, continuous miracles, signs that follow one another throughout the ages, and scholarly and practical virtues beyond enumeration. The indefiniteness (ibham) is for magnifying his status, and to convey that he is the unique distinguished one, without need of specification. It has also been said that he is Abraham, peace be upon him, since God singled him out with the honour of intimate friendship (khulla). It has been said that he is Idris, peace be upon him, since God raised him to a lofty place. It has also been said that he is one of the Messengers of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm), peace be upon them all. ﴿And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear signs﴾: the dazzling signs and manifest miracles, such as raising the dead, healing the blind and the leper, and informing of unseen matters. Or it means the Gospel. ﴿And We supported him﴾: that is, We strengthened him. ﴿With the Holy Spirit﴾: it is read with the vowel on the dal, and also read with it sukun; that is, with the holy spirit, as in your saying "a man of truth" (rajul sidq). It is the spirit of Jesus. It is described as holy because of its nobility, or because loins did not contain him and wombs did not carry him in their impurity. It has also been said that it refers to Gabriel, and it has been said that it refers to the Gospel, as has already been mentioned. The singling out of Jesus, peace be upon him, with what has been mentioned is to refute what exists between the People of the Two Books concerning his affair, peace be upon him, of deficiency and excess. The verse clearly states that the prophets, peace be upon them, differ in rank, so it is permissible to prefer some of them over others, but by a decisive proof. ﴿And had God willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another﴾: that is, those who came after the messengers, from the various nations. That is, had God willed that they not fight, they would not have fought, by making them agreed upon following the messengers, who are agreed upon the word of truth. Thus the object of the will is omitted, because it is implied by the apodosis, according to the well-known rule. It has been said that its estimated sense is: "Had He willed to guide all people, they would not have fought..." etc., but this is not the right reading. ﴿After the clear proofs had come to them﴾: from those messengers; the manifest miracles and evident signs that point to the truth of the truth, which necessitate following them and restrain from turning away from their path, which leads to fighting. So "after" (min) is connected to "fought." ﴿But they differed﴾: this is a corrective clause (istidrak) from the conditional sentence. It points to an exceptive syllogism (qiyas istithna'i), composed of positing the negation of its antecedent, which produces the negation of its consequent; however, the difference (ikhtilaf) has been placed in the position of the negation of the antecedent that follows from it, to indicate that the fighting arises from their side, not from His side (exalted is He) initially. As if it were said: "But He did not will that they not fight, because they differed with a gross difference." ﴿So among them were those who believed﴾: in what those messengers brought of clear proofs, and acted upon it. ﴿And among them were those who disbelieved﴾: in that, with a disbelief from which they do not refrain. Thus wisdom required (p-247) that He not will their non-fighting, so they fought according to what their states required. ﴿And had God willed﴾: that they not fight after this stage of difference and enmity, which entail fighting according to custom. ﴿They would not have fought﴾: and there would not have appeared from them a vein of arrogance or hostility, because all is under His dominion (exalted is He). So the repetition is not for emphasis, as has been thought, but to alert that their difference is not what necessitates His not willing that they not fight, as is understood from its placement in the corrective clause, rather He (glorified is He) is free to choose in that, such that even if He willed after that that they not fight, they would not have fought. This is made clear by the corrective clause with His saying (mighty and majestic is He): ﴿But God does what He wills﴾: that is, among affairs, both existent and non-existent, of which one is His not willing that they not fight, for abstention is also among the acts; that is, He does what He wills, as He wills, without anything obligating Him to it, or any hindrance preventing Him from it. In this there is clear evidence that events follow His will (glorified is He), whether good or evil, faith or disbelief.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 254:

﴿O you who have believed, spend﴾; in the way of Allah; ﴿from what We have provided for you﴾; i.e., some of what We have provided you with; with "mā" taken as a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah) whose returning pronoun has been omitted; and the mention of its coming from Him (exalted is He) is to urge spending, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾; and what is meant by it is obligatory spending, by the indication of what follows it of the threat; ﴿before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, nor friendship, nor intercession﴾: the word "min" (from) is connected to the same thing its sister (the first min) is connected to; and there is no objection to this because their meanings differ, for the first is partitive (tab'īḍiyyah) and this one is for the beginning of the limit (ibtidā' al-ghāyah); i.e., spend part of what We have provided you before there comes a Day in which you will not be able to make up for what you have neglected, since there is no buying and selling in it so that you might buy back what you spend, or ransom yourselves thereby from the punishment; nor friendship so that your friends might forgive you it or help you with it; nor intercession except for one whom the Most Merciful has permitted and with whose word He is pleased, so that you might seek the means through intercessors who intercede for you to remove what is upon your account. The three are given the nominative case together with the intent of generality, because in meaning they are the answer to "Is there in it trade, or friendship, or intercession?"; and it has been read with all of them in the accusative. ﴿And the disbelievers﴾; i.e., those who abandon zakat; and the choice of this term over the other is for severity and warning, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ in place of "and whoever does not perform Hajj"; and to signify that abandoning zakat is among the attributes of disbelievers; He (exalted is He) said: ﴿And woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakat﴾.

﴿They are the wrongdoers﴾; i.e., those who wronged themselves by exposing themselves to punishment, and who placed wealth in other than its proper place and spent it in other than its proper way.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 255:

﴿Allah—there is no god but He.﴾ It is a subject and predicate; that is, He alone is the one deserving of worship, and no other. Regarding the omission of the predicate of "lā" (there is no)—such as "in existence" or "it is possible that it exists"—there is a well-known difference of opinion among the grammarians (nuḥāt). ﴿Al-Ḥayy﴾: the Ever-Living, the one who remains, against whom there is no path to death and annihilation. It may be a second predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject, or an apposition (badal) to "lā ilāha illā Huwa," or an apposition to "Allāh," or an adjective (ṣifa) of Him. It is supported by the reading in the accusative (naṣb), as a praise (madḥ), because it is specified by the attribute.

﴿Al-Qayyūm﴾: the form fa'yūl from qāma bi-l-amr when one preserves it; that is, the one who constantly stands in managing the creation and preserving it. It has also been said (p-248): He is the one who subsists by His own essence and sustains others.

﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep seizes Him.﴾ "Sinah" is the languor that precedes sleep. ʿAdī ibn al-Riqāʿ al-ʿĀmilī said:

Drowsy, overcome by slumber, so that drowsiness settled
in his eye, yet he is not asleep.

"Sleep" is a state that affects living beings, from the relaxation of the nerves of the brain caused by moist vapors rising, such that the outward senses cease perceiving altogether. The purpose is to state the negation of either of these befalling Him—glory be to Him—because they are not befitting to Him (exalted is He); not because they are deficient in relation to divine power, for He is far removed from such a station of transcendence. Thus there is no way to interpret the noble wording as a method of hyperbole and gradation, based on the idea that one who can repel drowsiness may not be able to repel deep sleep, as in your saying, "So-and-so is alert; neither drowsiness nor sleep overcomes him." Sleep is mentioned after drowsiness only to preserve the order of external existence. The inclusion of the word "lā" serves to make explicit that the negation covers each of them, as in His saying—mighty and majestic is He—﴿And they spend no small nor great expenditure﴾, etc. As for expressing the non-befalling and non-occurrence by "not seizing," it is to observe the reality: the occurrence of drowsiness and sleep upon what they affect happens by way of seizing and taking hold. It has also been said that this is from the category of completion, and the sentence is an emphasis of what precedes it—regarding His being Living and Self-Subsisting—since whoever is affected by either of them would be deficient in life and lacking in preservation and management. It has also been said that it is a resumptive sentence emphasizing what came before, and it has been said that it is an emphatic circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun concealed in "al-Qayyūm."

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ This establishes His self-subsistence (exalted is He) and argues from it for His exclusivity in divinity. What is meant by "whatever is in them" is what is more general than their parts that enter into them, and the matters external to them that are established within them, among rational beings and others.

﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ This is an explanation of the majesty of His station, and that no one approaches Him such that he could alter what He wills, by intercession or supplication, let alone repel Him in obstinacy or opposition.

﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them.﴾ That is, what is before them and what is after them; or the reverse, since you face the future and turn your back on the past. Or: the affairs of this world and the affairs of the Hereafter; or the reverse. Or: what they perceive and what they comprehend; or what they apprehend and what they do not apprehend. The pronoun refers to "whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth," giving precedence to the rational beings among them over others; or to what is indicated by "who is it that," namely the angels and the prophets—peace be upon them.

﴿And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge﴾; that is, of what is known to Him,
﴿except what He wills﴾ that they should know. Its conjunction with what precedes it is because both together are evidence of His exclusive (exalted is He) essential, complete knowledge, which indicates His oneness.

﴿His Throne (kursiyy) encompasses the heavens and the earth.﴾ "Al-Kursiyy" is that upon which one sits, and it does not exceed the seat of the one sitting. It seems to be derived from "al-kirs," which is that which is packed down. There is no actual chair nor one seated; rather, it is an illustration of the greatness of His station—mighty and majestic is He—and the vastness of His dominion, and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of all things, in the manner of His saying—mighty is He in speech—﴿They did not measure Allah with the true measure, while the earth entirely is His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens are folded up in His right hand﴾. It has also been said that "His Throne" is a metaphor for His knowledge, taken from "the chair of the scholar"; and it has been said it is a metaphor for His sovereignty, taken from "the chair of kingship," since the greater the chair, the greater and more abundant the grandeur of the one seated; so He expressed the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, or the expansiveness of His kingdom and authority, by the vastness of His chair and its encompassing of the upper and lower regions. It has also been said that it is a body before the Throne, encompassing the seven heavens, based on the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The seven heavens and the seven earths, along with the Kursiyy, are but like a ring in a desert, and the excellence of the Throne over the Kursiyy is like the excellence of that desert over that ring." Perhaps it is the eighth sphere. From al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī it is reported that it is the Throne.

﴿And He is not burdened by guarding them﴾; that is, He is not weighed down by it, nor is it difficult for Him: ﴿guarding them﴾, that is, the guarding of the heavens and the earth. He did not mention what is in them because guarding them entails guarding what is in them.

﴿And He is the Most High﴾: exalted by His essence above things and rivals; ﴿the Most Great﴾: before whom everything other than Him is belittled.

Because of what you see of this noble verse's comprising the principal divine matters concerning the Exalted Essence and the manifest attributes—for it declares that He (exalted is He) exists, is singular in divinity, is characterized by life, is necessarily existent by His essence, is the originator of others (since al-Qayyūm is the one who subsists by His essence and sustains others); is transcendent above localization and indwelling, free from change and languor; has no resemblance between Him and bodily forms, and there befalls Him not what befalls souls and spirits; is the Owner of dominion and the realm of sovereignty; the originator of roots and branches; possessor of mighty force; none intercedes with Him except one whom He permits; alone knowing all things, the evident and the hidden, the universal and the particular; of vast dominion and power over all that can be owned and be subject to power; no difficulty burdens Him, nor does one affair preoccupy Him from another; exalted above what imagination can grasp, great such that understandings cannot encompass Him—it is distinguished by excellent virtues and surpassing special qualities that its sister verses lack. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, the greatest verse in the Qur'an is the Verse of the Throne; whoever recites it, Allah (exalted is He) sends an angel who writes down good deeds for him and erases his bad deeds until the same hour the next day."

And the Prophet ﷺ said—upon him be blessings and peace: "This verse is not recited in a house except that the devils abandon it for thirty days, and neither a sorcerer nor a sorceress enters it for forty nights. O ʿAlī, teach it to your children, your family, and your neighbors, for no verse has descended greater than it."

And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever recites the Verse of the Throne after every obligatory prayer, nothing prevents him from entering Paradise except death; and none persists in it except a truthful one or a worshipper. And whoever recites it when he takes his resting place, Allah (exalted is He) grants him security for himself, his neighbor, his neighbor's neighbor, and the dwellings around him."

And the Prophet ﷺ said—upon him be blessings and peace: "The master of mankind is Adam; the master of the Arabs is Muhammad, and I say this without boasting; the master of the Persians is Salman; the master of the Romans is Suhayb; the master of the Abyssinians is Bilal; the master of mountains is Mount Sinai; the master of days is Friday; the master of speech is the Qur'an; the master of the Qur'an is Surat al-Baqara; and the master of al-Baqara is the Verse of the Throne."

The specific mention of his mastery ﷺ over the Arabs within the enumeration of particular masteries does not indicate a denial of what the widely transmitted reports indicate, and on which there is consensus, of his mastery ﷺ over all of mankind.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 256:**

﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (*jumla mustaʼnafa*, a sentence that begins a new thought). It comes after the statement of God's unique attributes, which make belief in Him alone necessary. The implication is that a rational person should not need obligation or compulsion, but should choose the true religion without hesitation or confusion. It was also said that this is a declarative sentence with the meaning of a prohibition: "Do not compel anyone in religion." It was said that this verse is abrogated (*mansukh*) by His saying: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them.﴾ It was also said that it applies specifically to the People of the Book, who protected themselves by paying the jizya (poll tax). It is narrated that a man from the Ansar, from the Banu Salim ibn 'Awf, had two sons who had become Christians before the Prophet's mission (ﷺ). When they came to Medina, their father clung to them and said: "By God, I will not leave you until you become Muslims." They refused, so they brought the dispute to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed; so he let them go.

﴿The right course has become clear from the wrong.﴾ This is a causal resumptive sentence (*istiʼnaf taʻlili*), introduced by the particle of confirmation (*qad*) to strengthen the affirmation of its content, as in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿You have indeed received an excuse from me.﴾ The meaning is: since it has become clear, through the attributes of God (exalted is He) that were mentioned, which make it impossible to imagine that anyone shares any of them with Him, that faith, which is the right course leading to eternal happiness, is distinct from disbelief, which is error leading to everlasting misery.

﴿Whoever disbelieves in the false deity (*ṭāghūt*)...﴾ The word *ṭāghūt* is an intensive form (*bināʼ mubālagha*) derived from *al-ṭughyān* (transgression), like *malakūt* and *jabarūt*, with its middle and final radicals transposed. It was said that it is originally a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), and this is the view of al-Fārisī. It was also said that it is a collective noun (*ism jins*) in singular, masculine form; the plural and feminine forms are used only to refer to "the gods," and this is the opinion of Sibawayh. It was also said that it is a plural, the view of al-Mubarrad. And it was said that it is used uniformly for the singular and plural, masculine and feminine. The meaning is: whoever acts, after the truth has been distinguished from falsehood by the clear proofs and manifest signs, and disbelieves in Satan, or in the idols, or in everything worshipped besides God (exalted is He), or turns away from worshipping Him, after it has become clear to him that it is outside the right to be worshipped...

﴿and believes in God﴾ alone, because of what he witnessed of His sublime attributes, which require that divinity be exclusive to Him, mighty and majestic is He, and which necessitate faith and monotheism. The mention of disbelief in the *ṭāghūt* before belief in Him (exalted is He) is because the latter depends on the former, for clearing (*takhliya*) precedes adorning (*taḥliya*).

﴿then he has grasped the most reliable handhold.﴾ That is, he has greatly intensified his grasp of it, as if he, while holding it, seeks from himself an increase in it and steadfastness upon it.

﴿for which there is no breaking.﴾ *Al-faṣm* means breaking without separation, while *al-qaṣm* means breaking with separation. Negating the first implies, by priority (*bil-awlawiyya*), the negation of the second. This sentence is either a resumptive sentence confirming what precedes it regarding the firmness of the handhold, or a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to "the handhold," with the governing verb being "has grasped," or to the implicit pronoun in "the most reliable." The word "for it" (*lahā*) is in the position of the predicate, meaning: it belongs to it. The statement is an allegory (*tamthīl*), based on comparing a mental state, derived from constant adherence to a true belief that does not admit its opposite at all because it is established by clear and conclusive proofs, with a physical state derived from grasping a firm rope whose breaking is not feared. Thus there is no metaphor in the individual words. It is permissible, however, that "the most reliable handhold" be a metaphor for the true belief, which is faith and monotheism, not for the correct reasoning that leads to it, as some have said, since that is not mentioned in the conditional clause. "Grasping it" would then be a metaphor for the constant adherence mentioned, or an elaboration (*tarshīḥ*) of the first metaphor.

﴿God is All-Hearing﴾ of words, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of resolutions and beliefs. This sentence is an interjected concluding remark (*iʻtirāḍ tadhyīlī*), which urges faith and deters disbelief and hypocrisy through the promise and warning it contains.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 257:

﴿Allah is the Walī (Protector, Helper) of those who believe﴾; i.e., their helper (mu'īnuhum); or the one who manages their affairs (mutawallī umūrihim). By them is meant those whose faith, in general terms, is known in His knowledge (exalted is He) as to its outcome (mā'alan) or its present state (ḥālan). ﴿He brings them out﴾: an explanation of the walāya (guardianship); or a second predicate (khabar thānin), according to those who permit it to be a clause; or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "walī". ﴿From the darknesses﴾; which are more general than the darknesses of disbelief and sins, and the darknesses of doubts (shubah); indeed, even what is in some levels of the inferential (istidlālī) sciences, of a kind of weakness and obscurity, relative to their strong, clear levels; indeed, even what is in all their levels, when compared with the level of direct vision (ʿiyān), as you will come to know. ﴿To the light﴾; which encompasses the light of faith (īmān), the light of certainty (īqān) with its levels, and the light of direct vision (ʿiyān); i.e., He brings out, by His guidance and His enabling success (tawfīq), each one of them from the darkness into which he has fallen, to what corresponds to it of light. The singular "light" is because of the unity of the Truth, just as the plural "darknesses" is because of the multiplicity of the kinds of misguidance.

﴿As for those who disbelieve﴾; i.e., those whose disbelief is known in His knowledge (exalted is He); ﴿their guardians are the Ṭāghūt﴾; i.e., the devils and all others who lead astray from the path of truth. The relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) is the subject (mubtadaʾ); "their guardians" is a second subject (mubtadaʾ thānin); and "al-Ṭāghūt" is its predicate (khabar); and the clause is the predicate of the first; and the clause is conjoined to what precedes it. Perhaps the change of construction is to avoid placing the Ṭāghūt in opposition to the exalted Name, and for the purpose of emphasis by repeating the predication, together with an indication of the contrast between the two groups in every respect, even in the manner of expression. ﴿They bring them out﴾; by whisperings and other means of misguidance and seduction; ﴿from the light﴾; the innate light (al-nūr al-fiṭrī) upon which all people are created; or: from the light of the clear proofs (al-bayyināt) which they witness from the side of the Prophet (ﷺ), treating their capacity to be illuminated by them as if it were the proofs themselves; ﴿into the darknesses﴾; the darknesses of disbelief and of immersion in error. It has been said: it was revealed concerning a people who apostatized from Islam. The clause is an explanation of the guardianship of the Ṭāghūt, or a second predicate, as has passed. The attribution of bringing out, in terms of causation, to the Ṭāghūt does not conflict with its being ascribed, in terms of creation, to His power (exalted is He).

﴿Those﴾: a reference to the relative pronoun, in view of its being characterized by what is in the scope of the relative clause and the vices that follow from it; ﴿are the companions of the Fire﴾; i.e., those who are involved in it and bound to it, because of the crimes they have committed; ﴿they will abide therein forever﴾; remaining there eternally.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 258:

﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord﴾: This is offered as evidence for what was mentioned, that the disbelievers have as their protectors the tyrant (al-taghut), and as confirmation of it, in the manner of His (exalted be He) saying: ﴿Have you not seen that they wander in every valley?﴾; just as what follows it is evidence for His (exalted be He) guardianship of the believers, and a confirmation of it. This was begun with this for the sake of preserving the connection between it and what it implies, and because it stands on its own with a marvelous matter, worthy of being introduced by the speech: namely his audacity in disputing about God (mighty and majestic), and the great things he uttered in the course of it, which proclaim the perfection of his foolishness. Also, because what follows contains multiplicity and detail, whose placing first would produce a dispersal of the composition. Moreover, guidance by God (exalted be He) is also indicated within it, through the agency of Abraham (peace be upon him), for what is related of him concerning calling to the truth and refuting the arguments of the disbelievers is among the effects of God's (exalted be He) guardianship. The interrogative hamza is for denying the negation and affirming the negated, meaning: Have you not looked? Or: Has your knowledge not reached this towering tyrant, how he undertook to lead people astray and bring them out from the light into the darknesses? That is, the seeing has been realized and established, on the basis that his affair is so manifest that it can hardly be hidden from anyone who has a share of address; thus it became clear that the disbelievers have as their protectors the tyrant. In the mention of the title Lordship, together with its attribution to his (peace and blessings be upon him) pronoun, there is an honoring of him and a notice of his being supported in the disputation. ﴿Because God had given him the kingdom﴾: that is, because He had given it to him, whereby it made him exultant and drove him to dispute; or he disputed on account of it, placing disputation, which is the ugliest form of disbelief, in the place of the thanks that were incumbent upon him, as one says: "You opposed me because I did good to you." Or: at the time God gave him the kingdom. And this is an argument against those who deny that God gives the kingdom to a disbeliever. ﴿When Abraham said﴾: a temporal clause governing "argued"; or a substitute for "given him," on the last reading. ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾; with the ya' of "rabbiya" pronounced with fatha; and it was also read with its omission. It is related that when he (peace be upon him) broke the idols, the king imprisoned him, then released him, and said: Who is your Lord to whom you call? He said: My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death; that is, He creates life and death in bodies. He said: a resumption built upon the question, as if it were said: How did he dispute with him in this strong and true statement? So it was said: ﴿He said: I give life and cause death﴾; it is related that he summoned two men, killed one of them, and released the other, and said this. ﴿Abraham said﴾: a resumption, as before; as if it were said: What did Abraham say to one who was at this level of foolishness? And with what did he silence him? So it was said: He said: ﴿Indeed God brings the sun from the east﴾; as His will requires; ﴿so bring it from the west﴾; if you are able to do the like of His acts (exalted be He). He (peace be upon him) did not turn to refuting the statement of the accursed, indicating that its falsity is so clear and manifest that it can hardly be hidden from anyone, and that undertaking to refute it is of the kind of striving to obtain what is already obtained; and he brought an example in which the accursed finds no room for deception and confusion. ﴿So the one who disbelieved was dumbfounded﴾; that is, he became perplexed; and it was read in the active form, with the relative as its object, meaning: Abraham overcame the disbeliever and silenced him. The placing of disbelief within the relative clause serves to indicate the cause of the ruling, and to specify that disputation is disbelief. ﴿And God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾: a concluding clause confirming the content of what precedes; that is, He does not guide those who wronged themselves by exposing themselves to the everlasting punishment, because of their turning away from accepting guidance, toward the methods of reasoning, or toward the path of salvation, or toward the way to Paradise on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Or like the one who passed by a town﴾:

This is an illustration of what was mentioned of His (Exalted is He) guardianship over the believers, and a confirmation of it. It is conjoined to the preceding relative clause (al-mawsul al-sabiq). The choice of the disjunctive *aw* ("or") over the conjunctive *wa* ("and") is to guard against the supposition that the one being cited as an example is the same as the one already being discussed from the outset. The *kaf* (in *ka-alladhi*, "like the one who") is either a noun (*ismiyyah*), as a group of scholars have chosen, and is brought to draw attention to the multiplicity of examples and that they are not confined to what has been mentioned, as in your saying: "The past tense verb is like *nasara*" (a noun, meaning "like"). Or it is a superfluous particle (*za'idah*), as others have preferred. The meaning is: "Have you not seen the likes of the one who..., or [have you not seen] the one who passed by a town, how Allah guided him and brought him out of the darkness of confusion into the light of direct observation and witnessing?" That is, you have indeed seen that and witnessed it. Therefore there is no doubt that Allah is the Guardian of those who believe... etc.

This is one view. As for making the interrogative hamzah (*alif al-istifham*) merely for expressing wonder, so that the meaning in the first case is: "Have you not considered the one who disputed..." etc., meaning: look at him and marvel at his affair; and in the second case: "Or have you seen the likes of the one who passed by..." etc., as a notification that his condition and what befell him is so strange that no one like him is seen, as the view of the majority has settled, then this is not befitting the eloquence of the revelation and the grandeur of its exalted matter. So reflect upon this.

The one who passed by was Uzayr ibn Sharkhiya, as said by Qatada, al-Rabi', Ikrima, Naji ibn Ka'b, Sulayman ibn Yazid, al-Dahhak, and al-Suddi (may Allah be pleased with them). It was said: He was Armiya ibn Halqiya, from the lineage of Harun (peace be upon him), as said by Wahb and Ubayd Allah ibn Umayr. It was also said: Armiya is al-Khidr himself. Mujahid said: "The one who passed by was a man who disbelieved in the resurrection, but this is far-fetched." The town was Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), as said by Wahb, Ikrima, and al-Rabi'. It was said: It was Dayr Hiraql (the monastery of Heraclius) on the bank of the Tigris. al-Kalbi said: It was Dayr Sabir Abad. al-Suddi said: It was the dwellings of Salma Bad. The first view is the most apparent and the most well-known. It is related that when the Children of Israel went to extremes in engaging in evil and corruption, and exceeded every customary limit in arrogance and transgression, Allah (Exalted is He) empowered over them Bukhtanasar the Babylonian. He marched against them with six hundred thousand banners, until he trod upon the Levant (al-Sham), destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis, and divided the Children of Israel into thirds: a third of them he killed, a third he left in the Levant, and a third he took captive. They were one hundred thousand (p-253) youths, both those who had reached maturity and those who had not. He distributed them among the kings who were with him, so each king received four boys. Uzayr was among them. When Allah (Exalted is He) delivered him from them after a time, he passed by Bayt al-Maqdis with his donkey, and saw it in the most dreadful sight and the most desolate scene. This is the meaning of His statement (Mighty and Majestic is He):

﴿and it was fallen upon its roofs﴾: That is, collapsed upon its roofs, such that the roofs fell, then the walls, from *khawa al-bayt* ("the house collapsed"), when it fell; or from *khawat al-ardu*, meaning it was ruined. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *marra* ("passed"), or from *qaryah* ("town"), according to those who permit a circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun absolutely. He said, that is, out of distress over it, and longing for its restoration, along with a sense of despair regarding it:

﴿"How will Allah bring this back to life?"﴾: While it is in the strange state he sees, contrary to life. The placing of *hadhihi* ("this") before the subject (*al-fa'il*, i.e., Allah) is for emphasis, since the improbability arises from its side, not from the side of the agent. *Anna* was put in the accusative: if it means *mata* ("when"), it is in the accusative of time (*zarfiyyah*); if it means *kayfa* ("how"), it is in the accusative of circumstance (*hāliyyah*) from *hadhihi*. The governing word is *yuhyi* ("brings back to life"). Whichever it is, the intent is to express improbability of its being rebuilt with buildings and inhabitants from among the remnants of its people, who scattered like the dispersal of Saba', and from others. He expressed it as bringing back to life, which is by custom a well-known sign of remoteness from occurring, in order to make the address awe-inspiring and to emphasize the improbability. For the same reason he expressed its ruin as death, when it was said:

﴿"after its death"﴾. Since this expression clearly conveys the improbability of life after death in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, Allah (Mighty and Majestic is He) showed him the most remote of the two matters in his own self, and then in others, and then showed him what he had deemed improbable openly, to exaggerate the removal of whatever might stir in his mind. As for interpreting its bringing back to life as the bringing back to life of its people, this is ruled out by the fact that the mention concerns the state of the town rather than the state of its people, and by restricting the mention to their death rather than their being dust and bones, even though the latter would be more emphatically improbable, owing to its greater contrast with life and its utmost remoteness from accepting it. Furthermore, His (Exalted is He) will had not been directed toward bringing them back to life, as it had been directed toward the restoration of the town, and toward the passerby's witnessing it, as will be explained in detail.

﴿So Allah caused him to die﴾: and kept him in death

﴿for a hundred years﴾. It is related that when he entered the town, he tied his donkey and went around it, and saw no one in it. He said what he said. Its trees had borne fruit, so he took some figs and grapes and drank from their juice, and then slept. Allah (Exalted is He) caused him to die in his sleep, while he was young. He also caused his donkey to die. The remainder of his figs, grapes, and juice were beside him. Then Allah (Exalted is He) blinded the eyes of the creatures to him, so no one saw him. When seventy years had passed since his death, Allah (Mighty and Exalted is He) sent a great king from the kings of Persia, called "Yushk," to Bayt al-Maqdis to rebuild it, and with him were a thousand stewards (*qahramanah*), each steward having three hundred thousand workers. They began rebuilding it. Allah (Exalted is He) destroyed Bukhtanasar by a gnat that entered his brain. Allah (Exalted is He) rescued those of the Children of Israel who remained and returned them to Bayt al-Maqdis, and those who had been scattered among the regions returned to it. They rebuilt it for thirty years, and they multiplied and returned to their best condition. When the hundred years from the death of Uzayr were complete, Allah (Exalted is He) brought him back to life. This is His statement (Exalted is He):

﴿Then He raised him﴾. The choice of *ba'athahu* ("raised him") over *ahyahu* ("brought him to life") indicates its speed and the ease with which it is accomplished for the Originator (Exalted is He). It is as if He raised him from sleep, to indicate that He restored him in the same condition he was in on the day of his death: rational, understanding, and prepared for reflection and inference. He said:

﴿He said: "How long have you remained?"﴾. This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence not grammatically linked to what precedes), based on a question, as if it were said: "What did He say to him after raising him?" So it was said: "He said, 'How long have you remained?'" This is to show him his incapacity to comprehend Allah's affairs (Exalted is He), and that his revival was not after a brief period, which might be thought to be relatively easy, but after a long period. This would cut off the root of his improbability entirely, and he would become aware, in the midst of it, of another of the wondrous signs of His power (Exalted is He): that food, which naturally spoils quickly, remained as it was for a long time without any change. *Kam* is in the accusative of time, and its specified noun (*tamyiz*) is omitted. The meaning is: "How much time have you remained?" The speaker is Allah (Exalted is He), or an angel commanded by Him to do so. It was said: He was called from heaven: "O Uzayr, how long did you remain after death?"

﴿He said: "I remained a day or part of a day."﴾ (p-254) He said this based on approximation and estimation, or to minimize the length of his stay. As for what is said, that he died in the forenoon and was raised after a hundred years shortly before sunset, and then, before looking at the sun, he said "a day," then turned to it and saw some of it remaining, and so said "or part of a day," by way of retraction (*idrab*, a change from one statement to a corrected one), then this is far from precision, since there is no basis for asserting that it was a full day, even if reckoned from sunset, because a deficiency at its beginning is certain. He said:

﴿"Nay, you remained a hundred years"﴾: This is a coordinating clause (*'atf*) on something implied; that is: "You did not remain that amount, but rather this amount." 

﴿"So look"﴾: to witness another sign from the proofs of Our power:

﴿"at your food and your drink; they have not spoiled"﴾: That is, they have not changed during this long period, despite their tendency toward spoilage. It is related that he found his figs and grapes just as he had picked them, and his juice just as he had pressed it. The negated clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) without a *waw*, like His statement (Exalted is He):

﴿"no harm touched them"﴾. The pronoun is singular either because the food and drink are treated as a single thing, like "the food" (*al-ghidha'*), or it refers only to the latter, sufficing with the state of the latter as an indication of the state of the former. This is supported by the reading of one who read:

"And this is your drink, it has not spoiled." The *ha'* (in *yatasanna-h*) is either original or a *ha' al-sakt* (a silent pause *ha'*). Its derivation is from *al-sanah* ("year"), since its final radical is either *ha'* or *waw*. It was also said: its original form is *lam yatasannan*, from *al-hama' al-masnun* ("black molded clay"), so its *nun* was changed to a weak letter, as in *taqada al-bazi* ("the falcon swooped"). It has also been permitted that the meaning of *lam yatasanneh* is: the years that have passed have not passed over it, not literally, but figuratively. That is, it is in its state as if he had not remained a hundred years. It was also read: *lam yassanneh*, with the *ta'* assimilated into the *sin*.

﴿"And look at your donkey"﴾: how its bones decayed, scattered, separated, and disintegrated, so that what was mentioned of the long stay may become clear to you, and your soul may be reassured by it. His statement (Mighty and Majestic is He):

﴿"and that We may make you a sign for the people"﴾: is a coordinating clause on something implied, linked to a verb implied before it, by way of resumption (*isti'naf*), confirming the content of what precedes. That is: "We did what We did, of bringing you back to life after what has been mentioned, so that you may witness what you deemed improbable of bringing back to life after a long age, and that We may make you a sign for the people living in this generation, by their seeing you while you are from among the people of past generations, and by their taking from you what has been concealed from them for ages of knowledge of the Torah, as will come." Or it is linked to a verb implied after it. That is: "And that We may make you a sign for them, in the manner mentioned. We did what We did." On both interpretations it is evidence for what was mentioned of the long stay. For this reason, a separation was made between it and the command to look at his donkey. The repetition of the command in His statement (Exalted is He):

﴿"And look at the bones"﴾, even though the intended bones are also those of the donkey, is because the first command was to look at them from the viewpoint of their indication of the long stay mentioned, and the second command was to look at them from the viewpoint of life coming upon them and its beginnings. That is: "And look at the bones of the donkey, so that you may witness the manner of bringing back to life in another, after you have witnessed it in yourself."

﴿"how We raise them"﴾, with a *zay* with a dot (*nunshizuha*), meaning: We lift some of them up to others, and return them to their places in the body, assembling them in a fitting arrangement. Al-Kisa'i said: "We soften them and make them grow." Perhaps whoever interpreted it as "We bring them to life" meant by revival this sense. Likewise the one who read *nunshiruha* with a *ra'*, from *anshara Allah al-mawta* ("Allah revived the dead"), meaning: He brought them to life, not its literal meaning, due to His statement (Exalted is He):

﴿"then We clothe them with flesh"﴾, meaning: We cover them with it, as the body is covered with clothing. As for the one who read *nanshuruha* with a *nun* (*nanshuruha*) with the *nun* vowelled with a fatha and the *shin* with a damma, he perhaps meant by it the opposite of folding, as al-Farra' said. The meaning is then: "how We spread them out." The clause is either a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from "the bones," meaning: "And look at them assembled and clothed with flesh"; or a comprehensive apposition (*badal al-ishtimal*, an apposition in which the second term is a part of or connected to the first), meaning: "And look at the bones, [at] the manner of their raising and the spreading of flesh over them." Perhaps the reason for not addressing the manner of breathing in the spirit is that it is among matters for which wisdom does not require explanation. It is related that he was called: "O decayed bones, Allah commands you to come together." So every piece of them gathered together, those which the birds and beasts had carried off, and which the winds had scattered from every plain and mountain. Some of them joined others, and each limb adhered to what was fitting for it: rib to rib, forearm to its place, head to its position. Then the sinews and veins, then flesh spread over it, (p-255) then the skin, then hair grew from it, then the spirit was breathed into it, and behold, he stood up bray­ing.

﴿So when it became clear to him﴾: That is, what the command to look at it indicated, of the manner of revival with its beginnings. The *fa'* (in *falamma*) is for coordination with something implied, which the aforementioned command calls for. It was omitted to indicate that its realization was evident and that it needed no mention, and to convey the swiftness of its occurrence, as in the statement (Mighty and Majestic is He):

﴿"So when he saw it settled beside him"﴾, after His statement:

﴿"I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you"﴾. It is as if it was said:

Then Allah raised them up and clothed them with flesh. So when it became clear to him, that is, it became completely evident, he said: ﴿I know that Allah is over all things﴾, among the things of which is what he witnessed in himself and in others of the wondrous signs, ﴿Competent﴾, nothing among the matters is beyond Him. The use of the present-tense form (a'lamu) indicates that his knowledge of this is continuous, given that its essence has not changed or been altered; rather, only its attribute was transformed before his eyes. It also indicates that he spoke as he did on the basis of ordinary improbability and as a magnification of the matter.

It has been said: the subject of "tabayyana" is an implied pronoun, explained by the object of "a'lamu", that is:

"When it became clear to him that Allah (Exalted) is over all things competent, he said: I know that Allah is over all things competent." So reflect.

It was also read as "tubayyina lahu" (in the passive form), and it was read as "qala i'lam" (in the imperative form).

It is narrated that he mounted his donkey and came to his locality, and the people did not recognize him, and he did not recognize the people or the dwellings. He set off, by way of illusion from him, until he came to his house, and there he found an old woman, blind and paralyzed, who had reached the time of 'Uzair. 'Uzair said to her: "O woman, is this the house of 'Uzair?" She said: "Yes. And where is the remembrance of 'Uzair? We have lost him such-and-such a time ago." She wept a severe weeping. He said: "Indeed I am 'Uzair." She said: "Glory be to Allah! How can that be?" He said: "Allah caused me to die for a hundred years, then He resurrected me." She said: "'Uzair was one whose supplication was answered. So pray to Allah that He restore my sight to me, so that I may see you." He prayed to his Lord and wiped her eyes with his hand, and they became sound. He took her hand and said to her: "Rise by the permission of Allah." She rose sound, as though she had been freed from a bond. She looked at him and said: "I bear witness that you are 'Uzair." She went off to the locality of the Children of Israel, while they were in their assemblies. In the gathering was a son of 'Uzair who had reached one hundred and eighteen years, and the sons of his sons were elders. She called out: "This is 'Uzair; he has come to you." They denied her. She said: "Look, for by his supplication I have returned to this state." The people rose and came to him. His son said: "My father had a black birthmark between his shoulders, like the crescent moon." He uncovered him, and behold, it was so. Bukhtnasar had killed, at Bayt al-Maqdis, forty thousand men from among the readers of the Torah, and there was not then among them a copy of the Torah, nor anyone who knew the Torah. So he recited it to them from memory, without omitting a single letter.
