A man from among the sons of the captives, of those who had come to Bayt al-Maqdis after the destruction of Bukhtnasar, said: "My father told me, from my grandfather, that on the day of the captivity he buried the Torah in a jar in a vineyard. If you show me my grandfather's vineyard, I will bring it out for you." They went to his grandfather's vineyard, searched, and found it. They compared it with what 'Uzair had dictated to them from memory, and they did not differ in a single letter. At that point they said: "He is the son of Allah." Exalted is Allah above that by a great exaltation.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 260:**

﴿And when Abraham said﴾: this is another proof of His (exalted be He) guardianship (wilaya) over the believers, and of His bringing them out from the darknesses into the light. He did not follow the same manner of citation (istishhad) as the previous example, by saying "or like the one who said: My Lord... etc.", because his mention (peace be upon him) recurred in the course of the argument (muhajja). Also, he (peace be upon him) had no part in the very basis of the proof, as in the case of Uzair (peace be upon him), since what happened to him of being brought back to life after a hundred years is among the signs of His (exalted be He) power and His guidance. The adverbial phrase (zarf) is governed by an implied verb, of the kind that is stated explicitly in such constructions as His saying (exalted be He): ﴿and remember when He made you successors﴾. That is, "and remember the time when he (peace be upon him) said..." and the wondrous works of God's creation that occurred at that time, so that you may recognize the guardianship and guidance of Him (exalted be He) that have passed. The directing of the command to remember in such places to the time, rather than to the events that occurred in it, even though the events are the intended object of the reminder, is for the reason mentioned more than once: the emphasis on making their remembrance obligatory. For the obligation to remember the time is an obligation to remember what occurred in it by way of demonstrative proof (burhani), and because the time comprises them in detail, so that when it is called to mind they are present with all their particulars, such that nothing of what was mentioned in the narration, or was not mentioned, is absent from them, as if they were being witnessed directly.

"My Lord" (rabbi) is a word of entreaty (isti'tf), placed before the supplication for the sake of emphasis in seeking the answer. "Show me" (arini) is from the visual seeing (ru'ya basariyya) which is transitive to one object; with the addition of the causative hamza (hamzat al-naql) it requires a second object, which is the interrogative clause (al-jumla al-istifhamiyya) that is suspended (mu'allaqa) from it, for it is suspended just as visual looking is suspended. That is: make me see. ﴿How You give life to the dead﴾: that is, by Your giving them life while I look at them. The word "how" (kayfa) is in a position of accusative (nasb) by analogy to an adverb of time (zarf) according to Sibawayh, and by analogy to a circumstantial adverb (hal) according to al-Akhfash, and the governing element in it is "give life" (tuhyi). That is: in what state, or: in what manner You give life. Al-Qurtubi said: the question with "how" is only a question about the state of a thing whose existence is established for the questioner and the one questioned; so the question here is about the manner of the giving of life, which is established for the questioner. That is: show me the mode of Your giving life to the dead. He (peace be upon him) asked this so that his certainty might be confirmed by direct vision, and his heart might grow in tranquility upon tranquility.

As for what is said, that when Nimrod said, "I give life and cause death," Abraham (peace be upon him) said, "The giving of life by God (exalted be He) is by returning the spirits to the bodies," and Nimrod said, "Have you seen Him?" and he could not say "yes," and so he moved on to another argument, and then asked his Lord to show him that, this is refuted by the explanation of the question by tranquility.

He said: this is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), as has passed more than once. ﴿Have you not believed?﴾: this is a coordination (atf) upon an implied element; that is: "Do you not know, and have you not believed, that I am able to give life in whatever manner I will, that you should ask me to show it?" He (exalted and high be He) said this, while He knew that he (peace be upon him) was the most firm of people in faith and the strongest in certainty, so that he would answer with what he answered, and that would be a kindness (lutf) to those who hear.

He said: ﴿Yes﴾: I know, and I believe that You are able to give life in whatever manner You will. ﴿But﴾ I asked what I asked ﴿so that my heart may be at rest﴾: by combining direct vision with faith and certainty, and that I may increase in insight through witnessing it in a specific manner.

He said: ﴿Then take﴾: the fa' is the answer to an omitted condition; that is, if you wish that: ﴿then take four birds﴾. It has been said: it is a noun used as a collective for "bird" (ta'ir), like "riding party" (rakb) and "traveling party" (safr). It has been said: it is a plural of it, like "merchant" (tajir) and "merchandise" (tajr). It has been said: it is a verbal noun (masdar) used as a name for the genus. It has been said: it is a lightened form of "tayyir," with the meaning of "bird," like "hayn" in "hayyin." The preposition "from" (min) is connected to "take," or to an implied element that functions as a qualifier of "four"; that is: four being from among the birds. It has been said: they were a peacock, a rooster, a crow, and a dove; and it has been said: an eagle in place of the last one. The specification of birds for this is because they are the closest to humans, the most comprehensive of the special properties of animals, and because it is easy to carry out with them what is done to them of cutting up, separating, and so on.

﴿Then cut them into pieces﴾: from "sara-hu, yasuru-hu," meaning he inclined it; and it was read with a kasra on the sad, from "sara-hu, yasiru-hu," meaning incline them and gather them together. And it was read "fa-surrahunna," with a damma and a kasra on the sad and a shadda on the ra', from "sarra-hu, yasurru-hu, yasirru-hu," when he gathered it. And it was read "fa-sarrihinna," from "al-tasriya," meaning "gathering": that is, gather them ﴿to yourself﴾, so that you may contemplate them and know their markings in detail, so that after the giving of life you know that not a single part of them has moved from its original place at all.

It is narrated that he was commanded to slaughter them, pluck their feathers, cut them up, scatter their parts, mix their feathers, their blood, and their flesh, and hold on to their heads. Then he was commanded to place their parts upon the mountains, and that is His (exalted be He) saying: ﴿Then place upon every mountain a portion of them﴾: that is, divide them, and scatter their parts over the mountains that were in his presence. It has been said: they were four mountains; and it has been said: seven. So he placed on each mountain a quarter, or a seventh, of each bird.

It was read "juz'un" (juzu'an) with two dammas, and "juzz-an" with a shadda, by dropping its hamza for lightness, then doubling it at pause, then treating the connected reading as if it were pause. ﴿Then call them, and they will come to you﴾: in the position of jussive (jazm), as an answer to the command; but it was built (on the ending) because of its connection with the nun of the feminine plural. ﴿Running﴾: that is, hastening, rushing; or having a running, flying, or walking.

He only restricted himself to narrating His (exalted and glorious be He) commands, without addressing his compliance (peace be upon him), nor what resulted from it of the marvelous effects of His (exalted be He) power. As it is narrated that he (peace be upon him) called out, saying: "Come, by God's permission!" and every part of them flew to its companion, until they became bodies; then they came to their heads, and each body joined with its head, and each one returned to the form it had been in. This is to indicate that the consequences of those matters upon the sublime commands, and the impossibility of their failing to follow them, are so clear and manifest that there is no need to mention them at all. And sufficient is the story as evidence of the excellence of the Friend (khalil) [of God], of the blessing of humble supplication in prayer, and of the fine courtesy in asking, in that God (exalted be He) showed him what he asked for immediately, in the easiest of ways, and showed Uzair what He showed him after causing him to die for a hundred years.

﴿And know that God is Mighty﴾: overpowering over His affair, nothing can frustrate Him regarding what He wills. ﴿Wise﴾: possessing far-reaching wisdom in His actions. So the basing of His actions upon ordinary causes is not due to incapacity to bring them about by another, supernatural way, but because it contains wisdoms and benefits.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 261:

﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾: that is, in the channels of good works, whether obligatory or voluntary. ﴿is like a grain﴾: it is necessary to supply an elided noun (mudaf) on one of the two sides; that is, "the likeness of their spending is like the likeness of a grain," or "their likeness is like the likeness of one who sows a grain." ﴿that sprouts seven ears﴾: that is, it produces a stalk from which seven branches sprout, and on each one of them is an ear. ﴿In every ear there are a hundred grains﴾: as is observed in maize and millet in fertile lands, and even more than that. The attribution of the sprouting to the grain is metaphorical, like its attribution to the earth and the spring. This illustration is a depiction of the multiplication, as if it were present before the eyes of the beholder. ﴿And Allah multiplies﴾ that multiplication, or more than it, up to what Allah (Exalted) wills, ﴿for whom He wills﴾: that He multiply for him by His bounty, according to the state of the spender in his sincerity and his exertion. For this reason the ranks of deeds differ in the measures of reward. ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾: nothing constrains Him from the increase with which He bestows favour; ﴿All-Knowing﴾: of the intention of the spender, the amount of his spending, and the manner in which he acquired what he spent.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 262:

﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾: this is an independent sentence (jumla mubtada'a), brought to explain the manner of spending, whose excellence was shown by the example mentioned. ﴿Then they do not follow what they have spent﴾ (p-258): that is, what they spent, or their spending. ﴿with reproach (manna) or injury (adha)﴾: "al-manna" (reproach, i.e. reminding the recipient of one's favour) is to count one's kindness against the one to whom it was done and to show him that by it one has made a right incumbent upon him. "Al-adha" (injury) is to behave arrogantly toward him because of one's benefaction to him. Reproach was mentioned first because it occurs more frequently. The insertion of the word "la" (not) indicates that the negation covers the following of each of the two separately. "Thumma" (then) serves to show the high rank of what is joined by it.

It has been said that the verse was revealed concerning 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, when he equipped the Army of Hardship (jaysh al-'usra) with a thousand camels, with their saddles and their saddle-coverings. It was also said concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, may Allah be pleased with him, when he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with four thousand dirhams as charity, and nothing of reproach or injury nearly occurred to the minds of either of them.

﴿For them is their reward﴾: that is, as they were promised within the example. It is a sentence consisting of a subject and a predicate, which occurs as the predicate of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul). In the repetition of the predication, and in restricting the reward by His words ﴿with their Lord﴾, there is emphasis and honour that is not hidden. The predicate is left without the particle "fa" (so/therefore), which indicates that the preceding is the cause of the following, in order to signify that the reward's being due for what was mentioned, namely spending and abandoning reproach and injury, is a matter clear enough that it needs no explicit statement of causation. As for the impression that they are fit for this even if they did not do it, how much more so if they did? That is contrary to the context of encouraging the act and urging it.

﴿And no fear shall be upon them﴾: in both abodes, from befalling any of the disliked things. ﴿Nor shall they grieve﴾: over the loss of any sought object, whether small or great. That is, that which necessitates them does not befall them; not that such things befall them but they do not fear or grieve, nor that fear and grief do not befall them at all, but rather they persist in vigour and joy. How could it be otherwise? The sensing of fear and dread, out of magnifying the majesty and awe of Allah (exalted is He), and considering one's striving and effort in fulfilling the rights of servanthood as small, belongs to the elite of the elite and the near ones. The intended meaning is the explanation of the continuing negation of both, not the negation of their continuance, as the predicate in the second clause being in the present tense might suggest; for negation, although it enters upon the present tense itself, indicates continuity and persistence according to the context.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 263:

﴿A kind word﴾: that is, a beautiful speech that hearts accept and do not reject, by which the beggar is turned away without being given anything; ﴿and forgiveness﴾: that is, a covering over of what the beggar has done of insistence (ilhaf) in asking and of other things that weigh heavily on the one asked, and a pardoning of him. The beginning with the indefinite noun (nakira) in the first case is valid because it is specified by the descriptive phrase, and in the second case because of the conjunction; or by an implied qualifier, that is: and forgiveness proceeding from the one asked; ﴿is better﴾: that is, for the beggar; ﴿than a charity followed by harm﴾: because it is mixed with the harm that follows it, while the first two are free of harm. The sentence is resumed (mustaʼnafa), establishing the consideration of abandoning the following of reproach (mann) and harm. Interpreting "forgiveness" as obtaining forgiveness from God (Exalted is He) because of the good response, or as the pardon of the beggar, on the basis of considering the preferability in relation to the one asked, leads to the conclusion that the charity described as such has some good in relation to him, while it is entirely void; ﴿and God is Self-Sufficient﴾: He does not require the poor to bear the burden of reproach and harm, and He provides for them from another source; ﴿Forbearing﴾: He does not hasten to punish those who give reproach and harm, not that they do not deserve it because of these two. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for what precedes it, comprising promise and threat, and establishing the consideration of preferability in relation to the beggar with certainty.

﴿O you who have believed﴾: (p-259) He turned to them directly with address, after explaining the matter in the third person, to emphasize the obligation to act in accordance with the prohibition: ﴿do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾; that is, do not render their reward void by either of these. ﴿Like the one﴾: it is in the accusative position, either as an adjective (na't) of a deleted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: do not nullify them with a nullification like the nullification of the one ﴿who spends his wealth to be seen by people﴾; or as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "tubtilu" (do not nullify), meaning: do not nullify them while resembling the one who spends; that is, the one who nullifies his spending by showing off. It was also said that it is from the pronoun of the deleted verbal noun, according to the view of Sibawayh. The accusative of "ri'a'" (to be seen) is either as a reason (ʿilla) for "yunfiqu" (spends), meaning: for the sake of their showing off; or as a circumstantial clause from its subject, meaning: he spends his wealth showing off. What is meant by it is the hypocrite, due to His saying (exalted is He): ﴿and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾; until he hopes for reward or fears punishment. ﴿Then his example﴾: the "fa" (then) connects what follows it to what precedes it; that is, the example of the one who shows off in spending, and his strange condition. ﴿Is like the example of a smooth stone﴾; that is, a smooth rock. ﴿Upon it is dust﴾; that is, a small amount of it. ﴿Then a heavy rain strikes it﴾; that is, rain of great downpour. ﴿And leaves it bare﴾; there is absolutely none of the dust upon it. ﴿They have no power over anything of what they have earned﴾; they gain nothing from what they did for show, and they absolutely find no reward for it; like His saying: ﴿and We made it scattered dust﴾. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), built upon a question, as if it were said: "What then will their condition be at that time?" So it was said: "They have no power..." etc. And from the necessity of their example being as mentioned is that the example of those who resemble them, namely the people of reminders and injury, is likewise; and the two final pronouns refer to the relative pronoun in terms of meaning, as in His saying (Mighty and Majestic is He): ﴿and you plunged as those who plunged﴾; because what is meant by it is the category, or the group, or the faction. Just as the four preceding pronouns refer to it in terms of wording. ﴿And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾; to good and right guidance. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil) confirming the content of what precedes it; and in it there is an implicit indication that each of showing off, reminders, and injury is among the characteristics of disbelievers, and the believers must avoid them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 265:

﴿And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the approval of Allah﴾: i.e., seeking His pleasure; ﴿and for the firming of their own souls﴾; i.e., and to firm up some of their souls in faith. So "min" (from) here is partitive (tab'idiyyah), as in their saying: "he shook from his side (hazza min 'itfihi)" and "he stirred from his vigor (harraka min nashatihi)"; for wealth is the twin of the spirit (shaqiq al-ruh). Whoever spends his wealth for the sake of Allah (Exalted) has firmed up part of his soul, and whoever spends his wealth and his spirit has firmed it entirely. Or: and as an affirmation of Islam and a realization of the reward from the very origin of their souls; so "min" is then initial (ibtida'iyyah), as in His (Exalted) saying: ﴿out of envy from their own souls﴾. It may also be that the meaning is: and a firming from their souls before the believers that they are sincere in faith and sincere in it; and the reading of the one who read "wa-tabyinan min anfusihim" ("and a clarifying from their souls") supports it. In this is an alert that the wisdom of spending for the spender is the purification of the soul from stinginess and love of wealth, which is the head of every sin. ﴿Like the example of a garden on a height﴾; "al-rabwah" - with the three vowel-harakat, and it has been read with each of them -: an elevated place; i.e., the example of their spending in zakat is like the example of an orchard situated in an elevated place, safe from being struck by frost, due to the lightness of its air from the blowing of gentle winds upon it; for the trees of elevated ground are finer in appearance and purer in fruit, whereas low-lying lands rarely have their fruits safe from frost, due to the density of their air from the stillness of the winds. It was also read: "like the example of a seed (habbah)"; ﴿a heavy rain struck it﴾: rain of great drops; ﴿and it yielded its produce﴾: its fruit; it has been read with the kaf sukun, as a lightening; ﴿twofold﴾; i.e., double what it would bear at other times, because of what the heavy rain struck it with (p-260). The intended sense of "twofold" is "double"; it was also said: four times over. Its accusative is as a circumstantial state (hal) from "produce"; i.e., multiplied. ﴿But if a heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain (tall)﴾; i.e., a light rain that suffices it, because of its goodness, the nobility of its ground, and the lightness of its air. It was also said: then a light rain reaches it; and tall is the rain of small drops. It was also said: then what reaches it is a light rain. The meaning is that the spending of these people is growing (zakiyah) in the sight of Allah (Exalted), never lost in any state; though it varies according to the circumstances that accompany it. It is permissible that the comparison between their condition be considered in terms of the great and small amounts they spend, and the known garden, in terms of the heavy and light rain that reaches it; just as each of the two rains multiplies its produce, so too their spending, whether great or small, after it is sought for the face of Allah (Exalted), is growing, increasing their nearness and the goodness of their state in the sight of Allah. ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾; nothing of it is hidden from Him; and this is an encouragement to sincerity, together with a warning against showing-off (riya') and the like.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 266:

﴿Would any one of you wish﴾: "Al-wudd" (affection): love for a thing together with desiring it. For this reason it is used in the manner of these two (i.e., it takes the same construction as the verb of desire). The interrogative hamza (alif) here is for denying that the event occurs, as in his saying: "Shall I strike my father?"; not for denying the actual event, as in your saying: "Are you striking your father?" The point of the denial, however, is not every thing connected with the desire; rather it is the striking of the whirlwind and what follows it of burning: ﴿that there should be for him a garden﴾. It is also read "jannat" (gardens); ﴿of date palms and grapes﴾; i.e., made up of these two. This is on the basis that the origin and the pillar in it are these two noble kinds, which comprise the varieties of benefits, and the rest are among the things that follow from them, not on the basis that there is in it anything other than them, as you will come to know. And "al-jannah" (garden) is applied to dense, thickly intertwined trees; Zuhayr said:

"As if my two eyes, in the two channels of a twisted rope of the water-camels, water a garden of dense, tall palms"

and to the land that contains them. The first is more suitable to His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾; for according to the second it is necessary to posit an omitted noun; i.e., beneath the trees of it. Likewise it is necessary to make the attribution of burning to it in what follows metaphorical. The sentence is in the place of nominative case, as an attribute of "jannah"; just as His saying (exalted): ﴿of date palms and grapes﴾ is likewise; or in the place of accusative case, as a circumstantial clause from it, because it is qualified. ﴿For him therein of every kind of fruit﴾: The first adverbial phrase is the predicate; the second is a circumstantial clause; the third is the subject; i.e., it is an attribute of the subject standing in its place; i.e., for him is provision of every kind of fruit, as in His saying (exalted): ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾; i.e., there is none of us but has... etc. And "fruits" is not meant in its generality; rather it is meant to denote abundance, as in His saying (exalted): ﴿and she was given of everything﴾.

﴿And old age has struck him﴾; i.e., the age of old age, which is the occasion of intense need for its benefits, and the sign of complete inability to make up for the means of livelihood. The waw is circumstantial; i.e., while old age had already struck him. ﴿And he has weak offspring﴾: a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "asabahu" (struck him); i.e., old age struck him while the state is that he has offspring who are young, who cannot earn or arrange the beginnings of livelihood. It is also read "di'af" (weak); ﴿then a whirlwind with fire in it struck it, and it was burned﴾: "fa-asabaha" (then it struck it) is a conjunction; i.e., a whirlwind, violent, turning around on the earth, then rising from it in a column-like shape up to the sky, bright; ﴿with fire in it﴾, intense; ﴿and it was burned﴾: conjoined to "fa-asabaha" (then it struck it). This, as you see, is an illustration of the state of one who performs deeds of righteousness and good works, and then adds to them what nullifies them of blemishes; then he finds them on the Day of Resurrection, at the time of his complete need for their reward, as scattered dust, in regret and grief over them. ﴿Thus﴾: the singular "kaf" (that) with the addressee being plural has already been explained many times; i.e., like that clear explanation that proceeds to become manifest like perceptible matters; ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the signs, that you may reflect﴾; so that you may reflect upon them, take lessons from what they contain of admonitions, and act in accordance with their requirement.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 267:

﴿O you who have believed, spend from the good things you have earned﴾: This clarifies the condition of that from which spending is made, after clarifying the principle of spending and its manner; i.e., spend from the lawful (halal) of what you have earned, and from its excellent (jiyad) portion, in accordance with His (Exalted) saying: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of that which you love﴾.

﴿and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth﴾: i.e., from the good things of what We have brought forth for you of grains, fruits and minerals; the qualifier has been omitted because what precedes it indicates it. ﴿And do not aim at the bad﴾: with a fatha on the ta'; its original form is "wa-la tatayammamu" (wa-la tatayammamu), and it has been read with a damma; and it has been read "wa-la ta'ammamu"; and all of them mean "aiming" (al-qasd); i.e., do not aim. ﴿the bad﴾: i.e., the inferior, the base. It is like "the good" among adjectives that are commonly used and whose nouns are not mentioned. ﴿of which you spend﴾: the prepositional phrase is connected to "tunfiquna" (you spend); the pronoun refers to "al-khabith" (the bad), and the fronting is for restriction; the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "tayammamu" (aim); i.e., do not aim at the bad, restricting your spending to it; or from "al-khabith"; i.e., spending is specifically directed to it. In either case the restriction is for reproaching them for what they used to practise, spending the bad exclusively, not for permitting its spending alongside the good. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they used to give in charity the rotten dates and the worst of them; so they were forbidden from it. It was also said: the prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause from "al-khabith"; and the pronoun refers to the wealth implied by the context; or to the two relative pronouns, in the manner of his saying:

؎ ∗∗∗ as if on the skin it is the streaking of vitiligo

Or it refers to the second; and its restriction to that is because the disparity in it is greater. "Tunfiquna" is a circumstantial clause from the mentioned subject; i.e., do not aim at the bad as being part of the wealth, or of what you have earned, or of what We have brought forth for you, or from what We have brought forth for you, spending it. His (Exalted) saying: ﴿while you would not take it yourselves﴾: is a circumstantial clause, in every case, from the "waw" of "tunfiquna"; i.e., while you do not take it in your dealings at any time or in any way. ﴿except with closing your eyes to it﴾: i.e., except at the time of your closing your eyes to it; or: except by your closing your eyes to it. This is an expression for overlooking, by way of metonymy or metaphor; it is said: "He closed his eye" when he lowered it. It has been read in the passive form, meaning: "except that you be compelled to closing and be made to enter into it; or be found with eyes closed"; and it has been read "taghmudu" and "taghmiduu" with a damma and a kasra on the mim. It was also said: the speech is complete at His (Exalted) saying: ﴿and do not aim at the bad﴾; then it was resumed; and it was said, in the manner of reproach and rebuke: "of it you spend, while you would not take it yourselves except if you close your eyes to it"; and its implication is the rhetorical question of denial; as if it were said: "Is it from this that you spend...?"

﴿And know that Allah is Free of need﴾: from your spending; He only commands you with it for your benefit. In commanding them to know this, despite the evident knowledge they already had of it, there is a reproach to them for what they do of giving the bad, and an indication that this is one of the effects of ignorance regarding His (Exalted) affair; for giving the like of it usually occurs when the giver believes that the taker is in need of what he gives, or even compelled to it. ﴿Praiseworthy﴾: deserving of praise for His great blessings. It was also said: He is praiseworthy by accepting the good and rewarding for it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 268:

﴿The Shaytan promises you poverty﴾: "Al-wa'd" (promise): it is the informing of what will happen from the side of the one who informs, conditioned upon something of time or otherwise; it is used for evil just as it is used for good. He (Exalted) said: ﴿The Fire, Allah has promised it to those who disbelieve﴾. That is: he promises you poverty in spending, and says that the outcome of your spending is that you will become impoverished. He expressed this by "promise," although the Shaytan did not attribute the coming of poverty to himself, in order to signal the intensity of his assertion that its coming is certain; as if he made it, in the certainty of its occurrence, like his acts that occur according to his will. Or it is because it occurs in opposition to the promise of Him (Exalted), in the manner of parallelism (al-mushakalah). It has been read with a damma on the fa', with a sukun, with two dammas, and with two fathas. ﴿And he commands you to indecency﴾: that is, to the indecent trait; that is, he incites you to miserliness and withholding charity, the incitement of one who commands to the commanded to perform what is commanded. The Arabs call the miser "fahish" (indecent). Tarafah ibn al-'Abd said:

Ara al-mawta ya'tami al-kirama wa-yastafi * 'aqilata mali al-fahishi al-mutashaddidi

It was also said: it means sins and misdeeds. ﴿And Allah promises you﴾: that is, in spending; ﴿forgiveness﴾ for your sins. The preposition in His saying (Exalted) ﴿from Him﴾ is related to an omitted element; it is an attribute of "forgiveness," emphasizing its magnificence, which its indefiniteness conveys; that is, forgiveness of what forgiveness, forgiveness proceeding from Him, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿And bounty﴾: its attribute is omitted, because the mentioned element indicates it, as in His saying (Exalted): ﴿So they returned with blessing from Allah and bounty﴾, and its like; that is, and bounty proceeding from Him (Exalted); that is, a replacement for what you spent, increased beyond it in this world; and in this there is a refutation of the Shaytan. It was also said: a reward in the Hereafter. ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾ in power and bounty, so He will fulfill what He has promised you of forgiveness and of replacing what you spend. ﴿All-Knowing﴾: intensely knowing; He knows your spending, so He will hardly let your reward be lost. Or: He knows what will be of forgiveness and bounty, so there is no possibility of breaking the promise. The sentence is a concluding remark (tadhyil) confirming the content of what precedes it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 269:

﴿He gives wisdom﴾: Mujahid said: "Wisdom (al-hikmah) is the Qur'an; and knowledge ('ilm); and understanding (fiqh)." It is narrated from Ibn Najih that it is correctness in speech and action (al-isabah fi al-qawl wa al-'amal). And from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that it is knowing the meanings of things and comprehending them. It has been said: it is knowing the realities of things. It has also been said: it is undertaking good and correct actions. And from Muqatil that it is explained in the Qur'an in four aspects: sometimes by the admonitions of the Qur'an; another time by what it contains of the wondrous secrets; another time by knowledge and understanding; and another time by prophethood. Perhaps the most fitting to the context is that which encompasses the rulings clarified within the noble verses, from one of the first two aspects. The meaning of giving it is: clarifying it, and granting success in knowing it and acting upon it; that is, He clarifies it and grants success in knowing it and acting upon it. ﴿to whomever He wills﴾ from among His servants, that He give it to him, in accordance with the vastness of His grace and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, just as He has given you what He has clarified within the verses, of the profound wisdoms upon which the sphere of your benefits revolves. So seize them, and hasten to act upon them. The relative pronoun is the first object of "yu'ti"; the second was placed before it for the sake of emphasis on it. The sentence is a resumptive clause, confirming the content of what precedes it. ﴿And whoever is given wisdom﴾ is in the passive form; it has also been read in the active form, meaning: and whoever God (exalted is He) gives wisdom to. The explicit noun in the place of the pronoun is to show concern for its matter, and to indicate the cause of the ruling. ﴿then he has indeed been given much good﴾; that is, what abundant good; for he has been granted the good of both abodes. ﴿And none remember﴾; that is, none are admonished by what has been given of wisdom; or: none reflect upon it. ﴿except the people of understanding (ulu al-albab)﴾; that is, the intellects pure of the impurities of illusion and of inclining to following desire. In this is encouragement, beyond doubt, to maintain the rulings revealed concerning spending. The clause is either a circumstantial clause (hal) or a concluding parenthetical clause (i'tiraid tadhyili).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 270:

(p-263)﴿And whatever expenditure you spend, or whatever vow you vow﴾: This is an explanation of a general ruling, comprehensive of all the individual kinds of expenditure and what is in their ruling, following the explanation of the ruling concerning what was of them in the way of Allah. The "ma" (what) is either conditional (shartiyyah) or relative (mawsulah) with its returning pronoun omitted from the relative clause, i.e., "and whatever you spent of it (ma anfaqtumuhu) of expenditure," meaning: whatever expenditure it was, whether rightful or wrongful, secret or public, small or large. ﴿Or vowed﴾: "al-nadhr" (vow) is the binding of the self upon something, its obligation, and its performance, like "darb" and "nasr" (verbal noun forms). ﴿Of a vow﴾: whatever vow it was, whether in obedience or disobedience, conditional or unconditional, connected to wealth or to actions such as fasting, prayer, and the like. ﴿Then surely Allah knows it﴾: The "fa" (then) according to the first reading enters upon the apodosis (response); according to the second it is an additional particle in the predicate. The singular pronoun, despite the multiplicity of the object of knowledge, is because of the unity of the referent, based on the coordination being with the particle "aw" (or), as in your saying: "Zayd or 'Amr, I honored him," and one does not say, "I honored them both." For this reason, recourse to interpretation was made in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿If he be rich or poor, Allah is more concerned with both of them﴾; rather, the pronoun is sometimes returned to the nearer item, out of regard for priority, as in His saying (Mighty and Exalted is He): ﴿And when they saw a trade or amusement, they dispersed toward it﴾; and another time to the later item, out of regard for proximity, as in this noble verse, and in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And whoever earns a fault or a sin and then throws it upon an innocent one﴾. Reading the structure as an interpretation of it by what is mentioned and its like, or as an omission of the first on reliance upon the second's indication of it, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah﴾, and the saying of the poet:

"We are with what we have, and you are with what you have, content, and the opinion differs,"

and similar cases, in which the coordination is by the comprehensive "wa" (and), is an unnecessary strain (ta'assuf); yes, it is permissible to return the pronoun to "ma" if it is taken as relative. The opening of the sentence with "inna" (indeed) is to emphasize its content, for the benefit of confirming the recompense: that is, He (exalted is He) will surely recompense you for it; if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. So it is encouragement and warning, promise and threat. ﴿And for the wrongdoers﴾: by expending in sins and vowing in disobedience; or by withholding charities and not fulfilling vows; or by spending the wicked; or by showing off, reminding of favors, and harming; and other things that fall under the meaning of wrongdoing, which is an expression for placing a thing in other than its proper place, where it deserves to be placed. ﴿Any helpers﴾: that is, helpers who would defend them from the punishment and chastisement of Allah (exalted is He), neither intercession nor repelling. The use of the plural form is to correspond with "the wrongdoers": that is, for no wrongdoer among the wrongdoers is there any helper among the helpers. The sentence is a resumptive clause confirming what preceded of the threat, conveying the gravity of the state of those who do what the wrongdoers do, in order to obtain supporters and cultivate allies.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 271:

﴿If you disclose your charities, how excellent they are﴾: this is a kind of detailed explanation (tafsil) of some of what was left general (ijmal) in the conditional clause, and an elucidation of it; for this reason the conjunction (ʿatf) between them has been omitted. That is: if you make your charities apparent, then excellent is the thing their disclosure is, after it was not for show and reputation. It has been read with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the ʿayn, according to the original form (al-asl); it has been read with a kasra on the nun and a sukun on the ʿayn; and it has been read with a kasra on the nun and the vowel of the ʿayn concealed (ikhfa'). This applies to obligatory charities (al-sadaqat al-mafrudah). As for voluntary charity (sadaqat al-tatawwu'), concealment is more excellent, and it is this that was intended by His words (Exalted is He): ﴿And if you conceal them﴾; that is, you give them secretly; ﴿and give them to the poor﴾. Perhaps the explicit mention of giving them to the poor, although it is also obligatory in the case of disclosure, is because concealment is liable to confusion and uncertainty, for the wealthy man may claim poverty and accept charity in secret, whereas he would not do so before people; ﴿it is better for you﴾; that is, concealment is better for you than disclosure. This applies to voluntary charity and to one who is not known to be wealthy; as for obligatory charity, the matter is the reverse, to ward off suspicion (al-tuhma).

From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "Secret charity in voluntary giving surpasses its public form by seventy times; and public charity in obligatory giving is better than its secret form by twenty-five times."

﴿And He will remove from you some of your misdeeds﴾; that is, Allah removes them, or the concealment does; and "min" (from) is partitive (tab'idiyyah), meaning some of your misdeeds, as you have concealed them. It has been said that it is additional (mazidah), according to the opinion of al-Akhfash. It has been read with a ta' (tu-kaffiru), in the nominative and in the jussive, on the basis that the verb's subject is "the charities"; it has been read with a nun in the nominative (nukaffiru), as a conjunction with the position (mahall) of what follows the fa'; or as the predicate of an omitted subject, that is, "and We remove"; or as a fresh nominal clause consisting of a verb and subject. It has been read in the jussive, as a conjunction with the position of the fa' and what follows it, since it is the answer of the conditional.

﴿And Allah is All-Aware of what you do﴾, of concealment and of disclosure; ﴿All-Aware﴾. Thus it is an encouragement toward concealment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 272:

﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾: That is, it is not obligatory upon you to make them guided to performing what they have been commanded of good deeds, and refraining from what they have been forbidden of the abominable acts that are enumerated; rather, what is obligatory upon you is guidance to good, and urging toward it, and forbidding evil, and deterring from it, by means of what has been revealed to you of the verses and the Wise Reminder. ﴿But Allah guides﴾: with a special guidance, one that leads to the desired goal inevitably, ﴿whom He wills﴾: His guidance to that, from among those who take heed of what has been mentioned, follow the truth, and choose good. The clause is parenthetical; it has been brought in by way of varying the address and directing it toward the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, together with a shift to the third person amid the addresses relating to the responsible persons, for the sake of emphasis in moving them to compliance. For the report that it is not obligatory upon the Prophet ﷺ to make up for their affairs implies that it is obligatory upon them, as what follows in the conditional clause indicates.

It was also said: when the poor among the Muslims became numerous, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade the Muslims from giving charity to the polytheists, so that need would compel them to enter Islam; then this was revealed. That is: it is not upon you the guidance of those who oppose you, so that you withhold charity from them for the sake of their entering Islam. Then there is no shift in the discourse at that point, and the pronoun of the third person refers to the known poor polytheists; rather, there is only a variation in it. And His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And whatever you spend of good﴾: according to the first view, it is a shift from the third person to the address of the responsible persons, to increase their stirring toward compliance; and according to the second, it is a variation of the address by directing it toward them and diverting it from the Prophet ﷺ. "Ma" is conditional, jussive for "tunfiqu," governing it in the object position; and "min" is partitive, related to an omitted element that stands as a qualifier of the conditional noun, specifying and particularizing it; that is: whatever thing you spend is from wealth. ﴿Then it is for yourselves﴾: that is, it is for your own selves; no one other than you benefits from it. So do not confer favor upon those to whom you have given, nor harm them, nor spend from what is corrupt. Or: its religious benefit is for you, not for others among the poor, so that you withhold it from those who do not benefit from it in religious terms, namely the poor polytheists. ﴿And you do not spend except seeking the Face of Allah﴾: this is an exception from the most general of causes, or from the most general of states; that is, your spending is for nothing except seeking the Face of Allah; or: it is in no state except the state of seeking the Face of Allah. So what is the matter with you that you bestow favors through it, and spend the corrupt thing which is not directed to Allah (exalted is He) by the like of it?! It was also said: it is a negation with the meaning of a prohibition. ﴿And whatever you spend of good will be repaid to you﴾: that is, its reward and its recompense, manifold multiplied, as has been detailed before; so you have no excuse for being averse to spending in the best and most beautiful manner. Thus it is an emphasis and an explanation of the preceding conditional clause. Or: what you spend will be repaid to you by its replacement, and this is among the results of his supplication, upon him be blessings and peace, in his saying: "O Allah, grant the one who spends a replacement, and grant the one who withholds a loss." It was also said: Asma' bint Abi Bakr performed Hajj, and her mother came to her asking her for something, while she was a polytheist; and she refused to give her. It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that they used to avoid giving anything to their polytheist relatives; and it is reported that some Muslims had in-laws among the Jews and foster relations, whom they used to support before Islam; when they embraced Islam they disliked supporting them; so this was revealed. This applies to what is not obligatory; as for what is obligatory, it is not permissible to direct it to a disbeliever, even if he is a dhimmi. ﴿And you will not be wronged﴾: you will not be diminished in anything of the multiplied reward promised to you, or of the replacement.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 273:**

﴿For the poor﴾: it is connected to a word that is omitted, which the sentence implies, as in His saying, may He be exalted and glorified, ﴿among the nine signs to Pharaoh﴾. The meaning is: direct your efforts to the poor; or: make what you spend go to the poor; or: your charities are for the poor. ﴿Those who have been confined in the way of Allah﴾: by fighting and striving (jihad). ﴿They cannot move about the land﴾: because they are occupied with it. ﴿Travelling in the land﴾: that is, going about in it to earn a living and to trade. It has also been said that they are the People of the Suffa (the raised platform attached to the Mosque of the Prophet). They were about four hundred of the poor among the Emigrants, may Allah be pleased with them all, who lived on the platform of the mosque, spending their time in learning and in jihad, and they would go out on every raiding expedition (sariyya) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dispatched. ﴿The ignorant man thinks them rich﴾: because of their condition; ﴿because of their restraint﴾: that is, because of their abstaining from asking. ﴿You recognise them by their mark﴾: that is, you recognise their poverty and their need by what you observe of them, such as their weakness and the shabbiness of their state. The address is to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, or to everyone who is capable of being addressed, to emphasise how clear their poverty is. ﴿They do not ask people persistently﴾: that is, they do not press. Ilhaf is for the one asking to keep pressing the one asked until he gives. From their saying, "He pressed me (lahafani) from the surplus of his covering (lihafihi)", meaning he gave me from the surplus of what he had. The meaning is: they do not ask people for anything at all; and if they ask due to a need that compels them, they do not press. It has also been said that this is a negation of both matters together, in the manner of his saying:

*Upon a faint road whose landmark cannot be followed*

That is, there is no landmark, and no following of a path. ﴿Whatever good you spend, indeed Allah knows it﴾: so He will reward you with the best of rewards. This is an encouragement to give charity, especially to these people.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 274:

﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly﴾: that is, they encompass all times and all states with good deeds and charity. It was also said: it was revealed concerning al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr), may Allah be pleased with him, when he gave in charity forty thousand dinars: ten thousand of it by night, ten thousand by day, ten thousand secretly, and ten thousand openly. It was also said: it was revealed concerning 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, when he had nothing but four dirhams, so he gave away each one of them in one of the ways mentioned. Perhaps the mention of the night before the day, and of the secret before the open, is to signal the superiority of concealment over disclosure. It was also said: it refers to tethering horses and spending on them. ﴿Their reward is with their Lord﴾: "for them" is the predicate of the relative clause (alladhina), and the fa' (fa-lahum) indicates that what precedes it is the cause of what follows. It was also said: the fa' is for conjunction, and the predicate is omitted, i.e., "and among them are those who..." etc. For this reason, pausing on "openly" (ʿalaniyatan) was permitted. ﴿No fear shall be on them, nor shall they grieve﴾: its interpretation has already been given.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 275:

﴿Those who consume usury (riba)﴾; i.e., they take it. The expression "consume" for it is because it is the greatest part of what is intended by it, and because it is common in foodstuffs; along with the added reproach to them in it, which is the increase in amount or in term, as detailed in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh). It was written with a waw as in "al-salawah" (الصَّلَوَة), according to the dialect of those who emphasize in similar words, and an alif was added as an imitation of the waw of the plural; ﴿they do not rise﴾; i.e., from their graves when they are resurrected; ﴿except as one rises whom Satan has driven mad by his touch﴾; i.e., except rising like the rising of one afflicted with a fit (maṣrū'), and this is in accordance with what they claim, that Satan strikes a person so that he falls down in a fit. "Khabt" (الخَبْط) means striking without evenness, like the khabt of the blind camel (khabṭ al-'ashwā'). ﴿from the touch﴾; i.e., the madness; and this too is among their claims, that the jinn touches him so that his intellect becomes confused; therefore it is said: "the man has become possessed (junna al-rajul)." It is connected to what precedes it of the negated verb; i.e., they do not rise from the touch which is upon them, by reason of their consumption of usury; or it is connected to "yaqum" (rise) or to "yatakhabbaṭuhu" (strikes him), so that their standing up and falling down will be like that of those afflicted with a fit, not because their intellects are disordered, but because God (Exalted) increased in their bellies what they had eaten of usury, so it weighed them down, and they became unbalanced, rising and falling; that is their mark by which they are recognized among the people of the place of standing (ahl al-mawqif). ﴿That﴾: a reference to what has been mentioned of their condition; and the sense of distance in the demonstrative is to announce the monstrousness of what is pointed to; ﴿because they said: trade is only like usury﴾; i.e., that punishment is due to their having placed usury and trade in a single category, since both lead to profit; so they made it lawful as its lawfulness, and they said: it is permissible to sell one dirham for two dirhams, just as it is permissible to sell something whose value is one dirham for two dirhams; rather, they made usury the basis of lawfulness and analogized trade to it, despite the clear difference between them, for one of the two dirhams in the first case is necessarily lost, while in the second it is compensated by the need for the commodity or by the expectation of its marketability; ﴿And God has made trade lawful and forbidden usury﴾: a denial from God (Exalted) of their equating them, and a nullification of the analogy, since it occurred in opposition to the explicit text, together with what has been indicated of the absence of common ground in the underlying cause (manāṭ); and the sentence is independent, having no place in the grammatical analysis (i'rab); ﴿So whoever has received an admonition﴾; i.e., whoever has been reached by an exhortation and warning, such as the prohibition of usury; it was also read as "jā'at-hu" (has come to her); ﴿from his Lord﴾: connected to "jā'ahu," or to an omitted element functioning as a qualifier of "maw'iẓah"; and the mention of the title of Lordship (rubūbiyyah) with the possessive is to indicate that the coming of the admonition is for the purpose of nurture (tarbiyah); ﴿and desists﴾: coordinated with "jā'ahu"; i.e., he takes heed, without delay, and follows the prohibition; ﴿then he shall have what has passed﴾; i.e., what he had taken before the prohibition, and it is not to be reclaimed from him; and "mā" is nominative by the adverbial phrase if "man" is taken as a relative pronoun, and by the inceptive if it is taken as a conditional, according to the view of Sibawayh, since the adverbial phrase does not depend on what precedes it; ﴿and his affair is with God﴾; He will reward him for his desisting, if it was from accepting the admonition and sincerity of intention; and it was said: He will judge concerning his case, and there is no objection for you against it; ﴿And whoever returns﴾; i.e., to the permitting of usury; ﴿those﴾: a reference to "whoever returns"; the plural is according to meaning, just as the singular in "returns" is according to wording; and the sense of distance in it is to indicate the distance of their rank in evil and corruption; ﴿are the companions of the Fire﴾; i.e., its constant residents; ﴿they will abide therein forever﴾; remaining eternally; and the sentence confirms what precedes it.(p-267)

God destroys interest (al-riba): that is, He removes its blessing and ruins the wealth into which it enters. ﴿And He increases charities﴾: He multiplies their reward, blesses them, and increases the wealth from which the charity was given. It is related from him (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah accepts charity and nurtures it just as one of you nurtures his foal," and from him, upon him be prayers and peace: "Zakat has never decreased any wealth." ﴿And Allah does not love﴾: that is, He does not approve, because love is specific to those who repent (al-tawwabin); ﴿every disbelieving (kaffar)﴾: one persisting in declaring the forbidden lawful; ﴿sinner (athim)﴾: one who is engrossed in committing it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 277:

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾: in Allah (Exalted); and His Messenger; and what he brought them; ﴿and do righteous deeds and establish the prayer and give the zakah﴾; their being singled out for mention, despite their being included among the righteous deeds, is due to their excellence over the rest of the righteous deeds, in the manner of the mention of Jibril and Mika'il after the angels (peace be upon them); ﴿for them is their reward﴾: a sentence composed of a subject and a predicate, occurring as the predicate of "inna" (indeed); that is: for them is their reward that was promised to them. His (Exalted) saying: ﴿with their Lord﴾: is a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to "their reward". In the mention of the title of Lordship, together with the addition of a pronoun referring to them, there is added gentleness and honour for them; ﴿and no fear shall be upon them﴾: from a disliked matter that is to come; ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾: over a beloved matter that has passed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 278:

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾: that is, protect yourselves from His punishment; ﴿and give up what remains of interest (riba)﴾; that is, abandon what remains of the excess you have stipulated from people, abandoning it entirely; ﴿if you are [truly] believers﴾; in reality. For that necessarily entails complying with what you have been commanded, absolutely. This is a conditional clause whose consequent has been omitted, relying on what precedes it; that is: if you are believers, then fear Him, and give up... etc. It is narrated that the Thaqif had money owed to them by some of the Quraysh, and when the due date arrived they demanded the money along with the interest (riba), so this verse was revealed.

**Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on 2:279:**

﴿But if you do not do it﴾: that is, what you were commanded of heedfulness (al-ittiqa') and leaving off the remaining interest (al-baqaya), either while denying its prohibition or while acknowledging it. ﴿Then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger﴾: that is, know of it, from "adhina bi-al-shay'" (he came to know of the thing) when he knows of it. On the first case it is like the war against apostates (al-murtaddin), and on the second it is like the war against rebels (al-bughat). It has been recited as "fa-athinu" (then announce), that is, inform others. It was said that it is from "al-adhan" (announcement), which is listening, since it is one of the means of knowledge. It has been recited as "fa-ayqinu" (then be certain), and this supports the common recitation (al-qira'a al-'amma). The indefiniteness of "harb" (war) is for magnification. The "min" is attached to an omitted element that falls as a qualifier of it, emphasising its grandeur: that is, with a kind of war that is great, whose extent cannot be measured, coming from Allah (Exalted is He) and His Messenger. It is narrated that when this was revealed, the tribe of Thaqif said: "We have no power against war from Allah and His Messenger." ﴿And if you repent﴾ from usury (al-irtiba'), while believing in its prohibition, after what you have heard of the threat, ﴿then you shall have your principal﴾, which you take in full; ﴿you will not wrong﴾ your debtors by taking the excess. The clause is either resumptive (mustanafa), having no place in grammatical structure (la mahall laha min al-i'rab), or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "lakum" (to you), and the governing element is the stability (al-istiqrar) contained in the prepositional phrase. ﴿Nor will you be wronged﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it: that is, you will not be wronged by them through delay (al-matl) and shortfall. (p-268) It follows necessarily from making this ruling conditional on their repentance that it does not apply when they do not repent, because if their non-repentance is accompanied by denial of the prohibition, then they are apostates, and the wealth they earned while in apostasy is spoils (fay') for the Muslims according to Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him; likewise all their other wealth according to al-Shafi'i. According to us, it belongs to their heirs, and in every case they have nothing. If their non-repentance is accompanied by acknowledgement of the prohibition, then if they have power, they are on the verge of being killed, and their heads are not secure, so how much less their principal sums? Otherwise, it is likewise according to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, for he said: "Whoever deals in usury is to be asked to repent; otherwise his neck is to be struck." As for others, they are detained until their repentance becomes evident; they are not permitted to carry out any transactions at all. So as long as they do not repent, nothing of their wealth is handed over to them; rather, it is handed over only upon their death to their heirs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 280:

﴿And if the debtor is in hardship﴾; i.e., if one of your debtors falls into hardship; on the reading where "kana" (was) is complete (tammah); and it has been read as "dha 'usrah" (dha 'usratin), on the reading where it is incomplete (naqisah); ﴿then let there be postponement﴾; i.e., the ruling is postponement; or: upon you is postponement; or: let there be postponement; and it is al-inzar (granting respite) and al-imhal (allowing time). It has also been read as "fa-nazirahu"; i.e., the one entitled to it is his creditor (nazir), meaning his waiter (muntazir); or: the possessor of his respite (sahib nazratihi), in the manner of the relative noun (nisba). It has also been read as "fa-nazirhu" as an imperative from the form (mufa'alah); i.e., be lenient with him by granting respite; ﴿until a time of ease﴾; i.e., until a time of affluence. It has been read with a damma on the sin, and both are dialects (lughatan), like "mashraqah" and "mushraqah"; and it has been read with both as genitive-constructs (mudafayn) with the ta' dropped at the point of construction, as in his saying:

﴿They broke their promise to you, the matter they had promised﴾

﴿And that you give charity﴾; with one of the two taa's elided; and it has been read with the sad doubled, i.e., that you give charity (tatasaddaqu) to your debtors who are in hardship by releasing them; ﴿is better for you﴾; i.e., greater in reward than granting respite; or better than what you take, due to the multiplication of its reward and its permanence. So it is a recommendation that they give away their capital, wholly or partly, to their indigent debtors, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And that you pardon is nearer to piety﴾. It has been said: the intended meaning of charity is granting respite, based on his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "It is not lawful for a Muslim man's debt to be delayed by him except that for every day there is a charity for him." ﴿If you only knew﴾: its response is omitted; i.e., if you knew that it is better for you, you would do it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 281:

﴿And fear a Day﴾: It is the Day of Resurrection. Its being indefinite (nakirah) is for magnification (tafkhim) and awe-inspiring terror (tahwil); and attaching taqwa (guarding oneself, mindfulness) to it is for emphasis in warning against the hardships and terrors it contains. ﴿In which you will be returned﴾: read in the passive voice, from "al-rajk" (to return/send back). It was also read in the active voice, from "al-ruju'" (to return). The first (passive) is more suited to inspiring terror. It was read with the ya' (yatarji'un / yurja'un, third person), by way of iltifat (shift in grammatical person). It was also read as "turaddun" (you will be sent back), and similarly "tasirun" (you will come to an end/arrive). ﴿To Allah﴾: for the reckoning of your deeds. ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full﴾ of what it has earned (tuwaffa): from among souls, and the generalization (ta'mim) is for emphasis in magnifying the Day; i.e., it will be given in full. ﴿What it has earned﴾: i.e., the recompense of what it did, whether good or evil. ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "every soul"; it indicates that those who are punished, even though their punishments are everlasting, are not wronged in that, since it is from their own selves. The plural pronoun is used because it is more fitting to the state of recompense, just as the singular is more fitting to the state of earning.

From Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father), that it was the last verse revealed by Jibril (peace be upon him), and he said: "Place it at the head of the two hundred and eightieth (verse) of al-Baqarah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lived after it twenty-one days; it was said: eighty-one; it was said: seven days; it was said: three hours.(p-269)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 282:

﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term﴾: This begins the explanation of the state of the debt transaction (al-mudayanah) that occurs within the exchanges carried out among people, such as selling goods for money. It comes after the explanation of the state of riba (usury). That is: when some of you extend credit to one another and deal with each other on deferred terms, whether as a giver or a taker. The purpose of mentioning "debt" is to dispel the assumption that "tadayantum" means "requiting," or to draw attention to its division into immediate and deferred debt, and to the fact that it is what prompts the writing down, and to identify the referent of the pronoun object attached to the imperative. ﴿for a specified term﴾: "ila ajal" is connected to "tadayantum," or to an omitted word that serves as an adjective of "dayn." ﴿specified﴾: by days, months, or similar units, which give knowledge and remove uncertainty, not by harvest, threshing, or the like, which do not remove uncertainty. ﴿then write it down﴾: that is, the debt, with its term, because this is more secure and more effective in preventing dispute. The majority hold that writing is recommended (mustahabb). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that what is meant is the salam (advance-payment sale), and he said: "When Allah prohibited riba, He permitted it in salaf (advance payment)." ﴿and let a scribe write between you with justice﴾: This explains the manner of writing that was commanded, and specifies who should undertake it, coming right after the general command to write. The omission of the object is either because it is determined, or because the aim is to focus on the act itself, that is: let him perform the writing. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿between you﴾ indicates that the scribe should stand between the two parties to the debt and write down both their statements, and not rely on the statement of only one of them. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿with justice﴾ is connected to an omitted word which is an adjective of "scribe": that is, a scribe who is characterized by justice. That is: the one who takes on the writing should be one who writes impartially, without leaning toward either side, neither adding nor subtracting. It is also a command to the two parties to choose a scribe who is a jurist (faqih) and pious, so that his document will be trusted and certified by the Sharia. It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (hal) from him, that is: joined with justice. It was also said that it is connected to the verb: that is, let him write with truth. ﴿And let not a scribe refuse﴾: that is, let none of the scribes refuse ﴿to write﴾ the debt document ﴿as Allah has taught him﴾: in the manner of what He taught him regarding the writing of documents; or: as He explained it with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿with justice﴾; or: let him not refuse to benefit people by his writing, just as Allah, Exalted is He, benefited him by teaching him writing. Like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you﴾.

﴿So let him write﴾: that taught writing. He commanded it after prohibiting refusal of it, as an emphasis on it. It is also permissible for the particle "ka" (as) to be connected to the command, on the basis that the prohibition against refusing it is absolute, and then the command to do it is restricted. ﴿And let the one who owes the debt dictate﴾: "al-imlal" means al-imla' (dictation). That is: let the one who dictates be the one upon whom the right is due, because he is the one to whom testimony is made (al-mashhud 'alayhi), so he must be the one who acknowledges it. ﴿And let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾: The Majestic Name is combined with the beautiful attribute, for the sake of emphasis in warning. That is: let the dictator fear Allah, not the scribe, as it was said, because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and let him not diminish from it﴾: that is, from the right which he dictates to the scribe. ﴿anything﴾: for it is he from whom diminution is especially expected. As for the scribe, increase is expected from him as well as diminution. So if the prohibition were aimed at him, it would have been prohibited from both. Indeed, this was done where he is commanded with justice. The strictness was applied to the obligation of the dictator because the command to fear Allah and the prohibition of diminishing are combined in him, since there are motives in him toward what is prohibited. A person is naturally inclined to repel harm from himself and to lighten what is upon his obligation as much as possible. ﴿But if the one upon whom is the right is﴾: this is stated explicitly in the place of the pronoun for greater clarity and explanation, not because the command and prohibition are directed to someone else. ﴿foolish﴾: deficient in intellect, a squanderer, reckless. ﴿or weak﴾: a child, or a senile old man who is mentally impaired. ﴿or unable to dictate himself﴾: that is, unable to dictate by himself, due to muteness, incapacity of speech, ignorance, or other such impediments. ﴿then let his guardian dictate﴾: that is, the one who manages his affairs and stands in his place, such as a custodian, an agent, or a translator. ﴿with justice﴾: that is, without deficiency or excess. He is not charged with the same thing that the one upon whom the right is due is charged with, because excess is expected from him just as diminution is expected from him. ﴿And bring two witnesses﴾: that is, seek them, so that they may bear witness to what took place between you of the debt transaction. Calling them "two witnesses" is by way of treating the one who is about to become so as if he already is (tanzil al-musharif manzilat al-waqi'). ﴿from among your men﴾: "min rijalikum" is connected to "istashhidu," and "min" is for beginning (ibtida'iyyah); or it is connected to an omitted word which is an adjective of "two witnesses," and "min" is partitive (tab'idiyyah): that is, two witnesses from among the free Muslim men, since the discussion concerns their transactions. The rules of the Sharia do not, by way of direct address, include slaves, as has been explained in its proper place. As for when the debt is between disbelievers, or when the one upon whom the right is due is a disbeliever, then the testimony of a disbeliever is permissible according to us (the Hanafis). ﴿But if there are not two men﴾: that is, if the two witnesses together are not available, in the manner of negating the inclusiveness, not the inclusiveness of negation. This is either because they are unavailable, or for some other reason. ﴿then a man and two women﴾: that is, let one man and two women bear witness, or: a man and two women suffice. This applies to matters other than the hudud (fixed punishments) and qisas (retaliation), according to us; and in financial matters only, according to al-Shafi'i. ﴿from those whom you accept﴾: this is connected to an omitted word which is an adjective of "a man and two women": that is, they are people who are acceptable to you. Their being specified with the mentioned attribute, though this attribute must be met in every witness, is because women rarely have this attribute. It was also said that it is a qualifier of "two witnesses": that is, being among those whom you accept. This was rejected on the ground that it would require separating the two by a foreign element. It was also said that it is a substitute (badal) for "men among you," with the repetition of the governing verb. This was rejected on the same ground of separation. It was also said that it is connected to His saying: ﴿then bring﴾, so that there would be a separation between the condition regarding the two women and its reason. ﴿among the witnesses﴾: this is connected to an omitted word which is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the omitted pronoun that refers back to the relative pronoun: that is, those whom you accept, being some of the witnesses, because of your knowledge of their justice and your trust in them. The inclusion of women among the witnesses is by way of prevalence (taghlib). ﴿so that if one of them errs, the other will remind her﴾: this is a reason for counting the number for women. The real reason is the reminding, but since error is the cause of it, it is treated as having its rank, as in your saying: "I prepared the weapon in case an enemy comes, and I repel him." As if it were said: in order that one of them may remind the other if she forgets the testimony, by forgetting it. Perhaps the preference for the wording of the noble text over saying "that if one of them errs, the other will remind her" is to emphasize the vagueness, and to be more thorough in guarding against the assumption that error is restricted to one specific woman, and that the reminding is restricted to the other. It was read: "fatudhkira" from "al-idhkar" (causative form). It was also read: "fatudhakkira." It was also read: "in tadilla" in the conditional, with "fatudhakkiru" in the nominative, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him﴾.

﴿And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾: for the giving of testimony, or for bearing it. Calling them "witnesses" before they bear it is due to the treatment of the one about to be so as if he already is, as mentioned earlier. "Ma" is an extra (zaidah) particle. It is reported from Qatadah that a man would circulate in the large gathering place (al-hiwa' al-'azim) where a group of people was, and none of them would follow him, so this was revealed.

﴿And do not be weary﴾: that is, do not become bored because of the multitude of your debt transactions. ﴿of writing it﴾: that is, the debt; or: the right; or: the document. It was also said that it is a metaphor for laziness, which is a characteristic of the hypocrite, as it occurs in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when they stand up to prayer, they stand up lazily﴾. And the Prophet ﷺ said: "The believer does not say: I am lazy (kasilt)." ﴿whether small or large﴾: a circumstantial clause from the pronoun: that is, whether it is small or large, that is: little or much, or summarized or detailed. ﴿for its term﴾: connected to an omitted word which is a circumstantial clause from the "ha'" in "taktubuhu": that is, remaining in the obligation until the time of its falling due, which the debtor acknowledged. ﴿That﴾: a reference to what was commanded regarding writing. The address is to the believers. ﴿is more just﴾: that is, more equitable. ﴿in the sight of Allah﴾: that is, in His judgment, Exalted is He. ﴿and more suitable as evidence﴾: that is, more firm for it, and more helpful in establishing it. Both of these are derived from "aqsata" and "aqama," for it is analogical according to Sibawayh; or from "qasit" in the sense of "one who is just," and "qawim." The waw in "aqwamu" remained sound, as it did in the form of exclamation (ta'ajjub), because of its rigidity (judud). ﴿and nearer to preventing doubt among you﴾: and nearer to the removal of your doubt regarding the kind of debt, its amount, its term, its witnesses, and the like. ﴿except when it is a present trade that you conduct among yourselves﴾: this is an exception that is disconnected (istithna' munqati') from the command to write: that is, but at the time when your debt or trade is a present trade, with both exchanged items present, which you conduct among yourselves by exchanging them hand to hand. ﴿then there is no blame upon you for not writing it﴾: that is, there is no harm in your not writing it, because it is far from dispute and forgetting. It was read with the nominative "tijaratan," with it as the subject of "kana," and "hadirah" as its adjective, and "tudirunaha" as its predicate; or with it as a complete verb. ﴿And take witnesses when you conduct a sale﴾: that is, this sale; or in general, because it is more cautious. The commands in this noble verse are for recommendation according to the majority; it was also said they are for obligation. Then scholars differed regarding its rulings and its abrogation (naskh). ﴿And let no scribe or witness be harmed﴾: a prohibition against harm, which is open to both possible readings (as the reading of one who read "wa la yudarrir" with kasra and fatha indicates). It is the prohibition against them from refusing to respond, from altering, or from distorting the writing or the testimony. Or it is the prohibition against the one seeking them from harming them: by hastening them away from their business, or by requiring them to go beyond what is set for them, or by not giving the scribe his fee. It was read in the nominative, as a negation meaning a prohibition. ﴿And if you do﴾: what you were forbidden from harming. ﴿indeed, it is﴾: that is, your doing that; ﴿defiance on your part﴾: that is, departure from obedience, clinging to you. ﴿And fear Allah﴾: in violating His commands and prohibitions, of which His prohibition against harm is part. ﴿And Allah teaches you﴾: His rulings, which contain your benefits. ﴿And Allah is Knowing of all things﴾: so your condition is not hidden from Him, and He will requite you for it. The word "Allah" is repeated in the three sentences, to add awe and cultivate reverence, and to draw attention to the independence of each of them in its own meaning: the first is an exhortation to piety; the second is a promise of favor; and the third is a glorification of His majesty, Exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 283:

﴿And if you are on a journey﴾: that is, travelling; or, intending to travel. ﴿And you find no scribe﴾ for the debt transaction (al-mudayana). It is also read as "kuttaban," "kutuban," and "kitaban." ﴿then a pledge taken into possession﴾: that is, what is used for securing the debt; or, "then it is incumbent upon you"; or, "then let it be taken"; or, "then the prescribed course is a pledge taken into possession." This qualification is not a condition that travel be required for the legality of pledging (rahn, a pledge as security), as Mujahid and al-Dahhak supposed, because the Prophet (ﷺ) pawned his coat of mail in Medina to a Jew for twenty sa' of barley, which he took for his family. Rather, it is to establish security through pledging in place of security through writing, during travel, which is the situation where writing is likely to be unavailable. The verse did not mention the witness's situation because he is in the same legal position as the scribe in terms of securing the debt and its unavailability. The majority hold that taking possession is required for the completion of the pledge, unlike Malik. It is also read as "fa-ruhunun," like "suqufun," and both are plurals of "rahn," in the sense of "marhun" (that which is pledged). It is also read with the ha' sukun for lightness. ﴿But if one of you trusts another﴾: that is, one of the creditors trusts one of the debtors, because of his good opinion of him, and dispenses with a pledge due to his trustworthiness. It is also read as "fa-in uminya ba'dukum" (if one of you is trusted), meaning people have deemed him trustworthy and described him as such.
