It is said that in this case "ba'dan" is in the accusative by omission of the preposition, meaning "in respect of the property of someone." ﴿then let the one who is trusted discharge his trust﴾: this is the debtor. He is described by this title because he is identified as the means for the transaction, and because it is intended to compel him to repay. ﴿his trust﴾: that is, his debt. It is called a "trust" because he has been entrusted with it by the abandonment of a pledge against it. It is also read as "ai-tumina" with the hamza changed to ya', and read with the ya' assimilated into the ta'; the latter is an error, because a letter converted from a hamza is not assimilated, since it has the same status. ﴿And let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾: in observing the rights of the trust. Combining the title of divinity with the attribute of lordship carries emphasis and warning that is clear. ﴿And do not conceal testimony﴾: O witnesses; or the debtors; that is, your testimony against yourselves at the time of the transaction. ﴿And whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful﴾: "sinful" (athimun) is the predicate of "inna"; and "his heart" (qalbuhu) is raised by it as subject, as if it were said: "his heart sins." Or "his heart" is in the nominative as the subject, and "sinful" is a predicate preceding it, and the clause is the predicate of "inna." The attribution of sin to the heart is because concealment is something it commits; its parallel is the attribution of adultery to the eye and the ear. Or it is for emphasis, because it is the chief of the organs, and its acts are the greatest of acts, as if it were said: sin has established itself in his soul, has taken possession of its noblest place, and has surpassed all his other sins. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Indeed, the greatest of the major sins is associating partners with Allah, based on His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Allah has forbidden him Paradise﴾; and false testimony; and concealment of testimony." (It is also read as "qalbahu" with the accusative, as in "safiha nafsahu" [he deluded himself]. It is also read as "athdama qalbahu," meaning making it sinful.) ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾: so He will recompense you for it; if good, then good; and if evil, then evil.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 284:

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾; of the matters that are within their reality, and those that are external to them, and those that are settled within them, among the people of knowledge and others. That is, all of it belongs to Him (exalted is He) in creation, possession, and disposal, with no partner for anyone else in any of it, in any way whatsoever. ﴿And whether you show what is in your selves﴾; of evil and the resolve upon it, by manifesting it to the people through speech or through action; ﴿or conceal it﴾; by hiding it from them and not manifesting it in either of the two ways. What is not avoided by humankind, such as whisperings and the sayings of the soul in which there is no binding resolve or determination, is not included in this, since obligation is according to capacity. ﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾; on the Day of Resurrection. This is a proof against those who deny the reckoning among the Mu'tazilah and the Rafidah. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the subject is for the sake of giving it importance. As for the fronting of disclosing before concealing, contrary to what is in His saying (exalted and majestic is He): ﴿Say: Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or disclose it, Allah knows it﴾; this is because what is linked here to what is in their selves is the reckoning, and the basis of it is outward deeds; as for knowledge, its relation to them is like its relation to hidden deeds. (p-273) How could it not be so, when His knowledge (glory be to Him) of His objects is exalted above being by way of the acquisition of forms; rather, the existence of each thing in itself, in whatever state it is, is knowledge in relation to Him (exalted is He). In this respect the situation does not differ between things that are manifest and things that are latent, except that the stage of concealment precedes the stage of disclosure, since there is nothing that is disclosed except that it, or its beginnings before that, is hidden in the self. Thus the relation of His knowledge (exalted is He) to its first state precedes its relation to its second state. This has already passed in the explanation of His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they disclose?﴾.

﴿So He forgives﴾: with the nominative (raf'), as a resumption; that is, He forgives by His bounty ﴿whom He wills﴾; to forgive him; ﴿and punishes﴾; by His justice ﴿whom He wills﴾; to punish him; according to what His will requires, which is founded upon wisdoms and interests. The fronting of forgiveness before punishment is because His mercy precedes His wrath. It was also read with the jussive of both verbs, coordinated upon the response of the conditional; and it was read with the jussive without the fa', on the basis that they are a substitute for the response, a substitute of part or of inclusion. Its parallel is the jussive as a substitute for the condition in the saying:

Whenever you come to us and visit us in our abodes, you will find firewood, fine and a fire blazing.

The assimilation of the rā' into the lām is a solecism. ﴿And Allah is over all things capable﴾: a concluding statement affirming the content of what precedes it, for the perfection of His capability (exalted is He) over all things necessitates His capability (glory be to Him) over what has been mentioned of the reckoning and what is derived from it of forgiveness and punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 285 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The Messenger believes﴾. When it was mentioned at the beginning of this noble surah that what was sent down to the Messenger (ﷺ) of the Book, which is of great importance, is a guidance for those who possess the virtuous qualities detailed there, among which is belief in it and in what was sent down before it of the divine books, and that they attain both benefits, guidance and success, without specifying them individually or explicitly stating that these qualities are actually realized in them, since what is mentioned within the relative clause (al-ṣilah) does not contain a judgment of actual fact, this was followed by a statement of the condition of those who disbelieved in it, both the openly hostile and the hypocrites. Then, within its elaborations, there was an explanation of various kinds of laws, rulings, admonitions, wisdoms, and reports of past nations, and other matters that wisdom requires to be explained. At its conclusion, those who possess these qualities were identified, and it was judged that they actually possess them, by way of testimony in their favor from Him, Mighty and Majestic, to their perfect faith and good obedience. The Messenger (ﷺ) is mentioned here in the third person, although he was addressed in the second person there, because the right of a testimony that remains across the ages is that the one it is testified for not be addressed by it. Nor does it here address the attainment of their aims, among which are the supplications related of them that follow, as an indication that this is a certain matter, needing no explicit statement, especially after it was expressly stated earlier. The mention of him (ﷺ) by the title of Messengership, which indicates that he (ﷺ) is the possessor of a glorious Book and a new law, serves as a preparation for what follows in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿with what was sent down to him﴾, and as a further clarification of his inclusion among the Messengers in whom belief is held, peace be upon them.

By "what was sent down to him" is meant that which encompasses all of it and each part of its parts. Thus there is in this a specification of the manner of his belief (ﷺ) and a determination of his title. That is: he, peace and blessings be upon him, believed in all that was sent down to him ﴿from his Lord﴾, with a detailed belief, relating to all the laws, rulings, narratives, admonitions, conditions of the Messengers, the books, and other matters within it, insofar as it was sent down from Him (Exalted is He). As for belief in the truth of its rulings, the veracity of its reports, and the like, these are branches of belief in it from the aforementioned aspect. In this general statement there is a glorification of his station (ﷺ) and an indication that the connection of his belief to the details of what was sent down to him, and his comprehension of all that it contains, is so evident that there is no need to mention it at all. Likewise, in mentioning the title of Lordship together with its attribution to his pronoun, peace and blessings be upon him, there is an honoring of him, and an alert that the sending down to him is an upbringing and a perfecting of him, peace and blessings be upon him.

﴿And the believers﴾: that is, the group known by this name. The definite article here is of the known kind (ʿahdiyyah), not relative (mawṣūlah), because otherwise the speech would be left without benefit. It is the subject (mubtadaʾ); His saying (Exalted and Majestic is He): ﴿each﴾ is a second subject; His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿believed﴾ is its predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of the first subject. The link between them is the pronoun that the tanwin has taken the place of. The singularity of the pronoun in "believed," despite its referring to all the believers, is because the purpose is to explain the belief of each one of them individually, without considering collectivity, as was considered in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿and each of them came to Him humbled﴾. The change in the composition of the noble structure from what preceded it is to emphasize the notice of the clear difference and evident distinction between his belief (ﷺ), which is based on direct witnessing and eyewitness vision, and their belief, which arises from proof and demonstration, as though the two are different in every respect, even in the form of the construction that indicates them. There is also the repetition of the predication, in the judgment of the belief of each one of them in the manner that follows, which is a kind of obscurity requiring reinforcement and emphasis. That is: each one of them believed ﴿in God﴾ alone, without any partner in divinity or worship; ﴿and His angels﴾, that is, insofar as they are honored servants of His (Exalted is He), whose role is to mediate between Him (Exalted is He) and the Messengers by bringing down books and conveying revelation. For the basis of belief in them is not in the particular essences of their selves, but in their being attributed to Him (Exalted is He) in the aforementioned respect, as the ordering in the composition suggests. ﴿and His books and His messengers﴾: that is, insofar as they come from Him (Exalted is He) to guide creation to what has been legislated for them of religion, through commands and prohibitions. But not in an unrestricted sense; rather, in the sense that each of those books was sent down by Him (Exalted is He) to a specific Messenger among those Messengers, peace be upon them, as detailed in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿Say: We believe in God, and in what was sent down to us, and in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus, and in what was given to the prophets from their Lord﴾, and so on. Nor in the sense that the basis of belief is the particularity of that book or that messenger; rather, the belief in all of them is included within belief in the Book sent down to the Messenger (ﷺ) and is grounded in it, according to the recited noble verse. Nor in the sense that the rulings of the earlier books and their laws remain entirely valid; nor that what remains of them is binding in relation to them; rather, the rulings of each of them were true and established until another book came that abrogated them (naskh, the abrogation of a ruling by a later revelation). And what has not been abrogated of their laws and rulings until now is established insofar as it is among the rulings of this preserved Book, which is safe from abrogation until the Day of Resurrection.

The belief in the Last Day was not mentioned here, as it was in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿But righteousness is in him who believes in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets﴾, because it is included in belief in His books. It has been read as "and His book," meaning either the Qur'an or the category of the book, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿So God sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Book﴾. The difference between the singular form and the plural is that the singular is common to the individuals of the category, whereas the plural is for its collections. For this reason it has been said: "The Book is more than the books." This is a kind of detailing of what was summarized in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿with what was sent down to him from his Lord﴾. It was limited to this as an indication that it suffices for the general belief, which is realized in every individual of the believers, without denying any addition, given the differing levels of the believers and the great variation in their belief in the matters mentioned at the levels of detail. For the summarization in the report does not necessitate summarization in what is reported. How not? When the belief of the Messenger (ﷺ) was summarized as ﴿what was sent down to him from his Lord﴾, while it is obvious that it relates to the details of its sublime and subtle matters?!

Moreover, since the matters mentioned are unseen matters which can be known only from the side of the All-Knowing, All-Aware, belief in them is a fulfillment of what was mentioned at the beginning of the noble surah, namely belief in the unseen. As for belief in His books (Exalted is He), it is an allusion to what is in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿They believe in what was sent down to you and what was sent down before you﴾. This is what is fitting for the status of the revelation and what is worthy of its exalted measure.

It is also permissible that His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And the believers﴾ be conjoined to "the Messenger," in which case one stops at "the Messenger." The pronoun that the tanwin substitutes for refers to both conjoined terms together, as if it were said: "The Messenger and the believers believed in what was sent down to him from his Lord," and then this was detailed. It has also been said: each of "the Messenger" and "the believers" believed in God, and so on, except that the object of belief is placed before the conjoined term, out of care for its importance and as an indication of his (ﷺ) primacy in belief in it. However, it is not hidden that this reading, although it lacks what the first reading has of the perfection of honoring his station (ﷺ) and magnifying his belief, is detrimental to the eloquence of the noble composition. For if each of the two beliefs is taken as befitting his station (ﷺ) both in essence and in relation to details, it becomes impossible to attribute them to anyone else (ﷺ), and the repetition is wasted. And if both are taken as befitting the status of ordinary members of the community, that would be a demeaning of his lofty rank (ﷺ). As for taking each of them as befitting each of those to whom they are attributed among individuals, in essence and in relation, namely that with respect to the Messenger (ﷺ) they are understood as eyewitness belief related to all the details, and with respect to the individuals of the community as acquired belief from him (ﷺ), appropriate to their condition in both summary and detail, this is a clear distortion, and the sanctity of the revelation should be kept free from the likes of it.

His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ is in the accusative position by an implied verb of saying, in the plural form, observing the sense. It is either in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "believed," or in the nominative as a second predicate of "each." That is: they say, "We make no distinction between them, by believing in some of them and disbelieving in others, but we believe in the validity of the messengership of each one of them." They qualified their belief with this to establish the truth and to correct the People of the Two Books, who unanimously disbelieved in the Messenger (ﷺ), and the Jews alone disbelieved in Jesus, peace be upon him, as well. Yet their primary intent is to show their belief in what they disbelieved of his messengership (ﷺ), not to show their agreement with them in what they believed. As you see, this clearly indicates that those who speak are the ordinary believers in particular, for it is not possible for it to be attributed to him (ﷺ) to say, "I make no distinction between any of His messengers," while he intends by it to show his belief in his own messengership and his affirmation of its claim.

The non-mention of the negation of distinction between the books is because the mentioned negation implies it. It was not reversed, even though the implication holds in both directions, because the principal in the distinguishing of those who make distinctions is the Messengers, and their disbelief in the books branches off from their disbelief in them. It has been read with the "ya" (yuʾminūna/yufarriqu) as the verb is attributed to "each," and it has been read "they do not make distinction" (lā yufarriqūna), in consideration of the sense, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿and each of them came to Him humbled﴾. Then the sentence itself is a circumstantial clause from the aforementioned pronoun. It has also been said that it is a second predicate of "each," as was said about the implied verb of saying. Thus, the generality must be understood after the negation, not the reverse, since the intent is that the negation encompasses all, not the negation of totality. The discussion of the hamza in "aḥad" (any one) and of the entry of "bayn" (between) upon it has already been detailed at His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾. It contains, clearly, a proof of the realization of the non-distinction between each individual of them and anyone else, whoever he may be, which is not present in saying: "We make no distinction between His messengers." The choice to use the explicit noun "the messengers" rather than a pronoun, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿and what was given to the prophets from their Lord; we make no distinction between any of them﴾, is either to guard against the suspicion that the angels are included in the ruling, or to indicate the reason for the non-distinction, or to allude to their title, since what is considered is the non-distinction with respect to messengership, not the other particular aspects.

"And they say": a conjunction linking to "believed" (āmana); the plural form is used in view of the meaning. It is a report of their compliance with the commands, following the report of their faith.

"We hear": that is, we understand what has come to us of the truth, and we are certain of its soundness.

"And we obey": [what it contains of] commands and prohibitions. It has also been said: "We hear" means we answer your call, and "we obey" means we obey your command.

"Your forgiveness, our Lord": that is, forgive us, [granting] Your forgiveness; or: we ask You for Your forgiveness of our past sins, or of the shortcomings that humans cannot avoid in observing Your rights.

The mention of hearing and obedience before the request for forgiveness is because placing the means before the request is more likely to lead to its being answered and accepted. The use of the title "Lord" (rubūbiyya), together with the attribution to them, serves to emphasise the intensity of humility and supplication.

"And to You is the final return": that is, the return by death and resurrection, to no one other than You. This is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) to what precedes it, confirming the need for forgiveness, since the return is for reckoning and recompense.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 2, verse 286:

His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.﴾ This is an independent clause, placed directly after the report of their acceptance of His obligations with good obedience, in order to show what He, exalted is He, has bestowed upon them within the imposition of obligation, from among the fine effects of grace and mercy, bestowed as a beginning and not in response to a request, as will come later. Here.

It has been related that: "When His saying (exalted is He) was revealed: ﴿Whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾ (the verse)... this weighed heavily on the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They came to him, peace and blessings be upon him, then knelt on their knees and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we were charged with deeds we can bear: the prayer, the fast, the pilgrimage, and jihad. And this verse has been sent down to you, and we cannot bear it.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Do you wish to say what the People of the Two Scriptures said before you: "We hear and we disobey"? Rather, say: "We hear and we obey; Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return."' So the people recited it, and Allah, mighty and majestic, sent down: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord﴾, up to His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Our Lord, and to You is the final return.﴾" So what they asked for was forgiveness, which is made dependent on His will, mighty and majestic, in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾. Then Allah (exalted is He) sent down: ﴿Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity⦆, to ease the matter for them, by explaining that what is meant by what is in their souls is only what they had resolved upon of evil, and not what encompasses the passing thoughts that cannot be avoided.

"Taklif" (imposition of obligation) means requiring what involves hardship and difficulty. "Wus'" (capacity) is what embraces a person and does not constrain him. That is: it is His custom (exalted is He) that He does not impose upon any soul among souls except what its capacity comfortably embraces and what is made easy for it, short of the limit of its power and exertion, as a favour from Him (exalted is He) and as mercy to this community, like His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you.﴾

It is also read as "wus'ahā" with a fatha (wusʿahā, the accusative form). This indicates that the imposition of what is impossible does not occur, but it does not indicate that it is impossible in principle.

His saying (exalted is He): ﴿For it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has deserved.﴾ This is to encourage guarding the duties of obligation and to warn against neglecting them. It explains that the obligation of every soul, together with its accompanying blessing of lightening and facilitation, includes in observing it an additional benefit, and that this benefit returns to it and not to another; and neglecting it entails a harm that befalls it and not another. For the exclusive attribution of an act's benefit to its doer is among the strongest motives to achieving it, and restricting its harm to him is among the most severe deterrents from committing it. That is: for it is the reward of what it has earned of good, and what it was obligated to do, not for another, whether independently or jointly, because of the comprehensiveness of the word "mā" (what) to every part of what it has acquired; and against it, and not against another, by one of the two ways mentioned, is the punishment for what it has acquired of evil, which it was obligated to abandon. The use of "iktisāb" (acquiring) in the case of evil is because of the effort arising from the soul's concern with obtaining evil and its striving in seeking it.

﴿Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or err.﴾ This begins the relating of the remainder of their supplications, following the explanation of the secret of obligation. That is: do not hold us accountable for what proceeds from us of matters leading to forgetfulness or error, such as negligence, lack of care, and the like, which fall under obligation; or for the forgetfulness and error themselves, insofar as they result from what was mentioned; or absolutely, since there is no rational impossibility in holding one accountable for them. For sins are like poisons: just as consuming them, even by forgetfulness or error, leads to destruction, so too committing sins may well lead to punishment, even if not by deliberate intent. His promise (exalted is He) that this will not happen does not make its occurrence impossible, for that is among the effects of His grace and mercy, as is indicated by the lifting (of the blame) in His saying (peace and blessings be upon him): "My community has been relieved of error and forgetfulness." It has been related that the Jews, when they forgot something, had punishment hastened upon them. Their supplication, therefore, after knowing that the promise is realised, is for continuity and for acknowledging the blessing in that, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers.﴾

﴿Our Lord, and do not lay upon us a burden (iṣr)﴾: this is conjoined to what precedes it, and the insertion of the address between them is to display greater humility in supplication. "Iṣr" is the heavy load that binds its bearer, that is, holds him in place. Its meaning here is the arduous obligations. It was said that "iṣr" is a sin for which there is no repentance; so the meaning is: protect us from committing it. It is read as "āṣārā" (plural). It is also read as "wa-lā tuḥammil" with shadda (intensive form) for emphasis.

﴿As You laid it upon those before us.﴾ This is in the accusative position, as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, that is: a burden like Your laying it upon those before us; or as an attribute of "iṣr," that is: a burden like the burden that You laid upon those before us. This is what the Children of Israel were obligated with: the killing of the self in repentance, cutting off the place of impurity, fifty prayers in a day and night, giving a quarter of wealth as zakat, and other severities. For whenever they committed an error, some of the good foods that had been lawful for them were forbidden to them. Allah (exalted is He) said: ﴿Because of the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things which had been made lawful to them.﴾ Allah, mighty and majestic, by His grace and mercy, has protected this community from the like of that, and He sent down concerning them: ﴿And He relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them.﴾ He (ﷺ) also said: "I have been sent with the upright, easy, tolerant religion." And concerning the punishments with which the earlier peoples were punished, such as transformation, sinking into the earth, and others, he (ﷺ) said: "My community has been relieved of sinking, transformation, and drowning."

﴿Our Lord, and do not burden us with what we have no power to bear.﴾ This is conjoined to what precedes it, and is a plea to be spared from punishments that cannot be endured, after the plea to be spared from what leads to them through negligence in it, namely the arduous obligations, for one who is charged with them almost never escapes negligence in them. It is as if it were said: do not impose on us those obligations, and do not punish us for our negligence in guarding them. Thus the expression of sending down punishments as "burdening" is in terms of what leads to them. It was said: it is a repetition of the first, and a depiction of the burden in the form of what cannot be borne, for emphasis. It was also said: it is a plea to be spared from obligation with what human power truly cannot fulfil; this would be evidence for its rational permissibility, since otherwise they would not have asked to be delivered from it. The shadda here is for transitivising the verb to a second object.

﴿And pardon us﴾, that is, the traces of our sins; ﴿and forgive us﴾, and conceal our faults and do not disgrace us before the heads of the witnesses; ﴿and have mercy upon us﴾, and be tender toward us and show favour to us. The placement of the request for pardon and forgiveness before the request for mercy is because clearing away comes before adorning. ﴿You are our Mawla﴾, our master, and we are Your servants; or: our helper; or the one who manages our affairs. ﴿So help us against the disbelieving people﴾, for it is the right of the Master that He help His servant, and the one who manages his affairs, against enemies. The intended meaning is the disbelievers in general. In this there is an indication that raising the word of Allah and striving in His way, as He commanded throughout this noble surah, is the ultimate of their aims.

It has been related that: "When he (peace and blessings be upon him) had made these supplications, it was said to him at each supplication: 'I have done it.'" And from him (ﷺ): "Allah sent down two verses from the treasures of Paradise, which the Most Merciful wrote with His own hand two thousand years before He created creation. Whoever recites them after the final night prayer, they suffice him in place of the night prayer." And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever recites two verses of Surat al-Baqara, they suffice him." This is a proof against the one who disliked saying "Surat al-Baqara," and said: it should be said "the surah in which the cow is mentioned," just as he (ﷺ) said: "The surah in which the cow is mentioned is the tent-pole of the Qur'an; so learn it, for learning it is a blessing, abandoning it is regret, and the idle (baṭala) will not be able to master it." It was said: "What are the baṭala?" He (ﷺ) said: "The sorcerers."
